Certain <term>first-class heretics</term> <note>original: "Heretici p^a^ classis." In the context of the Catholic Church's *Index of Prohibited Books*, "first-class" authors were those deemed so dangerous that their entire body of work was banned, regardless of the subject matter.</note> were the translators of the works of Saint Cyril <note>original: "Dini Cyrilli"; "Dini" is likely a scribal variant or error for "Divi," meaning "Saint." Saint Cyril of Alexandria was a major 5th-century theologian.</note>, but they are permitted, and their names should be deleted, just as they have been deleted and <unclear>purged</unclear> in certain places. Read safely. <note>original: "Lege tutè." This was a standard formula used by censors to indicate that after the removal of forbidden names or passages, the book was now spiritually safe for a Catholic to read.</note>

<meta>The previous page provided was a title page for the works of Clement of Alexandria, printed in Antwerp. This page, however, is a preface to the works of St. Cyril of Alexandria, printed in Basel in 1566. It appears these are separate works or were bound together by a later collector. The catchword "IN IOAN" suggests the next section will begin a commentary on the Gospel of John.</meta>

# TO THE READERS STUDIOUS 
### OF ANCIENT THEOLOGY.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring a classical figure (possibly a deity or personification) seated within the letter's curve, surrounded by foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>THE various and divine monuments of Cyril, <note>St. Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444 AD) was a Patriarch of Alexandria and a central figure in early Christian theology, particularly known for his defense of the title "Theotokos" (Mother of God) for Mary.</note> a most holy man and most learned as well as prolific theologian—whatever works we have been able to obtain thus far, faithfully and elegantly translated from the Greek—we give to you again, readers studious of theological matters, and offer them up as if they were a new offspring. For we believe that what the Poet <note>The "Poet" is Virgil, the Roman epic poet. The following lines are from his *Georgics*, a poem about agriculture.</note> instructed should be done in livestock farming must be done with no less care in the "offspring" of good books. But why do I not include the most weighty sentiment of that excellent poet? For he said thus:

> *And supply new offspring by breeding one from another.*
> *The best days of life for wretched mortals*
> *Are the first to flee; diseases creep in, and gloomy old age,*
> *And toil; and the cruelty of harsh death carries them away.*
> *There will always be those whose bodies you would prefer to change.*
> *Therefore, always renew them, and lest you seek them after they are lost,*
> *Anticipate it: and choose new offspring for the herd every year.*
> <note>original: "Atq; aliam ex alia generando suffice prolem..." These lines from Virgil's Georgics (Book 3) emphasize the need for constant renewal to prevent the loss of a lineage—here applied metaphorically to the preservation of ancient books.</note>

There are also—yes, I say—diseases for books, their own old age, and their own destruction. This is testified by the works of countless others, as well as those of this great theologian Cyril, which have barely—and indeed scarcely—been rescued from the decay of time and ruin. For despite whatever diligence, labor, and expense we have used, we have not yet been able to obtain everything he left behind or that is said to still exist. However, we hope that by using such a thorough and accurate search, not a few works, and those most excellent, will come into our hands. If, as we hope with God as our guide, it happens that we achieve our wish, we promise to publish whatever that may be in a separate volume, so that those who have purchased this edition of Cyril are not forced to make new expenditures from scratch. 

To ensure that you, excellent readers, understand what has been added to this edition compared to the previous one, you should know that the former was comprised of only four volumes. But now a fifth volume has been added, and a most excellent one at that, containing the commentaries on the prophet Isaiah, <note>original: "HESAIAE". St. Cyril’s commentary on Isaiah is a significant work of patristic biblical exegesis.</note> completed in five books, produced from that most pure and abundant workshop of our Cyril. To these, if any addition is made hereafter, it will be gathered into a sixth volume, so that you may recognize that in this matter, as in others, we are watching over your interests. This we will continue to do in the future, so that we may keep you in the study and love of such authors. If we obtain this goal, we shall consider ourselves to have succeeded brilliantly. 

It remains for us to offer a reason why we have separated the index of the fifth volume from the one suited to the other four; but there is no need. For you will easily see for yourselves that it was done for your own convenience. These then, kind readers, are the matters we wished to discuss with you at this time. As for you—may God, the Best and Greatest, <note>original: "Deus Opt. Max." (Deus Optimus Maximus), a title borrowed from Roman religion (Jupiter) and applied to the Christian God.</note> grant that this be happy, auspicious, and healthful for you all and for the whole Christian Commonwealth—receive the long-sought Cyril with joy; and as for the rest, spend your time with him, and farewell. 

At Basel, in the year of Christ the Son of God and Savior, 1566, on the Kalends of September. <note>The "Kalends" refer to the first day of the month; September 1, 1566.</note>

<summary>This preface introduces a new 1566 edition of the works of St. Cyril of Alexandria, printed in Basel, highlighting the addition of a previously missing fifth volume containing his commentary on Isaiah. The editor uses metaphors from Virgil's poetry to explain the necessity of reprinting and preserving ancient theological texts to save them from "old age" and destruction.</summary>
<keywords>Cyril of Alexandria, Isaiah, Virgil, Basel, 1566, theology, book preservation, Christian Commonwealth, patristics</keywords>

<meta>Continuing the introductory material for the works of Cyril of Alexandria. The previous page ended with the publisher’s hope to find more of Cyril's lost works. This page provides biographical sketches and bibliographies of Cyril as recorded by two Renaissance-era scholars: Johannes Trithemius and Raffaele Maffei (Volaterranus).</meta>

->FROM JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT<-
->of Sponheim, on Ecclesiastical writers.<-

Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, a Greek by nation, once the glory and distinguished inhabitant of Mount Carmel <note>Trithemius, an early bibliographer, mistakenly identifies Cyril with the Carmelite order, a common pious legend of the time despite the order's medieval origins.</note>, a learned and holy man, presided over the Council of two hundred Fathers at Ephesus by the order of Pope Celestine. In that Council, condemning Nestorius and Pelagius <note>Nestorius taught that Christ had two distinct persons; Pelagius denied the doctrine of original sin. Cyril was their primary theological opponent.</note> along with their errors, he delivered many elegant opinions. Since he was most learned in the Holy Scriptures, he composed many short works, of which the following are reported:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| On the Faith against heretics, | Book | I. |
| Against Nestorius, | Book | I. |
| On the Falling Away of the Synagogue, | Book | I. |
| On the Birth and Praise of Saint Mary, | Book | I. |
| On the Paschal Cycle of 95 years, | Book | I. |
| Commentaries on the Gospel. | Books | IV. |

In addition, he composed many letters, homilies, and sermons, as well as various other treatises which have not come to my notice. He flourished during the Council of Ephesus, presiding under the Emperor Theodosius the Younger, in the Year of Our Lord 432.

---

->FROM RAFFAELE VOLATER-<-
->RANUS, Book XIV.<-

Cyril, the prelate of Alexandria, published treatises on various propositions and many homilies, which the Greeks still use. Furthermore, he wrote letters against Nestorius, in which he refuted all of Nestorius's hidden poisons; he also wrote against the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD), the last pagan emperor who attempted to roll back Christianity.</note> who attacked our faith, and many other works.

<summary>This page presents biographical and bibliographical entries for Cyril of Alexandria from two Renaissance authorities, Johannes Trithemius and Raffaele Maffei, highlighting his role in the Council of Ephesus and his writings against heretics.</summary>

# A Catalog of all the works of
## SAINT CYRIL, BISHOP OF THE 
### CHURCH OF ALEXANDRIA.

# THE FIRST VOLUME CONTAINS
The eight books of commentaries on the Gospel of John by Saint Cyril of Alexandria. To these, <term>Iodocus Clichtoveus</term><note>A Flemish theologian and humanist (1472–1543) who edited these works and wrote "supplementary" books to fill gaps in Cyril's original commentary on John that had been lost to time.</note> added four books in between the others.
Sixteen books on <term>Leviticus</term>, where everything that is established to be observed physically and literally is transferred entirely to a spiritual and life-giving understanding.

# THE SECOND VOLUME HOLDS
The distinguished work entitled the <term>THESAURUS</term><note>Original: "Thesaurus" (The Treasury). This is Cyril's major work defending the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit.</note>, concerning the <term>consubstantiality</term><note>The doctrine that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the very same "substance" or essence.</note> of the Son and the Holy Spirit with God the Father, against the heretics.
Seven books of Dialogues with Hermias on the Trinity, with an appendix of arguments proving that the Holy Spirit is God.
Book 1. That the Son is consubstantial and coeternal with God the Father.
Book 2. That the Son is coeternal with God the Father, and begotten from Him according to nature.
Book 3. That the Son is true God, just as the Father is.
Book 4. That the Son is neither a creature nor a created thing.
Book 5. That the properties and glory of the deity are naturally in the Son, just as they are in the Father.
Book 6. That the properties of humanity, and those things said of the Son which do not seem particularly divine, apply more to His <term>dispensation</term><note>A theological term referring to God's plan for salvation, specifically the Son taking on human flesh.</note> in the flesh, and not to the nature of the Word as He is understood to be God.
Book 7. Concerning the Holy Spirit: that He is both God and from God, according to nature.
Book 1. On adoration and worship in spirit and truth.

-> AN INDEX OF ALL THE CHAPTERS OF THIS BOOK, <-
-> which is called the Thesaurus. <-

### CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST BOOK.
How one should respond to the <term>Arians</term><note>Followers of Arius, who argued that Jesus was a created being and not fully God.</note> when they ask whether there is only one "unbegotten" being, or two. Chapter 1.
That it is better and worthier for God to be called "Father" than "unbegotten." Chapter 2.
That "unbegotten" is not a substance, but a term signifying the mode of the substance. Chapter 3.
That "unbegotten" is not a substance, but only signifies that God was not begotten. Chapter 4.
Against those who say there was a duration of time when the Son did not exist; and testimonies of Scripture from which it is gathered that the Word of God is eternal. Chapter 5.
That the Father did not exist before the Son, even though He is unbegotten, but the begotten Son was always coeternal with Him. Chapter 6.
That the Father begets the Son from Himself indivisibly and without corruption. Chapter 7.
To those who ask whether the Father begat the Son willingly or unwillingly. Chapter 8.
Against those who say the Son is similar not to the Father, but to the Father's will. Chapter 9.

### OF THE SECOND BOOK.
That the Son is consubstantial with the Father. Chapter 1.
That the Son is consubstantial with the Father, based on the proposed text: "I go to my Father and your Father: to my God and your God." Chapter 2.
Concerning the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son, based on the proposed text: "Because my Father is greater than I." Chapter 3.
That the Son is equal to the Father, based on the proposed Gospel text: "Among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist." Chapter 4.

### OF THE THIRD BOOK.
A refutation of the heretical interpretation, and an exposition of the true sense of the Gospel text: "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me." Chapter 1.
Concerning the likeness of the Son to the Father, and that the Son is not of a changeable nature, nor existing from the outside, but begotten from the very substance of the Father, as a true Son. Chapter 2.
That the Son is from the substance of the Father, and was not produced externally, as the heretics say. And since He was not produced externally, He is therefore like the Father. Chapter 3.
Concerning the likeness of the Father and the Son, likewise based on the proposed text: "No one is good, except God alone." Chapter 3.

### OF THE FOURTH BOOK.
That we are formed in the image of God through participation. Chapter 1.
Likewise, concerning the essential likeness of the Father and the Son, based on the proposed Gospel text: "For as the Father has life in himself,"

# THE FIRST BOOK OF CYRIL, PATRIARCH
## OF ALEXANDRIA, ON THE GOSPEL
### OF JOHN, TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF
### TREBIZOND. <note>George of Trebizond (1395–1482) was a leading Greek scholar and philosopher who helped reintroduce Greek patristic texts to the Latin-speaking West during the Renaissance.</note>

-> PROLOGUE OF CYRIL. <-

<margin>
On the authority
of holy
scripture
</margin>
The doctrine of all the Evangelists is indeed exquisite and flows from the divine. For as if looking around from a high watchtower, it gathers the advantage of listeners from everywhere with such diligent zeal that those who thirst for the truth of divine dogmas (if they inquire into the meaning of the scriptures with a right mind) may easily find in it whatever may benefit them. For the grace of the Spirit—which does not enter into a malicious soul, nor allows its most precious gems to be trampled under the feet of cattle—infuses truth not into those who rejoice in reckless investigation and human reasoning rather than the authority of scripture, but into simpler minds: those who, striving for no sophistry, follow the right and royal path with no small reverence. For "he who walks simply, walks with confidence," as it is written in Solomon <note>original: "apud Solomonem"; referring to Proverbs 10:9.</note>. Since, therefore, the doctrine of the holy Evangelists is wonderful and lofty (for as the Savior says, it is not they who speak, but the Spirit of the Father speaking in them), anyone who considers the sublimity of mind and the sharpness of John the Evangelist, and reflects on how great a weight of thought is in him, will rightly judge him the most outstanding of all. For even if the exposition of divine dogmas is set forth equally to all, and all are carried diligently toward the same finish line in their course, yet their speech is so diverse that although they all arrive at one city, it seems to me that they have entered different houses, one more magnificent than the other. For while the others most exquisitely recorded the genealogy of the Savior, either descending from Abraham to Joseph or ascending from Joseph back to Adam, one may see that John alone did not labor much over these things. Instead, with a burning spirit, beyond what is possible for man, he wished to fly and dared to express the ineffable generation of the Word in words.

Nor was he ignorant that the glory of the Lord surpasses all speech and every human mind, and that divine things can scarcely be signified by a human voice. But because it was now necessary to measure the heavens with a span, as it were, and to be carried into the highest things by human humility—lest a wide entrance be opened to simpler folk by malicious teachers if they were not restrained from their depravity by the voice of the Lord's disciples—he flew most vigilantly to the foundation of divine dogmas: *In the beginning was the Word* <note>original: "In principio erat uerbum"</note>, he cried out with a great voice, *and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: this was in the beginning with God.* But since it is right to receive all things that contribute to the truth gladly—so that, in the manner of a bee, we may glue together the sweet honeycombs of the Holy Spirit from many various things flowing into one—it will not be out of place to briefly set forth what we have received from certain very studious men.

For they say that after our Savior’s cross and His ascension into heaven, certain false pastors and destructive teachers, like savage beasts, rushed into the Lord’s flock, speaking from their own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord, as it is written. These men endeavored to hand down to the church the doctrine not only of their own heart, as we said, but even of their father, the devil. For if no one can say "Jesus is accursed" except by Beelzebub <note>original: "Beelzebul"</note>, how were those men free from the doctrine of the devil who impiously affirmed that the only-begotten Word of God (in whom we all move and exist) only then first came into existence when He took flesh from the undefiled Virgin and, according to the scripture, *was seen on earth and lived among men*? <note>This refers to the heresy of Photinianism or early Arianism, which denied the eternal pre-existence of Christ.</note> To these men, and all others who dare to deny the eternal and ineffable generation of the Son, that prophetic word is rightly said: *But come here, you sons,* says Isaiah <note>original: "Esaias"</note>, *seed of the adulterers and the harlot; over whom have you made sport, and over whom have you opened your mouth and stuck out your tongue?* [Isaiah 57:3-4]. For they do not bring forth good words from a good mind, but breathe out the poison of the deadly serpent, concerning whom the Psalmist cries out in a prayer turned to God: *You have broken the heads of the dragon.* [Psalm 74/73:13].

Since, therefore, there was a disturbance among the faithful that was not to be ignored, and the plague was devastating the souls of the simpler folk (with many sliding from the truth to their trifles), those who were firmer went to John, the disciple of the Savior. They explained the whole matter and the danger hanging over the church, and asked him to stretch out a hand to those in peril. Moved by this, John thought it right to look out for both those present and those to come by writing this Gospel. Therefore, whatever pertained to the flesh of the Lord, which had been or was to be spoken of more extensively by others, he passed over. He himself, most fiercely, like a very robust young man, cries out, leaping upon the madness of the heretics.

<margin>
Baruch 3.
Isaiah 57.
Psalm 73.
</margin>

Cyril argues that while other Evangelists focused on Christ's human genealogy, John "flew" toward the eternal Word to defend the Church.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from Cyril's prologue into the first chapter of his commentary. He begins to address the divinity and eternity of the Word (the Son) against Arian views that claimed the Son was a created being with a beginning in time. The catchword "fructus" (fruit) at the bottom of the previous physical page is not included in this prose translation.</meta>

THE HOLY CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>That the Only-begotten Son of God is eternal and before the ages.</margin>
<margin>He refutes the heretics by authority.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 81 <note>original: "Psal. 80" - following the Vulgate numbering.</note></margin>
<margin>John 8</margin>
**In the beginning was the Word.** What then can they say to this—those who preach to us that the Son is so recent that he is not even believed to be God? What, I ask, can they say? *There shall no new god be in you,* the Scripture cries out. <note>Psalm 81:9. Cyril uses this to argue that if the Son were a "new" or created being, he could not be God.</note> How then is he not "new," if he was born in the most recent times? How was he not lying when he said to the Jews: *Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am*? <note>John 8:58</note> For it escapes no one that Christ was born of the most holy Virgin many ages after Abraham. If, therefore, the Only-begotten was born in the final age, how can it be true that he was "in the beginning"? But we shall refute their trifles from the following words as well.

<margin>He refutes [them] by reason.</margin>
Let this be explained more subtly: what the Evangelist said, **In the beginning was the Word.** Indeed, if the definition of "beginning" holds firm, nothing is more ancient than it. For a "beginning of a beginning" can never be conceived. For if something else is understood to be before the beginning, the beginning will surely fail and not truly be a beginning. Furthermore, if something else can be found before a true beginning, we would have to proceed into infinity, always seeking one thing before another, and never resting in one simple beginning. Lest our consideration become inexplicable by seeking infinities—a path that could never reach an end—we shall neither grant a beginning to the beginning, nor concede that the Son was begotten of the Father in time. Instead, we shall confess that he is eternally with the Father. For if he "was" in the beginning, what mind could ever fly beyond that "was"? Or when he "was," shall we hold it in our mind such that it does not precede our thoughts? Justly, then, Isaiah cries out in awe: *Who shall declare his generation? For his life is taken from the earth.* <note>Isaiah 53:8. "Generation" here refers to the eternal origin of the Son from the Father.</note> For the logic of the Only-begotten's generation is indeed taken from the earth: for exceeding every mind and surpassing all human reason, it is ineffable. How then do some assert that he was made and created? For while our mind can easily circumscribe all things created by reason and time, it can in no way comprehend the generation of the Only-begotten. "In the beginning," he says, "was the Word." We can by no means understand a beginning of time in the Only-begotten Son of God. For he who is before all ages, his substance is eternal. Furthermore, since the divine nature refuses to reach an end (for it always remains the same, according to that: *But you are the same, and your years shall not fail* <note>Psalm 102:27. The margin cites "Psal. 121," but the text matches Psalm 102 (101 in the Vulgate).</note>), from what beginning, measured by spaces of time, shall the Son begin? Being God by nature, and therefore truly crying out, *I am the life*, <note>John 14:6</note> he cannot reach an end. For a beginning signified by a quantity of time can never exist in itself—nor even be understood—without looking toward its end and exit. For we call a beginning such in relation to an end,

<column-break/>

and we name an end by referring it back to a beginning. Since, therefore, the Son exists before the ages, he cannot have been begotten in time. Rather, he is always in the Father, as if in a fountain, just as he said: *I came out from the Father and have come.* <note>John 8:42</note> For we understand the Father as a fountain, in whom the Word is—existing as his wisdom, power, character <note>original: "character" - used here in the sense of 'exact imprint' or 'express image', as in Hebrews 1:3.</note>, splendor, and image. Therefore, if there was never any time when the Father was without his wisdom, power, character, splendor, and finally his image, it is necessary to confess that the Son also is co-eternal, who is the wisdom, power, and the rest—for he is the "character" <note>The Latin 'character' refers to the Greek 'charaktēr', meaning the precise representation of the Father's essence.</note> of the eternal Father. How or in what way is he the most exquisite image of the Father, unless he has perfectly attained the beauty of him whose image he is? It is not absurd that we said the Son must be understood as being in the Father as if in a fountain. For the name "fountain" signifies nothing else to us but "that from which" something comes. But the Son is in the Father and from the Father, not flowing out of him, but like splendor from the sun, or like the heat innate to fire. For in these examples, we see one produced by the other, and both are so co-eternal that one cannot exist without the other, nor retain the logic of its own nature. For how will there be a sun deprived of splendor? Or how will there be splendor unless there is a sun from which it flows? How will fire exist without heat? Or whence will heat flow, unless from fire, or perhaps from something else not far removed from the substantial quality of fire? Therefore, just as the things that flow from these are simultaneously with those from which they flow, and always show from where they flow: so it must be understood regarding the Only-begotten. For he is understood to be *from* the Father, but is also believed to be *in* the Father. Not alien in nature, nor second in nature after the Father: but always in the Father himself, and with him, and from him, according to the ineffable manner of generation. Now, the Father is called the "beginning" of the Son by Scripture in no other sense than "that from which" [he comes]. The Psalmist, moved by the grace of the Holy Spirit, shows this regarding the second coming of our Savior, saying to the Son: *With you is the beginning in the day of your power, in the splendor of your saints.* <note>Psalm 110:3 (Vulgate 109:3). The term "beginning" here translates 'principium' (Greek 'archē').</note> For that day of the Son's power is the one in which, as judge of the world, he will repay each according to their works. But he is to come in such a way that he is in the Father, and the Father in him; thus the Father is his eternal "beginning" only (as we have said) in that sense of being "that from which": since he is from the Father. "In the beginning," he says, "was the Word." Many and varied meanings of "beginning" suggest themselves to us as we investigate the truth of dogmas from every side. For rightly the Savior says: *Search the scriptures, because in them you think you have eternal life: and they are they which bear witness of me.* <note>John 5:39</note> It seems, therefore, that by the name "beginning" here, the blessed Evangelist signifies the Father. For in this way, he will place the divine nature above all things, if everything that is created is understood to be under his feet: so that as if sitting over all things he has created, he might nourish and preserve them all. In this, therefore, which is the "beginning" of all things and which is over all things—in this "beginning," I say, the Word was: not with all things under his feet, but apart from all created things: as if co-eternal [with the Father]...

<summary>In this opening chapter, Cyril argues for the eternity and divinity of the "Word" (the Son) against those who claim he was created in time, using both scriptural authority and logical analogies like the sun and its light. He explains that the Father is the "beginning" of the Son only in the sense of being his eternal source, not a chronological predecessor.</summary>

He moves from the first phrase of John 1:1 ("In the beginning was the Word") to the second phrase ("And the Word was with God"), specifically refuting the idea that the Son is a created "servant" or that the Father and Son are merely different names for the same person.</meta>

a 2

...the fruit is in him naturally, possessing (so to speak) the nature of the begetter. Therefore, since he is free, born of a free father, he has the principle of all things within himself. This is most strongly proven from this: because (as we said) some used to impiously contend that the Word of God first began to exist when he took up this temple of man <note>Cyril often refers to the human body of Christ as a "temple."</note> from the immaculate Virgin for our salvation. But if he were so created, and were of that nature which all things have that are produced from nothing, the name not of "Lord," but of "slave" would truly be applied to him. For no creature refuses the servitude of the Creator God and Lord; nothing at all was made that is not subject to the divine principle and power. Solomon <margin>Proverbs 8</margin> signifying this, said that by justice the seat of the principle is prepared. For the seat of the principle of all things is prepared and very fit for beautiful justice. But what is that seat of which he now speaks? You may hear God himself saying: *Heaven is my throne.* <margin>Isaiah 66</margin> Therefore the heavens—namely the holy spirits, whom we are also accustomed to call angels—are most ready for justice and servitude. Wherefore, lest you think the Son is subject to God the Father along with other creatures, and lest you reduce him to a servile place as if he were born recently and in time (for thus he would necessarily be a creature), John the Divine <note>original: "tiechemēus" - likely a corruption of the Greek *theologos*, meaning "the Theologian" or "the Divine."</note> not without cause drives out thoughts of this kind, vindicates the Son from every servile condition, shows that he emanates from a free and all-ruling substance, and asserts that he is in it naturally, saying: **In the beginning was the Word.**

Now, he most fittingly connects the word "was" to the term "beginning," so that the Son may be understood not only as beautiful but also as eternal and before the ages. For into that most profound and incomprehensible generation, which surpasses all time, he brings the sense of this "was." For "was" <margin>thought, counsel, indicator</margin> uttered by itself indeterminately, is never circumscribed by any limits, since it is born to always precede a laboring intellect; so much so that wherever you think it has reached its ultimate end and rest, that "was" is already there, and from there a new beginning of something higher immediately seems to be made. The Word was therefore in the beginning—in that, namely, which is above all things—whence the Word itself naturally possesses Lordly majesty. If this is so, as it certainly is, how will the Son be thought of as made or created? Or how, if "was" is truly and absolutely predicated of the Word (that is, of the Only-begotten Son of God), can "he was not" ever be preached?

<margin>That although the Son is consubstantial <term>consubstantial: sharing the same fundamental essence or "stuff" of divinity; Greek *homoousios*</term> with the Father, he is nevertheless in his own hypostasis <term>hypostasis: a distinct person or individual existence within the Trinity</term>, and similarly the Father.</margin>

### CHAPTER II.

**AND the Word was with God.** He now shows the empty opinion, far from the truth, of those who think the Son was produced from nothing. Therefore, just as a very good and skillful farmer, when he desires to root out all briars from the garden, diligently pulls up the roots with the long teeth of his rakes: so the most blessed John, most sharply and skillfully perceiving the false opinions of heretics that were about to sprout, overturns them with this Gospel as if with rakes, and preserves the studious reader in the right faith. For since he had the eyes of his mind illuminated by divine grace, he was not ignorant that certain men would come who would dare to say that the Father and the Son are one and the same, and that the most holy Trinity is distinguished only by names, not by their own *hypostases*. <note>This refers to Sabellianism, a heresy that claimed God is one person who simply wears different "masks" or names.</note> So that the Father may be understood truly as Father and not Son, and the Son again properly as Son and not Father—as if girded against the future wickedness of heretics already present—to that which was said, **In the beginning was the Word** (namely in God the Father, as we have said), he immediately added: **And the Word was with God.** Necessarily and most exactly he repeats "was" everywhere, so that he might more expressly designate the eternal generation of the Word. Since he preaches that the Word is "with God," he most clearly shows that the Son is one, subsisting in himself, and again that God the Father is one, with whom the Word is. For how could that which is numerically one be understood to be "with itself"? But it will not be out of place to show the falsehood of this pernicious opinion more broadly and exquisitely. The Son is indeed rightly believed to be consubstantial with the Father, and the Father with the Son. For there is such a supreme identity in them that the Father is seen in the Son, and the Son in the Father. "For he who sees me," <margin>On the divine hypostases.</margin> <margin>John 14</margin> says the Savior, "sees my Father." And again: "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me." Although this is so, he will not therefore deny that either the Son subsists in his own *hypostasis*, or the Father by himself. Nor does that supreme identity confound the persons (that is, the *hypostases*). Nor because the Father and the Son who is from him are one in substance, will they therefore be one in number; rather, the nature is the same in both, but each truly and properly subsists. For thus the Father will be truly Father, and the Son truly Son; and with the Holy Spirit counted in, the Holy Trinity will attain its fullness and its majesty. Furthermore, if the Son is himself also the Father, what reason introduced the variety of names? For if he in no way begot, why is he called Father? Or how is he called Son, if he was not begotten by a Father? For the names themselves necessarily declare this meaning to us. Therefore, since Scripture preaches him as begotten by the Father, and the truth is that the one begotten is necessarily distinguished in reality from the one begetting, both the Son subsists by himself and the Father truly subsists. Added to this is that the blessed Paul affirms to the Philippians that the Son is in the form of God, and did not achieve equality with God by robbery; is it not therefore necessary that he who attained equality with God (not by robbery) be someone other than the one in whose form he is known to be? Therefore, the Father and Son are not numerically the same; but each subsists, and one is seen in the other because of the identity of substance; and one is from the other—namely, the Son from the Father. The Savior also opens this very thing to us: "I," he says, "and the Father are one." For unless both subsisted, he would not have said "we are" (*sumus*), but "I and the Father am one" (*sum*). But because he said "we are one" in the plural number, he most fittingly showed both the unity of nature and the plurality of person—

<meta>This page continues the theological defense of the Trinity, specifically focusing on the distinction of persons within the Godhead while maintaining a single divine essence. The previous page discussed the Son as the eternal "Principle" of all things.</meta>

# THE DIVINE CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.

...shows the distinction of persons. For "we are" can never be predicated of only one, even if the heretics burst with rage. Furthermore, the Scripture records the words of God saying: <margin>Genesis 1</margin> "Let us make man in our image and likeness." <note>original Latin: *Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & ſimilitudinem noſtram*</note> If, therefore, the Holy Trinity is compressed into a single individual—as the impious contend—who is it that speaks, and to whom does he speak when he says: "Let us make man in our image"? Or why is it written "our" and not "my" image? Therefore, the use of the plural "Let us make," and the addition of "our image," is intended so that by this clear and great voice you may be able to hear and understand that the divine power in the Holy Trinity exists as three persons in one substance. Add to this that the Son is called the "Radiance of the Father," <margin>Hebrews 1</margin> as light from light; how can he be anything other than distinct from the Father? For that which emanates as radiance must necessarily emanate from another, and not from itself.

<margin>John 16</margin> Since the Son says of himself that he "went out from the Father and came [into the world]," and shows again that he "goes to the Father," how can he not be a different <term>hypostasis</term> <note>From the Greek *hypostasis*, referring to an individual, subsisting person or reality within the Trinity, distinct from the shared 'substance' or essence.</note> than the Father? For no reason allows that which flows out from another should not be distinguished from that from which it flowed. Furthermore, we are saved by believing in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit; for this reason Christ said to the disciples: <margin>Matthew 28</margin> "Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." If a single hypostasis and person were understood by this diversity of names, why would he want the faithful to be baptized into a Trinity rather than a Unity? It is clear, therefore, that we are baptized into the Trinity because the account of the persons reaches that number; and because these persons are recognized by an identity of nature, we believe in one God and piously worship one God. To this, the Scripture narrates that the cities of the Sodomites were burned up by the wrath of God. <margin>Genesis 19, Psalm 10</margin> "The Lord," it says, "rained fire and sulfur from the Lord." For this "portion of their cup" <note>A reference to Psalm 11:6 (Psalm 10 in the Vulgate numbering), where fire and brimstone are described as the portion of the wicked.</note> is reserved for those who commit such outrages. Which Lord, then, caused fire to descend from the Lord? It is evident, because the Father performs all things through the Son; for since the Son is the "arm" and "power" of the Father, <margin>Isaiah 53</margin> he himself sent the fire upon the Sodomites. But if the "Lord rained fire from the Lord," how is the Son not distinct from the Father, and the Father from the Son? For when it is said, "Lord from the Lord," it certainly signifies one proceeding from another. Add to this that the blessed Psalmist, moved by the spirit of prophecy by which he foresaw the future, knew that the human race could not be saved otherwise than through the appearance of the Son of God; therefore, he prayed to God the Father that he who alone could claim us from slavery into liberty might be sent to us, saying: <margin>Psalm 42, John 8</margin> "Send out your light and your truth." <note>Psalm 43:3 in modern numbering.</note> To learn who this light and truth might be, listen to the Son himself: "I am the light," he says, "and I am the truth." But if the light and truth of the Father—namely the only-begotten Son—is sent by him to us, how is he not someone other than the Father? And if so, how does he not subsist by himself, even though he is one with the Father in identity of substance? If the Father and Son were one in number <note>Meaning a single person rather than two persons sharing one nature.</note>, would not the praying prophet have said: <margin>John 14</margin> "Come to us, Light and Truth"? But since he said "Send," the Father—being divinely instructed—understood that it is one thing to send and another to be sent, and understood the manner of the mission as befits God.

<column-break/>

Lastly, that all things visible and invisible were made through the Son, <margin>Colossians 1</margin> both the Scriptures testify and all we who adhere to the truth and piety of divine dogmas believe. Let us therefore diligently examine what this phrase, "through the Son," implies. Does it not immediately demonstrate that there is one who acts, and another through whom he acts? Thus, when it is written that all things were made through the Son, two persons are undoubtedly designated. For how can one in number be truly and properly said to have created all things "through the Son" if no other person at all is understood? I do not think the adversaries can answer anything to this, if they admit the Scripture. Truly, that all things are made by the Father through the Son, both the Scripture proclaims and we <margin>Hebrews 1</margin> believe. How then is it not necessary that the Father subsists by himself, and the Son likewise? For the identity of substance is not harmed if we holily and piously confess a Trinity of persons.

-> That God the Son is in no way less than or unlike the Father. <-
-> CHAPTER III. <-

**AND THE WORD WAS GOD.**) The divine Evangelist was not ignorant that in later ages some would come who, denying the deity of the Son, would contend that the Word of the Father is not God by nature, but as if he were counterfeit <note>original Latin: *adulterinum*, meaning debased or not of the true stock.</note> and God in name only; who would think him called "Son" and "God," but not believe him to be true God. This especially the Arians, <margin>Arians</margin> conceiving Jewish impiety in their souls, seem to me to have suffered. For from their dark hearts flows not the life-giving word of piety, but the death-dealing doctrine of the devil; their tongue is entirely deceitful, and the words of their mouth are like arrows. Therefore, if they had contended against the Evangelist in this way: <margin>That the Son is consubstantial with the Father.</margin> "Although the Word is with God (for we believe you when you say this) and the Father is one person and the Son another, it does not follow from this that he is of the same substance with the Father. For since we find the Scripture preaching one God, we attribute that name truly only to the Father, with whom the Word was." As if hearing that they would say these things, [John] says: Not only was the Word with God, but "the Word was God." Thus, since he is with the Father, he says, he subsists by himself; but since he is God, and from God the Father, he is understood to be <term>consubstantial</term> <note>From the Latin *consubstantialis*, translating the Greek *homoousios*, meaning having the exact same essence or 'stuff' of divinity as the Father.</note> with the Father and God by nature. For since a single nature of God is believed by all, the most holy Trinity cannot fail to be contained within that identity of substance. Therefore the Word was God, not recently made, but eternal; for whoever is God is necessarily eternally so.

For that which is made in time, or which is found to be produced from nothing, cannot be God by nature; but the Word of God, since he is eternal and since he is God, is entirely consubstantial with the Father. Of what punishments, then, are they not worthy, who think the Only-begotten is somehow less than or unlike the Begetter? They have proceeded so far in impiety that they do not hesitate to bring these things forward, paying little attention to such great matters. For we shall learn by many and most firm reasons flowing from the fountain of the Scriptures that the Son is in no way less than the Father. For the Son of God is [described] by many and various names...

<margin>Philippians 2</margin>
...the spirit of the Begetter, as his own good in no other way than the Begetter himself possesses it: he is not, I say, in any way lesser than the Father. Add to this that, according to Paul, the Son exists in the form and equality of the Father. How, then, shall he be lesser than him? For the assumption of humanity—on account of which the Son is said to have humbled himself—by no means stripped the Son of the majesty and perfection of his <term>Deity</term> <note>The nature or essence of God.</note>. For though he was made man and humbled himself, he shall nonetheless come in the majesty and glory of the Father. How, then, is he in the majesty and glory of the Father if he is lesser than him? Especially since God has already spoken with a great voice through the prophet:
<margin>Isaiah 48</margin>
"I will not give my glory to another." <note>original Latin: *Non dabo gloriam meam alij*</note> Therefore, all those who are impious toward the Son must be questioned—or rather, those who are impious toward the Father (for he who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father either). If the Son is lesser than the Father, as they believe, is he <term>consubstantial</term> <note>From the Latin *consubstantialis*, meaning "of the same substance" or "of the same essence." This is the core term used to describe the unity of the Trinity.</note> with the Father, or not? For if he is consubstantial, those who think he is "lesser" will appear to be out of their minds. For whatever things are of the same nature and substance can in no way admit to being "more" or "less"; and this is exactly what we are investigating. But if they deny he is consubstantial—which follows from their claim that he is "lesser"—then he must be entirely alienated from the substance of the Father.

<margin>Daniel 7</margin>
How then shall he have his glory? Or how was the honor and kingdom given to him, as Daniel asserts? Either God the Father lies when he flatly denies that he will give his glory to another; or, if he is true (as he certainly is) and has given his glory to his Son, it is necessary that the Son be of the same substance, for he is the fruit—that is, the offspring—of the Father. If this is so, how can he who is of the same nature as the Father be lesser than the Father? To this we add: if the Father is <term>omnipotent</term> <note>All-powerful; from *omnis* (all) and *potens* (powerful).</note> and the Son is also omnipotent, how is he lesser? For the imperfect can never be equated in power to the perfect. If the Father is Lord, and the Son is similarly Lord, is it not madness to call him "lesser"? For if he is lesser, then his liberty and the dignity of his dominion must necessarily be lesser in him than in the Father. How then is he "Lord" if he does not possess the full dignity of dominion? Furthermore, the Father is light, and the Son is likewise; wherefore, if he is lesser, he will not be perfect light, and he would be overtaken in some way by darkness. In this way, the vice of falsehood would be attributed to the Gospel. For it is said:
<margin>John 1</margin>
"And the darkness did not overcome him." <note>original Latin: *Et tenebræ eum non comprehenderunt*</note> The Son is also life, just as the Father is; how then is he lesser? Or how do the faithful live because Christ has dwelt in the inner man, if the Son is not perfect life? For if the life by which we live is not perfect, we are not entirely alive, but are in some way dead. Fleeing these absurdities and inconsistencies with our whole soul, we confess that the Son is perfect, and equal in substance to the perfect Father. It follows that if the Son is lesser than the Father, and therefore not consubstantial, he would necessarily be neither the Son nor even God at all. For how will he truly be the Son if he was not begotten of the Father? Or how will he be God...

He concludes that any being who is "lesser" in nature cannot truly be God or the true Son of the Father.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument from the previous page, where Cyril uses biblical titles and divine attributes to prove that Christ (the Son) is equal to God the Father, specifically refuting the Arian claim that the Son is a "lesser" being.</meta>

# SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I

...who is not God by nature? For we all believe in the Son. Therefore, we would all be in error, and we would not yet have known the true God. Since this is absurd, those who believe in the Son also piously believe in the Father, and evidently in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the Son is not a stranger to the Father, nor is he lesser than him; rather, he is one with him, because he is from him according to nature, and therefore equal to him and perfect. For if the only-begotten Son truly shone forth from God the Father, one must confess—even if unwillingly—that he is from the substance and nature of the Father himself. For that is what true sonship signifies. How then is he "lesser," who naturally flowed forth from that substance in which nothing is found to be "lesser" or "greater," but all things are found perfect? 

But if he is not from the substance of the Father according to nature, he would not even truly be the Son; likewise, the Father would not truly be the Father. For if there is no Son because of whom the Father is a Father, how do we understand him to be a Father? But God is a true Father, for divine scripture proclaims this everywhere: therefore the Son is truly the Son, and is from the Father naturally. He is not, therefore, lesser than the Father who is from him; and because he is from him, he is for that reason entirely **consubstantial** <term>consubstantial: From the Greek 'homoousios,' meaning sharing the exact same essence or being. This was the central point of debate at the Council of Nicaea.</term> with him. 

Furthermore, the name of "fatherhood" did not descend from us into God, but from God into men. For from him all fatherhood in heaven and on earth exists, as Paul <margin>Ephesians 3</margin> says. By a certain imitation and likeness of him, we—who were made in his image—are called fathers. Tell me then, I ask, why are we fathers of our sons according to nature, if this is not present in the archetype whose imitation we possess? Or how did the name of fatherhood flow down from God into others if God is not truly a Father? For if that were so, the name of fatherhood would not descend from God to us, but ascend from us to God; and God would be called "Father" not in reality, but only according to our likeness. Therefore, the witness of truth would be lying when he testifies that all fatherhood, both in heaven and on earth, is from God. But he <margin>2 Corinthians 13</margin> in whom Christ spoke does not lie. 

Therefore, the name of fatherhood flowed down from God to us: for which reason the Word of the Father is from him according to nature. He did not beget someone lesser, nor someone unlike himself; for even we, who obtained the name of "father" from that source through the **incarnation** <term>incarnation: The doctrine that the second person of the Trinity, the Son, took on human flesh and became Jesus Christ.</term>, are able to produce sons equal to us according to the logic of nature, not unequal. For these reasons, let the heretics not arm themselves with quibbles against the truth, nor let them confess the Son of God with naked words while denying that he is from the substance of the Father. For how is he truly a Son who is not a Son by nature? Either they should throw off these veils of pretense and, confessing neither God nor the Son, blaspheme with an "uncovered head" (as the saying goes); or, if overcome by the authority of the scriptures and the doctrine of the saints they confess the Son, let them not say he is lesser than the Father. For if the Word was God, by what reasoning shall he be accepted as "lesser"? For not even a son of man, by the logic of being human, is lesser than his father. For in no way is one human lesser or greater than another human *insofar as they are human*, nor can anything be "more" or "less" of that whose logic of substance and nature it has received. Therefore, if the Son is truly the Son, it is necessary to confess that he is from the Father's substance; whence, if the Father is God by nature, then the Son who is begotten of him is also God by nature, necessarily possessing all

<column-break/>

the properties of that nature. How then shall God be "lesser" than God by the very logic that both are God? Tell me, I ask, how did you arrive at this? Or how did you believe it to be so? For I do not see by what reasoning you think the Son is lesser than the Father. Do you say it is because of **time**? But the Son is before the ages, and he himself is the founder of the ages; nor can he who was not born in time be contained by time. Is it because of **quantity**? But an incorporeal nature will never admit of any quantity. How then is he "lesser," if he is not lesser in these things? 

Perhaps you will say he is lesser in **glory, power, and wisdom**. Then explain to us how great and of what sort (if I may put it this way) the Father is in these things, so that the Son, measured against that by you, might be found to be "lesser." Or, if the glory, power, and wisdom of the Father is incomprehensible and immeasurable, by what reasoning do you dare to call the Son "lesser" after measuring him, and—as far as lies within you—deprive him of the dignity that is innate and natural to him? For the "lesser" is understood by the measurement of the "greater," which occurs through the comparison of the "minor." Since the dignity of the Father is immeasurable, from where do you say the Son is "lesser"? 

Rightly and truly, therefore, regarding heretics of this sort, we can exclaim what is commonly said: "Our adversaries are mindless and insane." For how are they not insane, since they understand neither what they say nor the things about which they dispute? We are moved to say these things because, while they confess the Son as God from God born of the Father, they contend that he is lesser than the Father. From this, many wicked and even horrible things to hear follow. For if the Son, though he is God by nature, admits of "lesser" in some way, there will necessarily be something "greater" than God. If that is so, then the Father himself, since he is God by nature, will be understood as being able to progress toward something greater. For if both the Father and the Son are God, and thereby something "greater" is understood, then something greater than the Father will also be understood. And if he has not yet received it, he could still receive it, or is capable of receiving it—which is shown to be so through the Son, <margin>Colossians 1</margin> who is his image. But how can such a potentiality exist in God that has not yet transitioned into action? 

Great blasphemy resides in these thoughts. For the Father will never receive "greater" or "lesser," because he is God by nature; therefore neither will the Son, since he is likewise God. Furthermore, if the Son is from God the Father according to nature, yet is "lesser" in dignity, or substance, or in any way at all, he is not depressed so much as the substance from which he is believed to be is dishonored. For while all things that generate produce things similar and equal to themselves by the logic of substance, only the divine nature would generate something lesser than itself. But the nature of the Father is not susceptible to any defect; indeed, the good things that are in us exist much more perfectly in him—as in the source from which they flow down to us—than they are in us. He will not, therefore, generate a Son lesser than himself, but one equal and consubstantial; lest he who infinitely exceeds human nature be found to fall short, in no small way, of the good that he has bestowed upon others. 

Add to this that Christ showed himself equal to God the Father: "He who sees me," he said to his disciples, <margin>John 14</margin> "sees also my Father." If therefore his nature is such that whoever understands him has understood the Father (as he himself asserts), how is he lesser? For if he shows the Father in himself with no perceived distinction (for the Father is seen in his immutable image), he is not "lesser."

<summary>Cyril argues that because the Son is of the same divine nature as the Father, he must be equal in power, wisdom, and glory, rather than "lesser" as the Arians claimed. He asserts that if a human father produces a son of the same nature, God—the source of all fatherhood—must do so even more perfectly.</summary>

Against those who dare to say that there is one internal and naturally implanted Word in God, and another who is called the Son of God by the scriptures: a pernicious opinion attributed to the Eunomians <note>The Eunomians were a radical wing of the Arian movement in the 4th century who argued that the Son was of a different nature than the Father.</note>.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>A</margin> **The same was in the beginning with God.** <note>original: "Hoc erat in principio apud Deum." This refers to John 1:2.</note>) When the Evangelist says, "The same was in the beginning," he seems to repeat his previous points very briefly through this demonstration, as if shouting with a loud voice: "I am speaking of this Word which was in the beginning, this one who was with the Father, this one who was God from God: this, I say, and no other, is the one about whom we write this book." For since he foresaw the future by divine inspiration, he was not ignorant (as it seems to me, and truly so, I believe) that there would be certain <margin>B</margin> snares of death, pushing simpler people toward the abyss of hell. These are the people who dare to say, to their own damnation, that there is one "internal and innate" Word in God the Father, and another "Son and Word of God" through whom God created all things—claiming this second word is merely a likeness of the internal one, so that he might be understood as a "word of a word," an "image of an image," and "brightness of brightness."

Foreseeing that such heretics would arise, and having already briefly determined that there is only one true Word—who is from God, in God, and with God—the Evangelist swiftly added in a wonderful and divine way: **The same was in the beginning with God.** He means: just as the Son is with the Father, just as he is innate and internal, just as he is from the substance of the Father, and just as he is the **only-begotten** <term>only-begotten: From the Greek 'monogenes,' emphasizing that the Son is the unique offspring of the Father's own nature, not a created being.</term>; he says "the same," because there is no second word. 

But so that this impiety may be openly exposed, and so that everyone might more easily flee from it as if from a venomous serpent, let us summarize their arguments. Once they are clearly refuted by the ancient reasoning of the scriptures which the wisdom of God has granted us, they will bring no destruction to the Church of God. 

<margin>
The impious opinion of Eunomius.
</margin>

"The only-begotten Son of God," they say, "is not properly the Word of God himself; rather, the internal and innate Word of God the Father is always in God himself. However, he who is said to be the Son begotten from him receives that internal Word, speaks all things from it, and therefore is called a 'Word' only because of his likeness to it."

<margin>D</margin> He later tries to strengthen this perverse opinion with arguments, so that the wretched man may be bound (as they say) by the chains of his own sins. "If," he says, "the natural, internal, and innate Word in God the Father is the Son himself, and is **consubstantial** <term>consubstantial: Having the same essence or substance (Latin: 'consubstantialis'). This is the orthodox view that the Father and Son are the same God.</term> with the begetter: what will prevent the Father from being, and being called, the Word?" 

Next, "if the Son of God is the Word, and there is no other besides him, by what 'word' did the Father say to the Son: *You are my Son, today I have begotten you*? <margin>Psalm 2.</margin> For since everything that is said is spoken by no other way than by a word, it is clear that the Father did not speak thus to the Son without a word." The Savior himself also says: "I know the Father, and I keep his word." <margin>John 8 & 14.</margin> And again: "The word which you hear is not mine, but his who sent me." 

"Since, therefore," they argue, "the Father addresses the Son by a word, and the Son himself also confesses at one time that he keeps the Father's word, and at another that the Jews were hearing not his own word but the Father's: how can it not be conceded that the Son is someone other than the internal and..." 

<margin>
Arguments for this impiety.
</margin>

### SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.
->B<-

...and innate, that is, existing only in the movement of understanding a word: having received this, is the word then brought forth in its fullness, expressing the substance of the Father, and thus called the "Word" and the "Son of God"? <note>Cyril is summarizing his opponent's argument—likely that of the Arians or Eunomians—who claimed the Son was not an eternal person but merely an "uttered word" of God’s internal thought.</note> That foolish man weaves such evils for himself, and does not fear to oppose all the scriptures, so that the saying might seem true of him: *When the wicked man comes into the depth of evils, then he despises all things.* <note>Proverbs 18:3</note> For that enemy of God and men has immersed himself in the very bottom of madness, so that, casting away the principles of truth, he follows his own empty thoughts. For it is the only-begotten Son of God and His Word that is truly meant, as can easily be recognized from what follows—although even things that are clear are difficult for <term>heretics<note>In the 4th and 5th centuries, this usually referred to groups like the Arians, who denied the full divinity or eternal nature of Jesus Christ.</note></term> to understand. For how shall wisdom enter into a malignant soul? <note>Wisdom 1:4</note> What could ever be devised more malignant than these men? They who, as it is written, turn their hearing away from the truth, and flow toward the fables of their own thoughts, so that the scriptural saying can rightly be applied to them: *Woe to you who prophesy from your own heart, and not from the mouth of the Lord.* <note>Ezekiel 13:3</note> For who, speaking from the mouth of the Lord, calls Jesus "accursed"? Yet some do this, insulting the dogmas of piety (as a certain prophet says) and perverting all that is right. We shall not be wrong to say of them: *O you who have abandoned the right paths to walk in the way of darkness.* <note>Proverbs 2:13</note>

But it is right for us to cry out toward heavenly teaching: *Turn away our eyes, lest they see vanity,* <note>Psalm 119:37</note> for the innovations of their impiety are truly vanity and nonsense. For the Son did not assert that he "kept the Father's word" because he possessed some other "word" within himself, nor did he ever affirm that he came to us bringing some sort of <term>pedagogue<note>original: "pædagogum." In antiquity, a slave who supervised a child; Cyril argues Christ isn't just an intermediary or teacher's aide to God.</note></term> along with him. Rather, he is the one who alone is in the Father according to nature, and who likewise has the Father in himself with nothing at all coming between them. He said: *I am in the Father and the Father is in me.* <note>John 14:10</note> He did not say some other "inner and innate word," but "I myself," he says, "am in the Father."

How then, one might ask, should we understand what he said to the Jews: *I keep the Father's word*? <note>John 8:55</note> The Savior was teaching the very stubborn Jewish people, and desiring to free them gradually from the observation of the Law, he frequently cried out: *I am the truth.* <note>John 14:6</note> This was as if to say: "O Jews, shake off the yoke of the Law, receive spiritual worship, cast far away shadows and figures, and follow the Truth who is now present." Thus did the Truth cry out. But they, having little faith, said: "If this man were from God, he would not break the Sabbath." Thus they accused him who knew no sin at all. Therefore, responding to these things (lest they be incited to fury if he had openly said how far he was from sin, claiming that such a thing belongs to God alone), he asserted more obscurely—since he was made man and placed under the Law—that he "kept the Father's word." He did this to show that he would say or do nothing that was outside the Father's will. For sin is committed through the transgression of the Law; but he, being God by nature, was far removed from every fault. Therefore, no one could rightly rebuke him who, though the author of the Law by nature, was made subject to the Law by his assumption of humanity.

15

Furthermore, he says he knows the Father, not simply as men do, because he is God; rather, because he is from the Father, he confirms that he knows the very nature of the Father. Thus, just as he knew the Father to be immutable, he suggests that he himself is also immutable, being from an immutable Father. Since he is immutable, he can in no way fall into sin. Therefore, the accusation of the Jews—who thought he was preaching against God the Father himself—was entirely empty and false. For he "keeps the word of the Father" and is naturally far from sin, being consubstantial with Him as a true Son.

But come, let us now turn to that which the Scripture introduces the Father saying to the Son: *From the womb before the morning star I begot you.* <note>original: "Ex utero ante luciferum genui te" - Psalm 110:3 (109:3 in the Vulgate). A key text for proving the eternal generation of the Son.</note> We should not understand that there is one "innate word" in the Father and another who is the "Son" just because the Father speaks these things to the Son. Instead, let us first know and carefully consider this: that the prophet, foretelling mysteries to us in the spirit, takes on the person of the Son, and thus asserts that he heard from the Father: *You are my Son.* <note>Psalm 2:7</note> Therefore, speech that is taken up according to human habit and capacity does not compel us to understand "two words." Rather, by attributing the dispensation of the language to our own customs, we—not without reason—adapt words of this kind of speech to the weakness of human nature. For we can neither express in words nor conceive in the mind divine mysteries; for divine reality surpasses both words and our intellect. Hence it happens that many things are understood not exactly as they are said, but as they befit the reality. Those who rightly deny these [heretical] things, when they hear that the Father "begets from the womb," do they understand it as a literal womb and the pains of labor? They would answer that "womb" in God signifies nothing other than the proper generation of the Son from Him. Therefore, let it be understood piously in that way, even if it is written in a human manner, and every deceptive sophistry will be dissolved.

But enough has been said on this for now; let us now rise up more ardently against the rest, and having set forth his argument, let us push back the flowing river of heresy with great force. 

"Unless," the opponent insists, "there is another, more internal 'Word' of God than the only-begotten Son (who is called the 'Word' by them only in imitation), then it will be necessary to admit that the Father is also the 'Word,' and ought to be called the 'Word,' because he is conceded to be consubstantial with his Son, who both is and is named the 'Word'." This is what he says.

But we say to this: there is no reason that compels the Father to be called the "Word" simply because he is consubstantial with His Word. For things that are of the same nature cannot be changed into one another, as if being contracted from a multitude or a duality into a unity. For even our father Adam was consubstantial with his son, yet he did not thereby "fall into" being the son, nor did the son "ascend" into the place of the father. Thus, while the Father is of the same substance as the Son, He retains His own property, just as the Son does. For he who is from the Father is understood to be the Son; but he who begot is called the Father. If consubstantiality forces you to confess that there is no distinction between consubstantial things, then what induced the Judge of all not to punish the Father for the Son, nor [the Son] by the Father...

He further maintains that sharing a "consubstantial" nature does not erase the distinct identities of Father and Son.</summary>

### TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND. <note>George of Trebizond (1395–1486) was a renowned Greek scholar and translator who brought many works of the Greek Church Fathers into Latin for Western readers.</note>

...from the son to take punishment for the father? The soul, he says, that has sinned, it shall die: nor shall the father take on the sin of his son. <note>This refers to Ezekiel 18:20, establishing the principle of individual identity.</note> You see that although a father is <term>consubstantial<note>Latin: *consubstantialis*. Having the same substance or essence. In this context, it means sharing the same "humanity" or "divinity."</note></term> with his son, nevertheless the things which one has sinned are not demanded of the other. Why, therefore, do you think that because the Word is consubstantial with God the Father, God the Father must also be called the "Word"? For God the Father is always the Father, and his Word—because he is the Word, therefore he is the Son—is always the Son; otherwise, the divine state would be understood to be in a worse condition than our own. Because the highest identity exists between the Father and the Son according to nature (for the Son is the most exquisite image and the very character of the Father's person <margin>John 14</margin>), he therefore said to his disciples: *He who sees me, sees also my Father.* If, therefore, because this is so, nothing shall prohibit calling the Father "Word" and "Son," and if the Son were understood to have ascended into the Father's place: let those words be attributed to him, so that he himself might say to the Father <margin>Psalm 109</margin>: "From the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you." <note>original Latin: "Ex utero ante luciferum genui te." A traditional Messianic prophecy from the Psalms used to describe the eternal generation of the Son.</note> If this were done, all things would be so confused that the most holy and consubstantial Trinity, which is always a Trinity, would be contracted into a single unit. And thus, that which properly belongs to each of the three persons would be destroyed by the reasoning of consubstantiality: and the identity of nature would overturn the distinction of persons—which is utterly absurd. The Father, therefore, because he is consubstantial with his Word, will not for that reason be the Word himself; but he will always be that which he is, immutably the Father. Furthermore, if every word is the word of someone—namely, of one who speaks with a tongue, or of one who thinks in his heart—but the Father were the Word because he is consubstantial with his Word, he would then be the Word of himself, or rather of no one, and thus would not be anything at all: for how can there be a Word unless it is the Word *of someone*? Therefore, though the Father is consubstantial with his Word, he never falls away into being the Word: but he will always be the Father, just as his Word is always the Son. Besides, the divine nature is always far removed from all change and alteration; how then shall the Father be changed into the Word? For he would not be the Father unless he preserved what he was. Therefore, if it is wicked to attribute change to the divine nature, the Father will never be changed into the Word, but will be immutably and always the Father.

Moreover, when the only-begotten Son of God wished to show himself as true God, and from true God <margin>John 16</margin>, he said: "All things that the Father has are mine." For of all things which naturally belong to the Father, since he is from him according to nature, the Son is the heir; he can never be the Father alone. <margin>That is to say, the Son can never be the Father.</margin> For that is the one thing that the Father is. But if the Son is the heir of all things that belong to the Father, he lacks nothing, even if he is never the Father. And just as he possesses all the good things of the Father, in the same way, all things that belong to the Son belong by nature to the Father, even though the Father can never be changed into the Word or the Son, but remains always that which he is: the Father. For in this way both Father and <margin>Ezekiel 18</margin> Son are understood to possess immutability. Finally, we are not ignorant that some were accused by God, the author of the Law, because they did not distinguish between the holy and the profane. For there is a great difference,

<column-break/>

and a contradiction between these things to all who judge correctly. But if it were possible for a consubstantial nature to be confused within itself <margin>If the Father is the Son, the Father would never exist.</margin>, so that the properties of individuals and <term>hypostases<note>Latin: *hypostasis*. The distinct, individual subsistence of a person, used here to distinguish the Father from the Son within the same divine nature.</note></term> passed to other hypostases of the same genus or species, what reasoning could distinguish the holy from the profane? If no difference between individuals—which makes a thing "this" or "that"—is found because of the identity of substance, then all things would be confused among themselves (our knowledge of individual things having been taken away): so that Judas the traitor would be Peter or Paul; and Peter or Paul, in turn, would be Judas the traitor, since they are of the same nature. But if it is more mad than any madness to say this—that individuals of the same genus or species and nature do not lose their individual and proper differences by which they are "this" and "that" simply because they share the same nature—then no human reason will ever be so strong as to force the Word to be and to be called "God the Father," simply because he is piously and truly believed to be consubstantial with his Word. For the Father remains always the Father; he can never lose the property by which he is who he is. We will never concede that the Father has nothing "proper" to himself because of the identity of substance; nor, because this is the case, will he have any more than the Son. The Son, since he is properly from the Father, possessing the immutability and eternity of the begetter, preserves his own sonship in such a way that he cannot be changed into the Father, just as the Father cannot be changed into the Son. But they say as a <margin>Quibble.</margin> <note>original: "Cauillus"</note>: "You insult us as if we were heretics, we who say the innate and interior Word of God is something other than the Son, when you hear him cry out with a great voice: 'I know the Father, and I keep his word.'" <margin>John 8</margin> For if it is necessary that the one who keeps be different from that which is kept, and these things can never coincide, you cannot deny that the Son of God is one thing, and his Word another. But tell us, I pray, if it were as you <margin>Refutation.</margin> <note>original: "Confutatio"</note> contend: whether that "interior word," which you imagine to exist in God the Father out of your ignorance, subsists or not? For if it subsists, since it would be understood to exist in its own hypostasis, there would not be one Son, but two. But if it does not subsist, since there is nothing between the Son and the Father that separates one from the other: how will the Son be third from the Father, if he is not connected immediately to the Father as a Son? For since they contend that the innate and interior Word exists in the Father for this reason, how do they want the Son to [keep?] the will of the Father? For the name of the Father is so related to the Son that it allows nothing at all to come between them. But if, according to their foolish opinion, some "interior word" explanatory of the Father's counsel is between the Father and the Son, and separates the Son from the Father like some sort of material barrier: clearly the counsel of God and the "word" explaining that counsel would be understood to subsist as their own hypostases; then the Father would no longer be the Father, nor would the Son retain the property of a Son. But if it does not subsist, the Son will be immediately in the Father: where then does that "interior word" go? Or what place would the counsel of God follow, if it is something other than the Son? Furthermore, that the holy and adorable Trinity is consubstantial...

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 17, where Cyril of Alexandria refutes opponents who distinguish between the "internal word" of God and the person of the Son.
