# SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.

...we believe rightly, even if the heretics are burst asunder <note>original: "disrumpantur"—a strong expression of the heretics' frustration or spiritual ruin.</note>.

<margin>Whatever things are **consubstantial** <note>original: "consubstantialia"—sharing the same essence or substance. This is the core doctrine of the Trinity.</note>, they agree in one with respect to the nature of all things. Therefore, if—as the rashness of some proclaims—there is some other word existing within the Father besides the Son, then the Son also will contain some other internal word within himself. For he is the most exquisite image of the Father and the "character of his <term>hypostasis</term>," <note>Hypostasis: the distinct person or individual reality of the Father. This quote is from Hebrews 1:3.</note> as it is written. But the Holy Spirit will likewise have such an internal word. Thus, for us, the Trinity will be doubled, and the divine composition will not create by nature—which is far absurd and wicked to think: for in a simple substance, nothing else can exist besides itself. Therefore, the holy and consubstantial Trinity is joined to itself immediately, with nothing mediating. 

That which is especially to be held is that whenever Divine Scripture places **articles** <note>Cyril is discussing a technical point of Greek grammar: the use of the definite article "the" (ho). He argues that "The Word" (ho logos) refers to a specific, unique person, not just a general concept.</note> before names according to the usage of the Greek language, it then signifies both a unity and that which alone is properly and truly called such a thing. However, when the article is not added, it designates all things generally. For example: "Many are called gods" <note>Referencing Psalm 82:6 or 1 Corinthians 8:5.</note>; but when the Greek language says "the God" with the article, then only the true God is designated. When "god" is uttered without the article, one who is called to this by grace is understood. So when "man" is said without the article, any person is designated; but when the article is added, it denotes a unique and singular man. Therefore we see "the Son of Man," with the article prefixed to both names, uttered by our Savior when he wishes to signify himself alone from the infinite multitude of men. 

Since these things are so, let them say, I pray: how is it to be understood, "In the beginning was **the Word**," since the article is added to this noun, "Word"? For a speech with an article cannot refer except to the one Word, which properly and truly was in the beginning. Why, therefore, do they pointlessly stretch things, bringing in another word for us, so that they may drive the Son away from the dignity and nature of the Father? Furthermore, if the only-begotten Son of God is and is called "the Word" for this reason—namely that (as they say) he, receiving an internal word, is formed according to it—why did he not say to the disciples: "I and the Father's word are one," or "He who sees me, sees also the Father's word"? Since he did not say so, but having surpassed all things, he compares himself in identity to the Father alone, it is surely impious to believe the Son is confirmed or taught by some other word, when he is joined to his Begetter by consubstantiality without any medium. 

But they say: "We believe there is another Son besides the internal and innate word, not persuaded by our own reasons, but by the authority of Scripture." For when we hear the Son saying to the Father, "Father, glorify your Son," and we see the Father in turn responding, "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again," <note>John 12:28.</note> is it not necessary to confess that the Father responds to the Son through a "word"? How then is that through which the Father responds to the Son not a "word" other than the Son? This does not seem so much a matter of wonder to me as a matter of weeping. For certainly those who invent these things are to be mourned. And that prophetic saying must be said over them: "Do not weep for the dead, nor mourn him; weep and mourn for..." <note>Jeremiah 22:10.</note></margin>

<column-break/>

...him <margin>Refutation of their reasoning.</margin> who dares to say such things of the Only-Begotten. For what more miserable thing can be devised for those who, when they ought to submit divine things to our minds—not in a dead way, but to understand them more deeply and sublimely (even if they are spoken in human custom)—have thought that the voice, which not only the Savior but also the multitude of disciples heard, was the "internal word" of the Father? For a bodily voice and sound is usually moved through the air from the lips or some other strike to move the sense of hearing. But the counsel of the Father, which is turned into his mind by an ineffable voice, the Son alone knows, who is naturally in the Father himself as his Wisdom. 

Yet it is entirely credible that God uses a voice formed by a strike of air. For one must not be ignorant that the nature of the Creator is above every creature. <margin>John 12.</margin> Although the Lord and our Savior himself affirmed that that was not the voice of God the Father, nor did he assert that he had need of it; for he did not hear the Father's voice, nor did he signify it was made for his sake, but for theirs: "This voice," he said, "was not made for my sake, but for yours." <note>John 12:30.</note> But if God the Father works all things through him, he also worked that voice through him. Indeed, he himself was that voice by which he opens the will of the Begetter—which he knows as the Son—not to himself, but to the disciples, so that they may be more easily brought to faith. 

<margin>Refutation.</margin> Furthermore, if the Son needs some innate word to learn the Father's will through it, what did he mean by saying, "Christ is the power of God and the **Wisdom** of God"? <note>1 Corinthians 1:24.</note> <margin>1 Corinthians 1.</margin> For how will the Son be the Wisdom of the Father if he himself lacks wisdom and learns what he does not know from another, or through something else? Or how <margin>1 Corinthians 2.</margin> will it not necessarily follow that the Wisdom of the Father is not perfect in the Father himself? Then, if the Son is the Father's Wisdom, how do they understand the Father's counsel to be something else besides the Son—unless perhaps they dare to affirm that the Father's counsel is in Wisdom? All of which are both said and thought impiously. Therefore, not taught by another or through another, the Son knows the Father's counsel, but since he is himself the **Word, Wisdom, and Counsel**, he searches even the very depths of God the Father, just as we are not ignorant that it is written concerning the Holy Spirit.

<margin>Hebrews 2. <note>Actually Hebrews 1:3.</note></margin> Furthermore, the Scriptures call the Son the image and character of the Father: "And he who sees me, sees also the Father," says the Savior. <margin>1 Corinthians 2.</margin> Therefore, having such identity with the Father, if he does not know the things that are the Father's through himself, but learns them as if from another narrating them, it will not <margin>1 Corinthians 2.</margin> be incongruous if someone also affirms that the Father needs an interpreter so that he might know the things that are hidden in the Son. For since he is entirely like his Son, he will be held by the same ignorance as the Son. Thus the divine nature would be susceptible to ignorance. 

Therefore, this impious heresy must be fled, fled with all one's strength, especially since the Spirit is written by the Apostle to search all things, even the depths of God. "For as no man," he says, "knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him; so also the things of God no one knows except the Spirit of God, who is in him." <note>1 Corinthians 2:11.</note> Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit, who searches the depths of God, is not only the Father's but also the Son's: how will the Son, who has the Spirit naturally in himself, be ignorant of anything that belongs to the Father? Therefore, it is not rightly said that the Father's will is [learned] by the Son from another or through another...

<summary>Cyril argues that the Son and the Word are the same unique person, using Greek grammar and the title "Wisdom" to prove the Son's perfect knowledge of the Father. He rejects the idea that a "voice" from heaven or an "internal word" acts as a teacher to the Son, which would imply divine ignorance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the nature of the Word (Logos). Cyril is refuting those who claim the Son is a "secondary" word or a created being, asserting instead that the Son is the Wisdom of God and the Creator of all things.</meta>

# TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.
<meta>catchword: I</meta>

...to be signified by the Son. For what need is there to devise another internal word, when He Himself is Wisdom in His own right, and possesses the Spirit who searches all things in common with the Father? Furthermore, let those who attempt to debase the substance of the **only-begotten** <note>original: "unigeniti"—referring to Jesus as the unique Son of God.</note> tell us this, since they claim He does not know the Father's will by Himself, but uses a word (I know not what kind) as a teacher and instructor: does that word, which they call "internal" (assuming it exists in its own right), have equality with the Son, or is it less or greater? For if they say it is less, this impiety ascends to the Father Himself. For there would be something in Him that is different from Him and less than Him. But if they contend it is greater than the Son, they sin against the Father in two ways. First, He would be found to have begotten a Son who is lesser than His own substance; and second, He Himself would appear lesser than His own word, while being **consubstantial** <note>original: "consubstantialis"—sharing the same divine essence.</note> with His Son, whom they call lesser than that inferior word. If, fleeing these conclusions, they affirm that this word is equal in substance to the Son, their whole argument immediately collapses. For how, if they are equal by nature, is one supposedly ignorant by nature and taught by the other, who is supposedly knowledgeable by nature? Thus, the falsehood of their opinion appears on every side. It is therefore impious to imagine anything as a "middle ground" between the Father and the Son; rather, it is pious to believe that the Son Himself is the Word of the Father, who was in the beginning, in which Word Paul says all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom are hidden.

<margin>Colossians 3 <note>The text likely refers to Colossians 2:3, which mentions the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.</note></margin>
But if this is so (for Paul does not lie), how does He need to be taught by another? Or in whom shall we say perfect knowledge and wisdom reside, if He who is Wisdom becomes wise through another's teaching? Or how shall He take for Himself the name of true and proper Wisdom if He learns from elsewhere? Therefore, one must not attend to the trifles of men, but to the teaching of the Holy Spirit. Wherefore, since the Holy Spirit has taught us through Paul that the treasures of knowledge and wisdom are hidden in the Son, we must believe that He does not learn from another, but since He is in the Father, He knows all things of the Father naturally, as His perfect wisdom.

### That the Son is the Creator according to nature, and not as a servant alongside the Father, because He is of His substance. CHAPTER V.

<margin>
Isaiah 44.
Jeremiah 2.
</margin>
All things were made through Him, and without Him was made nothing. When the blessed Evangelist had briefly overturned the various arguments of the impious heresies and handed down to us the precise doctrine concerning the only-begotten, he now proceeds to untie another snare of the devil, which, arising from ancient error, has deceived many, bound them, and finally led them down to the underworld. Since, therefore, the pagan world, clinging to the wisdom of this world and possessing the spirit of the prince of this age, despised the truth and worshipped inanimate idols—and one would say to a piece of wood, "You are my god," and another to a stone, "You brought me forth"—and some, though they seemed better than the masses, attributed the glory of the deity to the sky and the elements; it was necessary for John, the supreme Theologian of truth, to blunt their deceptions and open the right path for those paying attention. He thought it necessary to show with a loud voice that He is the Creator by nature, saying: All things were

<column-break/>

produced through the **only-begotten**, and without Him nothing at all was made. Since he judges that creatures were made by Him, he clearly teaches everyone that He is distinct from the things He created, by whose ineffable power all things were brought from nothingness into being. For thus, by the beauty of the creatures, we recognize the Maker by whom all things were made and by whom they are preserved. Thus we believe these words were written by the Evangelist against the pagans. Truly, because the false opinion of the heretics is also easily refuted from this, it is not irrelevant to write something against them as well. "All things," he says, "were made through Him, and without Him was made nothing." For these words also attribute the majesty of the Deity to the only-begotten Son of God, so that they may show that all things are naturally and truly in Him which are said to be in God the Father. For this title does not come to Him from the outside through grace, as it does to men, according to that saying: "I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High." For if all things were made through Him, He cannot be numbered together with all things. For when "all things" is said, there is nothing that is not contained within that "all." Surely Paul is also found to have understood "all things" in this way. For when he said that all things were subjected under the feet of our Savior, he immediately added: "For in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing that is not subject to him." Therefore, since we believe all things were made through the Son, we in no way understand Him to be one of those "all things," but separating Him from the number of all things, and placing Him far apart from the nature of creatures, we confess that He is nothing other than God from God by nature. For what can be found between God and the creature, so that something else might be understood besides the two? Or in what substance shall we place the Son, if He exceeds the nature of creatures to an infinite degree, as the Creator? For all things were made through Him, as through the power and wisdom of God the Father, which is not in God as a certain quality (as it is in men), but truly subsists through itself, although it proceeds from the Father in an ineffable mode of generation. For thus the Wisdom and Power of the Father is truly believed to be the Son. Yet He is not to be believed as a servant of another's will, nor as if He receives strength from another by which He is able to create, simply because all things that exist are said to be made through Him. On the contrary, since He is the very Power of the Father, just as He is the only-begotten Son, He created the universe together with the Father and the Holy Spirit: for all things are from the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. Nor do we understand the Son to be with the Father in creating because the Father is unable to create; but because, on account of His immutability and the identity of His <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substantiæ"—The underlying reality or essence of God.</note>, He is joined to Him by nature. It is as if someone, in smelling the scent that comes from a certain flower, in no way separates the action of the scent from the flower itself, from which the scent is naturally poured out. I am not unaware that the comparison of the example is small; but since the divine nature surpasses all things, it is necessary for us, according to our strength, not to despise the likenesses of even the smallest things. For how else do we rightly understand that saying: "My Father works even until now, and I work"?

1 Corinthians 15.
Romans 11.
John 5.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues Cyril’s argument that the Son is not a separate or inferior being to the Father. He focuses on the "co-operation" of the Trinity, arguing that when one person of the Trinity acts, they all act in unity, refuting the Arian claim that the Son is merely a "minister" or "servant" to the Father.</meta>

### ST. CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.

"I work." <note>original: "ego operor." A reference to John 5:17, where Jesus says, "My Father is working until now, and I work."</note> For it must not be understood that the Father works separately and by Himself, or that the Son works in turn while the Father remains at rest. For in that case, there would seem to be two creators and not one, the Father and the Son. Furthermore, if this were so, it would not be necessary for the Son to be always in the Father, and the Father likewise in the Son; thus that saying would be found false: <margin>John 14</margin> *I am in the Father and the Father is in me.* For we confess that the Son is in the Father—and the Father in the Son—not only according to an identity of substance, as if the Son were merely an "imprint" <note>original: "character." Referring to Hebrews 1:3, the "exact representation" or "stamp" of God's being.</note> and the Father merely the "original model," but also that the Son shines forth from the substance of the Father. He exists within that substance and from it, subsisting also in His own **hypostasis** <term>hypostasis</term><note>A technical theological term referring to an individual person or distinct reality within the Trinity. While they share one essence, they are three distinct "hypostases."</note>. We understand the Father to be likewise united by nature to the Son as one who is <term>consubstantial</term><note>Having the exact same essence or being; "of one substance."</note>, yet distinguished only by the fact that He is the Father. For the Father is the Father, even though He is naturally in the Son—just as we grant that the sun is in its own brilliance. The Son is the same: although He is and was in the Father, He is distinguished from the Father by no other reason than the fact that He is the Son. Thus, the Father is truly the Father and is understood as such, and the Son likewise is truly the Son. So too, when the Holy Spirit is mentioned, the number of the Trinity is gathered back into one and the same deity. For how else could God be understood as one, if the individual persons of the Trinity were to deviate into such entirely separate properties that each was named "God" while being wholly disconnected from a natural bond and a substantial relationship? 

Therefore, according to the reason by which the individual persons of the deity subsist in themselves, let us understand that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit exist without confusing the distinction of persons (that is, of names). We preserve for each that which He truly is and is called. Believing in this way, we confess that the Trinity is naturally contained in one deity, rejecting every other distinction besides that of the names—that is, the persons. For the Son is called the <margin>Wisdom.</margin> Word, the Wisdom, the Splendor, the Imprint, and the Power of the Father. He is called "Word" and "Wisdom" because He is from the Intellect immediately and indivisibly, and because of the (so to speak) reciprocal mutual indwelling <note>original: "reciprocam immissionem." In later theology, this is called *perichoresis*, the mutual indwelling of the three persons of the Trinity.</note> of these things: for the Mind and Intellect are seen in the Word, if it is Wisdom, and the Word and Wisdom are in turn seen in the <margin>Power.</margin> Intellect. Nothing stands between them or mediates to separate one from the other. He is called "Power" because He exists indivisibly in the one who possesses Him by nature; nor can Power be separated from Him, like an "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the essence of the thing. Cyril argues the Son's power is essential, not accidental.</note> that could leave without the subject being destroyed. He is called the <margin>Imprint</margin> "Imprint" because He is always naturally joined to, and cannot be separated from, that substance of which He is the imprint. For these reasons, since one is naturally and necessarily in the other, when the Father works, then the Son also works as His natural, substantial, and subsisting Power. Similarly, when the Son works, the Father is in the Son, just as fire always co-operates with its own heat which is in it. Therefore, it is clear that the thoughts of the heretics are false—those who impudently contend that the Son learns from another and creates in the place of a "minister" <note>The Arians argued the Son was an inferior assistant to the Father, rather than an equal creator.</note>, because all things are said to have been made through Him. I, however, cannot marvel enough at their impudence. For whatever

<column-break/>

appears to be said in a humble way by the Scripture regarding the Only-begotten, they hunt for all these things with great zeal from every side, and from every side they collect poisons for their own perdition. But those passages in which the Son is most clearly placed in the glory of the Father, they suppress with a strange silence, so that they seem to intend nothing else than to trample upon the majesty of the Son. For when they hear that all things were made through Him, they craftily cling to the word "ministry," dreaming that He is a servant instead of a free man, and a worshiper instead of the Lord. Yet immediately they see the Evangelist has added: *Because without Him nothing was made,* they are unable to be raised to more sublime thoughts. For since God the Father cannot create in any other way than through His own Son, who is His Power and Wisdom, for that reason the Evangelist asserts that absolutely nothing was made without the Word. For this reason also, the Only-begotten both is and is called the "glory of the Father"; for the Creator Father is glorified through the Son, working all things and leading them from non-existence into being. 

But regarding this Gospel passage, *because without Him nothing was made,* that verse from Genesis can rightly be brought forward: <margin>Genesis.</margin> *Let us make man in our image and likeness.* For He does not command, nor does He say to Him as if to a servant or minister: "Make man." Rather, He speaks and deliberates as if with one who is indivisibly and naturally joined to Him (I shall speak here in human terms). The Father does not precede the Son’s knowledge when He understands something, but is always manifest, just as the Word is indivisibly impressed and implanted in the Mind. However, these examples and analogies must be believed to be infinitely surpassed by divine realities. We say that the Father co-operates with the Son, not understanding two separate beings (lest we introduce two gods), nor contracting two persons into one (lest the Father be forced into the Son, or the Son into the Father). Rather, we mean it in the way that splendor co-operates with the light from which it shines. For in this and similar things, a distinction is understood in that the splendor shines *from* that which it indivisibly proceeds *from*. Yet both are one and the same in nature, and one cannot exist without the other. Nevertheless, He exceeds the likenesses of creatures, for He has no exact likeness among created things. Therefore, we use examples to declare what we wish to say, not as a perfect image of the Trinity. 

If they think that because it is written "through Him," the Son is taken by the Father into the position of a minister, and therefore falls away from a natural equality with the Father, what will they say of the Father Himself? For the particle "through" <note>original: "per."</note> is also applied to Him by the Scriptures: <margin>1 Cor. 1 / Eph. 1</margin> *God is faithful, through whom you were called.* And again: *Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God.* And elsewhere: *Therefore he is not a servant, but a son.* Paul says: *If a son by nature, then an heir through God.* <margin>Galat. 4</margin> For all these things refer to the person of the Father, and no one is so insane as to reduce the Father to the rank of a minister because of the particle "through." For divine Scripture often uses words in an inexact way <note>original: "abusionis modo." A rhetorical term (catachresis) where a word is used slightly outside its strict definition to describe something transcendent.</note> so that it may properly signify grand things to words, as much as is possible for a human. To these things must be added the fact that the glory of the Lord...

->GEORGIO TRAPEZONTIO INTERPRETE.<-
<note>original: "Translated by George of Trebizond." George (1395–1486) was a Greek scholar and philosopher who translated many patristic Greek works into Latin during the Renaissance.</note>

...obscures the word: for almost no power of words is so great that it can exquisitely express the ineffable glory of God. We ought not, therefore, to be troubled by the lowliness of words, when we know and piously believe that every sharpness of the mind grows dull in explaining divine matters.

<margin>That the Son is life by nature, and therefore not created, but of the substance of God and the Father.</margin>

### CHAPTER VI.

(*That which was made, in him was life.*) <note>original: "Quod factum est, in ipso uita erat." This refers to John 1:3-4. Cyril follows a specific punctuation common in the early Church where "That which was made" is linked to the phrase "in him was life."</note> Thus far the Evangelist speaks most exquisitely concerning the Word of God: so that while he diligently explains all things that belong to His nature, he may both deter the heretics <note>Likely referring to the Arians, who believed the Son was a created being rather than eternally God.</note> and confirm those who believe rightly—not by human wisdom or the strength of eloquence, but by the power of the Spirit. Since he has just shown Him to be the creator of all things, because He brought all things from non-existence into being, and *without Him nothing was made*: now, because the creature contains no power within its own nature to endure, but He Himself is, as it were, mixed with all things as their life, and preserves them in their own natural condition, for that reason he proclaims: *that which was made, in Him was life.* He says that not only were all things made through Him, but whatever things were made, the only-begotten Son of God—the principle and substance of all things, both visible and invisible—was the life within them. For since He is life by nature, He most kindly and in various ways bestows both being and living and moving upon things. This is not sent into individual things (which differ by nature) in a divisible or changeable way; rather, since He Himself is the one life of all, penetrating all things, He is received by individuals as far as is possible and fitting. Yet the creature itself, by the ineffable wisdom and power of the creator, is varied and changed within itself. And because that which is produced from nothing is corruptible, and all things that have begun hasten toward their end (for only the divine nature is without beginning and end), He attributed a kind of perpetuity to things as if by a certain art. For He devised successions and changes of things into one another, by which He made the individual species of things perpetual; and this is also what is written concerning plants: *Whose seed is in itself upon the earth,* <note>Genesis 1:11</note> which we see happen every year by the ineffable will of the Creator. Therefore, there was life in all things, as it is said. But what will the insanity of the heretics say to this, when they hear the Evangelical voice of the Holy Spirit, that in all created things the Word of God, who is in the beginning, was life? Will they even now dare to affirm that the Son is not from the substance of God the Father, but is something made and created? And how shall they not be justly condemned on the charge of ignorance? For if the Word of God, being life by nature, offers living to all things by the participation of Himself, He is certainly something other than those things which are believed to live by His presence. But if He is something other than what a creature is by nature, how shall He, who is above all things, not be God? If you contend that He is both created and yet do not deny that He is the life of things: since He is one of the creatures according to you, He Himself would be understood to have life by the participation of Himself. Since this is absurd, it is necessary that the God the Son, who is shared, be of a different nature than those who share in Him. Therefore He is not created, but exists in creatures as life by nature: which from what follows will appear more

<column-break/>

evident. For if the Son is not from the substance of the Father, but made, as they say, and created, how does He Himself give life to all things? Or how does Paul attribute this to God as something primary, when he calls Him the one who gives life? <note>1 Timothy 6:13</note> For if the Son, though He be created, gives life to all things, then the creature gives life to itself; why then should there be nothing primary in God beyond the creature? The creature would not even need God for its existence, since it would bring life to itself no less than God does; but the creature always stands in need of the Creator. Therefore, the Son of God is not to be placed among the creatures, since He is, and is understood to be, life through Himself. Furthermore, admiring the dignity of the divine nature, the Psalmist sang: *For with you is the fountain of life.* <note>Psalm 36:9</note> If, therefore, the Son, who they say is a creature, gives life to those things which were made, and as one who gives life is life according to nature, then the Psalmist in vain attributed the "fountain of life" to God alone as something primary. Indeed, the Son also—who according to them is numbered among the creatures—would be the fountain of life because He gives life. But God alone is the fountain of life; therefore the Son is life by nature, as God from God, and life from life. To this, if the Son were life according to nature and yet not from the substance of God the Father (as they blasphemously say) but a creature, then the nature of a creature would be life—if not in act, then at least in potential. For even if not every creature is life yet, because some creature is life, it would not be foreign to the nature of a creature that it could be life. Thus, being life would be something common to both God and the creature. Why then does the Son boast in vain, saying: *I am the life*? <note>John 14:6</note> when he ought rather to have said: "I and you together are the life." But since He did not say so, but attributed life to Himself as His own proper good, it is manifest that He does not number Himself among the creatures, but joins Himself to the nature of God the Father, which alone is life by nature. It follows that that which *participates* in life cannot properly be called life itself; for that which is shared is one thing, and the one who participates in it is another. If, therefore, the Son is shared by the creature as life, He will be something other than those who participate in life; but those participating are creatures: therefore He Himself is not created, nor does He stand in need of life from another. Thus He must be granted to be God who gives life, and <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "consubstantialis." From the Greek 'homoousios,' meaning having the same essence or being as the Father.</note> with the Father. For in this way we shall worship one God, nor shall we worship any other than He who is. Furthermore, when we diligently consider the nature of all things, we behold God and the creature, and nothing else beyond these: for whatever is not God by nature, that certainly is created; and again, whatever is denied to be a creature, that certainly is God. Since, therefore, we have divided these things most excellently, let them answer, I pray: how can the Son give life as life itself, when that is proper to the divine nature alone? If He can be life even though He is created, then "life" will also be predicated of the other member of our division [the creature], and all things will be life according to nature. What need then is there for the participation of the Son, or what more will the creature possess by this participation, if it is life through its own nature? But every creature necessarily needs the participation of the life which is the Son. Therefore nothing created is life according to nature, but only the Son is, and the Father is likewise consubstantial. Furthermore, since the Son is life, He is either a creature...

Cyril argues that if the Son were a creature, He would need to receive life rather than being the "fountain of life" Himself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument that the Son (the Word) is not a created being but is divine by nature. The previous page ended with a discussion on the Word being "life" itself; this page extends that logic to the concept of "light."</meta>

<page-num>26</page-num>
<header>ST. CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.</header>

<columns>
<column-break/>
<margin>John 6.</margin>
...[the Son] is either a creature, or he is not a creature, but true God. If the first is true, it is falsely said of him: "I am the bread of life, who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world." <note>original: *ego sum panis uitæ...* from John 6:35/51.</note> For a creature does not have life through itself; rather, that which is life does not need to participate in life. But if he is truly not a creature, he will possess that good which is beyond creatures: namely, to be life according to his very nature. It is characteristic of a creature to stand in need of life, being made alive by participating in it. Furthermore, if the Son is numbered among creatures even though he is life by nature, why does the Psalmist assert that the heavens grow old like a garment? 
<margin>Psalm 101.</margin>
For concerning the Son he says: "But you are the same, and your years shall not fail." <note>original: *Tu autem idem ipse es...* referring to Psalm 102:27 (101 in the Vulgate). Cyril argues that if the Son were a creature, he would be subject to decay like the rest of the universe.</note> For either he himself will fail and be corrupted just as we are, and thus he is not life itself; or, if he is a creature and yet is life itself, then the creaturely state would be perpetual and incorruptible. But he himself always remains in the same state, while the creature fails. Therefore, he is not created; but since he is life by nature, he gives life to all things that stand in need of life. It follows that nothing participates in itself; however, every creature participates in the Son as life. Therefore, the Son is not a creature, nor is the creature life itself. Finally, it is one thing to give life, and another to be made alive, just as acting is different from being acted upon. The Son gives life, but the creature is made alive. Therefore, the Son is something other than a creature, since that which acts and that which is acted upon cannot be the same thing.

->That the Son is light by nature: and therefore not<-
->created from the substance of God the Father.<-
### CHAPTER VII.
<margin>A</margin>
**And the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light.** <note>John 1:4-8. Cyril uses these verses to distinguish between Christ, who is the source of light, and John the Baptist, who is merely a witness to it.</note> Through these words, the Evangelist demonstrates to us that the Son is God by nature and the substantial heir of the Father’s goods. For he has already said that his nature is life itself, and that all things which are created are given life and preserved by him, since whatever was made was "life" in the Word. But because man on earth is a rational animal, capable of mind and discipline and participating in the wisdom of God, the Evangelist necessarily shows the Son to be the giver of human reason and wisdom through these words. This is done so that God the Father may be more easily understood to be "all in all" through the Son. He is life in those things that need life, and again, he is light and life in those things that need both light and life. Therefore, he proclaims with a great voice: **"And the life was the light of men."** Thus, the Son of God, who gives life to the universe and who is the life in all things, also illuminates the rational animal. To those capable of understanding, he grants intellect, so that what is said of the creature may appear true from every side: "For what do you have that you did not receive?" <note>original: *quid enim habes, quod nō accepisti?* from 1 Corinthians 4:7.</note> 
<margin>1 Corinthians 4.</margin>
For there is nothing that a creature possesses from itself; rather, it obtains both its being and its particular way of being through the bounty of God. But again, it was proper that this was written concerning life, so that the eternity of the Word might fall like a sharp axe upon the false thoughts of the heretics <note>Likely referring to the Arians, who claimed the Son was created "from nothing."</note> who, openly resisting all the scriptures, invent the idea that the Son of God was produced from nothing. But concerning the eternity of the Word,

<column-break/>

<page-num>27</page-num>
we have written briefly in the preceding sections, and more extensively in the book we have called the *Thesaurus*. <note>Cyril’s *Thesaurus de sancta et consubstantiali Trinitate*, a major work defending the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit.</note>
<margin>Cyril's book which is called the *Thesaurus*.</margin>
Therefore, let us speak as God opens our mouths on the subject at hand, which we think will be not entirely useless to those present and those to come. If the Son is not God by nature, nor the fruit of the Father's substance; if, moreover, he is not the true light who shone forth from the true light, but was produced from the outside (as some affirm) and numbered among creatures: how does he himself illuminate creatures, and how are creatures illuminated by him? Is not that which illuminates different from that which is illuminated? I certainly think so. For if they were seen to be the same in substance and reason, whatever is found separately in one of them would also be found joined in the other. Thus, that which needs light would itself be light, 
<margin>B</margin>
and light itself would indiscriminately both illuminate and be illuminated. No one of sound mind would grant that such a confusion of things is true. For the things that have been said are demonstrated by reason to be distinct, since that which illuminates by itself is one nature, and that which is illuminated is another. Therefore, since the Son has shone forth as true light from true light, he shall not be numbered among creatures, but is rightly believed to be consubstantial <note>original: *cōsubstantialis*, meaning "of the same substance," the key term from the Nicene Creed (homoousios) used to define Christ's divinity.</note> with the Father. Perhaps it is not difficult to apply what was just said about life—by which we demonstrated that those things which participate in life are different from life itself—to the subject of light. Therefore, lest sloth should seem to have removed us from serving the readers, we will try to transfer those arguments briefly to this passage. For just as life is something other than those things capable of receiving life, so also the "light of men" 
<margin>C</margin>
both is and is called something other than those things which, while being capable of receiving light, participate in it. This is confirmed by the following explanation: if the Word is light in creatures by nature, shining by the participation of himself, he is surely of a different nature than those things which are illuminated. Since, therefore, he is something other than a creature, how is he not God? Furthermore, if the Son is light by nature and illuminates creatures who lack light, and yet he is created (as they say), we would first understand him to be a specific "something"; then, since he would be from the number of creatures (whose nature it is to be illuminated by the participation of light), he would be, in respect to himself, both the participant and the participated. Since this is utterly impossible, it is necessary to confess that the Word of God is not created, but is God and light by nature. Moreover, if the Son illuminates 
<margin>D</margin>
creatures from the substance of God the Father, shall we find anything greater in the divine nature than in a created thing? Or how did the Psalmist sing of God, "In your light we shall see light"? <note>original: *in luce tua uidebimus lucem* from Psalm 36:9 (35 in the Vulgate).</note> 
<margin>Psalm 35.</margin>
For if, according to them, the Son is a creature and yet illuminates all things, the creature would not need the light of the Creator. These things are entirely absurd. Therefore, the Son is not a creature, but true God and light by nature, just as God the Father is. It follows that if the Son is the light of God the Father, according to the verse "In your light we shall see light," and "Send out your light and your truth," <note>original: *emitte lucem tuam* from Psalm 43:3.</note> and yet he is numbered among creatures, what will prevent all created things from being called the light of God the Father? For if the Son is light even though he is a creature, then surely this would apply to every creature in common...

<summary>Cyril argues that the Son (the Word) must be God by nature because He is the source of life and light, whereas creatures are merely recipients of these gifts. He emphasizes the logical impossibility of a created being acting as the universal source of divinity for other creatures.</summary>

Having previously established that the Son is "Life" by nature rather than by participation, the text now applies the same logic to the concept of "Light." It argues that if the Son were a creature, he could not be the source of light for others.</meta>

<columns>
...otherwise, light could be preached as something held in common by all. But no one will deny that this is false; for it is attributed to the Son alone that he both is, and is called, the light of God the Father. Therefore, the Son is not a creature, but God from God, and light from light, <note>original: "deus de deo, & lux de luce" – phrases famously used in the Nicene Creed to define Christ's divinity.</note> who illuminates all creatures through himself. Furthermore, if the Son were both a light by nature and a creature, how is it that he alone is the Light and called such? 
<margin>John 1.</margin>
For it is written of the Baptist: "He was not the light." <note>John 1:8.</note> And yet, both the Baptist and all other creatures could rightly be called light by nature if being "light" was simply a quality of being a "creature"; for whatever belongs to a creature as a creature must be common to all creatures. But it is denied that John was the light. The Son of God, however, is the Light; therefore, he shall by no means be numbered among creatures. To this we add: if the Son is Light because he is a creature, then every creature could be light, even if it is not yet light in actual practice. But if being light were common to all, why does the Son boast in vain, saying, 
<margin>John 8.</margin>
"I am the light," <note>John 8:12.</note> when instead he should have said, "I and you are the light"? Truly, since it is not so, but he calls himself alone the Light—attributing this to himself as his own proper good—it is manifest that he does not number himself among creatures, but joins himself to the nature of the Father, which alone is Light by nature. 

It must also be noted that the <term>participant</term> <note>original: "participans" – one who shares in or receives a quality from another.</note> is one thing, and the <term>participated</term> <note>original: "participatum" – the source or quality that is being shared.</note> is another. Therefore, that which participates in light cannot properly be Light itself. The Son, however, is participated in by creatures as Light; he is therefore not a creature, nor does he stand in need of light as creatures do. Rather, he is the God by whom the universe is illuminated, and he does not fall away from the <term>substance</term> <note>The essential "stuff" or being of God.</note> of the Father. In this way, we shall worship one God, believing that one nature is the Light. 

Furthermore, considering the nature of all things, we behold God and the creature, and nothing else beyond these. Since this division of things is the most accurate, let those who drive the Son far from the Father's nature say, I pray, how he joins himself to those natures, when such a thing belongs to the divine nature alone? For if the Son is both a creature and light, then every creature will be light. Thus, "light" would be predicated equally of both God and creatures. What need would there be, then, for a "participation" in the Son or in the light? What greater thing would a creature gain from this participation, since the creature would appear to be light in no different way than the Son? But the creature *does* need light, since it does not have it from itself. Therefore the Son, who is Light by nature and who illuminates creatures, is true God, not a creature. 

To this, we ask: is the Son—who is Light by nature—a creature according to the logic of his substance (as they contend), or is he not? If the first is true, then he spoke falsely when he said: 
<margin>John 12.</margin>
"I have come as a light into the world." <note>John 12:46.</note> For the world would already have light in itself as a creature. Moreover, that which *is* light cannot participate *in* light; for that which participates in light would not [otherwise] be light. But if the Son is not a creature (for 
<margin>1 Corinthians 4.</margin>
he is Light himself, whereas a creature stands in need of light according to that passage in 1 Corinthians 4: "For what do you have that you did not receive?"), <note>1 Corinthians 4:7.</note> then he is necessarily God himself, and it is his own proper good both to be and to be called Light by nature. A creature, however, needs light because it does not have light in its own nature. Additionally, nothing participates in itself; yet every creature participates in the Son as Light. Therefore, the Son is not a creature, nor is the creature Light. Finally, it is one thing to illuminate, and another to be illuminated, just as acting and being acted upon are different. The Son illuminates, while the creature is illuminated. Therefore, the Son is something other than a creature, since that which acts and that which 

<column-break/>

is acted upon cannot be the same thing. 

**And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.** 
Not without cause did the divine Evangelist [John] act; for he did not think it sufficient for the confirmation of the right doctrine to merely say that "the life was the light of men." Now, he explains the same matter more widely, and much more extensively. He did this lest anyone should think that the Word of God is indeed Light, but not for everyone—perhaps only for those he chooses or those he judges worthy to receive light. One might falsely assume that the rest of the universe possesses the power of wisdom or reasoning from themselves, or (as if the Son were less able to do it) that rational beings receive the power of understanding from God the Father alone. 

Lest anyone should think these or similar falsehoods, and so that all may clearly see that the Son of God is the light of *all* rational beings simply—the light by which they are wise and understand—he "mixes" himself (so to speak) in an ineffable way of participation, as Wisdom and Intellect. This is the light we call "reason" in rational beings. He does this so they may be able to have a mind, since they are capable of receiving a mind; for they could not attain this otherwise. Because of all these things, I say, he necessarily added: "And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it." 

Thus, he cries out as if with a great voice that the Life was not called the "light of men" because someone might merit light from the Son of God through a discipline of living. Rather, he says it so all may learn that just as the Word is Life in every created thing, giving life to all things capable of life, so in all things capable of reason, he is the Light. He makes those things that participate in reason to be exactly what they are—that is, rational beings. For the Father is all in all through the Son in the Spirit. 

By "**darkness**," he refers to that nature which stands in need of illumination, which was brought forth universally from nothingness into being. For since he called the Word of God "Light," in order to show that the nature which needs him is something else, he used the opposite term and called that nature "darkness." For those things which do not have light are truly darkness. 

From this, in my opinion, he taught that the nature of creatures has nothing entirely within itself by its own power. But receiving both its total existence (so to speak) and its total well-being from the Creator, the creature may rightly hear: "For what do you have that you did not receive?" Since, therefore, it receives light from God, it is clear that it does not have from itself what it receives from elsewhere. That which does not have light from itself is certainly the opposite of light, and is not unjustly called by the name of "darkness." It is not only likely, but even necessary, that the creature is darkness, while the Son of God, who shines in the darkness, both is and is seen to be the Light. For if the nature of creatures receives the Son of God as Light, there is no doubt that it receives him as darkness [receiving light], and the Son of God shines in it as Light in the darkness—even though the darkness did not know the Son of God. 

For this, I believe, is what is meant by: "and the darkness did not comprehend it." For although the Word of God illuminates all things that have a nature capable of receiving light, he is nevertheless ignored by the darkness. For the rational creature on earth, ignoring the Creator—who is the fountain of wisdom, the origin of intellect, and the root of prudence—worshiped created things. And yet, by the mercy of God, it was brought about that the light... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ae".</note>

### SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.

[Page 31]

...light and the power of understanding, which concurs with its own production and is implanted within itself, it has not lost. From this, it must again be noted most diligently that there is no way the Son of God can be understood as created or made. Instead, he is far removed from the nature of a creature, being entirely something other than a creature. He is so far from being a creature that, just as light relates to darkness (for it is the opposite of darkness), so the Son of God exceeds the nature of a creature beyond all comparison. **There was a man sent from God.** Since the Evangelist has already set forth many things concerning the Word of God, through which the Son is shown to share the nature of God the Father, he now employs a most weighty witness to bolster the faith of his readers. For since it was divinely said through Moses that *by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall be established* <margin>Deuteronomy 19</margin>, he joins to himself a witness of great authority. He thought it necessary to demand and, as it were, claim the faith of his listeners as a debt, since he was narrating wonders on his own that are beyond human capacity. But while he himself testifies that *in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God, and was in the beginning with God*, and that *all things were made through him*, and that *life was in created things*, and that *life was the light of men*—through all of which he shows the Son to be God by nature—he also uses the most weighty testimony of the Baptist, who cries out: *Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God.* <margin>Isaiah 40</margin> For he who possesses the dignity of lordship according to his nature cannot fail to be the true God. For even if many are called "gods" by grace, or if many are called "lords," nevertheless the Son, with the Father and the Spirit, is the one true God and the one true Lord. Nor is anyone else properly and truly God or Lord besides him. For as Paul says, there is *one God the Father, and one Lord Jesus Christ.* <margin>1 Corinthians 8</margin> Therefore, the duality of these holy men <note>John the Evangelist and John the Baptist</note> is entirely worthy of the listeners' faith, both because of the authority of the Law and because of the holiness and renown of the persons themselves. Then, passing over his own praises in silence—lest anyone should say, "You speak of yourself"—he did not omit the praises of the Baptist. Instead, he affirms that he was commanded by God and did not come forward to testify of his own accord, but ministered to the divine will. For he says: **There was a man sent from God.** <margin>Malachi 3</margin> I believe we must certainly observe diligently how he uses speech that is suitable, secure, safe, and adapted to the nature of things. For when he spoke of the Word of God, he used the word *was* <note>Latin: "erat"</note>, consequently adding it to show his eternity and to signify that he is the Creator, existing beyond every beginning of time, and not a creature. For how can that which always *is* be understood as being produced into existence out of nothing? But concerning the blessed Baptist, he appropriately exclaims *there was* <note>Latin: "fuit," implying a beginning or becoming</note>, as fits a mortal and created man. Not content with this alone, he most safely added **man**, overturning the rashness of some. For there were already rumors that the Baptist was not a man by nature, but was from the number of the holy angels and had merely used a human body. They affirmed this because it was written: *Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you.* They were evidently ignorant that the name "angel" <note>term: "angelus" (messenger)</note> signifies a ministry rather than a substance. For in this way—

<column-break/>

—we read of one messenger after another <note>original: "angelus," here used in the sense of a human messenger</note> running to the blessed Job, announcing new and unheard-of calamities. <margin>Job 1</margin> The blessed Paul also determines something similar regarding the holy angels. *Are they not all,* he says, *ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?* <margin>Hebrews 1</margin> Therefore, the blessed Baptist was called an **angel**—not because he was an angel by nature, but because he came to announce and cry out that the way of the Lord must be prepared. Moreover, he was sent **from God**, so that you would not think he announced anything foreign to the God who sent him. For the testimony of one who preached what he learned from God (for that is what being "sent from God" signifies) is true. In this way, Paul also affirms that he was sent through Jesus Christ: not by another, but by Jesus Christ himself revealing it, showing that he had learned the power of the mystery. <margin>Galatians 1</margin> For it follows entirely that whoever is sent by God to preach and announce something has learned what is to be said from God himself. **And his name,** he says, **was John.** By the name itself, he wished to make known the messenger sent from God, so that his great discourse might acquire credibility. For so the angel Gabriel, who stands before God (as he himself said), while announcing the son of Zechariah, added among other things: *John,* he said, *shall be his name.* <margin>Luke 1</margin> He gave the boy about to be born no other name than the one he received divinely. With how much honor, therefore, and with how much authority do we think him to be endowed, who obtained his name from God even before he was conceived in the womb? For these reasons, he necessarily mentioned the name. But since he affirmed that he was sent for a witness, and added *that all might believe through him*, some broke out into such rashness that they did not hesitate to object: "Why then did everyone not believe the one divinely sent? Or how did God’s messenger not persuade everyone?" This happened not through the fault of John, but through the hardness of those listening. For since everyone is in control of their own power, many who heard John did not believe because of the wickedness of their souls. Concerning them, that prophetic saying must be spoken: *He who hears, let him hear; and he who does not believe, let him not believe.* <margin>Ezekiel 3</margin> **He came for a witness, to bear witness of the light.** This word, **he** <note>Latin: "hic"</note>, seems to me to signify a singular and primary virtue. For **he**, he says—this man who was sent from God, who moved Judea by the excellence of his virtue, who was written of by the voice of the prophets as the one to come, of whom Isaiah predicted, *the voice of one crying in the wilderness* <margin>Isaiah 40</margin>, and whom the Psalmist called a *lamp prepared for Christ* <margin>Psalm 131</margin>—**he**, I say, **came for a witness, to bear witness of the light**, namely concerning the Word and the Son of God. For he shows that the Word of God alone is the light according to nature. How then can he be a creature, if he is properly the Light itself, while every creature is merely a participant in light? Or if he exceeds every creature, being in actuality the Light that illuminates all, how is he not begotten of the Light—that is, from God the Father? But if he is begotten of God and not made, as he certainly is, how is he not truly God and **consubstantial** <note>term: "consubstantialis" (of the same essence/substance)</note> with the Father? **He was not that light...**

Here, Cyril clarifies the distinction between John—the greatest of men but still a creature—and the Word, who is the "True Light" by nature. # WITH GEORGE OF TREBIZOND AS TRANSLATOR.

...light, but to bear witness to the light.) That divine Baptist despised cities and chose to dwell in the desert; he excelled in such a great number of virtues that, having reached the summit of human justice, he rightly stirred a profound admiration in men. From this, it happened that some thought he was the Christ, and for this reason, it is written that he was even asked whether he was the Christ.

<margin>Luke 3.</margin> The Evangelist, by no means ignorant of this, and in order to uproot this error at its source and show how great his authority truly was, necessarily added:

<margin>John 1.</margin> **He was not the light.** For how could that great man not be light, or why should his authority not be believed, when he shone with such a heap of virtue that he was believed by some to be the Light itself? Therefore, he says, he was not that light, but was sent for the testimony of the light. Moreover, he always brought forth the name of the light with the addition of the article <note>Cyril is referring to the Greek grammar of John 1:9 (*to phōs*), where the definite article "the" distinguishes the absolute Light from a general quality of light.</note>, so that he might show that the Light is of a single nature. For although that blessed Baptist, and indeed all holy men, are called "light" by the Scriptures (*For you are the light of the world*, says the Savior; <margin>Matthew 5. Psalm 131. John 5.</margin> and of the Baptist it is written again, *I have prepared a lamp for my Christ*, and: *He was a burning and a shining lamp*), we are nevertheless not ignorant of the source from which they obtained the grace and the distribution of light. For the holy are not illuminated by their own light, nor does a lamp possess its own light; rather, shining by the illumination of the Truth, they are like the luminaries of the world for those who hold fast to the words of life. But the Life whose words they hold—becoming light thereby—is surely none other than he who says: *I am the life.* <margin>John 14.</margin> Therefore, the Life is truly the light, by whose participation (and not by any natural consequence) all other things are seen to be light.

->That the true light is the Son, but the creature is not light, but a participant in light.<-

### CHAPTER VIII.

**That was the true light.** The Evangelist now openly separates the true light from the creatures which are not light in themselves. For that one [the Son] is light by nature, while these [creatures] are light through grace; the latter participate, while the former is participated in. These stand in need of light; that one bestows himself upon those in need. Therefore, nothing besides him is the true light, nor can anything else produce the fruit of light by its own power and nature. But just as they were brought forth from nothing, so, having received splendor from the darkness by the true light and being illustrated by participation in him, they pass into light by a kind of imitation. Thus, the Word of God is light substantially—not by a participation that happens through grace, nor by accident. But the creature is not so; it receives what it does not have. It is illuminated like the darkness; it acquires grace from without, and by the mercy of the Giver, it attains this kind of dignity. Therefore, the Son of God is indeed the true light, but the creature is light through grace by his illumination. 

Since, then, there is such a great difference between light and light, how will they not seem to be insane who, paying too little attention in my view, impiously count the Creator among the creatures? This is especially true since, to anyone considering it diligently from all sides, the truth of piety emerges: namely, that by no means can the Son of God be numbered among creatures, which is more broadly evident from what follows. For if the Son is the true light because he is the *radiance of the glory* <margin>Hebrews 1.</margin> of God the Father, then he is certainly not a creature; for otherwise, a creature would also be the glory of God the Father, and that which is the Son of God could be so according to nature. Furthermore, if a creature can be the true light, why is this said of the Son alone, when a creature could be called "true light" just as equally as the Son? But the substance of the Son is properly and truly light, while the creature is not at all; how, then, shall the Son be a creature? 

In addition, there must necessarily be a vast difference between the true light and that which is not true. Therefore, the Son of God, who is the true light, is one thing, and the creature is another. It also follows that no reason can be given why the Son of God *enlightens every man coming into this world* if the creature were also the true light. For it would be said in vain that one is illuminated through the Son if one possessed light substantially through oneself. But the Son of God illuminates us, and we are illuminated by him; therefore, the Son of God and the creature are not related according to substance, just as the participant and the thing participated in are not the same. 

Add to this that if the creature were also the true light, the Psalmist would be speaking in vain when he says: *Draw near to him, and be enlightened.* <margin>Psalm 33.</margin> For that which is the true light will never become light by the participation of another, since it is not illustrated by the splendor of another but shines perfectly by its own nature. But we see that this [being light by nature] is false for us; for we do not doubt that the human race lacks light, nor do we think the Psalmist lies when he cries out to the Word of God with a great voice: *For you, O Lord, light my lamp; my God, enlighten my darkness.* <margin>Psalm 17.</margin> Therefore, we are not the true light, but being naturally alienated from the true light (who is the Son of God), we are illustrated by participation. 

But if the human mind is called a "lamp" when it is said, *For you, O Lord, light my lamp*, how shall we be the true light? For light is granted to a lamp from the outside. If, also, the Only-Begotten alone illustrates our darkness, how is he not the only true light, and we ourselves darkness? If this is so, as it certainly is, how shall the Word of God, who so greatly exceeds creatures, be a creature? 

Furthermore, if the creature were the true light, and man (who is a not-insignificant part of the creature) were also light, to whom does God the Father promise when he says: *And for you who fear my name, the sun of justice shall arise*? <margin>Malachi 4.</margin> For the true light does not need the sun to illuminate it, but God the Father gave us the Sun, as he promised, for those of us truly in need, by which we have been illuminated. Therefore, the true light is one thing by nature, which illuminates those in need of light, and the creature is another, which is illuminated. 

Moreover, if we and the creature are the true light as created things, why do the saints cry out to God with a great voice: *Send out your light and your truth*? <margin>Psalm 42.</margin> For if the creature does not need an illuminator, as the true light does not, why did they call out in vain, needing nothing for this purpose? But those most holy men were not foolish; they sought to be enlightened, and to them in their need for light, God the Father in turn sent the Son. Therefore, the Son is not a creature. It follows that we clearly see the creature requires light; therefore, it is not the true light itself, but the Only-Begotten Son is, who illuminates that which cannot approach the light by itself. To this, since the light truly and naturally—

<meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria's defense of the divinity of Christ. On the previous page, Cyril argued that John the Baptist was not "the light" but merely a witness to it. Here, he broadens the argument to all created beings, explaining that only the Son of God is light by his very nature, while humans are light only through God's gift of grace.</meta>

### THE DIVINE CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.

...[that it might not] be overshadowed, if the creature were also the "true light." For this reason, it is written concerning the Son: *And the darkness did not overcome him.* <note>original: "Et tenebræ ipsum non comprehenderunt." Refers to John 1:5.</note> Regarding men, however, it is said in Paul's writings: *In whom the god of this world* <margin>2 Cor. 4</margin> *has blinded the minds of the unbelievers.* To these the Savior himself also says: *While you have the light, walk in the* <margin>John 12</margin> *light, lest the darkness overtake you.* These things would not have been said unless the human race was wrapped in darkness. How then are the Only-begotten and the creature similar in nature, since the Only-begotten is immutable <note>Unchanging and constant in his divine nature.</note>, while the creature is indeed mutable? For the creature does not have light implanted in its nature, since it can be overcome by darkness. Furthermore, if the "true light" were in men by nature, why do we cry out to God: *In your light we shall see light*? <margin>Psalm 35</margin> <note>Psalm 36:9 in modern numbering. Cyril argues that if we were light ourselves, we wouldn't need God's light to see.</note> For the true light itself cannot be illuminated by another light. We are not, therefore, joined to the Son of God by nature and substance. Moreover, this is the judgment in the Gospel, says the Savior: *Because light came into this world, and men loved darkness more than light,* which is said because they worked wrongly. *For everyone who does evil things hates the light.* <margin>John 3</margin> How then, if the creature is also the true light, <margin>John 3</margin> did the Son of God come to enlighten that which hates the light? Or how, if it is the true light, is it said to refuse to come to the light? For things that exist by nature endure along with that nature; but things that are applied by the will are very easily changed (when the will changes). For a man is rational not by his will, but by his nature. <term>Nature vs. Will</term> <note>Cyril distinguishes between "nature" (what a thing is essentially, like a human being rational) and "will" (choices like being good or bad). He argues divinity is Christ's nature, but righteousness is a human's choice.</note> Therefore, as long as he is a man, that rationality will necessarily be in him; but he is wicked or upright by choice and judgment, and therefore it is equally within his power which one he wishes to prefer. If, therefore, the creature is truly—that is, naturally <margin>C</margin> and substantially—light, how does it not come to the light, or how does it not hate darkness? It is manifest, therefore, that the creature is not itself light truly and naturally, but by the power of its own freedom, it pursues now better things, now worse. Therefore, let them [the opponents] either more openly deny that supernatural goods exist naturally in the Son—so that they may be heard by all as guilty of a greater impiety: *May the Lord destroy all* <margin>Psalm 11</margin> *deceitful lips, and the tongue that speaks great things*—or, if they firmly believe that supernatural goods exist substantially in the Son, let them not wish to join the creature to him according to nature. In addition to these things, if the creature is also the true light, how does the Savior say: *I am the light of the* <margin>John 8</margin> *world*? Or how can they bear to hear this voice of the Savior as if it were true? But our Savior is the truth, and he cannot speak falsely. He says, however, that he is the light of the world, because by a certain relationship to him, the creature both is and is called "light"; therefore, the creature is not of the same nature as him. Furthermore, if the Son is the true light and the creature is similarly so, what shall we answer to Peter writing to us: *But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood,* <margin>1 Peter 2</margin> *a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light*? For if we are light naturally and truly, how were we "called" as if from darkness to light, we who were never in darkness? But we were called to the light:

<column-break/>

the Son, therefore, is properly and truly the light, he who calls us to himself; but the creature, participating in the light, is in no way joined to him substantially. Moreover, since the Psalmist says: *The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us,* what "countenance" of God <margin>Psalm 4</margin> the Father does he mean, whose light is signed upon us? Is it not clear to everyone that the Only-begotten Son of God is called the "countenance" of the Father—that immutable image—who says of himself: *He who sees me, sees the Father*? He it is who is signed in us. For by making <margin>John 14</margin> us conformable to himself, and imprinting the illumination of his Spirit like a divine image upon believers, he renders them gods and sons of God through grace. How then is light "signed" in us, if we ourselves are also the true light? For light does not shine in light, but in darkness. Furthermore, it is sung in the Psalmist that "light has risen for the righteous." If, therefore, it rises for one who already has it and does not lack it, it happens in vain; but if <margin>Psalm 96</margin> it is for one who does not have it (which is the necessary conclusion), the Only-begotten alone will be the light. But the creature that participates in the light, for the very reason that it "participates," cannot be <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "consubstantialis." Meaning 'of the same substance or essence.' This is the key term from the Council of Nicaea used to describe the relationship between the Father and the Son.</note> with the Son of God. Furthermore, it is sung in the same Psalmist: *For they did not possess the land by their own* <margin>Psalm 43</margin> *sword, and their own arm did not save them: but your right hand, and your arm, and the illumination of your countenance.* Here he again names the "illumination of the countenance of God the Father" as the revelation of the Son through the Spirit, and a guidance as if by the hand toward each thing performed. For in this way he liberated the Jews from the greed of the Egyptians. Why then, if light is implanted in the nature of the creature, were they not liberated by their own light? Rather, as those lacking light, they are necessarily enlightened. It cannot be denied that the Son of God shone upon those in need. He himself, therefore, is the true light, and through grace the creature obtains light from him; therefore, it is not consubstantial with him. Likewise the Psalmist: *Blessed* (he says) *is the people that knows* <margin>Psalm 88</margin> *jubilation; they shall walk in the light of your countenance.* Since, therefore, they do not walk in their own light, or since seeking light from another they scarcely obtain salvation—but I think no one will doubt that the Son of God grants illumination to creatures, and when they have received it, they are saved—how then will the Only-begotten be of the same substance as the things which were made by him? Furthermore, *He sent forth* <margin>Psalm 111</margin> *light in the darkness for the upright,* it says. But how is an upright man in darkness if, just like the <margin>D</margin> Son, the creature is also the true light? If, however, light is sent to the upright as to those who do not have it, what need have we of more words? Since the very nature of things cries out with a loud voice that neither the perfect and the imperfect according to nature, nor the one in need and the one who gives out of his own fullness, are of the same substance. *Be enlightened, be enlightened, Jerusalem,* (it says) *for your light has come,* <margin>Isaiah 60</margin> *and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.* But if the nature of creatures through itself—that is, by its own nature, like the Only-begotten—is the true light, what need is there for light to come so that Jerusalem may be enlightened? But she is enlightened through grace. He, therefore, who enlightens her, he alone is the true light, and therefore he is above her in nature and substance. *Behold, I have given you* <margin>Isaiah 42</margin> *as a covenant for the people, for a light to the nations.*

<summary>Cyril argues that only the Son of God is the "True Light" by essence, while humans are in darkness by nature and only become "light" through the gift of divine grace. He uses numerous scriptural proofs to show that if humans were naturally light, they would not need to be enlightened, called out of darkness, or saved by God's "countenance."</summary>
