<meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria’s commentary on the Gospel of John, specifically focusing on John 1:9. The argument transitions from the previous discussion—that John the Baptist was not the light—to a broader theological proof that no created being (human or angel) possesses light by nature, but only through participation in the divine Word.</meta>

# TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.
<sig>b 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: illuminates</meta>

How then could this rational and mortal nature, if it were itself the true light, have stood in such need of light that God should now provide His own Son to it as if to one who did not have it? And now, it says: *House of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord.* <margin>Isaiah 1</margin> <note>Isaiah 2:5 in modern Bibles.</note> Why do they not walk in their own light, but are instead guided by the light of the Only-begotten as if they were lacking light? *I am the light of the world,* says the Savior. *He who follows me* <margin>John 8</margin> *will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.* Why also can a creature, if it too were truly light, not utter a voice of this kind? Therefore, since the creature would shudder to say such things, it most fittingly proclaims that no other light is true except the Son. *While you have the light,* says the Savior, <margin>John 12</margin> *believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light.* If they did not believe, was it going to happen that they would lose the light implanted in their nature? And in what way could that ever happen? For "privations" <note>A philosophical term referring to the absence of a quality that should normally be present.</note> due to neglect cannot occur in those things which are so substantially present that they cannot be absent without the destruction of the subject. Rather, they occur in those things which are acquired by will, and which, when lost, do not destroy the substance. For example: a human is rational by nature, a pilot by choice, and sick by chance. Therefore, a human can never become irrational by any accident; however, they will easily lose the skill of piloting through neglect, and will drive away the accident of sickness through a cure. Thus, things which have taken substantial root in nature are not destroyed without the destruction of the subject. How then do those who refuse to believe in the light lose the light, if they themselves are light truly—that is, substantially? Or how are those who believe "sons of light"? For if they themselves are light, they would be made the "sons of themselves." What then will be the reward of faith? Truly none. For they could be their own sons even while rejecting the faith. Therefore, we shall say that the Word of God alone is the true light, and we shall confess the creature to be of a far different nature. Similarly, one may reason from that Gospel passage: <margin>Ibid.</margin> <note>Referring to John 12.</note> *The light is among you for a little while longer; walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you.* For the true and natural light is never overtaken by darkness. And from that passage <margin>John 2</margin> <note>1 John 2:9.</note> in the epistle of John: *He who says he is in the light, yet hates his brother, is still in the darkness.* Therefore, we cling to the light by choice, and the rational creature receives light by will rather than by substance. This is shown to be so: because if you pursue your brother with hatred, you are still in darkness. But the Only-begotten is called light not by choice, but according to substance; for which reason he is demonstrated to be <margin>Ibid.</margin> <note>Above all creatures.</note> above every creature. Finally, *he who loves his brother remains in the light* (he says); thus charity provides light to the creature, but the Only-begotten *is* the light. Therefore, he is something far different from those things in which he dwells on account of charity.

->*That the soul of man does not exist before the body, nor does it fall into the body on account of preceding sins, as some falsely preach.*<-
<note>This is a refutation of Origenism, a theological movement that taught souls existed in heaven before being "imprisoned" in bodies as punishment for sins.</note>

### CHAPTER IX.
**W**HICH illuminates every man coming into this world, was in the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Most rightly and most safely, the blessed Evangelist has not only declared to us that the Only-begotten himself is the true light, but immediately added a demonstration as well: I affirm (he cries) that he is the true light who illuminates every man coming into this world. Will someone not say then, <margin>A Cavil</margin> <note>A "cavil" is a trivial or annoying objection used in debate.</note> who has skill in the Scriptures: do not angels also illuminate the human mind? Through whom then did Cornelius learn that he ought to be baptized if he wished to acquire salvation? And that Manoah, was he not taught future things by the voice of an angel? But Zechariah the prophet also did not hide this, saying: *And the angel who spoke in me said, I will show these things to him.* Then, showing that knowledge of hidden things is poured into his mind by angels: *Behold,* (he says) *the angel who spoke in me stood there, and another angel went out to meet him, and said to him: Run, and speak to that boy, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls, because of the multitude of men and cattle.* Similarly, Daniel also learned the meanings of visions from an angel, for he says: *And it happened when I, Daniel, saw the vision and sought understanding: behold, there stood in my sight as it were the appearance of a man, and I heard the voice of a man questioning, and he called out and said: Gabriel, make this man understand the vision.* And not only angels, but even man illuminates man. For that honest eunuch, not understanding the prophecy about the Lord, learned it from Philip. And the teachers of both the faith and of a disciplined life have been almost innumerable, by whom the world has been instructed. But why are so many of these things piled up for us, when this can be proved by divine authority? *For you,* says the Savior speaking to the apostles, <margin>Malachi 5</margin> <note>A misattribution in the margin; it refers to Matthew 5:14.</note> *are the light of the world.* Answering these things, we say <margin>The solution</margin> that there is nothing in creatures which is simple and uncomposed, but all things certainly consist of composition. Just as, therefore, a creature who makes another more learned and wiser is not wisdom itself, but a minister of the wisdom that is within him—for in wisdom the wise man is wise—and he who teaches others is not doctrine itself, but a minister of the doctrine through which he was taught; so he who illuminates others is not himself properly the light, but a minister of the light which is in him, spreading it to others through teaching, and making common the good which he had received. For this reason it was said to the apostles, *Freely you have received,* <margin>Matthew 10</margin> *freely give.* For whatever they had, they attained it by divine gift. For no creature can boast of any good of its own, not even the nature of the holy angels; but all things, called by God from non-being into being, do not obtain the nature by which they are well-off from anywhere else than from God; since there is nothing in a creature substantially which does not flow as a gift from the Creator, and which does not have its root in the Creator's grace. Since, therefore, every creature is found in composition, no light is in it properly and simply—that is, without some composition—but it has light by participation, receiving light from God no differently than it receives other goods. But the true light is that which illuminates...

Zechariah, Daniel, Gabriel: Prophets and the Archangel. Philip: The Evangelist who taught the Ethiopian eunuch. Lux mundi: Light of the world. Gratia: Grace. Substantia: Substance, the essence of a thing. Creatura: Creature, any created being (angels or humans).</vocab>

<summary>Cyril argues that while humans and angels can "illuminate" others, they are merely ministers of a light they received from God, whereas the Son is the "True Light" by his very essence and substance. He also explicitly rejects the idea that human souls existed before their bodies or were cast into them as punishment for prior sins.</summary>

### SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.

<margin>Objection.</margin>...illuminates those things that are not illuminated. This light is the only-begotten Son of God, who is simple in nature—that is, as God, He is far removed from any composition <note>In ancient philosophy, God was considered "simple," meaning He is not made of parts, unlike created things.</note>. But someone might object: If the saints are not light by their own nature, why did the Savior call them not merely "participants in light," but "light" itself? Or how is the creature not of the same nature as He is, if the creature is called "light" just as He is? For He said: 
<margin>Matthew 5.</margin> "You are the light of the world." <note>Quoting Matthew 5:14.</note> But those who devise these arguments against themselves fail to see that even "gods" and "sons of God" are what everyone is called in the Scriptures, according to the verse:
<margin>Solution.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 81.</margin> "I have said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High." <note>original: "Ego dixi, dij estis & filij excelsi omnes." This is Psalm 82:6 in modern bibles, 81 in the Vulgate.</note> Shall we therefore deny what we are because of these words? Do we think of ourselves as gods and sons of God in such a way that—after the true Word and Son of God is driven away from His union of divinity with the Father—we wish to sit beside the Father in His place? Shall we turn the grace by which we were honored as adopted sons into the subject matter of impiety? Far be this thought from us! For we worship the Son of God as truly God, and we recognize ourselves in such a way that we are not ignorant that we are made sons and gods by adoption—not by nature, but by grace. 

In this same way, therefore, we confess that the saints are "light." And we add this: that while every rational creature, once illuminated, then illuminates others, it does so by pouring a tradition of doctrine from its own mind into the mind of another. We call this kind of illumination "the power of learning" rather than "revelation." But the Word of God illuminates "every man coming into this world" (John 1:9), not by teaching like men or perhaps angels do, but rather by creating as God. He sows in each person a seed of wisdom—that is, He inserts the roots of piety and understanding. In this way, He makes the creature rational, granting a share of His own nature and sending into the human mind the bright vapors of His own ineffable splendor in a manner known only to Him. Because of this, our father Adam did not learn prudence over time (as we do), but was perfectly wise from the very moment of his creation, preserving the light given to him by God and retaining the integrity of his nature's dignity. 

Therefore, the Son of God illuminates in a "creative" way (if I may put it that way). For He Himself is truly Light, whereas the creature shines by participation in light. Thus, the creature is also called "light," rising above its own nature by the grace of the God who glorifies it and crowns it with various honorable gifts, so that we might step forward magnificently, as if crowned with the highest honors. Therefore, giving thanks with a loud voice, let us say: 
<margin>Psalm 102.</margin> "Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all His rewards; He who is gracious to all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities, who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you in mercy and compassion, who fills your desire with good things." <note>Quoting Psalm 103:2–5 in modern bibles, 102 in the Vulgate.</note> For the Lord is truly merciful, He who makes a creature that is small and lowly by nature into something great and wonderful by His own goodness. He has also adorned us abundantly and heapingly with His goods, so much so that He even calls us "gods" and "light." 

Next, because it was said: "Which illuminates every man coming into this world," and since this word "coming" <term>coming</term> <note>original Latin: "uenientem"</note> can be applied to both "man" and "light" in the custom of the Greek language, the Evangelist adds the following about the light so that it would not be ambiguous: "Because it was in the world." Thus, we should understand "coming into this world" to refer not to the Light, but to the man who is brought from nothingness into being. For "nothingness" itself is fashioned as a kind of place for creatures, from which, having set out in a certain way, they acquire (so to speak) a "place" of existence. It is therefore more fitting and decent to say of the nature of man that, from the very first moment of creation, he is illuminated and receives the power of understanding along with his existence from the Only-begotten Light which is in the world, and which fills all things with the power of ineffable dignity. He is with the angels in heaven,

<column-break/>

He does not abandon those on earth, He is present to those in the underworld; He never leaves any part of Himself empty. Moved by the miracle of this fact, the Psalmist did not hesitate to cry out: 
<margin>Psalm 138.</margin> "Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend to hell, you are present; if I take my wings at dawn and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me." <note>Quoting Psalm 139:7–10 in modern bibles, 138 in the Vulgate.</note> For His hand holds all places and every creature by His divine presence, containing and preserving in existence the things that have been made, infusing life into those things that need life, and sending intellectual light into those capable of receiving it. He is not "in a place," nor does He undergo the movement of passing through or crossing over. For these are properties of bodies, but God (as we have said) fills all things. 

<margin>Objection.</margin> But what are you saying? Someone might object: since the Savior Himself is found to have said, 
<margin>John 12.</margin> "I have come as light into the world," and since the Psalmist also prays, saying: 
<margin>Psalm 42.</margin> "Send out your light and your truth." <note>Psalm 43:3 in modern bibles, 42 in the Vulgate.</note> For the Son clearly says He has "come" into this world; therefore, He was not in this world before He came. Likewise, the prophet prays for one to be "sent" who was not present, but surely one who was absent. 

<margin>Solution.</margin> We, however, assert that the Evangelist used the proper word and spoke appropriately when he affirmed that the Son of God—who is by nature Life and substantially Light, not circumscribed by place, not measurable by space, held by no quantity, and not passing from place to place—is always present everywhere in the world. Therefore, He is said to have "come" into the world, even though He is always present in it, through the mystery of the Incarnation <term>Incarnation</term> <note>The Christian doctrine that the divine Son of God took on human flesh.</note>. 
<margin>Baruch 3.</margin> He dwelt on the earth and lived among men as a man, making His presence in the world more manifest to us. For He who formerly seemed to be present only to the intellect was afterwards perceived by physical eyes, sensibly instilling in us a more direct <note>original: "rudiorem," suggesting a more tangible or basic starting point for knowledge.</note> knowledge of piety, and becoming known through signs and miracles. It was in this way that the prophet prayed for Him to be "sent" to illuminate the world. 

In addition to these things, I think it should also be said that the mind is much swifter than speech, and the movement of the intellect is much sharper than the tongue. Therefore, as much as is permitted to human strength, let us contemplate the sublimity of divine things with the sharpness of our intellect; but let us speak with the speech of men, since we can in no way express what we think otherwise. And since...

<summary>Cyril explains that while humans are called "light" or "gods" by grace and adoption, only Christ is Light by nature. He clarifies that Christ "coming" into the world refers to the Incarnation, as His divine nature is already everywhere at all times.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria’s commentary on the Gospel of John. The previous page discussed how human beings are "light" only by grace and participation in Christ, the True Light. This page moves to refute the Platonic or Origenist idea that souls existed in a divine state before falling into human bodies as a punishment.</meta>

<page-num>40</page-num>
<header>TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.</header>
<meta>catchword: avoidances</meta>

<margin>Colossians 4.</margin> Since the tongue falls far short of being able to express the truth, let us imitate Paul, who, although he was a vessel for the mysteries of the Savior, sought a word from God for the opening of his mouth <note>Referring to Ephesians 6:19 and Colossians 4:3, where Paul asks for prayers so that God may "open a door" for his message.</note>. Therefore, the narrowness of our speech detracts nothing from the dignity of the Only-begotten <note>The "Only-begotten" refers to Jesus Christ as the unique Son of God.</note>: rather, all things said of Him are understood worthily. Indeed, words are spoken more humbly—both by the Savior Himself to us, and by the saints concerning Him—according to the measure of human nature. Truly, because we have asserted that "the light" coming into the world is to be understood as a man, we shall not find it burdensome to refute the frivolous thoughts of men’s hearts. <margin>The impiety of heretics.</margin> For there are those who abuse this authority of Scripture, belching forth not from the mouth of the Lord but from their own hearts, contending that souls existed in a blessed life in heaven before they inhabited human bodies. They claim that these souls, although they enjoyed the perfection of the Good, became "sated" with that better state and fell toward worse things through a foul thought and a desire for another life. The Creator, they say, took this poorly and cast them down, enclosing them in bodies as if in a sort of cave or prison, so that their inflamed desires might be extinguished. For the Creator willed (so they say) that souls should learn through danger how bitter and full of pain it is to despise the Good and turn toward worse things. They attempt to confirm these ideas partly from this text (as we have said), because it is said that "every man coming into this world is enlightened." Partly, they bring in other passages of the Scriptures which they misunderstand, especially this one: "Before I was humbled, I offended." <margin>Psalm 118.</margin> <note>original: "Priusquam humiliarer, ego deliqui." This is Psalm 119:67 in modern Bibles. The heretics argued that the "offense" happened in a pre-existent state before the "humbling" of physical birth.</note> Behold, they say, he confesses that he offended before he was humbled—that is, before the soul was joined to the body—and therefore he was justly humbled by being joined to a mortal body. For the body is mortal, or rather, it is death itself, as Paul shows, <margin>Romans 7.</margin> saying: "Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" <note>Romans 7:24.</note> Therefore, they say, if the soul is weighed down and made lower by coming into the world because it offended before it was lowered and joined to the body, it is clear that the soul surely existed before the body. Furthermore, if it comes into this world from elsewhere, it must have existed before it was connected to the body. Those who say these things against the true doctrines of the Church, deceiving the simple-minded with trifles of this sort, shall be truly rebuked in this way: <margin>Jeremiah 23.</margin> "Woe to you who prophesy from your own heart." <note>Jeremiah 23:16.</note> For they fashion certain wonders from their own hearts, like prophecies, and apply them to divine and spiritual doctrine, not noticing the great impiety into which their efforts erupt. <margin>Refutation of the said impiety.</margin> Now is the time to disprove the falsehood of this opinion. If, therefore, souls existed before the bodies of men and were connected to bodies as a place of punishment due to a certain inclination toward evil (as they say), how can they be said to be "enlightened" when coming into this world? For enlightenment seems to bring a greater grace and is surely a matter of honor, not of punishment. He who is honored is not punished, nor is he who participates in divine light tormented by tortures. Therefore, it is certain that the soul is not punished by its connection to the body, as it is honored within that very body. Furthermore, it would be—

<column-break/>

<page-num>41</page-num>
—entirely false for the soul coming into this world to be enlightened if it were previously a mind and an uncorrupted intellect. For if it is enlightened while it comes into the body, it must have lacked light before it came. How then could the intellect be uncorrupted and pure if it only then began to be enlightened when it descended into this world and into the mass of the flesh? Furthermore, if the soul existed before the body as a pure mind and uncorrupted intellect, it was more closely joined to the Good itself; but if it was pressed down to earthly things by wickedness and a desire for worse things, how is it not a great injustice to that soul, which, having now been pressed down into this body, is commanded to live rightly and not to sin? It would have been more appropriate to command this when it was not yet bound to the body and was farther away from all disturbance. Surely they cannot say either that the opportunity to admonish the soul was unknown to God, or that it was treated unjustly by Him who cannot sin. Therefore, we are commanded to not sin while in this flesh at the appropriate time and justly, since we began to exist at the same time we came into this world with the body, arriving, as if from a certain place, from nothingness into being. Furthermore, I would gladly ask them what likelihood of truth their speech has when they say that, because of the offenses the soul previously committed, it is thrust into the body so that it might learn the foulness of its own desire through the experience of things. How are they not ashamed to say these things? For it seems the soul ought to have been freed from wicked thoughts rather than thrust into the deepest depths of the most foul pleasures. For that method, not this one, could have cured it. If the soul was thrust into the body so that it might enjoy the pleasures of the body—and in that way become even more sick—then the Physician <note>Referring to God as the "Great Physician" of souls.</note> could be rightly accused of both ignorance and injustice, thinking that a sick soul could be healed by being driven through injustice into greater and more numerous offenses. But if it was done so that the soul might make an end of offending, how could He think it would emerge from the ultimate depth of misery and desire rather than retaining its status through a small correction at the very beginning of its evils, when it lacked the "fuel of sin"—that is, the body? To this, if the soul offended before the body and was joined to the body to pay the penalty, it would certainly be necessary for believers, who are freed from sins by faith, to be freed immediately from the punishment—that is, from the body. For tell me, I ask, how can the soul be understood to have fully obtained the remission of sins while it is still held enclosed in the body because of sin? Yet we see it happens much differently: not only do the faithful not fly away from their bodies immediately, but by the profession and faith of the resurrection, they believe they will live immortally with their bodies. Therefore, the body is not joined to the soul for torture, especially since it has been so divinely honored that it bears witness to the omnipotence of the Savior who will live again, and it is a life that shall possess immortality. Add to this that according to the law, greater offenses are punished by death, while those who have sinned more lightly are permitted to live; but those who are seen to be entirely innocent are even [led] to living by certain rewards... <margin>Leviticus 20.</margin>

He argues that physical life is a gift of "enlightenment" from God and that the body is destined for resurrection, not a mere prison for the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria’s defense against the idea that souls exist before bodies and are joined to them as a punishment for prior sins. This line of reasoning was common in Origenist thought, which Cyril vigorously opposes here by appealing to the goodness of the resurrection and various biblical examples.</meta>

### SAINT CYRILL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.

[...so that they] might be affected by hindrances. It would follow, however, if the soul were joined to the body to pay the penalty for crimes committed, that wicked men should rather be invited to live longer, so that they might be more greatly vexed by the mass of the body; conversely, the innocent should be more quickly liberated from this body—that is, from their punishment. But by right, the law orders the murderer and others of this sort to die, while the just are decorated with honors. Therefore, it is falsely said that souls are attached to bodies for the sake of punishment. Furthermore, let them tell me, I ask: if the body is joined to the soul for punishment, what good did the Savior bring to us by destroying death and granting immortality to the body through the resurrection? We ought to have desired a limit to be placed on the body's perpetual corruption for the sake of ending the punishment, rather than giving thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ (whom we believe has granted resurrection to our bodies). But the Church does not act this way; instead, she gives thanks to Christ, regarding Him as a Savior in truth because He has liberated us from death. Therefore, bodies were not given to souls for punishment. For if it were so, the resurrection would bring greater evils upon us, perpetually enclosing miserable souls in bodies and thrusting them back into that from which they had escaped through death. But it was given by Christ as a singular gift, not as an evil, but for the renewal of nature; therefore, bodies were not given to souls for punishment. Besides, the prophet, announcing a certain singular joy <margin>Isaiah 26</margin> to us, cried out: *The dead shall rise again, and those who are in the tombs shall be awakened, and all who are in the earth shall exult.* <note>original: "Resurgent... mortui"</note> It should instead have been said that they would be affected by great sorrow, returning again into bodies. Or, if he truly wished to affect the human race with joy, he would have affirmed not that the dead would rise, but that the nature of the flesh had been given over to perpetual corruption. But since, inspired by the divine Spirit, he announces the resurrection of the flesh as a cause for joy, we are not joined to the body for punishment—for we are commanded to rejoice and exult in its immortality. Added to this is the fact that <margin>Genesis 15</margin> God, when He blessed the blessed Abraham, promised that his descendants would be as numerous as the stars of heaven. Wherefore, if the soul is introduced into the body as if into a punishment, He is promising a crowd of souls divinely damned, and, as it were, fugitives from the good; He would be promising the seed of malice, a slave of the curse rather than a blessing. But in reality, Abraham was blessed by God. Therefore, the union of body and soul is free from all blame. Similarly, that divine man Moses, when he admired the multitude of the Jews (and not without reason), said: *Behold,* <margin>Deuteronomy 1</margin> *in your multitude, you are as the stars of heaven today.* He added a prayer: *May the Lord God of your fathers add many thousands to this number.* If lapsed souls are punished in the body, this thing should not have been hoped for, but rather repelled by the prayer and intercession of Moses to God; yet it was hoped for. For we do not say that Moses was some empty-headed man. Therefore, wicked men devise these types of falsehoods falsely and from themselves, not from the scriptures. Furthermore, we are not ignorant of the fact that nothing is granted by <margin>James 4, 1 Kings 1</margin> God to those who ask wrongly. For he says: *You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly.* If, therefore, the incarnation of the soul is given (as they would say) to pay penalties, then Hannah, daughter of Phanuel, <note>The text names her as "Anna Phanuelis filia," likely conflating Hannah (mother of Samuel) with Anna the Prophetess (Luke 2), though the context of praying for a son refers to the former.</note> sinned not a little, asking for a son from God in long prayer. 

<column-break/>

For she was asking first for the fall of a soul, and then for its punishment; and if the woman erred as a human being, how did she prevail upon God? For a woman could not conceive in the womb unless a soul had sinned in heaven, so that on account of the sin it might enter the woman’s womb and assume a body. But God was moved by her prayer because she asked well; therefore, souls are not joined to the flesh because they sinned beforehand, since we did not exist before the body. To this, if we are connected to the body for the sake of punishment, why did Hezekiah, a holy and <margin>2 Kings 20</margin> upright man, ask for the extension of this life? Or how did God, moved by his piety and tears, add fifteen years to him as a benefit? He would seem to have bestowed calamity and torture upon him, rather than a gift and grace, if those trifles [of the opponents] had any truth in them. But the extension of life was certainly a gift and a grace; therefore, bodies are not given to souls for punishment. Furthermore, if the body was given to the soul for punishment, God returned a vain grace to him who drew Jeremiah out of the pit, and to him whom He promised would escape the onslaught of the Chaldeans and <margin>Jeremiah 39</margin> live longer; whereas He ought rather, if He wished to honor him, to have liberated him as soon as possible from the vexation of the body. Nor, moreover, did He impart any good to those three youths <margin>Daniel 3</margin> whom He saved from the Babylonian flame, nor to Daniel, whom He rescued from the ferocity of the lions. But this is altogether false: for He is praised, and thanks are given to Him, because He bestowed a chief benefit upon them. Therefore, that from which this follows is also false. Add to this that before the Lord's judgment seat each of our works will be made manifest, as Paul says: *For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive the things proper to the body,* <margin>2 Corinthians 5</margin> *according to what he has done, whether good or evil.* If, therefore, retribution is made for the works we have done wrongly, or otherwise, while in the body, and no mention is made of those things we might have done rightly or otherwise before the body: how do they dare to say the soul existed before the body, if only those things done with the body are sought out? Then, how does the same Paul say: *Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God*? For if bodies <margin>Romans 12</margin> were given to souls for punishment, how can we offer to God as a sweet-smelling fragrance that through which we are punished? Or how will that possess virtue which, born for punishment, has struck great roots in sin? To this, on account of the transgression of the first man, corruption invaded our race, as Paul says: *But death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin after the likeness of the transgression of Adam.* How, <margin>Romans 5</margin> therefore, does he affirm that death reigns even over those who did not sin, if a mortal body is attached to us for the sake of ancient crimes? Or how did they not sin, if they fell into the body because of sins? Furthermore, the disciples questioned the Savior regarding a certain man blind from his mother's womb, saying: *Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?* For since it is written in the prophetic books that God returns the sins of the parents upon the children, for this reason the apostles thought that man had been born blind. What then did Christ say? *Neither this man,* <margin>John 9, Exodus 20</margin> he said...

It is therefore clear and conspicuous that the words of the Lord refer to the time that preceded their birth, at which time they neither existed nor could have sinned. For in this way, the integrity of truth will be seen in the words of Truth, that is, of Christ. Furthermore, Isaiah, showing the reason why the earth was made, says: "It was not created in vain, but so that it might be inhabited." <note>Isaiah 45:18</note> However, it cannot be suitably inhabited by naked spirits or incorporeal souls, but only by ensouled bodies. From this fact it follows: if we grant that souls existed beforehand and fell into bodies by sinning, then they must have sinned by the will of God so that there would be humans to inhabit the orb of the lands. But this is entirely false; therefore, the alternative is true. Add to this that Wisdom, the artisan of all things, is introduced in the book of Proverbs saying words of this kind about herself: "I was," she says, "the one in whom the Creator of all things rejoiced. I was glad before him every day and at all times, when he rejoiced at the completion of the world, and was glad over the sons of men." <note>Proverbs 8:30-31</note> If, therefore, God rejoiced when man was created, how can those be so insane as to think that souls are thrust into bodies because of sins? For if he rejoices because they are paying penalties through their bodies, he would not be good, as he would be one who triumphs in the punishment of others. But he is good by nature and the producer of good creatures; therefore, bodies are not instruments of punishment, as many falsely proclaim. 

Furthermore, if souls that sinned before bodies are punished by being joined to bodies, why was the flood sent against the impious and the just Noah saved in the retribution of his faith? <note>Genesis 7</note> For it ought to have happened in the opposite way: namely, that the just should be more quickly released from the body, while the wicked should be tortured by the mass of the body for a longer time. But the just Lord punished the impious with death and honored the just man with a longer span of this life. Therefore, that opinion is false and must be entirely cast out from our minds. In addition to this, why did the Savior raise Lazarus, whom he loved, and bring his friend, who had been liberated from punishments, back into punishments? <note>John 11</note> But he raised him, honoring the one he loved. Therefore, it is said against the truth that souls sinned before bodies. Add to this: if it were so, this rational animal called "man"—and indeed the very nature of man—would seem to have been produced through sin. But then again, death entered into the world through sin; <note>Romans 5</note> thus sin would seem to struggle against itself, since it would dissolve earlier things with later things. Satan also would be divided against himself; how then would his kingdom stand? <note>Luke 11</note> But these things are false; therefore, the things opposed to them are true. Finally, the Church denies that death was produced by God. For Scripture confirms that it came into the world through the envy of the devil. <note>Wisdom 2:24</note> But if the body is joined to the soul to punish it, why is the devil blamed, who dissolves the punishment of the soul through death? And why do we give thanks to the Savior for restoring our bodies to us again through the resurrection? But we rightly both do give and owe thanks to the Savior, who liberated us from the corruption which envy

### CHAPTER X.

**And the world was made through him.** <note>John 1:10</note> The Evangelist necessarily signifies that the world was made through the only-begotten of God, through the true light. For even though he said above that all things were made through him, nevertheless, so that no room for error is left, he proclaims again that he is the creator. For since he spoke of the light, that it was in the world: lest anyone should suspect this light to be one of the parts of the world—just as the sun, moon, and stars are in the world and are believed to be members of the world as if of one body—he necessarily confirms that this light is the artisan of the entire world. Thus he has instructed us once again that the world was made by the only-begotten of God. For who is so unrefined and rustic as not to see that he is different from the world, through whom the world was made? Or who, hearing these things, will not separate the creator from the creature according to nature? For that which makes and creates is of one nature, and that which is created is another; otherwise, the same thing would create and be created. But if that were so, and there were no difference according to the logic of substance, the creature would surely pass into the nature of the creator, and the creator would descend into the nature of the creatures. Nor would God alone create, but there would even be in creatures the force of creating—or at least the potential—if they were united to God in any way by the logic of substance. Thus the creature would also be a creator. And the Evangelist attributed the authority and dignity of creating to the only-begotten with more than just bare words, saying: "He was in the world, and the world was made through him." But he did not say this with bare words, for he knew that the creator of all things is one in nature. Therefore, it is not possible—nor can it be understood by the pious—that the creature and creator are the same in nature. Rather, the creature, not being ignorant of the limit of its own nature, will subject itself to servitude. But the Son will reign over it, who alone together with the Father and the Spirit can call those things which are entirely nothing as if they were beings, and can produce that which is nothing at all into existence by ineffable power. But since we shall demonstrate more extensively in the book on the Trinity that the nature of God the Son is not a creature, we will not be longer now. However, this must not be overlooked: that since he affirms the world was made through the Son, he easily leads our memory back to the Father. For when "through whom" is said, "from whom" is also understood: for all things are from the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit.

Romans 11.
</margin>

### CHAPTER XI.

**And the world did not know him.** <note>John 1:10</note> With the greatest skill and the greatest vigilance, he strives to anticipate and prevent the empty thoughts of men. For this order of sublime things and the overturning of objections is marvelous: he was just now adding that the true light comes into this world; and besides this, he was asserting that he was also in the world, and the world was made through him. Therefore, someone could easily object: "If the Word of God is light, and if this light illuminates the hearts of men, and indeed piety and the knowledge of things..."

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary by Cyril of Alexandria, transitioning from a defense against the pre-existence of souls to an exposition of the Prologue of John (specifically John 1:10-12), discussing why the world failed to recognize its Creator and the distinction between the ignorance of the Gentiles and the rejection by the Jews.</meta>

### ST. CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.
<meta>catchword: seed</meta>

...instills an understanding of things suitable for the human race. If, moreover, He was always in the world and is Himself the maker of the world, how was He ignored for such long periods of time? For it would seem to follow that since He was ignored, either the world was not illuminated by Him, or He is not entirely the light. Lest anyone should raise this objection, he divinely introduced the following: *And the world knew him not.* <note>original: "Et mundus ipsum non cognouit." A quote from John 1:10.</note> Let the world, he says, accuse its own weakness, not the Word of God or this eternal light. For the Son illuminates, but the creature—which has abused the sharpness of understanding given to it to know God by nature and has, like a prodigal, turned its power of vision toward created things—rejects grace. It neglected to run further; it undermined the illumination out of laziness and contempt for this grace. Lest a <margin>1 Timothy 4</margin> disciple of Paul suffer this, he is warned to watch diligently. Therefore, the wickedness of those who should be illuminated will not justly reflect back upon the light. For just as the sun rises for everyone, yet a blind man receives no benefit from it—and no one would rightly accuse the sun's splendor for this, but would attribute the fault of not seeing to the blindness—so, I believe, it must be understood regarding the <term>Only-begotten</term><note>A title for Jesus Christ (the Son of God), emphasizing his unique relationship to the Father.</note>. For He is indeed the true light, and He emits His splendor to all; but <margin>2 Corinthians 4</margin> "the god of this world" (as Paul says) "has blinded the minds of unbelieving men, lest the light of the knowledge of God should shine in them." <note>original: "deus huius seculi... mentes infidelium hominum obcæcauit."</note> Now, we say that blindness has come upon man not because he is entirely deprived of light—for nature always preserves the power of understanding granted to it by God—but because man, through poor habits, dulls it, and by turning toward worse things, weakens the measure of grace as if by a faintness. Therefore, when such a state comes upon a <margin>Psalm 118</margin> man, the Psalmist then rightly prays to be illuminated, crying out to God: *Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law.* <note>original: "Reuela oculos meos, & considerabo mirabilia de lege tua." Psalm 119:18 in modern bibles.</note> For the Law was given so that the light within us might be kindled through it, the bleariness of the mind's eyes wiped away, and the darkness that occupied us through ancient ignorance driven out. Thus, by these words, the world is accused of being ungrateful and senseless, for it ignored its own Author and did not produce the proper fruit of illumination. It seems that what was preached by the <margin>Isaiah 5</margin> prophetic voice concerning the Jews can now truly be said of all: *I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.* <note>original: "Expectaui ut faceret uuam, & fecit uepres." Reference to the Parable of the Vineyard in Isaiah 5:2.</note> For the proper fruit of the Only-begotten’s illumination was knowledge, hanging from the human mind like a grape from a fertile vine-branch. But when rashness draws the multitude toward the error of many gods, they arise like sharp thorns and mortally wound the mind of man.

### CHAPTER XII.
**He came unto his own, and his own received him not.**

Now the Evangelist casts the blame for ignorance upon the world in a more explanatory way—that the world, though illuminated by the Only-begotten, ignored Him. He also demonstrates the sin of the nations alongside the error of the Jews, placing the ignorance and hardness of the world as if before our very eyes. In a marvelous way, he descends from that "high theology" <note>The study of Christ's divine nature and pre-existence.</note> into the discourse on the Incarnation and the exposition of this mystery which was done for our sake. For it is no wonder, he says, if the world

<column-break/>

did not know the Son of God, since it turned away from the right path of understanding and did not remember that it was made in honor, but made itself like <margin>Psalm 48</margin> the beasts (as the Psalmist used to say). This happened even when the very people whom God chose as His own "peculiar" people refused to receive Him when He was present in the flesh and coming for the salvation of all, even though He would have repaid them with the kingdom of heaven for their faith. It should be noted, however, how carefully the discourse is woven. For the "world" <note>Referring here to the Gentile nations.</note> is accused of not having known Him at all, and a certain pardon is prepared for it, seemingly leading it toward the grace of knowledge. Regarding the Jews, however, whom He chose as a "peculiar" people, he added: *they received him not.* For ignorance cannot truly be spoken of them at all, since the Law first preached of Him, and then the Prophets foretold Him. Therefore, by a just judgment, they are cut off, and the nations obtain mercy. For the world—that is, the nations—driven away from connection with God by the onset of wickedness, was entirely ignorant of the Illuminator. But those others, enriched by the knowledge of the Law and called back to a life pleasing to God, through the insolence of their souls, did not receive the Son of God who was already known in the Scripture and coming to His own. By right of creation, the entire world is God’s own property, for it was made from Him and through Him. But much more fittingly is Israel called "His own" because of the election of the holy patriarchs. And for this reason, he is called the "firstborn" among the sons of God, whom He specifically named as His own when speaking <margin>Exodus 14</margin> to Pharaoh, the tyrant of Egypt. For He said: *Let my people go.* <note>original: "Emitte... populum meum." Exodus 8:1.</note> Which <margin>Exodus 8</margin> Moses also confirms, saying: *When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he appointed the bounds of the people according to the number of the angels of God. And the Lord's portion <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> became the people of Jacob, the cord of Israel's inheritance.* <note>original: "Et facta est pars domini populus Iacob, funiculus hæreditatis eius Israel." Deuteronomy 32:8-9.</note> To these, therefore, He came as if to His own; for this reason <margin>Psalm 104</margin> He says: *I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.* <note>original: "Non sum missus, nisi ad oues quæ perierant domus Israel." Matthew 15:24.</note> Since He was by no means received by them, <margin>Matthew 15</margin> He transferred grace to the nations. Thus, the world is indeed illuminated by faith and repentance—the world which previously ignored the Word of God—while the people of the Jews return to the darkness from which they had been led out. Therefore, the Savior also said: *For judgment I have <margin>John 9</margin> come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.*

### CHAPTER XIII.
**But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe in his name.**

By a certainly fair judgment, and one worthy of God, Israel the firstborn is cast out. For he did not wish to remain in kinship with God; he did not receive the Son of God coming to his own; he rejected the granter of nobility and repelled the author of grace—whom the nations received by faith. Therefore, he justly reaps the fruit of this rashness and will weep for this kind of loss, by which he is driven away from the adoption of the sons of God. The nations, however, will enjoy the benefits of faith and will find no small rewards for obedience; they will be transplanted into the place of the others, cut off from the wild olive tree according to nature and grafted into the fertile nature of the olive. And Israel hears: <margin>Romans 11</margin> *Woe to the sinful nation, a people full of sins...* <margin>Isaiah 1</margin>

C
<meta>Catchword: only</meta>

<margin>1 Peter 2</margin>
...an evil seed, wicked children, you have forsaken the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger. But the Gentiles hear something far different from the apostles or one of their company: *But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for His own possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.* <note>original: "Vos autem genus electum, regale sacerdotium..." A quote from 1 Peter 2:9.</note> For since the Gentiles received the Son through faith, they also receive the power to become the children of God. They receive this, however, from the Son, in whom alone this status exists by nature; and therefore He can offer this in common to others as a sign of His mercy and love. For it was not otherwise possible to escape the image of the earthly man—that is, the corruption we put on through sin—unless the image and beauty of the <term>Heavenly Man</term><note>A title for Christ, contrasting Him with Adam, the "earthly man."</note> were impressed upon us through the calling of adoption. For having been made participants of Him through the Spirit, and marked by His own seal, we rise to His likeness and into the original form of the image in which divine Scripture testifies we were created. For thus, finally recovering the ancient beauty of our nature and being conformed to that divine nature, we shall overcome the evils which happened to us through the great fault of transgression. Let us, therefore, ascend to supernatural dignity through Christ—not, however, as if it were our own property, as it is His, but so that by His likeness we may be children of God through the grace of the Son. For He is the true Son of God the Father; but we, adopted by His mercy through grace, hear the words: *I have said, you are gods.* <note>original: "Ego dixi, dij estis." A quote from Psalm 82:6 (81 in the Vulgate).</note> Since a creature is a servant, he is called to supernatural things only by the birth and will of the Father. But the Son is both God and Lord, not only because the Father willed it, but because He shone forth from the very substance of the Father, drawing His own good according to nature. We recognize Him as the true Son also by comparison to ourselves. For the principle of nature is one thing, and that of adoption is another; the principle of the true Son is one thing, and that of the adopted son—who is called a son by likeness and imitation of the Son—is another. We are the children of God by adoption. Truly and naturally, therefore, He is the Son through whom we, having been adopted into sonship, are distinguished by the title of "sonship." For one is a son either by nature, as He is, or by adoption, as we are, having obtained the good of grace in place of natural dignity.

### CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>Psalm 109</margin>
<margin>The Evangelist explained the power given to them when he said a little earlier: "He gave them power to become the sons of God."</margin>
*Who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.* <note>original: "Quoniam ex sanguinibus..." A quote from John 1:13.</note> Those who are called into the adoption of sons by faith in Christ, he says, have set aside the humility of their nature, and by the grace of Christ who honors them, they ascend to supernatural dignity as if clothed in splendid purple. For they were made children not of the flesh, but of God by adoption. But notice how carefully he speaks. For because he was about to say that the faithful were born of God, he wanted to prevent anyone from thinking either that they proceed from the substance of God the Father (and thus become unchangeably like the <term>Only-begotten</term>), or that the phrase "From the womb before the morning star I begot you" <note>original: "Ex utero ante luciferum genui te." A quote from Psalm 110:3 (109 in the Vulgate).</note> was said of the Only-begotten merely in a figurative or improper sense. Lest he should join the Son of God to the nature of created things, he necessarily placed these premises first. Thus, since he explained the power given to them and the servant-nature to the Son, and the adoption and grace 

<column-break/>

<margin>He likewise explained the nature of the Son in the Gospel when he says: "And the Word was made flesh."</margin>
that he understood through this "power," he very safely introduced afterward: *They were born of God.* This is to show the greatness of the grace that joins those who were strangers to God and makes them children of God, and out of love grants the nobility of the Lord to servants. But someone might say: "In what way did the believers in Christ obtain more than Israel?" For even the Jews are said to have been born of God. For He says: *I have nourished and brought up children, but they have rebelled against me.* <note>original: "Filios enim... enutriui." A quote from Isaiah 1:2.</note> First, it is clear that because the Law contained a shadow of future goods, these things were ascribed not according to truth but figuratively, until the time of grace. Then, those were to emerge who—more fittingly and truly because of the indwelling Spirit of the Only-begotten—would call God "Father." For the former had the spirit of slavery in fear, but the faithful have the Spirit of adoption of sons in liberty, in which we cry: *Abba, Father.* <note>original: "Abba pater." A quote from Romans 8:15.</note> Therefore this people, who were adopted by faith in Christ, were depicted in the former people as if in a shadow. Just as circumcision, which is performed in the spirit, was marked in their flesh, so all other things (to speak briefly) which are expressed in us were foreshadowed in them. Furthermore, we add that Israel was also called into adoption through Moses as mediator; therefore, they were baptized into him (as Paul says) in the cloud and the sea, and thus they were restored from the worship of idols to the law of servitude, receiving commands through the ministry of angels. But those who are adopted by God through faith in Christ are baptized not into any creature, but into the Trinity itself with Christ as mediator, who joins humanity to Himself by the assumption of man, and is joined to the Father by nature. In this way, the serving nature ascends into sonship, called to His natural dignity by participation in the true Son. For these reasons we are both called and truly are children of God, we who receive by faith the regeneration worked by the Spirit. Regarding this Holy Spirit—since some even dare to number Him among the creatures—it is not irrelevant now to say a few things for our benefit and that of the readers.

<margin>Refutation of the Macedonians.</margin>
For if the Spirit is not God by nature, nor essentially within God, but is placed in the number of creatures, how are we who have been regenerated through Him said to be "born of God"? Either you must say the Evangelist is lying, or if he is truthful—as indeed he is—then the Holy Spirit is God by nature from God. By participating in Him through faith in Christ, we participate in the divine nature, are made children of God, and are "gods"—not only because we fly toward supernatural glory by grace, but also because we possess God dwelling within us, as it is written: *He will also give life to your mortal bodies because of His Spirit dwelling in you.* <note>original: "Viuificabit... propter inhabitantem spiritum." A quote from Romans 8:11.</note> Otherwise, let them say, I ask, how are we "temples of God" according to Paul because we have the Spirit dwelling in us, unless the Spirit is God by nature? For if He is a creature, why would God destroy us, as if we were destroying the temple of God, when we defile our body in which the Spirit dwells, who possesses all the natural properties of the Father and the Son? If this were not so, how could the Savior's word be true?

<margin>Romans 8</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin>

<header>SAINT CYRILL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.</header>

<margin>John 14</margin>
...provided it were the true prayer of the Savior: "If anyone loves me," he said, "he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our home with him." And certainly, it is the Spirit who dwells in us, through whom we believe we possess both the Father and the Son simultaneously, as this same John says in his epistles: "In this we know that we abide in him, and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit." <note>original: "In hoc cognoscimus, quoniam in eo manemus..." from 1 John 4:13</note>

### How indeed shall he truly be called the Spirit of God, unless he exists by nature from him and in him?

But if he were a created thing, why are other creatures not called the "Spirit of God"? We would not be burdened to say more on this, but since this was stated sufficiently (as I judge) in the book *On the Trinity*, it is appropriate to be briefer now.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>Joel 2</margin>
**And the Word was made flesh.** Having now clearly entered upon the discourse of the incarnation <term>incarnation: the doctrine that the second person of the Trinity took on human flesh</term>, he most openly narrates that the only-begotten Son of God was made man. For when he says, *And the Word was made flesh*, he says nothing other than that the Son of God, being God by nature, was made man. Nor is anything new brought forward, since Divine Scripture often signifies the whole human being (if I may put it so) by the single word "flesh." "I will pour out," says Joel, "from my Spirit upon all flesh." <note>original: "Effundam à spiritu meo super omnem carnem" from Joel 2:28</note> Here, unless you understand the whole man from this one part, it would seem ridiculous that the Spirit is given to inanimate meat. 

The reason why he speaks this way rather than another must be rendered by us. Man is a rational animal composed of a soul and this mortal flesh, but brought into being by God. Since by his own nature he could not be incorruptible and perpetual (for this belongs substantially to God alone), he was sealed with the spirit of life through a relationship with Him, and thus followed the good of immortality beyond his own nature. For "He breathed," it says, "into his face the breath of life, and man was made into a living soul." <margin>Genesis 2</margin>

But because, on account of his transgression, he rightly heard that he was earth and to the earth he would return, having been stripped of grace, he lost the breath of life according to the flesh—namely, the Spirit of him who says: "I am the life." <margin>Genesis 3</margin> <margin>John 14</margin> Thus man fell into death only on the part of the flesh, while the immortality of the soul was preserved. For it was said to the flesh alone: "Dust you are, and to dust you shall return." <margin>Genesis 3</margin> Therefore it was necessary that what in man is corrupted should be recalled to immortality through a reunion with natural life. For this evil could not otherwise be dissolved unless the power of that decree—"Dust you are, and to dust you shall return"—were destroyed by an ineffable assumption <term>assumption: the act of the Word taking human nature into himself</term>, the mortal flesh of man being taken up by the Word who gives life to all things. Thus, when it became the flesh of Him who is truly immortal, it might participate in His immortality. 

For it would be entirely unbefitting if fire could impart its own quality to the matter joined to it, and in that way transmute the matter into itself, but the Word of God were unable to infuse his own proper and natural good—that is, life—into the flesh joined to him. For this reason especially, I judge it was written by the Evangelist: *and the Word was made flesh*. He wished to signify the restoration of the whole through the part that was most corrupted and then vivified by union with the Word. For thus the magnitude of the wound and the power of the remedy are easily seen: thus the sick man and the physician; thus what has fallen into death and he who raises from death to life; thus what is corrupted and the expeller of corruption; thus what death overcame and he who conquered death; thus what was deprived of life and he who bestows life, are seen as if with the eyes. 

He did not say, however, that the Son of God *came into* flesh, but that he *was made* flesh—lest anyone should judge that he came merely by a disposition <note>original: "habitudine," referring to a temporary or external relationship</note>, as he came into the prophets and other saints, but rather that he truly was made flesh, that is, man. Therefore he is also God according to nature in the flesh, and with the flesh. For he made that flesh his own, and yet he is understood as something distinct from it, and is adored in it and with it (as Isaiah says). <margin>Isaiah 45</margin> "Men of stature," he says, "shall pass over to you, and they shall be your servants, and they shall follow after you bound in manacles; they shall adore you and make supplication to you, for God is in you alone, and there is no God besides you." Behold, he says God is *in him*, not separating the flesh (that is, the man) from God. And again he confirms there is no other God besides him, joining the temple taken from the Virgin to the Word as his own, for Christ is one from both.

### CHAPTER XVI.

**And dwelt among us.** The Evangelist now explains what he had just said. For since he signified that the Word of God was made flesh, he immediately added *and dwelt among us* as a safeguard, lest anyone out of ignorance should think the divine nature was completely changed into flesh—which is entirely impossible, for the substance of God is far removed from all mutation. Thus, you must necessarily understand two things: the one who dwells, and that in which he dwells. You should not think the divine nature was commuted into flesh, but rather that he dwelt in the flesh, and used the temple which he took from the holy Virgin as his own. 

For in him "the whole fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily," as Paul says. <margin>Colossians 2</margin> He confirms that he dwelt "in us," revealing a certain sublime mystery. For we are all in Christ, and the person of our common human nature has lived again in Christ. <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> For this reason he is also named Adam <note>The "Last Adam" concept from 1 Cor 15:45</note>, because through the commonality of our nature, the glory and immortality which the first Adam took away from everyone, now flows to all. Therefore the Word dwelt in all through the assumption of one; and since the one Son of God is defined in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, this dignity is poured out upon the whole human race. 

And thus through one of our race, that saying reaches us as well: "I have said, you are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High." <margin>Psalm 81</margin> Therefore, in Christ our nature, though in the form of a servant, was truly liberated, ascending to a mystical union with him who put on the form of a servant; and in us, it is liberated on account of the affinity of the flesh by which we are joined to him. <margin>Hebrews 2</margin> For for no other reason "did he not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham." <margin>1 Corinthians 8</margin> Whence it was necessary that he be made like his brothers in all things, in all things similar to his brothers... <note>original: "fratribus per omnia similis"</note>

->TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.<-

<margin>2 Cor. 8</margin>...similar, and truly made man: so that by descending into a servant's nature, he himself indeed acquired nothing, but brought himself to us as a gift. Thus, through his poverty, he might enrich us <note>original: "per paupertatem sua nos ditaret"</note>, as we who have climbed toward his primary good through a likeness to him are established as gods and sons of God through faith. For he who is by nature the Son of God dwelt within us; therefore, in <margin>Rom. 8</margin> the spirit we cry out: "Abba, Father." The Word of God dwelt in us in a single temple, which he built for himself for our sake and from our own nature, so that having all people <margin>Ephes. 1</margin> within himself, he might reconcile them in one body to the Father (as Paul says).

### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>A</margin> **A**nd we saw his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the father, full of grace and truth. Although he asserted that the Word of God was made flesh—that is, made man—he nevertheless showed that the Word preserved the complete dignity of the Father's deity, no less full of good things than before. For that supernatural nature is firm and immutable, and always remaining in the same way, it always abounds equally in its own proper dignities. Therefore, even though the Word was made flesh, he says, it was neither overcome by the weakness of the flesh, nor did it fall from its ancient majesty and omnipotence because it was made man. For we saw, he says, the glory of Christ from God, a glory higher than that of the creatures; so that anyone of sound mind would confess that such glory belongs to no other than the only-begotten Son of God. For he was full of truth and grace. Indeed, if one were to consider the multitude of saints and diligently count the wondrous deeds of each, one would not deny that they were full of the <margin>John 3</margin> glory of God. Yet one will see the glory and grace of the Son as being sublime beyond any comparison. For grace is not given to him by measure as it is to others <note>A reference to John 3:34, implying Christ has the Spirit without limit</note>, nor does it come to him from the outside; rather, it exists substantially within him as a perfect thing in a perfect being, held naturally from the Father. Additionally, the saints are like servants in the house, but the Son moves within his own house. For of the only-begotten it is written: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the <margin>Psalm 117</margin> Lord." But concerning the saints, the Father says: "And I sent to <margin>Jer. 7</margin> you my servants the prophets." Furthermore, the saints performed signs not by their own power, but by a higher power; Christ, however, worked as the Lord of all powers. "If I do not do," he said, "the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even if you do not believe me, believe <margin>John 10</margin> my works." If, therefore, the strengths of the only-begotten are as great as the Father’s, as demonstrated by his works, he shall be glorified with glory equal to the Father, since he works equally. Therefore, although he was made man <margin>Heb. 2</margin>, he is nevertheless as superior to those he calls "brothers" as God truly and naturally stands above men—as much as a true Son exceeds those who are sons by adoption. But if his glory is full of grace and truth, you might ask, how is it written in <margin>Luke 2</margin> Luke that he "progressed in wisdom, age, and grace"? Or what can be added to that which is "full," beyond which there is nothing? But he is not understood to have progressed as the Word and God; rather, because men wondered at him more every day, it was their opinion of Jesus that grew, rather than his grace being perfected. As they recognized him more day by day, they thought he was proceeding further and growing in grace.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>B</margin> **J**ohn bears witness of him, and cries out, saying: In his usual manner, the blessed Evangelist, since he had said "we saw the glory of the Word, as the glory of the only-begotten," and because the word "we saw" is not properly applied to only one person, he cites the Baptist, who was similar to himself in both name and piety. He did not say only that John attested to him, but excellently added "because he also cries out." For he was not ignorant that it was written of him: "The voice of one crying in the desert." <margin>Isa. 40</margin> He added that John "cried out" so that no one could say: "When did the Baptist ever bear witness to Christ, or to whom, since he never spoke of Christ?" He cries out, therefore, he says: that is, not in secret, nor with a low or stammering voice, but he cries out more loudly than a sounding trumpet. "I am not the only one who heard him," he says, "but his cry was scattered far and wide among all." For he was a splendid preacher, not obscure, but distinguished and very great.

### CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>C</margin> **T**his was he of whom I said: "He who is to come after me was made before me, because he was prior to me." Since he has cited a witness by name and shown that he used a great cry for the ministry of preaching, he now explains the manner of his testimony. Certainly, the whole question turns on this. What, therefore, was he crying out? "He who comes after me was made before me." This speech is deeply hidden and requires very diligent consideration; however, here is the ready and well-worn meaning. The birth of the Baptist preceded the incarnation of the Savior; for by six full months (as is perceived from the <margin>Luke 1</margin> Gospel of Luke), Emmanuel was later. Therefore, they think this is what is signified: that according to age, he who comes after me was made before me. But if one raises the mind to higher things, the speech is pulled far away from its purpose toward alien meanings. For the Baptist was cited as a witness not to affirm that Christ was sometimes later and sometimes earlier merely in the time of birth, but so that he, who just like the Evangelist, might see the glory of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. Therefore, this speech cannot be accommodated to any span of time. For even if we do not deny that the Lord was born after the Baptist according to the flesh, this meaning is by no means suited to what precedes (as we have said) and is said quite inconsistently. <margin>D</margin> Secondly, that which is found to be later than a thing in time cannot have preceded that same thing in time. It pleases us more, therefore, to accommodate the meaning of this context to the condition of spiritual things, taking our speech from the image and likeness of human affairs. For it is common in the world that he who precedes always seems more glorious to those who come after; just as one who has absolutely mastered a certain craft or any other skill precedes or is more glorious than the one who is still learning, following the master and continually stepping toward further things. Yet, when the student surpasses his master in the knowledge of the craft, he could rightly hear from the surpassed master: "He who comes after me was made prior to me." By applying the meaning of this speech through this image to the Savior and the Baptist, you will, in my opinion, understand it correctly.

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary on the Gospel of John, specifically contrasting the ministry and status of John the Baptist and Moses with the divine preeminence of Jesus Christ.</meta>

->SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.<-

Everyone marveled at John; he gathered many disciples from all sides, and a great crowd of people who wished to be baptized by him flocked to him daily. But Christ, though superior to him, was unknown; it was hidden that he was truly God himself. Because he was unknown, he seemed much later and lesser than the Baptist. For the Baptist received greater honor and glory from men; but he who was to come after was made prior, being daily regarded as greater and more excellent. For he was revealed to be God by his very works, while John, not exceeding the limits of a man, was left behind. 

Therefore, the blessed Baptist spoke enigmatically: "He who is to come after me has been preferred before me" <note>original: "prior me factus est"</note>; and he who was inferior to me in honor has become more glorious, and surpasses by incomparable excellence the measure of glory suited to me. Certainly, this meaning is not taken up in vain or outside the purpose, but is said consistently and in harmony with what came before. For when he is cited as a witness to the glory of the Only-begotten <term>Unigenitus: a title for Christ emphasizing his unique status as the only Son of God</term>, since there was a great opinion among men concerning him, when he testifies that Christ is greater than himself, what else is he doing but attesting to Christ's preeminent glory? And since he said he "was made prior," he necessarily added, "because he was before me," attributing to him an ancient and most venerable glory, because he is prior to all things—not in time, but by nature as God. For he said, "he was before me," which means he was always superior to me, always more glorious. Understand this comparison, made to one of the creatures (that is, to John), as being made to every creature. For we consider the glory of the Only-begotten to be superior not only to John’s glory, but simply to the glory of all.

### CHAPTER XX.

**AND of his fullness we have all received.** With these words, the Evangelist seems to confirm that John's testimony is true: for he clearly demonstrates that [Christ] is substantially superior not only to the Baptist but to every creature, both in glory (which was just discussed) and in the number of other good things. Most rightly, he says, it was said of the Only-begotten by John: "because he was before me," that is, much more sublime and glorious. For even all of us, who hold the place of the saints, have been enriched by his own goods, and human nature rejoices in his goods more than its own. 

For from the fullness of the Son, like an ever-flowing fountain, the gift of graces wells up and flows down into every soul that is worthy. If, therefore, the Son bestows gifts as if from a natural fullness, while the creature is the one upon whom he bestows them, how will he not possess a glory unlike all others? Namely, that glory which befits the Only-begotten Son of God, who possesses as the fruit of his own nature every dignity and excellence which the Father is understood to have. Concerning this matter, I believe the most wise Paul was moved to say to the creature:

<margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin>
*For what do you have that you did not receive?* For not only to exist, but also to exist well, and to exist in this or that way, is granted to creatures by God; since they have nothing from themselves, they are enriched solely by the freedom of the Giver. This also must not be overlooked: that by affirming the Son to be full—that is, perfect in all things—he shows he is so far from lacking anything that he himself abundantly bestows upon everyone as they lack, and yet he always preserves his fullness as the same and unchanged.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER XXI.

**AND grace for grace: because the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.** Since he said the Son's glory was more excellent than the glory of all men, he now sets this forth by a demonstration, comparing him to those who surpassed other men in the magnitude of their holiness. For concerning John, the Savior himself says: *Amen I say to you, among those born of women there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist.* But he introduced this very man, so great and sublime, crying out: "He who is to come after me has been preferred before me, because he was before me." 

Therefore, since John yields to Christ, it must be that none of the saints can ascend to the measure of Christ's glory, which is seen in the splendor of his works. But the saints who lived in former times, since they yield to the virtue of John and cannot reach his virtue, they together with him concede the palm <note>The "palm" refers to the prize of victory or supreme status.</note> to the Savior. Indeed, John, the most excellent of them all, preferred Christ as the only one truly holy, not by the voice of others, but by his own preaching. Necessarily, therefore, so that Emmanuel <note>The name "Emmanuel" means "God with us."</note> might appear far greater even than the ancient saints, he mentions Moses, to whom it was said by God:

<margin>Exodus 33</margin>
*I know you above all others: and you have found grace in my sight.* We can know from this that he was better known to God than others: *If there be a prophet among you,* says the Lord, *I will appear to him in a vision, and I will speak to him in a dream. But not so with my servant Moses, who is most faithful in all my house: for I speak to him mouth to mouth, and plainly, and not through enigmas and figures does he see the Lord.* 

Since, therefore, Moses far excelled the more ancient saints, he shows the Only-begotten is superior to him so that he may be seen as the first of all; and he says, *grace for grace, because the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.* This is the meaning of what he says, in my opinion. Truly, he says, John's testimony concerning the Only-begotten is certain when he says: *He who is to come after me was made before me, because he is before me: for from his fullness we have all received.* 

Nor should anyone think that while Christ excels John and the other saints who were present at the time of his coming, he is surpassed by the glory of the ancients. For he can see that Moses is much inferior to Christ—Moses, who excelled all the ancients in holiness and was known by God above all others. But John indeed, by his own voice, places himself after [Christ], and thus left no ambiguity in this matter. But how shall we say that Moses is less than Christ? Examine carefully, he says, and compare the Gospel grace given to us through the Savior to the legal grace which Moses seems to have brought to us. For since the Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth were made through Jesus Christ: by as much as the teaching of Christ excels the discipline of the Law, and by as much as the grace and truth of Christ excel the legal commandments, by so much is it necessary to confess that Christ is more excellent than Moses. But how great the difference is between the Law...
