<meta>This page continues the theological comparison between the Law given through Moses and the grace brought by Jesus Christ, following the discussion of John the Baptist's testimony from the previous page.</meta>

->TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND<-

c 3

...the Law and the grace of Christ. Although it is outside our current purpose, a few things out of many must be said: for we believe that almost infinite things could be spoken on this subject. First, therefore, because the Law condemned the world (for <margin>Romans 11</margin> God, as Paul says, enclosed all things under sin through it), it showed us to be rightly subject to punishment; but the Savior liberated us. For he did not come to judge <margin>John 3</margin> the world, but to save it. Furthermore, although the Law also gave grace—by calling people back from the worship of idols to the knowledge of the true God and teaching them to discern good from evil—it did not do so perfectly, but rather as a schoolmaster <note>The Latin 'pædagogice' refers to the 'paidagogos', a tutor or guardian who led children to school in antiquity.</note> and in a practical way. The truth and grace of the Only-begotten, however, bestows good things upon us not in figures or shadows, but openly and clearly, leading us by his teaching to the perfect knowledge of faith. Moreover, the Law gave a spirit of servitude leading to fear, but Christ <margin>Romans 8</margin> gave a spirit of adoption leading to freedom. The Law introduced the circumcision of the flesh, which is nothing (as Paul says); the Lord introduced the circumcision of the spirit and the <margin>1 Corinthians 7</margin> heart through faith. The Law baptizes those defiled with water; the <margin>Matthew 3</margin> Savior baptizes in the Holy Spirit and fire. The Law led into the Tabernacle, which was a figure of true things; the Savior led us into heaven itself, and into the true Tabernacle, which not man, but the Lord established. There is no need to pile up more examples now, but it is timely to say that the blessed Paul, <margin>Hebrews 9</margin> comparing the Law with the grace of the Savior, resolved this question in very few words. For if the ministry of <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> condemnation was glorious, he says, how much more shall the ministry of righteousness overflow with glory! For he called the commandments of the Law the "ministry of condemnation," but he calls the grace of the Savior the "ministry of righteousness," to which he attributes an abundance of grace, judging rightly about the nature of things as a man of divine insight. If, therefore, the Law which condemns was given through Moses, but the grace which justifies was made through the Only-begotten, how could it not be more glorious? Truly, therefore, the Psalmist cries out in the spirit to the radiant multitude of the saints that Christ presides over them, saying: Who in the clouds shall be <margin>Psalm 89 (88 in Vulgate)</margin> equal to the Lord, or who among the sons of God shall be like the Lord? For the prophets are the "intellectual clouds" who all yield to Christ, in no way striving to be equal to him. For they are not ignorant that Moses—who above all others was known by God—conceded the first place to him. Moreover, the sons of God, who shone brightly at the time of his coming, will not be entirely like the Son, nor should they attribute this to themselves; but they will not be ignorant of their own measure, hearing the Baptist (of whom it was said: no one greater has arisen among those born of women) saying that he comes after Christ. Truly <margin>Matthew 11</margin> therefore, the Evangelist says he saw the glory of Christ, as the glory of the Only-begotten from the Father—of such a kind, certainly, that everyone would confess it belongs to the Only-begotten Son of God the Father, and not to those who are called to his <margin>Romans 8</margin> brotherhood (among whom he is the firstborn).

### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>D</margin> **No one has ever seen God. The Only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has revealed him.** Once again, the divine Evangelists noted the sharpness

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> of this point. He was not ignorant that some would say: "You describe the glory of the Only-begotten from the Father to us, but you do not bring forward anything great and sublime. For his glory could not be seen otherwise, except that he was more excellent than Moses and John—who were most singular men (we do not deny this)—and so you have called it the glory of the Only-begotten from the Father." But the blessed Isaiah did not speak thus: For I saw, he said, the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and the house was full of his majesty; and <margin>Isaiah 6</margin> seraphim stood around him, six wings to one, and six wings to another; with two they veiled the face, with two the feet, and with two they flew; and they cried to one another, saying: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Sabaoth <note>original: "dominus sabbaoth", meaning the Lord of Hosts.</note>, all the earth is full of his glory. Ezekiel <margin>Ezekiel 1</margin> <margin>B</margin> also said: Behold, a voice was made above the firmament that was over their heads, and above the firmament that was hanging over their heads: like the appearance of a sapphire stone was the likeness of a throne, and upon the likeness of the throne was a likeness as the appearance of a man above it. And I saw as it were the appearance of electrum <note>original: "electri". This refers to a glowing alloy of gold and silver, or amber, used to describe divine radiance.</note> from his loins upward, and from his loins downward I saw as it were the appearance of a shining fire all around, like the appearance of the bow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day; this was the appearance of the brightness round about. This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord. Since he was not ignorant that some would say such things out of impiety and ignorance, he necessarily suppressed their attempts long before by saying: "No one has ever seen God." For he says the Only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of God the Father, has revealed this to us. He said clearly to Moses: "no one shall see my face and live." He also taught the disciples: "no one <margin>Exodus 33</margin> <margin>C</margin> has seen the Father, except he who is from him." For <margin>John 6</margin> the Father is visible only to the consubstantial <term>Consubstantial: of the same essence or substance, translating the Greek 'homoousios'</term> Son, and to no one else besides him. Always understand "vision" in these cases in a way that is appropriate to God. Nevertheless, the speech of the prophets is not false when they cry out that the Lord of Sabaoth was seen by them. For they do not claim to have seen that which the nature of God is substantially; rather, they explain openly how they saw it, saying: "it is a vision of the *likeness* of the glory of the Lord." Therefore, it was formed enigmatically from corporeal things, as a figure of divine glory; which likeness, like a symbolic painting on a tablet, showed the excellence of divine glory to be beyond the mind and speech of man. Most excellently, therefore, the sublime Evangelist, when he <margin>D</margin> affirmed that he had seen his glory as the glory of the Only-begotten from the Father, confirms that he speaks truly by that excellence by which Christ surpassed everyone. For just as we perceive the power of the Creator through the beauty of his creatures—since the heavens without a <margin>Wisdom 13</margin> voice declare the glory of God, and the firmament <margin>Psalm 19 (18 in Vulgate)</margin> announces the works of his hands—so the Only-begotten is shown to be superior to others in glory by his works. But escaping the sharp sight of man's eyes as God, because he surpasses every creature, he is therefore understood and glorified as uncreated—that is, as God. This, in my judgment, is the sense of the proposed text.

But it must be noted again that he called him the Only-begotten Son and affirmed that he is in the bosom of the Father, so that he might separate him from every creature, and [show him to be] from the Father...

<meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria’s commentary on the Gospel of John, specifically interpreting the relationship between the Father and the Son. # SAINT CYRILL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.

...to have his own substance, and to show that he is in the Father. For if the Only-begotten is truly God, how will he not be of a different nature than those who are "gods" and "sons" by grace and adoption? For if he is the Only-begotten, he is not understood to be among brothers, but <margin>2 Corinthians 8</margin> <note>The text cites 2 Cor. 8, though the quote "one God the Father... and one Lord Jesus Christ" is found in 1 Cor. 8:6.</note> alone from the Father. For since according to Paul, although many are called gods in heaven and on earth, yet the Only-begotten God is separate from those other brothers who are gods through grace: "to us," he says, "there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." For since he is the one God and Father according to nature, the Word will not be outside the nature of God, since the Word is from him and in him; and, shining forth with the natural goods of the Begetter, he substantially ascends to an equal dignity, since he is God according to nature. For this reason, he asserts that he is in the "bosom of the Father," so that even from this you may understand that he is in him and from him, just as <margin>Psalm 109</margin> <note>original: "Ex utero ante luciferum genui te"; Psalm 110:3 in modern Bibles.</note> it is written in the Psalms: "From the womb, before the daystar, I have begotten you." For just as here, to specifically signify that he is *from* him, he used the word "womb" by analogy to humans—for those who are generated by us come forth from the belly—so when he says "in the Father’s bosom," he certainly meant in the Father’s "womb," from which the Son is born by an ineffable generation befitting of God. His offspring is not like a body cut off from the begetter, but the Son is in the Father, and has the Father in himself: for the proper goods of the Father’s substance, naturally flowing into the Son, show that the Father is in him. But again, the Father has the Son in himself—that is, fixed and (so to speak) rooted by an immutable identity of substance, germinating from him without any cutting or division, but in such a way that he is both within him and exists together with him. For in this way we piously understand the Son to be in the bosom of the Father, not as some who fight against God and (as the prophet says) pervert all right things, <margin>Micah 3. Romans 14. A Cavil.</margin> <note>The margin notes a "cavillatio," or a deceptive argument used by opponents (likely Arians) to undermine the Son's divinity.</note> attempting to seduce the simpler brothers for whom Christ died. For they say incorrectly: "Because the Son is said to be in the bosom of the Father, you rightly understand him to be from the Father and in the Father, and you preach that he was begotten from his substance as being of the same nature. But have you not heard," they say, "what Christ says regarding the rich man and Lazarus? For he says that <margin>Luke 16</margin> Lazarus, after death, was carried into the bosom of Abraham: and yet, because Lazarus was afterwards in the bosom of Abraham, it does not mean he is naturally from him or in him. Rather, by the word 'bosom,' the Scripture," they say, "understands 'charity' or 'love.'" Therefore, they argue the Son is in the bosom of the Father only in the sense of delight and love, just as the Father says he "loves the Son." But let them tell me, I pray: if "bosom" in the Scriptures signifies only <margin>Refutation. John 3. Psalm 124. Exodus 4.</margin> delight and love, then because God (according to the Savior’s word) "loved the world," or because the Lord "loves the gates of Zion," can we safely say that both the world and the gates of Zion are "in the bosom of God the Father"? Furthermore, when God commanded Moses to put his hand into his bosom, was he commanding him to *love* his hand, or rather to hide it in his bosom? We would certainly be ridiculous saying such things. Indeed, we would even act impiously against the Father himself if, believing that all things (for he loves all things) are in his bosom, we grant to creatures that which is attributed to his Son, so that the Son possesses nothing greater or worthier than the creatures do. Therefore, leaving these things aside, when-

<column-break/>

-ever the Son is said to be in the bosom of the Father, we understand nothing other than that the Son is from him and in him. This will be most clear to all who diligently consider the words of the Evangelist. For he says, "The Only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father." He first said "God" and "Only-begotten," and then immediately added, "Who is in the bosom of the Father," so that the Son might be understood to be from the Father naturally and substantially. He used "bosom" to represent "substance" by an analogy to bodies, which are more manifest to us than spiritual things. For images of sublime things are often taken from bodies, although many historical things are also understood as they are set forth, such as that regarding Moses: that he put his hand into his bosom. <margin>Exodus 4</margin> But as for what they say regarding Lazarus, <margin>Luke 16</margin> it not only does not oppose us, but even supports us. For Lazarus, having departed this life, was brought into the bosom of Abraham—that is, he was placed with the <margin>Genesis 17</margin> sons of Abraham; for God appointed him the father of many nations.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>I in the first place, John the Baptist: but in the second, John the Evangelist.</margin> **AND this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him, to ask him: Who are you? And he confessed, and did not deny: and he confessed, "I am not the Christ."** Now the Evangelist sets down the manner of John’s testimony more expressly, as if the event were currently happening, recording what he said when questioned. For when, he says, the leaders of the Jews according to the laws sent Levites and priests to ask him who he said he was, then he openly confessed the truth, saying: "I am not the Christ." Therefore, he implies: "Neither did I lie when I wrote concerning him, that he was not the Light, but that he might bear witness to the Light."

### CHAPTER XXIV.

**AND they asked him: What then? Are you Elijah? And he said: I am not. Are you the Prophet? And he answered: No. They said therefore to him: Who are you? That we may give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say of yourself? He said: I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, make straight the way of the Lord, as said the prophet Isaiah.** The Evangelist narrates each detail minutely, so that both the manner of the confession is placed before our eyes, and the ignorance of the Jews is stripped bare—those who, saying they are wise, have become fools. For while boasting of an exquisite knowledge of the Law and believing they hold the sense of the prophets, they reveal their ignorance by these questions. For that famous Moses, <margin>Deuteronomy 18</margin> signifying that the Lord would come as a prophet, foretold to the Jews: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from the midst of your brothers, like unto me; him you shall hear." And Isaiah, signifying the precursor to us, <margin>Isaiah 40</margin> said: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God." A third comes, Malachi, <margin>Malachi</margin> <note>Malachi 4:5-6.</note> who says of the Tishbite <note>term: "Tishbite" refers to the prophet Elijah.</note> that he will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the incredulous to the wisdom of the just, lest I come and strike the earth. Therefore, since there are three who were expected, those men, thinking more would come, truly hear: "You err, not knowing the scriptures." For when they had asked if he were the Christ, and it was answered to them that he was not <margin>Matthew 22</margin> the Christ, they then asked: "What then, are you Elijah?" He then...

...denying this, it remained for them to ask about the forerunner. But having unskillfully fallen back to the matter of Christ himself, and poorly understanding Moses, they ask: "Are you the Prophet?" Because of the preceding definite article, <note>original: "praescientem articulum"; Cyril is referring to the Greek grammar where the use of "the" (ho) implies a specific, expected figure rather than just any prophet.</note> this refers to that unique prophet and the lord of all prophets, whom the Baptist again affirmed he was not. Therefore they said to him: "Who are you? So that we may give an answer to those who sent us, what do you say about yourself?" He said: "I am the voice of one crying in the desert, <margin>Isaiah 40</margin> make straight the way of the Lord," just as the prophet Isaiah said. He sharply rebukes them as being ignorant of the Scriptures, explaining the ministry committed to him by prophetic authority. "For I come," he says, "to say that he who is expected is already at the doors, so that you may be ready to set out wherever he commands. Until now you have walked in the way of Moses; now take up the way of Christ, which all the prophets foretold to you." For Isaiah <margin>Isaiah 2</margin> exhorts you, saying: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will announce his way to us, and we shall walk in it." And <margin>Isaiah 35</margin> again: "There shall be a clean way there, and it shall be called the holy way; no lion shall be there, nor shall any small beast go up upon it; and those who were scattered shall walk in it." And again: "I will give a beginning to Zion, and I will exhort Jerusalem to the way." Jeremiah likewise <margin>Isaiah 41</margin> <margin>Jeremiah 6</margin> says: "Stand in the way, and seek the everlasting paths of the Lord, and see which is the good way, and walk in it, and you shall find the purification of your souls." What then is the good way, which purifies those who walk in it? Christ himself cries out, <margin>John 14</margin> "I am the way."

### CHAPTER XXV.

And those who had been sent were of the Pharisees. And they questioned him and said to him: "Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?") See what great audacity they use against the Baptist: "Why," they say, "do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor that Prophet?" For they do not think him worthy to be counted among the number of the one who was expected. Instead, out of their innate arrogance—even though they heard, "I am the voice of one crying in the desert, prepare the way of the Lord"—they pay little attention and, neglecting the Baptist’s dignity, they openly rebuke him, saying: "Why then do you baptize? Why have you dared to undertake such a great thing when you are not worthy?" For the Pharisees, out of their insolence, were always accustomed to utterly despise those who were present and to bestow a feigned honor upon the one yet to come. So that they might be great among the Jews and accumulate vast riches for themselves, they permitted no one but themselves to be honored. For this reason they also killed the heir himself, <margin>Matthew 21</margin> saying: "Come, let us kill him, and we shall retain his inheritance."

### CHAPTER XXVI.

John answered them, saying: "I baptize in water: but there has stood one in your midst whom you do not know. It is he who is to come after me, who was made before me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to undo." These things were done in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.) The blessed Baptist returned no insults for their abuse, but answers very kindly for the sake of their salvation, and teaches these unwilling men that Christ is already at the doors—indeed, even within the doors. "For I," he says, "by preparing, wash those defiled by sins with water at the beginning of repentance, and by this means I will prepare you from these lesser things for more sublime ones. For I was sent for this, and I do this as much by the act of baptizing as by words, preaching to prepare the way of the Lord. But the giver of greater things and of the highest perfection has stood in your midst, whom you have not yet recognized because he is clothed in flesh. He so far surpasses me that I am not worthy, like a servant compared to the master’s son, even to be the one who undoes the strap of his sandal." By this, I believe, he signifies that he is not worthy to perform even the lowest service for him; thus he speaks the truth and, by his own example, tries to lead the Pharisees from arrogance into humility. These things were done in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing. This is a sign of his diligence and of the greatness of these events. For men are certainly accustomed to commit to memory more carefully the individual places where great things were done or explained.

### CHAPTER I.

The next day John saw Jesus coming to him, and said: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.") In a very short time, he was made a prophet and an apostle together with being the Baptist. For the one whom he preached was coming, he now shows to be present. Therefore he exceeded the measure of the prophets, as the Savior said of him to the Jews: "What did you go out into the desert to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet." For <margin>Matthew 11</margin> the prophets foretold that Christ would come, but this man, preaching his coming, also showed him present. "For the next day," it says, "he saw Jesus coming to him, and said: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world." He does not say now, "Prepare his way," as before; but since he for whom the preparation was to be made was perceived present before their eyes, it was not to be preached in that old way, but explained more openly who this present person was, and for what reason he descended from heaven to us. "Behold therefore," he says, "the Lamb of God," that is to say, the one of whom Isaiah said: "He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before his shearer <margin>Isaiah 53</margin> he was silent." The entire Law of Moses signified him in figures; he who, in the times of the Law, did not pour out his mercy in this way nor to all—for the Law was wrapped in figures and shadows. But now, he who was preached enigmatically as the most perfect lamb, the immaculate victim, goes spontaneously to the slaughter so that he may drive away the sins of all, overturn the enemy of the world, destroy death by dying, and dissolve the curse given to men—lest that sentence, "Earth you are, and to earth you shall return," should forever subject the human race. This is the second Adam, <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> not from the earth but from heaven, the beginning of all goods and the destruction of death itself, the giver of eternal life, the cause of our reformation, by which we are refor...

-> SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK II. <-

we are reformed to God, the foundation of piety and justice, and the way to the kingdom of heaven: for one lamb is slain for all, so that he might offer the entire human race to God the Father. One died for all, so that he might win everyone over, so that all might no longer live for themselves, but for Christ (who died for all and rose for all). For since we were in sin, and therefore owed to death and destruction, the Father gave his own Son as a redemption for us—one for all. For all are in him, and he is better than all: one dies for all, so that we might all live in him. For when death swallowed the lamb slain for all, it could not hold him, but vomited him out—and all others with and in him. For if we are all in Christ, who died and rose for us after sin was destroyed, how will death, which is the fruit of sin, not also be destroyed? And once the root is torn up, how will the branches sprout? Or for what reason will we still be owed to death once sin, which was the cause of death, is destroyed? Therefore, in the slaying of the Lamb of God, we solemnly cry out, exulting with a loud voice: **Where now is your victory, O death?** <margin>1 Corinthians 15; Psalm 106</margin> **Where is your sting, O hell?** For "all iniquity" (as the Psalmist sang) "has shut its mouth," since, having been weakened, it can no longer accuse sinners; for it is God who justifies us. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having himself become a curse <margin>Galatians 3</margin> for us, so that we might escape the curse of sin.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>Luke 1</margin> **This is he of whom I said: After me comes a man who was made before me, who was prior to me; and I did not know him, but so that he might be manifested in Israel, therefore I came baptizing in water.** The Baptist brings to mind what he had said before, and of his own accord yields to the glory of Christ; he does this not only out of charity but also out of the necessity of truth. For the creature is subject, even if unwillingly, to the Creator, the servant to the master, and the gift to the Giver. Regarding how Christ, who was prior to John, "came after" John, enough has been said in the preceding sections. **And I did not know him, but so that he might be manifested in Israel, therefore I came baptizing in water.** He who rejoiced while recognizing the Lord in the Virgin's womb, who prophesied before his birth, and who was a disciple from his mother's belly, now confesses that he does not know the Savior—and in this, he does not lie. For God alone knows all things from himself without the teaching of anyone else; every creature, however, learns not from itself but from the teaching of another. The Spirit dwelling in holy men fills what nature cannot provide, and bestows its own good upon human nature; thus illuminated, the soul knows future things and hidden mysteries. Therefore, when he says he did not know the Lord, he speaks most truly according to the measure of the human race and of the creature, yet also very usefully. Although he asserted he did not know the Savior, he nevertheless confesses that he came for this reason: to manifest him to the Jewish people, so that he might not seem to run ahead to give testimony of his own will, but as a minister of the divine dispensation and will. God revealed to his mind who it was that would take away the sins of the world. Therefore, the Jews ought to have believed his testimony more easily,

<column-break/>

since they understood that he did not know the Savior by his own power, but had come to know him through God's revelation. They could also infer how great the Master was from the dignity and greatness of the servant. For clearly, when he confesses that he came to manifest him in Israel, he clearly shows that he himself is the servant and the other is the Lord.

<margin>That the Spirit does not flow into the Son by participation, nor from the outside as in the saints, but is in him substantially and according to nature. Chapter III.</margin>

### CHAPTER III.

**And John bore witness, saying: I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven and remaining upon him. And I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.** Since he had said in the previous sections that he did not know him, he now reveals that divine mystery more extensively. For he shows both the manner in which he learned what he had been ignorant of, and that God the Father was the teacher; in this way, he leads the minds of his listeners to the truth by many various paths. For when he says he learned the mystery from God the Father, he shows that everyone who opposes his preaching—thereby setting themselves against the great counsel of the Father—is resisting God. Thus, he tries to persuade everyone in a clear and fitting way to receive the Savior, especially since he testifies that he saw the Spirit descend in the sign of a dove and remain upon Christ. In addition to this, he affirms that he heard from the one who sent him to baptize in water that he who baptizes in the Spirit is the one upon whom the Spirit would descend and remain. This witness is certainly worthy of belief, as is this new and unheard-of sign; and the one who said and showed these things to the Baptist is the Father and God of all. But enough on these things for now. 

Perhaps the crowd of <term>heretics</term> <note>Cyril is likely targeting the Arians, who argued that if Jesus received the Holy Spirit, he must have been "lesser" than God or lacked something in his divine nature.</note>, eager for contention, will insult us again and again, saying: "We have nothing unless we wish to quibble, for how can we escape from this?" "Behold," they say, "the Spirit descends to the Son; behold, the Son is anointed by God the Father; clearly he is receiving what he does not have." The Psalmist also attests to this, saying to the Son: **Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.** <note>Psalm 45:7</note> How then can the Son be <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: 'consubstantialis' — meaning of the exact same substance or essence as the Father, a core doctrine of the Trinity.</note> with the Father if he is not as perfect as the Father and therefore had to be anointed? To such men, who pervert the truth of Christian dogma and the sense of the Scriptures, we can appropriately say: **Wake up, you drunkards, from your wine!** So that, seeing the most brilliant light of truth, you may cry out with us to the Son: **Truly, you are the Son of God.** For if you believe him to be God by nature, how can he be imperfect? Or how will this impiety not also reach the Father himself? For from where will the Father have perfection if the Son is imperfect? Or how will the Father himself not be driven toward the diminishment of the Son (who according to you is imperfect), if the divine substance once admitted imperfection in the Son? For you will not dare (I think) to divide the divine and immortal nature into different categories of substance so that it appears perfect in one and imperfect in the other.

He also defends the divinity of Christ against heretics who claimed that Christ's baptism and anointing implied he was an imperfect being inferior to the Father.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria’s defense of the equality of the Son with the Father. The previous page discussed Christ as the Lamb of God; here, Cyril refutes the argument that Christ is inferior to the Father or that he only became "holy" when the Spirit descended upon him at his baptism.</meta>

<page-num>64</page-num>
-> WITH GEORGE OF TREBIZOND AS TRANSLATOR <-
<meta>catchword: holy</meta>

...one should see: especially since you see that the nature of human essence is one and the same in all people. One person does not possess "more" or "less" of humanity than another, insofar as they are human. In the same way, one angel can never differ from another angel by the very fact that both are angels—by which, clearly, all are included in one species and nature. How, then, shall the nature of the Godhead, which is incomparably above all these things, possess fewer good things than a creature? How shall that incorruptible nature admit inequality, when even corruptible things do not admit it <note>Cyril argues that within a single "type" of thing (like humans), the essence is equal; therefore, God cannot be "more" or "less" God than himself</note>? How shall God be simple and uncomposed, if both the perfect and the imperfect exist within Him? For these things are dissimilar, and you falsely judge that His nature consists of them. For if the perfect and the imperfect were similar and did not differ from each other, then everything perfect would be imperfect, and vice versa. Therefore, the Son is not more imperfect than the Father, nor the Father more perfect than the Son, even though you <note>Addressing the Arian heretics who claimed the Son was subordinate to the Father</note> say so repeatedly. But if there is a great difference between the perfect and the imperfect, and the nature of the Godhead is capable of receiving both, it will not be simple, but composite. 

<margin>
A quibble.
</margin>

But perhaps someone will say that contrary things cannot exist in the same subject at the same time, but rather separately and through succession—just as in a body, a color is now white, now black. You have fought well for us, my friend, and have quickly turned to our side! For if the nature of the Godhead is one, and no other besides it can be imagined, how is it capable of receiving contraries? Or how shall things that are contrary to each other happen to the one and the same subject at the same time? 

<margin>
The solution.
</margin>

For the Father is God by nature, and the Son is likewise God by nature. Therefore, there is no difference of "perfect" and "imperfect" between the Father and the Son, who flowed forth from the most perfect substance of the Father. Is it not necessary that the offspring of the most perfect parent be perfect? He is the "unchangeable image" and the "stamp of his <term>hypostasis</term>" <note>original: "character suae hypostaseos." Hypostasis refers to the distinct "person" or "individual reality" of the Father, of which the Son is the exact representation.</note>. I believe everyone will utterly agree with this. For how else shall the Son be the unchangeable "stamp" of the perfect Father, if he is not perfect by nature, as some recklessly claim? For since he is the stamp and the image, he is certainly perfect in the same way as He whose image he is.

<margin>
A quibble.
</margin>

But, the opponent says, John saw the Spirit descending from heaven upon the Son. Therefore, the Father from above sanctified the Son, upon whom the sanctifying Spirit descended as if he did not already possess him. 

<margin>
The refutation.
</margin>

Do you notice how clearly you preach that the Son of God is a creature? You hardly attribute anything great to him when you judge that he is perfected and sanctified by an external gift of goods, just like other creatures. And how will the Evangelist not be a liar when he says, "From his fullness we have all received"? <margin>John 1</margin> For how shall he be full by his own nature if he receives from another? Or how shall God truly be the Father if the Only-Begotten is a creature and not a Son? For then He would be "Father" in word only, not in reality; and likewise the Only-Begotten would be "Son" in name only, not truly a Son. But if God is truly the Father, He will likewise have Him whose Father He is, born naturally from Himself. Furthermore, how shall the Father, who is holy by nature, beget a Son who is void of holiness, and produce an offspring alienated from His own natural goods? For if he acquires sanctification from the outside...

<column-break/>

<page-num>65</page-num>

...as those fools babble, one must admit (even if unwillingly) that he was not always holy, but was only sanctified at the moment when the Spirit (as John says) descended upon him. How then, even before the incarnation, did the Seraphim in the first rank glorify him as holy, saying "Holy" three times? <margin>Isaiah 6</margin> If, therefore, he was holy even before the incarnation—or rather, if he is always holy, just as the Father is—how did he, having become man in these last ages, stand in need of sanctification? 

But I cannot help but wonder why this point escaped them, though they seem so studious. For if sanctification is not substantially within the Son, but comes to him from the outside as it does to a rational creature, it must be possible for him to at some point shake it off. He who shakes off and casts away sanctification from himself would surely fall into worse things, weighed down by the bond of sin, not preserving or retaining in himself that which kept him from sin before. Therefore, the Son would not be unchangeable. The Psalmist would also be lying when he cries out to him: "But you are the same." <margin>Psalm 101</margin> 

To this, I shall not omit something similar to the previous points: everyone led by reason will admit that the "thing participated in" is different by nature from the "participant." Otherwise, the participant and the thing participated in would be the same, which is intellectually impossible. For how shall something participate in itself? If, therefore, the participant and the thing participated in are of different natures, let those who contend that the Spirit exists in the Son through "participation" consider what great impiety they have fallen into without realizing it. For if the Son is a participant in the Spirit, and the Spirit is holy by nature, then the Son will not be holy by nature, but will have been reformed by grace from worse things to better things through participation in another. 

From this, many absurdities follow. First (as we said), he will be susceptible to change; or rather, he has already changed (for he progressed toward the better, as you say). Thus, he is not only "not less" than the Father, but in some way he has even been made greater! For Paul writes of him: "Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient." <margin>Philippians 2</margin> 

Since, therefore, before the incarnation he was established in the form and equality of the Father, but after being incarnated he was (according to you) sanctified by receiving the Spirit from heaven, he will now appear better and greater than himself. Consequently, he has also become greater than the Father, to whom he was previously equal. If this is so, and he exceeded the Father by receiving the Spirit, then the Spirit through whom the Son achieved this would also be greater and better than the Father. 

I judge these things to be horrible even to hear and full of danger; but we cannot otherwise drive away the harm that the church suffers through their impiety. Therefore, I think we must pursue this: if the Only-Begotten Son of God, having become man, is only then sanctified by the Spirit as if he were not holy before the incarnation (though he was, according to them, in the equality and form of the Father), it follows that God the Father, who is holy by nature...

# SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK II.

<margin>Psalm 140 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 141:3-4.</note></margin>
A ...with the river <note>Likely referring to the "river of the Spirit" or the flow of grace discussed on the lost end of the previous page.</note> poured out, they might cry out with a loud voice among us:
> Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint for my lips; do not turn my heart toward words of malice.

For wicked and unjust are the speeches which, when uttered thoughtlessly by them, cause the greatest harm to those who hear. But we, banishing their trifles from our hearts, shall follow the right path of faith, mindful of that passage of Scripture: *destroying counsels, and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every intellect into captivity to the obedience of Christ.* <margin>2 Corinthians 10</margin> Come then, bringing every understanding of the proposed theorem <note>In this context, a "theorem" is a theological proposition or a subject of contemplation.</note> into captivity to the glory of the Only-begotten [Son], let us wisely subject it to him in all things, just as we attribute it to him as a man: *who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, that he might enrich us by his poverty* <margin>2 Corinthians 8</margin>—which we shall not find it burdensome to explain more broadly to those with receptive ears.

B Man is said by Moses to have been made *in the image and likeness of the true God* <margin>Genesis 1</margin>; Moses was the one who, by the Spirit, composed the first books of Scripture for us. We have also learned from the same Spirit that man was sealed in the divine image. *And he breathed into his face,* it says, *the breath of life.* <margin>Genesis 1 and 2</margin> For at once the Spirit instilled life into the creature and impressed his own character <note>original: "characterem." In this sense, it refers to a distinctive mark or a seal-impression, like that on a coin.</note> upon him, as befits God. Thus, a rational animal <note>The standard philosophical definition of a human being in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> was established by God the craftsman, received a command for salvation, and remained in paradise as long as he preserved the grace of the Creator through the indwelling Holy Spirit.

C But afterward, having been seduced by the devil's deception, he despised God's precepts; and having scorned the command, he lost that grace and heard that he was earth and to earth he would return. And the likeness of God, in which he had been created, did not preserve its character so clearly because of sin, but retained it in a way that was darkened and weakened. Then, as the human race multiplied, sin also grew to such an extent and so oppressed wretched souls that humans, stripped of the grace of God—since the Spirit had utterly flown away from them—became as if completely devoid of reason, and they even ignored the Creator himself.

D Therefore, moved by mercy, the Creator wished to recall human nature to its ancient image through the Spirit. For man could not recover the divine impression <note>The "imprint" or "stamp" of God's likeness.</note> in any other way than through the Spirit. Now we must discuss how this was done, and how the Spirit planted roots in us, or how he firmly planted his grace within us, or how our reformed nature took root in the Spirit. For since the first Adam, by his own freedom, chose not good as he ought, but evil as we have said, and thus, being sentenced to death, had lost the Holy Spirit—who, as it is written, *flees from the wicked and does not dwell in a body subject to sins* <margin>Wisdom 1</margin>—the mercy of God sent us a "second Adam" from heaven. For he sent his Son, immutable by nature and far removed from all sin, to take on our flesh; so that just as by the transgression of the first Adam we were subjected to a curse, so by the virtue of the obedience of the second Adam we might both escape the curse and no longer fear the losses that followed from it. Therefore, the man [Christ] who truly became the Son of God, as one of the humans, receives the Spirit from the Father—not because he himself needed it, he who is the giver...

<meta>Catchword: largitor (the giver/bestower)</meta>

<summary>Cyril explains that humanity was created with the Holy Spirit as a divine "seal" but lost this grace through Adam's sin. He argues that Christ, the "Second Adam," became human to restore this lost Spirit and divine image to mankind.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section where Cyril explains that Christ, as the "Second Adam," restores the Holy Spirit to human nature. The previous page discussed how humanity lost this divine grace through sin, and how Christ—being sinless—is the perfect vessel to reclaim it for us.</meta>

# TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.

He is the giver of the Spirit itself, but He preserves the Spirit received as a man so that He might keep it for us, and so that grace, which we had lost, might take root in us through Him who was entirely ignorant of sin. For this reason (as I believe), the Baptist says he saw the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon Him. For the Spirit, which flew away from us because of sin, remained in Him because it found no sin in Him. Therefore, He received the Spirit in Himself for our sake, and He renews our ancient blessings; in this way, He is also said to have been made poor for us. <margin>1 Corinthians 8</margin> For although He is God and in need of nothing, He became a man lacking all things, of whom it is rightly written: *What do you have that you <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin> did not receive?* <note>original: "Quid autem habes quod nõ accepisti?"</note> Therefore, just as He is Life by nature, yet died as a man for our sake so that—having conquered death—He might raise our entire nature with Him (for we are all in Him, insofar as He is man), so also He receives the Spirit for our sake, so that He may sanctify our whole nature. For He did not become man for His own benefit, but so that He might become the way and the door to heavenly blessings for us. For if He had not received the Spirit as a man, or if He had not suffered as a man, how could anyone show that He had been humbled? Or how could the nature of a servant be rightly recovered, unless certain things were truly written about Him as if about a servant? Let no one, therefore, mock the most wise logic of the <term>dispensation<note>The "dispensation" (or "economy") refers to the divine plan for human salvation, specifically how God works through the Incarnation of Christ.</note></term>, which the divine Paul admired, crying out: *that the multiform wisdom of God <margin>Ephesians 3</margin> might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavens through the church, according to the eternal purpose which He made in Christ Jesus our Lord.* For the sublime mystery of the Incarnation is certainly a wisdom worthy of God. In this way, I believe, we must piously believe that the Spirit descended upon Christ. For we shall never descend to such recklessness as to believe that the Spirit is in the Son by "participation" <note>In Greek theology, "participation" implies a created being receiving a gift from outside itself; Cyril argues the Spirit belongs to Christ's very essence.</note>, whom we confess to be in the Son substantially (just as He is certainly in the Father). For we read in the Scriptures that the Spirit belongs to the Son, just as He belongs to the Father: *When they had come <margin>Acts 16</margin> to Mysia,* it says, *they tried to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them.* <note>original: "spiritus Iesu"</note> If, however, anyone still dares to contend that the Spirit is in the Son by participation, or that the Spirit first came upon Him when He was baptized by John, let him consider, I pray, how many impious consequences follow. For first, we see John—<margin>Matthew 11, John 1, Luke 1</margin> than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women, and who reached the very peak of virtue—approaching Christ as God. For he says, *I am not worthy to untie the strap of His sandal.* How, then, is it not impious to believe that the Lord of John and of all people—when John himself was filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb (for so it is written of him)—only then first received the Spirit when He was baptized? Yet Gabriel certainly said to the holy Virgin: *The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and <margin>Ibid. <note>Refers to Luke 1:35</note></margin> the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore, the holy thing that shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God.* Attend, I pray, to how deep a meaning this discourse contains.

<column-break/>

For while it is written of John that he "shall be filled" with the Holy Spirit (for John possessed the Spirit as a gift from without, not substantially implanted), regarding the Savior it is written quite properly: He will not "be filled," <margin>Ibid.</margin> but rather: *the holy thing that shall be born of you.* Nor did the angel add that He "would become" holy, because as God by nature, He is *always* holy; rather, He *shall be called* holy. But since we must gather evidence from every side, come, let us also consider the words of the angel. He says, *The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore, the holy thing that shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God.* Let the adversaries of the Church say, I pray, whether the Word of God was the Son of God before the Incarnation, or whether He was being worshipped under a false name, as if He were illegitimate? For if they deny He was the Son, they must also deny there was a Father. For of whom was He the Father, if there were no Son? But all Scripture cries out that there was a Father and a Son. If, however, they confess that He was the Son even before the Incarnation, why does the angel announce that what was to be born of the Virgin "would be called" the Son of God, when He was this naturally from eternity? Therefore, just as He is the Son eternally with the Father, yet is called the Son of God as if starting a new beginning from the time of the Incarnation (since He then lived in the world as a man among men), so also, although He has His own Spirit substantially within Himself, <margin>Baruch 3</margin> He is nevertheless written to "receive" it as a man, preserving the dignity appropriate to a human being, and attributing the properties of our nature to Himself for our sake. For how can the Word be understood without His own Spirit? Would it not be absurd if someone were to separate the spirit that is in a man from the man himself, yet think the nature of his reason and his whole soul remained intact? I think so entirely. How then shall we separate the Spirit from the Son, who is so innate to Him, so substantially joined, and proceeding through Him? He is so naturally in Him that, because of the identity of their nature, He cannot be understood as something else separate from Him. *If you love me,* (the Savior says to His disciples) *keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of Truth, whom the world cannot receive.* Look, He most clearly called the Spirit of Truth the "Holy Spirit." Yet there is no other Truth besides the Son. He says, *I am the Truth.* <margin>John 14</margin> See what a great identity the Spirit has with that Truth. For this same John writes in his epistles <margin>1 John 5</margin> about the Savior: *This is He who came by water and blood and the Spirit: Jesus Christ; not in water only, but in water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies, because Christ is the Truth.* Therefore, when the Spirit dwells in the inner man, Christ Himself is said to dwell there. And certainly, this is the natural state of things, which Paul taught most clearly: *You,* he says, *are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. If <margin>Romans 8</margin> anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not His. But if Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness.* If Christ is in you, he immediately added, to show the identity of the Son with the Spirit, who is His own, and who is from Him according to nature...

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cyril of Alexandria, translated into Latin by George of Trebizond, focusing on the baptism of Christ and the subsequent testimony of John the Baptist. It addresses the nature of the Holy Spirit and the divinity of the Son against heretical views.</meta>

# BLESSED CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK II.

...is poured out, he might show. For this reason, he is also called the Spirit of <term>adoption</term><note>The theological concept where believers become children of God through the Holy Spirit.</note>, in whom we cry: **Abba, Father.** 
<margin>1 John 4</margin>
And as John writes in his epistles: *By this we know that he is in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.* I think these points suffice to repel the darts of the heretics. But if anyone does not wish to unlearn their impiety from the Son, but instead contends that the Holy Spirit was first received from the Son only when he became incarnate: let them show us from the scriptures that he was not the Son of God before then, and we shall be silent. 

However, one must marvel at how carefully the Evangelist everywhere maintains what is fitting for the divine nature. For although in the preceding passages he asserted that no one has seen God, and now he confirms that the Spirit was seen by the Baptist, he did not forget to immediately add that it was seen not in its own nature, but in the form of the gentlest of animals <note>original: "mitissimi animalis specie" — referring to the dove.</note>. Thus, by this also, he is seen to be naturally joined to the Son. For he says: 
<margin>Matthew 11</margin>
*Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart.* Therefore, the Spirit does not fall away from the nature of God; as he is immutable, he was never seen except by the wood and figure of the dove for the benefit of the learner. 
<margin>John 1</margin>
For the Baptist himself confesses that this was given to him as a sign, when he said in his testimony: *He who sent me to baptize in water, he said to me: Upon whom you see the Spirit descending, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.* Whence the rash opinion of the heretics must be exploded, who translate what was done as a sign into a reality of things, even though it was done through <term>dispensation</term><note>The divine plan or arrangement of events in salvation history.</note> for the benefit of our race, as we said above.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Proverbs 25</margin>
**I saw, and I have borne witness, that this is the Son of God.** This is the testimony of a most weighty witness, who is not ignorant of what is written: *What your eyes have seen, that you shall speak.* For see, he says, the sign given to me, and I understood that it was he who was signified, and I bear witness that this is the Son of God, who is described by the figures of the Mosaic law, and who is foretold by the writings of the prophets. 

The title "Son of God" is most safely used with the addition of the <term>article</term><note>Cyril emphasizes the Greek definite article "the" (ho huios) to distinguish Jesus as the unique Son by nature, rather than a son by grace like humans.</note>, so that he alone might be shown to be the heir of all the Father's goods according to nature; we are confirmed in this same dignity through <term>adoption</term>, having been invited to it by his grace. 
<margin>Ephesians 3</margin>
For just as all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is from the Father, because he himself is primarily, properly, and truly the only Father; so also all sonship is from the Son, because he himself is primarily, properly, and truly the only Son. He is not a bastard, nor is he falsely so called, but he is from the very <term>substance</term><note>Greek: "ousia." The core essence or being of God.</note> of God the Father. This is not by cutting, or flowing out, or division, since the nature of the deity admits of no suffering or change; but as one from one, he is always together with the begetter, co-eternal with him and innate. For he is in him, and proceeds from him indivisibly and inseparably. 

For the nature of the deity is not a body, nor is it circumscribed by place, nor does it pass through the spaces of locations; but just as heat is innate in fire, so he proceeds from him and is in him. Thus, although he may seem to be something else, he is nevertheless not separated from him, but remains as the whole in the whole fire. So must we understand regarding the Son

<column-break/>

of God, adapting our understanding to more sublime things by this likeness. We believe that he subsists indeed in his own <term>hypostasis</term><note>A technical term for "person" or "individual reality" within the Trinity.</note>, but we shall neither place him outside the one and ineffable deity, nor shall we confess him to be of any other substance than the Father's. For otherwise he will not be truly and truly the Son; and a "new god" would be discovered by us if we thought him to be anything other than the one and only God. For if he is not <term>consubstantial</term><note>original: "consubstantialis" — of the same substance (Greek: homoousios).</note> with God the Father, how does he not fall away from the true title of God? But since we have the Baptist as a most weighty witness, who bears testimony that *this is the Son of God*, we shall not hesitate to preach him as true God, and as the Son from the substance of the Father. For the name of true sonship can signify nothing other than this.

### CHAPTER V.

**The next day John stood again, and two of his disciples; and looking upon Jesus as he walked, he says: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.** He had already shown him before, and called him truly and properly the Son of God by adding the article; now again he shows him to his disciples, and naming him the **Lamb of God**, he affirms that he is the one who takes away the sin of the world. He calls them back to the memory of that prophetic saying: 
<margin>Isaiah 43</margin>
*I, even I, am he who blots out your iniquities.* Thus, by frequently preaching the same things about the Savior, he performs the duty of an excellent teacher. For it is certainly the work of a teacher to diligently repeat what the listeners have not yet rightly understood. 
<margin>Philippians 3</margin>
For this reason, the blessed Paul also writes: *To say the same things to you is not troublesome to me, and it is safe for you.*

### CHAPTER VI.

**And the two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed him.** You see how quickly the fruit followed from the Baptist's teaching; you see how great a benefit the repetition of the discourse brought to the listeners. Let him, therefore, to whom the work of teaching is entrusted, learn from these things: that silence is not to be praised in a pastor, nor is the Lord's talent to be committed to the silence of unfruitful earth; 
<margin>Matthew 25</margin>
rather, it is to be distributed to the money-changers, so that the Savior may demand it back with interest, like a fertile seed bringing life in productive soil. You have learned the confirmation of all these things by the example of the Baptist, who did not grow weary of showing the Lord again and again. By this iteration of teaching, he contributed so much to his disciples that he has now persuaded some; for two of his disciples immediately followed the Lord.

### CHAPTER VII.

**But Jesus turned, and seeing them following him, says to them: What do you seek?** The Lord turned opportunely to those following him, so that you might learn that what we sing is true in reality: 
<margin>Psalm 33</margin>
*I sought the Lord, and he heard me.* For as long as we seek the Lord neither with right faith nor with honest morals, we are found to be behind him, as it were; but when, knowing his divine mandates, we search for the chief way of justice, he immediately visits us, turning and crying out: 
<margin>Zechariah 1</margin>
*Turn to me, and I will turn to you.* Moreover, he asked what they were seeking—not because he was ignorant, as he who knows all things as God, but so that the question might become the beginning of a conversation.

<summary>Cyril of Alexandria discusses the baptismal sign of the dove and the consubstantial nature of the Son, emphasizing that Christ is the "Son of God" by nature rather than adoption. He also highlights John the Baptist's role as a teacher whose persistent testimony leads the first disciples to follow Jesus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cyril of Alexandria, translated from Greek into Latin by George of Trebizond. It moves from the testimony of John the Baptist to the calling of the first disciples: Andrew, Peter, Philip, and Nathanael.</meta>

->TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.<-

### CAP. VIII.

**T**hey said to him: Rabbi (which is translated as Master) where are you staying? <note>original: "Rabbi (quod dicitur interpretatum magister)"</note> Responding learnedly to his questions, they first called him "Master," for they desired to learn from him. Then they asked where he lived, as if they intended to discuss more weighty matters more appropriately at home; for they did not think it right to speak of serious things just anywhere. This action of theirs is set before us as a very useful example to follow.

### CAP. IX.

**H**e said to them: Come and see. He did not simply tell them where he lived, though they had asked this very thing, but urged them to go there at once. He did this first to teach that no delay should be praised when seeking good things, since a delay in usefulness always brings harm; and secondly, to show that it is not enough for someone to learn where the house of Christ—that is, the Church—is founded, but rather one must come into it through faith and behold with a fervent heart the mysteries celebrated within it.

### CAP. X.

**T**hey came and saw where he stayed, and they stayed with him that day; it was about the tenth hour. <note>The "tenth hour" in Roman timekeeping was late afternoon, approximately 4:00 PM.</note> The disciples of the divine mysteries were taught with exceeding fitness through this knowledge. For it is not right that we, quickly satisfied, should depart from divine doctrine; rather, we must maintain our fervor throughout the entire span of our lives. I believe this is what is signified when it says: "because they stayed with him that day." Moreover, he says the hour was about the tenth to remind us that the mystery of our Savior was not enacted at the beginning of the ages, but after they had already progressed a great deal. For in the last days (as it is written), <margin>Jeremiah 31. John 6.</margin> we have all been made teachable by God. Furthermore, he says they turned aside and stayed with God at the tenth hour so that those who cling to Christ through faith may learn that they must not be alienated from him by sin or unbelief.

### CAP. XI.

**A**ndrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who heard John and followed him. He first found his own brother Simon and said: We have found the Messiah (which is translated as Christ), and he led him to Jesus. <note>original: "Messiam, quod est interpretatum Christus"</note> When the disciples of John had received such a gift, they immediately returned it to the Lord multiplied. This is certainly the mark of an attentive and teachable soul: that it does not need a long speech, nor does it produce the fruit of doctrine only after many years or months. Instead, as soon as it hears, it both benefits itself and strives to be useful to others. For "Give a reason to a wise man," it says, "and he will be wiser; teach a just man, and he will increase." <margin>Proverbs 9. Matthew 13.</margin> Thus Andrew saved his brother Peter by briefly signaling such a great matter: "We have found the Messiah," he said—like a treasure hidden in a field, or a pearl of great price, according to the parables of the Gospel itself.

### CAP. XII.

**J**esus looked at him and said: You are Simon, son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas (which is translated as Peter). <note>Cephas is the Aramaic word for "Rock," translated into the Greek "Petros" and Latin "Petrus."</note> He looks upon him as becomes God, who searches hearts and minds; <margin>Psalm 7.</margin> and since he is ignorant of nothing, he sees to what height of faith and virtue this disciple will reach.

<column-break/>

Even before he had asked anything about him, he called both the man and his father by name. By this act, he instructed the disciple that he is the one who knows all things even before they happen. <margin>Matthew 16.</margin> He predicts that his name will no longer be Simon, but Peter—fittingly signifying by that very name that he would build his Church upon him as upon a rock and most firm stone.

### CAP. XIII.

**T**he next day, he wanted to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip and said to him: Follow me. Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. Philip also (as I suspect) was of an upright soul and very inclined to follow Christ. Knowing his future faith and virtue, Jesus called him with a single word; and by that word, the great grace that was in him is revealed. For indeed, the life of a man is proven worthy when he is commanded to follow Christ; for Jesus would not have chosen him unless he were upright.

### CAP. XIIII.

**P**hilip found Nathanael and said to him: We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the law and the prophets, Jesus the son of Joseph from Nazareth. Very quickly, like those mentioned before, Philip also returned fruit. For he did not find Nathanael by chance, but found him after seeking with great zeal. He knew him to be a man most studious and diligent in the scriptures, and therefore he addressed him as one skilled in the law and all prophecy, saying that he had now found the Christ who is predicted by all scripture as the one to come. Now, there was an opinion about our Savior among the Jews that he was a Nazarene, even though scripture calls him a Bethlehemite, saying: "And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrata, are by no means the least among the princes of Judah, for from you shall come a leader who will rule my people Israel, and his going forth is from the days of eternity." <margin>Micah 5.</margin> For scripture testifies that he was brought up in Nazareth. "And they came," says the Evangelist, "to Nazareth, where he was raised." <margin>Luke 4.</margin> Philip therefore followed the common opinion: "We have found him," he said, "who was expected as foretold in the scriptures, Jesus the son of Joseph from Nazareth."

### CAP. XV.

**N**athanael said to him: Can anything good come from Nazareth? Nathanael could not easily believe that something great and preeminent could have its origin in Nazareth. This did not command the faith of a man skilled in the law and all prophecy since (as we have said) the prophets predicted that Christ would come not from Nazareth, but from Bethlehem. [Philip replies]: "If you will only see," he says, "if you will speak with him, you will most easily agree with me that he is undoubtedly the one who is expected." For we must believe that there was an ineffable grace in the speech and words of Christ, by which the souls of his listeners were drawn with great joy. For it is written that "all wondered at the words of grace that came from his mouth." <margin>Luke 4.</margin> For just as divine power was present in his words to perform signs, so also did he possess great power to persuade.

### CHAPTER XVI.

**Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said: Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile.** Before he drew men to faith through the miracle of signs, he showed himself to be God by nature in another way—no less wonderful—having come in human form for the salvation of mankind. What was that way? The knowledge of hidden things, which is attributed to God alone. Therefore, he does not flatter Nathanael with the pursuit of adulation, but by exposing those things of which Nathanael was aware, he confirms that he knows the hearts of men (which belongs to God alone).

### CHAPTER XVII.

**Nathanael said to him: How do you know me?** Nathanael is amazed, and moved toward faith, he seeks to learn how Christ knew him. For a studious mind desires exact and exquisite instruction in matters before it. However, he perhaps suspected that these things had been told to the Lord beforehand by Philip.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

**Jesus answered and said to him: Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I knew you.** The Savior shook off all his suspicion when he asserted that he had seen him under the fig tree—even though he was physically far away—before Philip had even spoken with him about Jesus. The specific mention of the **fig tree** describes the place more certainly; thus, Nathanael, who was conscious of his own location, is invited to a firmer faith by a witness of the truth who carried weight within himself.

### CHAPTER XIX.

**Nathanael answered him and said: Rabbi, you are the son of God; you are the king of Israel.** Nathanael knew well that the hearts of men are open to God alone, and he held fixed in his mind that saying of the Psalmist: *God searches the hearts and the reins* <note>original: "Scrutans corda, & renes deus." Reins is an archaic term for kidneys, historically viewed as the seat of emotions and hidden intent.</note>. For the prophets attributed this power to no one else but the divine nature. When he perceived this quality in the Lord, he confessed him as teacher, Son of God, and King of Israel.
<margin>Psalm 7.</margin>

### CHAPTER XX.

**Jesus answered and said to him: Because I told you I saw you under the fig tree, you believe; you will see greater things than these.** You shall be more fervent in faith, he says, when you see greater things than these. For if you were led to faith by one sign, how will you not be better when you behold more wonderful things?

### CHAPTER XXI.

**And he said to them: Amen, amen, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.** Behold, once Nathanael’s faith was established, Jesus turned his speech to everyone in common. He announces that angels will come up and down to the Son of Man, by whose commands it will be believed (and rightly so) that he is most truly the Son of God. For the heavenly powers do not serve just anyone, but God. For although some are subject to others in a certain order, such subjection is not slavery; yet of the Son of God it is written: *because angels came and ministered to him.*
<margin>Matthew 4.</margin>

### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>John Chapter Two.</margin>
**And on the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there; and Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding. And when the wine failed, the mother of Jesus said to him: They have no wine.** He now opportunely arrives at the beginning of his signs. For since the wedding was being celebrated honorably, both the mother and he himself with his disciples were present as invited guests; he went more for the sake of the miracle he was about to perform than for the sake of the feast, and further, so that he might sanctify the beginning of our birth, as far as the flesh is concerned. It was certainly fitting—since he was restoring the whole nature of man for the better—not only to bless those already born, but also to prepare grace for those yet to be born, and to make their entrance into this life holy by his presence and the authority of a miracle. Furthermore, it was said to the woman because of sin that she would give birth to children in pain <note>A reference to the "curse of Eve" in Genesis 3:16.</note>. How else, then, was this curse to be driven away—lest the sanctity of marriage seem condemned—except by the presence of the Savior? Since he is true joy, he drove away the ancient sorrow of marriage by his presence. For every creature is new in Christ; old things have passed away, as Paul says, and all things have been made new. The disciples were also present so that they might confirm their faith by the miracle. When the wine failed, his mother, who was not ignorant that all things were possible for him, urged him to use his customary goodness and mercy. For she said, "They have no wine."
<margin>Genesis 3.</margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 5.</margin>

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER XXIII.

**Jesus said to her: Woman, what is that to me and to you? My hour has not yet come.** The Lord is not accustomed to proceed to the performance of miracles on his own, nor without being asked. For he is used to offering his grace for the necessity and use of men, although those things which are requested are even more pleasing if they are delayed a little while. Additionally, he easily shows how much honor is owed to parents, since he immediately proceeded to the act on account of his mother, which he would have delayed a little longer as far as it depended on him.

### CHAPTER XXIII. <note>The original text repeats Chapter XXIII; this likely refers to the continuation of the scene often indexed as Chapter XXIV.</note>

**His mother said to the servants: Whatever he says to you, do it. Now there were six stone water jars placed there according to the purification rites of the Jews, each holding two or three measures.** The mother was certainly not ignorant that great authority and dignity were deferred to her by the Lord; this persuasion, as was fitting, prepares the servants for the son, and she urges them to do everything he commands.

### CHAPTER XXV.

**Jesus said to them: Fill the jars with water. And they filled them to the brim. And Jesus said to them: Draw some out now, and take it to the master of the feast. And they took it. When the master of the feast tasted the water made wine, and did not know where it came from (but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him: Every man serves the good wine first, and when they have drunk freely, then that which is worse; but you have kept the good wine until now.** The servants did as they were commanded; by the ineffable power of Christ, the water was transformed into wine. For what is difficult for the almighty God? Or how could he, who calls all things from nothing into being, not much more easily change one thing into another
