->TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND<-

...will change and translate to another: However, the **master of the feast** <note>original: *architriclinus*, the person in charge of managing a banquet</note> marvels at the quality of the wine as something exceptional; and indeed, it could not be anything but the best, since it was miraculously created by Christ. He even—quite appropriately, it seems to me—reproaches the **bridegroom** because he had offered the best wine only after the feast was nearly over, and not before.

### CHAPTER XXVI.

**This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days. And the Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.** Many and great things were accomplished by this same sign: marriage was sanctified, and the curse upon women—the origin of our birth—was destroyed by a blessing. The glory of the Savior shone forth like a ray of the sun, and finally, the faith of the disciples was strengthened. But let this be the end of the explanation of the literal history; let us now explain the more hidden meaning signified here by a deeper sense, as I perceive it. Therefore, the Son of God descended from heaven so that, like a bridegroom (as he himself says), having embraced human nature, he might bring forth the fruit of spiritual and true wisdom. Thus, the nature of human life is called the "bride" by this reasoning. The bridegroom, however, is the Savior himself—a comparison not improperly adapted from our world to higher things, according to the custom of Scripture. Indeed, the wedding is celebrated on the **third day**, because the Savior appeared in the final times of this age. For this number signifies the beginning, middle, and end, by which all time is measured. But that prophetic word can rightly be applied: **He will strike, and he will heal; he will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight; we shall know and follow on to know the Lord.** <margin>Matthew 9</margin> <margin>Hosea 6</margin> <note>Cyril interprets the "third day" of the wedding as the "third age" of the world or the resurrection.</note> For he struck us because of Adam’s transgression, saying: *You are dust, and to dust you shall return.* <margin>Genesis 3</margin> But having been struck by corruption and death, he himself healed us again on the third day—that is, not in the first or middle times, but in the most recent times—when, having become man for our sake, he raised up and healed our whole nature in himself. For this reason, Paul called him the "firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep." <margin>1 Corinthians 15 <note>The text cites 1 Cor 3, but the reference is to chapter 15.</note></margin> Therefore, the final times are signified by the name of the "third day." Furthermore, the wedding is celebrated in **Cana of Galilee**, not in Jerusalem; the banquet is prepared outside of Judea, as if among the regions of the Gentiles. For Galilee is often called "of the Gentiles" by the prophets. <margin>Colossians 2</margin> It is surely clear that the bridegroom, rejected by the Jews, was gladly received by the Church of the Gentiles. Moreover, he came to the wedding having been invited—he who was called by the voices of the saints while they were yet dead. The wine failed the guests because, just as innate and natural reason was unable to save man, so also the **Law** <note>The Old Testament Law of Moses</note> was not a complete joy for us, nor did the Mosaic scripture satisfy men. Therefore, it can truly be said of us as much as of the Law: *they have no wine.* But God, the giver of graces, does not allow human nature to be weighed down by a lack of good things; instead, he produces for us a much better wine than before. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life; and while the Law brings no perfection of good things, the Gospel teach-

<column-break/>

-ing brings a most full blessing. Moreover, the **master of the feast** marvels at the excellent wine because he stands in for the high priests to whom the house of the Savior is entrusted; he is stunned by the reason of this mystery. Christ commanded that the wine be brought to him first because (as Paul says) it is necessary for the hardworking farmer to be the first to taste the fruits. <margin>2 Timothy 2</margin> Let each person understand this for himself.

### CHAPTER XXVII.

**And he found in the temple those selling and buying sheep and doves, and the money-changers sitting there.** From this, the Jews are also rebuked, as if they had no care for the laws and were greatly devoted to greed. For while they ought to have been purified in many and various ways according to the law before entering the temple, the money-changers and other men of this sort—who are devoted to profit, usury, and money above all—had filled the temple. They did this to such an extent that those who ought to have prohibited these things seemed to command them to happen. Thus, the Scripture truly spoke of them: **Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard, they have trampled my portion, they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness, they have laid it in ruins.** <margin>Jeremiah 12</margin> For the vineyard of the Lord was certainly corrupted; having been left uncultivated by the greed of the prelates, it learned to trample upon piety.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

**And when he had made a whip as if of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and the oxen; and he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned the tables; and to those who sold doves, he said.** The Savior is rightly moved by the contempt and greed of the Jews; for the temple was not a place of business, but of prayer (as it is written). <margin>Matthew 21</margin> And he showed that he bore this with annoyance not only by words, but even with lashes, justly driving them out of the temple as if they were wicked servants. They were certainly slaves <note>Cyril uses a wordplay on "servants/slaves" (servi) who are bound by their sins.</note>, and they remained in that condition, since they refused to receive the Son of God, the liberator, through faith. Thus, that apostolic saying was depicted as if on a tablet: **If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him.** <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin>

### CHAPTER XXIX.

**Take these things away, and do not make my Father’s house a house of business.** He commands as a Lord, and he encourages them toward what is fair and just as a teacher, exposing their sins so that, overcome by shame, they might recognize they are justly excluded from the temple. It must be carefully noted, however, that as the only Son of God by nature, he calls God his Father alone. For if he were a son by grace in the same way that a creature like us is, for what reason would he seize a dignity common to all by saying not "our Father's house," but **"my Father's house"**? For he would have spoken more fittingly in that way if he were a son by adoption and not by nature. For we, who are sons by a certain added dignity, say in prayer: **Our Father.** <margin>Matthew 6</margin> But the **Only-begotten** <term>Unigenitus: The unique, single-natured Son of God</term>, who is a son not by grace but begotten from the substance of the Father, truly and properly calls God his Father alone. But look deeper, I pray, at how the future state of things is designated by these two recent acts of Christ: for having been invited to the wedding and honored by the Galileans who lived in Cana...

...honored, and he provided help through a miracle, and he filled them with the joy of wine, and sat at the same table and banquet with them. Thus, from the very beginning of Christ’s teaching, through the Galileans <note>The author interprets the people of Galilee as a symbol for the non-Jewish nations (Gentiles) who would be the first to embrace the faith</note>, all the nations that were to receive the faith of Christ were shown. These nations, arriving at the heavenly bridal chamber through faith, will eternally enjoy a spiritual banquet together with the holy apostles and Christ himself, deprived of no joy. For "eternal joy," it says, "shall be upon their heads" <note>original: "Læticia enim æterna... super caput eorum"; a reference to Isaiah 35:10</note>, which is stated more clearly by the Lord elsewhere: "For many," he says, "shall come from the east and the west, and shall sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." But the unbelieving Jews he will thrust away from the company of the saints, and he will hand them over, bound in the chains of their own sins, to punishments—in no way appeased by their unfairly performed sacrifices. For he says, "Take these things out of here." Isaiah seems to me to have prophesied these things: "I did not want the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of well-fed beasts, and the blood of calves and lambs and goats. When you came before my sight, who required these things from your hands? You shall not walk in my courts, nor offer sacrifice in vain any longer. Incense is an abomination to me; I will not bear the new moon and the sabbath, and other festivities; my soul has hated your fasts and solemnities; you have become a weariness to me" <note>A translation of Isaiah 1:11-14, where the prophet critiques hollow religious ritual</note>. This is perfectly illustrated by the whip made of cords—for it is an instrument of punishment—which serves as a kind of foreshadowing figure.

### CHAPTER XXX.

<margin>Psalm 69</margin>
**For his disciples remembered that it was written: The zeal of your house has consumed me.** Every day and in every detail, the disciples, comparing the events to the Scriptures, progress toward a greater strength of faith.

### CHAPTER XXXI.

**The Jews then answered and said to him: What sign do you show us, since you do these things? Jesus answered and said to them.** The multitude of Jews wonders at the power of Christ, and all those who sat in the temple seeking profits (of which they are now justly deprived) are annoyed. Indeed, they cannot deny that the temple of God should not be made a house of business; but to maintain their own customs, they flee to this argument: that he should not be believed as the Son of God unless he demonstrates this to be so by a sign.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

<margin>Luke 11</margin>
**Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.** Just as God easily grants all things to those who ask well, so to those who ask while testing him, he not only provides nothing, but even rejects them as malicious. Thus, in another place, when the Pharisees asked for a sign, he rebuked them more sharply, saying: "A malicious and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and none shall be given it, except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so also the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights" <note>A reference to Matthew 12:39-40</note>. He responds to these people now in the same way with another example, as they are similarly testing him. Indeed, if this sign were not going to happen for the salvation of all, he would never have given it to those who were testing him; this is the very thing that, being poorly understood by them, they later used to falsely—

<column-break/>

<margin>Matthew</margin>
accuse him, saying: "This man said, I can destroy the temple of God." The prophets predicted these false testimonies of theirs: "Unjust witnesses rising up asked me things I did not know" <note>Psalm 35:11; in the Latin Vulgate this is Psalm 34</note>. And again: "Unjust witnesses have risen up against me, and iniquity has lied to itself" <note>Psalm 27:12; Vulgate Psalm 26</note>. He does not drive them toward his own slaughter when he says, "Destroy this temple," but rather he partially reveals what he knew they would do, for their own benefit, if they had any sense.

### CHAPTER XXXII. <note>The chapter numbering repeats in the source text</note>

<margin>Psalm 35</margin>
<margin>Psalm 27</margin>
**The Jews said to him: This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?** Not understanding the depth of the mystery, they mock it as a sign of recklessness. Proposing the difficulty of the task, they think they have found a reason not to obey him; though even if he had said something easier, they would by no means have complied. Thus the truth of Scripture was already emerging: "Let their eyes be darkened so they do not see, and always bend their backs" <note>Psalm 69:23; Vulgate Psalm 68</note>. For as if they were stooped over by their wicked crimes and looking only at earthly things—with the protection of God justly taken from them—they are unable to behold the sublime teachings of Christ. For they despise Christ’s teaching as if it were for an infant, rushing against their own salvation. For our Lord called God his own Father, saying: "Do not make my Father’s house a house of business." But they, despising these words of his as if he were a mere man, object with the great length of time in which the temple was built. But O men, captured in mind by pride—someone might rightly say—if you believed that temple was your God’s, how did you not understand that he is the Son of God by nature, who without any trembling or danger was confident enough to cry out with a loud voice: "Do not make my Father’s house a house of business"? For if this had come into your minds, you would not be in doubt that he who produced the universe from nothing in the space of seven days <note>A reference to the creation narrative in Genesis</note> could restore a house in three days; nor does he who has all things obeying his command have any need for a length of time.

<margin>Psalm 69</margin>
<margin>a rebuke</margin>
<margin>Genesis 1</margin>

### CHAPTER XXXIII.

**But he was speaking of the temple of his body. When therefore he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this about his body, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.** Just as a wise man easily retains the words of wisdom, so the Savior's word was preserved and impressed upon the disciples of Christ as if in soft wax. Therefore, just as upright men are not contentious, they are also tenacious in true doctrine. But men of "stiff necks" <note>A common biblical idiom for the stubborn or rebellious</note> do not retain words, though the disciples ascended daily toward a greater state of piety. Truly, since the body of Christ was called a temple, how shall the Only-begotten Son of God, who dwells in it, not be God by nature? For it is not said that one who is not God dwells in a temple; nor will anyone ever find it said in Scripture regarding the body of a mere man. Who is greater than the blessed Baptist? Who reached the pinnacle of virtue, who was second to none in piety, who offered his head to tyrannical fury for the sake of the divine law: yet now he is so...

<meta>This page continues Saint Cyril of Alexandria's commentary on the Gospel of John, specifically addressing the nature of the human body as a temple versus a corpse, and transitioning into the encounter between Jesus and Nicodemus. It emphasizes Christ's divine nature through his ability to know the secrets of the heart.</meta>

->TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.<-

Scripture speaks of his body: "But his disciples," it says, "namely John's, coming, took his corpse" <note>original: "cadauer"; refers to a dead body or carcass.</note>. If, therefore, John’s body is called a "corpse," how can the body of any man be called a "temple"? I am not unaware that the faithful are called the temple of God; but this is said because of the Spirit dwelling in us: we are God's temples, not our own. But perhaps someone will object, how then did the Savior himself name his own body a "corpse" <note>original: "cadauer"</note>? For he said, "Where the carcass is, there the eagles will gather." But this was not spoken of his body, but rather to signify by a likeness the future rushing of the saints toward him when he shall appear from heaven in the majesty of the Father. For just as he says the flocks of the most predatory birds are carried with swift flight to carcasses, so also you will fly to me. Paul, explaining this, says: "The trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised." And elsewhere: "We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." Therefore, nothing stands against the truth if something said through image and likeness places another thing before our eyes.

<margin>Matthew 14.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 6.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 24.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 15.</margin>
<margin>1 Thessalonians 4.</margin>

### CHAPTER XXXV.

<margin>A</margin>
**When he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name, seeing the signs which he did.** Christ does not stop drawing some to faith by words and doctrine, and others by the truth of miracles; thus, those wiser than his words were persuaded by his miracles and believed him to be God, who was able both to say and to do such things.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

<margin>B</margin>
**But Jesus himself did not trust himself to them.** The faith of those who have recently believed is not stable; nor is a firm mind present in those new to the faith, since they are not yet strengthened in piety. Therefore, Christ did not trust himself to such men; although from this he also shows us that the habit of good is not strengthened suddenly, but by long meditation. Let all those to whom the mysteries of the Savior are entrusted learn, therefore, not to receive <term>neophytes</term> <note>From the Greek for "newly planted," referring to recent converts to the faith.</note> into the divine mind too quickly, nor to commend Christ to them through the mystery of baptism before it is appropriate, until the <term>catechumens</term> <note>Individuals undergoing instruction in the Christian faith before receiving baptism.</note> are more firm. For we have, as in all other things, the example of Christ set before us, who indeed receives those who believe, but does not yet seem to have handed himself over to them entirely: so that you may not doubt that those recently coming to the faith are to be kept for no small time in the status of catechumens. For thus, having been strengthened by long exercise in our ways, they can be received more safely.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

<margin>C</margin>
**Because he himself knew all people, and because he had no need for anyone to bear witness concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man.** This dignity is attributed to the true God alone, and not to any of the creatures. Whence the Psalmist also says: "He who fashioned their hearts individually, who understands all their works." If, therefore, God alone understands what is in our hearts, how is the Savior not true God, who knows the deep and hidden things of hearts? For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? Since, therefore, no one knows, God alone is not ignorant, because he is not numbered with all others: concerning whom "no one" is rightly added. For God is outside the number of all things, nor is he ignorant of anything placed under his feet. For the word of God is living and effective (as Paul says) and sharper than any two-edged sword, and reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and a discerner of the thoughts of the heart. And there is no creature invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes. Indeed, he who planted the ear hears all, and he who formed the eye considers all. Whence he himself says to Job: "Who is this that hides counsel from me, but holding words in his heart thinks to hide them from me?" So that we may believe the Only-begotten is God by nature, it was diligently written by the Evangelist that he had no need for anyone to bear witness concerning man: for he himself knew what was in man.

<margin>Hebrews 4.</margin>

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.

<margin>D</margin>
**Now there was a man from the Pharisees, Nicodemus by name, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night, and said to him.** Nicodemus seems to have been inclined toward faith, but overcome by a wicked shame and defeated by the glory of men, he does not dare to approach openly: thus, with a certain ambiguous opinion and a limping judgment, he labors on both "knees" (as the saying goes). For his conscience indeed pushed him toward faith by the magnitude of the miracles, through its own stings; but the leadership of his people (for he was a ruler of the Jews) easily persuaded him not to adhere to Christ openly: for they considered the loss of their leadership to be no small calamity. Desiring, therefore, to retain both faith and the glory of men, he committed himself to the darkness: which openly accuses the duplicity of his mind.

<margin>Gospel of John, Chapter 3.</margin>

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

<margin>E</margin>
**Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher: for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God were with him. Jesus answered and said to him.** He thought that by these words he could obtain the goodwill and piety of Jesus toward him, and that it was enough for salvation if he merely admired things worthy of admiration. Therefore, he asks for nothing else, but confirms that Christ is a teacher come from God, whom he still addresses as if he were a mere man.

### CHAPTER XL.

<margin>F</margin>
**Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a man be born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God. Nicodemus said to him.** It is not as you think, Nicodemus (he says), that you obtain piety and faith, nor can you attain justice by bare words. For not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," but he who does the will of my Father, shall possess the kingdom of heaven. But the will of the Father is that a man receive the Holy Spirit, and, regenerated in an unheard-of and new way, be made a citizen of heaven. When indeed...

->ST. CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK II.<-

<meta>catchword: would seem,</meta>

But he who asserts that this regeneration, which happens through the spirit, is "from above," clearly demonstrates that the spirit is from the substance of God the Father. Indeed, he certainly says the same of himself elsewhere: *I am from above*: and the Evangelist says, <margin>John 3</margin> *He who comes from above is above all,* about which we shall speak more extensively in its proper time.

### CHAPTER XLI.

(**Q**uow can a man be born when he is old? can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born again?) Since Nicodemus was still a natural man <note>original: "animalis homo," a term used by St. Paul to describe someone living by human instinct rather than by the Holy Spirit</note> and did not understand the mysteries of the spirit at all, he thought what was being said was foolishness rather than something sublime. For not grasping a spiritual birth, and thinking of nothing beyond human affairs, he was forced to imagine a physical womb and a man’s return to birth again: thus, weighed down by the magnitude of the matter, he wallowed in these lower things. For just as thrown stones bounce back when they strike a harder obstacle, so a weaker mind, confused by matters higher than it can bear, recoils; this is what the ruler of the Jews suffered, and clinging to earthly things, he did not accept divine and spiritual regeneration.

### CHAPTER XLII.

**A**men, amen, I say to you, unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. Since Nicodemus did not understand what it meant to be born again "from above," the Lord explains the whole mystery to him more clearly and briefly. For the Lord called the regeneration that happens through the Holy Spirit "being born from above": so that from this we might also learn that we are made partakers of God because we acquire through baptism the Spirit who proceeds substantially from God; by this we are reformed into our original beauty, born again to a new life, and adopted as sons by God. However, since Nicodemus could not grasp what he meant by "from above," he suspected it meant being born again from the womb, and therefore he resisted, thinking it an impossible thing. Therefore, casting aside the veils of mystery, the Savior speaks to him as to one who is weak: *For unless a man,* he says, *be born of water and the spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.* For since man is not simple but composed of a perceptible body and an intellectual soul, he needs a twofold manner of generation, which by its duality can be adapted to both: for the spirit of man is sanctified by the Holy Spirit, but the body is sanctified by water. For just as water heated by the intensity of fire burns no differently than fire itself, so by the operation of the Holy Spirit, waters are reformed into a divine power, by which they cleanse the body of those baptized.

### CHAPTER XLIII.

**T**hat which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the spirit is spirit.) Now he leads Nicodemus to recognize higher things in another way, so that when he hears of spiritual generation, he does not fall back into bodily thoughts. For just as it is necessary, he says, for that which is born of the flesh to be flesh, similarly that which is born of the spirit is spirit. Truly, all things whose reason for being is different also have a different manner of generation. But that which is born of the spi-

<column-break/>

rit, we call the spirit of man: not because it is from the Spirit according to nature—for that would be entirely absurd—but in one ancient sense: because it was brought from nothingness into being through the spirit; and in another sense which we call "dispensational" <note>The "dispensation" refers to God's plan of salvation through Christ and the Church</note>, because through the Spirit we are reformed toward God, and marked with his own character, we are transformed in soul to his own quality (if I may put it that way). In this way, that saying of Paul can also be rightly understood (as I judge): *My little children, for whom I am again in labor,* <margin>Galatians 4</margin> *until Christ be formed in you.* And again: *For in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the Gospel.* <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin>

### CHAPTER XLIV.

**D**o not wonder that I said to you: You must be born from above: the spirit blows where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes; so is everyone who is born of the spirit.) It is the singular virtue of a teacher to touch the minds of his listeners in many and various ways. For in this way, the difficulty of the subject is gradually opened up at last. Thus Nicodemus is led toward knowledge by examples and figures. For this "spirit" <note>In Latin, "spiritus" can mean both "spirit" and "wind." Cyril here interprets the verse as referring to the physical wind as an analogy for the Holy Spirit.</note> here, he says—the airy wind—blows daily throughout the whole world, as you see, and running everywhere, it is known to be present by its sound alone: yet it is seen by no one, but touching human bodies with a very thin breeze, it leaves an impression of its operation on the senses. Thus, therefore, led by the hand from small things to greater ones, you may understand spiritual generation: just as in a certain image given by the likeness of a perceptible thing, gather the imperceptible from the perceptible.

### CHAPTER XLV.

**N**icodemus answered and said: How can these things be?) Nicodemus gained nothing from Christ's long discourse. Wisely, therefore, it was written by Solomon: *Speak into the ear of those who listen:* <margin>Sirach 25; Romans 11</margin> yet no fault should be given to a master who fails to persuade. For he who is placed in this rank must perform the duty of a teacher properly, even if it profits little: although we also learn from this that *blindness has happened in part to Israel,* for hearing they do not understand.

### CHAPTER XLVI.

**J**esus answered and said to him: Are you a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things?) By this one man, all the Jews—who thought themselves much more learned than other nations—are rebuked by Christ for having only the bare name of doctrine and piety without any fruit, as if they were endowed with such ignorance that they not only cannot teach others but cannot even understand themselves. For if Nicodemus, who was a teacher among them, is found to be so ignorant, what kind of disciples do we think they had? Since a disciple does not exceed the measure of his master, as the Savior says: *A disciple is not above his master.* Rightly, therefore, did the Lord compare such unlearned and boorish men to whitewashed tombs. <margin>Luke 6; Matthew 23</margin> Paul also said politely to the leader of the Jews: *God shall strike you, you whitewashed wall.* <margin>Acts 23</margin>

### CHAPTER XLVII.

**A**men, amen, I say to you, that we speak what we know, and we testify what we have seen.) Since in reality he was too ignorant to grasp divine dogmas, and a long speech having now been spent, Nicodemus...

->TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.<-

...it seemed best, leaving aside more exquisite diligence in investigation, to advise him that he ought to receive with a simpler faith what he could not understand. Indeed, he [Christ] testifies that he certainly knows what he says, blocking the way of contradiction with his own authority. For Nicodemus ought to have remembered what he had recently said: that he was not ignorant that Christ had come from God as a teacher. How was it not dangerous to contradict God, or his messenger, when nothing is more perilous than to resist God? Let us, I pray, who have received the power of teaching, take heed that it is better to hand down faith to new converts <term>neophytes: those newly initiated into the faith</term> simply, rather than through a more profound and diligently explained reason. For Paul also says that he nourished some with milk, <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> specifically those who were not yet able to digest more solid foods. And you should prudently know the souls of your flock: for this reason Solomon advised <margin>Proverbs 27</margin> that he might warn that doctrine must be proportionately accommodated to the talents of each individual.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.

<margin>Deuteronomy 17</margin>
**And you do not receive our testimony.** <note>original: "Et testimonium nostrum non accipitis"</note>) Since the Savior naturally possesses the Father and the Spirit within himself, he brought forth the persons of those testifying in the plural number. This was done so that, in a way, according to the Law of Moses: *By the mouth of two or three witnesses, every word shall be established.* <note>original: "In ore duorum uel trium, omne uerbum firmetur"</note> But the Jews, as if utterly rejecting salvation, are carried by an inconsiderate impulse toward the deep pit <note>original: "barathrum," a Greek-derived word for a dark abyss or pit of destruction</note> of perdition. For if they can neither understand higher things because of their lack of skill, nor wish to receive the preaching of Christ by faith: what other way of salvation shall be found for them? Therefore, the Savior rightly said that Jerusalem would be without excuse, <margin>Matthew 23</margin> because it would rush headlong into ruin of its own accord: *Jerusalem, Jerusalem* (he says), *who kills the prophets, and stones those who are sent to you: how often I wanted to gather your children together, just as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings? Behold, your house is left to you desolate.*

### CHAPTER XLIX.

**If I have told you earthly things, and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? And no one has ascended into heaven, except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.**) If, he says, you do not receive a doctrine suitable to men, which hardly exceeds these sensible things, out of great lack of skill, how shall I explain more divine things to you? If you do not understand human affairs, how will you be wise in supernatural things? If you cannot bear lesser things, how will you sustain greater ones? If you do not believe me when I speak, but demand many witnesses for each thing: who can I bring to you as a witness because he has seen the heavenly mysteries? For no one has ascended into heaven, except the Son of Man who descended from heaven. Moreover, although the Word of God descended from heaven, he says the Son of Man descended, refusing to divide Christ into two persons after the Incarnation. <note>Cyril is emphasizing the "Hypostatic Union," the belief that Christ is one person with two natures, rather than two separate beings joined together.</note> Nor does he permit anyone to preach that the temple <note>meaning the physical body</note> which was taken from the Virgin is one son, and the Word of God is another: although those things which are naturally in each receive a proper distinction. For just as the Word is from God, so the man is from a woman. Therefore, there is one Christ from both, indivisible in his sonship and divine majesty. For how else could those things which belong to the Word of God alone be suited to the Son of the Virgin? Or how, conversely, could those things which belong to the flesh alone be attributed to the Word of God? For now he says the Son of Man descended from heaven, but at the time of his passion, the Word of God himself is written to have feared, as if he himself were suffering those things which are suitable only to his humanity.

<margin>Mark 14</margin>

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER L.

**And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life.**) Since he has brought forth the reason why his discourse does not go out to more sublime things, he descends to those things which were done in shadow by Moses. For he was not ignorant that Nicodemus could reach a knowledge of the truth through figures <note>symbolic foreshadowing</note> rather than through spiritual doctrine. He asserts that it is entirely necessary for himself to be lifted up in the manner of the Mosaic serpent: thus he encourages the investigation of history and the searching out of the hidden figures within it, and he as it were hammers this in again: <margin>John 5</margin> *Search the scriptures, because they are they which bear witness of me.* For serpents once jumped upon the Jews in the desert. <margin>Numbers 21</margin> And when they fell like stalks of grain at harvest time, they sought divine help as suppliants. But the merciful Lord commanded Moses to lift up a serpent made of bronze, so that in that matter they might learn to hope for salvation through faith. For those suffering from the bite of a serpent, the only remedy was to look upon the uplifted serpent with faith. This indeed is history, in which, as if on a tablet, the whole mystery of the figured incarnation is shadowed forth. For the serpent signifies sin, which fed upon the human race and which pours poison into men through various diseases, which human nature could escape by no other means except by divine help and aid. Therefore, the Word of God, made in the likeness of sinful flesh, <margin>Romans 8</margin> condemned sin in his own flesh, as it is written. And to those looking upon him with sincere faith, he is shown as the giver of eternal salvation. But that the serpent was lifted up on high denoted that the passion of Christ would reach that knowledge: so that just as he himself had also predicted, <margin>Matthew 20</margin> there is no one who is ignorant that he suffered on the cross.

### CHAPTER LI.

**For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son: that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life.**) Plainly by these words he signifies that he is God by nature. For it is necessary that the only-begotten Son of God, being like the Father, be God; he who does not have the dignity of sonship from the outside (as we do), but truly is that very thing which he is called. Moreover, he opportunely made mention of the charity of God the Father toward men, so that the hardness of Nicodemus might either be softened or more clearly exposed. For what else is it to not believe God when he preaches, than to accuse the truth with the crime of a lie? Furthermore, since he affirms that he is given for the life of the world, he warns that great punishments hang over all those who, in their arrogance, finally neglect the grace of God the Father. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son. Let all those who oppose Christ hear these things again, I pray.

It emphasizes that salvation comes through faith in the "Only Begotten Son" who was "lifted up" for the world's healing.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria’s commentary on the Gospel of John, specifically Chapter 3, regarding the nature of Christ’s divinity and the purpose of his coming into the world as shared with Nicodemus. The text continues to argue against those who view Christ as a mere "creature" rather than of the same substance as the Father.</meta>

->### SAINT CYRILL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK III.<-

...and let them explain to us as we ask: what greatness does the love of the great God the Father possess, according to their view, or how shall we rightly admire it? They will answer (I think) that the love of God the Father toward us is to be wondered at because he gave his own Son for us, and his **only-begotten** <term>only-begotten: The unique, one-of-a-kind Son, emphasizing his divine nature</term> Son. Therefore, so that this love of God the Father may be truly wonderful, the Son who was given must not be believed to be a mere creature. But I call him a Son who, since he is from the substance of the Father, is **consubstantial** <term>consubstantial: of the very same essence or being as the Father</term> with the one who begot him, and is truly God. For if, as you say, he is not from the substance of God the Father, he cannot be the Son of God according to nature. In that case, that "wonderful love" of the Father will be seen as nothing. For he would have given a creature for the sake of creatures, and not his true Son. 

Furthermore, the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> terrifies us in vain when he says: *If anyone who spurns the Mosaic law on the evidence of two or three witnesses is punished with death, how much worse punishment do you think he deserves who has trampled the Son of God?* <margin>Hebrews 10</margin> For he who spurns him, tramples him. Why, then, if he is not the true Son, but a fellow servant of Moses—for one creature is related to another creature by the very fact of being created, even if one seems to surpass the dignity of the other by some excellence—why shall he who spurns him pay a greater penalty than he who despised the law of Moses? It is clearly because he did not sin against a creature, nor against a fellow servant of Moses. Therefore, the love of God the Father is immense and wonderful, for he mercifully gave his own Son (who is of his own substance) for the life of the world.

### CHAPTER LII.

*For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him.* Since he clearly called himself the Son of God, he proves it by the quality and magnitude of his deeds, as if by the firmest testimony. "For I was not sent," he says, "to condemn the world by the law, as Moses did, nor to deliver mandates for the rebuke of sins, nor to perform a servant's ministry; but that through a mercy befitting God, as the Son and heir of the Father, I might redeem men from slavery, changing the condemning law into justifying grace, and thus rescue the human race from the chains of sin." 

"I have come, therefore, to save, not to condemn. For as it was fitting," he says, "for Moses (who was a servant) to be the minister of the condemning law, so it befits me (since I am the Son of God) to free the world from the curse of the law and to heal the sickness of the world with an abundance of mercy." But if justifying grace is more excellent than the condemning mandate of the law, how can it not be understood, consequently, that he entirely exceeds the condition of a servant, who by divine power, as God, frees humanity from the chains of sin? 

And this is one reason for these words of the Gospel; another is closely connected to what came before: he perceived that Nicodemus clung too much to the Mosaic mandates and was horrified by **spiritual regeneration** <term>regeneration: being born again through the Spirit</term>, and thus despised the Gospel's way of life because he thought it would be more difficult than the legal mandates. As God, knowing these things perfectly, he dissolves the fear of this unskilled man by a single argument: showing that the law is excessively burdensome, which does not 

<margin>Romans 7</margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>

<column-break/>

free the world, but condemns it, while he himself is the giver of grace and mercy. *For God did not send his Son into the world,* he says, *to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him.*

### CHAPTER LIII.

*He who believes in the Son is not judged; but he who does not believe is already judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.* Since he had proven by his very actions that he was the Son of God, and said that a more sublime grace was offered to the world through him than the Mosaic law provided (for it is better and higher to be justified by grace than to be condemned by the law), he urges men toward a certain wonderful salvation. For to the believer, he proposed a singular and divine reward, affirming that he would not come into judgment; but to the unbeliever, he says certain punishments are imminent, compelling both toward one and the same path. For he mercifully calls the former to faith through a laudable desire for grace, and the latter through the terror of torture. Moreover, he shows that the crime of unbelief is great, since he is the only-begotten Son of God. For the more excellent that which is despised, the greater the punishments he who spurns it will undergo. He says the unbeliever is "already judged" because the man has brought the sentence of condemnation upon himself by not accepting the giver of non-condemnation.

### CHAPTER LIIII.

*And this is the judgment: that light came into the world, and men loved darkness more than light.* He brings forward the causes for the condemnation of unbelievers, and shows that it is very rightly said in the Proverbs: *Not in vain are nets spread for birds.* <margin>Proverbs 1</margin> For if they preferred to remain in darkness when they could have come to the light, how are they themselves not to be condemned, who by their own perverse judgment bring tortures upon themselves, preferring worse things to better, and darkness to light? By these words, he also shows the **free will** <note>original: "liberum iudicium"</note> of man, who can proceed toward either side according to the judgment of his own soul. For thus we shall justly find praise if we act well, and the opposite if we commit evil. He also said this through a certain prophet: *If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the earth; but if you are unwilling and do not listen to me, the sword shall devour you.* <margin>Isaiah 1</margin>

### CHAPTER LV.

*For everyone who does evil hates the light, and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be exposed.* He explains what he had said more broadly, showing that men are hindered by laziness from attaining good things because they love perverse things. Moreover, the roots of laziness are that they do not want to learn or weigh those things by which anyone might become good and wise. "For everyone who acts wickedly," he says, "refuses the illumination of the light; not because he is ashamed or tired of his evils (for he would be saved if that were the case), but because he prefers to be ignorant of better things, so that he is not tormented daily by the stings of conscience as he sins; and because he thinks he will undergo greater punishments if, while possessing a more refined knowledge of good things, he refuses to do the will of God."

<summary>Cyril argues that Christ's divine nature makes God's love meaningful and explains that Christ came to save rather than condemn, contrasting his grace with the law of Moses. He also explores why people reject this "light," attributing it to a preference for "darkness" and a fear of moral accountability.</summary>

The previous page concluded a discussion on the divinity of Christ and his relationship to the Mosaic Law. This section moves into the transition from the ministry of John the Baptist to the ministry of Jesus Christ, emphasizing the superiority of Christ's spiritual baptism over John's preparatory rite.</meta>

->## TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.<-

### CHAP. LVI.

<margin>Psalm 19 <note>Original: Pfal. 18. In the Latin Vulgate, this is Psalm 18; in English Bibles, it is Psalm 19.</note>, Psalm 8.</margin>
*But he who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God.*) He who "does the truth" does not despise spiritual illumination. Indeed, he is led especially toward that knowledge so that he may understand whether he has performed all things according to divine precepts and has not transgressed the will of God. Therefore, it is a most certain sign of unbridled lust if someone refuses to learn those things by which he might be recalled to better ways. Conversely, it is a sign of virtue and piety if someone considers that life to be pleasing to God which is conducted according to His commands. The Psalmist was not ignorant that this is so when he said: *The law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, providing wisdom to little ones. The justices of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts; the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes.*

### CHAP. LVII.

*After these things, Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea, and there he stayed with them and baptized. But John was also baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there; and they came and were baptized. For John had not yet been sent into prison.*) Having finished the conversation with Nicodemus, the Evangelist <note>Referring to St. John the Evangelist</note> now narrates another most useful matter. For, illuminated by the grace of the Spirit, he saw how necessary it was to recount those things by which it would be revealed how much the baptism of Christ surpasses the baptism of John. He perceived that not long after, there would be some who would either make no distinction between the two baptisms—crowning both with equal praise—or, through ignorance and human error, might even think the baptism of John was better. For there is no deed so shameful that ignorance does not dare to attempt it. No blasphemy is so great that it is not willingly spoken against the dogmas of the most sacred Church by those who (as it is written) pervert all right things. Therefore, lest rash men should dare to prefer the water of John, with which he baptized unto repentance, to the spiritual baptism of Christ, the Baptist himself—overturning the causes of such shameful rashness—is shown to have dissolved this fragile knot of a question for his doubting disciples. For Christ baptized through his disciples, while John baptized not through others, but with his own hands; and not in the same springs where Christ did these things, but near Salim and in a certain specific and nearby spring. This was so that even by this distinction of location, he might subtly and enigmatically reveal that his baptism, since it was imperfect, was merely an introduction to perfection. For just as the Mosaic Law was a certain preparation for future things and spiritual worship, giving birth to a hidden truth, so the baptism of John, when compared to the baptism of Christ, held the power of preparation.

### CHAP. LVIII.

<margin>Numbers 19.</margin>
*A question therefore arose among the disciples of John with the Jews regarding purification; and they came to John and said to him.*) When the Jews could not defend their legal sprinklings, nor show that their purifications performed with the ashes of animals <note>A reference to the "Red Heifer" ritual in Numbers 19 used for ritual cleansing.</note> were better than John’s baptism, they sought to disturb his disciples. These disciples already seemed more sublime than the Pharisees, as they preferred their master's baptism to legal purification. To do this, the Jews extolled the baptism of Christ with praises to the depression of John—not doing this from the heart, nor because they truly felt that way, but so that by depressing and confusing the Baptist’s disciples, they themselves might appear victorious. They did not prefer Christ’s baptism by any reason or authority of Scripture (for how could such ignorant men have thought of such things?), but they brought forward only this: that very few were flocking to John, while many were rushing to Christ in great herds. For they thought that if the Baptist’s disciples were overcome by this fact, they would report no small victory over them. Thus they went out as if victors, though they were much more conquered and prostrate, since even against their will they decorated the Lord with praises—the very Lord whom they did not accept.

<column-break/>

### CHAP. LIX.

*Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, behold, he is baptizing, and all are coming to him.*) The disciples of John took this offense of "victory" painfully, especially because, considering the state of affairs, they could not refute the Pharisees. They were disturbed to see their master made of lesser account, and with a mixture of shame and wonder, they modestly asked why the one to whom John himself bore witness was growing more in glory and anticipating him by baptizing such a great multitude. I would contend that this question arose by divine dispensation <term>divine dispensation: the providential plan or arrangement of God in history</term>. For from this, the Baptist was incited to a long and exquisite sermon about Christ, clearly showing how great the difference is between the two baptisms.

### CHAP. LX.

*John answered and said: A man cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.*) Nothing, he says, is good in men that has not been given by God. For what does a creature have that he has not received? Therefore, it is fitting for a man to be content with the measure of honor granted to him from heaven, and not to demand more than he can carry, lest he seem to despise the decree given from above with an ungrateful soul and resist the divine judgment. For he ought not to be disturbed by shame if perfections are preferred by divine will, but should rather magnify those things with which he has been mercifully decorated by God. Let none of my disciples, therefore, take this badly. I preserve my own measure; I am by no means ignorant of a greater one, and I am not unaware that I am but a man.
<margin>1 Corinthians 4.</margin>

### CHAP. LXI.

*You yourselves bear me witness that I said: I am not the Christ, but that I have been sent before him.*) He now brings back to his disciples' memory the words they had often heard from him: partly to rebuke them for being sluggish toward noble things, and partly to persuade them to seek more diligently from the Scriptures how great a future Christ they predict, and how great a precursor his Baptist is. For in this way, having a more certain knowledge of things, they will not be disturbed when they see appropriate things happening to both. "And I have no need of other witnesses now," he says, "since you yourselves heard these same things from me long ago. For I profess that I am a servant, who was sent to proclaim—"
<margin>He proclaims; the Scripture, clearly.</margin>

to be proclaimed: because I am not the Christ, but He is. Therefore, let His glory, who is Lord and God, surpass and hold all things.

### CHAPTER LXII.

**He who has the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom's voice. This joy of mine, therefore, is fulfilled.** By drawing again from a comparison with human affairs, he leads us into the knowledge of divine things. For these bodily matters are <term>figures</term><note>Figures: Symbols or physical analogies used to represent spiritual or "intellectual" truths.</note> of spiritual realities: since they are felt by the senses, they often make clearer those things which we otherwise could hardly understand. Therefore, the leader of the celebration and the festivity (he says) is Christ: but I am the steward of the feast. And my dignity is this: that being numbered among his friends, I may hear the voice of the bridegroom: and I have indeed already obtained what I hoped for. For I did not merely preach that Christ would come: but I see Him present, and I perceive His voice with my ears. But you, when you see the human race and nature—which I call the bride of Christ (and which previously fled from Him)—spiritually joined to her bridegroom through the spiritual grace of baptism: do not take it poorly that they flock from all sides to the spiritual bridegroom rather than to me (as is right). For he is the bridegroom, who has the bride. Do not, he says, seek the bridegroom's crown in me. For it is not on my account that the prophet exhorts the bride, saying:
<margin>Psalm 44. Song of Songs 1.</margin> <note>Psalm 44 in the Vulgate is Psalm 45 in modern Bibles.</note>
> Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house.

Nor does the bride seek my bed-chamber when she says: "Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture your flock, where you lie down at midday." This bridegroom is heavenly; but I triumph in the joy of the <term>Only-begotten</term><note>original: "unigeniti." A traditional title for Jesus emphasizing his unique relationship as the Son of God.</note>, because, having set aside the condition of a servant, I enjoy friendship both in name and in reality.

### CHAPTER LXIII.

**He must increase, but I must decrease.** Now he more seriously rebukes those who are troubled over a small matter, especially since they were stirred up even before they knew who <term>Emanuel</term><note>Emanuel: "God with us," a name for Jesus from the prophecy of Isaiah.</note> was. For He surpasses my glory (he says) not only in this fact, that more people are baptized by Him: but He will rise to such a point that, just as He is God, so He may also be seen as such by men. For He grows daily, and His splendor will illuminate the world: but I shall be diminished, nor shall I exceed the measure given to me, but remaining in the same state, I shall seem to be diminished as much as He runs ahead toward greater things. This the holy Baptist foretold to us. But let us also place what is said before our eyes with examples. Surely, then, let us imagine seeing a piece of wood of a certain size, and next to it, let us imagine the seedling of a great future tree now first emerging from the earth. If that wood were to take a voice and say: "it is necessary for this plant to grow, and for me to be diminished," would we understand that some loss was to happen to the wood? I think not. But we say it is "diminished" because, while it is compared to the plant, it is found to be less and less every day. Fittingly, the brightest of the stars might also say of the sun: "He must increase, but I must decrease." For as long as the depth of the air is obscured by the shadows of night, everyone proclaims with great admiration that <term>Lucifer</term><note>original: "luciferum." Here referring to the "Light-bringer" or the Morning Star (the planet Venus), not the fallen angel.</note> shines with golden brightness and full glory. But when the sun is seen to hasten toward its rising, and when its light has illuminated this world of ours even a little, the morning star gradually yields to the greater light, and the words of John can be said without injustice: He must increase, but I must decrease.

<column-break/>

<margin>That the Son is not of the number of creatures, but above all.</margin>

### CHAPTER LXIIII.

**He who comes from above is above all.** It is not a great thing (he says), nor a wonder, if Christ exceeds human glory. For His glory, who is God, is not limited to this, but surpasses every creature. He is above all creatures (he says): not as if numbered among all, but as separated from all, and yet present to all, as befits God. He proposed the reason for this matter so that he might suppress the tongues of his adversaries with shame. For he who comes from above, he says—that is, he who sprouted from a higher root—he, preserving the nature of the Father, will truly and surely be believed to be above all things. For it is impossible for the Son not to be such by nature as his generator is. But how shall He who prevails by the same nature, who is the brightness and character of the Father, be of lesser glory than the Father? For if we do not give the Father's own goods to the Son, but wish to despise His "character" (His exact image), we shall also despise the Father Himself. For it is written, that all should honor the Son, just as they honor the Father: so he who does not honor the Son, also makes little of the Father. But He who is glorified with no other honor than the Father’s, since He is from Him according to nature, how does He not exceed the substance of all creatures? For this is what is signified when it is said: He is above all. It does not escape me that the adversaries will cry out from here with a loud voice and say: what reason, since "from above" is written, compels us to understand that the Son is from the Father's substance rather than from the sky, or from an innate excellence, because of which He is proclaimed to be above other creatures?
<margin>Hebrews 1. John 5.</margin>
<margin>A sophistical objection.</margin>
<margin>Answer to the first part of the arguments.</margin>
Against these things we shall not hesitate to respond thus: We do not investigate the sense of Scripture by your empty and frivolous reasons: but following the sacred letters, we search more deeply into the whole. It must be asked, therefore, how Scripture usually accepts this phrase "from above" or "from over." *Every best gift* (one of the saints full of the Spirit says) *and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.* 
<margin>James 1.</margin>
Behold, this "from above" can signify nothing other than "from the Father," and not without cause. For what is above creatures, besides the ineffable nature of God, to which "from above" and "over" (which the Greeks call *ἄνωθεν*<note>original: "ἄνωθεν" (anōthen). This Greek word can mean both "from above" and "again" or "from the beginning."</note>) can be properly applied? For all other things are pressed under the yoke of servitude, but God alone reigns by nature. Therefore, He alone is truly above all: which dignity we also piously attribute to the Son as God, and from God according to nature. But if "from above" signifies nothing other than "from heaven": why is it not said of every angel and rational power? For they come to us from heaven, and "they ascend and descend," he says, "upon the Son of Man." Why, then, does it compel the Baptist to attribute to the Son alone, as if something unique, that which is common to many, and with what faith could he have said it of the Only-begotten: "He who comes from above," when it would have to be said...
<margin>anōthen (from above).</margin>
<margin>John 1.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the translation of St. Cyril of Alexandria’s commentary on the Gospel of John, specifically addressing the theological distinction between the divine nature of the Son and the created nature of humanity, using the testimony of John the Baptist as a guide. TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.

...it should rather be said that those who come from above are over all, so that this dignity would appear common to many. He certainly was not ignorant that a phrase of this kind belongs to Him alone, because He sprouted from a higher root. Therefore, the very word <gloss>from above</gloss><note>original: "ἄνωθεν" (anothen), which can mean both "from above" and "from the beginning."</note> shows us—piously and truly—what we have said. For how will He truly be over all things if we think the word signifies "from heaven above" rather than "from the Father"? For in that case, any of the angels who is truly said to come from heaven would truly be over all things. And since that which is "above all" is not counted among "all things," what kind of creatures shall we place "above all"? Or how is He completely and purely "above all" simply because He comes from above? For if that were the case, the vast multitude of angels would by no means be included among "all things," since they also come from heaven in a similar way. We cannot understand "all things" if we think any part of "all things" is not included. 

But the Word who shone forth from God the Father, who was properly born from above—who flowed from the fountain of the Father’s <term>substance</term><note>Substance (substantia): The underlying essence or "whatness" of a thing. Here, Cyril argues Christ shares the same divine essence as the Father.</note>—is not placed among "all things," since He is not a part of them at all. Instead, as something distinct from all things, shining naturally with the good qualities of the Begetter, He will surely be over all things. 

But if you think that "from above" does not mean "from heaven," they will say that you still cannot deny it signifies the excellence innate to the Son. I ask you to look more closely at where this reasoning will eventually lead you. First, it seems quite ignorant to say that the Son "comes" from a dignity innate to Himself, as if coming from some place, or as if one coming from one thing should ascend above everyone. Next, I would also gladly ask them whether they say this excellence—by which the Son is written to be over all—is substantial and inseparable from the Son, or <term>adventitious</term><note>Adventitious: Coming from outside; non-essential. In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the nature of the thing itself (like hair color), whereas "substance" is the thing's core nature.</note> and acquired from the outside like an accident? 

For if this excellence is adventitious to Him, and the Word of God is merely adorned with an external dignity, they will be unable to avoid confessing that He could at some point suffer the loss of this excellence. For every "accident" of a substance is understood to be able to be absent from its subject. Therefore, the Son of God would be <term>mutable</term><note>Mutable: Changeable. Cyril argues that if Christ can change, He cannot be the eternal God.</note>, and the Psalmist would be glorifying Him with empty words when he predicts in song that the heavens will perish, but He Himself will remain forever. "And all of them," he says, "will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will fold them up, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail." How then is He "the same" if He is changeable like a creature according to you—and changeable for the worse? Or does He speak falsely of Himself when He says: "See, see, for I am He, and there is no God besides me"? 

How could this mutability of the Son not also touch the Father? Since the Son is His image and His character, if the Son is mutable, then God the Father will also be mutable, and He will be "over all" only through some external excellence. I remain silent about what follows. For they will not be able to deny that everything in the image is also inherent in the original model. But if, because of these inconsistencies, they confess that He does not shine with an adventitious dignity but with one that is substantial and inseparable, will they not then—even against their will—concede that the Son is God according to nature, and thus is over all and comes from the very substance of the Father?

<margin>
The second part of the objection.
The reply.
</margin>

<margin>
Psalm 101.
Isaiah 45.
</margin>

<column-break/>

For if nothing has been created that is not contained within the category of "all things," and yet the Son is "over all," He is clearly something other than all things, and He thrives with a substantial excellence over all. Since He is not the same in nature as a creature, how is He not the true God? And since He escapes the nature of creatures, what else shall He be but God? For according to the reasoning of substance, nothing is found as a "middle ground" between the created and the uncreated; rather, the creature is under the kingdom of created things, but God reigns over the creature. If, therefore, the Son is God according to nature, and was ineffably born from God, this "from above" truly signifies nothing other than the nature of the Begetter. Therefore, the Only-Begotten is also over all things because He proceeded from that nature itself.

->CHAPTER LXV.<-

> **He who is of the earth, is of the earth, and speaks of the earth.** He who is of the earth, he says, will not be able to persuade men in the same way as God, who is over all. For he who is of the earth, since he is a man, will hold the place of an advisor, and will necessarily commit the entire power of believing to the listener. But He who comes from above, like God, sends His words into the souls of the listeners by His own power; and the more excellent His nature is, the more effectively and quickly He works. The Baptist instills these things very usefully into his disciples, who were quite disturbed because they saw the glory of the Savior obscuring him; and therefore they approached him saying: "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, behold, he baptizes, and everyone comes to him." Since, I say, they were disturbed, the Baptist, wishing to cast away the agitation of their minds, handed down to them the correct doctrine about such great matters. Thus he showed the Savior’s excellence over all, and he provided the reason why everyone should flock to Him. For he says that all people—not without cause—flow together toward the Superior One, who baptizes in the Spirit.

<margin>
John 3.
</margin>

->CHAPTER LXVI.<-

> **He who comes from heaven is above all.** This, he says, is a sign that the Son of God, who comes from heaven (that is, He who descends from above), stands at an infinite distance from those who are of the earth. For neither am I sufficient to teach, nor can my words satisfy you. The Son Himself also taught that this difference is incomprehensible when He said to the Jews: "You are from below, I am from above." For "beneath" and "below" signify the nature of creatures, which is so called because it is a servant and subject to God, who called it into being. But "above" refers to the divine, ineffable, and sovereign nature, because all things created by it are subjected to the yoke of its power. The Baptist added these things to the previous ones not in vain. For he did not want his disciples to think these things were invented because he was moved by shame and did not want to appear surpassed by a man; so that it would not seem strange for a man to be conquered by God, he thought this should also be confirmed by the Savior’s own words, so that these things might be believed not as false, but as truly told by Him.

# ST. CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK I.

...and hearing, by which we are especially born to be made more certain of the truth of things by their own evidence. For when we ourselves have heard and seen, we speak what we have seen and heard without any doubt. Therefore, so that he might more quickly compel them to faith in Christ, he testifies to that which (he says) he knows best, because he has seen and heard it. We shall understand that the Son of God has "seen and heard" not in a human way, but as befits God.

### CHAPTER LXVIII.

<margin>Matthew 16.</margin>
**AND no one receives his testimony.** These things are not said because *no one* receives the testimony—namely, that he is God by nature, and is from above, and has come from heaven (that is, from the Father) and is above all. For many have indeed received his testimony, and before all others, Peter, who said: *You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.* Rather, these words are spoken because John the Baptist, perceiving the dignity of Christ much better and more quickly than others, and shaking his head, so to speak, and clapping his hands <note>The Latin "pedes manibus cedens" suggests a physical gesture of astonishment or grief at human stubbornness.</note>, marvels at the great unbelief of men.

->*That he is God and by nature the Son from God.*<-

### CHAPTER LXIX.

**HE who receives his testimony has certified that God is true.** He could not have placed the impiety of the unbelievers before our eyes in any other way than by showing the virtue of the believers. For the foulness of evil is easily seen by the opposition of good, and shameful things are immediately rebuked by the knowledge of what is better. Therefore, he says that he who receives the words of him who comes from above has, by his own wisdom, certified (as if by a seal) that the divine nature cannot lie. From this, the opposite emerges: for those who refuse the faith of Christ testify falsely that God is not true. We must notice, however, how by these words he again removes the Son from the <term>consubstantiality</term> <note>The doctrine that the Father and Son share the exact same divine essence or "substance."</note> of created things, and shows him to be true God. For if he who receives his doctrine and his testimony about himself has rightly certified and distinguished that "God is true," how shall Christ not be God by nature, since he is confirmed to be true? Or if they deny this, let them answer, I pray: how is the nature of the Deity honored as "true" if the Savior's testimony is not received? For if he is not God by nature, then he who believes in him as one who is "true" is found to be pious not toward God, but toward some very beautiful creature. But since the judgment of this truth is that if Christ is believed to be true, he demonstrates not a creature but God, it is clear that he is God not by a mere title, but in reality, and is adorned by the praises of those who agree and believe. But perhaps some great <margin>The slander of the faithless and their vain offering</margin> enemy of the truth will laugh, and, being unwilling to confess that the Son is God by nature, will cry out with a loud voice: "Why do you darken the simple and upright sense of Scripture with such quibbles and perverse reasonings? For since the Son of God descended from heaven, he openly preaches about himself, saying: *I do not speak of myself, <margin>John 12. John 15.</margin> but the Father who sent me gave me a commandment what I should say and what I should speak.* and again: *All things that I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you.* For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God. Therefore he now says: 'He who receives his testimony has certified that God is...' "

<column-break/>

**...true.** "For God the Father is surely true, but you are trying to transfer what is owed to the Father onto the Son." But we respond to these things: Will you then <margin>The clearing of the unspeakable slander</margin> place the <term>Only-Begotten</term> <note>original: "unigenitum"</note> among the prophets, and attribute nothing else to him than that he performed a prophetic office? For to whom is it not most clearly evident that the voices of God were brought to us through the ministry of the prophets? And what special thing will you give to the Son, if he did only that? How is he "above all" if, being numbered with the prophets, he is measured by the standard of a servant? Furthermore, how does he say of himself, as if his glory were superior to theirs: *If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and the Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?* For by openly calling himself the Son of God in these words, he removes himself from the flock of the prophets; and he affirms that they were indeed called "gods" because the word of God came to them, but he himself is the Son of God—and not without right. For a certain partial grace of the spirit was bestowed upon the prophets, but in Christ the Savior *the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily*, as is written in Paul. <margin>Colossians 2. John 1.</margin> Wherefore John asserted that *from his fullness we have all received.* How then is he who bestows equal to those who receive? Or how shall the "fullness of the Godhead" be placed among the ministers? Let them consider, therefore (I pray), into how great an impiety their speech falls. But as for how that is to be understood—*I do not speak of myself, but the Father who sent me gave me a commandment what I should say or what I should speak*—we shall speak more extensively in its proper place. For now, it is enough if we admit that the dogmas of piety are strengthened by these very reasons of his. They contend that the Son receives commandments from the Father and speaks nothing of himself, but says what he has heard. Granting these things, we affirm that nothing—as far as the nature of his substance is concerned—stands in the way of Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the universal, orthodox Christian faith as defined by the early Church councils.</note> truth. Therefore, when they hear him saying, *I and the Father are one*, and, *He who sees me sees the Father*, and, <margin>John 10. John 14.</margin> *I am in the Father and the Father is in me*, let them receive this testimony of his and let them certify that God the Father is true, and let him persuade them that what the Father knows most truly, he speaks to the Son. Therefore, they do not disagree with the words of the Lord, who explains the mind of the Father to men.

### CHAPTER LXX.

**FOR he who is sent by God speaks the words of God.** The Father knows, therefore, that his Son is in himself by nature. For I think this, and nothing else, is what *I and the Father are one* signifies. He knows the Son is not a creature; and I say "Son," not one adorned with the mere title of sonship, but one proceeding from the substance of the Begetter. He knows him to be the unchangeable image of his nature, in whom he himself is perfectly seen, since he is depicted (so to speak) in the Father himself, who has shone forth from him according to nature in an ineffable way. For the Father has the Son in himself, and he in turn is in the Son because of the identity of their substance. If you are willing to confess these things, you will escape unharmed from the pestilential disease of heresy, and we shall be freed from this multitude of words.
