TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.

### CHAPTER LXXI.

<margin>Exodus 3.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 1.</margin>
<margin>John 8.</margin>
**(For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God.)** If you understand this only according to the surface meaning, what great thing is there in the Son? Was not every one of the prophets sent by God? Did they not speak the words of God? Indeed, it was said to Moses: *And now I send you into Egypt, and you shall say to Pharaoh, "Thus says the Lord."* And to Jeremiah: *Do not say, "I am too young"; for you shall go to whomever I send you, and you shall speak whatever I command you.* What, then, is greater in the Son being sent by God and speaking the words of God? For he would not seem to have done anything greater than the prophetic ministry. Therefore, his "sending" in these instances must be understood either according to the reason of the Incarnation—because he came into this world with flesh—or in a higher and more sublime way, as befits God. For he shone forth from the nature of the Father like the radiance of light, according to the ineffable manner of divine generation. He showed this himself, saying: *I proceeded from God and have come.* For the Son proceeds from the Father into his own <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substantiam," referring to the Son's distinct yet shared essence with the Father.</note>, even though by nature he is in the Father. Therefore, what "proceeding" signifies there, being "sent" signifies here. Thus the Word, who shone forth from the Father, because he is God from God, will use words fitting for God. Furthermore, those words are fitting for God which are true and are not stained by any foulness of lying. Whoever, therefore, accepts the Savior’s testimony has firmly sealed it as if with a signet, because God is truthful. For the Son is truly God according to nature.

### CHAPTER LXXII.

**(For God does not give the Spirit by measure.)** Now, lend your most attentive ears, so that you may once again marvel with us at the Baptist's wonderful teaching. For since he said the Son was sent by God and asserted that Christ speaks the words of God—since these words could also be applied to prophetic dignity—he now separates the Son far from the prophets by what he says. And by this one sign, he shows that the difference between men and the Son is immense. For he says it is impossible that those who received the Spirit by "measure" <note>By "measure," Cyril means a limited portion or gift, whereas Christ possesses the Spirit infinitely.</note> should also bestow it on others; for never was a holy man a bestower of the Spirit to another holy man, but the Son bestows it upon all out of his own fullness. Therefore, he does not give by measure, nor does he possess the Spirit by measure or participation as they do. Since, therefore, he is the giver of the Spirit, no one will doubt that he possesses the Spirit <term>substantially</term> in himself. He who exceeds the prophets by such great excellence will not speak the words of God as they did, but as God from God, he will preach things becoming to God. But someone might object: "We are not ignorant that the Spirit was given through the hands of the Apostles." O friend, they *prayed* for the Spirit, and when he came in response to prayer, he was said to be provided through their hands. For not even the blessed Moses was seen to take from the Spirit that was in him and provide it to others; rather, this was reserved for divine power alone. For only God can perform these sublime things worthy of God. For the Father’s goods are in the Son, not by participation, but by nature and substance.

<margin>The solution of Canillus.</margin>
<margin>Acts 8.</margin>
<margin>Numbers 11.</margin>

### CHAPTER LXXIII.

**(The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.)** He has already said that because the Son is God from God, he cannot use any words other than the truest ones which the Father uses. For he who is sent by God speaks the words of God. Now opening this more widely, he says: *The Father loves the Son.* We do not offend God the Father, he says, if we render equal honor to the Son, crowning the Son with glory befitting God, since he is known to be the heir of the Father’s goods substantially. For since the Father loves the Son, he rejoices in his equal glory and is always offended by the contrary. Nor did he give this dignity only to his own heir, but he gave *all things into his hand*. I say "all things" simply: whatever things are substantially in the Father are also in the Son. By "hand" here, he names <term>power</term>, as it is said elsewhere: *My hand established the heavens.* Truly, all the Father’s own substantial goods are not given to the Son by participation. For if that were so, the divinity of the Son would be found to be accidental rather than natural. Rather, it is like the heat that proceeds from a fire: the property of the fire is said to be given naturally. This "giving" brings no loss to the giver (since those things which appear to be given suffer no division), and they bring no disgrace to the one who receives. For all these things signify nothing other than the source from which they come: for the natural quality (so to speak) of the producers appears in the products, showing what the substance of the producer is and adorning the natural action of its own fountain. But we say these things regarding examples taken from the world; however, God is above all these things. Therefore, human mind and speech should not be blamed if they use bodily examples for explanation; for *the glory of the Lord obscures speech*, as it is written. For since we understand through mirrors and riddles and only in part, it is necessary that we are even less able to express it with the tongue. Either you will understand it as we have said, or you will refer these things to Christ as a man, so that he may seem to say with a loud voice: "Let no one be indignant when he sees that the Lord and Creator of all things is a man, nor let him refuse to believe in him as God because he sees him with flesh; but let him receive his testimony with a willing mind, and let him seal that God is truthful." For in this way, he can avoid offending the Father, who loves his Son—the sign of which love is that he has handed over to him the power of all things. For he himself said, *All things have been delivered to me by my Father,* and again: *All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth.* Nor will he seem lesser than the Father who gives it simply because power was "given" to him. For he received it as a man when he humbled himself; otherwise, how could he be said to have been "humbled" and to have descended from equality with God the Father? Do you not see that in these things, the Father gives as God, but the Son receives as a man those things which he already had as God? Therefore, the Father does not "give" so as to provide the beginning of power to the Son, but so that the Son, with his flesh, may return to the power which he always possesses naturally without flesh. For this power did not first belong to him when he was made man. For to what "humility" would he be said to have descended if, having been made man, he then received power over all things? Or how would he be believed to have taken the form of a servant...

->SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK II.<-

...was he [the Son] then made Lord only when he received it? Let us cast these impious thoughts from our minds: for having been made man, he begins to rule as a man, though he never lost the dignity befitting God; rather, having been made man, he ascended with his flesh to that state which he always is. <margin>John 17.</margin> He himself showed that these things are so, saying: *Father, glorify me with that glory which I had with you before the world was.* You should consider that he does not seek a beginning of glory, but a renewal, so to speak: not because he fears losing it, but because he begins to reign as a man. That these things are said on account of the Lord's flesh, though it can be proven by many examples, is best shown from that awesome vision of Daniel, <margin>Dan. 7.</margin> in which he says he saw the Ancient of Days <note>Ancient of Days: a title for God the Father used in the Book of Daniel.</note> on his throne, and a thousand thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand were ministering to him and standing by. To which he added: *And behold, with the clouds of heaven, one like a son of man was coming, and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they brought him into his presence, and he gave him power, and honor, and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him.* You see how the Son receives the kingdom from the Father as the Son of Man; for he humbled himself, as it is written, <margin>Philip. 2.</margin> being found in appearance as a man for our sake: so that when he, as the first, returned to his kingdom, the beginning and the way of eternal life and royal glory might be set before us. And just as he is life by his very nature, yet he descended for our sake as a man unto death, so that in this way—having been, so to speak, truly mixed into all parts of our nature—he might both free us from destruction and make us sharers in eternal life. Thus, although he is God, he took on our lowly state <note>original: "dedecora nostra," literally "our disgraces" or "lowliness"</note> so that he might lead the nature of man back to royal honor. For he was the first (as Paul says) to become for everyone the way, the door, and the source <margin>1 Cor. 1.</margin> of our blessings; he restored us from death to life, from corruption to immortality, from weakness to strength, from slavery into the adoption of the sons of God, and from disgrace and infamy into honor and glory. Therefore, when he seems to receive as a man those things which he had and always has as God, let us not be troubled: but being mindful of the **dispensation** <term>Dispensation: (Greek: oikonomia) The divine plan by which God became human in Jesus to save humanity.</term>, let us keep our understanding sound and without harm.

### CHAPTER 74.

> He who believes in the Son has eternal life: but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life.

Not without reason does he testify that life is reserved for those who believe in Christ, but he brings forth the demonstration of such a great matter from the facts themselves. For the Only-Begotten Son of God is Life by nature: <margin>Acts 17.</margin> for *in him we live and move and are.* For he enters into us through faith, and dwells in us through the Holy Spirit, as this same Evangelist testifies in his epistles. For in this, he says, <margin>1 John 4.</margin> *we know that he is in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.* Therefore, Christ gives life to those who believe in him, because since he is Life by nature, he dwells in the faithful. That this happens through faith, Paul shows, saying: *For this reason I bow my knees to <margin>Ephes. 3.</margin> the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may give*

<column-break/>

to us the power of his goodness, to be strengthened through his Spirit, that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts. Since, therefore, the Son himself is substantially Life, and dwells through faith in believers, how can it not be truly said: *He who believes in the Son has eternal life: but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life?* Will someone then say <margin>A Quibble.</margin> <note>original: "Cauillatio," a sophistical objection or quibble.</note> that the Baptist wished to impress this opinion upon us because the mystery of the resurrection is diminished? For he proves that believers will have eternal life, but says the unbelieving will not see life: thus it seems the Baptist's speech signifies that not all, but only the faithful will live again. But where will that go, <margin>The Solution.</margin> which was said simply concerning everyone: *the dead shall rise*? And what did Paul mean when he said: *We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that <margin>2 Cor. 5.</margin> each one may receive the things proper to the body, according as he has done, whether good or evil*? I cannot help but praise those who hesitate, if the believers doubt for the sake of learning. For the meaning of the proposed speech is this: To the believer, he says, eternal life is set forth. Regarding the unbeliever, the words imply something else. For he did not say that the unbelievers would not have life—since they certainly will be raised by the common law of the resurrection—but *they shall not see life*, he says. That is, as far as the simple experience of it goes, they will not be able to reach the life of the saints; they will not attain that blessedness, they will not taste those joys, they will not see that true life. For they will be tortured with punishments, which is sadder than any death, retaining the soul in the body only for the sensation of pains. Paul also preaches this distinction of life; hear, I ask, what he writes to those dead to sin for <margin>Coloss. 3.</margin> Christ: *For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. For when Christ, your life, shall appear, then you also shall appear with him in glory.* Do you see how he calls that manifestation in glory with Christ "the life of the saints"? Furthermore, when the Psalmist sings: <margin>Psalm 33.</margin> *Who is the man who wants life, loving to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil.* Shall we not say that the conspicuous life of the saints is signified by these words? As I judge, it is clear. For he does not exhort them to abstain from evils so that they may live again in the flesh (for even those who do evil shall rise), but he invites them to that life in which one can see "good days," living eternally in blessedness and glory.

### CHAPTER 75.

> But the wrath of God remains upon him.

Most clearly now, by this addition, he has explained what we just said: let him who desires to learn look upon these things more diligently, I pray. *He who is unbelieving toward the Son*, he says, *shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.* If it were true that the unbelieving would not rise, he would not have immediately added: *But the wrath of God remains upon him.* But because he named the "wrath of God," he clearly seems to distinguish the bitter torture of the impious from the joyful life of the saints: and indeed to call the glory with Christ "life"—which is truly life—but the punishments of the impious "the wrath of God"; for Scripture is often accustomed to use "wrath" for punishment. Witnesses of this are...

<margin>Ephesians 2.</margin>
Paul and John—the former said to the converts from among the nations: *By nature you were children of wrath, just like the rest.* 
<margin>Luke 3.</margin>
The latter said to the Pharisees and scribes: *You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?*

### CHAPTER LXXVI.

<margin>John Chapter 4.</margin>
*When therefore Jesus knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did—he left Judea and went again into Galilee.*

It is worthwhile to explain why this discourse proceeded in this way, or from what beginning of events the Lord is said to have known that the Pharisees had heard this news. For when it is said, "When therefore Jesus knew," a certain past event is clearly indicated. To be sure, as God, he knows all things even before they happen, without any messenger. However, he waits for the opportune moment for each thing, and in many instances, he follows the order of events in a marvelous way rather than acting solely on his own divine foreknowledge.

Therefore, a question having arisen between John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification, as has been said, both sides defended their own opinions with great contention. For some, being zealous for the glory of John, affirmed that his baptism was more sublime than the legal sprinkling and every Jewish purification. The sign of this, as I believe they asserted, was likely this: that many people, despising ancient customs, were flocking to John. Others, when they could not diminish the high speech of those disciples (for the force of truth is great), unwillingly fled to Christ's baptism because of the confusion of their adversaries. For the same reason, because many more were openly flowing to Christ than to John, they contended that Christ's baptism was better. 

From this, I believe, the disciples of John were incensed with great heat and went to their master, saying: *Teacher, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, look, he is baptizing, and everyone is going to him.* <note>original: "Rabbi, qui erat tecum trās Iordanem, cui tu testimoniū perhibuisti, ecce ipse baptizat, & omnes ueniunt ad ipsum."</note> For by changing their way of speaking, they put forward the argument of the Jews in the form of an interrogation. Thus, the Lord is said to have known from this that the Pharisees had heard he was making more disciples than John. Therefore, avoiding their seething envy and reserving his passion <note>The "passion" refers to his eventual suffering and crucifixion, which he intended to happen at a specific ordained time.</note> for the opportune moment, he departed from the region of Judea and went back into Galilee.

### CHAPTER LXXVII.

*And he had to pass through the middle of Samaria. He came therefore to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.* 

O, what admirable prudence and sharpness of mind! By beginning a narrative of unheard-of things, he immediately resolves what someone might ask shortly thereafter. We might certainly wonder why our Lord Jesus Christ enlightened the Samaritans before the appointed time. To that Tyrian woman, when she was a suppliant seeking the health of her daughter, he said: *It is not good to throw the children’s bread to the dogs.* <note>Referencing the story of the Syrophoenician woman in Matthew 15 and Mark 7, where Jesus initially prioritizes his mission to Israel.</note> Before Israel drove him away, he signified that the grace previously reserved for the Jews should not yet be given to the Gentiles.
<column-break/>
Did he not say that he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel? How then was he now teaching the Samaritans before Israel had entirely rejected its salvation? 

To answer all these objections, he stated first that he "had to pass through Samaria." He did not go into Samaria for the sake of teaching foreigners and transferring the entire blessing of the Hebrews to them; rather, since it was necessary to pass through there, he necessarily performed a work of wisdom even there. For just as fire will never lose its natural power to burn, so it is entirely impossible for a work of wisdom not to proceed from Wisdom itself. 

Therefore, although he said that the children's bread should not be given to dogs, he nonetheless mercifully provided grace to the poor woman who was weeping and constantly clinging to him. In the same way, he also received the Samaritans—not because a convenient opportunity was now being given by another, but because he himself, along with the Father and the Spirit, determined it as God and Lord. Thus, showing the ineffable virtue of his power, he enlightened the whole region as he passed through, even though it might seem to pressure the Jews who were already contemplating the same things. For by this transition to foreigners, he seems to threaten those who were driving him out, suggesting he would transfer grace from them to others unless they repented. Thus, this journey through Samaria was a kind of figure <note>A "figure" is a symbolic foreshadowing of future events.</note> of things to come.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII.

*Now Jacob's well was there. Jesus, therefore, being weary from his journey, sat down.* 

When he had left the borders of Judea and entered the region of the foreigners, he sat upon Jacob's well. This was to signify enigmatically that, although the truth was about to depart to the nations once the Jewish race was left behind, the honor and dignity of the Patriarchs would not fall. Instead, it would grow, as if irrigated by the constant waters of Christ. 

He sat down, "weary from the journey." Thus the impiety of those driving him away seems even greater; for while they ought to have treated him with honors, they exhausted him by pursuing him with sweat and labor. This matter was predicted by the Psalmist: *They rewarded me,* he said, *evil for good.* <note>Psalm 35:12.</note> Truly, the pride of the Jews in these matters is easily understood. 

But what, in turn, shall the Arians <note>Arians were followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal or of the same substance as God the Father. This was one of the most significant theological conflicts in the early Church.</note> say to us? We can rightly say to them: *Sodom has been justified by you,* for you have exceeded the madness of the Jews. 
<margin>A rebuke against the Arians.</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel 16.</margin>
By the Jews, Christ was crucified; by the Arians, the ineffable nature of the Word is blasphemed. What, I ask, will they say to: "being weary from the journey, he sat down"? Will you, because of these words, think the Lord of all powers is weak and infirm? Will you attribute the labor of the journey to the only-begotten Son of the Father, so that he is found by you to be "passible" <note>capable of suffering or feeling pain</note> when he is the one who can least suffer? Or will you reject these thoughts as impious and correctly attribute these things to the human nature he assumed and to his body? 

For since two natures came together into one person, therefore the one Christ is not split into two sons, and he is said to be able to do all things as God. And although he is impassible, he nevertheless attributes the pains of a man to himself—pains which he endured not as God, but as man. Let us beware, then, lest when we most need a certain skill and sharpness of mind to attain piety, we then, like unrefined and rustic people, cast the reason for the incarnation and the assumption of man far away—

->SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK II.<-

<meta>catchword: from water</meta>

let us not cast this far from us, nor place burdens on our shoulders greater than we can bear. For if He had not become man, if He had not taken the form of a servant <note>Original: "formam servi." A reference to Philippians 2:7, describing Christ's humility.</note>, you might rightly be troubled when something humble or servant-like is said of Him. But if we firmly believe that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, then when He is said to have spoken or suffered things that befit our nature, you should attribute these things to His humanity. <margin>John 1</margin> For we could not have known in any other way that the Word of God had become man, unless He had spoken and suffered certain things as a man.

### CHAPTER 79.

**Now it was about the sixth hour.** <note>Midday, when the sun is at its peak.</note> The author provides the reason why Jesus rightly wished to sit by the spring. For when the more intense heat of the day is added to labor, He rests—not because He was captivated by the pleasure of the spring, but because He was fatigued by the heat and work as a man. He writes that the hour was not exactly the sixth, but "about the sixth," so that we too may learn to have no small care for the truth, even in the smallest matters.

### CHAPTER 80.

**A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her: "Give me a drink." For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food. The Samaritan woman then said to him...** The Lord, as God, was not ignorant of the woman's arrival; but because He knew she was coming to the waters, He stretched out the "nets of doctrine" for her, beginning the conversation from the very act the woman was doing. <margin>Leviticus 5</margin> Since the Law commanded the Jews to beware of every unclean thing and not to associate with foreigners or the uncircumcised (from which they went to even greater lengths, moved more by vain superstition than by a precise desire for the Law), they would not even touch the body of a foreigner, or eat and drink together. They considered themselves "unclean" <term>unclean</term> <note>Ritually polluted according to Jewish purity laws.</note> if they agreed with the Samaritans on anything. Therefore, so that the woman might be moved by this novelty—who He was, where He came from, and why He, appearing in Jewish dress, would ask a Samaritan for a drink—and so the conversation could proceed further, He asked for water as one who was thirsty, saying: "Give me a drink." She then replied:

### CHAPTER 81.

**How is it that you, being a Jew, ask a drink from me, who am a Samaritan woman?** A question is the beginning of instruction, and prudent doubt is usually the root of coming to know things that are ignored. The Savior wisely seized upon this origin of the conversation, as she seemed to hold the customs of the Jews in contempt.

### CHAPTER 82.

**If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to her: "Give me a drink," you would have asked of him, and he would have given you living water.** The woman, being ignorant of the divine nature of the Only-Begotten and not knowing that the Word of God had been made man, called Him a Jew. Christ, however, said nothing to this, but raising the woman's mind to higher things, He said she did not know who it was asking for a drink from her, nor how great the grace is that God bestows. "For if you knew," He said, "you would have first asked for living water from me." By these words, He urged her to diligently seek instruction in these matters.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, one must observe more vigilantly how, without any arrogance, He shows Himself to be God. For first, He suggests to the woman (who is slow to understand) that she ought to marvel at the grace of God; then He professes Himself to be the giver of that grace. "For if you knew the gifts of God," He says, "and who it is who asks a drink from you, you would certainly have asked of Him." Now, no one can bestow the gifts of God unless He is God by nature. Moreover, He calls the "living water" the grace of the Holy Spirit which gives life. Through this grace, human nature—having been driven from the dryness and barrenness with which it had been infected by the devil's arts—is irrigated and returns to its original beauty and greenness, blossoming with a great number of virtues and producing the sweetest fruits through love toward God. God foretold through Isaiah that this would happen: <margin>Isaiah 43</margin> *The beasts of the field, the dragons and the ostriches, will glorify me, because I have given waters in the desert and rivers in a parched land, to give drink to my people, whom I formed for myself, that they might declare my praise.* <note>Original: "Glorificabunt me bestię agri..." quoting Isaiah 43:20-21.</note> <margin>Psalms</margin> Another writer also described the soul of the righteous man as being like a most fruitful tree planted beside streams of water. There are many other testimonies of Scripture in which the Holy Spirit is understood by the term "water." However, a very deep and great sea still remains for me to navigate.

### CHAPTER 83.

**The woman said to him: "Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep; where then do you get that living water?"** The woman understands nothing beyond common things, and therefore she thought He would suddenly draw water from the very springs of the well without any tool (as some do by magic arts). For she thought that "living water," in common parlance, referred to water that had just been drawn from the springs.

### CHAPTER 84.

**Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well, and he himself drank from it, and his sons, and his cattle?** The woman quickly realized that she had not thought piously of Christ by suspecting He was some kind of sorcerer. Nor could she (and rightly so) resist the grace of Him whose words she was listening to so attentively. Therefore, as if He were not a magician but a prophet who could suddenly bring living water without a tool, either from this or another spring, she changed the conversation to more honorable things. Comparing one holy person to another, she said: "Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well?" Thus she no longer speaks of the difficulty of drawing, but of the quality of the water. Now, although the Samaritans had been sent as a colony from Babylon, nevertheless, either <margin>4 Kings 17</margin> because they were neighbors to the Jews or because they had approved some parts of the Hebrew religion, they were not ashamed to call the fathers of the Jews their own ancestors—even though many of them did indeed draw their origin from Jacob. For Jeroboam the son of Nebat, at the time when Solomon’s <margin>3 Kings 11</margin> son Rehoboam was reigning, drew ten and a half tribes (the portion of Ephraim) with him, and departing from Judea, inhabited Samaria.

### CHAPTER 85.

**Jesus answered and said to her: "Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water...**

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cyril of Alexandria, translated by George of Trebizond. It follows the dialogue between Jesus and the Samaritan woman at Jacob’s Well. The previous page ended with Jesus beginning to explain the "living water" He offers, contrasting it with the physical water of the well.</meta>

->TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND.<-

...from the water that I shall give him, he will never thirst; but the water I give will become in him a fountain of water springing up to eternal life.) <note>Original Latin: "ex aqua, quam ego dabo ei, nō ſitiet in æternum..." quoting John 4:14.</note> The woman brought forth a speech as if to refute Him, considering it impossible. She asked: "Are you greater than our father Jacob?" The Savior, however, did not openly attribute such greatness to Himself in words (lest He seem arrogant), but He persuaded her of this very fact through the reality of the situation. He showed that these sensible and earthly waters differ infinitely from spiritual <note>Original: "intelligibilibus," referring to things understood by the mind or spirit rather than the physical senses.</note> waters. He said: "Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water I provide will not only never thirst but will contain within himself a fountain that can lead him to eternal life." Therefore, He who bestows greater things is greater than he who can barely provide lesser things. Furthermore, He again called the grace of the Spirit "water." Whoever has obtained this grace has obtained a gushing fountain of divine knowledge, such that he does not lack the precepts of men; instead, he can easily exhort others to drink of the heavenly word—just as the prophets and apostles once were, and as are those who are now the successors of their ministry, of whom it is written: <margin>Isaiah 12</margin> "You shall draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior."

### CHAPTER 86.

**The woman said to him: Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst, nor come here to draw.**) Again, the woman thinks of earthly things and does not understand anything sublime. She believes that the full extent of the Savior’s generosity might only result in her being freed from the great labor of drawing water when she is thirsty.

### CHAPTER 87.

**Jesus said to her: Go and call your husband, and come here.**) It can be said rightly and truly that the mind of all women is feminine. For their intellect is soft and slow, while the nature of men is more teachable and shrewd. <note>This reflects a common historical trope in Patristic and Renaissance commentary, characterizing the woman’s slow realization as a "feminine" trait to emphasize the pedagogical patience of Christ.</note> For this reason, I believe, the woman is commanded to call her husband as her own; thus, the unrefined woman is rebuked, and the discourse is marvelously prepared for what follows.

### CHAPTER 88.

**The woman answered: I have no husband. Jesus said to her: You have spoken well, "I have no husband"; for you have had five husbands, and the one you have now is not your husband; in this you have spoken truly.**) Since it is now clear that the Savior was not ignorant that she was not then living with a legitimate husband, He nevertheless asked for her husband so that an opportunity might be given to manifest the woman’s hidden secrets—so that, at the very least, through this she might perceive something about Him that is above man. Moreover, He approves of her answer—that she said she had no husband, though she had been attached to so many. For it is not those who have come together out of pleasure, but those who have consented according to the law out of charity, who are said to live together in holy marriage.

### CHAPTER 89.

**The woman said to him: Lord, I see that you are a prophet.**) The woman recovered her senses—not perfectly, but a little bit. For she supposed that the Lord of prophets was merely a prophet. Yet she gradually became better, bearing the rebuke in no way resentfully, and gathering great benefit from the sign. From slowness and a feminine disposition, she gradually ascended to a masculine understanding, now raising the eyes of her soul to higher things. In this, the patience and performing power of the Lord are greatly to be admired, who makes even the rustic merits of men ascend to sublime heights most easily and in almost a moment of time.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER 90.

**Our fathers worshiped on this mountain; and you say that Jerusalem is the place where it is necessary to worship.**) Although she thought Christ was a prophet, because she saw from His appearance that He was a Jew, she boasted of the Samaritan custom of worship and looked down upon the arrogance of the Jews. For the Jews, not having a correct opinion about the nature of God, contended that God must be worshiped only in Zion, which was in Jerusalem, as if He were enclosed in a temple made by hands. Wherefore He speaks to them through the voice of the prophets in this way: <margin>Isaiah 66</margin> "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What house have you built for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?" The Samaritans, also near to the Jews in both region and ignorance, thought it necessary to worship God only on the mountain named Gerizim. <note>Mount Gerizim was the center of Samaritan worship, contrasting with the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem.</note> This ridiculous religion arose because (as it is read in Deuteronomy) the blessing was given on Mount Gerizim. <margin>Deuteronomy 27</margin> Therefore, she proposed this difference between Samaritans and Jews in worshiping to Christ as if it were inexplicable, saying: "Our fathers worshiped on this mountain."

### CHAPTER 91.

**Jesus said to her: Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.**) He condemns the arrogance and ignorance of both, showing that the mode of worship must be transferred to something more sublime and true. For, He says, a place where God dwells would not be sought; but as one who fills and preserves all things, He will be worshiped everywhere, as one of the prophets predicted. <margin>Malachi 1</margin> Moreover, no one doubts that the "hour" and time of this transition was the time of His conversation with men. I believe it should be noted how marvelously the woman is invited by the Savior’s speech to think of Him as the Son of God. For He called God "the Father"; furthermore, "Father" can in no way be understood unless there is a Son to Him.

<margin>That the Son is not among the number of those worshiping by the reason that He is God, but is worshiped together with the Father and the Spirit.</margin>

### CHAPTER 92.

**You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.**) Again, because it had to be dispensed in this way, He speaks as a Jew, and attributes a bit more knowledge to the religion of the Jews. For the Samaritans did not worship God by the doctrine of the Law or the prophets as the Jews did, but by some more unrefined reasoning. Therefore, He affirms that they do not know, while the Jews in some way do know, from whom the salvation of all—even the Samaritans themselves—comes. For from the seed of David, who was of the tribe of Judah, Christ was born according to the flesh. <margin>Romans 1</margin> However, He numbers Himself among those worshiping, He who—together with the Father and the Holy Spirit—is worshiped both by angels and by us. For since He had assumed the form of a servant...

### SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK II.

<margin>Philippians 2</margin>
...he took up the service suitable for a servant: yet he did not lose his status as God and Lord, worthy of adoration; he himself was also made man, preserving the logic of both natures in all things. When you hear of such unheard-of humility, you ought to marvel and imitate it, not use it as an accusation. For Paul also exhorts us to be like this, saying: *Let this mind be in you, brothers, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself.* <note>original Latin: "Hoc sentite in uobis fratres..." quoting Philippians 2:5-8. The "emptying" of Christ is often called the <term>Kenosis</term>.</note> You see how, having been humbled, he became an exemplar for us; though he is equal to God the Father, he voluntarily descended to the lowest humility for our sake. For how else could the character of obedience or humility be known, except through the lowest deeds and words—things far beneath the Word and Son of God—unless he had been made man? For how shall we say he "descended," unless we attribute to him something <unclear>unworthy</unclear> of his divinity? How was he "made in the likeness of men" (as Paul says) if he did not take on what is fitting for men? Now, it is most fitting for men to offer adoration to God as his due. Therefore, Christ also adores, after he was made man, **as a man**. Yet he is always adored together with the Father and the Spirit, because he is
<margin>Refutation of error.</margin>
true God by nature. I am not ignorant of the fact that the adversaries of Christ will despise these words; they will say that the Father is adored by the Son, not as we or the angels adore Him, but by some other "more sublime" adoration. To them, we shall not hesitate to say: O, what a "special" dignity of a servant you attribute to the Only-Begotten! Cease, I pray, from offending the Son with this kind of "honor" if you wish to glorify the Father. For he who does not honor the Son, does not honor the Father either, as it
<margin>John 5</margin>
is written. For what honor is returned to the Only-Begotten if he adores the Father more sublimely than the rest? Surely, if he is numbered among those who adore, he will be a servant, even if he is the "chief" adorer. He would not differ from the <term>creatures</term> <note>In theology, a "creature" is anything created by God, as opposed to God the Creator.</note> in essence, but would only be more excellent by some other degree of standing—just as angels are known to be more excellent than men, surpassing them either by their substance, their degree of holiness, or by a heap of glory (as it seemed fit to God the Creator). But in the fact that they are creatures, and according to the logic by which they were truly produced out of nothing, they agree with all other creatures. Therefore, if the Son is said to adore the Father in any way *as God*, he will not escape being believed to be a created being. How then is he the Son, if he is created? Or how is he Lord, if he is an adorer and a servant? In my opinion, royal and lordly dignity is perceived in the fact that one **is adored**; whereas a subject and servile condition is defined by the fact that one **adores**. For this reason, Moses exhorts the entire
<margin>Deuteronomy 6</margin>
creation, saying: *You shall adore the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.* To him who is a servant by nature and is subjected to the yoke of the deity, it is necessary to worship and adore God. For when it is said, "You shall adore the Lord," such a command refers to a servant; but when it says, "God,"

<column-break/>

it refers to the creature. For just as the "servant by nature" is understood simultaneously with the "Lord by nature," so that which is produced from nothing is understood alongside the "creating Deity." Since the Son is eternally in the Father, and since he is Lord by nature because he is God and Creator, how can the condition of "adoring" befit him? I certainly do not see it. But those men talk nonsense, saying: "He will adore the Father not as a servant, nor as a creature, but as the Son." It would then be necessary for this "adoration" to exist within the very logic of his Sonship; it would follow that the Son must adore because he was born for this purpose. Just as we are rational and mortal beings, possessing souls and capable of mind and learning—not because we wish to be, but because we were born for this. If, therefore, it is naturally innate to the Son to adore the Father, and they understand and preach it thus, how will they not be seen as impious toward the Father himself? For the Father's own nature would necessarily be of the same kind as his Image, Character, and Son. For those things which exist in the Father's nature also exist unchangeably in the Son. But if the Son adores the Father of his own free will—and that is what they believe—they are moved more by conjectures than by true reasons. And what will stop these pretenders of piety from saying that the Father also adores the Son of His own free will? But they say, "It is right and equal that the Son offer the gift of adoration to the Father, not the Father to the Son." Is this how you prophesy to us again, as if from the inner shrines, the tripod, and the laurel of Apollo? <note>Cyril is mockingly comparing his opponents to pagan oracles who spoke in riddles or inspired frenzies.</note> Are you belching out words from the heart and not from the mouth of the Lord, following the "Samian Elamite"? <note>This likely refers to Pythagoras (the Samian), whose followers were known for secretive, dogmatic assertions.</note> Are you not ashamed to speak of "good and equal" in this matter? Is it not "equal and good" that the Son of the true God should be true God? And that He whom every creature adores should be and be called the Father of a Son who is not an adorer, but is by nature adorable? I think these things will not seem inconsistent to wise men. For how shall we say it is "equal" for the Father to be adored by his own Son, when that would bring detriment to both? First, he who adores will not retain the unchangeable image of nature. Indeed, he adores as a lesser being—and lesser not in quantity or by some accident (for all such things are absent there), but by the logic by which the substance of each is defined. Furthermore, how could he truly say: *He who sees me, sees my Father also*? <margin>John 14</margin> How, moreover, can he say he is to be honored no less than the Father, when he does not possess the same glory by reason of his adoration? Next, the Father himself will also suffer detriment, as we have said. For it is a great glory to Him to have begotten a Son who is by nature such as He Himself is. Just as, on the contrary, it would be no small disgrace if He produced a Son of a different nature—a thing which not even the nature of a creature suffers. For all things that possess the power of generating by the will of the Creator bring forth things similar to themselves according to nature. It says, *Let the earth bring forth the grass of the field, and the fruit tree having seed according to its kind and likeness.* <margin>Genesis 1</margin> Therefore, in this respect, the nature of the deity would be inferior to the creatures. That which he has rightly bestowed upon creatures, he alone would lack. Who, then, can endure the nonsense of those who say the Father ought to be adored by the Son? Truly, since they claim this is done voluntarily by the Son...
<margin>Refutation of calumnies.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 2</margin>

<summary>Saint Cyril argues against heretical claims that Jesus is inferior to God the Father because he "adores" or worships Him. Cyril explains that Christ adores only in his human nature, while in his divine nature, he is equal to the Father and worthy of the same worship.</summary>

...they were saying, and they believed this was confirmed by nothing more than equity and goodness: let us again examine the truth from the Holy Scriptures, from which such things must chiefly be drawn. The Law, therefore, commanded that a <term>didrachm</term> <note>A Greek silver coin equivalent to a half-shekel, paid as a Temple tax.</note> be offered to God by every individual of the Jews as a kind of tribute:

<margin>Exodus 30</margin>

not because God wished to collect money, but because He taught greater things through symbols. First, because no one is master of his own life, but we all have one Lord, whom we acknowledge by the laying down of this tribute; second, it described a spiritual tribute within a physical one. "Honor," it says, "the Lord from your

<margin>Proverbs 3</margin>

just labors, and offer Him the firstfruits of your fruits of justice": which has now been fulfilled through the Gospel doctrine, as the legal worship has ceased. For we do not think that God should be worshiped with corruptible matter and outward things by assigning a didrachm; rather, as true worshipers, we adore in spirit and truth. It must be thought that this meaning lay hidden in that Law. Therefore, when the Lord was in Jerusalem, it is written that the collectors of the didrachm said to Peter: "Does your teacher not pay the didrachm?" But Jesus,

<margin>Matthew 17</margin>

before he had heard anything from Peter, anticipated him, saying: "From whom do the kings of the earth take tribute? From their own sons, or from strangers?" And when Peter answered "from strangers," Jesus replied, "Then the sons are free." He added, "But lest we should offend them, take a hook and go to the sea, and take the first fish that comes up, and opening its mouth, you will find a <term>stater</term> <note>A silver coin worth four drachmas, exactly enough to pay the tax for two people.</note>; give that for me and for you." You see that the Son does not wish to be placed under tribute; you see that he does not allow himself to be believed to be under the yoke of servitude like the others. For since he knows his own nature is of a free dignity, he affirms that he owes nothing servile to God the Father. "For the sons," he says, "are free." Therefore, if he rejected even the symbol of the thing, how would he allow himself to perform the thing itself of his own accord, as you claim? Or does it not seem to you that adoration is like a spiritual tribute, a kind of profession of servitude? And for what reason did the Law join adoration to servitude, saying:

<margin>Deuteronomy 6</margin>

"You shall adore the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve"? For adoration is like a door and a way to the works of servitude; let it stand as a mark of the service by which we profess to serve God. Therefore the Psalmist exhorts everyone, saying: "Come let us adore, and fall down

<margin>Psalm 95 <note>The text cites Psalm 49, following a different numbering system or a scribal error; this is Psalm 95:6.</note></margin>

before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us." You see that adoration is joined to prostration: by this fact, if anyone rightly understands the conditions of things, I think nothing more clearly signifies the state of servitude. But if our adversaries still dare to contend, and do not blush to pile up frivolous reasons, let them show us, through all of Holy Scripture, where adoration is attributed to the Word and Son of God when he is bare of the flesh? For while as a man he rightly adores, it is never shown in the Holy Scriptures that he did this before he became man. But using false

<margin>Matthew 22</margin>

conjectures, they deservedly hear: "You err, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God," and being ignorant of the glory of the Only-begotten. For because he does not adore in his capacity as the Word of God, but having been made man for our sake, he took this up on account of the flesh—we shall know this from no better source than his own words. "For you," he says, "adore

<column-break/>

what you do not know, but we adore what we know." Is it not clear then, since he uses the plural number and counts himself among the servants, that these things are said as if by a man in servitude? For what prevented him from using the singular number (if he wished to be proclaimed as a worshiper of the Father) and saying: "I adore what I know, you adore what you do not know"—so that he might attribute this to himself without being numbered with the others? But now, since he is teaching us, because of the Incarnation—because he was made man for our sake—he numbers himself with the Jews who adore because of their region.

->CHAPTER XCIII.<-

"But the hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers will adore the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father seeks such as these to adore Him. God is spirit, and those who adore Him must adore in spirit and truth." <note>John 4:23-24</note> The "present" signifies the time of his arrival, in which he suggests that the symbols of the Law are transformed into truth, and the shadow into spiritual worship, and into a way of living pleasing to God the Father through Gospel doctrine. He asserts that the "true worshipers" will be spiritual men, so that they may run to Him on a clearer path. For God is understood to be Spirit when compared to bodies; and the spiritual worshiper is pleasing to Him—the one who is not overshadowed by Jewish forms and symbols in his piety, but shining with Gospel power, performs true adoration through the correct discipline of dogmas.

->CHAPTER XCIIII.<-

"The woman said to him: I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; when he comes, he will announce all things to us." <note>John 4:25</note> When the Lord said that the time was coming, or rather was already present, in which true worshipers would offer spiritual worship to God the Father: immediately, even beyond her own natural wit, the woman was brought back to the memory of the Messiah, who was then commonly expected by the Jews. She confessed that Christ would come, and although she was given to the pleasures of the flesh, she was not entirely ignorant that Christ would be a teacher of a more sublime doctrine.

->CHAPTER XCV.<-

"Jesus said to her: I am he, who speaks with you." <note>John 4:26</note> Not to the unrefined or the contentious, but to those laboring to bring forth faith <note>original Latin: "fomone parturientes" likely a typo for "sermone," meaning "laboring in word/discourse."</note>, those more inclined toward the light of perfection, and those bringing forth the roots of believing through simple speech—these ascend more easily to a more perfect knowledge. Such the Samaritan woman seems to have been: for although she considered higher things in a somewhat rustic and unrefined way, she did not lack good will, nor was she entirely removed from understanding. For first, she did not give drink to Christ when he asked, but seeing him scorning the customs of the Jews, she sought the reason for this transgression; then, as the conversation progressed (and she benefited from the clarification), she diligently sought greater things. "For our fathers," she said, "adored here, but you say that in Jerusalem one ought to adore." And thus she learned that the time had already come when true worshipers, having left behind adoration fixed to specific places, would worship the Father spiritually. The knowledge of this matter...

<sig>iii</sig>

you will attribute those things to Christ alone. "We know," she says, "that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ: who, when he comes, will explain all these things to us." You see by what sequence of speech the woman was prepared for faith, and as if ascending by steps, from small little questions she leaped into a more sublime state. It was not, therefore, inappropriate to declare the whole matter to her in a single word, and to say: "I am he who speaks with you." Admonished by this example, we who possess the rank of teaching in the church of God ought to begin from lesser things; when the **neophytes** <term>neophytes: Literally "newly planted," referring to new converts or beginners in the faith.</term> have chewed on these, then they are to be led from small to greater things in such a way that they now see Jesus Christ. However, those who introduce those tender in faith into the inner parts of the holy things, and committing the Lamb of God with "unwashed hands" (as the saying goes) <note>original: "illotis manibus" — a proverb meaning to handle something sacred without proper preparation or reverence.</note>, decorating those not yet well-**catechized** <term>catechized: Instructed in the basic principles of Christian doctrine.</term> with priestly dignity, let them know they will give no small account of this matter on the day of judgment.

### CHAPTER CXVI.

AND immediately his disciples came.) The presence of the disciples brought an end to the conversation with the woman. For a spark of faith had already stuck in the woman’s mind, which by the favor of Christ could bring in a great flame. For I think it must be understood thus, according to what was said by him: *I came to cast fire upon the earth.*
<margin>Luke 12</margin>

### CHAPTER XCVII.

AND they wondered that he was speaking with a woman.) The disciples are stunned by such great humanity <note>In this context, Cyril uses "humanity" to describe Christ's kindness, approachability, and lack of social prejudice.</note> of the Savior: for he did not avoid conversations with women (as some do by a pretense of holiness), but offered his mercy to all, in reality attributing life through faith not only to men but also to women. Therefore, let those who perform the office of a pastor not repel poor women, and let them serve not their own will, but the utility of preaching.

### CHAPTER XCVIII.

YET no one said, what do you seek, or why are you talking with her?) It is the duty of an upright disciple to honor the teacher with such great reverence that he dares to ask nothing rashly, nor let him go out into shameful thoughts if the master speaks with a woman: but rather out of modesty and fear, let him keep his tongue "under the hedge of his teeth" <note>A vivid metaphor for keeping silent and guarding one's speech.</note>, and wait for an explanation of this matter to be brought forward by the master. We ought therefore to wonder at the humanity of Christ, who was speaking with the woman, and also at the prudence of the disciples, who were not ignorant that nothing should be said concerning this matter.

### CHAPTER XCVIII.

The woman therefore LEFT her water jar, and went into the city.) Now superior to the cares of this world, the woman who was a little before devoted to pleasure was changed; having no concern for thirst or water, she was being established in a more sublime state through faith. Kindled by the strength of charity <note>Charity here refers to "agape" or divine love for one's neighbor.</note>, which is the best of virtues, she was eager to offer the good that happened to her to others by running to them. Nor is it a wonder; for Christ was speaking more secretly within her, saying: "Freely you have received, freely give." Therefore, that servant who buried the talent is not to be imitated, but what we have received must be multiplied: which that noble woman did rightly, who
<margin>Matthew 10 and 25</margin>

<column-break/>

proposed to all the Samaritans what she had received. She did not draw water from a terrestrial fountain, nor carry a terrestrial water jar back home: but full of the heavenly grace and doctrine of the Savior, she immediately set out to teach others. From which we learn that we shall obtain greater and better things from God if we neglect these small and temporal things.

### CHAPTER C.

AND she said to those men: come and see a man who told me all things whatever I did; is he not the Christ?) O wonderful prudence of the woman, O ineffable power of Christ: she now speaks skillfully, who a little while before, understanding nothing, heard: "Go, call your husband, and come here." It is certainly worth the effort to look at how skillfully she speaks: for she does not say she has found the Christ, nor beginning immediately, does she weave a narrative about the Savior, lest she be laughed at by the Samaritans (who knew her character) as if she were foolish and saying things greater than she could understand. Therefore, the narration of the miracle, placed first, prepared the listeners for faith. "Come," she says, "and see." For sight alone will suffice for faith: he will make you more certain by many and great miracles. For he who knows the secrets of hearts, and possesses this divine dignity, how will he not accomplish all things that he wishes?

### CHAPTER CI.

THEY went out therefore from the city, and were coming to him.) The hardness of the Jews is rebuked by the Samaritan facility; and their cruelty is rebuked by the humanity of these people. Consider the minds of both, so that you may much more admire Jesus, because he withdrew from the Jews and bestowed himself upon foreigners. For the Jews, to whom Christ was preached as coming by the Mosaic law, to whom a multitude of prophets now showed him almost at the doors, saying: "Behold the Lord our God, behold the Lord"; <margin>Isaiah 40</margin> to whom most recently John, the great among those born of women, showed him present, saying: "Behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world"; <margin>John 1</margin> to whom—what was greater and more wonderful—the Savior revealed himself by the marvelous power of signs. The Jews, I say, instructed in all these things, meditate upon injustice, plot impiously, and are unable to restrain the fury of envy. They drive away from themselves the life, the light, the savior of all, the way and the gate of the heavenly kingdom, the giver of the remission of sins and the adoption of the sons of God. Justly therefore did Christ say: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets, you who seek with stones all who are sent to you: how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and behold, your house is left desolate." <margin>Matthew 23</margin> But the Samaritans are far better, overcoming their innate desire by the goodness of their character and obedience. When they heard a single miracle narrated, they pour out from the city to Christ: not forewarned by the voice of the prophets, not instructed by the Mosaic law, not strengthened by the doctrine of John: but at the narration of a single woman, and she a sinner and lowly, they hasten running to Christ. Wherefore let us also, admiring the judgment of the Savior, cry out: "You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgments are right."
<margin>Psalm 118</margin>

### CHAPTER 102.
**Meanwhile his disciples asked him, saying: <term>Rabbi</term> <note>original: "Rabbi"; a Hebrew title of respect meaning "teacher."</note>, eat. But he said to them.** Nothing so small is found in the sacred scriptures that does not yield great utility for us; for all things were written by holy men for our instruction. Let us look therefore, I pray, at how the Lord is set forth as a primary model for the teachers of the church. For since he was not ignorant that the Samaritans would soon come to salvation, he was so intent upon it that, although he was tired from the journey, he nevertheless had no regard for his physical needs. Thus, by his example, he persuades the pastors of the church to devote themselves to the salvation of humanity rather than to their own bodily comfort, lest we hear that prophetic <margin>Jeremiah 48</margin> warning: *Woe to those who do the work of the Lord negligently.* <note>original: "Væ qui opus domini facitis negligenter." This refers to Jeremiah 48:10, often cited in the Middle Ages and Renaissance to exhort clergy to diligence.</note> So that we might not be unaware that the Lord fasted especially in such times, the text did not omit how he was asked by the disciples to eat.

**118 SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK II.**

...the faith of the nations having been demonstrated, he led the Savior back again to Jerusalem, where He freed a man worn down by a long illness. Therefore, the nobleman <note>Latin: *regulus*; referring to the royal official whose son Jesus healed in John 4:46-54</note> believed along with his entire household. The Jews, however, although they ought to have marveled at and loved Him, impiously persecuted their benefactor as if He were a lost man. By their actions, they showed themselves to be much worse than the foreigners, and were left far behind them. <margin>Psalm 21:12</margin> <note>The original margin cites Psalm 10, but the quote "You shall make them turn their back" is found in Psalm 20:13 of the Vulgate or 21:12 in modern English bibles.</note> This is certainly what is said in the Psalms to the Lord Jesus: *For You shall make them turn their back.* For those who were the first of all because of the virtues of their fathers shall be saved only after the calling of all the nations. <margin>Romans 11:25-26</margin> *For when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, then all Israel will be saved.* This meaning emerges from the very arrangement and order of events; now let us consider the rest.

<margin>The word "to be able" <note>original: "posse"</note> has another power, a different force and meaning.</margin>

...power: for it sometimes signifies a stable operation of nature, which cannot be otherwise. For example, if a rational human being, born naturally rational from a rational human, were to say he "cannot" do anything of his own accord that he does not see as belonging to his father’s nature. In this way, therefore, the Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing. Therefore, do not criticize the works of the Son, who cannot do anything other than what the <term>substance</term> <note>The underlying essence or "being" of God.</note> of the Father likewise does. For example: if the Father’s nature is merciful, the Son also, who is from him, is naturally merciful, and cannot be otherwise than the Father is. For just as he has his substance from the Father, so too he possesses the virtues of that substance simply and far removed from all composition, as God possesses them. Moreover, he himself declared that this meaning is most perfect when he immediately added: *For whatever he does, these things the Son also does likewise.* Truly, if you also consider the reason why these things were said by Christ, you will not stray from the true meaning of this passage. For because he was merciful toward the sick man on the Sabbath day, and because the Jews persecuted him as a lawbreaker, he wished to reconcile them with these words; thus he affirms that God the Father also acts mercifully on the Sabbath. For He has never ceased from those things which lead to our salvation. This is why he said: *My Father works until now, and I work.* Lest they be more agitated by these words, he added: *The Son cannot do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it. For whatever he does, these things the Son also does likewise.* For he says, "Because I see that the Father is always merciful, even on the Sabbath, I also act mercifully on the Sabbath. For I cannot change the Father’s substance, since I am one and the same with the Father according to nature; therefore, as I am from him, I do all things that he performs." But those who say that the Father acts first, and then the Son imitates his works, suffer from great ignorance. For how can the Father ever work separately (so to speak) and alone without the Son? For his <term>power</term> <note>In Greek theology, Christ is often identified as the "Power" and "Wisdom" of God.</note> by which he works is the Son, who exists eternally within him, and is the expression of his will and movement (if I may call it that) in acting. If they contend that the Father's operation is awaited by the Son so that he might imitate it, let them show us if anything has ever been made by the Father without the Son, or—what pertains to the matter at hand—let them bring forward some person with withered limbs cured by the Father without the Son, so they might persuade us that this man was cured by the Son through imitation of the Father.

**CHAPTER 136.**
*For the Father loves the Son.* He argues that they are provoked in vain because of the Sabbath, since he asserts that he is loved by the Father. For the Father does not love one who offends him, but rather one who fills him with joy. Therefore, they persecute him in vain who brings joy to the Father by his works; they themselves are clearly fighting against God the Father when they persecute with hatred the one whom He loves. It is evident, moreover, that he who disregards the will of the parent and follows his own

***

**SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK II. 227**

counsel would not be the beloved Son to the Father. But, since the Father loves the Son, it is clear that He consents to him even in the breaking of the Sabbath. It is also clear that this matter contains nothing for which God, the Lord of the Law, could rightly be offended.

**CHAPTER 137.**
*And he shows him all things that he himself does.* He necessarily added these words to the ones above. For human fathers, by a certain natural love for their children, endure and tolerate even disobedient sons, driven to this by a certain force of nature. But God the Father, he says, does not love the Son in that way. For the Son can do nothing that the Father does not do. For since the substance of the Father and the Son is one, they are led by a certain natural law (so to speak) into one power and one will. Therefore, the Son does nothing contrary to the Father’s will, but performs what he sees Him doing, since because of the identity of their substance he cannot fall away from the Father’s will. For he is entirely free from change; he always remains the same, as the Psalmist sang. <margin>Psalm 101 <note>Specifically Psalm 102:27 in modern numbering: "But you are the same."</note></margin> Again, the Father shows the Son what he himself does, not as if they were painted on tablets, nor as if helping one who is ignorant with instruction (for the Son, as God, knows all things), but rather by painting his whole self into the nature of the Son, so that whatever he has in himself, he demonstrates in the Son. Thus, just as the nature of the Father is known from certain things, the nature of the Son is demonstrated from those same things. For this reason it was said that *no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son.* <margin>Matthew 11</margin> This knowledge is in both of them, not through instruction, but naturally. The Father sees the Son in himself, and the Son in turn sees the Father in himself; therefore he says: *I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.* <margin>John 14</margin> However, "seeing" and "being seen" should be understood not in a human way, but in a manner befitting God.

**CHAPTER 138.**
*And he will show him greater works than these, so that you may marvel.* It was mentioned above that the Jews sought to kill Jesus because of the Sabbath, and because he said God was his Father in a unique way, making himself equal to God. First, therefore, he rejected the accusation concerning the Sabbath when he demonstrated that the Father himself likewise works on the Sabbath. Now, although he was made man for our sake, he nevertheless shows that he is equal to the Father. For this followed after the other; therefore he says: *and he will show him greater works than these, so that you may marvel.* He says, "The man who was troubled by disease for thirty-eight years was healed, and this event revealed the divine power and authority of the one who performed it." No one can rightly criticize him who acts so miraculously and with such authority if he says he is God and the Son of God, equal to the Father in all things. "But," he says, "since you are agitated because of this work and do not wish to believe, you will see much greater things, and you will marvel that such great power is placed in me that I can even raise the dead—a power and glory that belongs to God alone, whom you now accuse of the crime of iniquity and persecute because I called myself the Son of God." How God the Father shows works to the Son was explained above.

### CHAPTER 139.
**For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son gives life to whom he will.** <note>original: "Sicut enim pater suscitat mortuos & uiuificat, sic & filius quos uult uiuificat"</note> Observe again how equality is most clearly demonstrated in these words. For if he raises the dead in no other way than the Father does, how can he be lesser than him? Or how can he not be of the same substance as him, since he possesses the properties of the same nature? For it is characteristic of the supreme substance to be able to give life to the dead, a power which belongs equally to the Father and the Son. Moreover, the Father does not give life at one time and the Son at another, nor does one give life separately from the other; for the Son performs all things because he has the Father within himself, and the Father likewise works all things through the Son. Therefore, since it is naturally inherent in both to be able to give life to the dead, this power is attributed to both without any division in their operation.

### CHAPTER 140.
**For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.** <note>original: "Non enim pater iudicat quenquam, sed omne iudicium dedit filio"</note> He brings forth another divine and primary argument by which he shows himself to be God truly and by nature. For to whom else is it appropriate to judge the world than to God alone? <margin>Psalm 82</margin> <note>The original cites Psalm 81, following the Vulgate numbering.</note> whom alone the divine Scripture calls upon to judge, saying: *Arise, O God, judge the earth.* <margin>Psalm 75</margin> <note>Original cites Psalm 74.</note> And again: *Since God is the judge: he humbles one, and exalts another.* Now, he says that judgment has been "given" to him by the Father, not because he does not possess this power by his own nature, but through the <term>dispensation: the theological concept of God's plan for salvation, specifically the Incarnation of Christ</term>, as a man, he teaches that all these things exist within divine power. Therefore, insofar as he is the Word of God and is God, he possesses this power naturally; <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin> but insofar as he became man (for it is said to man: *For what do you have that you did not receive?*), he openly professes that he has received this power.

But the adversaries will say again: "Behold, the Son himself teaches that he received judgment from the Father; but one receives what one does not have. How then is the one who abounds and gives not of a greater nature than the one who is in need and receives?" <margin>Refutation of cavils</margin> We, however, affirm that this was said appropriately and fittingly because of the dispensation of the Incarnation, by which he humbled himself, being made in the likeness of men.

Truly, since you neglect these simpler dogmas of the Church and, curiously seeking higher things, compel me to respond more sharply to your arguments, we say this first: it is not necessary, nor is it always the case, that something is given only to one who lacks it, nor is the giver always greater than the receiver. <margin>Psalm 68</margin> <note>Original cites Psalm 67.</note> For what will you answer if you hear the Psalmist saying: *Give glory to God*? Will you think that God lacks glory, or will you judge created men to be greater than the Creator because they are commanded to bring glory to God? The Godhead is full of glory, even if it receives nothing from us. But if he receives as an honor that which he already has from himself, he is not therefore lesser than the one who offered it. Therefore, the Father is not greater than his own Son because he has given him all judgment. 

Furthermore, it must be considered more carefully that "to judge" is an act rather than a substance. For if it were a substance and not an act, when someone ceased to judge, they would immediately cease to exist—which is clearly false. Therefore, judging is nothing other than a certain act and operation. What then

->[Column 2]<-

has the Father given to his Son, if he granted him all judgment? Nothing else, indeed, than a certain action over those who are judged. How then is the Father of a greater nature than the Son, or what did he provide to the Son that he did not already have? Does he not clearly say: *All things that the Father has are mine*? 

How then, you will ask, are we to understand that judgment was "given" to him? Listen and pay attention, I pray. For just as God the Father is able to create all things, yet he does so through the Son as through his own Power; so, although he is able to judge the world, he performs it through the Son as through his own Righteousness. It is as if someone were to say that fire had "given" the power of burning to its own natural heat; they would not wander far from the truth, because the act of burning is completed in this way. By understanding the giving of judgment to the Son in this manner, we shall not be caught in the snares of the devil. But if they impudently contend, saying that honor was added to the Son when he was made judge, let them show us how he was the Lord of all things who is only crowned with this praise in these last times.

*That all the dignities of the Godhead are in the Son, not by participation, or from the outside, but by nature.*

### CHAPTER 141.
**That all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father, who sent him.** <note>original: "Ut omnes honorificent filium, sicut honorificent patrem. Qui non honorificat filium, non honorificat patrem, qui misit illum."</note> A certain reason is now given for what has been said: but so that we may more fully grasp the entire power of the discourse, let us look back a little at the preceding points. He was saying in a unique way that God was his own Father, and he was making himself equal to God. Similarly, he was showing himself to be no less almighty than the Father, saying: *For whatever he does, the Son does likewise.* He also declared himself to be Life and a giver of life by nature, just like the Father. *For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son gives life to whom he will.* He also affirmed himself as Judge by the consent of the Father. *For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.* 

For what reason, then, were all these things said? *So that all* (he says) *may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father.* <margin>Objection of the ungodly</margin> For if he is everything that the Father is, regarding the majesty of the Godhead, how is it not right that he be honored equally with the Father, since nothing is lacking for the identity of their substance? 

But what do they object to us—those who, as Micah says, pervert all that is right? <margin>Micah 3</margin> "If," they say, "it is written that all should honor the Son *just as* they honor the Father, and for that reason you honor the Father and the Son equally, you wander far from the truth. For the word *just as* <note>original: "sicut"</note> is an expression of similarity, and signifies a certain likeness, not an equality of things." For so the Savior advises, saying: <margin>Luke 6</margin> *Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.*

<summary>This page argues for the divine equality of the Son with the Father, specifically through their shared power to give life and execute judgment. It refutes Arian-style objections by explaining that "giving" judgment to the Son refers to the economy of the Incarnation rather than a lack of inherent power.</summary>
