--- Page 83 ---
134 OF THE BLESSED CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK II. 135

...strikes [them] with fear, showing that he will raise the dead and lead them into judgment: so that those hearing that they must give an account of all these things to him—having been made slower to persecute him by this dread—might listen to his teaching with a quiet mind. Therefore, we all believe as faithful people that a time will eventually come in which all the dead will hear the voice of the one who raises them. But such a time is also present now, either because (as is commonly said) Lazarus heard the voice of the Savior <margin>John 11</margin> or because the faithful were dead before they received the Savior’s teaching. These things seem more likely to us than more refined interpretations; therefore, let us examine a more suitable meaning for these same words as they were proposed. 

"The hour is coming," he says, "and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God: and those who hear shall live." When, therefore, he says the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, he signifies the time in which all shall rise by his voice, will, and power to give an account of this life; thus (as we have already said), he drives them toward the right path through this fear. However, when it is added: "And those who hear shall live," he shows that the time for believing in him is already here, and he promises that the reward for this obedience will be eternal life. Thus, he testifies as if shouting: "You will certainly come into judgment at the time of the resurrection; if you consider it a bitter thing to be condemned there, or if you dread paying eternal penalties to me, do not miss this suitable time for believing, but embrace my present teaching now if you wish to reach eternal life."

### CHAPTER 144.

**"For as the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son also to have life in himself: and he has given him power to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man."** See again, see with what wonder—regarding the <term>dispensation</term> <note>original: "dispensationem"; here referring to the "Divine Economy" or the way God manages the salvation of humanity through the Incarnation</note> of these words and the character of this speech—you will escape the thoughts of the ignorant and avoid utter destruction. For the <term>Only-Begotten</term> <note>original: "unigenitus"; a title for Christ emphasizing his unique status as the only Son of God</note> Son of God was made man and was seen on earth, as it is written <margin>Baruch 3</margin>; and inducing the Jews toward salvation in many and various ways, he claimed for himself two great things worthy of God. For he was saying, not obscurely, both that he would raise the dead and that he would lead them to judgment before his own tribunal. Therefore, those hearing these things were troubled and were moved by various thoughts toward persecution, because he both said that God was his Father and made himself equal to Him. For this reason, joining the speech of his humanity to the splendor and power of his divinity, he softens their anger when he speaks more humbly of himself. "For as the Father," he says, "has life in himself, so he has given to the Son also to have life in himself." 

"Do not wonder," he says, "if, though you see me as a man, I nevertheless promise that I will raise the dead and threaten that I will lead them into judgment. For the Father has given me the power of giving life, he has given me the power of judging." But just as he strove to restrain the slippery minds of the Jews with these words, so he also had no small care for others. For that reason, he immediately added the cause for why he said these things were given to him by the Father, saying: "Because he is the Son of Man." This is so that we may understand that all things were given to him as a man, who—since he is a creature—has nothing from himself. Truly, the Only-Begotten Son is not a participant in life, but is life by nature just as the Father is; which we showed more extensively when explaining that "what was made in him was life."

### CHAPTER 145.

**"Do not wonder at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God: and those who have done good will come forth unto the resurrection of life: but those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment."** By these words, the time of the resurrection of all is signified. When (as the divine Paul writes <margin>1 Thessalonians 4</margin>) the Lord himself—with a command, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God—will descend from heaven to judge the world in justice, rendering to each according to his merits. Moreover, this is a repetition of what was said a little while before, so that the slow minds of the Hebrews might be able to understand that he would do greater things than the healing of one sick man. "Therefore," he says, "do not wonder at this—that one man, dissolved by a long illness and strengthened by a word, even carried his cot and departed—since I am to utterly destroy death and judge the whole world." 

We must not think, however, that the splendor of that miracle is diminished by Christ himself. For he does not forbid them from wondering at it, but he shows that this is a small thing compared to the others. Therefore, he was exhorting them to believe that he could deliver them not only from disease but even from death; for this reason, he relates these greater things. "Because the hour is coming, in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God." For how could he who produced all things from nothing not be able to recall those things once produced from destruction back to life again? Certainly, both acts belong to the same immense power. He most usefully added that they would "come forth" from the tombs: the sinners indeed into everlasting punishment, but those others, conversely, into eternal life. Thus, he demonstrates that he will be the judge and moderator of all these things; he deters them from vice through terror, and invites them to virtue by the magnitude of the rewards.

**Because God from God is the Son by nature, and is the most just image of the parent, he is therefore honored and glorified equally with the Father.**

### CHAPTER 146.

**"I can do nothing of myself: but as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just: because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me."** Attend again diligently, so that you may look into the power of the words. ->CYRIL’S COMMENTARIES ON JOHN
Book Three.<-

->PROLOGUE.<-

Having only just reached port at the completion of the second volume, we see another sea before us that must no less be sailed. But, since <margin>Wisdom 3</margin> the matter itself is worthy, and the rewards of honest labor (as they say) are glorious, we will gladly commit our sails to the winds, attributing the whole matter to the mercy of God. Therefore, unfolding the breadth of our mind like the curves of sails, and having received the breeze of the Spirit's grace through prayers, let us not shudder at the depth of the questions. <margin>Psalm 76</margin> For it is Christ who shows the way in the sea, and prepares straight paths in the waters.

->Why the Baptist is called not only a lamp, but a burning one.
CHAPTER I.<-

**H**e was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for an hour in his light. The most blessed Baptist is called a lamp because, as far as the measure of a human being is capable, before the manifestation of Christ he shone forth—not by his own light, but by another’s. For a lamp does not possess its own inherent or rational light, but one that is added and comes from the outside: just as in all the saints, illumination proceeds from Christ in the Holy Spirit. As most grateful <margin>John 1</margin> men proclaim, saying: *From his fullness we have all received.* For the Only-begotten is light by nature, who shone forth from the light, that is, from the substance of the Father. But the rational creature, whatever it seems to know and understand, knows and understands by participating in the true light, with its whole power of understanding derived from there. In this way, therefore, the Baptist was a lamp: *I have prepared <margin>Psalm 131</margin> a lamp for my Christ.* These things were necessarily added to what came before. For since, in order to shake off every cause of unbelief and

141

<margin>A</margin> to urge them toward faith from every side, he said that he does not receive the testimony of man, he did not want the Baptist to be thought of little value by him. He himself seems to say nothing of him now, but reminds them that he is called a lamp by the voice of the Father. For in this way, those who contradicted him could either be pacified by the fear of God the Father, or they would appear even more impudent in despising Him as well. "He," he says, "was a lamp, but you were willing to rejoice for an hour in his light." Thus he shows the Pharisees to be not only alienated from piety and faith, but also—even if they tasted something good in words—to be quickly affected by loathing because of their inconstancy. For this is what it means, I believe: that they "wished to rejoice for an hour" in the light of John. For though they admired him from the beginning as an example of virtue and piety, when they heard him <margin>B</margin> <margin>Isaiah 40</margin> saying, "Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God," they suddenly grew weary of him. But this is the common exposition of this text. Yet, since the Savior raises us to higher things, calling the Baptist not simply a lamp, but a *burning and shining* one, we must sharpen the edge of our mind for more sublime matters. "He was a lamp," he says; this would have been enough if he only wished to remind them of the prophecy concerning the Baptist. For the Psalmist sang of him, saying: "I have prepared a lamp for my Christ." But because he added, *burning and shining*, he did not only send his listeners back to the prophecy, but also to a certain figure of the Law <note>The "figure of the Law" refers to the Old Testament types or shadows that prefigured New Testament realities.</note> which denoted John’s light in the shadow. In this way, he shows that they, though nourished in the Mosaic Law, appeared to be skilled in the scriptures rather than actually being so. And this indeed is the sense of this discourse; but it is necessary, having brought here the passage of scripture <margin>C</margin> that pertains to the matter, to show more broadly that the Baptist was a burning and shining lamp. When the sacred Tabernacle was divinely established and the feasts of the Lord were set, he said to Moses: "Command <margin>Leviticus 24</margin> the children of Israel that they bring to you the purest and clearest oil for tending the lamp continually outside the veil of the testimony in the Tabernacle of the Covenant; and Aaron and his sons shall set it from evening until morning before the Lord, by a perpetual rite and worship throughout your generations." Oil, removed from all dregs and most pure, seems to me to signify the nature of the Holy Spirit. This Spirit, having entered into our souls ineffably like oil, nourishes, preserves, and increases (like oil placed in a lamp) the illumination granted to us. Thus, therefore, we believe the light of the blessed Baptist also burned. <margin>D</margin> For he did not have the power of illuminating from anywhere else than from this intellectual oil <note>original: "oleo intellectuali" — here meaning spiritual or non-material oil.</note>, by which the fire of this divine illumination is kindled in us. The Savior signified this elsewhere enigmatically, saying: "I <margin>Luke 12</margin> came to send fire upon the earth; what do I wish, if it is already kindled?" Therefore, the blessed Baptist was a burning and shining lamp always in the Tabernacle of the Testimony. For the fact that he shone in the Tabernacle of the Testimony signifies that his illumination is not cast out by the Church, but is received and is pleasing. But the fact that the lamp burned *outside the veil* denoted nothing else (as I <margin>Matthew 3</margin> think) than that his illumination would be simpler and introductory: saying "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand," for it contains no interior or hidden mystery...

For John did not baptize into the participation of the Holy Spirit, nor did he introduce anyone to the light within the veil <note>Referring to the veil in the Temple, which separated the holy place from the Most Holy Place, symbolizing access to God's presence</note>. And he says, "Aaron and his sons shall set it <note>original: "ponet eam"</note> from evening until morning before the Lord." <margin>To the writer, namely the legislator, who circumscribes the spiritual sense for some.</margin>

But again, ruminating on the more sublime sense of this passage, we shall arrive (as I believe) at the spiritual sense intended by the writer. The placement of the lamp is located at the end of the tabernacle, after the access and use of the priests is described: because at the end of the Law and the Prophets, the "voice of one crying" sounded like a trumpet in the desert, saying: "Prepare the way of the Lord: make straight the paths of our God" <note>Matthew 3:3 / Isaiah 40:3</note>; and this was after the ordination and preaching of the apostles shone forth. He again rebukes the obstinacy and ignorance of the Pharisees, who did not understand the things they professed to know; instead, wandering far from the true sense of Scripture, they showed themselves off with empty doctrine. For since he called John a burning and shining lamp, he shows that they had not yet understood the shadows and enigmas <note>term: "enigmas"—symbolic riddles or veiled meanings in the Old Testament that point to Christ</note> of the Law. But when he added, "But you were willing to exult for an hour in his light," he reveals that the divine will was neglected by them. For though the founder of the Law commanded that the lamp must always burn and shine, He says, "You willed" that it should shine not always, but only for an hour and a very brief space of time. For having admired John at the beginning, you lit his light in this manner. But afterward, you yourselves were not baptized by him, and you prohibited others from being baptized, falling into such insanity 

<margin>John 1.</margin>

that you even rebuked God’s messenger. For you sent people to him who said: "Why then do you baptize?"—that is, why do you lead the people by your light toward repentance and the knowledge of Christ? Thus, they are seen to be briefly accused by the Savior of the crime of ignorance and iniquity. 

<margin>Luke 7.</margin>

Luke also shows their ignorance, saying: "And all the people hearing the words (namely of the Savior) justified God, being baptized by John: but the Pharisees and the teachers of the law rejected the will of God for themselves, not being baptized by him."

### CHAPTER II.

"BUT I have a testimony greater than John: for the works which the Father gave me to finish, these very works that I do bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me." Although the 

***

143

Baptist was a lamp, although he was denoted by the figures of the Law, and although 

<margin>Isaiah 40.</margin>

he was preached by the voice of the prophets as coming to prepare the way of the Lord and the paths of our God; nevertheless, He says, because he does not seem worthy of faith to you, nor is the testimony of such a great man accepted by you because of your arrogance, I am compelled to offer you a greater witness, the brilliance of which will so dazzle the eyes of your mind that you will be able to say nothing at all. For I do not prove my case with words, nor by the authority of men, but by the brilliance and glory of miracles I show that I am born of God and am God by nature. Nor do I do any injury to anyone if I so moderate the laws which I myself brought forth, that I may transfer the things spoken enigmatically from literal rudeness to spiritual intelligence. Therefore, in these words, He clearly teaches that no virtue or operation fitting for God can exist in anyone unless he is God by nature. For works are a certain and necessary testimony. For if He performs the works of God the Father, and accomplishes by His own command those things which no one but God can do, how will it not be plain that He possesses the same nature as God the Father and shines with the perfections of the deity? 

Moreover, He affirms that He received these works from the Father, either speaking of Himself more humbly because of the dispensation <note>term: "dispensation" (original: "dispensationem")—the theological plan of the Incarnation, where God the Son took on human form and limitations</note> in the flesh, or calling the consensus of the Father in performing miracles by the name of "giving." For in this way He is also said to have been "sent," because He humbled Himself for our sake. But "humbling Himself" is understood in no other way than through the assumption of humanity, by which it came to pass that He often speaks as a man. 

<margin>Psalm 2.</margin>

Wherefore the Psalmist also sang more humbly of Him, as of a man, in this way: "But I have been set as king by Him over Zion, His holy mountain, preaching His precept." For He who always reigns with God the Father confesses that He was "set" as king. For having been made man, for whom it is not natural to reign, He is said to receive a kingdom which He always possesses naturally as God.

### CHAPTER III.

"AND you have never heard His voice, nor seen His form, and you do not have His word abiding in you: because you do not believe Him whom He sent." These words again contain no simple meaning, but various sublime understandings are hidden in them. For someone might perhaps object: why, when He had said that He has the testimony of the Father, did He immediately drop down to these things which seem to have nothing to do with what went before? For what does it matter to the testimony of the Father if the Pharisees never heard the voice of God the Father, nor ever saw His form? Someone might rightly object to these things. But we, with the help of the grace of the Spirit, shall say that it was Christ's custom—especially when He spoke to the unskilled Pharisees—to look into their hearts and examine the movements of their thoughts as God, and sometimes to accommodate His speech to the things they were turning over in their minds. And for this reason, His discourse sometimes does not proceed directly from the preceding words, since the speech is most sharply composed to address those things which they were debating within themselves. In this way, He most especially showed Himself to be God by nature. For no one except God [knows] the hearts...

...the law was sent down from the beginning with a divine voice, yet it was subtle and soft on account of human weakness, not yet capable of bearing the full blast of the trumpet; for this reason, Moses was "slow of tongue" <margin>Exodus 4</margin>. <note>Cyril interprets Moses’s speech impediment as a symbol for the "quiet" or limited nature of the Old Testament Law compared to the Gospel.</note> But as the ages progressed—once people were led back from the literal shadow to spiritual worship by Christ—the sound of the divine trumpet became much more powerful, spreading the preaching of the Gospel throughout the entire world. He simply said "with a voice," which miraculously sounded in the ears of the listeners through the sound of words in the human manner.

What, after all, is God unable to accomplish? But these things are indeed symbols; now let us look upon the truth itself. We read, therefore, in the most holy Gospels that the Lord said, "Father, glorify your son," and the Father responded, "I have glorified it, and will glorify it again" <margin>John 12</margin>. You see that he says the voice "happened." For it is not fitting that we should think the divine nature uses this sonorous voice—which is produced by the striking of air—even if He is said to have spoken in the human manner for our benefit and through a <term>dispensation</term> <note>original: *dispensationem*. In this context, a "dispensation" is a divine arrangement where God adapts His infinite nature to human limitations to communicate with us.</note>. These things were said to us so that the truth of the Savior's words might appear: because they never heard the Father's voice, nor have men seen His form, nor did the Pharisees have His word abiding in them, because they did not believe in the one whom He sent.

Truly, the lying pen of the scribes has produced a lie; the wise are put to shame, they are terrified and captured, and there is no wisdom in them, for they have cast away the word of the Lord" <margin>Jeremiah 8</margin>. For how could the living and subsisting [Word] of God... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

<margin>Moses’s mediation</margin> Therefore, the mediation of Moses between God and the people of the Jews was a <term>figure</term><note>A "figure" (figura) is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows a reality in the New Testament.</note> of the mediation of Christ. But while that first mediation was servile, employed in the manner of a servant, this mediation of Christ is free and mystical. For having been made the mediator between God and men, he truly touches both natures. For he who is God by nature, as the only-begotten Son of God—not separated from the substance of the Father, but from it and in it—has also been made man, so that the nature of men, which was separated far from God, might be joined to God through him.

<margin>Deut. 18</margin> Therefore, what Moses says—"The Lord will raise up for you a prophet like me"—must not be understood in any other way than what we have said. For God himself also affirmed this, saying: <margin>Acts 3</margin> "They have spoken rightly. I will raise up for them a prophet like you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him." <note>Deuteronomy 18:17–18</note> For the Son carries all things by the <margin>Heb. 1</margin> word of his power, as Paul says. And he thunders the voice of the Father to us, having been appointed mediator by him, just as the <margin>Psalm 2</margin> Psalmist sang concerning the person of Christ himself: "But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, preaching his precept."

Someone might bring forward this point on account of that phrase, "Like you," since Moses was the minister of the Law: <margin>Matt. 5:b</margin> "You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not commit adultery; but I say to you, You shall not covet." <note>Cyril is contrasting the Mosaic Law with Christ’s "internalized" law.</note> One might also understand Christ as the teacher by whom we ascend into heaven and to eternal life, just as Moses was the leader of the ancients to the land of promise; whence he often says: <margin>Deut. 18</margin> "And the Lord your God will lead you into the land which he swore to your fathers; and keep these precepts, that you may live for a long time." 

Truly, because it is written: "But whoever will not hear his words, I shall stand as an avenger." Let the Jews hear, I pray, and understand how, through their ignorance and arrogance, they have called down eternal vengeance upon themselves. How they are tortured by eternal punishments, deprived of all hope of honors, because they did not believe Moses—whom, if they had believed, they certainly would have believed Christ, about whom he wrote.

#### CHAPTER X.

**BUT if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?** This speech seems to pour out great darkness here. For someone could certainly reach such a point of falsehood as to think the writings of Moses are of greater dignity than the words of the Savior. Indeed, the very style and figure of the speech seems to show the writings of Moses as much more worthy than the words of the Savior. But the very nature of things persuades us that this sense is far from the truth and full of madness. For how can those things be greater or more worthy which were nothing other than figures and shadows? How, I ask, shall they be greater than the Truth which was prefigured by them? It would not be difficult to write a long discourse on this matter due to the abundance of material. However, since it is so clear that it shines by its own light, such labor would be superfluous. Therefore, let us continue our journey; the sense of this passage is as follows:

->### SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK III. 151<-

"If you," he says, "who hold the written Law of Moses and read it daily with zeal, nevertheless make little of it and transgress it, as if forgetting those things you read every day, how will you be rightly disposed toward my words? Or how will you believe my words, which you have heard scarcely once and then negligently, when you do not believe Moses, whom you profess as your master and read every day?" 

Either we shall understand it in this way, or (for a pious variety of interpretations is useful in these matters) we shall say that the Mosaic Scripture, with its figures and shadows, leads us toward the mysteries of Christ (as a <term>pedagogue</term><note>A "pedagogue" was a tutor or guardian who led a child to their teacher; Cyril uses the Pauline image of the Law leading believers to Christ.</note> is accustomed to do); and we shall assert that the things written there are like certain <margin>Gal. 3</margin> elements of the Evangelical Scripture. For Christ is the end of the legal discipline, as it is written: <margin>Rom. 10</margin> "Christ is the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets." He, therefore, who [rejects] the elements...

<margin>The Lake of Tiberias is called a sea.</margin> When He was supposed to set out for Jerusalem, the Lord, avoiding the feast day, sailed across the Lake of Tiberias—which the Jews called a "sea" because of its great size. We understand the day of this Feast of Tabernacles <term>scenopegiæ: The Feast of Tabernacles or Booths, a Jewish autumn festival commemorating the desert wanderings of Israel and the harvest.</term> spiritually as the gathering of the saints to Christ. This occurs when, from the entire circle of the earth after the resurrection of the dead, they shall be gathered to the heavenly Jerusalem to celebrate the solemnity of the true "Tabernacles" forever, giving thanks to the Lord for the resurrection of their bodies and the destruction of death. 

It is said in historical accounts that a nearly infinite multitude used to go up to Jerusalem for that feast day. During that time, the Pharisees were able to exert a necessary and powerful influence. Because they appeared to be the defenders of the Law, they could easily incite the crowds among such a large and unlearned multitude by shouting against transgressors (or those they deemed to be transgressors). These crowds tend to behave like waves or a fire that has found abundant fuel: they are tossed violently here and there by the "winds" of the leaders' words. 

Being well aware of this, the Lord departed from there secretly with His disciples and crossed over the Sea of Tiberias. The Evangelist himself declares to us that He avoided the Jews who were seeking Him, saying: *After these things Jesus walked in Galilee. For he would not walk in Judea, because the Jews sought to kill him.* 

<margin>John 7</margin> "But," someone might say, "I do not deny that this is how things were; however, I desire to learn why He also avoided the feast day itself." Listen, then, to those who were considered His brothers, who said to Christ in Galilee: "Go up from here into Judea, so that your disciples may see the signs you perform." To whom the Lord replied: "You go up; I am not going up to this festival, because my time has not yet come." Clearly...

You also hear that those who were just described as having followed him were moved by the signs he performed upon those who were sick; they did this with great zeal, progressing from witnessing miracles to a knowledge of him, understanding that divine honors should be bestowed upon him because of the power he used as God.

However, I believe a sharper meaning lies hidden in these words. The Jews were more violently disturbed because of the healing of a sick man; these people not only marvel at such signs but even follow him as God because of them.
Therefore, I pray that we who profess Christ as God and Lord may flee the shameful ignorance of the Jews. Let us cling to Christ through patience; let us imitate those most patient disciples who never departed from him, who cried out in deed what Paul later explained in words: *Who shall

he has already promised us: *You who have followed me in my trials, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty in the regeneration, you also shall sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.* For I believe this is signified by the fact that the disciples climbed the mountain with the Savior and sat there with him.

### CHAPTER XIII.
**When Jesus then lifted up his eyes and saw that a great multitude was coming to him, he said to Philip: "Where shall we buy bread, so that these may eat?" (But he said this to test him. For he himself knew what he was going to do.)** Christ now proposed an excellent discipline—one consistent with holy men—to his disciples. For even in the mountains and the wilderness, he taught that they ought to be prepared for the virtue of hospitality. Indeed, what greater thing can be devised for a person who wishes to attain the love of God? For when countless people flowed toward him like streams of water, he commanded his disciples to sustain them with food.

<column-break/>

155
Given the sheer number of people and the solitude of the location, what wealthy man would not have been terrified by the magnitude and difficulty of such a task? But he warns that all such fear should be cast aside by the hope of his grace. Historically, the meaning of the words is easy to grasp.
But spiritually, we say that from the high mountain of his foreknowledge, God foresees all those who seek him with fervent faith, just as Paul says:
<margin>Romans 8</margin>
*Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son; these he also called.* Therefore, with eyes lifted up, Christ sees those who are worthy to be visited by him (because they seek and love him). Just as it was said to Israel in a
<margin>Isaiah 26</margin>
blessing: *May the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace.* But grace does not end with the visit alone; nourishment and a feast are also prepared, so that you may know the truth of what is said in the proverbs: *The Lord
<margin>Proverbs 10</margin>
will not kill the righteous soul with hunger.* For he will set himself forth as the bread from heaven and nourish the souls of the faithful, preparing all the necessities of life for them, as it says in the
<margin>Psalm 64</margin>
Psalms: *You have prepared their food, for so is your preparation.* And Christ himself says in the Gospel: *Amen, amen, I say to you, whoever comes to me
<margin>John 6</margin>
shall never hunger.* For he will give (as we have said) heavenly food and various, copious graces of the Spirit, and he will prepare them before anything is asked of him.
For we do not know how to pray and ask as we ought. Therefore, he himself reaches out to us with those things that lead to eternal salvation.
He said to Philip: *Where shall we buy bread?* It is not out of place to consider why he spoke to Philip. Philip was eager to learn and asked questions often, but he was not so sharp as to be able to understand deeper things. This is evident because, though he followed the Savior for a long time and saw various signs of his divinity daily—drawn toward knowledge by both deeds and words—he speaks to Jesus almost at the very end of his
<margin>John 14</margin>
earthly mission as if he had learned nothing: *Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.* And because he asked without malice, he was taught rightly. *Have I been with you for so long,* Jesus said, *and you still do not know me, Philip?* Therefore, he questions him to call and strengthen him, leading a simpler mind to achieve more sublime insights.
The Evangelist signified this when he said that Philip was tested by the Lord. *For he himself,* it says, *knew what he was going to do.* He said, *Where shall we buy bread?* to show the poverty of the disciples, who had long since cast aside the pursuit of gathering money and had nothing with which to buy.
He also does this most skillfully. For the word "where" was not said in vain; because he closed off every way for them to collect money, he forced them by his questioning to break out into a realization: if he wished to feed the multitude while knowing the disciples had nothing, it would be necessary for him, as Lord, to produce nourishment by ineffable virtue and power. This was the only thing left, and he provoked them to this, as the poets of the nations say: <note>original: "ferro ulceri opus est" — a classical medical proverb meaning "the ulcer needs the knife" or "drastic measures are required."</note> "the ulcer needs the knife."

<margin>Psalm 6</margin> Do not neglect to remember. From the Psalms: *For in death there is no one who remembers you; in the underworld, who will acknowledge you?* <note>original: "Quia non est in morte qui memor sit tui, in inferno aut quis confitebitur tibi?"</note> For what fruit will there be after death? Or how shall anyone remember God, or how shall he perform the commandments, once he has descended to the depths? <margin>Regarding one who has died</margin> For God has concluded the matter in him, as it is written. Therefore, Paul also teaches, saying: *While we have time, let us work for the good.* <note>original: "Donec tempus habemus, operemur bonum"</note> History itself provides us with this useful lesson.

Truly, we must look at this spiritually (as is necessary in the Scriptures). We previously stated that the **five barley loaves** signify the books of Moses <note>The Pentateuch: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note>, while the **two fish** signify the writings of the Apostles and Evangelists. Now, concerning the gathering of the fragments, let us draw a spiritual conclusion consistent with what came before. By the Lord’s command, the crowds sat down, and the blessed bread and fish were placed before them through the ministry of the disciples. When everyone was satisfied, twelve baskets were filled with the fragments, one for each disciple. What do we understand by this? Christ is the master of the feast for the faithful; he receives his guests with heavenly and divine teachings—both the legal and prophetic commands, as well as the evangelical and apostolic ones. He does this not directly by himself, but through the ministry of the Apostles, who administer his grace to us. <margin>Matthew 10</margin> For it is not they who speak, as it is written, but the Spirit of the Father who speaks through them. Nor did the Apostles endure this labor without a reward: for when they set the Savior’s feast before us through their ministry, a most full measure of divine grace was returned to them. In my opinion, this signifies nothing other than the fact that after the labor and service of the feast, each man carried back a basket full of fragments at Christ’s command. Do not doubt that this same grace has passed down to the leaders of the holy churches through succession.

### CHAPTER XIX.
Therefore, when those men had seen the sign he had performed, they said: "This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world." They marveled at the novelty of the sign, for they judged these things to be fitting for God. They were moved by human reason rather than by the animal-like recklessness of the <margin>John 6</margin> impious inhabitants of Jerusalem. While the latter could have been helped by a correct judgment of the miracles, they instead thought of stoning Jesus, even though he performed many miraculous deeds beyond the powers of nature every day. These people, however, being not a little better, were so affected by the excellence of this unheard-of sign that they firmly believed and proclaimed that he is the one written of who would come into the world in the role of a Prophet. But a still greater difference is seen here between the Jews and the foreigners. For although the Jews saw many things most worthy of admiration, they are not only harsh and rustic, but they even meditate on killing their Savior. Yet these people, who lived far from Jerusalem (and for that reason we call them <term>foreigners</term><note>The Latin 'alienigenas' likely refers to the Galileans or Gentiles who, though geographically or socially distant from the religious elite in Jerusalem, showed greater faith.</note>), are so moved by a single sign that Israel justly condemned itself, and the Gentiles were similarly received by God.

### CHAPTER XX.
Therefore, when Jesus realized they were coming to seize him and make him king, he fled again to the mountain by himself. The intention of those people was certainly praiseworthy, for they judged that what is considered the highest honor among men could worthily be conferred upon Christ. Indeed, this offering of a kingdom signifies nothing other than their heart's high opinion of Christ. But Christ, fleeing the kingdom in his contempt for glory, serves as an example for us. He teaches us by his actions that the things considered greatest in this life are actually small. For the honor and glory of the world must be fled by those who wish to attain the glory of God. It is entirely foolish to seek the kingdoms of this world if you desire eternal kingdoms. Let us therefore flee fleeting glory, which is joined to pride and status, as if it were a bitter enemy. Let us instead embrace the beauty of humility, yielding to one another, as the blessed Paul advises, saying: *Let this mind be in you, <margin>Philippians 2</margin> which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in human form: he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Because of this, God also exalted him, and gave him the name which is above every name.* <note>The translator provides a full English rendering of the famous "Christ Hymn" from the Latin Vulgate text.</note> You see how this voluntary humility brings about a most radiant end. You see how a mind that is by no means arrogant becomes the root of many good things. For the only-begotten Son of the Father humbled himself for our sake, and from this humility of the flesh, he returned with that very flesh into the dignity and glory of God. We must understand it in this way for ourselves as well. For when we have been humble in this life for the sake of Christ, we shall attain heavenly glory and become gods by grace, called the adopted sons of God. Therefore, let us refuse even the highest honor of a kingdom if it is offered, if we savor heavenly things rather than earthly ones.

But let us briefly repeat what has taken place so that we may more easily see the spiritual truths which the Evangelist is partially revealing and proposing for our necessary investigation. *Jesus,* he says, *withdrew again to the mountain alone.* Spurning the cruelty of the Jews, <margin>Jeremiah 11</margin> he departed from Jerusalem. *He left his house, he abandoned his inheritance,* as it is written, and having gone across the Sea of Tiberias far from them, he ascended the mountain with his disciples. As we have said, this signifies that the way to Christ has been made inaccessible to the Jews because of their stubbornness until the appropriate time. Furthermore, it shows that Christ, having turned with his disciples from the Jews toward the Gentiles, will be conspicuous and illustrious as his grace is transferred to them. When he lifted his eyes from the mountain and saw the multitude, he prepared himself to nourish them. As we said, this enigmatically points to the visitation of God owed to the saints, according to the verse: <margin>Psalm 33</margin> *The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.* Moreover, that multitude was miraculously fed to satisfaction with five loaves and two fish; thus we understood that the old and new commandments of Scripture are set before the faithful by the Apostles, and both the Apostles and their successors in the churches will possess the full grace of this ministry. Finally, the spectators, marvelling at the sign, thought to seize the Savior for a kingdom; and he, not being ignorant of this, withdrew alone to the mountain. For when he was held in admiration by the nations as a worker of miracles and as God—when all received him as their king and Lord—then alone (with no one at all following...

<meta>This page continues a theological commentary—likely by Cyril of Alexandria as translated by the Renaissance scholar George of Trebizond—concerning the Gospel of John. It specifically addresses the nature of Christ's divinity and his relationship to God the Father using the metaphor of a "seal."</meta>

# 168 TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND 169

<unclear>He</unclear> assumes? For who can grant food that remains unto eternal life? Surely no mortal; but God alone, who both created and governs all things. Therefore, the Savior came forward and restrained such talkativeness, saying that this food, which nourishes for eternal life, is given by the Son of Man; and he immediately added that he himself was **sealed** by God the Father. Moreover, he used the word "to be sealed" either in place of "to be anointed" (for he who was anointed was being sealed) or he denoted by the name of "sealing" that he was naturally formed (so to speak) according to the form of the Father. He seemed to be saying: "It is not difficult for me to bestow upon you the permanent food by which you will be led to the unheard-of delights of eternal life. For even if I am a man, like one of you, I am nevertheless anointed by God the Father and sealed to his immutable identity."

<margin>John 14</margin>
**A** "For I am seen naturally in the Father and the Father in me." <note>original: "Ego in patre & pater in me"</note> Therefore, although for your sake, through the reason of the **ineffable dispensation**, I was made a man from a woman, I nevertheless possess that power by which I can perform all things as God; nor is my power in any way less than that of the Father. Thus, if the Father can provide you with spiritual food leading to eternal life, the Son can likewise do the same. Although he assumed flesh, he is nonetheless his immutable image; this supreme identity is seen not in the lines of a body, nor in any physical shape, but in substance, glory, and the royal power of the deity.

This must be observed above all: because when he said the Son of Man would give this divine food and was sealed to the image of God the Father, he allows no separation that could sever the temple assumed from the Virgin from the true Son of God. Rather, he wishes himself to be understood as one, just as he is: for there is truly one Christ, composed of the whole man—namely of soul and body—just as if clothed in royal robes.

**B** Thus, Christ is one from two natures. But the great adversary of Christ will cry out, and by cavillations will contend to drag the explanation of this passage to a place where we do not wish it to go. 

<margin>The cavilling of the impious.</margin>
For he will clearly say that these words do not show the Son to be of the substance of the Father, but only a certain likeness of that substance. For just as a seal (he says) which we use to mark wax or another material suitable for being marked, imprints only its own likeness, and is seen neither to do nor suffer anything else, so the Son, being sealed by the Father, received indeed an exquisite likeness of him, but the substance of the Father was not communicated to him, just as the substance of the seal is not transferred into the thing marked.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
Let whoever is a student of Christ hear and attend, I pray, how even now iniquity insults us, raising itself up like a venomous serpent. But he who broke the heads of dragons will, I know for certain, break this one too; and he will give us strength, he who...

<margin>Psalm 71</margin>
...concedes that one can mark a seal with a <term>character</term> <note>In Greek theology, "character" refers to the distinct expression or "stamp" of a person's being (hypostasis).</note>, and cannot mark without a character. Since, therefore, the divine Scripture testifies that the Son is the character of the Father's <term>hypostasis</term> <note>The underlying reality or distinct personhood of God.</note>, because he is in it and from it by nature, by what other character did the Father seal his Son? Or by what character was the Father himself sealed, so that he might be able to seal the Son? For no one will say that the Father is not in the form of the deity, while the Son is the form of the parent; whom if anyone sees intellectually, he has seen the Father himself entirely.

**C** Wherefore he also says he is in him naturally, although he is also from him, because he subsists: just as perhaps splendor is in a thing, and from the thing which shines. For it is understood to be something else by reason, and the thing itself which shines is another thing; but it is not "something else" if you look at the nature of both, since splendor is from the shining thing and is in it again. Nor, because they are the same in nature, is it believed that any part of it is from itself. For those things proceed, which are thus from another, so that they are understood to subsist as their own, although not separated or cut off. Therefore, he who is the Son from the substance of the Father is sealed: not to a naked likeness, nor without flesh, but rather in the flesh, so that through him, those who ascend to the likeness of God through grace may be sealed.

For in this way we also understand that verse: "The light of your countenance, O Lord, is sealed upon us." 

<margin>Psalm 4</margin>
For he calls the Son the "countenance of God the Father," that is, the character of the Father; but his "light" is the grace of the Spirit, which penetrates to all creatures, through which we are conformed to God by faith, as if conformed to the Son by a certain seal, who is the image of the Father. And thus it is rightly preserved in us, namely, that we were created "to the likeness and image." Since, therefore, the Son is the countenance of God the Father, he himself will also be the character in which God seals.

<margin>A new objection.</margin>
"Let these things be," the adversary of Christ will say; "for we believe that the holy are sealed by God through the Spirit, but this has nothing at all to do with the proposed question." For just as a seal (as we said) made of iron or gold imprints its likeness on another material and suffers no loss, but leaves the likeness in the suitable material by impression alone, so the Son, sealed by the Father, has nothing of his substance. Instead, while God the Father is one thing, the Son possesses only an exquisite likeness of him (as the image of the original).

<margin>Rebuke of the adversaries.</margin>
**D** O immense madness! O mind headlong into danger, how quickly it has forgotten all that was just said! For we asserted that the Son is the character of the Father, and we understood that in him, not himself (for nothing is a character of itself), but something else is sealed. But you, with this reason not rightly pushed back, are not ashamed to speak only of the likeness of the impression. For in the figures of the impression alone, according to you, the Son is God—but not at all by nature—but only by a certain form and figure by which he is similar to the parent.

Here, Cyril refutes the idea that the Son's likeness is a secondary quality that could be lost.</meta>

[Left Column]

...do you yield? Or even if it is not implanted in nature, do you still deny that it can nevertheless be removed? But it is clear, even while you remain silent, that those things which are not inherent by nature could be taken away. Therefore, by this comparison, the Son could be deprived [of his likeness]. For if, as you feel, he is similar to the Father not naturally, but by the impression (as it were) of a seal, then he is indeed something other than the parent by nature, and far removed from his substance. For you have said clearly and safely that nothing except "likeness" was given to the Son by the Father—lest, presumably, some detriment or <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passio" – in ancient theology, this refers to undergoing change or physical suffering, which was thought impossible for God's pure essence.</note> should seem to have disturbed the substance of the Father. 

But you are ignorant that God the Father generates the Son as far removed from all "passion" as he produces all things without "passion." For he is much better than the fire which we see (for we are compelled to use even cruder examples), which, I say, we see generating heat from itself without [B] "passion," nor by any cutting or separation such as is found in physical bodies. 

Pay attention, therefore, I pray, all you who think it a virtue rather than a vice to dispute so incautiously about divine matters. Pay attention, I say: because if the Son is joined to the Father by only this kind of likeness, no good will be permanent for him, and he can be seen to not be God by nature; furthermore, he will be susceptible to changing for the worse. For we read <margin>Ezekiel 28</margin> that it was said by divine decree to the Prince of Tyre—whom we are persuaded by a certain necessary reason to identify as the Devil—"You are the impression of similarity." Yet it is found that he, whoever he was, fell away from this similarity; from which one can see that the Son could also cast away that likeness. For being "sealed" according to the nature of the Creator is not sufficient for an unchanging eternity of goods: for even intellectual substances <note>i.e., angels or spiritual beings</note> fall away by the choice of some shameful thing. 

Therefore, if the Son is not similar to the Father by identity of nature, but only by a certain "accidental" similarity which he preserves by the merit of an upright will, he could also be changed. And if he is not changed by his will, he will possess this immutability not naturally (as God does), and therefore he will not be the true God. And why then do we adore him? Why is he also glorified together with the Father? Or why is he worshiped by the higher powers? Do you believe that those blessed <margin>Isaiah 6</margin> Seraphim also wander far [from the truth] when they glorify one who is not God by nature, and call him "Lord of <term>Sabaoth</term>"? <note>Sabaoth is a Hebrew title meaning "of Hosts" or "of Armies," used to denote God’s supreme authority.</note> For you will not deny that all those heavenly virtues, powers, and dominations strive, as much as is possible for them, to achieve conformity to God. For if man—a small animal when compared to them—is honored with such dignity by the grace of the Creator, who will deny that even more excellent gifts have been divinely conferred upon them? 

How then, calling him Lord of Sabaoth, do they perform their service as attendants, as if to the King of all things? For what reason is it written <margin>Hebrews 1</margin> that he "sits at the right hand" of God the Father himself? Does a servant sit with the Lord, or a creature with the Creator? It is therefore clear on all sides that the Son is not a creature, but is substantially and naturally God, unchanging by nature and impassible. How then are those who say these things to be endured?

[Right Column]

...or how can it not rightly be said of them: <margin>Isaiah 5</margin> "Woe to you who are drunk without wine"? Truly they do not yet blush, but they assert that the Son was "sealed" by the Father with an exquisite likeness to God, so that although he is not from the Father by nature, he is nevertheless unchanging. <margin>Refutation of a new objection.</margin> 

Tell me, I pray: how shall he who is not from God according to nature possess the property of deity by nature? Who will deny that a creature cannot obtain the property of an uncreated nature? Who will not confess that those things which naturally inhabit the deity can never be found in the same way in another besides God? Immutability exists in God naturally; it cannot exist in creatures in the same way. Rather, by a certain zeal, vigilance, and care, through the grace of God which prevents rational creatures from sliding into shameful things, they are conformed to divine immutability as much as they are able to receive it. 

But if any property or perfection of the deity were to inhabit another besides Him in a similar way (as they say), what prohibits all those properties of that nature from inhabiting everyone else too? For if one "immutability" is known to pass over to another in this way, and other properties pass over likewise, it must be confessed that all things will be confused for us: God will differ in nothing at all from creatures, and creatures will ascend to the nature of the deity. For since God has offered all good things to his creatures without any envy, as much as they can receive, there would be no doubt that many would turn out to be gods for us according to nature, capable of creating the earth, heaven, and other such things from nothing. 

Consider, therefore, I pray, how great a force of blasphemies gushes forth from this position of yours! God, therefore, preserves his own [C] nature, and the creature does not at all ascend to His immutability according to nature, but is made a participant in immutability by a certain spiritual union. The Son, however, who is immutable by nature, is also God by nature—and therefore necessarily "from the Father." For there is no dignity, no perfection, no property of the deity that is not naturally within the Son. 

But since they strike us with that "firm" argument (as they call it), saying that the Son is one thing and the Father another—since the image is one thing and the original another—and they think that from this the diversity of the substance of the Father and the Son is demonstrated: they will be said to babble frivolous and empty trifles if, putting aside all contention, they will choose to consider these things rightly. For why do they contend in vain? <margin>Refutation of another quibble.</margin> Or why [do they flee] from the properties of substance...

<meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria’s commentary on the Gospel of John, specifically addressing the relationship between the Father and the Son through the lens of biblical law and the transition from the Old Covenant to the New. The previous page discussed the nature of the Son as the "seal" of the Father; here, Cyril uses the Jewish Temple tax as a metaphor for their shared essence.</meta>

172 TRANSLATED BY GEORGE OF TREBIZOND 173

An example is not out of place for the confusion of heretics, taken from the authority of the Law: for the redemption of his own head, each person according to the Law <margin>Exodus 30</margin> was required to contribute half a <term>didrachm</term> <note>original: "didrachmi medietatem" – a Greek silver coin; in the Jewish context, this refers to the half-shekel temple tax.</note>. However, the value of the didrachm was contained in a single <term>stater</term> <note>original: "statere" – a silver coin worth four drachmae or two didrachms.</note>. By these shadows of the Law, Christ—who offered himself to God the Father for the redemption of all—was depicted. For in one coin, a drachma was understood which was not separated from the other. Indeed, as we have said, two drachmas were in one very small unit. So the Father relates to the Son, and the Son to the Father, in one nature: yet they are distinct, because each exists as a person; and yet they are joined, because one is not without the other. And just as two drachmas were in one small coin, differing by no measure of quantity, so the Father and the Son are in one substance, differing by no reasoning of nature. If you follow this truth, you will understand in their integrity all things written about the Son.

### CHAPTER XXX.
**They said therefore to him: What shall we do, that we may work the works of God? Jesus answered and said to them.** This question did not proceed from a good heart, nor from a desire for learning, but rather from arrogance; for they asked as if they already knew everything and nothing remained for them to learn. "The precepts of Moses are enough for us," they say; "we know no less than those ought to know who wish to do the work of God. What new or unheard-of thing can he himself teach us that has not been said in the Scripture?" You find something similar in Matthew: <margin>Matthew 19</margin> for a certain young man, surrounded by a great heap of riches, asked how he might obtain eternal life. To whom the Lord said: "You know the commandments well: do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not bear false witness, and those things joined to these." But he, thinking these things beneath his knowledge, said: "All these I have kept from my youth; what is still lacking to me?" Therefore, what that man brought forward out of ignorance and pride—"what is still lacking to me?"—these people also do out of arrogance, saying: "What shall we do that we may work the work of God?" Humility is a proven thing, and a sign of a noble soul to believe teachers and to yield to them as to those more learned, when they strive to lead us to better things by instructing us. For how shall they hold the dignity of a teacher unless they can perceive better things to bestow? "The disciple is not," <margin>Matthew 10</margin> he says, "above his master."

### CHAPTER XXXI.
**This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent.** Although somewhat hiddenly, he opposes them with a great rebuke of their arrogance. Someone might think that Jesus is commanding nothing else here except that the listeners should believe in him; but if one considers more diligently, he will see a wider and fuller sense lying hidden in these words. For when they—impiously scorning the Savior’s teaching and thinking the Law of Moses was enough for them to know the work of God—said "What shall we do, that we may work the work of God?", he appropriately reveals that they are far from the true worship of God, and teaches them that they know nothing. Because they cling to the letter, they are full of figures and shadows, not the truth. Thus, separating the fruit of faith from legalistic worship, he says: "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent." "This," he says, "is the work of God, not that which you think, looking only at the shadows and figures of the Law." Learn, even if you are unwilling, that the Author of the Law never desired the slaughter of oxen or sheep. And what is incense, even if it fills the surrounding air with a sweet odor? <margin>Psalm 49</margin> Furthermore, how can a goat help, or an offering of cinnamon? Will God eat the flesh of bulls? <margin>Isaiah 1</margin> Will he drink the blood of goats? He knows all the birds of the heaven, and the beauty of the field is with him. He hates and rejects your solemnities, nor will he smell anything of your festivals, as he himself says; nor did he speak to your fathers concerning burnt offerings and the slaughter of sacrificial victims. <margin>Jeremiah 7</margin> Therefore, this is not the work of God, but rather this: that you believe in him whom he sent. For faith brings salvation, and grace justifies, but the mandates of the Law rather condemn. Therefore, the work of God is faith in Christ; wherefore his doctrine does not belong to those who cling to the shadows of the Law. This is altogether worthy of wonder: for while Christ was accustomed to take no care for those who questioned him through temptation, in the present case—although he saw they would follow no utility—he answers for their condemnation, just as he said elsewhere: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin." <margin>John 15</margin>

### CHAPTER XXXII.
**They said therefore to him: What sign then do you perform, that we may see and believe you? What do you work? Our fathers ate manna in the desert, as it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat.** The mind of the Jews is revealed little by little. For although they said out of arrogance, "What shall we do, that we may work the work of God?"—thinking, as we said, <margin>Psalm 77</margin> that the Mosaic Law sufficed to provide all knowledge by which they might know the work of God—nevertheless, this opinion of theirs remained hidden. But now, stripped bare, it comes into the open. For what they mean when they say "What sign do you perform?" is: "That blessed Moses is deservedly honored. For he was accepted by God as a mediator between God and men, and he gave a preeminent sign of this: everyone who was with him ate manna in the desert. But you, since you seem to seek greater things than Moses, and since you strive to change his precepts, with what signs do you corroborate this, or by what miracle do you strive to lead us back to a new doctrine?" Here the Savior is shown to have spoken truly. For they are rebuked for following Christ not to see miracles, but because they ate and were filled. For they do not ask for just any sign, but the one they thought Moses had performed, when not for the space of a year, but for forty whole years, God had nourished the Hebrew <margin>Exodus 16</margin> people with the food of manna in the desert. Thus they seem to understand nothing at all. Indeed, they most foolishly attribute that sign of the manna not to divine power, but to Moses. Therefore they demand such a sign from Christ, thinking it too little that they were miraculously fed in a single day...

He contrasts the "shadows" of Old Testament animal sacrifices and the manna in the desert with the spiritual reality and salvation offered by the Son.</summary>

He is, therefore, the true manna; he himself, I say, is the bread from heaven which is offered by God the Father to every rational creature. In this way, the grace and mercy of God is accustomed to recall human nature from the desire for fleeting things <note>original: "caducarum rerum" — things that are perishable or destined to fall away, as opposed to eternal things.</note> in various and many ways. 

For when the appetite of the flesh presses down like a stone of great weight toward these unstable things, and tyrannically brings us under its own rule, Christ leads us around—as if with a bridle—toward the desire for better things; having gifted us with health of mind, he confirms us in the habit of virtue. For you see that even those people who were captured by the lure of bodily food and a life of idleness are now being recalled, by the doctrine of Christ, to the desire for heavenly bread, to spiritual manna, and to the consolation of the Holy Spirit. 

Therefore, let us be fortified with all patience, and let us not, through weakness of mind, desire those things which are not permitted, so that Christ our Lord, the intellectual manna <note>In this context, "intellectual" (intellectuale) refers to the spiritual or noetic realm—food for the mind and soul rather than the physical stomach.</note>, may confirm us in his piety. <meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria’s commentary on the Gospel of John, specifically Book 3. The previous page concluded with a transition back to the scriptural analysis of the manna in the desert as a type or foreshadowing of Christ.</meta>

That is to say, let the rough and frosty <note>original: "pruinosa" — referring to the frost-like appearance of manna, here allegorized as the "cold" or "lifeless" nature of the Old Law's literal observation.</note> observation of the law's commandments cease and come to an end (for Christ is the end of the law and the <margin>John 10</margin> prophets); then the true manna descends from heaven, then the Gospel doctrine shines forth—not merely within the congregation and synagogue of the Hebrews, but throughout the circuit of the camps in the face of the desert and the <margin>Isaiah 54</margin> wilderness—namely, among all the nations, in the Church of the Gentiles, of whom it was said: *Because many more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.* For the grace of the intellectual <note>In this context, "intellectual" refers to the "noetic" or spiritual realm, feeding the mind rather than the belly.</note> manna has been poured out over all the earth. This manna is compared to coriander, and is called "minute" or small, because the power of the divine word is indeed subtle and rather cooling, extinguishing the heat of passions by its own coolness; for the essence of coriander is said to be very cold. When the children of Israel saw this, they said to one another: *What is this?* Since they had <margin>Exodus 16</margin> no prior experience of this thing, and were struck by its novelty, they asked each other what it might be; and from this, the thing received its name. For *Manna* in the language of the Syrians <note>original: "Syrorum lingua" — Cyril refers to Aramaic/Syriac here.</note> signifies "What is this?" From this, in my judgment, it was denoted—as we see now in the reality itself—that the Jews would not recognize Christ. And Moses said to them: *Let no one leave any of it until morning.* Those who did not listen to him, but left some of it until the morning, found that it began to swarm with worms and it rotted; and Moses was angry with them. Here, "morning" signifies the most splendid times of the Savior's arrival: when the shadow of the law was driven away, and the darkness of the nations was illuminated, the only-begotten light—the spiritual dawn—shone upon us. Moses commanded that the manna should by no means be left until morning: because when the sun rises, the shadows of the law vanish, and at the presence of the truth, the figures <note>original: "figurae" — symbolic foreshadowings or "types" in the Old Testament.</note> entirely cease. For this reason, Paul also showed the righteousness of the law to be useless once Christ began to shine, saying of himself: *For whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things*—meaning all those things <margin>Philippians 3</margin> in which the law most boasted. *For I say,* he says, *that all things are refuse, provided that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having the righteousness of the law, but that which is through faith in Jesus Christ.* Therefore, Paul, as a wise man, preserved nothing until the morning. However, those who then preserved that sensible manna <note>original: "sensibile" — that which can be perceived by the physical senses, as opposed to "intellectual" or spiritual.</note> prefigured the unbelief of the Jews; for them, the untimely preservation of the law will surely produce rot and worms. Hence we read that Moses was affected by grief and moved to anger. And Moses said to <margin>Exodus 18</margin> Aaron: *Take one golden jar, put manna there, as much as a gomer can hold, and place it before the Lord to be kept.* In admiration I would now exclaim: *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!* Truly, an incomprehensible wisdom lies hidden in the Scriptures, and a great height of depth is found in them. Consider, I pray, more diligently what is concealed in this last portion. For since Christ was prefigured by that sensible manna, it now necessarily teaches with what glory and power he is filled—he who hides Christ within himself, who carries Jesus firmly fixed in his heart through truth and right faith. For you hear how the golden jar is filled with manna by Aaron and is placed before God for perpetual preservation. For the pious and holy soul, which has conceived the faith of Christ and stored the whole heavenly treasure within itself, is a precious and golden vessel; it is offered by the High Priest to God the Father, and it shall be preserved in His sight forever. Justly, therefore, does Christ refute the Jews who were puffed up by the doctrine of Moses and thought that the manna had been given to the ancients by him, understanding nothing beyond the physical figure, saying: *Amen I say to you, Moses did not give you the manna.* For it was entirely necessary that they should not be ignorant that Moses was merely a minister; for the thing itself could not be the work of a man, but was the gift of God, by which the life of the whole world—not just of one nation—was signified by the heavenly bread.

### CHAPTER XXXV.
**[D]**hey said therefore to him: Lord, give us this bread always.) The mind of the Jews is now completely stripped bare (although they had tried to keep it hidden); it is evident also that Christ cannot lie: for it is not because they saw signs that they follow, but because they ate until they were satisfied. Regarding their ignorance, I might aptly say: *Behold a foolish and heartless people; they have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not <margin>Jeremiah 5</margin> hear.* For even if the Savior removed them from their fleshly understanding with many words, and even if he recalled them to spiritual contemplation by his wonderful doctrine, they nevertheless make no progress, nor do they depart from fleshly things in any way. Indeed, hearing of "bread" by which life is given to the world, they understood earthly bread. Therefore, serving their bellies as if they were a god, they shall deservedly hear: *Whose glory is in their shame.* For they are like that Samaritan woman who, when <margin>Philippians 3</margin> she had heard a long discourse from Christ about the intelligible water—him saying openly: *He who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall <margin>John 4</margin> give will have within him a fountain springing up into eternal life*—yet, understanding nothing, she slipped back into the memory of physical waters, saying: *Lord, give me this water so that I may not thirst, nor come here to draw.* But she was both a Samaritan and a woman, so it is no wonder if she was slower to understand; but these men, both Jews and males, have nothing of manly prudence, but are made effeminate by the desire of the belly, showing that it was truly said of them: *The fool will speak foolishly, and his heart will understand vain things.* <margin>Isaiah 32</margin>

### CHAPTER XXXVI.
**[D]**esus said to them: I am the bread of life.) Although Christ was accustomed to explain mysteries in a somewhat enigmatic way and not too openly—lest divine things be exposed to the derision of wicked men—nevertheless, sometimes on account of the ignorance of his listeners, when he sees they understand nothing, he removes all ambiguity of speech and explains the whole power of the mystery clearly and briefly, so that no excuse is left for those who do not believe. That he usually used a shaded and somewhat obscure manner of speaking, he himself teaches in the Psalms, saying: *I will open my mouth in parables.* <margin>Psalm 77</margin> Isaiah also demonstrates this very thing, crying out: *Behold, your just king shall reign, and princes shall rule with judgment, and there shall be a man hiding his <margin>Isaiah 32</margin> words,* for he foretold that He would reign, who says:

<summary>Cyril allegorizes the manna as a foreshadowing of Christ, interpreting the golden jar as the faithful soul and rebuking the Jews for their materialistic misunderstanding of Jesus' promise of the Bread of Life.</summary>

...opinion, this kind of food was provided. It was gathered not in the tabernacle, nor within the camp, but outside in the desert, beyond the circuit of the camps. This surely signified that the Gospel doctrine (through which Christ dwells in our hearts) is not the exclusive property of the Jews, nor of those who are under the law. For the <term>Synagogue</term><note>The traditional assembly of the Jewish people.</note> was within the camp; but the Church (which was called from the <term>Gentiles</term><note>A term used by early Christian writers to refer to non-Jewish nations.</note>) seemed to be as if in solitude and the desert. 

As for the statement: *One gathered more, another less; yet he who gathered more had nothing over, and he who gathered less had no lack*— <margin>Exodus 16</margin> this signifies that the grace of the Spirit is distributed equally to every person, because grace does not admit of physical measure. And just as the sun is common to all, so also is grace. 

Likewise, the fact that some kept the manna for the next day, and it rotted and began to swarm with worms, signifies this: in those who receive Christ but then afterwards return to the old law, or who attempt to mix the grace of Christ with the legalistic observances of the <margin>Galatians 5</margin> old law, the gift of the Spirit is corrupted and lost. For the Apostle Paul says that those who seek to be justified by the law have fallen away from grace. 

Therefore, let the manna be understood as the bread of life, which is Christ. For He is that bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world. But let us see how He says this to the Jews: *Amen, amen, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.* <margin>John 6</margin> He does not say, "He gave," but "He gives"; for the Father is always giving this bread, which is the Son.

<summary>Cyril explains that manna was gathered outside the camp to show that the Gospel belongs to all nations, and that divine grace is distributed equally to all believers regardless of their standing.</summary>
<keywords>manna, grace, Gentiles, Synagogue, equality of grace, Bread of Life, Exodus allegory, Law vs. Gospel</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria’s theological argument regarding the nature of Christ’s submission to the Father. He is responding to Arian or Eunomian claims that the Son is "subjection" by his very essence, rather than being a distinct person who chooses to obey.</meta>

In that same way, certainly, **subjection** <term>subjection</term><note>original: *subiectio*; in this theological context, it refers to the state of being under authority or the act of obedience. Cyril is arguing that subjection is an attribute of a person, not a person's entire identity.</note>, since it shows an inclination of the will to obey someone, does not exist as a separate nature in its own right, but exists within one of those things that already are, just like a passion, or a will, or a desire. Furthermore, both the reality of subjection and the name itself, if uttered alone, are scarcely understood with certainty; nor is it known whether it is a good or <margin>B</margin> an evil thing, unless it is added to what thing the subjection belongs. 

For someone is said to be subject now to God, and now to the devil. And just as the name **shrewdness** <note>original: *calliditas*; Cyril uses this as an analogy for a "neutral" quality that depends on its application—one can be shrewd for good or for evil.</note> is a neutral term (for many are shrewd for doing evil, and others are shrewd again for escaping troubles and seeking advantages), so subjection is a certain neutral and uncertain thing until you know whose subjection it is. Therefore, if the Son has a nature, we cannot say that he *is* subjection. For if, according to you, the Son is subjection itself, then the nature of the Son would be something uncertain and doubtful.

<summary>Cyril argues that "subjection" is a quality or a movement of the will rather than a substance or nature. He concludes that if the Son were merely "subjection" itself, his nature would be ill-defined and dependent on external factors, which contradicts the stability of the divine nature.</summary>

### CHAPTER III.

*The Jews then murmured at him, because he said, "I am the bread which came down from heaven," and they said.* They take offense again, understanding nothing. For the minds of the ignorant are usually recognized most clearly in such matters. For when a person does not understand a thing by which they might be turned toward something better, they are led from a sense of helplessness into annoyance; we see that this is exactly what happened to them. 

For by what other reason were they driven to murmuring? Certainly, it would have been more fitting, if they had understood anything at all, to examine—based on the very facts and the **signs** <note>original: *signis*; refers to the miracles Christ performed as evidence of his divine mission.</note> performed by him—whether Christ was lying when he called himself the bread that came down from heaven, or whether he was speaking the truth. For in this way, through right judgment, they could have been led to the discovery of the truth. But now, seeking nothing, they only murmur in vain.
