...that he is the teacher, and that one must cling to him alone, who is able to lead us to eternal life. For in this way, having entered into the church of the firstborn <note>original: "primogenitorum ecclesia"; a reference to Hebrews 12:23, referring to the community of the faithful</note>, we shall enjoy ultimate blessedness. However, that Christ alone must be followed, and that from him alone salvation is obtained, although the nature of things makes it clear, it will not be out of place to confirm this from ancient scripture as well. When the Hebrews, fleeing Egypt, were hurrying toward the land of promise, they were commanded not to go wherever they wished, lest by proceeding without a leader they should wander in confusion. For thus it is written in the Book of Numbers: <margin>Numbers 9</margin> On the day that the tabernacle was set up, a cloud covered it; and from evening until morning it was over the tent as it were the appearance of fire. So it was continually: the cloud covered it by day, and the appearance of fire by night. And whenever the cloud that protected the tabernacle moved forward, then the children of Israel set out; and in the place where the cloud stopped, there they camped. At the command of the Lord they set out, and at his command they pitched the tabernacle.

You see how they are commanded to camp when the cloud stands still, and to follow it when it moves. For it is very beneficial to always obey the leader. Wherefore just as the people of Israel were then, we are now commanded to be joined to Christ. For he himself is the tabernacle, the cloud, and the fire; so that this may be clear to all, let us translate the whole matter into a spiritual history. Therefore, when Wisdom built a house for herself <margin>Proverbs 9</margin> (as Solomon says) and more truly established for herself that tabernacle—that temple which he took from the Virgin, into which he descended ineffably from the Father's bosom, having become man—then, having become a cloud for those already illuminated and walking in the day <margin>Romans 13</margin> according to Paul, he extinguishes the heat of sins. But for those still wandering and living as if in nocturnal darkness, he is established as an illuminating fire, transforming them into the heat of the spirit. For we believe that the good and faithful burn in the spirit; nor do we think the appearance of the cloud by day and the fire by night over the tabernacle signified anything other than what we have said.

Now, they were commanded to stay or follow at the movement and stopping of the cloud, so that you might understand what was said by Christ: *Whoever serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will also be.* <margin>John 12</margin> For it is necessary for the believer to be fixed and indivisibly stuck to Christ, which is signified by the will and work of walking with him. For this is not understood as a journey of the body, but is accomplished by virtue and the soul. Whence the most wise disciples, because they were fixed upon Christ with their whole soul, and thought it ruinous to go back with the unbelievers, said: "To whom can we go?"—that is, we will always be with you, we will follow your commands, we will hear your word; nor like the unskilled do we accuse you or think your words are "hard," but rather we say: *How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!* <margin>Psalm 118</margin> <note>This is Psalm 119:103 in modern numbering.</note>

Such is the sense of the passage set before us. That the tabernacle was granted to the ancients as a figure <term>figura; a symbolic foreshadowing</term> of Christ, we will best know if we examine more attentively the words spoken divinely to Moses; nor should we fear a digression, for we must not fear those who accuse us of too much exactness in the scriptures. But first let us set down the words of scripture. The Lord spoke (it says) <margin>A</margin> to Moses, saying: <margin>Exodus 40</margin> "In the first month, on the new moon <note>original: "neomenia"; the first day of the lunar month</note> of the month, on the first day, you shall set up the tabernacle." For this reason, the Lord of all commanded Moses to set up the tabernacle in one day, not in many, and on the new moon—not of just any month, but of the first.

[Column 1]
The ark and the golden altar, upon which incense was burned, were placed inside; and at the entrance of the tabernacle, a tent-curtain was stretched out so that nothing of the interior might be seen by the common people. However, the altar of burnt offering <term>holocausti; refers to a "whole burnt offering" where the entire animal was consumed by fire</term> was set up near the doors of the tabernacle, outside the tent. Thus, through the altar of incense, which sends up a sweet-smelling odor, Christ is understood as offering himself to God the Father. Through the altar of burnt offering, he is understood as the victim led to the slaughter for our sake. The first was hidden because the glory of Christ is secret and concealed. The other, however, was open to the public because his death is visible to all. But the golden altar was also set up in the presence of the ark, so that it might enigmatically <note>original: "ænigmatice"; Cyril uses this to mean a symbolic or "riddling" representation of a spiritual truth</note> show that the glory of the Son is wondrous and precious in the sight of God the Father, according to that saying: <margin>Matthew 11</margin> No one knows the Son except the Father. But the altar of burnt offering stood at the entrance of the tabernacle, which signified the death of Christ which he endured for all, as we have said: so that we may understand that we can in no way approach God the Father except through the sacrifice of Christ. He said: <margin>John 10</margin> I am the door, and no one comes to the Father except through me. <margin>John 14</margin> Moreover, the tabernacle was stretched out and contained all things, so that all might appear as one thing and not many. For although he is understood among us in many ways, Christ is one. He is the tabernacle because of the covering of his flesh. He is the ark, having the law hidden within, as the Word of God. He is the table, as our food and life. He is the lampstand, as our spiritual light. He is the altar of incense, as the sweet fragrance in sanctification. He is the altar of burnt offering, as the victim led to the cross for the life of the whole world. All these things are sanctified, because in whatever way you understand Christ, he is entirely holy. Therefore, as the Hebrews followed the tabernacle when it moved and camped when it stood still, let us learn that no other leader has been given to us for salvation than the Word of God made man. In this way, let us strive to attain eternal life by keeping his precepts. This was not done by those who, despising the teaching of Christ, went backward and did not walk with him. But Peter and all the twelve rightly saw, as holy men, that they could not acquire life from anywhere else but from Christ; therefore, they clung firmly to him.

**CHAPTER 29.**
And we believe, and we know, that you are the Christ, the Son of God. The faith of the apostles was wonderful, this manner of confession was most fervent, and their wisdom was exceptional and singular. For they did not go backward like the ignorant, nor were they led to believe lightly without cause; rather, having been made more certain by many signs that Christ was full of the words of life and that he preached heavenly doctrine, they truly believed. Indeed, when faith is not so firmly established, since it has no root, it is accustomed to fly quickly out of the soul—similar to that seed which fell upon the rock, <margin>Luke 8</margin> and because it could not take root, it was easily dried up. Here, he enigmatically called the "rock" a hard mind, which the doctrine of God does not penetrate into the interior. Such a mind the Jews had and still have, and therefore it is said to them through the prophet: <margin>Joel 2</margin> Rend your hearts, and not your garments. For just as we are taught by the laws of agriculture that fields must first be broken up by the plow

[Column 2]
[Marginal letter: A] before the seeds are entrusted to them, so I believe that before faith is entrusted to us, our hearts must be broken down by a desire for it. Therefore, the disciples say they have firmly "known" that he is the Christ, the Son of God. They spoke very wisely in joining these two words, "to believe" and "to know," together so vividly. For we do not entirely despise reason because we believe; rather, we strive to have some knowledge, as if in a mirror or a riddle. But they excellently placed faith before knowledge. For faith precedes, and knowledge follows, according to that saying: <margin>Isaiah 7</margin> If you do not believe, you will not understand. <note>original: "Si nõ credideritis, non intelligetis"; this is the Latin translation of the Septuagint version of Isaiah 7:9, a foundational concept in Patristic theology</note> For unless you cast the foundations of faith without any doubt, you will not be able to build up bit by bit the knowledge that is in Christ, and thus emerge as a spiritual man. Behold, <margin>Isaiah 28</margin> [Marginal letter: B] he says, I will place in the foundations of Zion a stone, an upright, angular, and precious stone. For the beginning and the foundation for sanctification and righteousness is Christ—namely, through faith and not otherwise—for in this way he dwells in us. Consider also carefully that they everywhere say, specifically with the addition of the article: *You are the Christ*, and *the Son of the living God*. By this, they separate the true and natural Son from other "sons of God" who are called and adopted by grace; we are called sons only by being joined to him through likeness. They call him "the Christ" because Christ and the Son of God are one and the same. Yet he is not called Christ because the Son of God and Christ are substantially the same thing <note>Cyril is clarifying that "Christ" (the Anointed One) refers to his human mission, while "Son of God" refers to his divine nature, yet they are one person</note>; rather, he is the one Christ in a certain preeminent way. For no one is Christ as he is; rather, others are called "christ" <note>original: "christus"; meaning "anointed one" in a general sense, like kings or prophets</note> by likeness to us. [Marginal letter: C] For while he is properly and uniquely the Son of God both in name and in reality, the name of "Christ" is common to him and to us. For he was anointed insofar as he is man, and for that reason he is Christ. Since, therefore, being anointed is attributed to the human race, he is understood to be Christ by a likeness to us (as we said), not as the Son of God. Nevertheless, he is uniquely and preeminently one Christ, both before the flesh and after the flesh—not two, as some assert, being ignorant of the depth of the mystery. <note>This is a critique of Nestorianism, which Cyril fought against, arguing that Christ was one single person, not two separate beings (one divine and one human) joined together</note> For the Word of God did not descend into a certain man (as the grace of the Spirit descended upon the prophets), but truly became flesh—that is, became man—as it is written. <margin>John 1</margin> Therefore, he is not split into two persons after the incarnation, although it must be entirely believed that the Word of God is one thing according to nature, and his humanity is another. [Marginal letter: D] The apostles themselves teach us this faith, who say they have known that he himself is the Christ, the Son of God. Therefore, those who dare to say otherwise are not to be accepted.

For the path of destruction is exceedingly slippery: <note>original: "Lubrica enim admodum perditionis est uia"</note> it does not only pull apart a weak mind, but sometimes even deceives firm souls with pleasure. That this is so is confirmed not by the example of those who went back, but by your own. For I chose you as good men; I was not ignorant, but as God I knew your hearts. For man is a creature of free will, <term>animal; here meaning a "living being" or "creature" endowed with a soul</term> and he is able to choose whichever path he wishes, whether the right or the left (by which I mean virtue or vice). Therefore, he makes them all more vigilant, because he does not say clearly who is going to betray him; but by affirming generally that the burden of such great impiety hangs over one of them, he makes them all anxious, and rouses them to greater vigilance through dread. He also does this for another reason: for when they asserted that they believed and knew him to be the Son of God, he demonstrates that this confession of theirs is true by his prediction of future events. ### CHAPTER XXXI.

<margin>John Chapter 7</margin> **After these things Jesus walked in Galilee. For he did not wish to walk in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.** After these things, he says—those things which were done and said (as was clear in the preceding sections)—he walked, that is, he lived and moved in Galilee. The added reason shows that this was done not of his own will or for pleasure, but out of necessity. For this reason, he says, he was in Galilee with the foreigners for a long time: because the Jews were seeking to kill him. This is surely a great accusation against the Jews, by whose cruelty it came about that he lived among foreigners. Jeremiah predicted that this would happen: <margin>Jeremiah 12</margin> **I have forsaken my house, I have left my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hands of her enemies.** For the Gentiles, since they neglected the Creator and worshipped created things, were enemies of God. For he says, <margin>Luke 11</margin> **He who is not with me is against me.** No one will ever doubt that before the time of Christ, the Gentiles were ignorant of the true God. Therefore, they were against God and placed in the position of enemies. Great, therefore, was the cruelty of the Jews, which made him prefer to live among enemies rather than with his own people, who ought to have loved him at least because he was joined to them in the flesh. Rightly, therefore, did he later transfer himself to the Gentiles, which he was already threatening to do by his very actions—crying out as if with a great voice that unless they stopped their persecution, he would depart entirely to the Gentiles. What he now seems to threaten by his actions, he showed in ancient times through a certain figure, signifying secretly through riddles that he would leave Jerusalem. For when he brought the laws concerning sacrifices, as he writes in Leviticus: <margin>Leviticus 1</margin> He first commanded a calf to be offered to the Lord as a gift in the figure of Christ for a burnt offering. Then, if the offering is from the flocks, he says, he shall offer a male from the lambs and goats for a burnt offering, without blemish; and he shall lay his hands upon the head of the victim, and sacrifice it at the side of the altar which looks toward the North <note>original: "Aquilonem"</note>

<column-break/>

before the Lord. By these words, it was signified that the mystery of Christ would be transferred to the Gentiles. This will easily be revealed if we first explain the location of the temple and the arrangement of the altar. For thus it will become clear what was meant by the fact that the offered animal did not face directly forward, but toward the side and toward the North. The region of the Jews is situated in the southern parts; however, the temple that was in Jerusalem faced the East in such a way that it immediately admitted the rays of the rising sun. The altar itself also faced one entering directly; hence one side looked toward the north, and the other toward the south. That these things were so is proven by the spiritual vision of Ezekiel. <margin>Ezekiel 8</margin> **And I saw,** he said, **and behold twenty-five men, whose backs were toward the temple of the Lord, and they were worshipping the rising sun.** Surely, he who worships the rising sun turns his face of adoration toward the sunrise; if the front of the temple looks at their backs, it is necessary that the face and the gates of the temple look toward the rising sun. The altar was also positioned in this way; therefore, the front of both the temple and the altar looked toward the sunrise, while one side looked to the south, the other to the north, and the rear part looked toward the west. Since these things were so, Galilee—that is, the region of the Gentiles (for so it is written of it) <margin>Isaiah 9</margin>—is joined to Judea from the north. Therefore, because after his passion our Savior was going to pass from Judea into Galilee, that is, to the Church of the Gentiles, he was for that reason sacrificed at the side of the altar that looked toward the north and Galilee. This is also what the Psalmist sang: <margin>Psalm 65</margin> **For his eyes,** he says, **look toward the Gentiles.** Therefore, the Lord avoided Judea, not as if he were fearful, but because the fitting time for the cross had not yet arrived.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

**Now the Jews’ feast day, the Feast of Tabernacles <term>scenopegia; from the Greek 'skenopegia', referring to the Feast of Booths or Sukkot</term>, was at hand. His brothers said to him: Leave here and go into Judea, so that your disciples may also see the works you are doing. For no one does anything in secret while seeking to be known publicly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world. For even his brothers did not believe in him.**
Not yet knowing that the Word of God inhabited him—those who were thought to be the Savior’s brothers—they were moved by common opinion, thinking he was born of Joseph. But seeing the miracles being done by him more privately in Galilee, they urged him toward vainglory; as if he performed signs for the purpose of obtaining praise from men. They advise him to go up into Judea and perform signs for them: not so that his disciples might believe in him, but so they might see miraculous works. For they say, if you wish to be known, do not do these things secretly, but in Judea, so that you may make more disciples in a crowded region. He added by necessity that even they did not yet believe in Jesus, lest they should seem to speak such frivolous words as believers. However, after they did believe, they reached such a point of piety that they were numbered among the apostles. Jeremiah, in a discourse turned toward Christ, predicted this very thing: <margin>Jeremiah 12</margin> **Even your brothers,** he said, **and the house...**

<summary>Cyril interprets Jesus’s withdrawal to Galilee as a symbolic movement toward the Gentiles, using the architectural layout of the Jerusalem Temple and Levitical sacrifice laws to explain the transition. He also addresses the human motivations and initial lack of faith among Jesus's kinsmen regarding his miracles.</summary>

house of your father have despised you, and they themselves have cried out after you: Do not believe, for they will speak good things to you. <note>Cyril is quoting Jeremiah 12:6 to explain the hostility Jesus faced from his own kin.</note> For those who, before they firmly believed, followed so lightly as if crying out against him, having later been gathered to him through faith, spoke well of him, preaching the saving Gospel to others. <margin>Here he seems to want them to be the sons of Joseph.</margin> <note>Cyril follows the tradition that the "brothers of Jesus" were children of Joseph from a previous marriage, maintaining the doctrine of Mary's perpetual virginity.</note> But since the prophet called them brothers by divine inspiration, he immediately added: *And the house of your father*: lest the sons of the Virgin should be thought to be his brothers.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.

**Jesus said to them: My time has not yet arrived, but your time is always ready.** The meaning of his speech is mostly hidden. For it is written, that there will be a man hiding his words, <margin>Ecclesiasticus 20</margin> <note>The original text cites "Eccl. 30," but the reference to "hiding words" for the benefit of listeners is a common theme in the Wisdom of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), particularly chapter 20.</note> which no one but an infant would deny was done for the benefit of the listeners. Therefore he says, the time for making all things public is not yet present. Since the mind of the Jews cannot bear or endure my teaching without anger: nor indeed is the time present for these things to be handed over entirely to the Gentiles, since the Jews have not yet completely fallen away from grace. Therefore (he says) the time of my manifestation is not yet here, but yours is here, and is ready: for nothing prevents you from being able to approach better things. Furthermore, whatever things are subject to a greater dispensation <term>dispensation; from the Greek 'oikonomia,' referring to God's divine plan or the specific timing of salvation history</term> are not conveniently done at every time, as were the affairs of Christ: but the affairs of those who neglect greater things and follow humbler ones can be undertaken at any time. For these reasons, my time is not yet, but your time is always ready.

### CHAPTER XXXIIII.

**The world cannot hate you: but it hates me, because I bear witness concerning it, that its works are evil.** He conveniently rebukes with these words those who are still somewhat gasping after earthly things, and most skillfully brings a second response: because he shows that they still do not know who he is, and therefore are cast far from him, as those who admire the life of this world more than the life of virtue. Now, it was the custom of our Savior, when a small occasion was given, to say many useful things to the listeners. Therefore, he says, each person always tends to love one similar to himself, and a similarity of character marvelously glues them together in love. You see that the world does not hate you: for you feel as it does: but it hates me, because I accuse it of acting wrongly: wherefore you can set out for this festival without danger, but I cannot at all. For if I come, I will speak entirely those things which are beneficial to it. But truth gives birth to hatred, and inflames the anger of a pleasure-seeking soul, when it is unwilling to despise a life of luxury. Hence we say, that one should not be rebuked inconsiderately, nor reproved in front of men. Do not rebuke, he says, <margin>Amos 5</margin> <note>original: "Amos 5:10 - They hate him who reproves in the gate."</note> the wicked, lest they hold you in hatred. For hatred cannot be without detriment: wherefore one must speak rather to the ears of the listeners: for the world is prone to sinning, but sins are abandoned through correction, of which even the mere naming alone [is] a correction...

<summary>Cyril discusses why Jesus delayed his journey to the festival, arguing that divine actions follow a specific "dispensation" while worldly actions are random. He also explains that the "world" only hates those who challenge its sinful nature.</summary>

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

### CHAPTER LI.

**<margin>Deuteronomy 1</margin> Do not judge according to appearance: but judge a just judgment.** <note>Quoting John 7:24, where Jesus references the legal principles established in the Old Testament book of Deuteronomy.</note> The Law, he says, which you seem to defend, openly cries out that no person's status should be considered in judgment, because judgment belongs to God. <note>original: "iudicium dei est." <meta>This page continues Cyril of Alexandria’s commentary on Book 4 of the Gospel of John. Having previously discussed the Sabbath as a symbolic "rest," Cyril now moves to an allegorical interpretation of circumcision, explaining why it was performed on the eighth day and how it prefigures the spiritual purification brought by Christ’s resurrection.</meta>

->238 SAINT CYRIL ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK 4.<-

Every male infant of eight days shall be circumcised. Showing this figure of a mystery to be necessary, he <note>God, speaking in Genesis 17.</note> adds a penalty for transgressors, saying: "And my covenant shall be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant: and the male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall be destroyed from his people, because he has not kept my covenant." The divine Paul indeed asserted that circumcision was given to Abraham as a sign of the faith which he had while still uncircumcised. For he wished, as it seems to me and as the matter itself proclaims, to show that the calling and the righteousness of faith are prior and superior to every legal mandate. He did this so that he might more easily persuade the Hebrews not to think that the righteousness of faith was a transgression of the Law, but rather a return and a restoration to the original state of man. 

But he is also found to hand down another B mode of circumcision. For advising the Jews not to boast in the flesh, he says: "He is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from men, but from God." From this he clearly shows that circumcision was not given solely as a sign, but that it signifies something greater and more spiritual. 

Let us therefore consider more deeply what this spiritual circumcision might be, of which the fleshly one was a figure. Let us also examine why it was applied not on just any day, but only on the eighth day. It is clear, then, that we must be prepared and cleansed in every way so that we may be joined to Christ through faith. For our whole intention is to be connected to God through the meditation of Christ. You have an image of this matter in what is said by God to Moses: "Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day; for on the third day the Lord will descend upon Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people." This signifies that the integrity of morals must be studiously acquired. By the washing of garments, he shows the purity of the body. For in a certain way, the body is the garment of the soul. 

Since, therefore, it is necessary for all who strive to be joined to God to be prepared and pre-cleansed (for he says, "Be holy, because I am holy"), the sign of purification was given to the men of old through the circumcision of the flesh. We will understand this easily if we consider our own condition. A certain pleasure <note>original: "voluptas"</note> precedes every sin, and a burning desire <note>original: "cupiditas"</note> is accustomed to entice us toward offenses. This desire resides within us before the act of sinning and seizes the consent of the mind, easily persuading us that we must go the way we crave. The true disciple of Christ shows this, saying: "Let no one who is tempted say that he is tempted by God. For God tempts no one, but each person is tempted, being drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then, after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is finished, generates death." You see how wickedness takes its origin from desire. You see how offenses are produced from the seed of pleasure. For this reason, God commanded that part of the body in which and through which the 

<column-break/>

239

A fountains of pleasure spring up to be cut around with iron. We learn through this riddle <note>original: "aenigmate"</note> that we shall never be clean by any pact unless, holding the action of the divine word in our heart like the sharp double-edged axe of the Spirit, we cast out every foul desire from the soul. We should do nothing that the pleasure of the flesh seeks, however delightful it may seem, but only those things which please God. 

Since this is the true circumcision, we rightly say to those who glory in the circumcision of the flesh: "Circumcise yourselves to God, and circumcise the hardness of your hearts, all you who dwell in Jerusalem." For he who is circumcised in the flesh does nothing except that he is circumcised in the flesh. But he who performs this in the spirit on the eighth day (that is, in the resurrection of the Savior) shall live in Christ, as Paul says: "For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory." For we can truly say that all are dead to the world who despise the pleasures of the world for the sake of God, who can say with Paul: "We glory in nothing except in the cross of Christ, through whom the world is crucified to us, and we to the world." For having been made partakers of him through the Spirit, who without hands cuts away our inward impurity at the root, we are dead to the world but live for God. 

Therefore, circumcision was performed on the eighth day, and not before the eighth, because it was a figure of the resurrection. For the Spirit was not given before the resurrection of Christ, but after it, when he breathed on the disciples and said: "Receive the Holy Spirit." 

C But for the Jews, who were still under the Law and were slaves, circumcision of the flesh performed with iron was appropriate; for iron is received from the Law for punishment. But for us, who are free and spiritual, a spiritual circumcision and purification is fitting, which exterminates all the filth of the soul and brings perfection through the piety of faith. 

That our glory is filled by this spiritual circumcision, which is perfected through piety, we shall easily recognize if we consider more diligently what is written about Abraham. It is written that Abraham was ninety-nine years old when God gave him circumcision. By this, it is openly shown that circumcision is a kind of door to perfection, and that no one can be perfected by any pact unless he possesses the purification overshadowed by circumcision. For the number ten <note>original: "denarius... numerus." In ancient numerology, ten represented completion or perfection.</note> returning upon itself is a sign of perfection. Therefore, circumcision is given before perfection, which easily leads us to perfection. 

Moreover, this spiritual circumcision is owed only to those made free through Christ. For no one is free unless he has shaken off the yoke of sin and the slavery of the devil through Christ, and, having broken the chains of offenses, is crowned with the glory of righteousness—that righteousness, I say, which is held in the faith of Christ. But that it is appropriate for the free, not slaves, to be circumcised on the eighth day, Scripture itself will teach us. For Ishmael, the son of Abraham born of a slave woman, was circumcised not on the eighth day, but in the thirteenth year. Thus he shows that the son of the enslaved Jerusalem—that is, the Jewish people—has fallen away both from the eighth day and from the twelfth. For he fell away from the eighth because...

<summary>Cyril provides an allegorical reading of circumcision, arguing that the physical act was a "riddle" representing the spiritual removal of sinful desire. He links the "eighth day" of the rite to Christ's resurrection and the gift of the Holy Spirit, contrasting the spiritual freedom of Christians with the "punitive" physical law of the Jews.</summary>

244 ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, BOOK V.

# THE FIFTH BOOK ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, 
## Added to the explanation of Cyril by Jodocus Clichtoveus of Nieuwpoort, Doctor of Theology. <note>Jodocus Clichtoveus (1472–1543) was a prominent theologian who completed the missing sections of Cyril's commentary for publication in the Renaissance.</note>

### CHAPTER I.

**THEN** said some of them of Jerusalem: Is not this he, whom they seek to kill? Lo, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Do the rulers know indeed that this is the Christ? <note>This text corresponds to John 7:25-26.</note>

Those who were from Jerusalem knew the wicked efforts of the rulers and Pharisees to bring about the death of Christ better than the outsiders; for they lived among them and had more knowledge of their pursuits and plans than others. Therefore, seeing Christ speaking to them with such great constancy <note>The Latin "constantia" implies a steady, unshakable firmness of character or speech.</note> in public, they were led to wonder that he had been sought with such diligence before, and now when he is present in person, he is not at all detained by those who pursue him. For indeed they were ignorant of what power caused him not to be held; they did not know that this was the work of divine virtue <note>original: "virtutis" — in this context, it refers to supernatural power or miraculous strength.</note>, and

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Jodocus Clichtoveus on the Gospel of John, specifically addressing the arguments made by the people of Jerusalem regarding the origins of the Messiah. Clichtoveus continues his project of filling the gaps in Cyril of Alexandria’s commentary, focusing here on the dual nature of Christ as both human and divine.</meta>

->**246 ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.**<-

They strive to support this truly wicked opinion with reason as well. "We know this man," they say, "whence he is." They knew his parents according to the common estimation of men, believing him to be the son of Joseph (as was supposed) and Mary. They likewise knew the place of his upbringing, and that he had been raised in Nazareth, as the Evangelist says; from this they profess to know where he draws his origin. [*Marginal note:* Luke 4.] But concerning the Christ, they say that no one will know whence he is, perhaps relying on the testimony of Isaiah, who says of Christ: *Who shall declare his generation?* [*Marginal note:* Isaiah 53.] <note>Isaiah 53:8. In the Latin tradition, this was often interpreted as the mystery of Christ's eternal or miraculous birth.</note> From these things they conclude that our Lord should by no means be accepted as the Christ. They do not pay enough attention to the fact that in him there is a double substance and nature: **B** namely, the human, according to which they did indeed know in part where he was from, though not entirely, because they naturally thought Joseph was his father and were ignorant of the Virgin birth; and the divine, which they neither perceived in him, nor recognized from whence he had obtained it. Furthermore, the prophet spoke concerning his divine and eternal generation from the Father, which is inexpressible not only by the tongues of men but even by those of angels. For how the Father begot the Son from the womb before the day star, [*Marginal note:* Psalm 110.] <note>original: "Psal. 109" — in the Vulgate numbering. The verse "ex utero ante luciferum" refers to the eternal birth of the Word before the creation of light.</note> neither the tongue can sufficiently speak, nor any mind can grasp. However, these men—who failed while searching with their scrutiny—thought that the prophet spoke only of the temporal and human generation of Christ. [*Marginal note:* Psalm 64.] <note>original: "Psal. 63" — the Latin text quotes a phrase about those "failing in their search."</note> And for that reason their heart was made foolish, and believing themselves to be wise (as Paul says), they became fools. [*Marginal note:* Romans 1.] Furthermore, although that oracle of Isaiah just cited is rightly understood to refer to the eternal generation of Christ from the Father according to his divinity, it nonetheless also holds truth regarding his generation according to the flesh; it is also cited in that sense by the prophet in that place when speaking of the human nature, birth, and passion of Christ. For who can sufficiently describe how a Virgin, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, brought forth God and man to the world in a blessed birth, with her virginal integrity preserved? Therefore, that prophetic word is true concerning both births of Christ. And those who were making these quibbles could indeed have taken the occasion from that text to assert that "when Christ comes, no one knows whence he is," either from that word of Isaiah: *Truly thou art a hidden God, the Savior of Israel,* [*Marginal note:* Isaiah 45.] or from any other place of Scripture. But that matters little, since that saying of the people of Jerusalem was spoken not so much according to the truth as according to their own opinion. Indeed, for one who unrolls the Scriptures more attentively, it will be clear that it was foretold by the prophets, and signified long before, from where Christ was to have his origin even according to both natures. According to the divine nature indeed, that he proceeded from God the Father, the Psalm attests when it says: *The Lord said to me, thou art my son, today I have begotten thee.* [*Marginal note:* Psalm 2.] This is clearly designated to be understood concerning the Christ of the Lord expressed at the beginning of the psalm. Likewise, that he was to be sent into the world by God the Father,

***

->**ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 247**<-

**a** Isaiah suggested when he said: *And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.* [*Marginal note:* Isaiah 48.] According to the human nature, however, that he was to take his origin from the seed of David, Isaiah had predicted, saying: *A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall ascend from his root, and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him.* [*Marginal note:* Isaiah 11.] That he also ought to be born of a virgin mother, that oracle of Isaiah had pre-signified: *Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.* [*Marginal note:* Isaiah 7.] Finally, the place of his birth—namely, that he was to be brought into the light in Bethlehem—this prophecy of Micah had designated: *And thou, Bethlehem, land of Judah, art by no means the least among the princes of Judah; for out of thee shall come a leader who shall rule my people Israel.* [*Marginal note:* Micah 5.] You see, therefore, in what way it could have been discovered from a diligent search of the Scriptures whence Christ was. **B** With what face, then, with what confidence, and finally with what reason do the enemies dare to speak and assert that "when Christ comes, no one knows whence he is"? But because they have not searched the Scriptures, which bear witness of Christ, they thought that what they themselves were ignorant of through their own laziness could not be known by others either, and ought to be known by no one.

### CHAPTER III.

**C** Jesus therefore cried out in the temple teaching, and saying: *You both know me, and you know whence I am, and I have not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know.* <note>John 7:28</note> They were whispering into one another's ears in Jerusalem what was just said about having sensed the Christ, and with lowered voices they were muttering these things among themselves. But Christ, to whom every thought speaks and to whom every heart lies open, [*Marginal note:* 2 Chronicles 6.] responded with a free and loud voice to their words uttered in silence, testifying by this one sign that he is God, who alone knows the secrets of the heart. Therefore, Christ did not murmur in a lower voice to the ears of others to respond to them, but cried out in the temple, so that his voice might be carried to many. "You say rightly," he says, "that you recognize me and whence I am; for according to the condition of human nature, you well distinguish both my lineage, and my birthplace, and the features of my face. Nevertheless, there is something remaining in me which you do not know: namely, the truth of the divine nature, which I do not have from myself, but from the Father, from whom all things have been delivered to me." [*Marginal note:* Matthew 11.] Since, therefore, **D** you are ignorant that this is in me, you surely neither know me, nor know whence I am. And so that the mystery of this higher nature may be more open to you, I have not come into this world by my own authority or judgment alone, through the assumption of the flesh and its union to the deity; but the heavenly Father himself sent me into the world, that I might save it. The *true* Father, I say: because what he had promised long times before through the prophets—namely, that he would send a savior...

<summary>Clichtoveus argues that the people of Jerusalem failed to recognize Christ's divinity because they misinterpreted prophecy and focused only on his human origins. He explains that while Christ's earthly family was known, his divine generation from the Father remains a mystery that requires diligent study of the Scriptures.</summary>

and proclamations, against which envy is stirred. For when one is affected by a malicious spirit toward another and greatly desires their ruin, hearing that person extolled with praise tortures the poisoned soul and goads it with sharper stings of pain. The Pharisees were suffering from this serious disease, bearing it with difficulty that the crowd—even with unspoken words and nearly pressed lips in silence—testified that about Christ which contradicted their own opinion. Hence, raging more violently than usual, they sent officers to seize Jesus. But they labored in vain, not knowing the power of God, which they had experienced as many times as they had attempted to seize him; instead, they were restrained from their wicked attempt by a certain hidden power. They ought, therefore, to have considered that he could not be seized by officers unless he willed it—he who had so often prevented them from laying hands on him when he was unwilling. Moreover, the Pharisees sent officers so that if any riot should arise among the people against those wishing to seize Jesus, the officers would be exposed to that danger, while they themselves would be exempt and safe from the risk. Thus does human wisdom cast others into danger which it does not dare to undergo itself.

                                        CHAPTER VIII

[Drop cap D] Jesus therefore said to them: "Yet a little while I am with you, and then I go to him who sent me; you will seek me and not find me; and where I am, you cannot come." Officers were indeed sent to seize Jesus, but he, on the other hand, puts forth words to them by which they, in turn, might be captured. They were sent to bind him, but he, conversely, binds them with the happy chains of his doctrine. He predicts to them that he will be with them for a little while yet—namely, until the hour of his passion and the completion of the mystery of human redemption. When this is finished, he says he will return to the Father by his ascension, by whom he was sent. Lest they be negligent in seeking him while he still 
<margin>Isaiah 55</margin> shows himself present to them, let them follow the warning of Isaiah, who says: **Seek God while he may be found; call upon him while he is near.** <note>original: "Quærite Deum, dum inueniri poteſt..."</note> He foretells to them that when he has gone away, they will indeed seek him with great desire, longing to see "one day of the Son of Man," but they will not find him. Truly, after the ascension, those who were pierced to the heart by Peter's preaching sought him with pious affection, 
<margin>Acts 2</margin> saying: **What shall we do, brothers?** <note>original: "Quid faciemus uiri fratres?"</note> Yet they did not find him present in the body, although according to the presence of his divinity he was not lacking to them—according to which he is with us always, even 
<margin>Matthew 28</margin> to the end of the age. In the wretched destruction of the city of Jerusalem <note>original: "Solymæ," a poetic shortening of Hierosolyma.</note> carried out by the Romans shortly after the passion of Christ, the Jews who were then surviving and had seen the miracles of Christ—when the memory of his remarkable power and signs came to their minds—certainly wished to have Christ present then for their liberation from the imminent slaughter. They conjectured well enough in their minds that this was sent upon them because of the unjust death inflicted upon Christ. Nevertheless, they did not find him as a defender or helper, because their house had already been left to them desolate.

<margin>A</margin> Finally, lest they should think him to be merely a man, <margin>Matthew 23</margin> mixing high things with humble things in his usual manner, he suggests the nature of his divinity—by which he is immutable with the Father—saying: "And where I am, you cannot come." He did not say "where I will be," because that would have pertained only to his human condition, by which he was going to the Father; but "where I am," according to the substance of his deity, by which he is always in the Father and with the Father, and never departs from the Father’s glory. Just as he said earlier in this Evangelist: **The Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him** <margin>John 1:18</margin> and **The Son of Man, who is in heaven.** <note>original: "Vnigenitus, qui eſt in ſinu patris... & filius hominis, qui eſt in cœlo."</note> To

<margin>B</margin> them were going to believe and later arrive there—because the gate of heaven was not yet open; or never, because of the unbelief of those who were going to persevere in their sin until the end. For these could not reach heavenly glory because they refused to repent of their evils; by the weight of these sins, they shut the way of heaven against themselves and voluntarily placed an obstacle so as not to enter into life.

                                        CHAPTER IX

<margin>D</margin> [Drop cap D] The Jews therefore said among themselves: "Where is this man going, that we will not find him? Is he going to the dispersion of the Gentiles and to teach the Gentiles? <margin>2 Corinthians 2</margin> Corinthians says: **The carnal man does not perceive the things that are of God.** <note>original: "Carnalis homō non percipit ea quę dei ſunt."</note> For because he is carnally minded, he judges all things according to the flesh. So the Jews, in their usual way, understanding the words of God carnally and not grasping that he was speaking of a return to the heavenly kingdoms from which he had descended to us, slipped into a worldly sense, far removed from true understanding. For they ask (since the truth was hidden from them) whether Jesus meant by those words that he would go into the dispersion of the Gentiles <note>The "Diaspora" or the regions where Jews lived among the non-Jewish nations.</note> and teach the Gentiles; they spoke this with a certain insult and contempt for the Gentiles, and a silent boasting of their own. <margin>D</margin> But they characterized the Gentiles as scattered everywhere, wandering throughout the whole circuit of the world and inhabiting various places far apart; by this very fact, they preferred themselves to them. But now the order of things is changed, and the condition of both peoples is turned into the opposite. For the Gentiles, because they promptly and greedily received the offered grace of faith, were led from the dispersion of diverse worship, rites, and superstitions to the unity of faith and gathered into the one fold of Christ the true shepherd. 
<margin>Luke 21</margin> But the Jews, because they did not know the time of their visitation and rejected from themselves the Good Shepherd (who 
<margin>Matthew 15</margin> proclaimed that he had come for the sheep that were lost of the house of Israel), were given over to pillage, dissipation, and dispersion by the just judgment of God. Our Lord had clearly predicted that this would happen to the Jews.

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological argument for due process, moving from the Old Testament examples (Sodom and Nicodemus) to the practices of the Roman Empire and finally to the words of Jesus Christ himself in the Gospel of John.</meta>

272 BOOK FIVE.

<margin>Acts 25</margin>
The judge appointed by the Romans <note>referring to Porcius Festus, the Roman procurator</note>, when the chief priests and elders of the Jews demanded a sentence of condemnation against the blessed Paul, responded: "It is not the Roman custom to hand over any man (that is, to permit him to be surrendered to the will of others for execution and the infliction of punishment) before the accused has his accusers present and receives an opportunity to defend himself to clear away the crimes of which he is accused." Indeed, it is so manifest that the same thing is commanded by Divine Law that it hardly requires proof, 
<margin>Psalm 57</margin>
since the Prophet says in the Psalm: "Judge rightly, you sons of men." 
<margin>John 7</margin>
And the Lord says in the Gospel: "Do not judge according to appearances, but judge a just judgment." How, then, can anyone judge rightly or deliver a just judgment if he condemns the accused without the case being heard and without any investigation of the alleged crimes? Could you recall to life one who has been put to death, if, after the final punishment has been carried out, his innocence is perceived and recognized, when no remedy for his life can any longer be applied? 

Furthermore, when the Pharisees persisted with their insistent questioning about what the Lord felt should be done in this perplexing and doubtful case, he, struck by their relentless voices, stood up and said: "He who among you is without sin, let him be the first to cast a stone at her." He meant that Moses commanded adulteresses to be stoned according to the law—but only by those who are observers of the law, not its violators. For it is not right, nor do the laws permit, that the transgression of a law be punished by those who themselves transgress it. Therefore, "whoever among you is conscious within himself that he has not violated the law, that he has never committed anything against the law, let him cast the first stone at her. I do not forbid the adulteress to be stoned, but I would not have it done by those who have trampled the law no less than she, or perhaps even more gravely." 

With this marvelous sentence, he blocked the mouth of those speaking iniquity. 
<margin>Psalm 26</margin>
For he dictated that the law of Moses must indeed be kept, but he attached a condition which none of the accusers dared to claim for himself or saw present in himself; each was conscious of his own evils and struck in his soul by this sentence. Having given this answer, the Lord stooped down again and wrote with his finger on the earth, turning his face away as was his custom, so that they might have more freedom and confidence to leave—those whom he foresaw would depart more quickly than they would ask further questions. 

Now, what the Lord wrote in the earth the first time he stooped, and what he wrote the second time, the Evangelist does not explain, nor is it easy for anyone to define. Although there are those who assert that during this second stooping, the Lord inscribed certain marks on the ground by which each of the accusers saw his own sins before his eyes and beheld them set against his mind. From this, overwhelmed by a blush of shame and affected by disgrace, they easily recognized that they were not leading lives free from sin, and were moved to learn rather than to inquire so sharply. Furthermore, by this second stooping

<column-break/>

BOOK FIVE. 273

[A] and his writing, the Lord teaches us that before we rebuke a sinning brother, and after we have rebuked him, we ought to stoop into the depths of our own heart. There, we should investigate more attentively whether we suffer from a similar vice to the one we rebuke in another, or perhaps something more serious. If we discover this, we ought to humbly punish it in ourselves first, and only then rebuke our neighbor with gentleness. For we do not rightly reprehend the sins of others if we are weighed down by the same or greater ones. 
<margin>Romans 2</margin>
Regarding such people, Paul says: "In that which you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you do the same things that you judge: you who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say one should not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abominate idols, do you commit sacrilege?" 
<margin>Galatians 6</margin>
[B] Paul teaches us the correct law of correction in his letter to the Galatians: "Brethren," he says, "even if a man is overtaken in some fault, you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted." For when we discuss our own life with diligent examination, being conscious of our fragility, we more easily forgive the fragility of another; and when we have amended our own fault, we are led by a pious affection to kindly wipe away the fault of another as well.

CHAPTER XVII.

[C] Hearing these things, they went out one by one, beginning from the elders; and Jesus remained alone, with the woman standing in the midst. Then Jesus, straightening himself, said to her: "Woman, where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?" She said: "No one, Lord." And Jesus said: "Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on, sin no more." 

Just as Goliath the Philistine (as the history of the Kings records) 
<margin>1 Kings 17</margin>
was struck by David’s sling and stone, prostrated on the ground half-dead, and, deprived of his strength, was cut down; so the Pharisees, struck by the sword of the word of God, were dismayed in spirit. Truly, this sentence of the Lord struck the hard forehead of their minds like a stone and made each one conscious of his own fault. Therefore, having heard it, and thinking they should stay there no longer, they went out one after another, covered in silent shame, following the order of their age—so that the elders and those of greater years left first, and then the others followed. 
[D] I would easily believe that the elders were conscious of more serious evils in themselves and were guilty, and that the word of Scripture was fulfilled in them: 
<margin>Daniel 13</margin>
"Iniquity came forth from the elders" <note>a reference to the story of Susanna and the Elders</note>. For that reason, affected by a more vehement shame, they were the first to depart, followed by the others younger in age as if following their leaders and chiefs. 

The adversaries having been cleared out, Jesus was left alone with the woman accused of the crime of adultery, upon whom the Lord—the fountain and origin of all goodness—bestowed great mercy. Indeed, he asked where those were who had just now accused her—not because he was ignorant that they had departed, but so that he might show an example to those who, in a judgment, are about to acquit someone of a charged crime: that they ought to grant a free [opportunity...]

274 ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

...a place for the accusers to be heard, and to admit anyone to bring a legitimate accusation. For if no accuser is excluded, the innocence and integrity of the one who is acquitted in judgment will be more clearly established. Therefore, when the woman replied that she had been condemned by no one, he immediately promised that he would not condemn her either, and by the sweetness of his kindness, he ordered her to go free. He enjoined only this upon her: that from now on she should guard herself against sin and watch with the greatest zeal lest she fall back into her former evils. 

<margin>One must beware of relapsing into sins.</margin>
For medicine is taken in vain if, after health has been restored, the person who recovered falls back into the original disease through a lack of self-control. Indeed, a relapse into sickness is usually more dangerous and closer to death than that first illness; often, a recurring sickness after health has been returned carries away from this life those whom the first bout of ill health did not kill. In the same way, the medicine of penance is taken in vain if, after it is completed, one returns to the filth of a past life. This second fever of the soul is extremely dangerous. 

<margin>John 5</margin>
Hence our Lord is read to have said to the paralytic <note>The man at the Pool of Bethesda</note>—who had lain ill for thirty-eight years, was now healed, and ordered to take up his mat and walk—: "Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happens to you." By these words, he certainly signified that through the repetition of sin, a person falls into worse evils. What does it profit, I ask, to diligently wash clothes and then soil the washed garments again with mud? What does it profit to wash hands and then contaminate the cleansed hands again with filth? 

<margin>Proverbs 26</margin>
"As a washed sow," says the Wise Man, "in the wallowing-place of mud: so is a fool who repeats his folly, for he is like a dog that returns to its own vomit." 

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 34</margin>
Hear the Preacher <note>referring to the book of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus</note> gravely condemning this repetition of sins: "One building up, and one pulling down: what profit have they but labor? One praying, and one cursing: whose voice will God hear? He who is baptized after touching a corpse, and touches it again, what does his washing profit him? So is the man who fasts for his sins, and doing the same things again, what does he profit by humbling himself?" 

<margin>Genesis 19</margin>
Lot's wife, having turned back toward Sodom which she had left, was changed into a pillar of salt. 

<margin>Luke 17</margin>
The Lord warned us that we should take an example from this, so that we do not return to the wretched allurements of sins, saying: "Be mindful of Lot's wife." 

<margin>2 Samuel 19, 1 Kings 2</margin>
When Shimei had obtained pardon for his first offense against David and was ordered not to go beyond the walls of the city of Jerusalem, he was punished with death because he was caught transgressing a second time and neglecting the king's command. What else does this case of Shimei suggest to us, except that the wrath of God is to be feared and greatly dreaded if we perpetrate the same outrages again and again? 

<margin>Luke 11</margin>
The unclean spirit, having been cast out of a man and finding no rest elsewhere, said: "I will return to my house from which I came," and finding it not fortified by the protection of God, he took seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they entered and dwelt there, and the last state of that man became worse than the first. 

<margin>Numbers 11</margin>
The children of Israel in the desert,

sighing after the meat-pots of Egypt and the bread eaten to fullness—when the melons, onions, and other things came to their minds—were struck down by the wrath of God. 

<margin>Numbers 14</margin>
Those who said, "Let us appoint a leader for ourselves and return to Egypt," were routed by their enemies. They serve as a type <note>a symbolic foreshadowing</note> for those who, having entered the path of virtue, labor to turn their feet back to the darkness of their past life. "For no one putting his hand to the plow and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God." 

<margin>Luke 9</margin>
However, some have been so anxious to condemn relapsing into sin severely and rigidly that they deny penance or the granting of pardon to those who fall into vices after the saving washing of sins in the font of baptism. Likewise, if anyone should commit the same sins again after having undertaken penance, they refuse to grant him the benefit of absolution and the remission of sins a second time. For they say that this easy granting of pardon, offered promptly whenever someone has transgressed, would be a kind of incentive and occasion for sinning more boldly and licentiously. 

[Center gutter marker: B]

To be sure, the ease of pardon incites a mind naturally prone to evil to sin more confidently, since after a crime is admitted, a path to pardon is ready and open to wash away the fault. But these people seem to begrudge men the fountain of divine mercy, which most generously communicates to us the abundant streams of its grace. They seem to want to enclose the immense within certain limits and constrain it by boundaries, so that it might only delete the first sins, but for deleting others, it is either not sufficient or not applied. 

[Center gutter marker: C]

Nor do they see clearly enough that if a medicine is established for the human body that is so effective and healthy that whenever someone falls into a disease, they are immediately healed upon taking it—if someone willfully incurs a disease, led by the hope of recovering health through the medicine, which causes them to be less cautious against the disease—the cause of this frequent relapse into disease is not the medicine (which was ordained only for the expulsion of the disease), but rather the negligence and wickedness of the man, misusing what is good for evil, contrary to the order and nature of that thing. 

But if anyone were to contend that this medicine should by no means be administered to one who is sick a second time, but rather should be withdrawn lest it seem to give men a handle for living more licentiously: 

[Center gutter marker: D]

who would say this person is of sound mind, or who would bear it with a calm spirit? Likewise, who would rightly care for human health in this manner? In no other way was penance ordained by God for the preparation of the deletion of crimes: but if anyone makes the frequent receipt of it a matter for sinning more freely, they do that only by their own wickedness, taking an occasion of evil from good, and not from the nature or ordination of penance itself. For it was instituted to abolish committed sins, not to perpetrate future ones. 

<margin>The objection of the adversaries and its solution. Hebrews 6.</margin>

### CHAPTER 19.
**The Pharisees therefore said: You bear witness of yourself; your testimony is not true. Jesus answered and said to them: Even if I bear witness of myself, my testimony is true; for I know where I came from and where I am going; but you do not know where I come from or where I am going.** [Marginal note: A]) Everywhere the Pharisees show themselves to be very inclined not toward learning, but toward slander. [Marginal note: B] They always strive to contradict the words of Christ, to resist them, to oppose them as false, and to hurl insults. For when the Lord called himself the light of the world, they, with hardened minds, struggled against this light lest it shine into their minds. They are very much like those who, lest they behold the offered light of the sun, cover their eyes with their eyelids or turn their faces away. And because they consider him a mere man, covered by the cloud of the flesh, <note>original: "nube carnis obductam" — a common theological metaphor suggesting that Christ's divinity was hidden by his human body like a cloud hiding the sun.</note> they do not notice the Deity revealing itself in him through the splendor of his signs. Indeed, a man's testimony about himself is usually invalid and by no means worthy of trust; for less credit is given to one who praises himself and his own deeds, or extols his own works with words. Therefore, the Pharisees throw it in the Lord's face that he bears witness of himself, not considering that he had previously been promised by the heralds—Moses, David, Isaiah, and the other noble prophets—who bore witness of him with most celebrated proclamation before he arrived. Then they vomit out that voice full of blasphemy: [Marginal note: 1 Cor. 1, John 14] *Your testimony is not true.* By this, they graze Christ—the power and wisdom of God—with the mark of a lie, and with impious mouths, they babble that he who is the supreme Truth tells a false testimony. But notice what the Lord answered them. Indeed, he provides an answer first to the latter point they pressed: that even if he bears witness of himself, it is nonetheless true, because God is true, in whom no lie or falsehood can fall. He likewise [Marginal note: D, 1 John 1] is the light, and there is no darkness in him. Now, light is by its very nature self-manifesting; <note>original: "suapte natura suiipsius est manifestativa"</note> and although it is made bright by no external thing, nor is it illuminated by a lamp or a torch brought near, it nonetheless truly introduces itself to the eyes of mortals. Thus Christ, the spiritual light, even if he had not been declared by the testimony of others, his own testimony which he spoke of himself would have been no less consistent with the truth. Moreover, he asserts that the testimony he bears of himself is true: *because I know,* he says, *where I came from and where I am going.* For he came from the Father into the world to complete the mystery of human redemption, and by the good pleasure and will

***

BOOK FIVE. 281

of the Father, he assumed the substance of our flesh. [Marginal note: A] Having completed the sacred mystery of our salvation, he goes again to the Father, and returns to the glory of the Father as an extraordinary triumpher and victor. But the Pharisees neither received him as the Son of God sent by the Father, nor believed that he would return to the glory of the Father’s majesty. Therefore, he aptly testifies that they do not know where he comes from or where he is going.

### CHAPTER 20.
**You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. And yet if I do judge, my judgment is true; for I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me. It is also written in your law that the testimony of two men is true. I am one who bears witness of myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness of me.** [Marginal note: A]) Those who have bodily eyes that are weak from blear-eyedness <note>original: "lippitudine" — a medical term for inflammation or "runny eyes," used here as a metaphor for spiritual blindness.</note> or dullness do not judge colors correctly; [Marginal note: B] rather, they give judgment otherwise than the matter stands because of their inherent weakness, repeatedly saying of white that it is black, and of black that it is white. So the Pharisees seem to be affected: for because of a grave disease of the soul—the zeal, envy, and hatred by which they were incited against Christ—they had the edge of their mind dulled and clouded. They were not able to penetrate to the knowledge of the divinity hiding within the flesh, which nevertheless clearly revealed itself through manifold signs. And sticking only to what they gazed upon externally in Christ, and fixed only upon his bodily figure, they thought him to be a mere man. For this reason, Christ said they [Marginal note: C] judge according to the flesh: because they thought nothing else remained in him beyond the flesh and human nature. Christ, however, denies that he judges anyone in this way, according to the flesh and the appearance, because he searches even the secrets of the heart and knows what is in man. Or, he denies that he judges anyone now, [Marginal note: John 2, John 3] in his present coming. For he did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. In his second coming, however, he will judge all by a discussion and examination of their works previously done in life; regarding which judgment to come at the end of the age, he adds: *And if I judge, my judgment is true.* Or, in this second place, he speaks of the present judgment of discernment, <note>term: "judgment of discernment" (iudicio discretionis) — the idea that Christ's presence automatically separates the faithful from the unfaithful even before the final Judgment Day.</note> by which he separates the good from the evil by the examination of his secret knowledge, and distinguishes the faithful from the wicked, just as Paul says to Timothy: [Marginal note: 2 Tim. 2] *The Lord knows those who are his.* Both judgments of Christ—the discussion of works, which is deferred to the end of the world, and the discernment of merits, which is always exercised in the present time—are true, because they proceed from the highest truth and the most just scale of justice. For how could it be that the supreme Truth does not correctly discern the hidden merits of each person, or that the first Justice wanders from the right law of judgment? Furthermore, he brings forward the cause of the truth of his judgment: *Because,* he says, *I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.* Do not, he says, [Marginal note: John 14] think that I wander from the path of truth by the reason of my judgment;

Furthermore, to make it clear that he was speaking of God the Father, and not of any other parent according to the flesh—and also to show that he was not resistant or opposed to God, as the Jews commonly boasted—he protests that he does nothing of himself, by his own will or judgment. Instead, he speaks those things which he received and learned from the Father, in the same consensus and concord with him. Moreover, the Father "taught" the Son, not because he instructed one who was ignorant or previously lacked divine knowledge, or led him into understanding; but because he begat him knowing all things before the ages, and by begetting him, he bestowed wisdom upon the Son just as he bestowed the divine essence. Therefore, the Son did not first become ignorant and then wise; but being wise from eternity, he refers his knowledge back to the Father as its author, and confesses that he has it from him. Finally, he repeats the same things that were mentioned above: namely, *he who sent me is with me, and he has not left me alone,* lest those things which contain the arduous mystery <term>mystery — here used in the sense of the Latin "sacramentum," a sacred and profound reality that is revealed by God</term> of his divinity and his inseparability from the Father should pass by fruitlessly if heard carelessly. Rather, by being repeated again and again, they are fixed more firmly in the minds of the listeners. Thus, he maintains that his Father, by whom he was sent, is with him: because he himself is in the Father, and the Father is in him, immovably and inseparably; nor has the Father left him alone, as he who is one with the Father in inseparability and identity of nature, and is always in the bosom of the Father. Moreover, with this most close connection of the substance of the Father and the Son, there is also

I know that you are children of Abraham: but you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you. I speak what I have seen with my Father: and you do what you have seen with your father.) Children of Abraham according to the spirit <margin>Luke 19</margin> are pleasing to me: such as Zacchaeus, who by my own testimony <margin>Genesis 17</margin> was called a son of Abraham. Abraham was the first to receive circumcision according to the flesh; so that you may be true children of Abraham, receive circumcision according to the spirit, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart. Thus he killed him, because he turned a righteous man into a sinner, an immortal into a mortal, and one living through grace into one dead through guilt. Furthermore, that it is the devil's desire to kill man and to shed innocent blood is shown by the Lord's following words. *He,* he said, *was a murderer from the beginning.* <note>original: "Ille homicida erat ab initio."</note> The devil came against the first man not girded with iron, but armed with lying and lethal persuasion. He did not slay him with a sword, but with a word, when he suggested to him: *You shall by no means die; but you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.* <margin>Genesis 3</margin> Therefore, everyone who persuades another toward evil with a pestilent tongue kills them while dragging them into sin—not indeed according to the body, but according to the soul. <margin>Psalm 57</margin> Of such people the Psalm says: *The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.* <note>The author cites Psalm 56 in the Latin Vulgate, which corresponds to Psalm 57 in modern bibles.</note> For if a man kills his own soul through malice, as the <margin>Wisdom 16</margin> Wise Man says, while he instills the poison of his own evil into another's soul, does he not kill it? And if hatred for a brother is the death of the soul, as <margin>1 John 3</margin> John says in his epistle: *He who hates his brother is a murderer; and we know that a murderer has no part in the kingdom of God,* then by the same reasoning, are not greed, anger, and other capital sins of that kind the destruction of the soul? And he who drags his neighbor to those things cruelly kills him; and indeed more monstrously, insofar as the soul is more excellent and worthy than the body, and the death of the soul is more ruinous than that of the body. He also (who is called the father of the Jews) *did not stand in the truth, and the truth is not in him.* He did not stand in the truth because he fell away from the truth, nor did he wish to remain in the holiness of his origin. For he had been made in the image and likeness of God. But by becoming proud, he did indeed retain the image, because he did not lose the nature of immortality; yet he lost the truth of the likeness, because from a righteous and good angel, he became an unjust and evil devil. Concerning this, for a stronger proof of what was said, the Lord adds: *When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own: because he is a liar, and the father of it,* <note>original: "pater eius, ſcilicet mẽdacij"</note> namely, the father of lying. The devil was plainly a liar from himself, because he heard it from no one else first, nor did he learn the lie, but he himself fathered his own lie. Turning away of his own accord from the truth and from God, who is truth, he ran into the horrific darkness of lying; nor did he receive that darkness from anywhere else but himself. Just as someone turning their eyes away from the splendor of the sun does not have the darkness and the horror of night from another, but from themselves alone, because they departed of their own will from the source of light. For that reason, when the devil speaks a lie, he speaks from his own. And <margin>Romans 3</margin> just as God is true and the father of truth, so also the devil is a liar and the father of lies. But man, because he did not learn the lie from himself but from the teaching and

305

suggestion of the devil, when he speaks a lie, he does not speak from his own, but from what is foreign and what he received from elsewhere. Nor is he the father of the lie, but the son of the father of lies, whom he imitates by a likeness of malice, turning away from the truth and God through sin. Furthermore, it would not be out of place <margin>Objections of adversaries and solutions.</margin> here to destroy the assertion of some who feel that evil was established in the devil by God, and that he was created in depravity. They take the opportunity to support this opinion from this place where it is said: *He was a murderer from the beginning,* thinking that by these words it is signified that from the very start of his production—indeed, in the very beginning of his origin—he was addicted to malice. But these people do not sufficiently discuss the Lord's words, nor do they keenly attend to their sense. For it was not said that *in* the beginning he was a murderer, but *from* the beginning—namely, of sin, as Augustine says—since sin and transgression began with him. Or he was a murderer from the beginning of human creation and the production of the physical world, because he then brought death to the human race, and never ceased afterward to bring destruction and ruin by whatever means he could. And yet, when this sensible world was produced and man was formed, the angelic substance already existed as a created thing, having been brought into being first of all (as is the opinion of many). Therefore, the angel himself existed in the condition of his nature before he fell and became a murderer. Moreover, they bring forward what was said by <margin>1 John 3</margin> John in his epistle: *He who commits sin is of the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning.* If he sins from the beginning, they say, then he was produced in sin and created evil; otherwise he would not have sinned from the beginning, from the start of his constitution. But almost the same dilution must be applied to this reasoning: it was not said that the devil sins from the beginning because he was formed evil by God, but because from the very start of sin (which took its origin from him, for before his fall there was no sin) he transgressed the law of God, and falling away from his native goodness, he fell into depravity, from which he never ceased. Instead, he continues in it constantly, always piling <margin>Psalm 104; Job 40</margin> evils upon evils and suggesting wicked things. Furthermore, they rely on this verse of the Psalm: *This dragon which you made to play in it.* <note>The author cites Psalm 103 in the Vulgate; modern Psalm 104:26.</note> And on this word of Job: *Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you.* Where by the names of the dragon and Behemoth the devil is understood, called by these names by reason of his malice. The Lord, however, bears witness that He made him, so that his temptations and the machinations of his frauds might be mocked by good men who overcome him. Consequently, they say, he was created evil by God. But those who devise these things to attack the truth do not exactly distinguish the substance of the devil from his accidental malice. If they did so diligently, they would recognize that this malice proceeded from the fallen angel himself, but that his substance proceeded from God, and that the scripture intends to signify only that. In scripture, the cause of the subject at hand is not always suggested, but sometimes the outcome is implied; as in other places...

It distinguishes between the devil's created nature (which is good) and his chosen malice (which is the source of lies and death).</summary>
