[The Jews asked:] **"Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died: who do you make yourself out to be?"** <note>original: "Nunquid tu maior es patre noſtro Abraham..." This refers to John 8:53.</note> Just as a good person becomes better when an insult is received, so a wicked person becomes worse when a benefit is offered. <margin>Romans 8</margin> This is not without reason: for those who love God, all things—even the bad—work together for good. <note>A reference to Romans 8:28, a central tenet of Christian providence.</note> But those who hate God turn everything, even good things (as was said before), into evil. See how the Jews do not strive to hear or learn the truth, but resist and contradict it with open hostility. The Lord had just spoken of the death by which the soul is separated here from God, the fountain of life, through guilt, and in the future through Gehenna <note>term: Gehenna (a historical valley in Jerusalem used as a metaphor for the place of spiritual punishment or hell)</note>. The Jews, however, with the eyes of their minds growing dim and not perceiving the brilliance of the light which the Truth showed them, thought the Lord spoke of the death of the body. From this, they took material for their false accusation, objecting that both Abraham and the prophets had died, even though it is certain they kept the word of God. They wished to conclude from this that what the Lord had said before was false. Abraham indeed died according to the body, as did the prophets; however, they did not experience the death of the soul, but according to the soul, they live for God. For whether we live, we live for the Lord; or whether we die, we die for the Lord: therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord's. <margin>Exodus 3. Luke 20.</margin> And God himself is called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob: but he is not the God of the dead, but of the living: for all live to him. <note>Jesus uses this argument in the Gospels to prove the resurrection and the continued existence of the patriarchs.</note> 

Indeed, in this place, both from the words of the Jews and from the words of our Lord, a two-fold death is suggested to us, one far different from the other. One, of course, is of the body, which is the dissolution of the soul itself from the **prison of the flesh.** <note>original: "ergaſtulo carnis." This metaphor views the physical body as a temporary confinement for the eternal soul.</note> And this should be called not so much death as a "falling asleep," a passage and migration from this life, and a laying down of the burden of the body. Furthermore, this type of death is by no means linked to the account of guilt, since it is common to all people—both the just and the unjust—by the law of nature and inevitable necessity. For it can be delayed, so that one might die later, but it cannot be avoided so that one might entirely escape and not feel the death of the body. Therefore, it is by no means to be dreaded, although many are seized by a heavy fear of it; yet one can find those who have longed for it with burning prayers, as the Prophet <margin>Psalm 119. Philippians 1.</margin> crying out with sorrow: "Woe is me, for my exile is prolonged." And the blessed Paul, writing to the Philippians: **"I desire to be dissolved, and to be with Christ."** 

The other death is truly of the soul, which is its separation from God through guilt in this life, and from His kingdom through Gehenna after the course of this present life. This, however, is born from guilt alone, and a heavy and pestilential guilt indeed, as the Wise Man says: <margin>Wisdom 16.</margin> **"A man through malice kills his own soul."** Therefore, it can be avoided with God's help by those who are anxious for their own salvation and not careless. Nor can it be imposed on anyone by any necessity or violence; it is summoned and contracted only by one's own will. Nor is it common to all, but is peculiar only to the wicked and those of corrupt life. It is, however, to be dreaded above all else, because it is not temporary or momentary, but 

->ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 315<-

endless and perpetual. The Lord also healthily warned of this in the Gospel: <margin>Matthew 10.</margin> **"Do not fear those,"** he said, **"who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna."** But because the Jews paid attention only to the flesh in Christ, and thought him a mere man, they considered him to be of far lower dignity than Abraham and the prophets had been. Therefore, when they ask with resentment and anger: **"Are you greater than our father Abraham?"** they thought it a great wickedness if he should call himself greater than him—he who is greater than both men and angels. And because they judged all these things to be said by him through arrogance, they ask with reproach and bitterness: **"Who do you make yourself out to be?"** as if they were saying: "Your pride, by which you puff yourself up so grandly, is not to be endured with a calm mind."

### CHAPTER XI. <note>This likely refers to a chapter or section in the commentary volume, as the scripture text continues from John 8:54.</note>

**Jesus answered: If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me: whom you say is our God, and you have not known him: but I know him. And if I say that I do not know him, I shall be a liar like you. But I know him, and I keep his word. Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day: he saw it, and was glad.** The more stubbornly the Jews strive against the words of Christ, the more kindly the Lord tries to lead them to the way of righteousness. See how he sees them resisting him with open hostility, and yet he does not cease to communicate the words of salvation to them. He shows that he by no means seeks his own glory, because they had insolently objected, "Who do you make yourself out to be?" He says he is glorified by God the Father: because in his baptism, transfiguration, and works of miracles, the Son was glorified, declared, and manifested by the Father. 

Therefore, the false accusation of the heretics—who quibble that the Father is greater than the Son because He glorifies the Son—has no place. For the Son himself often says in the scriptures that he glorifies the Father; from which, however, they do not rightly conclude that the Son is greater than the Father. <margin>John 17. Matthew 5.</margin> **"Father,"** he says, **"glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you."** Indeed, even humans are said in scripture at times to "glorify" God. **"So let your light shine,"** (said the Lord on the mount to his disciples) **"before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven."** Now, who but one lacking in mind and insane would say that men glorifying God are greater than the Heavenly Father, who is glorified by them? Truly, this kind of glorification does not consist in the addition of *new* glory to the one who is glorified, but in the *manifestation* of the glory already possessed. Therefore, the one who glorifies is not always greater than the one who is glorified. Furthermore, because the Jews claimed a special knowledge of God for themselves, and they alone... <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing with "the worshippers of God."</note>

But when the Jews saw that they were making no progress, they turned once again to insults and blasphemies; since they could not resist Christ's words and reasoning, they seized the weapons of fury. From which it follows:

**"Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad."**
<margin>John 8</margin>
This is not to be understood as a physical vision, since Abraham did not see the day of Christ's incarnation <note>The "incarnation" refers to the moment God became human in the form of Jesus.</note> with his bodily eyes, but through the spirit and faith. For Abraham was a prophet to whom the salvation of the world had been revealed. Because all nations were to be blessed through him, he had known the day of the Redeemer, which is the day of joy and salvation. He desired to see this day, and he saw it, just as it is written in Genesis: for he saw three men and worshiped one <note>original: "vidit tres viros, & vnum adorauit." A standard medieval interpretation of Genesis 18, where Abraham's three visitors are seen as a prefiguration of the Holy Trinity.</note>; and because he was commanded to sacrifice his son Isaac, he understood that through that figure, Christ would one day suffer.

**"Then the Jews said to him: 'You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?'"**

The Jews received Christ's words according to the flesh, and they speak in a worldly way. They think He is speaking about the length of His human life, whereas He was speaking about the eternity of His divinity. Abraham had lived a long time before Christ’s birth; therefore, they think He is lying when He claims to have seen Abraham.

**"Jesus said to them: 'Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham was made, I am.'"**

Because Abraham was a creature, but Christ is the Creator: Abraham was born and had a beginning, but Christ always remains. Therefore, He did not say, "Before Abraham was, I was," but **"I am,"** just as it was said to Moses: **"I am who I am."** <note>original: "Ego sum qui sum." This is a reference to Exodus 3:14, where God reveals His name to Moses, signifying eternal existence.</note> By this, He shows that He is eternal and exists before all time.

**A** do they not fear to assert his nature? Is it not true that those who share the same operation also share the same nature? And those whose nature is different also have a different manner of action? If, therefore, the works of the Son are also the works of the Father himself—just as he says in another place: **"If I do not the works of my Father, believe me not"** <margin>John 10</margin> <note>original: "Si nō facio opera patris mei, nolite credere mihi."</note> and again: **"The Father dwelling in me, he does the works"** <margin>John 14</margin> <note>original: "Pater in me manens, ipse facit opera."</note>—then the substance and nature of the Father and the Son will be entirely the same. But if anyone should stubbornly assert a different nature, the Son would be a creature; and a creature would then ascend to such power and dignity that he would perform the work of God and hold that same work in common with God. And since God, by his immense power, performs those things which transcend the strength and measure of a creature (for the prophet sings to him: **"You alone are the one who does wonders"** <margin>Psalm 71</margin> <note>original: "Tu es solus, qui facis mirabilia." Historically, this is Psalm 72:18.</note> and again: **"Who alone does great wonders"**), **B** <margin>Psalm 135</margin> <note>original: "Qui facit mirabilia magna solus." Psalm 136:4.</note> then the creature itself, relying on its own strength, would be doing things that transcend its own limits and laws. But let these trifles vanish: let us instead confess that the Son, who performs the works of the Father, is of the same substance as the Father, so that from the fellowship of their works, the identity of their nature may shine forth. 

Furthermore, when Christ says in this place that this man was born blind **"so that the works of God might be made manifest in him,"** he says this concerning himself, not the Father, and by that word he implies that he himself is God. For already the works of the Father were manifest in the creation of the whole world, in its most wise arrangement, and indeed in its continuous administration and governance. But regarding Christ, clothed in human form, it was not yet so clearly perceived that he was the creator and ruler of the world; rather, through this miraculous illumination of a man, people were led, as if by a guiding hand, to believe that truth. And so the **C** Son of God manifested his glory, to show that he was the author of creation. For indeed, faith regarding a greater matter also confirms that which is lesser. Among the entire multitude of sensible creatures, man is the most honorable. From the fact, therefore, that Christ showed himself to be the creator of man, he strengthens this faith in all things: that he is also the maker of the entire sensible creation. 

Of those members which are within us, the most honorable is the eye; for it governs the entire human body and directs the feet: **"The lamp of your body,"** he says, **"is your eye."** <margin>Matthew 6</margin> <note>original: "Lucerna... corporis tui, est oculus tuus."</note> It likewise adorns and beautifies the face of man. For what the sun is in the world, the eye is in the body; **D** hence it is allotted a higher place than the other members, situated as if on a certain royal summit. Therefore, since in this illumination of the blind man Christ shows himself as the maker and creator of the eye (for neither the clay placed upon him, nor the flowing water, had any power to form an eye; rather, Christ's divine power alone produced it), by that act he proves that he is the creator of the remaining members of the body, and indeed of the whole man. And since by showing himself to be the maker of man, he also creates this faith in all: that he is the producer of the entire fabric of the world, as has already been shown. It follows that Christ himself, through this illumination of the blind man and the new production of his eyes, clearly reveals himself as the founder of the entire machinery of the world,

**A** and so manifests his glory—which was the point proposed at the beginning. But indeed, someone might ask here: Did this blind man suffer unjustly, because he was born blind without fault? Not at all; rather, he received a benefit through this blindness. For he received his sight more miraculously than if he had received it from the moment of his birth; and by that occasion, he was also enlightened in his inner eyes and led fully to the faith of Christ. For what did it profit the Jews to have had the eyes of the body intact from the beginning of life, when they were utterly blind in their souls? Has not this blind man attained a greater benefit, who, though deprived of bodily sight for a time, was afterward granted the faculty of seeing both inwardly and outwardly? 

Nevertheless, there are some who, in this passage of the Gospel, say that the word **"That"** (**Vt**) is not causative, but signifies the **B** outcome; just as in that word of Paul: **"The law entered so that sin might abound."** <margin>Romans 5</margin> <note>original: "Lex subintrauit, ut abundaret delictū."</note> For the law itself was not the effective cause of the abundance of sin, since it forbade fault; rather, it followed from the introduction of the law that sin abounded. So too it followed that the Lord, opening closed eyes and correcting other defects of natural infirmity, demonstrated his own power. But the former opinion seems more suited to this passage. 

Nor should we pass over this lightly: that the Lord says he must work while it is day; as long, namely, as he is present in this world. But you will say: if the operation of Christ is extended only through that interval of time in which he was present in this world, since he has now long since departed hence to the Father, then he no longer performs the works of the Father, nor is he the light of the world, since he is no longer in the world. We are therefore wandering in that horrendous night in which no one can work. But observe carefully here: **D** that although he has withdrawn the presence of his body from here, he is nevertheless always present by the majesty of his divinity; just as he promised when about to depart from his disciples: **"Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age."** <margin>Matthew 28</margin> <note>original: "Ecce ego uobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi." For [the old law] prevented anyone from descending into the water and being cured before others. But now, anyone at all can approach the basin of baptism. For it is not an angel who stirs the water, but the Lord of angels, who works all things. And in this font of baptism, it is not just one person at one time who is cured, as it was in the pool; on the contrary, even if the entire world were to come, grace is not consumed, but remains the same. For just as the rays of the sun illuminate each day and are not consumed, nor is the light of the sun made less by its great abundance, so too—and much more so—the action of the Holy Spirit is in no way diminished by the multitude of those who receive it. However, that previous healing used to happen—namely, that only one person was healed after the moving of the water—so that those who had learned that bodily sicknesses were healed in water might, having been practiced in this for a long time, easily believe that water can also heal the sicknesses of the soul.

Therefore the neighbors, and those who had seen him before because he was a beggar, said: "Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?" Some said, "This is he." A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; <note>original: "Non potest ciuitas abscondi supra montem posita"</note> nor do they light a lamp and put it under a basket, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to everyone who is in the house. Thus, neither could the brightness of Christ's signs be obscured or concealed. For it was first perceived by his neighbors and acquaintances, who knew this enlightened man previously as blind and a beggar. 

Here we must observe toward what sort of men the wonderful mercy of God inclined itself. He healed those who begged with great compassion; and by this he blocked the mouths of the Jews, because he deemed not the famous, not the distinguished, nor the princes, but the lowly <term>ignobiles</term><note>Referring to those of low social birth or status</note> worthy of his providence; for indeed, he had come for the salvation of all. Thus also, <margin>Luke 19</margin> descending from Jerusalem into Jericho, he healed a blind man sitting by the way and begging; and having called him to himself, he kindly enlightened him. And because his opened eyes had changed his face and the appearance of his mouth somewhat, some said he was not the same man who had been blind, but another similar to him. But he himself was neither ashamed of his former blindness, nor did he fear the fury of the common people, nor did he refuse to show himself, so that he might proclaim his benefactor. Questioned about the manner of the enlightenment he received, he was proved entirely truthful. For what he did not know, he did not say. For he did not know that [Jesus] had spat on the ground, and therefore he did not express that to the others; but that he had anointed them, he learned through the sense of touch. That he had ordered him to go to the pool of Siloam, he testified from hearing. He expressed the name of his benefactor; for he recognized his voice from the discussion with the disciples, and from previous times 

329

<margin>A</margin> he had already heard his name for a long time, through the widespread fame of his signs, which he had learned from the reports of others. Finally, when the neighbors asked, "Where is he?" they seem to be meditating on a conspiracy against the Lord, so that they might accuse him before the Pharisees, just as their subsequent actions show. Christ, however, was not present with this man whom he had healed, nor with others who were healed by him; for he did not seek his own glory, nor to show himself off. The Lord always withdrew after performing the benefit of a healing: so that he might teach us that we ought not to seek human glory from our good deeds, but only to meditate on the honor of the divine name. Our Lord, the teacher of all virtue, also healthfully <margin>B</margin> taught us this, admonishing us that in fasting, prayer, and almsgiving we should not seek the applause of the people, but the glory of God alone: so that our left hand does not know what the right is doing, otherwise we have received our <margin>Matthew 6</margin> reward. But if we have taken care to work what is right in secret before the eyes of God, our heavenly Father who sees in secret will repay us. Paul also, agreeing with this same opinion, exhorts us that we should not be desirous of empty glory, nor do anything through vain glory: but whether <margin>Galatians 6</margin> we eat, or whether we drink, or whether we do anything else, <margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin> let us refer all things to the glory of God; let our intention be turned to that alone.

They lead him who had been blind to the Pharisees. Now it was the Sabbath when Jesus made the <margin>C</margin> mud and opened his eyes. The Jews, previously asking "Where is he?", wanted to find him so they could lead our Lord to the Pharisees; but because they did not have him, they lead the blind man. Furthermore, the Evangelist adds that it was the Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud: namely, to demonstrate <margin>D</margin> their evil mind, full of iniquity, and the reason for which they sought him—namely, that they might find an occasion against him, and that they might disparage the miracle through a supposed transgression of the law; which shines forth more clearly from their subsequent questions. But it must be diligently considered how the blind man is not disturbed. For since he spoke to the crowds when questioned without danger, it was not such a great thing to speak the truth. But it is wonderful now that, placed in greater danger, he neither denies nor says things contrary to his previous statements, but more succinctly crushes [their arguments] with the same ones. And in this way they suffered the opposite of what they wanted. For they led him and questioned him as one who would deny; but [they received] from him more certainly the truth and the wonderful power of the Lord.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of John 9, focusing on the debate between the Pharisees and those who witnessed the healing of the man born blind. It addresses the legalistic objection to Christ performing "work" on the Sabbath.</meta>

# 330 COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

learned of His power. But indeed, once the manner of this performed enlightenment was heard, different people felt various ways about the Lord. Some, in fact, argued that He was not sent by God but was a transgressor of the law who did not keep the Sabbath, since He had made clay on the Sabbath and anointed the man's eyes. Truly, these people were held by a great blindness of the soul. For while they should have been led to faith by this sign and should have proclaimed the author of such a great work, they did not turn their minds toward what appeared worthy of praise or commendation. Instead, they focused on what they judged to be open to rebuke and objection. They immediately charged Him with a violation of the Sabbath—which, however, the Lord had not violated in the least, even according to the literal meaning of the law. For those works performed by the exercise and service of the hands that pertained to the service of God, or to the manifesting of His glory, were not prohibited from being done on the Sabbath; such works included circumcision and the preparation and sacrificing of victims in the temple. Moreover, this mixing of clay and the anointing were intended to demonstrate the power of God and to make it known to others. 

<margin>John 7</margin> If, therefore, a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses is not broken, and the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath <note>The author refers to the physical labor of the priests in the Temple, which was technically "work" but legally permitted for religious duty.</note> and are without fault, who could rightly think the Sabbath was violated by the mixing of clay or the anointing of eyes—from which the glory of God shone out most brightly among men? Others, however, illuminated by even a small spark of the truth, said (trying to block the mouths of those speaking iniquity): "If this man were not from God, He could not do these signs." Since He restored sight to a man blind from birth, that is a sign that He is not a sinner. Thus, taking their argument from the effect of the deed, they prove that He is from God because He performed such a stupendous sign. 

But someone might ask whether the ministry and office of performing miracles might sometimes fall to the wicked, since in Matthew the Lord says of the rejected: 

<margin>Matthew 7</margin> "Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name, and prophesy, and perform many signs?' And then I will declare to them, 'I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity.'" In what way, then, does it follow that the Lord Himself, if He were a sinner, could not do these signs? 

The answer is that those who possess a depravity of life are not the *primary authors* of signs, even though they have the power to perform miracles; they only exercise the ministry of them and function as certain instruments for their performance. For God often uses even the wicked to perform wonderful works. 

<margin>John 10</margin> Christ, however, was the primary author of these signs, and He testified that they were the works of the Father, which He performed not through another's power nor by a power arriving from the outside, but by the command of His Word alone—a work demonstrating nothing but the primary Operator. Therefore, He Himself—witnessing that He did these things in the name of the Father and calling them the works of the Father—could not be a sinner; otherwise, the very works of God the Father would have been perfected by a sinful man, and God would have been a co-operator with him. And since the Jews, holding different views of the Lord, could not agree on one opinion concerning Him, there was a **schism** among them, with each person defending his own side.

Is it not the duty of disciples to follow the teacher's doctrine to the letter, <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for perfect precision.</note> and in no way to deviate from his precepts? If therefore you are disciples of Moses, as you protest in word, O Pharisees, why do you not observe his teachings? He forbade a curse to be brought against anyone: "You shall not curse the deaf," he said, "nor put a stumbling block before the blind." <margin>Leviticus 19</margin> But you curse a man who is constantly confessing the truth. He furthermore forbade innocent blood to be shed, and the righteous to be killed. <margin>Exodus 23, Deuteronomy 6</margin> <margin>C</margin> But you are carried headlong toward the slaughter of the innocent one, and of Him who is the author of all justice. Finally, Moses commanded God to be adored, and His glory to be sought in all things: but you, by slandering this sign worked for the blind man, diminish and deny the power of God as much as you can. Yet you confess one thing that is true, namely, that you know that God spoke to Moses. And we also freely confess that very thing, having been taught by the Sacred Scripture, which says: <margin>Exodus 33, Numbers 12</margin> "God spoke with Moses, as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend." And God said of Moses: "I speak to him mouth to mouth." But your damnation and iniquity are all the more serious because you neglect the precepts of him to whom God spoke. You trample upon the mandates he received from God <margin>Deuteronomy 18</margin> and consider them as nothing. You now despise that Prophet, whom he foretold would be raised up from among you and <margin>D</margin> should be listened to, as He speaks before you, saying: "But as for this man, we do not know where he is from." But did you not know the place of His birth and His country, or even His lineage according to human genealogy? Did you not say earlier: "We know where this man is from"? <margin>John 7</margin> But these words of yours proceed not from ignorance of Him, but from contempt, by which you make light of Him. For you, seeing the miserable Son of God, judged Him to be a man altogether contemptible and the lowliest of all; hence you say you do not know where He is from, in the usual manner of men who say they do not know those whom they reject. We read something similar in the Book of Kings. <margin>1 Samuel 17</margin> For when the youth David had laid low Goliath, who was formidable to brave men, Saul said to Abner: "Whose son is this boy, Abner?" Surely David had been his armor-bearer, and had frequently played the lyre before him, and yet now he asked who he was. For he spoke as if he did not know him, in whom he despised the youth's age and his pastoral clothing. 

<column-break/>

But so that your blindness may shine forth and become even more known, you estimate those things which you know through sight as being of less value than what you hear. For those things which you say you know—namely, that God spoke to Moses—you heard from your ancestors. But is he not more worthy of belief who has certified that he comes from God through miracles, which you have not only heard of, but have seen? Wherefore, the blind man himself, now rightfully bathed in the clarity of both mind and body, refutes your words, taking his argument from the greatness of the sign performed upon him. "It does not seem," he says, "consistent with the truth, or at all coherent with what is true, that you do not know where <margin>B</margin> this man is from, and that you despise him as an ignoble man or a man of obscure name, who has worked such a magnificent sign and testament of divine power in me." Certainly, God turns away from and hates sinners, nor are their prayers pleasing to His ears. But if anyone worships God most intently and keeps His commandments, He graciously hears him. For "the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous," <margin>Psalm 33</margin> as the prophet says, "and His ears are open to their prayers." And again in another place: "If I have looked upon iniquity <margin>Psalm 65</margin> in my heart, the Lord will not hear me." But God heard this man, my enlightener, and bestowed such power upon him that he drove away from me a blindness that was implanted and innate from my cradle. Therefore, he is not a sinner, as you believe; but he is from God, by whose power he performed this admirable work. <margin>C</margin> For from the beginning of the world it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind; wherefore, unless the author of such a great sign were from God, he would not have been able to achieve such a thing. 

But how, someone might say, does God not hear sinners? Was the Publican not heard, who, standing far off in the temple of God <margin>Luke 18</margin> and casting his eyes down to the ground and beating his breast with his fists, said: "God, be merciful to me, a sinner"? By which confession he was so heard that he returned from the temple justified, though he had come to the temple as an unjust man. Furthermore, have we not been taught by our Lord to use a daily prayer to God: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive <margin>Matthew 6</margin> our debtors"? But what are our debts to God, except the sins by which we offend Him, <margin>D</margin> on account of which we are made debtors of death and guilty of damnation before the Divine Majesty? Again, the blessed John says in his epistle: "If we say that <margin>1 John 1</margin> we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." Finally, the Wise Man says: "Who can <margin>Proverbs 20</margin> say, 'My heart is clean, and I am pure from sin'?" If, therefore, no one lives this life free from crime, and the prayers of a sinner are not received by God, then God hears no one, but turns away from the prayers of all. How then does the Psalm say: "The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping, <margin>Psalm 6</margin> the Lord has heard my supplication, the Lord has received my prayer"? However, sinners are heard by God if they repent of their sins, if they wash away past evils with tears, and from their heart deny being what they were; for having been transformed through these...

### CHAPTER 21.

And Jesus said to him: "For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see: and those who see may become blind." And some of the Pharisees who were with him heard this, and said to him: "Are we also blind?" Jesus said to them: "If you were blind, you would not have sin: but now because you say, 'We see,' your sin remains."

Simeon, the patient waiter for the Lord, ardently sighing for His coming in the flesh, when he had received Him into the Temple when He was brought in on the fortieth day after His birth, and had embraced Him with eager arms—after giving divine praises and being enlightened by the prophetic spirit— <margin>Luke 2</margin> said: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and the resurrection of many, and for a sign that shall be contradicted."

He is for the fall of those who stumbled over the <margin>Isaiah 8</margin> "stone of offense and rock of scandal," <note>original: "lapidem offensionis, & petram scandali." A common biblical metaphor for something that causes people to trip or be "scandalized" because it does not fit their expectations of God.</note> and who, through the unbelief of their minds and the hardness of an obstinate soul, refused to believe in Him. But He is for the resurrection of those who embraced His doctrine and kept His commands; through these, they were raised from the lowest pit <note>original: "barathro." A term often used to describe a deep abyss or the depths of ruin.</note> of damnation to the peak of virtues, and finally to the height of heaven.

The Lord offers the same sentiment in this place, saying that He has come into this world for judgment—not indeed for condemnation or the final retribution, which is reserved for the end of the age, but for the discernment <note>original: "discretionis." Here meaning the ability to distinguish or separate one group from another.</note> of the good from the wicked, and believers from the unbelieving. He came so that those who do not see might see: that is, those who realize they do not see and seek to see may be enlightened by an inner light and led to the knowledge of faith and truth. For the simple and humble, confessing and acknowledging their own ignorance, are illuminated by Christ.

And He came so that those who see might become blind: that is, so that those who think they see and do not seek a physician to enlighten them—even though they dwell in great blindness—might remain in their unbelief and in the darkness of their errors. Such were the proud "wise men" <margin>Isaiah 5</margin> and the Pharisees, who were wise in their own eyes <margin>Romans 1</margin> and prudent in their own conceit. Truly, as Paul says, "claiming to be wise, they became fools; they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened."

And these words of the Lord clearly show us how much weight it carries toward virtue and toward deserving divine gifts to think humbly of oneself, to know one's own fragility, and to confess one's weakness. This clearly humble <margin>Humility is most fitting for the perception of divine grace.</margin> estimation of oneself and the confession of one's own neediness abundantly obtains the bounty of divine grace and impetrates <note>term: impetrate. To obtain something through a formal request or prayer.</note> heavenly help. On the contrary, those who think something grand and sublime of themselves, and extol themselves above themselves, arrogating more than is actually in them, are left dry and destitute of divine protection, unworthy and needy of all good things. The Prophet teaches us this, <margin>Psalm 130</margin> <note>Psalm 131 in modern numbering.</note> saying: "Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes raised up: neither have I walked in great matters, nor in wonders above me. If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul, like a child weaned upon its mother, so is the retribution in my soul."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on John 9, specifically interpreting Jesus's statement about coming for "judgment." It explains the paradox of spiritual sight and blindness, using the metaphor of a physician, before concluding Book 6 and beginning Book 7, which covers the parable of the Good Shepherd in John 10.</meta>

342 ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

Even though the primary cause of the Lord’s coming into the world was that those who do not see might see—since He Himself is the primary source and author of internal enlightenment—He must not, however, be thought to have come so that those who see should become blind. Darkness cannot proceed from Him in any way; rather, what followed His arrival was that those who imagined they saw became even more blind. This did not happen by the nature of the Light itself (which by its own nature illuminates), but rather through the hardening of the hearts of the wicked.

Consider a most skilled physician who gives instructions to all his patients on how to recover their former health. Those who obey the physician are restored to safety; but those who refuse to follow the habits of the one giving sound advice grow sicker and are eventually consumed. In such a case, that physician would rightly say he came to bestow the benefit of health upon everyone, yet by his arrival it happened that many became worse and exchanged life for death. No one of sound mind, however, would attribute their death to the fault of the physician, but rather to the lack of self-control <note>original: "incontinentiæ"</note> of the patients, who, by indulging their own whims, neglected the life-saving instructions given to them.

It is a very frequent custom of Holy Scripture to express things that happened as an eventual result or consequence as if they were intended by a cause, even though no actual reason for the cause exists there. As this Evangelist says in another place: *But though he had done so many signs before them, yet they believed not on him: that the saying of Isaiah might be fulfilled, which he spoke: "Lord, who has believed our report? and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?"* <margin>John 12.</margin> <margin>Isaiah 53.</margin> Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah had foretold it. Again, in another place: *But now they have both seen and hated both me and my father: but this happened that the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law: "They hated me without a cause."* <margin>John 15.</margin> <margin>Psalm 68.</margin> In these and similar passages of Scripture, the prediction and announcement made by the Prophet is not denoted as being the *cause* of the unbelief and hatred of the Jews; rather, because they were blinded and hardened of their own will, it followed that the testimonies of the prophets—which predicted this very blindness and hardening—were fulfilled and completed in them.

Furthermore, some of the Pharisees, suspecting that those words of the Lord were spoken because of them—specifically that "those who see might become blind"—asked with pride and indignation: "Are we also blind?" For they took it poorly and were annoyed that they themselves were marked by the shame of blindness in those words, since they considered themselves to see with the mind more sharply and perceptively than others. 

But it is worthwhile to hear what the Lord replied to those boasting of their mental perception and failing to recognize their own blindness: "If you were blind," He said, "you would not have sin." That is to say: if you called yourselves blind and turned to the physician so that He might drive away this blindness, you would be free from sin and worthy to be enlightened by the physician. "But now because you say, 'We see,' your sin remains." This means: because you imagine that you see, and refuse to implore the help of the physician, you are bound by a heavier offense

<column-break/>

ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 343

and labor under a greater burden of sins.

Indeed, there was a double evil in them: first, that they were held by a most heavy blindness, not recognizing the true Light that radiated among them with the splendor of signs; and second, that they did not weigh this great blindness of theirs, but persuaded themselves that they were most sharp-sighted and enlightened beyond others in the grace of knowledge. Thus, they were very similar to those suffering from a frenzy <note>original: "phreneticis," referring to those in a state of delirium or mental agitation</note> who, when they are gripped by a most serious disease and are clearly raving, do not recognize their own illness, but persuade themselves—and assert in words to others—that they are sound in mind and body. 

It would likewise not be unsuitable to interpret these final words of the Lord according to another meaning: namely, "if you were blind," meaning ignorant of the scriptures that speak clearly about my coming and works, a sin so heavy would by no means weigh upon you, as you would be sinning through ignorance and would have some excuse for that reason. But now, because you assert that you are wise and experts in the law, you are condemnable by your own selves, because no excuse through ignorance can be held out for you. 

But even those who have received the talent of understanding the scriptures from the Lord must greatly fear lest that talent, if improperly managed, should provide the material for heavier sin and damnation. For to whom much has been communicated, much will be required from him <margin>Luke 12.</margin>; and a person is guilty of a crime that much greater the more gifts he has received which he misuses, or the more he performs his duty wrongly, or the more <margin>John 14.</margin> he knows what ought to be done and neglects to do it.

THE END OF BOOK SIX.

The Seventh Book on Cyril’s Commentary on John, added by Jodocus Clichtoveus. <note>Jodocus Clichtoveus (1472–1543) was a Flemish theologian who completed or edited several patristic commentaries.</note>

### CHAPTER I.

**A**MEN, amen, I say to you, he who does not enter by the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up another way, the same is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. To him the doorkeeper opens; and the sheep hear his voice. <margin>John chapter ten</margin> 

Because the Pharisees were boasting that they saw—which they indeed could have done if they were Christ's sheep—the Lord, against their arrogance, proposes a comparison about his flock and about the door by which one enters the fold. He shows that neither wisdom, nor observance of the law, nor a good life is worth anything except through Him, through whom alone entry and access to salvation is given, just as He says in another place: "No one comes to the Father except through me." <margin>John 14.</margin> Therefore, in this proverb <note>or "parable"</note> He proposes four main things: the door, the sheepfold, the thief, and the shepherd. By "the door," He intends Himself to be understood, as He declares later. By "the sheepfold," He designates the Catholic Church and the fellowship of the faithful, into which no one enters rightly except through Christ.

By **the thief and the robber**, we must understand the one who either does not think rightly about Christ, or who seeks his own glory rather than God’s; such a person infects and undermines the sheep with pestilential doctrine <note>original: "pestifero dogmate"</note> or ruinous behavior. For indeed, it is the nature of a thief not to enter the sheepfold through the door, but to climb up by some other way: such as by scaling the stone wall <note>original: "maceriam"</note> or preparing an entrance for himself by breaking through the wall, so that he may steal what belongs to others. Those who wish to enter the church not through Christ, but by any other way whatsoever, are just like him.

### [Page 350]

350 

<margin>Acts 5</margin> ...[forbade the people] from paying taxes to Caesar, asserting that they should acknowledge no Lord but God alone. These men, therefore, are the **thieves and robbers**; they did not enter through the **door**, which is Christ, but climbed in by another way—that is, led by their own pride and a thirst for worldly glory.

For this reason, the **sheep**—that is, the elect of God—did not listen to them. For even if some were momentarily led astray by their deceptions, they were never drawn away into eternal destruction, because the Father’s hand protects those who truly belong to the flock.

**I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; and he will go in and go out and find pasture.** <note>John 10:9</note>

In this passage, Christ explains the three-fold benefit granted to those who enter through Him:

First, **he will be saved** <note>original: "saluabitur"</note>, meaning he is rescued from the power of the devil, the sting of sin, and the sentence of eternal death. 

Second, **he will go in and go out**. <note>original: "ingredietur et egredietur"</note> This suggests a life of spiritual freedom and security. He "goes in" to the secret places of the heart to find rest in grace through faith, and "goes out" into the world to perform good works and exercise charity. Some also interpret this as "going in" to contemplation and "going out" to action. 

Third, **he will find pasture**. <note>original: "pascua inueniet"</note> Just as a physical sheep needs grass to live, the soul finds its nourishment in the Word of God and the hope of eternal happiness. This pasture is found both in this life, through the scriptures, and in the life to come, where the thirst of the soul is fully satisfied.

**The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy.** <note>John 10:10</note> The false teacher or "thief" seeks only his own profit, feeding himself rather than the flock, and ultimately leading souls to ruin. 

**I have come that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.** <note>original: "ego ueni ut uitam habeant, et abundantius habeant"</note> Christ did not come for His own gain, but to give. This **abundance** refers to the overflowing richness of the Holy Spirit and the gift of eternal life, which far exceeds the mere earthly promises of the false prophets.

<summary>This page concludes the historical warning against false messiahs like Judas the Galilean and provides a detailed commentary on Christ as the "Door," emphasizing the salvation, freedom, and spiritual nourishment found in Him.</summary>

<margin>Scripture's testimony against wicked shepherds. Ezekiel 34</margin> ...lest he lose what he loves. The Lord truly complains bitterly through Ezekiel about such hirelings who seek their own advantage and are shepherds in name only, saying: "You ate the milk, and clothed yourselves with the wool; you killed what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen what was weak, nor did you heal what was sick. You did not bind what was broken, nor did you bring back what was cast away. You did not seek what was lost. These words of the prophet must be explained one by one with a clearer light. Idle shepherds indeed "eat the milk," "clothe themselves with the wool," and "kill what is fat" when they seize the goods of their subjects for their own food, dress themselves in a variety of garments woven from the fleeces of their sheep, and claim all the best things of those under them for their own use. For they seek "their own interests" (as Paul says) "not those of Jesus Christ." <margin>Philippians 2</margin> Shepherds do not "strengthen what is weak" and do not "heal what is sick" when they do not bolster those prone to vice with words of encouragement, nor do they call those who have fallen into spiritual sickness back to health through penance. They do not "bind what is broken" when they do not restore those who have fallen from a life of integrity into deadly sin through proper correction. They do not "bring back what was cast away" when they do not convert back to the purity of doctrine those led away from the truth of the faith by grave error or the heretical plague <note>The author uses "heretical plague" to describe the rapid and "contagious" spread of dissenting religious ideas during the Reformation period.</note>. They do not "seek what was lost" when they do not restore those turned away from God in despair to the hope of salvation by promising pardon through God’s mercy. The sheep were scattered because there is no shepherd: this happens when subordinates wander through the steep cliffs of vice because of a lack of right guidance and teaching from their leaders. The sheep became "food for all the beasts of the field" when they were subjected to the yoke and slavery of unclean spirits, who receive power over humans as they wander and stray through the pathless ways of vice. The flocks were scattered "over the whole face of the earth" when they seek earthly rather than heavenly goods, gasping for works and fleeting riches because they are not warned to "seek the things that are above." There is no one to search for the scattered flocks because shepherds who seek their own pleasures or comforts do not care about the losses of the Lord's flock, nor are they moved by any zeal or desire for the salvation of the souls of their subordinates. They give little thought to how great a price was paid for them, for they were redeemed "not with corruptible gold or silver, but with the precious blood of the spotless lamb." <margin>1 Peter 1</margin> The Lord also threatens such shepherds through Jeremiah, saying: <margin>Jeremiah 23</margin> "Woe to the shepherds who scatter and tear apart the flock of my pasture, says the Lord. Therefore, thus says the Lord God of Israel to the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock

### CHAPTER VI.

**I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and my sheep know me. Just as the Father knows me, and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for my sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they will hear my voice; and there will be one fold and one shepherd.** The Lord demonstrates that He is the good shepherd by a two-fold proof and argument. First, that He knows His sheep, choosing and foreseeing them for eternal life; just as the Apostle says: <margin>Romans 8</margin> "The Lord has not rejected His people, whom He foreknew." For just as the Lord is said not to "know" those whom He rejects—as He says to the foolish virgins, <margin>Matthew 25</margin> "Amen I say to you, I do not know you"—so He is rightly judged to "know" those whom He predestines and preordains for salvation. And by a reciprocal and mutual recognition, the sheep of Christ recognize Him because they love Him and obey His commands. Truly, he who does not believe in the Lord or despises His commands is said to be ignorant of the Lord and not to know Him. Just as the hardened Pharaoh answered Moses: <margin>Exodus 5</margin> "I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go." By a reversed and retrospective way of speaking, those who keep His faith unshaken and observe His commands are rightly said to know Him. Next, so that you do not think the measure of knowledge between Christ and the sheep is equal, He consequently adds: "Just as the Father knows me, and I know the Father." The Son indeed knows the Father with a divine, immense, and (to humans) inexplicable knowledge, because He is the wisdom of the Father. And by that same notion entirely, the Father knows the Son as the radiance <margin>Hebrews 1</margin> shining forth from Himself, as the character <note>original: "characterem" — used here in the theological sense of an exact imprint or "the express image" of God's person, as in Hebrews 1:3.</note> and image of His substance, as the word co-eternal with Himself. But the sheep do not know Christ, nor His Father, in that specific kind of knowledge, because <margin>John 1</margin> "no one has ever seen God; but the only-begotten [Son], who is in the bosom of the Father, He has made Him known." <margin>Matthew 11</margin> Also, "no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." And as He testifies in another place: <margin>John 6</margin> "Not that anyone has seen the Father except He who is from God; He has seen the Father." Since, therefore, the Son knows the Father and the Father knows the Son with an entirely similar knowledge, who of sound mind would call the Son inferior to the Father, or imperfe—

The Psalmist, enlightened by the divine spirit, mentions this stone: <margin>Psalm 117. Ephesians 2</margin> The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. And blessed Paul says of Christ: He is our peace, who has made both one. Indeed, he made both one because he connected the Jews and Gentiles into one confession of faith and one fold.

...cept to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. <margin>Matthew 15:24</margin> <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "Although... he had not been sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."</note> However, because the labor of Christ was not so restricted that it would not also benefit the nations of the world, he immediately adds: **“And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold.”** <margin>John 10:16</margin>

By this <term>fold<note>The Latin *ovile* refers to an enclosure for sheep. In this theological context, it symbolizes the specific religious and legal boundary of the Jewish people under the Mosaic Law.</note></term>, he refers to the people of the Jews, who were kept within the "fences" of the Law and the specific ceremonies of the Old Testament. The **“other sheep”** are the Gentiles, who at that time lived outside those boundaries, wandering without the guidance of the Law. Christ shows here that his power as a Shepherd is not confined to one nation alone, but extends to the whole world.

**“I must bring them also,”** he says. This "must" does not imply a necessity forced upon him by another, but rather the "necessity" of his own divine plan and his burning desire for our salvation. He does not say "I will send someone else," but "I must bring them," showing that he is the primary actor in the conversion of the world. **“And they will hear my voice.”** <note>original: "vocem meam audient"</note> This is a mark of the true sheep: they recognize and obey the call of Christ through the Gospel, distinguishing it from the "voice" of false teachers.

The result of this gathering is the ultimate unity of the faithful: **“And there shall be one flock and one shepherd.”** <note>original: "fiet unus grex, unus pastor"</note> He does not say there will be "one fold," but "one flock." <note>A subtle but important distinction in the Latin text: the "fold" (enclosure) of the Jewish Law is gone, replaced by a single "flock" (the people) united by their one Shepherd, Christ, regardless of their ethnic origin.</note> Thus, the distinction between Jew and Gentile is abolished, and all are made one in Christ.

<margin>John 10:17</margin> **“For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it up again.”** Here, the Lord reveals the profound relationship between his sacrifice and the Father's love. The Father does not love the Son because of the death itself, but he loves the Son’s perfect obedience and his voluntary devotion to the safety of the sheep. 

**“No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.”** <margin>John 10:18</margin> This is a crucial point for the reader: Christ was not a helpless victim of the Jews or the Romans. He possessed the divine power to avoid death, yet he chose to submit to it. He describes this as a **“command”** <note>original: "mandatum"</note> received from the Father, emphasizing that the entire plan of the cross was not a tragedy of human history, but the fulfillment of a divine decree for the redemption of mankind.

...by dismissing them, he would take it away, and render them anxious and tormented—he who had come for this very purpose: to save the souls of those believing in him. **“If you are the Christ,”** they said, **“tell us plainly.”** The Jews believed that the Christ <note>original: *Christum*. Meaning the Messiah or "Anointed One."</note> would be merely a pure man, a king who would come in the manner of earthly princes, more excellent than the rest. Their descendants falsely persuade themselves of this even to the present day. For they thought the kingdom promised to Christ by the prophets ought to be only temporary and worldly, like other kingdoms, since they read in Jeremiah: *And a king shall reign, and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice.* <margin>Jeremiah 23</margin> And in the Psalm: *But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, preaching his commandment.* <margin>Psalm 2</margin> Yet a kingdom of this kind is not found in outward power or worldly dominion, in armor, the conscription of armies of warriors, or the enlistment of attendants. In this kingdom, once the prince of this world <note>A common title for the Devil.</note> has been cast out, Christ was to reign in the souls of the faithful throughout the whole circuit of the world. They wanted, therefore, by this fraudulent questioning, for the Lord to say he was the Christ, so that they might hand him over to the protections of the [Roman] power to be punished, as if he were rebelling against the Roman Caesar and usurping a kingdom for himself against the decrees of the Romans (to whom the Jews were taxpayers). 

For this reason, the Lord directed his response so prudently and temperately that he blocked their path to slander, yet revealed with an open voice to future believers that he himself is the Christ. For he answered them, saying: **“I speak to you, and you do not believe.”** My words, he says, openly testify that I have been sent by the Father and that I am the true Christ; but because of the hardness of your heart, you do not apply faith to my words. Furthermore, the works that I do in the name of my Father—giving light to the blind, healing the paralytics, curing the demon-possessed, and calling the dead back to life—those bear witness of me, that I am the true Son of God and the Christ promised by the Law and the Prophets. ### **That Christ, as the Son of God, is one with the Father not only by consent of will, but also by <term>consubstantiality<note>original: *consubstantialitate*. ### **CHAPTER 10.**

**“But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: and I give them eternal life, and they shall not perish forever, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all. I and the Father are one.”** The reason why the Jews do not believe his words and works, Christ adds: because they are not of his sheep, nor of the number of those who were foreseen for eternal life, but are instead addicted to perpetual perdition. And lest he should seem to have said this without cause or reason, he sets forth a manifest sign by which his sheep are discerned from those who do not belong to him. My sheep, he says, **“hear my voice,”** embracing, of course, a sincere faith and obeying my commands; **“and I know them,”** by a free election to eternal life; **“and they follow me,”** namely, by the imitation of good works and the attainment of blessedness. The Lord calls the faithful and those who obey him his sheep, who love and follow him as their shepherd, and who arrive at the pastures of eternal satisfaction by following the footsteps of the Good Shepherd. 

Therefore, he said that those who were unwilling to believe in him were not of his sheep: because he saw that they were already prepared for eternal destruction, and were not to be purchased for perpetual life by the price of his blood. But the Lord affirms that he gives eternal life to his sheep—namely, the most fertile pastures, flowing with an abundance of all good things, where there is the clearest light, secure peace, sweetest rest, and perpetual glory. **“And they shall not perish forever”**: because their shepherd and savior is such that nothing at all can perish in his care. To be sure, the holy martyrs seemed to perish when they lost this mortal life through torments; but they shall not perish forever, because, being loosed from the bonds of the flesh, they received the rewards due to them from Christ, just as the Sage says: *In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to die, but they are in peace.* <margin>Wisdom 3</margin> The souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of malice shall not touch them. **“And no one shall snatch them out of my hand,”** that is, out of my power, says the Lord. For those whom Christ has once taken up by predestination, no force of the devil’s temptation, nor any cruelty of human persecution, can take away from his strength and his side. But did not Judas (someone might say) perish forever? Was he not snatched by Satan from the hand of the Lord? And do not many walk the way of the Lord, from which they eventually fall away? In truth, only those who persevere in good until the end are, and are called, the sheep of the Lord. Therefore, those who perish from the number of Christ’s sheep after having received grace were certainly not sheep in the eyes of God; wherefore neither Judas nor others who turn back belonged to the fold of Christ.

For they were thinking most foolishly about his death, since they could not only do nothing against him if he were unwilling, but they also lacked the power to take anyone away from his followers. But lest by saying these things he should seem to seek his own glory, he refers all this power to the Father, adding: **“What my Father has given to me is greater than all.”** This clearly means that what God the Father gave to the mediator between God and men <note>Referencing 1 Timothy 2:5</note> is that he should be his only-begotten Son: God from God, neither different in nature, nor inferior in power, nor later in duration. And he gave this by begetting him: because the true God begat the true God, eternal light begat co-eternal light, and life begat life. This indeed is that which is greater than all, because it exceeds every creature, both human and angelic. And no one can snatch that which the Father gave me from my Father's hand: because since he himself is of immeasurable power, no violence can be inflicted upon him by anyone. Previously, the Lord indeed said, **“No one will snatch them from my hand,”** but here he says, **“No one can snatch them from my Father’s hand,”** so that we might clearly understand that his power and the Father’s are exactly the same (for he himself is the hand and power of the Father). We should believe without doubt that this very one is Christ, who did not receive grace for a temporary time as other saints do, but has always existed as the true Son of God. He also shows this in the following sentence, when he says: **“I and the Father are one.”** He says, **“We are one”**: one essence, one divinity, one equality. By these words, he not only resolved the question of the Jews—who were testing him by asking if he were the Christ—but he also showed how detestable is the madness of the heretics whom he foresaw in the future. Listen to both "one" <note>original: "unum" (neuter), implying one substance.</note> and "we are" <note>original: "sumus" (plural), implying distinct persons.</note>, and you will be delivered from both Charybdis and Scylla <note>A classical metaphor for two equal dangers on either side of a narrow passage.</note>. The fact that he said "one" delivers you from Arius <note>Arius taught that the Son was a created being, separate from the Father's substance.</note>, who separates the Son from the substance of the Father. The fact that he said "we are" delivers you from Sabellius <note>Sabellius taught that the Father and Son were not distinct persons, but merely different names or "modes" of one person.</note>, who confuses the person of the Father and the Son without distinction. If they are "one," then they are not different; if "we are," then there is both a Father and a Son. But the impiety of both of these was abundantly refuted at the beginning of the first book. Yet because the heretics cannot deny these words of the Lord, <margin>Objections of the adversaries and their solutions.</margin> they corrupt them with the falsehood of their own impiety and an absurd explanation. For they try to refer this to a consensus of unanimity: suggesting that there is a unity of *will* in the Father and the Son, but not of *nature*. That is, they claim they are "one" not because of what they *are*, but because they *will* the same thing. But through the birth of nature (since God, by begetting God from himself, does not degenerate), they are in truth one. And while they are not snatched from the hand of the Son, they are not snatched from the hand of the Father. <margin>John 14</margin> While the Father works in the working Son, while he is in the Father and the Father is in him, this is not granted by a created status, but by birth; it is not produced by will, but by power; it is not unanimity speaking, but nature. We do not deny the unanimity of will between the Father and the Son. For the heretics are accustomed to lie about this: that when we do not look to mere concord as the only source of unity, they claim we are affirming that they are in discord. But let them hear that we do not deny unanimity,

but beyond that, the Father and Son are one by nature, honor, and power; nor can the same nature want diverse things. But the adversaries of truth raise a cavil <note>A trivial or deceptive objection.</note> again from the fact that Christ, praying to the Father for his disciples, said: **“Holy Father, keep them in your name, those whom you have given me, so that they may be one, just as we are.”** <margin>John 17</margin> <margin>Isaiah 66</margin> And yet the disciples cannot be "one" except by a conspiracy of will and concord; for they cannot coincide into one single number and the same substance. Therefore, they argue, neither are the Father and Son one by identity of substance and nature. However, since they seek to cast slurs rather than to clarify the truth, they completely subvert the correct sense of the scripture. For it is false that the disciples cannot be one with God except by concord of will. For above that is their unity with God through a certain conformity of deity and "deiformity," <note>original: "deiformitatem" - the process of being made like God.</note> by which, a participation in divinity having been communicated to them, they pass into and are transferred into God (so to speak), while the truth of their own nature is preserved. It is just as when iron is fired and glowing: through the communion of the fire, it becomes fire-shaped, and with the substance of the iron seemingly removed, it appears to be entirely fire. And by this kind of union—which is far superior and more sublime than union through love and concord of wills—our Lord asks that the disciples be one in God: namely, that they may be grafted into him and intimately joined through the reception and participation of the deity within themselves. This union, moreover, comes closest to that supreme and ineffable union by which the Father and the Son, mutually permeating each other <note>original: "immeantes"</note> and intimately remaining within each other, are one by unity of nature. This is indeed the supreme unity and the truest of all, and Christ here asks for a close assimilation of this to be given to the disciples through their grafting into God. But come, let us demonstrate from the nature of things that the Son is of one and the same substance with the Father. For we see that which is proper...

Then he inquires exactly where Lazarus has been placed, not because he was ignorant of the place of his burial. For he who, while absent, knew the man had died, also knows where he is buried; nor was he unaware of where he had been placed, whom he intended to raise up. Rather, he asks because he does not wish to thrust himself forward to perform the miracle, but prefers to learn everything from others, to act upon being asked, and to be informed of those things which occurred in his absence, so that he might strip the sign <note>The "sign" (signum) refers to the miracle itself, which serves as a proof of his divinity.</note> of any suspicion. Therefore, to demonstrate that Lazarus had indeed died while he was away and had been committed to the earth, he seeks the location of his tomb from others. Finally, the Lord also wept, because he was the fount of piety <note>original: "pietatis," meaning here compassion or dutiful love.</note>; but those tears were destined to give birth to inexplicable joy. For the Lord wept for him according to his human nature, whom he was about to raise by the power of his divinity. The Lord also instructs us by his tears how we ought to mourn our deceased loved ones with moderate tears, tempered by the law of reason. For to feel no compassion or sorrow at all is beastly and harsh; yet an excess of these is womanish <note>The author reflects common Renaissance/Early Modern views on the "Golden Mean" of emotion, citing the Stoic-influenced idea that grief should be balanced.</note>. The book of Sirach <note>original: "Ecclesiasticus"</note> also admonishes us, saying: **Weep over the dead, for his light has failed.** <margin>Sirach 22</margin> **Weep but a little over the dead, because he is at rest; the mourning for the dead lasts seven days.** <margin>Sirach 38</margin> And the same author says in another place: **My son, shed tears over the dead, and begin to wail as one who has suffered dreadfully.** For this reason, Scripture has left it carefully noted that after Aaron died on the peak of Mount Hor, the entire multitude of the people of Israel, seeing that Aaron had fallen, wept over him for thirty days throughout all their families. <margin>Numbers 20</margin> Also, when Moses died in the plains of Moab, the children of Israel wept for him for thirty days. <margin>Deuteronomy 34</margin> Finally, when Judith, that most esteemed widow and courageous slayer of Holofernes, had completed the course of her life, all the people mourned her for seven days. <margin>Judith 17</margin> Truly, such mourning ought to be moderate and tempered by the right law of reason, and not excessively beyond what is just, lest it appear to be evidence in us of faithlessness or a lack of belief in the immortality of the soul or the future resurrection of the flesh. For when we waste away with heavy grief because a friend has been taken from us by death, and we indulge in tears alone, we seem to grieve either as if his soul perished along with the body and did not remain surviving after the dissolution of the flesh, or as if it were never again to be joined to the body at the end of the age. Consequently, we bewail it as though it were a perpetual separation from our friend, as if we were never to see him thereafter. But the blessed Paul restrained this impious thought, writing thus to the Thessalonians: **We do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who are asleep, so that you do not grieve like the rest who have no hope.** <margin>1 Thessalonians 4</margin> Furthermore, how can we pray to God daily with a sincere heart, **Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven**, <margin>Matthew 6</margin> if, with sighs drawn from the depths of our chest and a great flood of tears, we bewail a friend snatched away from us? Shall we not be judged to contradict God in some way, and to bear with an unjust mind that which is the good pleasure of his will, as if struggling and opposing him in our hearts? Therefore, it is altogether to be feared lest we provoke divine

wrath against ourselves by so obstinately refusing that which he, who holds command over life and death, has determined should be done. Moreover, it is not the work of a prudent and mature man to bewail with constant grief one who cannot be recalled to life by tears, nor rescued from the tomb by weeping; for that would be to waste labor in vain upon that which cannot be recovered or changed. Considering this prudently within himself, David, when he learned that his son was dead—for whom, while he was still living, he had severely afflicted himself with fasting and weeping—laid aside his mourning and ordered food to be set before him and he ate. <margin>2 Samuel 12</margin> When his servants wondered at this, he answered: **While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept. For I said: Who knows whether the Lord may perhaps grant him to me, and the infant may live? But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him instead, but he will not return to me.** We ought to set before ourselves this prudence of the excellent King David for imitation, and define mourning itself by moderation.

CHAPTER XXI.
The Jews therefore said: **Behold how he loved him.** But some of them said: **Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the one born blind, have caused this man not to die?** Jesus therefore, again groaning <note>original: "fremens," often translated as "deeply moved" or "troubled in spirit."</note> within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it. Jesus said: **Take away the stone.** Martha, the sister of him who had died, said to him: **Lord, he stinks by now, for he has been there four days.** Jesus said to her: **Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?** They therefore took away the stone. It is the custom for humans to mourn the dead whom they previously held dear and were joined to by love. According to this custom, the Jews thought the Lord was weeping, saying: **Behold how he loved him.** Yet he was instead bewailing the human misery of the world, which is subject to the slavery of harsh death; and he was weeping for the sad lot of Lazarus, who had to be recalled to this mortal life full of misery and sorrows. Others, however, who were rivals and enemies of Christ, immediately turned to disparagement and speaking against his almighty power. From the very things for which they ought to have admired his power—namely, the healing of the man born blind—they find a reason to revile him. For they ascribe it to the powerlessness of Christ that Lazarus had died, as if he were not strong enough to preserve him from death. Although the Lord could indeed have done this, he permitted Lazarus to die so that he might be raised by a greater miracle. Just as when the Lord was nailed to the cross, those blaspheming said: **He saved others; himself he cannot save. whereby he accomplished what was more conducive and useful for our salvation. In this, these detractors also show themselves to be corrupted in their judgment of mind, because even before Christ arrives at the tomb, they take up accusations, not waiting for the end of the matter, which is far more wonderful than the preservation of a sick man from death. For it is a greater thing to raise a man dead for four days than to keep a suffering man from dying; therefore, why would he who could do the former not be able to do the latter? Then Jesus **groaned** again in himself, expressing the indignation of his soul with this second groan at the malice and wickedness of the Jews, who did not cease to constantly slander his works and gnaw and bite at them with a <term>dog-like tooth</term> <note>original: "canino dente." A classical idiom for a biting, cynical, or viciously critical person.</note>. Yet let no one believe that this groaning of Christ, or any other passion in him, occurred with a precipitation of mind or an unbridled impulse, but rather with the greatest tranquility and a calm moderation of mind, always directed by right reason: for in him was the most orderly harmony of all powers. Nor did those passions in Christ precede reason by their own movement or anticipate it—as they do in us—but they followed it, being stirred by the will and reason. Consequently, when and how he willed, he was affected by them. Indeed, the Evangelist frequently and studiously records that he groaned and that he wept, so that you might learn more clearly and openly that he truly put on our human nature. For because this Evangelist <note>John</note> speaks more of his great and divine nature than the others do, he also speaks of the more humble things regarding his physical reality. Finally, so that the resurrection of the dead man might be more obvious to the eyes and more conspicuous, the Lord ordered the stone to be lifted. But why (someone might ask) did he not raise him while the stone was still in place? Could he who moved a dead body with his voice not even more easily move a stone? He did not do this, however, so that he might make those present witnesses of the miracle, so that they could not say—as they had said of the blind man—**This is not he.**
<margin>John 9</margin> For their own hands and their access to the tomb testified that it was indeed Lazarus. But Martha wished to prevent the removal of the stone, saying: **Lord, by this time he stinks, for he has been dead four days.** She says this as if distrusting, as if believing it impossible for her brother to be raised because of the length of time passed; or, out of a sincere affection of mind, she feared for the Lord himself, lest by removing the stone, he might be offended by the heavy odor of the corpse; therefore, by leaving the stone in its place, she was perhaps asking for her brother to be raised in a way that the bystanders would not be harmed by the foul smell of the buried man. But the Lord—as if she had forgotten those things she had heard from him a little while before, namely that he is the resurrection and the life—strengthens her in her faith: calling those things back to her memory and promising that, even if stubborn cruelty were present, she would behold the glory of God in the remarkable novelty of this miracle.

He did not need prayers, but he prayed for our sake so that the Son would not be ignored. He also cried out more loudly to restrain the mouths of the pagans, who tell fables that the souls of the departed remain in their tombs: for as if she <note>The author refers to the soul, which is feminine in Latin (*anima*).</note> were waiting outside, he summons her by a shout. Here meaning the realm of the dead.</note> lay open and unlocked. All the dead were waiting for their names to be called. Finally, when one was called by name, the others were held back.
