Finally, the Lord did not say, "Arise," but "Come out": so that speaking to the one who had been dead as a living man—not as if he were dead, but as if healthy, as if living, as if ready to hear—he called him from the tomb: because all things live for Christ <margin>Luke 10 <note>This likely refers to Luke 20:38, "for all live to him," though the marginal note in the source text cites chapter 10.</note></margin>. Nor did the Lord say, "In the name of my Father, come out," or "Father, resurrect him." But setting all these things aside, after he had taken the form of one praying, he showed his authority through the deed itself: since it belongs to his wisdom to show condescension through words, but to demonstrate power through deeds.

**CHAPTER XXIII.**

**E**T immediately he who had been dead came forth, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face was wrapped with a shroud. Jesus said to them: Untie him, and let him go. Many of the Jews, therefore, who had come to Mary and Martha and had seen what Jesus did, believed in him. Just as the universal resurrection of the dead will be completed in the twinkling of an eye—as the Apostle says: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin>—so also this singular resurrection was accomplished: for immediately and without hesitation, he who had been dead came forth, without retardation or delay. Moreover, he came out bound, so that he would not be thought to be a phantom <note>original: *phantasma*. A spirit or ghostly apparition without a physical body.</note>. The Lord ordered him to be untied so that, evidently, those touching him and approaching him might see that it was truly he. ## CHAPTER II.

**O**ne of them, named Caiaphas, being the high priest of that year, said to them: "You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, so that the whole nation does not perish.") While the other Pharisees hesitated on what ought to be done and proposed their opinions in the order of the council, Caiaphas—more impudent and shameless than the rest, and shouting with irritation—rebuked the others for their ignorance and sluggishness. He complained that they did not see as quickly as was necessary what needed to be done, just as he himself seemed to have foreseen it. However, a question arises in this place that should not be passed over lightly: how is Caiaphas called the "High Priest of that year," when the Lord had commanded through the law <margin>Exodus 28</margin> that there should be only one High Priest, and upon his death, his son should succeed him and administer the priesthood in his father's place? But the answer must be given that, at that time, the law of the Lord was not observed among them; it had been abolished through the ambition of the Jews and the greed of the Romans, who now sold the high priesthood every single year for money. Therefore, in that time, the high priesthood lasted only for a year, and when the year’s course was finished, another succeeded who had purchased the high priestly dignity for himself with money. Indeed, reliable historians report concerning this Caiaphas that he redeemed the priesthood for himself for one year at a price paid to Herod. It is not difficult to discover from the history of the Maccabees <margin>2 Maccabees 4</margin> that this corruption of morals had crept into the synagogue even then, where several men are recorded to have competed for the high priesthood by giving a great sum of money. When the Evangelist refers to Caiaphas being the "High Priest of that year," he clearly demonstrates the magnitude of his impiety and the gravity of his crime. For because he surpassed the others in priestly dignity and authority, he ought to have shone with greater piety and religious devotion toward God, so that he might be an example to others in cultivating virtue and keeping the divine commands. He, however, being more cruel than the rest, more headlong toward crime, and more ready for slaughter, urges the others—as if they were acting too slowly—to commit the deed, saying: "You know nothing, nor do you consider that it is expedient to neglect the safety of one man for the sake of the whole state <note>original: "republica," here referring to the Jewish nation as a political body</note>: since a private good must be secondary to the public, and the common good is to be preferred to the private and particular." He said this, however, with a depraved intention: wishing to lead that entire assembly to the opinion that it would be beneficial for the Jewish state to put Christ to death. He believed that if this death were carried out, the whole nation would be 

<column-break/>

391

free from the fear or incursion of the Romans; as if, if Christ were not killed by them, destruction from the Romans would hang over the Jews. But if He were killed, as they had pre-conceived and determined in their minds, the Jewish nation would be free from the death and ruin they feared was imminent from the Romans. Yet the matter turned out far differently than they had planned. For because of the death inflicted upon Christ by the Jews, the entire Jewish nation suffered a miserable extermination, captivity, death, and dispersion. This the Lord had predicted to them in these words: "And they shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led away captive into all nations." <margin>Luke 21</margin> And when He wept over the city of Jerusalem with holy tears, He said: "Because your enemies shall encircle you with a trench, and hem you in on every side, <margin>Luke 19</margin> and shall level you to the ground, and shall not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation." All these things predicted by the Lord have long since been proven by the actual outcome of events.

### The Preparation at Bethany

The **feast** <note>original: "festum"</note> had its **beginning** <note>original: "exordium"</note> on that **day** <note>original: "diem"</note> in **Bethany** <margin>John 12:1</margin>. **However** <note>original: "autem"</note>, a **banquet** <note>original: "convivium"</note> was prepared for him there. In this account, there are several points **to be observed** <note>original: "attendenda"</note> regarding how one is **to be devoted to** <note>original: "inserviendum"</note> Christ and the nature of the **ministry** <note>original: "ministerium"</note> or service performed for him. 

A great crowd **of the Jews** <note>original: "Iudæorum"</note> had gathered. <margin>Matthew 26. Mark 14.</margin>
**A** [The house] was filled with the **aroma** <note>original: "odore"</note>. Regarding the fact that the Evangelist calls the **ointment** <note>original: "unguentum"</note> **"pistic"** <note>original: "pisticum"; a rare term likely derived from the Greek "pistikos," meaning genuine or liquid</note>, we ought to believe either that it refers to a certain place from which this precious ointment was obtained, or it was called "pistic," meaning **pure** <note>original: "syncerum"</note> and **genuine** <note>original: "fidele"</note>, not adulterated with foreign substances. Since **"pistis"** <note>original: "pistis"</note> among the Greeks signifies **faith** <note>original: "fidem"</note>, it is rightly called "pistic" because it is sincere and not at all mixed or confused with things of another kind.

**B** However, because **Matthew** and **Mark** say in this supper at Bethany that the Lord's **head** <note>original: "caput"</note> was poured over with that ointment, while **John** in this passage says the **feet** <note>original: "pedes"</note>: let us understand that the woman poured it not only on the head, but also on the Lord's feet. John records the latter, while the other Evangelists record the former; nevertheless, none of them departs from the truth. Some ancient authors, distinguished for their great learning, thought and left in writing that the woman mentioned here by John was one person, and the one of whom Matthew and Mark speak—who poured the ointment over the Lord's head—was another. Truly, they do not seem to have paid enough attention to the fact that the circumstances of the anointing itself are the same here and there, from which it is discovered with no great effort that it is the same woman anointing, and likewise the same anointing. For the anointing described here by John was offered to the Lord in **Bethany**, a short time before his **passion** <note>original: "passione"; the suffering and death of Jesus</note>; similarly, that anointing recorded by Matthew and Mark is read to have been bestowed upon Christ at the same place and time. Again, just as in John, **Judas** is said to have grumbled because of that pouring out of ointment, so in Matthew and Mark the **disciples** are written to have taken the anointing with a bitter spirit and to have rebuked it with almost the same words. Finally, just as the Lord here in John commended the work of the woman anointing him and restrained the rising murmur with a reason, in a very similar way in Matthew and Mark, the woman's dutiful anointing is commended by the Lord, and the disciples' murmur is repressed with almost the same words. Nor does it stand in the way of this proposal that in John the woman anointing is named **Mary**, the sister of Lazarus, while in Matthew and Mark she is designated by the common name of "woman." For the very same woman can be expressed in different ways by different Evangelists—namely, by her proper name in this one, but in the others by only a general title. Indeed, no one would deny that the title of "woman" fits Mary the sister of Martha, and that she is included in that general term expressing her gender. Likewise, there have not been wanting writers who think this anointing of the Lord's feet recited here by John is the same as that which **Luke** describes in his seventh chapter. But these also have not considered with enough care the different circumstances and conditions of this anointing and that one, from which a wide distinction and <margin>Luke 7.</margin> difference is gathered between the two. Indeed, the anointing described in Luke is recorded to have been done in the middle of the Lord's time of preaching, nearly two years before the Lord's passion; whereas the one here in John was done a few days before Christ would suffer.

->EIGHT. 397<-

**A** Again, the anointing done in Luke was offered to Christ in **Galilee** (as is easily gathered from the Gospel) and in the house of **Simon the Pharisee**. But the one narrated by John in the present passage was performed in the village of **Bethany** in **Judea**, and in the house of **Simon the leper**, as Matthew and Mark testify. To this, in Luke, the woman anointing the Lord's feet first watered them with **tears** <note>original: "lachrymis"</note>, then wiped them, and finally anointed them. In John, however, in the present passage, no mention is made of tears, nor of a washing of Christ's feet performed with weeping, or a wiping after tears were poured over the Lord's sacred feet; he reports only the anointing of the feet and the wiping of them with her hair after the anointing was done.

**B** Finally, in the anointing narrated by Luke, only the **Pharisee** grumbled within himself, to whom Christ responded by proposing the **parable** <note>original: "paradigmate"</note> of the two debtors, and commended the woman's service bestowed upon him. But in that anointing of the Lord's feet which John describes here, **Judas** especially is said to have been indignant and to have rebuked that pouring out of ointment as if it were superfluous and done for luxury. Responding to him, the Lord said that the **poor** <note>original: "pauperes"</note> would not be lacking to those who wished to be kind to them, and he foretold that the memory of that deed would be celebrated forever to the <margin>Luke 7.</margin> glory of the woman who had performed that anointing. Lastly, to her who anointed the Lord's feet in Luke, it is written that many **sins** <note>original: "peccata"</note> were forgiven because she loved much, and her **faith** <note>original: "fides"</note> is proclaimed to have made her whole, and she was ordered to go in peace. In John, however, in the present passage, no mention is made of the sins of the woman who bestowed the anointing on the Lord, nor of salvation obtained through her faith, nor of a departure in peace; nor is such mentioned in Matthew and Mark when they describe the same anointing as John does here. Therefore, the anointing read in Luke is far different from the one here in John.

### CHAPTER VII.

But he said this, not because he cared for the needy, but because he was a **thief** <note>original: "fur"</note>, and having the money box, he carried what was put into it. Jesus therefore said: "Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you will always have with <margin>2 Corinthians 2.</margin> you, but me you will not always have." Our mind must be recalled to the words of the **Apostle** <note>referring to St. Paul</note>, who says: "To some the **aroma of life** <note>original: "odor uitae"</note> leads to life, to others the **aroma of death** <note>original: "odor mortis"</note> leads to death." And we shall hear concerning this ointment how it was a good aroma unto life for some, such as Mary; and for others an evil aroma unto death, namely for Judas, who rebuked the service performed for the Lord under the pretext of piety, and cloaked the most foul crime of his **avarice** <note>original: "auaritiæ"</note> <margin>Matthew 26.</margin> with the duty of showing care for the poor. ## THE TRIUMPHAL ENTRY INTO JERUSALEM
-> Matthew 21, Mark 11, Luke 19, John 12 <-

On the next day, a great multitude that had come for the feast day, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took up branches of palm trees and went out to meet him. They cried out:

-> **"Save us, we pray! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!"** <-

And Jesus found a young donkey and sat upon it, just as it is written in the prophets: *Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey’s colt.* <note>A quotation of the prophecy from Zechariah 9:9, emphasizing the peaceful nature of the King.</note>

<column-break/>

His disciples did not understand these things at the time; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and that they had performed these things for him. 

The crowd that had been present when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness to the miracle. It was for this very reason—the news of this great sign—that the people went out to meet him. The Pharisees, seeing this, said to one another: "Do you see that we are accomplishing nothing? Look, the whole world has gone after him!"

<margin>The significance of the palm branches</margin>
The palm branches carried by the people represent victory <note>original: "victoriam"</note>. In ancient times, it was the custom to welcome victors with palms. It was appropriate that he who was about to conquer death through his own death and triumph over the devil, the prince of death, should be received with the emblems of victory.

<margin>The donkey and the horse</margin>
Furthermore, he chose to sit upon a donkey rather than a horse. A horse is an animal used in war, but a donkey is a humble beast of burden. By this, he demonstrated his humility <note>original: "humilitatem"</note> and signaled that his kingdom is not of this world, nor does it rely on the violence of weapons, but on the peace of the spirit.

Previously, the demon held a princely rule through tyranny over the entire human race, and he exercised his cruel lordship over all. Far be it from us, however, to think that the devil is called "prince of the world" in such a way that we believe he could rule over heaven and earth. For he is not himself the author or governor of the world, as some falsely believe. <note>This likely refers to the Manichaean heresy, which claimed the physical world was created by an evil deity.</note> Instead, "this world" is used here to refer to wicked men who follow secular <note>original: "secularia," meaning worldly or temporal</note> desires and indulge their own cravings. <margin>C</margin> Satan is the prince of these people because he rules over them according to his will, and at his nod, he drives and thrusts them headlong into grave crimes. 

He, however, was to be cast out through Christ’s death. Why, then, was it said, "Now he shall be cast out," unless because what was done back then in only a very few men is now predicted to happen soon among many and great nations. 

What then, someone may ask: because the devil is cast out, does he no longer tempt any of the faithful? On the contrary, he does not cease to tempt them; <margin>D</margin> but it is one thing to reign from within, and another to attack from the outside. For an enemy excluded from the city walls does not cease to shake the walls with battering rams and engines of war <note>original: "machinis," referring to siege engines</note>, so that he may break an entrance for himself and prepare a way back in. ...is so cast out from the world that he no longer remains outside, or no longer persecutes, or no longer tempts the faithful. <margin>A</margin> On the contrary, he is cast out from the inner sanctuary of the mind, so that he no longer holds dominion in the hearts of the believers. Even though he has been excluded from the interior life of the soul, he still prowls around the exterior; though he has lost the fortress of the heart, he continues to besiege the walls. Therefore, the Lord says: *Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world will be cast out.* <note>original: "nunc princeps hujus mundi ejicietur foras." See John 12:31.</note> <margin>B</margin> And He immediately adds: *And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.* <note>John 12:32</note> By the phrase "lifted up," He signifies His death on the cross, the means by which He was to die for the salvation of the world.

<column-break/>

It is often asked why He said *all things* <note>original: "omnia," the neuter plural in Latin, implying "all things" or "the whole"</note> rather than "all men." <margin>C</margin> He says *all things* to encompass every variety of person—from every nation, language, and status—or perhaps to signify that both the soul and the body of a person are drawn to Him, as both are redeemed. He draws us to Himself through the power of faith and the sweetness of His love, so that we might cling to Him and obey His commandments. <margin>D</margin> One might wonder how He draws "all things" when there are so many who do not believe and are not drawn. To this, we must respond that Christ, as far as it depends on Him, draws everyone, because He offers His grace to all and calls all to Himself. <note>The author is addressing the theological tension between universal salvation and individual rejection of faith.</note> That some are not drawn is not due to a failure in the One who calls, but is the fault of those who resist. Just as the sun shines for all, yet those who keep their eyes closed do not see the light, so too does Christ, the sun of justice, offer Himself to all; but those who turn away through pride or malice are not drawn. <note>This solar analogy was a common way for medieval theologians to explain the relationship between divine grace and human free will.</note>

#### CHAPTER XXII.

**Nevertheless, many even among the leaders believed in Him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be cast out of the synagogue. For they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God.** <note>See John 12:42-43.</note> The Pharisees had said earlier: **Has any of the leaders believed in him?** <margin>John 7</margin> — wishing to imply that none of the rulers had joined themselves to Christ through faith. The Evangelist <note>The Gospel writer, John.</note> now proves that this was false, and writes that many of the leaders did indeed believe in Christ.

Truly, however, their faith was weak and powerless; for it was kept only in the heart and was not spoken aloud with the mouth, nor fulfilled in action. This is despite the fact that the God-spoken Paul says: **With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation** <margin>Romans 10</margin> — especially when the opportunity and necessity for such a confession arises. But these leaders, fearing to offend the Pharisees if they openly confessed Christ, and fearing to be cast out of the synagogue with shame, strove to please men rather than God. For this reason, they walked less uprightly in the way of the Lord, since the Psalm says: **The Lord scatters the bones of those who please men.** <margin>Psalm 51</margin> <note>This refers to Psalm 53:5 in modern Bibles (52 in the Vulgate).</note> And Paul says: **If I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of Christ.** <margin>Galatians 1</margin> And the Lord speaks of such people in the Gospel: **Whoever is ashamed of me before men, I also will be ashamed of him before my Father.** <margin>Luke 9</margin>

Finally, the Evangelist adds the reason why they did not dare to confess Christ openly: because, he says, **they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God.** Indeed, the glory of God is to confess Christ publicly; but the glory of men is to boast in worldly things. They loved the glory of men because they wanted to be seen as part of the fellowship of the synagogue rather than that of Christ. They feared offending the Pharisees more than God, lest they incur a mark of shame among men. Yet, by contrast, it was said of the true disciples of Christ: **Blessed are you when men hate you, and when they separate you, and reproach you, and cast out your name as evil on account of the Son of Man. Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven.** <margin>Luke 6</margin> Again, we read it said of the Apostles: **The Apostles went out from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they were counted worthy to suffer shame for the name of Jesus.** <margin>Acts 5</margin> But the Jews had conspired that if anyone confessed Jesus to be the Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue. <margin>John 9</margin> Therefore, lest they be touched by that disgrace, they suppressed their confession of Christ and remained silent. They were truly less constant than that blind man healed by the Lord, who fearlessly confessed the name of Christ in public and before a great crowd of men; having been cast out of the synagogue, he was kindly received by Christ.

#### CHAPTER XXIII.

**But Jesus cried out and said: He who believes in me, does not believe in me, but in Him who sent me. And he who sees me, sees Him who sent me. I have come as a light into the world**

<column-break/>

421

**so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.** <note>See John 12:44-46.</note> Because the love of human glory prevented the believing leaders from confessing Christ—and this is no surprise, for that same love kept many others from even believing, just as the Lord had said earlier: **How can you believe, you who receive glory from one another, and do not seek the glory that is from God alone?** <margin>John 5</margin> — for this reason, the Lord cries out against this, exalting the fruit of faith based on the majesty of the One in whom they believe.

That "crying out," however, designates not so much a raising of the voice as the greatness of the mysteries being spoken, and the devotion of His soul toward human salvation. Since the fire of devotion sounds louder in the ears of God than the volume of a voice, the intensity of feeling is often denoted in Scripture by the word "cry," as in the Psalm: **Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my voice.** <margin>Psalm 129</margin> <note>Psalm 130 in modern Bibles.</note> And in another place: **Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.** <margin>Psalm 101</margin> <note>Psalm 102 in modern Bibles.</note>

Furthermore, because Christ appeared as a man to men while His divinity remained hidden, He did not want them to think He was only what they saw. Wanting Himself to be believed as such and as great as the Father is, He says: **He who believes in me, does not believe in me** — that is, in this which is seen here with physical eyes — **but in Him who sent me** — that is, in the Father, who is of the same substance as I am, and whose only-begotten Son I am by nature. Therefore, let it not be considered a small or trivial thing to believe in me, even if it means despising human glory; for that very act is likewise to believe in God the Father and to cling to Him through true faith. If, therefore, no one for any reason ought to refuse to believe in God, neither should they refuse to believe in me, since faith cannot be had in the one without the other.

To further show the complete identity and equality of Himself with the Father, He adds: **He who sees me, sees also Him who sent me.** It is as if He said: there is so little difference between Him and me, that he who sees me immediately sees also Him who sent me, because of the likeness in nature and the natural properties of both. He would say this later to Philip: **He who sees me, sees also my Father.** <margin>John 14</margin> However, "vision" is not used here to mean the sight of a physical body present before one—for God is not a body, but a spirit—but the consideration of truth, which is through the intellect, and faith in God; this is what is called "vision" here.

Finally, He invites them to faith because of the abundant fruit and utility springing up in those who embrace the right faith. He signifies that something different and greater must be believed about Him than about other men, saying: **I have come as a light into the world.** <margin>John 1</margin> He called Himself "light" here, just as in previous passages, because He rescues people from error and dissolves intellectual darkness. And in truth, He Himself is the primary light, illuminating everyone and not receiving illumination from any other. Other people who participate in divine light are sometimes called "light," but they are illuminated by Him first, and then they distribute the received gifts of heavenly illumination to others. This true light came into the world so that everyone who believes in Him should not remain in darkness; but if someone was previously wandering in the gloom of vices, he might be rescued from that horrific night and be transferred...

This page defends the equality of the Father and the Son against those who suggest the Son is inferior because he receives "commands."</meta>

424 ->BOOK NINE.<-

...the Father commanded him to speak: therefore, he might seem inferior to the Father either according to his substance, or according to some logic of status. But let the reader turn this over in his mind and answer our question: whether he thinks the title and the reality of a "prophet" belongs to God by his very nature? I do not doubt that it would seem absurd to everyone for God to be called a prophet—He who speaks *through* the prophets, "who multiplied visions," as it is written. <margin>Hosea 12</margin> <note>original: "Oseæ. 12." — referring to Hosea 12:10.</note> However, because he truly took upon himself the name and condition of a servant in our likeness, and was called a "prophet" in this manner, those things which belong to a prophet are appropriately attributed to him by the scriptures. Thus, he truly writes that he "heard" from the Father, and "received commands" regarding what he should say and what he should speak. 

Furthermore, the Jews—preoccupied with an overly literal <note>literally "ruder" or "unrefined"</note> understanding of the Law and believing it was given by God—would by no means have accepted the words of the Savior as he translated everything toward a [Marginal note: B] spiritual worship. For they did not know that he was God by nature, nor did it enter their minds that the only-begotten Word of the Father had taken on our flesh for our sake. If they had believed that, they would never have rejected his teaching; but because they believed him to be a "naked" man <note>meaning a mere human being without divinity</note>, they could not endure the Law being dissolved by him, as they thought. From this arose their frequent, impudent shouting: "We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because [Marginal note: John 10] you, being a man, make yourself God." <note>John 10:33</note> 

Therefore, by an excellent <term>dispensation</term> <note>The Greek term *oikonomia*, referring to God's strategic plan for human salvation through the Incarnation.</note>, our Lord Jesus Christ, removing them from this false opinion and urging them to respect his words, redirected his speech from a "naked man" toward God the Father. He softened the hearts of the Jews by every means and method, [Marginal note: C] treating their minds in various ways. Although I think these points are sufficient to repel the false arguments of the heretics—who think the Son is less than the Father because he speaks nothing of himself but only the commands he has heard—I will nonetheless add something more to completely expose their insults. 

Come now, setting aside for a moment the mystery of the Incarnation, let us show that this can be rightly said of the Son of God himself: "For I do not speak of myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a command, what I should say and what I should speak." For since he himself is the living and subsisting Word of God the Father, he necessarily interprets those things which are from the Father. Bringing the will of the Father into the light, he says he has received a "command" from there. 

This will become clearer by an example taken from ourselves. [Marginal note: D] For this speech which we produce, which is composed of words and flows outward through the voice, brings the thoughts of our mind into the light as if they were its "commands." It does not take a long time to do this; for as soon as the mind conceives, it delivers what it has conceived to the voice. The voice, poured out externally, interprets what is in the depths of the mind, changing nothing of the "commands" given to it. What wonder is it then, or what is so impossible, if the Son—being the Word of the Father (though not like our "fictional" word, for God exceeds all things)—interprets the counsel of the Father? Is he not, therefore, called the "Angel of Great Counsel" by prophetic [Marginal note: Isaiah 9] authority? <note>Isaiah 9:6 in the Septuagint version.</note> Therefore, no diminution of substance or dignity is understood to exist 

<column-break/>

425 
[Marginal note: A] in the Son because it is written that he "received a command" from the Father. This is especially true since we ourselves also give commands to others and order them to act. Yet we do not, for this reason, exclude them from our natural likeness; they are the same according to nature and <term>consubstantial</term> <note>of the same essence or "stuff" (Latin: *consubstantiales*).</note> with us, both before we commanded them and after they followed our orders. 

But perhaps someone will say: they are indeed consubstantial, but those who serve the commands of others are lesser in dignity. But if it were not written concerning the Only-begotten—O you, whoever you are who says these things—"Who, being in the form of God, did not [Marginal note: Philippians 2] count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in human likeness, humbled himself" <note>Philippians 2:6-8</note>—then perhaps your logic might seem to carry some weight. But since the manner of his subjection and humiliation is most clearly evident, why do you thus rise up against him who was humbled for our sake? Therefore, bringing these words back to the correctness of doctrine from every side, we assert that they were spoken by Christ according to the "dispensation."

### CHAPTER II.

For what reason does he seem to say so pointedly "before the feast day of the Passover, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father"? Or what is it that, "having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end"? 

To touch upon this briefly at first: it seems to me he is saying that before his saving passion, since Jesus knew the time was very near for him to pass to the heavens, he showed perfect love toward his own who were in this world. But so that they may embrace the whole matter more broadly, I will not be burdened to repeat what has been said elsewhere. Intellectual and rational substances—powers, dominions, and others of this kind—belong properly to the Savior by right of creation. But rational and earthly substances are also his own by that reason by which he is Lord of all, even if some do not worship him. He loved, therefore, his own in this [world]...

### THE HUMILITY OF THE WORD

Then He poured water into a basin and began to wash the feet of the disciples and to wipe them with the towel with which He was girded. What a sight to behold! The Lord of Majesty, the King of Glory, assumes the form of a servant. He who sits upon the <term>Cherubim</term><note>A high order of angels often associated with the presence of God.</note> sits at the feet of men. He who measures the heavens with a span and the earth in a handful of dust, washes the dust from the feet of His servants. 

Through this act, Christ demonstrates that spiritual leadership is not found in the exercise of power over others, but in the washing away of their burdens. He shows that the teacher must be the first to descend to the lowest place so that the students may follow. He who was rich became poor for our sake, and He who was high became low, so that by His humility He might heal our pride.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Gospel of John, chapter 13, following the discussion of Christ’s humility in washing the feet of His disciples. The text moves from the physical act to the moral and spiritual obligation it imposes on all believers.</meta>

->430 ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN<-

He imparts the power of understanding. And just as He Himself is life and gives life to all things capable of receiving it, so because He is the wisdom of the Father, He instills wisdom into all who are capable of it. Therefore, the Son is Lord and teacher **by nature**. "Since I," He says, "who am so great in glory, did not disdain to come to such great humility that I even washed your feet, how can you refuse to wash one another's feet?" From this we learn that we ought not to leap over the honor of our neighbors, but always consider our neighbors as those to be preferred. This is indeed the finest discipline; for what can be compared to a mind that is not arrogant? This is especially true when we see that nothing separates brothers and friends more than an excessive desire for **miserable glory**. For we always choose what is greater; the fleeting and unstable honor of this [B] life always drives our slippery minds to long for more brilliant things. Therefore, if we wish to be freed from this detestable disease and empty desire (for this desire is nothing other than a deception), let us embrace Christ our Savior with our whole soul. He washed the feet of the disciples so that we might also wash one another's feet. In this way, every path of arrogance will be blocked, and every appearance of vainglory will vanish. For if He, who is Lord by nature, was like a servant among His disciples, how shall we, who are servants by nature, escape terrible punishment if we do not profit from such a great example?

### CHAPTER IX.

[Initial A] "Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is an <term>apostle</term><note>The word 'apostle' comes from the Greek 'apostolos,' meaning 'one who is sent.'</note> greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them." He confirms virtue by these laws, as if by firm examples, showing that the transgression of the precept is full of ruin. For that which is confirmed by an oath is not disregarded without guilt. For He says it is certainly an inexcusable crime for servants to think themselves greater than their masters. To be arrogant is to desire things greater than you can bear. Similarly, apostles are to be blamed if they demand more preferential treatment for themselves than the one who sent them possesses, especially since the dignity of the sender ought to be enough for them. Thus, He seems to me to be saying nothing other than that no small punishment threatens men if, being servants by nature, they are unwilling to do for one another what He, being God and Lord by nature, did for His disciples. For it is shameful and entirely full of madness [D]: "Since you are servants," He says, "to blush out of arrogance to do for your fellow servants what your Lord did for you." "If you know these things," He says—that is, if you can understand these things deeply—"you are blessed if you do them." For it is not a great thing to know virtue, but to act upon it studiously; that is certainly the greatest thing. I even consider it better in a certain way not to know, than to neglect through laziness what you do know, and to pass over out of sloth what you have believed to be good. "The one who did not know his master's <margin>Luke 12</margin> will," He says, "and did not do it, will be beaten with few blows; but the one who knew and despised it, will be beaten with many." For the one who was entirely ignorant, even if he is held in guilt because he perhaps neglected to learn, nevertheless the plea of ignorance seems to be a suitable petition for pardon. But for the one who knows, his very 

->ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 431<-

condition condemns him. For he showed contempt and did not do what he clearly knew. Therefore, let us not neglect to carry out what we know to be good. For since we are not ignorant of the proper discipline of living according to Christ, we shall have a great reward in the opportune time by living rightly. For "He who does and teaches," as the Savior says, "shall be called <margin>Matthew 7 <note>The author likely means Matthew 5:19, though the margin cites Chapter 7.</note></margin> great in the kingdom of heaven." For what is lacking to that man, as far as piety is concerned, who is upright in both word and deed? Or how shall such a man not be honored by God? When knowledge is joined to works, and works to knowledge, then no small benefit follows. For if someone knows by nature that there is one God, and confesses it with both heart and tongue, although he does so rightly, he will nevertheless die unless the brightness of works is added to his knowledge. How then is it not utter madness if one knows what is good and yet despises living well? For this reason, He says the disciples—that is, those believing in Him—will be blessed if they have not only understood what He taught, but have also carried it out sincerely and with integrity.

### CHAPTER X.

[Initial N] "I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But so that the Scripture may be fulfilled: 'He who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me.'" A place of no small obscurity is hidden here. For when He had said they would be blessed who, having knowledge of virtue, strive with care, zeal, and deeds to do as they have known, He immediately added that He was not speaking of all of them, signifying the traitor (as it seems to many and to me). For now, one held in such great impiety will be numbered among the blessed. And this is indeed one sense; but another can rightly (as I think) be added to this. For since He was about to speak according to the Scripture: *He who eats my bread has magnified <margin>Psalm 40 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 41:9.</note></margin> his supplanting against me*—that is, he has lifted up his heel against me—and since all the disciples were eating His bread, living together with Him, He first mitigated the statement so that He would not seem to say it of everyone, saying: "I am not speaking of all of you. For I know whom I have chosen, but so that the Scripture may be fulfilled, which says: 'He who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me.'" Let each person approve whichever of these senses they prefer. For we say all things for the edification of the readers. But someone will ask first: if Christ is believed to know all things, <margin>A separate question.</margin> why did He choose Judas, who was to be the traitor? For why did He count him among the others, whom He was not ignorant would fall into the snare of the devil, captured by the desire for gain? Secondly, if he lifted his heel against Christ *so that the Scripture might be fulfilled*, it was surely not caused by the event itself, but by that force which compelled the fulfillment of Scripture. In responding briefly to these things for the common <margin>Response to the first part.</margin> benefit, we say first that such reasons will never be lacking to us, nor shall we ever make an end of rebuking and plucking at God—who, because of His immense mercy, called all things into being from nothing—if we are so unskillfully affected that in all things made by God, we find similar...

### CHAPTER XXI.

**Little children, yet a little while I am with you.** He called the disciples "little children"—as if they were newborn infants—even though they shone with many virtues and were each fortified with prudence. He did this to show that a human being is like an infant before God and is of small importance, even if they were the most perfect of men. For what is human prudence when compared to the wisdom of the Creator of all? <margin>Psalm 72</margin> Thus the Psalmist sang to God: *I have become like a beast of burden before you.* <note>original: "Psal. 72." In the Vulgate numbering, this is Psalm 72:22; in modern English Bibles, it is Psalm 73:22.</note> Nor can anyone say—unless they are gripped by great madness—that the Psalmist called himself senseless like a beast because he clung to God; for great impiety arises from such a thought. For if someone clings to a wise person, they become wiser; how then could one who clings to God become mindless and senseless?

The phrase "immediately" <note>original: "continuo"</note> signifies that the time of His exaltation was not far off. The betrayal, the sacrifice, and the subsequent return to life were to follow one after another in swift succession, fulfilling the divine plan for the salvation of the world. By saying this, He strengthens the hearts of His followers, showing that death would not be a defeat, but a rapid passage into supreme honor.

### **John 13:33**

**"Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going you cannot come,’ so now I say to you."**

Having spoken of His impending glory, He now addresses the grief of His disciples. He uses the tender address "Little children" <note>The Latin *filioli* (and Greek *teknia*) is a diminutive expressing deep affection, often used by a teacher or father nearing the end of his life.</note> to soften the impact of the news of His departure. By this name, He reminds them that they have been reborn through Him and that He feels for them the protective love of a parent.

He warns them that he is with them only "a little while," preparing them for the physical absence that will follow His death and ascension. He notes that they will "seek Him," just as He previously told the Jews <margin>John 7 and 8</margin>. However, there is a great difference: the Jews sought Him in their sins and with malice, or would later seek a Messiah in vain because they rejected the True One. The disciples, conversely, seek Him out of love and faith. Yet, even for them, the path He takes to the Father’s presence is one they cannot yet travel; He must first go alone to prepare a place for them and to conquer death as their pioneer.

A silversmith or a blacksmith cries out that he has learned his craft. In the same way, I believe that those who are held together by charity cry out by the very reality of their actions that they are disciples of Charity itself—that is, of Christ, who possesses the supreme charity. For He so loved the world that He even laid down His life for us, enduring the cruelty of the Judean customs. No one, as He Himself says, 

<margin>1 John 4</margin>

possesses greater charity than this: that a person lays down their life for their friends. For since God is charity <note>The Latin *charitas* (or *caritas*) refers to the highest form of Christian love—selfless and divine.</note>, He did not attain this perfection through training, study, sweat, or practice. No one of sound mind would dare to say that the divine nature "received" or acquired its goodness. No form of goodness is accidental or external to Him, as if it were one thing added to another; rather, it exists within the very substance of the Godhead. For it is not as it is in a human being, where knowledge is one thing and the person who receives that knowledge is another; instead, whatever God is believed to be, that is Goodness itself. I say that this Ineffable Nature is Goodness itself, a kind of fountain, so to speak, in which every form of virtue resides and from which it flows forth. Most truly, then, He is the fruit of charity, and for that reason, He is charity itself, just as the Father is, from whom He comes. Therefore, through charity, He is most especially imprinted upon our souls. 

Thus, the charity impressed upon us, by which we love one another, is a sincere and complete footprint of His union. Furthermore, if Christ is our peace, 

<margin>Ephesians 2</margin>

as Paul says (for in Him the lower things are joined to the higher, and through Him we are reconciled to God the Father—we who were once far from Him because of our impiety, divided into two primary peoples, the Gentiles and Israel), and if we are built up into one "new man" in Him, the middle wall of the partition having been dissolved and the power of enmity destroyed through the teaching of the Gospel—the shadows now passed and the law falling silent—how could it be known that they were disciples of Peace if they did not have peace among themselves? For what else is the absence of love but the origin of war, the overturning of peace, and a duplicity of the soul? For just as the blessings of peace are preserved by the bond of charity, in the same way, the evils of war arise through the rupture (so to speak) of love. From this rupture come contentions, rivalries, insults, detraction, anger, envy, and every vice. 

Since, therefore, the full count of virtue is contained and perfected in love, let no one think they have achieved anything great through hunger and fasting, or by prostrating themselves on the ground, or through other exercises of virtue, unless they truly love their brothers. For such a person is not heading toward the finish line <note>original: "ad calcem," literally the lime-line or chalk-line marking the end of a racecourse</note>, but elsewhere. They are like an unskilled charioteer, or like a pilot who has never sailed but holds the tiller, steering the ship toward rocks and reefs. For this reason, Paul, if you seek a proof, 

<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>

of Christ speaking in me (he says), placed this proof not in simply following, but in following rightly and with intention. He certainly knew that charity was, as it were, a golden crown placed upon all the virtues. Listen to how excellently he philosophizes about it: *If I distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing. If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity,*

*I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.* Therefore, the face and image of Christ engraved upon us, by which we are recognized as His own, is the glory of charity.

### **CHAPTER XXV.**

**Simon Peter said to him: "Lord, where are you going?"**

Peter did not understand what those words meant: *Where I am going, you cannot come.* Therefore, out of a longing to follow Christ, he asks where He intended to go. The modesty of the disciples is wonderful. The others do not remain silent because they understood; rather, they were entrusting the matter to this greater one <note>Likely referring to Peter's role as the leader or "spokesman" of the apostles.</note>. Peter also seems to me worthy of no small praise; considering the shame of slowness that often weighs upon those who ask questions to be nothing, he desires to know, and he places the utility of knowing above all the disgrace of being slow to understand. Thus, he became an example to those who come after, that we should not bypass a teacher’s discourse if it is somewhat obscure, nor should we allow ourselves to seem to both understand and approve through our silence. Let no one, therefore, be ashamed to ask, since the utility of asking and learning is much greater than a false opinion of knowledge and an empty reputation.

Indeed, all who are wise are accustomed to cover with shadows those things that bring grief to their listeners. For although He was ascending into heaven to give Himself as the firstfruits to the Father—which is most useful for the entire human race (for He made a way for us, which our nature could not previously attain...

## BOOK NINE

...our labors <note>original: "sudores nostri"; literally "our sweats," referring to the arduous work and suffering of the disciples</note>, which we hoped would bring us life. For I believe that they either thought these things to themselves, or would have thought them, if Christ had not quickly recalled them; for He alone is accustomed to even prevent the wounds of the soul with His help and remedy. 

He heals them, therefore, saying: **Let not your heart be troubled.** <note>original: "Non turbetur cor uestrum"; John 14:1</note> Observe, however, how He promises them pardon for this excessive hidden fear; for it was not safe to say openly that He would grant pardon to those who would flee and deny Him, lest, by treating the crime of offense as something small, they might think that denying Him and fleeing from Him carried no guilt at all. 

Yet, by saying they ought not to be troubled, He placed them between hope and fear. This was so that if they should suffer any human weakness <note>original: "si quid humanum patiantur"; a common theological idiom referring to falling into sin or error because of mortal frailty</note>, they might be able to find relief in the hope of pardon, yet be kept from offending by the dread of doing so. For they did not yet possess the inability to fall, which they later received when strengthened by a higher power—that is, when they were fortified by the grace of the Spirit <note>A reference to the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, which the author argues changed the disciples from fearful men to "invincible" martyrs</note>. He commands them, therefore, not to be troubled, so that He might teach those who are about to struggle...

<summary>This page analyzes Jesus's command "Let not your heart be troubled" as a medicinal remedy for the disciples' secret fears. The author explains that Jesus balances the hope of forgiveness with the fear of sinning to prepare the disciples for their upcoming trials before they receive the Holy Spirit.</summary>

**Believe in God, and believe in me.** <note>original: "creditis in Deum et in me credite"; John 14:1</note>

He speaks of "many" dwellings to demonstrate the great abundance of heavenly grace and to show that there is space enough for all who follow Him. He implies that their labors will not be in vain, and that His departure is not a desertion, but a preparation of the way for their own eventual arrival in the presence of the Father.

# 454 BOOK NINE.

...law of sin, and He will lead us back to that life which consists in holiness and blessedness.

**"No one comes to the Father except through me."**

For since He Himself is the Way, He leads us to the Father—not through any other person, but by making an entrance for us through Himself. This is the true and unshakable logic of our <term>doctrines</term> <note>original: *dogmatum*; refers to the essential religious teachings or established truths of the Christian faith.</note>. For since there is no other Word of God except the one who is from Him by nature, and likewise no other Father except Him who begat Him, how is it not true that he who has known the Son has also known the Father? 

**"If you had known me, you would have known my Father also; and from now on you know Him and have seen Him."** <note>John 14:7</note>

Having said that He is the Way, the Truth, and the Life, and that no one comes to the Father except through Him, He now observes that the disciples have not yet reached a perfect understanding of who He is. For although they believed He was the Christ and the Son of God, their understanding was still somewhat clouded by the limitations of His human <term>appearance</term> <note>original: *habitu*; this refers to the physical "garb" or outward form of Christ's humanity, which can sometimes distract from His divine nature.</note>. They did not yet clearly see the full dignity of the divine nature within Him. 

Therefore, He gently reproaches them, saying: "If you had known me"—that is, if you had clearly understood that I am the Word originating from the very substance of the Father—"you would have known my Father also." For the Father is known within the Son as if in a living and natural image. 

<margin>Philip's Request</margin>
**"Philip said to Him: 'Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.'"** <note>John 14:8</note>

Philip, being more eager than the others but still not grasping the spiritual depth of the mystery, asks for a physical manifestation. He likely recalled how the ancients were granted visions of God, such as when Moses or the prophets were allowed to see a glimpse of the divine glory. He says, "It is enough for us," meaning that such a visible sign would satisfy all their doubts and settle their hearts once and for all.

<summary>Cyril explains that knowing the Son is the only way to know the Father because they share the same divine nature. He interprets Philip's request for a physical vision of God as a sign that the disciples did not yet fully grasp Christ's divinity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the refutation of an Arian teacher who argued that the Son’s "dwelling" in the Father is merely a moral or relational connection, similar to how humans "dwell" in God, rather than a shared divine nature. 468 LIBER NONVS. 469

...[if he believed] this, we would not say it; rather, we drive from the fellowship of the brothers all those who do say it. For persons are distinguished not by nature, but by personal properties. For Peter is indeed Peter, and not Paul; and Paul is Paul, and is not Peter. Yet they are indistinct in their nature. For there is one account of substance in both, and those things which are natural are the same in both. To what end is this? It is to show that those people impiously drive the Son away from the nature of the deity, who attribute to him nothing other than a "conjunction of habit" <note>original: "coniunctionem habitudinis"; a technical term used by opponents to suggest Christ was only "joined" to God by a shared attitude or will, rather than being God by nature.</note>. For why, using our own example, do you say that just as we have a substance separate from God—although we are in Him—so the Son, though he is in the Father, nevertheless has a substance distinct from Him? Is his cunning not pulled out into the open? Might someone not rightly call that man one of those mockers who were predicted by the Spirit? Listen to what Jude, the disciple of Christ, writes to us: *But you, beloved, be mindful of the words which were predicted by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, who told you that in the last times mockers would come, walking according to their own desires, not in piety. These are they who segregate themselves, <term>unspiritual</term> <note>original: "animales"; from the Latin 'anima' (soul). In theological texts, this refers to people living on a purely human/sensory level, lacking the Holy Spirit.</note>, <margin>1 Cor. 12.</margin> not having the Spirit.* For no one speaking by the Holy Spirit says anything against the glory of the Only-begotten; for to do this is nothing other than to say "Jesus is anathema." Unspiritual and miserable men, possessing hearts desolate of the Holy Spirit, banish the Son from the Father, thinking that the Father differs substantially from the Son, just as the things which were produced by Him differ; and contending that the Son is in the Father in no other way than we are in Him.

We shall attempt to demonstrate from the Scripture itself that this is far from the truth. For the Son is said to be in the Father both by identity of substance and because He is the image and <term>character</term> <note>original: "character"; here meaning the "exact imprint" or "stamped representation," referencing Hebrews 1:3.</note> of the Father. We, however, are in the Son through faith and virtue, having been reformed toward Him. That most wise John testifies that this is so in his epistle: <margin>1 John 1.</margin> *Our fellowship,* he says, *is with the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ.* For if this logic of fellowship does not look toward a similarity of will, but rather we are in the Father and the Son because we "mix" our substance with the substance of His nature—how shall we be substantially with the Father and the Son if the Son is not <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "consubstantialis"; the key orthodox term (homoousios) meaning "of the same essence."</note> with the Father? For according to them, it would be necessary to say that ridiculous thing: that we are understood to be in them because we assign a part of our nature to the Father and a part to the Son. 

Because that is full of madness, we say instead that our souls are reformed toward divine beauty by the ardor of the will, by fervent faith, and by every kind of virtue; and we affirm that the grace of communion is acquired by us in this way. The Son, however, is in the Father not through this "habitual" <note>Meaning a relationship based on "habitus" (disposition or behavior) rather than being.</note> and studiously maintained communion, but through natural identity. Moreover, John again testifies that we are said to be in God through virtue, saying: <margin>1 John 2.</margin> *In this we know that we are in Him. He who says he abides in Him ought himself to walk just as He walked.* And again: *What you have heard from the beginning, let it abide in you; for if it abides in you, you also shall abide in the Son and in the Father.* 

But what is it that we have heard from the beginning? He himself declares it, saying: <margin>A</margin> *And this is the commandment which you have heard from the beginning, that you love one another.* Do you hear that we are in God if we have charity among ourselves, if we imitate the virtue of the Savior (as much as is possible for us)? Now, I speak of the virtue of the Savior—not that by which He created the heavens, nor that by which He rebuked the sea, raised the dead, or cleansed the lepers—but that of which He Himself says: <margin>Matt. 11.</margin> *Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.* Thus, following Him as the leader of virtue, we are said to abide in the Father and in Him. 

The Son, however, led the disciples to believe that He is in the Father and the Father in Him through those things which He did with supreme power as God. But perhaps someone will say: <margin>B</margin> the Son is in the Father in the same way we are in the Son, because just as we are said to be in the Son through the study of virtue, so the Son himself is conformed to the Father by virtues. Why then, when Philip had said, *Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us,* did He not take all the apostles as an image of the Father? Why did He not say, "For so long a time we have been with one another, and you have not known the Father"? Instead, passing over all the others because they offered no "exquisite image" of God, He attributed the supreme likeness—indeed, the identity—to Himself alone, saying: *He who sees me, sees the Father.* and immediately added: *Believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.* For where there is supreme identity, how can one not be in the other? 

Consider that this can even be said of men. For the son of Abraham, showing the nature of his father in himself, would rightly have said: <margin>C</margin> "I am in my father and my father is in me." And he would have rightly proved this by his works, saying: "Believe it is so because of the works. For everything that my father does naturally, I also do." Why then, neglecting the straight and royal road, do they set out toward harsh, trackless places and compel others to do so as far as they are able? But we, fortified by the authority of the sacred writings and walking along the royal road, believe the Son is consubstantial with God the Father, and therefore we confess Him to be in the Father, and the Father in Him.

### CHAPTER XLI.

<margin>D</margin> **Truly, truly, I say to you, the works that I do he also shall do, and greater works than these shall he do, because I go to the Father: and whatever you ask the Father in my name, this I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.**

Great is the depth of this speech, but for the utility of the readers, we shall briefly set forth its sense. Since He wished to demonstrate that He is consubstantial with the Father and His most exact representation—so that He might be believed to be in the Father as in the original, and the Father in Him as in His own representation, not by some bodily figure, but naturally and substantially—He said: *I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.* Then, so that we might understand this unchangeable equality to exist in no other way than by nature and the perfections of nature, He added: *believe because of the works themselves.* Certainly, whoever considers that He prevails with the same supreme power in the same works as the Father, will understand the Son to be the natural representation and image of the Father. For never would one who [is] from God by nature...

<summary>The author argues that Christ's unity with the Father is one of shared divine substance and "natural identity," unlike the unity of believers which is based on the imitation of virtue. He uses the dialogue with Philip from the Gospel of John to show that only Christ is the "exact representation" of the Father's nature.</summary>

Never <margin>A</margin> will a creature receive those attributes which belong to infinite power; never can the qualities of that nature, which has always existed, be properly attributed to those things which were <term>produced from nothing</term> <note>original: "producta ex nihilo"; the Christian doctrine that the universe was created out of nothing, distinguishing created beings from the eternal Son.</note>. For it must be carefully noted that he did not say here that the Father would do something, <margin>B</margin> but "whatever you ask in my name, [I will do it]."

He immediately explained in words to whom this promise was made. Therefore, the grace of spiritual blessings is granted only to those who love him and keep his commandments. For the disciple of Christ shows elsewhere that these things are not prepared for everyone indiscriminately, saying: *You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may consume it upon your pleasures.* <margin>James 4</margin> And again, concerning those who are double-minded: *Let not that man think he will receive anything from the Lord; for a double-minded man <note>original: "uir duplex animo"; literally "a man double in soul," referring to someone whose loyalty is divided between God and the world.</note> is unstable in all his ways.* <margin>James 1</margin> Indeed, God has completely closed his ears to all who ask for anything from Him not for the sake of acting with devotion, but to fulfill their cravings and carnal desires. For how could He grant to others the very things He hates because they are shameful? How could a fountain of sweetness pour forth something bitter? 

Isaiah also shows that He provides all things with a generous hand to those who desire spiritual graces, saying: *While you are still speaking, I will say, "What is it?"* <margin>A, Isaiah 65</margin> The Psalmist says something similar: *The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous,* he says, *and his ears are open to their prayers.* <margin>Psalm 33</margin> Therefore, since He said these future blessings—which are poured out from the Father through Him—would belong to those who love Him, He immediately revealed how this love is held and what its method is. For not everyone who says God is loved by them will be seen to speak truly; the strength of virtue does not consist in naked words, nor is the shining glory of piety confirmed by a spoken word. Rather, it is known by good works and a rightly disposed mind. Thus, the observation of the divine mandates demonstrates our charity toward God and constitutes a living and true virtue, which consists not only in word, but much more in deed. 

The Lord himself demonstrates this, saying: <margin>C</margin> *Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father.* <margin>Matthew 7</margin> For faith is proved to exist not in flattering words, but in the heart of the one acting. Therefore, Scripture teaches that faith without works is dead. <margin>James 2</margin> For not only men, but even the impure demons, trembling at the power of the Creator, confess the unity of God. But to perform works consistent with faith belongs only to those who love God. Therefore, the most perfect boundary of faith and the demonstration of the love of God is the observation and keeping of the Gospel’s precepts. Much could be said on this matter, but it is not pleasing to wander too far. *If you love me,* he says, *keep my commandments.* 

I ask you to notice and remember this diligently: He is often found saying both to the disciples and even more commonly to the Jews: <margin>D</margin> *The words that I speak are not mine, but His who sent me.* <margin>John 7</margin> And again: *I do not speak of myself, but the Father who sent me gave me a commandment as to what I should say and what I should speak.* <margin>John 12</margin> And again: *The things I speak are not mine, but His who sent me.* <margin>John 14</margin> But now, those things which He used to say were the Father's, He clearly affirms are *His* commandments. No Christian would think these things were said lightly or falsely, for He is the Truth itself. Therefore, he did not explain the Father’s speech to us as one of the prophets or in the place of a servant, but as <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "consubstantialis"; meaning of the same essence or 'substance.' This is a key technical term in the Nicene Creed to explain that the Son is fully God just as the Father is.</note> and identical in nature with the Father. As a Son born from the substance of the Father, as the 

<column-break/>

Word, substance, and counsel of the Father, He spoke the Father’s words and His own. Yet, He says He had a commandment from the Father regarding what to say and speak. We perceive this even in ourselves, when we understand that "commands" are given by the mind to the speech we usually produce, which the speech then explains as it goes forth. I am not unaware that the power of this example is very small; however, since we understand the deep mysteries of God in a mirror and a riddle <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly."</note> when we apply even a tiny likeness from things we understand to supernatural things, this point should not have been omitted.

<margin>John 20</margin> For it is written that he breathed upon the disciples, saying: **A**
**Receive the Holy Spirit.** <note>original: "Accipite spiritum sanctum"</note> Must it not therefore be said—indeed, must it not be entirely believed—that because the Son substantially shares in the natural blessings of the Godhead together with the Father, He possesses the Spirit in the same way the Father is understood to possess Him: not as something added from the outside, nor from without? For it is foolish and even mad to think such a thing. Instead, just as each of us contains our own breath <note>original: "spiritum"; here used as a double meaning for both "spirit" and physical "breath."</note> within ourselves and pours it out from our innermost depths to the exterior, for this reason Christ breathed physically. He showed by this sign that just as the human breath proceeds physically from the human mouth, so from the divine substance the Spirit—who is from that substance—is poured forth in a manner befitting the Godhead. Since, therefore, the Spirit is Himself the Spirit of the Father and the Son, how can the Father and the Son not have one power, both distinctly and jointly at the same time? For the Father **B**
is indeed the Father, and not the Son; and the Son is not the Father, but the Son. And yet the Father is in the Son, and the Son is in the Father. Moreover, the Father does not provide the Paraclete <note>term: Paraclete (from the Greek "Parakletos," meaning one called to one's side as an advocate, helper, or comforter).</note>—that is, the Holy Spirit—separately, nor does the Son provide Him separately. Instead, when the Son is said to give Him, the Father, from whom all things exist, is also understood to give Him. Truly, although no one of right mind doubts that the Spirit is of the same substance as the Father and the Son, this is also proven by reason. For if the Spirit is not God by His very substance, how is a created being made a "partaker of God the Father" by receiving Him? Or <margin>1 Cor. 3</margin> how shall we be "temples of God" if we are receiving a created spirit and not rather Him who is from God? How do those who have received the Spirit become "partakers of the divine nature" (as holy men testify), if the Spirit **C**
is counted among created things and does not proceed from the divine nature? Therefore, He does not come to us as a stranger, but as one consubstantial <note>term: Consubstantial (sharing the same fundamental essence or substance; a key concept in the doctrine of the Trinity).</note> with the Father and the Son. Wherefore those who are wise in the ways of the world, and prefer these earthly things, cannot be capable of receiving Him; but the holy are capable of Him. For this reason, because the former are entangled in filth and labor as if with a blurring of the mind's eyes, they do not behold the splendor of the divine nature and cannot receive the grace of the Spirit, being entirely conquered by the desires of the flesh. But upright men, since they possess a clean heart, are made receptacles of the Paraclete (as far as is possible for men in this life); they understand that they will obtain great and unheard-of rewards. For they shall be sanctified by the Spirit and made partakers of all good things; having cast aside the shame of slavery, they shall be decorated with the dignity of the "adoption of the sons of God," which Paul showed when he said: **D**
<margin>Gal. 4</margin> **And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying: Abba, Father.**

CHAPTER XLV.
**I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.** <note>original: "Non relinquam uos orphanos: ueniam ad uos."</note>
Necessarily, even now our Lord shows the consubstantiality of the Holy Trinity. This He also did in the preceding sections, demonstrating both in words and in deeds that He was born naturally from God the Father, and possesses the same power and will. For this reason He was just saying: *Because I do not speak from myself*; and again: *If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even if you do not believe me, believe my works.* However, it was also necessary to hand down to us a correct faith regarding the Spirit, so that the

He does this. He had just said that "another Paraclete" from God the Father would come to us; yet, lest it be understood that the Spirit was "another" in terms of substance and nature, He promised that He Himself would come, to show clearly that the Spirit is "another" only in personal substance from the Father and the Son (for He is the Spirit, not the Father or the Son). Thus He showed that the Holy Spirit is not something other than what He Himself is. For He is the Spirit of the Father, and is also understood to be the Spirit of the Son, and is therefore called "His Mind." Paul also denoted this when he said: **But we have the mind of Christ.** <margin>1 Cor. 2</margin> Therefore, as those who think rightly and follow the divine Scriptures, we preach that the Spirit is not something other than the Son in substance and nature, yet we profess that He subsists in His own Person. **B**
For this reason, Paul also (as I believe) frequently joins the Spirit to the Son. Let no one think that the distinction of the Persons is being confused by us; we do not profess it so, nor was that Paul's intention. For that divine man most correctly knew the enumeration of the Holy Trinity; and therefore he teaches that each Person subsists properly and distinctly, and yet he openly preaches the unchangeable identity **C**
of the Trinity. Otherwise, how could He be called "the Spirit" and "God"? He says: **Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God [dwells in you]?** <margin>1 Cor. 3</margin>

**A** Therefore, weaving together the consequences from what came before, we say that the Paraclete <note>term: Paraclete (from the Greek "Parakletos," meaning one called to one's side as an advocate, helper, or comforter).</note>—that is, the Holy Spirit—is given by the Father through the Son, for all things are from the Father through the Son. We shall understand this passage either in this manner, or—especially since this is added: **because I live, you also shall live**—we shall explain it thus: When, through His resurrection, He first repaired the immortality of our nature in His own body, He ascended into heaven to the Father; and after some time, He will descend again to us with the angels in the majesty of the Father. That the faithful who have followed Christ will be with Christ, beholding that ineffable beauty, Paul shows by saying: <margin>1 Thess. 4.</margin> **For the Lord himself, with a command, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven; and the dead in Christ will rise first. ### CHAPTER 47.

**B In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.**) The sense of the proposed text seems difficult for me to find, and therefore must be sought with greater vigilance. For I believe that Christ, who is the truth, will direct us to the true meaning. <margin>Refutation of a cavil.</margin> <note>term: Cavil (a petty or unfair objection used in an argument).</note> Some of those who even seem to be leaders, impiously driving the Son away from the substance of the Father, assert that a "habitual" rather than a "natural" connection is signified when the Son is said to be in the Father. <note>note: This refers to a theological debate where "habitual" means a connection based merely on behavior or friendship, while "natural" means sharing the same divine essence.</note> Thus, writing from themselves and not from the Holy Spirit, they say that because the Father loves the Son, and is in turn loved by Him, He is therefore written to be "in Him." They believe they can take a demonstration of their own impiety from this place. Defending themselves with a "staff of reed" <note>note: A biblical metaphor for a weak or unreliable defense.</note>, they say: "If we are in Him and have Him in us—not joined by reason of substance, but by an affection of love, since we love and are loved in return—then the Son also, being in the Father in this way, is separated from the Father by reason of His nature." 

But we, since we have already demonstrated at length that the Son is in the Father naturally and is substantially joined to Him, will now more briefly refute their malicious sophistry. If the Son is in the Father only because He loves and is loved—in the same way that we are in Him and He in us—and if no other bond is hidden by which either the Son is joined to the Father or we are joined in the Son, then tell me, I ask: why did He say, <margin>John 15.</margin> **In that day you will know** this mystery? For by these words He shows that we do not yet properly know it. Are we perhaps ignorant that the Father loves the Son, and is loved by Him in return? And who would not say that we are loved by Him who endured the most bitter passion for us? For no one has greater love than that he lay down his life for his friends. And He plainly sought why He loves us, saying: **If you love me, keep my commandments.** Therefore, he who keeps His commandments (as much as lies within him) is loved. If, then, we are not ignorant that the Son is loved by the Father, and that we are loved by the Son and love Him when we keep His commandments, we must understand this differently. For He clearly introduced another mode of being when He said: **In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.**

Therefore, man was made from the beginning according to the image of the creator, as it is written. 

<margin>Genesis 1</margin>
And although "image" is used in many ways, the most important sense is that man was made according to the image of God, which is to say, according to the likeness of incorruption <note>term: incorruption (the state of being free from decay or physical death)</note> and immortality—something which he could never possess by the mere logic of his own nature.
