For we do not say that; and we would gladly ask those who do: was the breath of God changed from its own nature when it became the human soul, or did it remain the same? For if they say the former, they are condemned for the crime of impiety by asserting that an unchangeable nature was changed. But if it remained what it was, how did it become a vessel for the fall into sin and passion, when it is entirely impossible for the divine nature to fail? 

Therefore, the human soul was not made from the breath of the divine substance. Rather, the creator fixed the breath of life—that is, the Holy Spirit—into the living human being and the properties of his nature (both soul and body) as a kind of seal of his own nature. By this, man was reshaped toward his original beauty and led back to the image of the creator, conforming himself to every kind of virtue through the grace of the Spirit dwelling within him. 

But since man held the reins of his own will—for liberty is also a part of that image, since God is of free power—he fell through change (Scripture clearly teaches the manner of this change and fall). 

<margin>Genesis 3</margin>
God wished to restore human nature to its original state. How he restored it, let us now consequently examine. It was not possible for man, who is corruptible by nature, to escape death in any other way unless, having obtained his first grace, he once again became a participant in God, who gives life to all things through the Son in the Spirit. Therefore, he shared in flesh and blood—that is, the Only-begotten

<margin>1 Timothy 2</margin>

When, therefore, you yourselves, who are corruptible by nature, see yourselves living in my likeness, then you will clearly know that since I am naturally Life, I have joined you to God the Father (who is also Life in his essence) through myself, and I have made you partakers of his immortality. 

Thus I am naturally in the Father, because I am born from him; but you are in me, and I in you, also naturally, by the logic of my becoming man. And so I made you partakers of the divine nature when I caused my Spirit to dwell in you. For Christ is in us through the Spirit, changing our corruptibility into incorruptibility. 

<margin>Romans 8</margin>
Therefore Paul says: **He who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will give life to your dead bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.** For if the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, he nevertheless comes through the Son and is his own; for all things are from the Father through the Son.

You see how the removal of the Spirit because of sin led us back to destruction. But when God sent his Spirit and made us partakers of his nature, the face of the earth was renewed through the Spirit. For we have been reshaped into a new life, casting far away the corruption toward which we were being carried because of sin, and we have obtained eternal life through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. With whom, and through whom, to God the Father be glory with the Holy Spirit forever and ever.
->Amen.<-

OF THE COMMENTARIES OF CYRIL
on John, Book Ten.

### CHAPTER I.
**He who has my commandments, and keeps them, he is the one who loves me. But he who loves me, is loved by my father: and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him.** Very clearly, then, the mystery will be revealed in us when we see ourselves living in his likeness. For he says, **Because I live, you also will live.** <margin>A</margin> For then our mind—not only through those things which we have heard and believed, but also through the outcome of the promise which we will possess in its completeness—will be more certain through the experience of the things themselves. 

But lest we believe that such a gift can happen to everyone simply, he immediately mentions those who love him, showing that this grace is not set aside for any others except those who keep his commandments. For these are the ones who love him. For although all people, both the good and the wicked, will rise again by the power of Christ, <margin>B</margin> they will not all return to life for glory. Rather, some will endure a life more cruel than any death, while others will live blessedly in Christ. 

That those who rise for punishment are never to taste the sweetness of blessedness, he shows by saying: **He who believes in the son has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the son shall not see life, but the wrath of God shall remain upon him.** <margin>John 3</margin> Pay close attention here: although all will rise, he asserts that the wicked are not even "living" in the true sense, calling only that state "life" which is found in rest, delights, and glory. 

By "delights," we mean in a spiritual sense the perfect knowledge of God and the exquisite revelation of God's mysteries—not in a mirror and a riddle <note>original: "in speculo & ænigmate"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12, often translated as "through a glass darkly."</note> as it is now, but openly, perfectly, and (so to speak) totally. For **that which is in part shall be done away with**, <margin>C</margin> <margin>1 Cor. 13</margin> as Paul says. Therefore, since our Lord Jesus Christ wished to show the future grace of perfect knowledge to those who love him and keep his commandments, and not to the wicked, he most appropriately added: **He who has my commandments, and keeps them, he is the one who loves me.** 

Now, whoever receives the faith and retains a clear knowledge of the Gospel precepts with a tenacious memory "has" the commandments. But he "keeps" them if he lives according to them. Thus, the foster-child of piety is made perfect, being recognized as one who lives holily in Christ through both faith and action. For **in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand**, <margin>D</margin> <margin>Deut. 19</margin> as it is written. God the Father and the Son also will love this person no less. For they are of one substance, one will, and one intention in all things. 

To those who are loved by God, he promises the most radiant rewards and a most brilliant crown. **I will manifest myself to him**, he says. To the pure, the vision of God is certainly the highest reward, in whom Christ will shine through the Spirit, illuminating every detail and raising their minds to the knowledge of himself with ineffable splendor. <margin>Psalm 48</margin> Those who reach this state will be truly blessed. It seems to me the Prophet sang of this in advance, saying: **I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me.** <margin>2 Cor. 13</margin> Paul also says:

### CHAPTER II.
**Judas (not the Iscariot) says to him: Lord, what has happened, that you are going to manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?** The disciple asks this out of love, but he did not correctly understand Christ’s words. For our Lord Jesus Christ promised an extraordinary knowledge to the saints, in whom the understanding of mysteries shines more expressively. 

For in those who have not reached such a level of goodness that they can attain the knowledge of supernatural things by the gift of the Spirit, knowledge is simpler and more unrefined <note>original: "rudior"; referring to a basic or foundational understanding compared to the "extraordinary" insight of the saints.</note>—such as the basic fact that Christ is the Son of the true God. Since there is such a great difference between the knowledge of the saints and the ignorance of the wicked, the disciple, making no distinction between these, asks out of love why he is going to manifest himself only to the saints and not to everyone. 

**What has happened?** he says, as if to say: "The intention of your coming, Lord, is not so that one part of humanity should know you and another part should be ignorant (for we have heard that **all flesh shall see the salvation of God**)." And you yourself proclaimed with a loud voice: **Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Sion, for behold I come, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord; and many nations shall rise up to the Lord on the day of the Lord, and they shall be a people for you.** 

From you also we have heard: **When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.** And to the Jews you said: **Because I have other sheep which are not of this fold, and those I must bring together, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd.** Since, therefore, your knowledge is preached as something that will pass to everyone, both by the voice of the prophets and by your own: what has happened...

For sin derives its origin from contempt for the commandments. For just as the deprivation of light produces the opposite—that is, darkness—so too wickedness originates from a will that chooses not to act uprightly. For opposites can never be seen simultaneously in one and the same subject, and virtue and vice are most distant from one another. Therefore, when one is absent from us (for we are necessarily always subject to one or the other), the other is certainly present. Consequently, if keeping the commandments is virtue, it is clear that wickedness arises from not keeping them. And just as the Father and the Son dwell in the one who keeps them—which is the origin and foundation of supreme glory and blessedness—likewise, the divine nature will never dwell in the one who does not keep them. This is nothing other than to never participate in any good. <note>Cyril uses the philosophical concept of "participation" (sharing in the nature of another) to describe the believer's relationship with God.</note> For these reasons, if the participation in God seems to anyone a glorious and excellent thing, if anyone desires the Father...

### CHAPTER 3

-> *If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our home with him.* <-

Where he spoke above <note>original: "vbi supra" — referring to verse 21 of John 14</note>, he said: *If anyone loves me, he will keep my commandments.* Therefore, we will find again in these words no small fruit of benefit already now emerging. For from these things which have been said here, it is clear that to love God is nothing other than to keep his commandments. Therefore, in this way Paul <note>The text attributes this to Paul, though the phrasing "This is the love of God, that we keep his commandments" is found in 1 John 5:3. This reflects a common practice where "the Apostle" could refer to the general body of apostolic teaching.</note> also wrote: *This is the love of God, that we keep his commandments.* And elsewhere: *But whoever keeps his word, truly in him the love of God is perfected.* 

But by what words do they say they will show they are "coming" to the one who loves him? *We will come,* he says, *and make our home with him.* Now, what is the manner of this "coming"? Will they migrate from place to place? Far be it! For the divine nature is incorporeal <note>original: "incorporea" — meaning God has no physical body and is not restricted by space or location</note>. 

How, then, do they come? They come, certainly, by illuminating our minds with their light and leading us to the knowledge of them. They come by manifesting themselves through those qualities that are proper to them. They come by dwelling within us—specifically through the Holy Spirit, who conforms us to himself so that we might be partakers of the divine nature <note>original: "diuinae naturae participes" — a reference to the concept of theosis, or the human person's participation in the life of God</note>. For through the Spirit, God dwells in us. Whence Paul also says: *Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you?* And elsewhere: *In whom you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.* 

Indeed, he is said to "dwell" in those whom the Holy Spirit sanctifies and illuminates with his grace. For in this same way, he also dwelt of old in the prophets, as Isaiah says: *I say to you, that I will dwell in the holy ones, and walk among them.* <note>Isaiah 57:15 and Leviticus 26:12 are often combined in patristic citations regarding God's indwelling.</note>

<summary>Cyril explains that loving God is synonymous with keeping His commandments and describes the "coming" of the Father and Son as a spiritual illumination rather than a physical movement. not only for his own benefit, but rather for this glorious purpose: that he might openly return to the dignity, power, and glory of the Godhead, and sit at the right hand of the Father—the Father himself willing it so, for he loves his own Son as the fruit of his own substance. "Therefore," he says, "**if you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father.**" <note>original: "Propterea si diligeretis me, inquit, gauderetis utique, quia uado ad patrem." — John 14:28.</note> And certainly, it would have been a proof of the disciples' love toward Christ if they did not grieve at his departure, but rather remembered that he was returning from the mob of the Jews to the glory of the Godhead. For this reason, his disciples and friends ought to rejoice greatly. However, he calls the Father "greater," not insofar as he sits at his right hand as God, but insofar as he was still with us—that is, he was made like us. The time had not yet come in which he was to fully assume the dignity of the Godhead. Hence, when vinegar and gall were given to him on the cross in his thirst, he said after he tasted it: **It is finished.** <margin>John 19</margin> For then the time of his state of humility reached its end. For he was crucified as a man, but he cast down the empire of death not as a man, but as God. The Father is therefore "greater" because the Son was still in a state of servitude. For this reason, he also called the Father "his God," attributing this even to his humanity. For it is clear that he descended from supreme excellence to a servant’s nature, and from equality with the Father to our condition—none of which, we believe, happened to the Father. Therefore, by this reasoning, the Father is greater than the Son who humbled himself, until he restored his humility to its original glory. But since we have already said much regarding the equality of the Father and the Son in earlier sections, it would be appropriate to move on with the exposition of the Gospel. Truly, however, because a certain heretic <margin>Heretics write for the sake of blasphemy.</margin> <note>Cyril is likely attacking a contemporary opponent, possibly from the school of Antioch or an Arian writer, who used this verse to argue that the Son is naturally inferior to the Father.</note>—illustrious among the Jews for his skill in sacred letters—wrote intolerable blasphemies against the Only-begotten while explaining this passage, I considered it my duty to argue against the falsehood of his speech. But I think I should first transcribe some of his own words.

"He calls the Father 'greater,'" he says, "not only to avoid the crime of ingratitude, but also to refute the false opinion of those who think the same things exist in both, and simultaneously to exterminate the opinion of Sabellius." <note>Sabellius taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were the same person; the opponent argues that "greater" proves they are distinct and unequal.</note> And after a few more words, he says, "Some have proceeded to such arrogance that they will in no way allow themselves to hear that the Father is greater than the Son in deity, but think the Father’s nature exceeds the Son’s only in humanity. These people are unable to understand that things of different kinds cannot be compared to one another. For no one calls a man wiser than a beast of burden, nor a horse faster than a tortoise; rather, everyone compares man to man and horse to horse. Since this is the case, they must—even if unwillingly—concede that the Father is greater than the Son in deity. For those who think this refers to the humanity of the Only-begotten diminish the dignity of the Father as much as they can." These are his trifles. And consider, I pray, how his speech contradicts itself, if nothing else. He praises the Son because he seems grateful to the Father by professing himself to be lesser; but he has not considered for what reason Christ touched upon these theological sentiments just now. For it is no small thing to say all things at the appropriate time. Why, then, was it necessary to say these things just now to his sorrowful disciples? What consolation could these words have brought to those who were mourning? Why, as if rebuking them sharply, does he say: "If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I go to the Father: because the Father is greater than I"? Do you think they could have cast off their inner turmoil because he was leaving them to seek someone "greater"? In what way is this a form of consolation? And certainly, when Philip asked, saying: **Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us,** then he opportunely showed the highest equality, affirming that the Father was in him, and he in the Father. **Have you not known me yet, Philip?** he said, **He who sees me, sees the Father. Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me? I and the Father are one.** <margin>John 10</margin> <note>Combining John 14:9 and John 10:30.</note> But then indeed, as we said, he opportunely revealed that he was equal to the Father. But now, by what reasoning—when he wanted to soothe the grief of the disciples—could this remedy be applied: that they should instead rejoice because he goes to the Father? Will it not be clear to everyone that he was returning to the glory of the Father, from which he had descended of his own accord? Was he not right to command his friends to rejoice for this reason? But let these things be set aside for now. As for their thought that we use a useless comparison when we compare the humanity of Christ to the nature of the Godhead—saying the Son was "emptied" because of his humanity—they err vehemently. For we believe the Son is lesser than the Father insofar as he was made man, and we confess that he returned to equality with the Father after he ascended into heaven; not as if to a new or foreign equality and glory, but to that...

->496<-

Are you unaware that a comparison is typically only made between things that belong to the same kind and nature? <note>Cyril is applying a principle of logic here: for a comparison of "greater" or "lesser" to be meaningful, the two things being compared must share the same category of existence.</note> For no one would say, for example, that a man is "greater" than a dog, or a dog "greater" than a mouse; rather, a man is compared to a man, and a dog to a dog. 

Since, therefore, our Savior compares himself to the Father when he says, "**The Father is greater than I**," who cannot see that he must be of the same substance <term>substance: the Greek *ousia* or Latin *substantia*, referring to the essential nature or "stuff" that makes God what He is</term> as the Father? Otherwise, on what grounds could we say he is a "creature" <term>creature: a created thing (*creatura*); Cyril argues that if Christ were a different kind of being than the Father, the comparison "greater than I" would be as nonsensical as comparing a man to a dog</term>, when he is being measured against the Father according to his nature?

<summary>Cyril explains that meaningful comparisons of "greater" or "lesser" can only exist between things of the same nature, using the analogy of humans and animals. He concludes that because Jesus compares himself to the Father, they must share the same divine essence.</summary>

498 ->ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN<-
->That the Son is of one substance with the Father.<-
### CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>Chapter of John 15</margin>
"**I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.**" <note>original: "Ego sum uitis uera, et pater meus agricola est."</note>

In order to show how much we ought to cling to him and depend upon him, and how much this benefits us, he called himself a "vine" by way of example, and those who believe in him "branches" fixed to that vine. Through the participation of the Spirit, by whom we are joined to the Savior, we share in his nature. For the bonding of the branches to the vine—as it relates to us—is voluntary, since we approach Christ by our own will. However, as it relates to the vine binding us to itself, it is a matter of our state of being <term>habitualis: referring to an essential condition or "habit" of being rather than a fleeting feeling</term>. For by a righteous will, we approach him through faith. We are made, so to speak, of his own "kind," having obtained from him the dignity of being adopted as children of God. For as Paul says, "He who adheres to the Lord is one spirit with him." <margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin>

Therefore, just as he is called the "base and foundation" in the prophetic voice—for in him we are built up as living stones, <margin>Isaiah 28</margin> made into spiritual beings for a dwelling place of God in the spirit and a holy priesthood, and we cannot be built up except through Christ—so too is he called the "vine," as the mother and nourisher of the branches. For we are reborn from Christ and through him in the spirit to bear the fruit of life—not that old life, but this new one, which consists of faith and love toward him. We are preserved in this state and, as it were, "grafted" into him in a certain way: that is, by firmly holding onto the commandments delivered to us by him, and striving to preserve the goodness of this noble status. This happens if we do not offend the Holy Spirit, through whom God dwells in us. 

For John clearly shows how we are in Christ: "**By this,**" he says, "**we know that we are in him and he in us: because he has given us of his Spirit.**" <margin>1 John 4</margin> And again: "**He who says he remains in him ought himself also to walk just as he walked.**" <margin>1 John 2</margin> And elsewhere even more clearly: "**He who keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in him.**" For if keeping the commandments produces love toward him, and through love we are joined to him, how is it not true that those who keep the commandments remain in him?

But just as a root sends its own quality into the branches, so the only-begotten Son of God imparts a kinship <note>original: "affinitatem"</note> of the Father's nature and his own (so to speak) by giving the Spirit to the saints. He joins them to himself through faith and holiness, nourishing them toward piety and every kind of virtue. 

Furthermore, he calls the Father the "vinedresser" <note>original: "agricolam," literally "farmer" or "cultivator"</note> so that this work—which is the miraculous labor of the entire Trinity—might not seem to be done by the Son alone. For not only our salvation, but indeed all things that are done by God, are done by one will and power of the supreme nature. And therefore, giving thanks to God because he has had mercy on us, we call him "Savior"—attributing this not to the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit separately, but to the Godhead simply. Therefore, the Father nourishes us toward piety and faith through the Son in the Spirit, and performs the work of a vinedresser: looking after us, cherishing us, and bringing us to virtue with all care through the Son, likewise in the Spirit. 

For in my judgment, we will understand this more correctly in this way. For if we assign some things to the Father and other things separately to the Son—since the Son is called the "vine" and the Father the "vinedresser"—we would seem 

499
->ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN<-
to be sustained and nourished by the Son alone, while being "cultivated" by the Father only through a mere visit. For a vine nourishes its own branches, but a vinedresser only visits and cultivates the vine. Therefore, this work is not to be separated from the Father, nor that work from the Son, nor either from the Spirit. For all things are from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. 

The reason he called the Father the cultivator of the vine was to prevent anyone from attributing our salvation to the only-begotten Son alone; and furthermore, so that we might learn that we stand in need of divine visitation. Most fittingly, then, when he named the vine and the branches, he also made mention of the cultivator, demonstrating that we are led to virtue and sustained by the care, providence, and governance of God. 

If, however, we believe that the Son is naturally in the Father, and the Father in the Son, and that all things are from them in the Spirit as from one Godhead, then the Father will not be separated from nourishing us, nor will the Son be a stranger to the "cultivation." And this is only right. For where there is a supreme identity of nature, even though some things may seem to be done in many and various ways, there is nevertheless one operation, in no way distinct. Truly, there is one nature in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. How then can whatever is done divinely not be the work of the one Godhead? 

Wherefore our Lord Jesus Christ also, wishing to show that he works together with the Father, said to the impious Judeans: "**I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of them do you stone me?**" <margin>John 10</margin> And again: "**My Father works even until now, and I work.**" For no one (I think) would suppose the Father works anything separately from the Son. For since the Son is the Wisdom and Power of the Father, <margin>The quibble of the impious</margin> through whom the Father does all things, he says for this reason that he does nothing of himself, but that the Father, who remains in him, performs the works himself. 

Therefore, Christ holds the place of the vine, and we the place of the branches; we, depending on him, draw the nourishment of the virtues and the grace of the Spirit for our sustenance and for spiritual fruit. But I cannot follow the work I have set out for myself in such a way that I neglect those things which certain people...

<summary>Cyril interprets the metaphor of the vine and vinedresser from John 15, arguing that while Christ is the vine who nourishes believers, the work of salvation is a unified operation of the entire Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit).</summary>

Cyril is refuting heretical interpretations (likely Arian or Eunomian) that use the metaphor of the "Vinedresser" and the "Vine" to suggest the Son is of a different nature than the Father.</meta>

to bring across that meaning which was spoken through a likeness. For I think, if we wish to rightly understand what is being said, we must always consider the intention and the purpose for which Christ was speaking. Therefore, I pray you who are about to read this, consider it diligently. Christ did not intend merely to show himself to be different from the Father in nature, nor for this reason did he name himself the vine and the Father the vinedresser. For if this had been his purpose, why did he bring up nothing else? Or why did he use a likeness at all, when he could have done so much more briefly and clearly using only the names of "Father" and "Son"? It was not, therefore, what those men have devised from their own minds, but rather this that he wished to show: that just as the quality and nourishment are provided to the branches of trees from the root, so too the fruit of spiritual virtues is granted to us by him. <margin>James 1</margin> For every good thing we have is not from ourselves, but is given by God; to God, however, nothing is given. For he himself is the origin of all things; therefore Christ is the root and, as it were, the vine, and we are the branches. But if the Father is the vinedresser, he is not for that reason understood to be of a different nature, nor did Christ wish to signify this; rather, by showing the root and origin, the supreme nature of all good things, he attributed to the Father the practice of love, by which he visits us like a vinedresser.

But since they <note>The "they" refers to Cyril's theological opponents who denied the full divinity or the physical union of Christ with believers.</note> think that we cannot by any reasoning attribute these things to the humanity of Christ—because they think we are joined to him by faith and love, not by the flesh—come, let us say a few words about this, and show that the sense of the sacred scriptures is being expounded perversely by them. We do not, however, deny that we are spiritually joined to Christ by right faith and sincere love. But we utterly deny that there is no manner of connection according to the flesh with him, and we say that such an idea is entirely foreign to the divine scriptures. For who has doubted that Christ is a vine in this way too, and we are the branches, who acquire life from there? Listen to Paul saying: *Because we are all one body in Christ.* <margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin> Because even if we are many, we are still one in him. For we all participate in the one bread. Or perhaps he thinks the power of the mystical blessing <note>original: "mysticae benedictionis" — a common patristic term for the Eucharist.</note> is unknown to us? When this occurs in us, does it not also bodily make Christ dwell in us by the communication of his flesh? For why are the members of the faithful the members of Christ? *Do you not know,* he says, *that your members are members of Christ?* <margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin> Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot? Heaven forbid! The Savior also says: *He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.* <margin>John 6</margin> From this it must be considered that Christ is in us not by disposition <note>original: "habitudine," meaning a mental or moral inclination.</note> alone, which is understood through love, but also by natural participation. For just as if someone mixed wax melted by fire with other wax similarly melted, so that one thing seems to be made from both: so by the communication of the body and blood of Christ, he himself is in us, and we in him. For this corruptible nature of the body could not otherwise be brought across to incorruptibility and life, unless the body of natural life were joined to it. If you do not believe me saying these things, 

<column-break/>

BOOK TEN. 501

(I beseech you) give your faith to Christ. *Amen, amen,* he says, *I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you.* <margin>John 6</margin> *He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.* You hear him openly crying out that they will not have life unless we drink his blood and eat his flesh. And he says *in you*, that is, in your body. Now, life itself can rightly be understood as the flesh of Life: for this raises us up on the last day. And I shall not find it a burden to say how: the flesh of the Only-begotten, having been made the flesh of Life, was brought across to the power of life; therefore it cannot be overcome by death. For this reason, having been made in us, it drives out destruction from us. For the Only-begotten Son of God is not absent from it. Since he is one with his own flesh, he says: *I will raise him up.*

Why then does he <note>The heretical opponent.</note> deny that we are called branches according to the flesh? Can it not be fittingly said that his humanity is the vine and we are the branches because of the identity of nature? For the vine and the branches are of the same nature. Thus, both spiritually and bodily, we are branches and Christ is the vine. But the adversary of Christ contends that Christ is called a vine only by reason of his deity: so that since the Father is called the vinedresser, he can show a diversity of substance against the dogmas of the Church. But I wonder, if he thinks the Son is different by nature from the Father, how he can use the names of Father and Son. For how will he truly be a Son if he was not born from his substance? He who denies the Son also denies the Father; and he who confesses the Son also confesses the Father, as John says. <margin>1 John 2</margin> And certainly it is so. For if one is taken away or placed, the other is removed or placed. He will not be a Father unless there is a Son, nor will a Son be understood unless a Father is understood. But he who thinks the Only-begotten is diverse in substance from the Father denies that he is the Son, and therefore also denies that the Father is the Father. And where is the faith of the Church? Where is the glory of the Trinity in naked names? Do you not see that all things which have been said by the scriptures concerning the supreme nature are being dragged down?

But perhaps, fearing the magnitude of this impiety, he will say the Son is indeed different in nature, yet he understands him to be born from the Father. For if he does not feel that he is fixed in the same impiety by which all things are said to be "from God"—as some creatures are said to be through a disposition found in love according to the will—but instead says he is truly born from the Father, yet not of the same substance <note>original: "consubstantialem" — the Latin equivalent of the Greek *homoousios*.</note> with him, then he will also be impious toward the Father himself; since the Father alone would have suffered what the nature of creatures cannot endure. And what is worse, the Father himself will be dragged down to the level of creatures. For he says the Only-begotten is the vine, not according to the flesh, but only according to the deity. Let him say, then, whether he thinks the Son is the true God, or a counterfeit <note>original: "adulterinum" — used here to mean a "fake" or illegitimate Son.</note> one by name only. If by name only, and not according to nature, let him hear what the Savior cries out: *I am the truth.* <margin>John 14</margin> Truth, however, in no way accepts empty names. Let him also hear what this John cries out elsewhere: *And may we be in the true God, Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life.* <margin>1 John 5</margin> If, therefore, the Only-begotten is the true God, and the Father is distinct from him...

<summary>Cyril argues that the "Vine and Branches" metaphor proves a real, physical union between Christ and believers through the Eucharist, and defends the Son's shared substance with the Father against heretical claims of a "different nature."</summary>

### BOOK TEN

...be joined to him only through the **affection of the will** <note>original: "sola voluntatis dilectione" — Cyril is arguing against those who claimed our connection to Christ is merely psychological or moral, rather than a real, ontological union.</note> and the disposition of the mind, let us demonstrate that it is necessary to believe that we are also joined to Him by a physical participation. For just as the vine is joined to its branches, so too the Savior is joined to us. 

**"Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he takes away; and every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit."** <margin>John 15:2</margin>

Observe here the dual operation of the Vinedresser. For the Father, who is the Vinedresser, removes the sterile and useless branches—those who perhaps bear the name of Christ but do not produce the works of faith. But he does not leave the fruitful branches to their own devices; instead, He *prunes* them. <note>original: "purgabit" — This Latin term means both "to prune" a plant and "to cleanse" or "purify" a person. Cyril plays on this double meaning.</note> 

This pruning is not a cutting away of our nature, but a removal of the superfluities and "wild" growth of the soul—those worldly cares and carnal desires that hinder us from producing spiritual fruit. It is an act of divine cultivation, ensuring that the strength of the branch is not wasted on vanity but directed toward virtue.

<column-break/>

We must also understand that the Father performs this cleansing work through the power of the Word. For as Christ says a little later, *“You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.”* <margin>John 15:3</margin> The Word of God serves as the pruning hook, separating what is healthy from what is diseased within the soul.

Therefore, when the Father is called a "Vinedresser," it does not imply that He is of a different or superior nature to the Son. Rather, it signifies His providential care for us, the branches. He tends to us with love, pruning away what is dead so that we might more abundantly share in the life-giving sap that flows from the true Vine, which is Christ. <note>Cyril is careful to ensure that the metaphor of the "Vinedresser" (Father) and "Vine" (Son) is seen as a description of how God works in the world (the "economy"), not a statement that the Son is a created being subordinate to the Father.</note>

<summary>Cyril argues that believers are physically and substantially united to Christ, not just through shared intent. He explains that God the Father prunes the faithful to remove worldly distractions and increase their spiritual productivity.</summary>

### CHAPTER XVII

*I am the vine, you are the branches: he who abides in me, and I in him, the same brings forth much fruit: for without me you can do nothing. If any man abides not in me, he is cast out as a branch, and is withered, and they gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they burn.* Here, he clearly shows why he called himself a vine: so that we might see with our own eyes, through this example, that by remaining in him like branches and drawing out the "sap" of the vine, we are able to bring forth spiritual fruit. But those who leap away from him—either because they fail in faith or in the keeping of the commandments—will not only produce no fruit but will also suffer eternal fire. For whoever falls away from the piety or the love of Christ hands themselves over to punishment, just as a cut-off branch is useful for nothing else but the fire. The apostles themselves are the best example for us; because they remained in Christ and could be separated from him by no force, they attained eternal praise and brought forth the fruit of their virtue: the conversion of the world. Therefore, we do not doubt that they will hold unfading crowns in the presence of God. But the servant Judas, cut off from the spiritual vine by his greed, lost the grace of the Spirit, was cast out, and like a useless twig, was handed over to the fire. Thus, Christ leads us to remain with him in two ways: partly by the desire for glory, which the fruitful branches will obtain, and partly by the fear of the fire, to which those who separate themselves from him will be delivered. Moreover, he names the Father as the "vinedresser" <note>original: "Agricolam"</note>, attributing this to the divine nature, as we have said. For the Son himself is the "Hand" of the Father, through whom all things were made. *My hand,* <margin>Isaiah 66</margin> he says, *has made all these things,* and the Scriptures testify that all things were made through the Son. For this reason, the Son is called the "Hand of the Father." Paul also understood this "grafting" <note>original: "incisionem" — specifically the process of being cut into or grafted onto a plant.</note> which is understood here, saying: <margin>Romans 11</margin> *Behold therefore the goodness and severity of God: on them which fell, severity; but toward thee, goodness, if thou continue in his goodness: otherwise thou also shalt be cut off.*

### CHAPTER XVIII

*If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, you shall ask what you will, and it shall be done unto you.* He says that the root of heavenly benevolence and its firm foundation is if they keep the dogmas and commandments of the Gospel teaching as a spiritual deposit. To those who keep them, he promises that the good things they ask for will be present without delay: *If you abide,* he says, *in me, and my words abide in you, you shall ask what you will, and it shall be done unto you.* For it is possible to abide in Christ and yet not have his words in you. For there is a double path, as we just said: through faith and through love, for the sake of which the commandments are kept. Since this is the case, those who confess Christ with empty words, but are not shaped toward perfection by the observation of the commandments—that is, by love—even though they cling to Christ by faith and "abide" in him in this sense, they nevertheless do not have his words. They have not <margin>Matthew 7</margin> forgotten the Gospel preaching, but...

<column-break/>

->507<-

...captured by the enticements of pleasures, they cast away the grace of the Spirit. Concerning these people, the Savior himself says: *Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that does the will of my Father who is in heaven.* Moreover, the disciple of Christ shows that faith alone is not sufficient for salvation, writing: <margin>James 2</margin> *You believe that there is one God; the demons also believe and tremble.* If, therefore, faith alone were sufficient, the multitude of demons could not perish. For this reason, the works of love must be added to faith. For he who does this remains in Christ through faith and preserves his words in his heart, as it is said in the Psalms: <margin>Psalm 118 <note>Psalm 119:11 in modern Bibles.</note></margin> *In my heart have I hidden your words, that I might not sin against you.* For just as one who hides fire in a bronze vessel does not lack the heat of the fire, so he who retains the divine words in his soul and strives to keep them always burns with the love of virtue. For it is written: <margin>Psalm 118 <note>Psalm 119:140 in modern Bibles.</note></margin> *Your word is exceedingly refined <note>original: "Ignitum" — literally "set on fire" or "fiery," often used to mean purified or burning with power.</note>, and your servant has loved it.* Therefore, he who remains in Christ with sincere faith and keeps his commandments will be granted immediately whatever he asks. Will he then obtain it, you ask, if he asks for something evil? Not at all, I say, not at all. It is not possible that one who remains in Christ and keeps his commandments would ask for anything that does not please God. Therefore, he promises this to those who retain and keep his doctrine in their souls. Thus, if we wish to receive when we ask, let us live rightly: and whatever we ask for, Christ will provide for us without delay.

### CHAPTER XIX

*In this is my Father glorified, that you bear much fruit, and so shall you be my disciples.* He says that his Father is glorified because His ineffable goodness and mercy, made known to all, has brought Him a crown of glory, as it were. <margin>John 3</margin> *For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son: that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.* The life of all, therefore, is the work of the Father, which was accomplished through Christ. <margin>John 17</margin> For this reason, he said to the Father: *I have glorified thee: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do.* For he himself brought us salvation from the Father—not as a servant, but as the Wisdom and Power of the Father, without whom nothing at all can be done. For all things are through him. Wherefore, David also, praying to the Father, refers the management of our salvation to the Power and Wisdom of the Father <margin>Psalm 67 <note>Psalm 68:28 in modern Bibles.</note></margin> (the Son), saying: *Command, O God, thy strength; confirm, O God, that which thou hast wrought in us.* And again: <margin>Psalm 71 <note>Psalm 72:1 in modern Bibles.</note></margin> *Give the king thy judgment, O God.* For it is the work of him alone, who reigns with the Father, to be able to reform the entire nature of man to its original state. The Father, therefore, is glorified by giving his own Son for the redemption of men, whom he willed to become man—not to acquire any good for himself, who is always most perfect, but so that men might bear much fruit and be made disciples of Christ. For unless the Son of God had become man, we would never have produced fruit by participating in the Spirit, clinging to him like branches to a vine; this fruit he calls "much" in comparison to the fruit of the Law. For the <margin>Philippians</margin> Law [made] nothing perfect...

### 514 BOOK TEN

...the grace of **adoption**. <note>original: "per adoptionis gratiam." In a theological context, this refers to humans being brought into God's family, no longer as mere subjects but as children and "friends."</note> For he does not say that he has revealed absolutely all the secrets of the Father, but rather those things which he "heard"—that is, those things which were fitting and necessary for his listeners to hear and understand at that time.

**For a servant does not know what his master is doing.** <note>Quoting the latter half of John 15:15.</note> 

By this, he means that the condition of a servant does not carry with it the right to share in a master's private counsel or secrets. He uses the term "servant" to describe anyone who has not yet been raised to this high dignity of friendship. On the other hand, he calls those "friends" whom he has already renewed through the **Holy Spirit** and elevated to the glory of adoption. 

<margin>John 15:15</margin>

While a servant is kept at a distance from his master's inner will and serves merely as an instrument for carrying out commands, a friend is made a participant in the master's very mind. Therefore, the Lord shows that the knowledge he shares is the ultimate proof of this bond. Just as a master does not disclose his private thoughts to his slaves but only issues orders, Christ opens the "ears" of the soul to the mysteries of the Father for those he loves.

### CHAPTER XXIX.
**But all these things they will do to you for my name’s sake, because they do not know him who sent me.** He asserts that there will be no cause for the wicked to persecute the apostles other than the name of Christ. For this "crime" and this "fault" is attributed to believers by the unbelieving; but with a certain hope of reward, all things brought against us for the name of Christ must be endured with a great heart. For this name alone renders things that are terrifying even to hear, pleasant to those who believe. Whence, when the apostles had been beaten by the Jews, they went out
[Marginal note: Acts 5.] (as it is written) **rejoicing, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus Christ.** For this reason, they gave us similar counsel: **Let none of you suffer**, they say, **as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoer; but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this name.**
[Marginal note: 1 Peter 4.] Therefore, the danger undertaken for Christ is exceedingly sweet when it proceeds from the love of God. It must be carefully considered, however, how Christ—here again binding himself into <term>one nature</term> <note>original: "unam naturam." This refers to the doctrine of the Consubstantiality, meaning the Father and the Son share the same divine essence.</note> with the Father—says the Father is unknown to the persecutors. For he who disparages the Son is ignorant of the Son; and he who is ignorant of the Son is surely also ignorant of the Father, because of the <term>identity of substance</term> <note>original: "identitatē substantiæ." A technical theological term asserting that the Father and Son are the same "stuff" or being.</note>. Conversely, he who is not ignorant of what the Father truly is, cannot be ignorant of the Son. Therefore, that the Father is unknown to the persecutors is proven by the fact that they sin against the Son. But since he does not say "my Father," but "him who sent me," he shows that the iniquity of the persecutors is twofold. For they do not only ignore him from whom the Son originates, nor will they be condemned for this impiety alone; but they also find fault with the very wisdom and good will of God. For since God sent his own Son to raise the fallen, to restore the corrupt, and to give life to the world, they did not hesitate to oppose the ministers of this <term>dispensation</term> <note>original: "dispensationis." In this context, it refers to the "divine plan" or the "management" of human salvation through the Incarnation.</note> with all their might. Thus, by the word "sending," he signified the whole <term>mystery of the incarnation</term>. He who has been ignorant of the one who sends, has at the same time been ignorant of God, and despises the mystery of the sending—that is, the Incarnation.

Anyone examining more closely will never deny that all things are said and done through the Son—who is **consubstantial** <term>consubstantial</term> <note>Meaning of the same essence; sharing the same divine nature as the Father.</note> with the Father—according to the Father's will. Just as there is one shared glory for both, so one cannot be neglected without the other being held in contempt. Furthermore, the harassment of the Apostles also ascends to Him who raised them to the peak of the apostolate. For we have learned that it was said even to Samuel regarding the children of Israel: <margin>1 Samuel 8</margin> "It is not you," He said, "but me they have rejected." <note>original: "Non te, inquit, sed me contempserunt."</note> It is therefore exceedingly dangerous not to attribute proper honor to the saints, since contempt for them passes through to Him by whom they were sent.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.
**But these things I have spoken to you, that when the hour comes, you may remember them, because I told you.**
He says: I did not speak these things for this reason—that the strength of your mind might be weakened or that you might be terrified before the dangers arrive. <margin>B</margin> Rather, I spoke first so that, having remembered that these things were foretold to you by me, you might wonder all the more; and in the very time of the dangers, your faith in me might be made more certain by the outcome of events and more stable. For how is He not God by nature who knows future things as if they were present? Furthermore, coming dangers are softened by forethought, and the mind is better formed by long consideration (for sudden things usually seem very bitter, which is why <margin>Psalm 119</margin> the Psalmist also said: *I am prepared, and I am not troubled*). Therefore, He commands them to remember that all these things had been foretold to them, so that from this they may firmly believe Him to be the true God and not doubt that they can easily be liberated from dangers through Him.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.
**But these things I did not say to you from the beginning: because I was with you. And now I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, where are you going? But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.**
He now confirms the minds of the disciples by another very useful reasoning. For since they had lived with Him for a long time and had perceived His omnipotence in many things, they could not doubt that they would overcome all dangers by His power. But because they have now heard, contrary to their expectations, that great sorrows are coming to them, He brings forward the necessary cause for why He did not explain these things to them from the beginning—lest, being troubled, they think to themselves and say: "Our hope has deceived us, we who believed we were called to good things, and now calamities and hardships are predicted to be imminent." He says, "I did not say these things because I was with you." Indeed, His presence was sufficient to snatch them from every temptation. But since He now goes to the Father, He explained everything to them at the opportune time. Previously, however, it was a time for silence, when there was no need for them to know these things. How then, someone might ask, did He promise <margin>Matthew 28</margin> that He would be with them even to the end of the age, yet now say He fortifies them with the prediction of future things because He is not going to be with them? No one doubts that when He ascended into heaven, although He has always been present by the power of the Spirit, He has nevertheless been absent in the presence of the flesh. This matter affected the hearts of the disciples with great grief, nor did they ask Him for what reason He would do so, understanding that He had already determined it thus. Therefore, He grants them pardon of His own accord, even though they were unseasonably silent; for by asking,

<column-break/>

495
<margin>A</margin> they could have learned the cause more extensively, from which they would have obtained the greatest benefit.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.
**But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go. For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you: but if I go, I will send him to you.**
I perceive, He says, that you are moved by great grief because I have entirely resolved to depart. Nor is this undeserved, especially since you have heard that great temptations are coming to you. But since utility must be preferred to pleasant things, I will open the truth to you: it is expedient for you that I go. But some simpler person might be troubled. For if it was better for Christ to depart, His presence seems to have been somewhat of a hindrance; why then, such a person might ask, was He present for so long? <margin>B</margin> We, however, although we rightly leave all such things to the knowledge of the Savior, nevertheless concede that something [on this matter] can be said. If anyone considers more diligently, he will in no way be troubled, remembering that there is a convenient time for every thing, and all things are good in their own time. Therefore, the Lord was present in this world corporally at the opportune time. And again, when He knew it was necessary, He returned to the Father in the body. Nor do we entirely deny that the presence of Christ was always expedient for the disciples, nor because His presence had been useful was His departure (which was of maximum benefit) to be despised; for both were applied most usefully in their own time. But come, for the benefit of the readers, let us briefly touch upon the cause of the incarnation of the Only-begotten and the great utility of His departure to the Father. <margin>C</margin> Man, therefore, was made [in Christ], so that He might liberate us from the destruction which the ancient curse had brought in; and since there is no inclination in the divine nature toward sinning, He assumed all of us through that very flesh: for in Him we all are, by that reasoning by which He is man. <margin>This earthly shadow of the flesh assumed by Christ.</margin> He assumed us, therefore, so that He might extinguish this earthly shadow—that is, the passions of the flesh and the law of sin which had broken into the members of men; and additionally, that He might sanctify our nature and become the leader to piety and the best discipline of living for the human race. And these things He indeed effected by being made man. But He did not only wish to liberate us from destruction and sin, but also to lead us back to the heavens themselves, and make us participants of the highest good, numbered in the company of the angels. And just as through His resurrection He destroyed death, <margin>D</margin> so He might place [us] before the Father Himself. <margin>Hebrews 9</margin> Correcting understanding this, Paul says: *For Christ did not enter into holy places made with hands, nor into copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, that he might appear before the face of God for us.* You hear that although He is always with the Father because of the identity of substance, He appears to the Father not for Himself, but for us. Thus, since He is the **firstfruits** <term>firstfruits</term> <note>original: "primitiæ." A biblical metaphor for the first part of a harvest which consecrates the rest; Christ is the first of humanity to enter heaven, opening the way for others.</note> of our race, when He ascended into heaven with His flesh, He established us (as I just said) before the Father. And just as, although He is life according to nature, He nevertheless died for our sake; so also, even if He Himself always sees the Father and is seen by Him, now however—that is, after He was made man—He is said to have appeared to Him as a man, not for His own sake, but for ours. Therefore, it seemed that this was lacking to the [divine] dispensation, so that we also might ascend into the heavens themselves in Christ...

### CHAPTER 41.

"I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. However, when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will teach you all truth. For he will not speak on his own authority; but whatever he hears, he will speak, and he will tell you things to come." Seeing that they already desired to have knowledge of future things, he does not rebuke them, but promises that they will receive it from the <term>Paraclete</term> <note>From the Greek 'paraklētos,' meaning a helper, comforter, or legal advocate. Perhaps, because he knew they were too weak to receive greater things without the Spirit—for as the Evangelist says <margin>John 7</margin> "the Holy Spirit had not yet come, because Christ was not yet glorified"—because, I say, he saw they were weak in the face of higher things, he speaks these words. He affirms that many profound things remain for him to say, which are beyond what the human soul can carry. "I pass these over in silence," he says, "because you have not yet been reformed by my Spirit." For when, by his help, you emerge as different men—when you cast aside the <term>legal figures</term> <note>Refers to the symbolic laws and ceremonies of the Old Testament (the Mosaic Law), which the author views as "shadows" of the spiritual reality brought by Christ.</note> under his protection, and when by his aid you prefer the beauty of spiritual worship over those shadows—then, and only then, will you understand the full power of the mystery concerning me. I believe this passage should be understood in the same way the Savior signified elsewhere through a certain similarity, <margin>Matthew 9</margin> saying: "No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, nor do they put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the skins burst and the wine is spilled. Instead, new wine must be put into new wineskins." For those who have not yet been reformed by the Spirit into a new way of living and a new doctrine, the fresh preaching of the Gospel and the sublime mystery of the Trinity must not be handed over. Rightly, therefore, the interpretation of higher matters is reserved for the future renewal through the Spirit. It is very easy to prove that before the Savior’s resurrection and before the coming of the Spirit, the disciples lived in the Jewish manner. <margin>Matthew 16</margin> For Blessed Peter, the prince of all the disciples, resisted the Savior when he told them what he was about to suffer, crying out: "Lord, be kind to yourself; let this not happen to you." Even though the prophets had clearly foretold everything, he was unable to understand it. <margin>Acts 10</margin> It is also written in the Acts of the Apostles that when he was hungry and wanted to eat something, he saw a certain vessel, like a large linen sheet, being let down from heaven by its four corners, in which all kinds of earthly, aerial, and aquatic animals appeared to be. And when he heard a great voice saying, "Kill, Peter, and eat," he did not hesitate to answer, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything common or impure." Rightly, then, was he rebuked with these words: "What God has purified, you must not call common." And certainly, he ought to have remembered the words of the <margin>Matthew 15</margin> Lord...

## CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>Chapter 17 of John</margin>
*Jesus spoke these things: and lifting up his eyes to heaven, he said: Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may also glorify you.* <note>original: "Pater uenit hora, clarifica filiū tuum..." — The opening of John 17, often called the "High Priestly Prayer."</note> When Christ had delivered the truth of his teaching to his apostles as a kind of provision for the journey <term>viaticum</term> <note>A "viaticum" was originally money or supplies for a journey; in a religious sense, it refers to spiritual nourishment for the soul's journey.</note> toward salvation, and had rendered them stronger against temptations, he immediately turned himself from this conversation into a state of prayer. He did not allow any time to intervene between his speech to the disciples and his prayer to God the Father, chiefly establishing for us in this act a rule for the discipline of living. For it is necessary to know that if anyone wishes to live piously and holily, he ought either to speak usefully to his brothers or to employ the use of speech in the work of prayer, lest empty wordiness seem to find a place. In this way, the honor of the tongue is preserved, for vain speech is not without blame. <margin>Proverbs 10</margin> And from much speaking (as a certain Wise Man said) sin cannot fail to arise. <margin>James 3</margin> But he is wise who spares his lips. This is truly wonderful and most useful to us: he begins his prayer from his own glorification and that of the Father, and then he joined ours to it. Why so? He delivers to us a certain duty of prayer. <margin>Matthew 5</margin> For just as we ought to act well, not for our own glory but for the glory of God (for he says, *let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven*), so when the time for prayer arrives, the glory of God must be sought first. In this way he taught us to pray, for he commanded us to say: <margin>Matthew 6</margin> *Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread.* This very thing he now establishes by his own deed. It was certainly necessary that he himself should become our leader toward every good thing. But let us consider more diligently what he says to the Father, and through a minute observation of the words, let us inspect the truth of the doctrines. *Father,* he says, *the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may also glorify you.* Perhaps someone will think

# ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 539

A that he who says these things is in need of that glorification and glory. But if one is not forgetful of the dignity of the Only-begotten, he will easily cast these empty thoughts out of his mind. For it is foolish to say that he is lacking in glory who is the Lord of Glory, and is called such by the scripture. <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> Whence in another place he is read to ask for that glory from the Father: *The glory,* he says, *which I had with you before the world was.* <note>original: "Quam apud te... habebam antequam mundus esset" — John 17:5.</note> Thus it should be clear that no one, unless they are mentally captive, would say the Only-begotten is in need of glory—that glory which is fitting for God. <margin>Philippians 2</margin> But because, though he was in the form and equality of God the Father, he did not think it a thing to be grasped to be equal with God, but emptied himself, assuming a little human body <note>original: "humano assumpto corpusculo" — The use of the diminutive "corpusculo" emphasizes the humility of Christ taking on a frail, mortal frame.</note> and absolutely putting on our smallness; and now that the opportune time was present—in which, the mystery of the incarnation being consummated and the human race called to the life and knowledge of God, B he might return to his former glory—he addresses the Father in this way to show that the Father is also the author of these things. He demonstrates that it is now the time to ascend with his flesh to the dignity of his nature. Moreover, he ascends not by the ministry of another, but as the wisdom and power of God the Father. <margin>1 Corinthians 1</margin> For thus, and not otherwise, he performs the works of the deity with supreme power; for all things are from the Father, but not without the Son. For how shall God the Father work anything without his natural wisdom and power cooperating? <margin>John 1</margin> *All things were made through him,* it says, *and without him nothing was made.* Therefore, since the logic of the identity of substance persuades us that all things are from the Father through the Son in the Spirit, C he is about to set aside death and the tyranny of the devil, because the entire world, illuminated by the doctrine of the Spirit, was going to recognize that Christ is, according to nature, the true God. Therefore he says, *Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may also glorify you.* No one who is not out of their mind would say that the Son wishes to be glorified by the Father as if receiving and returning it in turn as one man from another (for it is entirely foolish to think such things about God), but he asks for glorification from the Father and promises he will return the like to the Father, so that the equality and identity of nature might appear. For just as the Father seems to be dishonored unless one believes he has begotten such a Son as he himself is, so it is his glory to have produced a Son entirely like himself. The Father is therefore glorified in the glory of the Son, because, as we were just saying, while it is understood D from what Father he was born, glory is returned to both the Father and the Son. Glory, therefore, completely overflows from the Father—who begot such a Son—to the Son, and from the Son—who is like the Father—to the Father. But if someone thinks this is also said by the Savior in a humbler way because of the man he assumed, they will indeed speak correctly, yet they will not explain the force of this theorem <term>theorematis</term> <note>In this context, a "theorem" refers to a fundamental theological proposition or truth.</note> so exquisitely. For if Christ only asked to be glorified by the Father, we would attribute this to his humanity. But because he promises that he too will glorify the Father in turn, it is necessary to interpret the passage as has been said.

->CHAPTER XVI.<-

**This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.** <note>John 17:3</note> He affirms that the root and origin of eternal life is faith and the virtue of true piety; we assert that true piety is that upon which the crime of foreign and false worship cannot be branded. For many have worshipped the creature, passing over the Creator, and have not feared to say to a piece of wood: "You are my Father," and to a stone: "You gave birth to me." For many—alas, almost everyone—have fallen into such a depth of ignorance that, lacking sense, they have attributed the ineffable glory of the deity to matter. For these reasons, distinguishing the Father from those who are gods in name only and false gods, He calls Him the "only and true God." Most usefully, when He called the Father alone the true God, He also remembered His own glory, saying: *and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.* For the Father is not otherwise rightly known unless the Son is also known together with Him. When, therefore, He called the Father the only true God, He did not separate Himself from this glory: for He is in the Father and from the Father. Wherefore He is true God according to nature, and the "Only in the Only" <note>This refers to the mutual indwelling of the Trinity.</note>; for no god is true except the Trinity, since the gods of the nations are demons, and since every creature is subjected to slavery—a creature which many, having fallen into a wicked sense, adore. There are many in this world falsely called "gods" by men; but there is only one true God: the Father, and He who is in Him and from Him according to nature, both distinctly and at the same time conjointly by a natural union. Distinctly, indeed, because He is understood to exist in His own subsistence <note>original: "subsistentia" — In theological terms, this refers to a "person" (hypostasis) of the Trinity.</note>. For He is the Son, and not the Father. Conjointly, truly, because the Father and Son exist together. For He is the Father for this reason: because He brought forth the Son. *This, therefore,* He says, *is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.* But if the knowledge of God is eternal life, how...

**550 ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN**

For I shall soon ascend into the heavens to reign alongside You, while these men remain on earth; it is for them I pray, for they are already Yours, since they were given to Me. Therefore, I rightly have no small care for what is both Yours and Mine. **And I am glorified in them**, because all things that You gave to Me are Yours, and Yours are Mine. This is a true saying: for just because they have been given to Christ, and therefore belong to the Father as well, they do not cease to glorify Him through whom they are joined to God the Father. For although they have been brought to the Father through Him and have become the Father's, they nevertheless remain His own, since all things are held in common by the Trinity, in both divinity and power. For one God is adored in the Trinity, to whom we are all subject by the condition of our service.

### **CHAPTER 20**

**Holy Father, keep them in Your name, those whom You have given Me, that they may be one, even as We are.** Consider diligently the interweaving of two things into one: I mean the humility of His humanity and the supreme glory of His divinity; for His prayer embraces both. For as we touched upon in the earlier sections, He is neither raised up entirely to the sublime heights, nor does He descend completely to our lowly measure. For since He is truly both God and man in an ineffable <note>indescribable or beyond words</note> union, He occupies a sort of middle ground, so that He never leaves the boundaries of divinity, yet still contains the nature of man. For He voluntarily humbled Himself for our sake, so that we also might be called "sons" and "gods"—not by nature as He is, but by grace, having been reshaped toward Him through the participation of the Spirit. 

Therefore, when He says nothing in a way that suggests human lowliness is joined to the glory of divinity, do not be disturbed. Instead, marvel all the more that there is such power and miraculous craftsmanship <note>original: "artificium"</note> in His speech, so that the Speaker clearly appears to be as much God by nature as He is man. We do not say this because the nature of the Word was dragged down to something lower (for we judge that to be the height of madness, since the nature of divinity suffers no change), but because the manner of His voluntary emptying <note>This refers to *kenosis*, the theological concept of Christ "emptying" himself of his glory to become human.</note>, while always retaining His humanity, necessarily makes the Son appear in some way "lesser" than the Father due to His state of humility—though He is equal and consubstantial <note>sharing the same fundamental essence or "stuff" of God</note> with Him, the only-begotten God in Him and from Him. 

Do not wonder, then, if the Father's glory seems greater because of Christ's humanity, since Paul even wrote that He was surpassed by the angels for this reason. **We see Jesus**, he says, **who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor.** Yet the angels are commanded to worship Him; for when He brings the Firstborn into the world, He says: **And let all the angels of God worship Him.** The holy Seraphim were also seen by the prophets standing in the posture of servants before Him as He sat upon a high and lofty throne. Therefore, as far as His ineffable generation from the Father is concerned, the taking on of human nature is not an inherent property of the Son's divine nature <note>meaning: His being human is an act of will for our salvation, not a requirement of His eternal existence as God</note>.

<summary>This page provides a theological commentary on Christ's prayer in John 17, explaining how Christ balances His divine equality with the Father and His humble human nature. It emphasizes that Christ's "lowliness" is a voluntary act (kenosis) intended to elevate humanity to the status of God's children.</summary>
