...to rescue from evils. But it was necessary (for I shall say it plainly) if they were later to become the lights of the world, that they should look not only upon the flesh of Christ, but also upon His deity; which, although it cannot be discerned by the eyes, is nevertheless always present with supreme power. Nor is there anything that can prevent Him from filling all things and accomplishing what He wills: for the divine nature is not circumscribed by place or dimensions. Therefore, since Christ is truly God and man, it was necessary for them to have understood that, by the ineffable <note>indescribable</note> power of His deity, He would always be with them, even if He were absent in the flesh. For this reason, He also said in the preceding verses: *Holy Father, keep them in Your name, whom You have given to Me.* Clearly signifying that they could be saved by the power of His deity, not merely by the physical presence of His flesh.

Indeed, even the flesh itself was not holy of itself, but having been in some way reformed by its union with the Word <note>the 'Logos' or second person of the Trinity</note> and the power of the Word, it became the cause of salvation and sanctification for those who participate in it. Therefore, we do not attribute the power of divine operation to the flesh insofar as it is flesh, but to the nature of the Word. For this, and nothing else, is what it means that they were kept in the name of the Father. For they were certainly saved for the glory of God.

Driving away the dread of being left alone, therefore, He repeats the same point through the same words several times: showing that their salvation would come not through the bodily presence of the flesh, but by the power of His deity. But observe, I pray, how much hidden force is contained in this prayer for our edification <note>spiritual improvement</note>. For while He asked that they be kept by God the Father, He Himself affirms that He has done it, demonstrating that He is of equal power with the Father—indeed, demonstrating the subsisting power of the Father. For He who can do the same things that the true God does, how shall He not be both the same in nature and equal in power? And He who, as God, kept them in the name of God, and obtained the glory of deity from His works: how shall He be of any other nature than the Father’s? Or how shall He not be demonstrated to be the true God? For nothing can do the works that are proper to God unless it is substantially God. 

However, the prayer again retains a duality of perspective. For the fact that He can save whom He wills is far removed from the nature of created beings. But in that He attributes it to the name of the Father, He spoke as a man. Thus, as a man, He in a certain way placed Himself under this law: but as God and the omnipotent power of the Father—a power not produced by external effort, but proceeding ineffably from the nature of the Father and manifesting it—He attributed it to Himself. 

But if, again, He asserts that the name of deity was given to Him, He will not be believed (as we have said) to have ever lacked the glory of deity for this reason, since it is seen to be perfectly suited to His humanity. For a creature has nothing of its own accord. Moreover, He says He has kept the disciples in such a way that none of them perished except the **son of perdition**: and He called him the "son of perdition" because he perished by his own wickedness. For it must not be believed that the traitor fell into the snare of the devil by a divine and inescapable judgment. For if it were so, he would in no way be blamed, since no one can resist the judgment of God. But now he has been made so wretched that it would have been better for him if he had never been born. <margin>John 10</margin> For he did what he did by no necessity, but by his own judgment. Therefore, he is rightly called the **son of perdition**...

[Column 2]

...who chose perdition. For it was not because it was written of him that he was to perish that he proceeded to such wickedness as to betray the precious blood of Christ for a few pieces of silver. But because he was entirely destined to perish by his own malice, for that reason the Scripture foretold that it would entirely happen—and it is impossible for Scripture to say anything false. For God Himself speaks through the Scripture, who knows the character and life of all: for the Psalmist attributes the knowledge of all things, both past and future, to Him, saying: *You have understood my thoughts from afar; You have searched out my path and my cord, and foreseen all my ways.* <margin>Psalm 138 <note>original: "Pfal. 138." In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 139:2-3.</note></margin> 

Therefore, He who knows all things, who sees future things as if they were present, also foretold this to us through Scripture. But God does not either will or command all things that He knows will happen, nor does a prediction encourage evil any more than it discourages it. For he who was foreknown, since he was of free will, could certainly much more easily have avoided the snare of the devil. 

But someone might perhaps say: "If the others escaped the snare of the devil by their own will and free power, but Judas alone fell in, how did Christ 'keep' them? Or why did this salvation not benefit Judas?" 

But zeal and watchfulness, O noble reader, however upright and laudable they may be, are nonetheless not sufficient for the perfect work of virtue: rather, we acquire salvation by being vigilant and attending to it diligently. But that is not enough for us, since we necessarily need divine grace, which makes difficult things easy and renders the steep path of righteousness level for us. For our own strength, unless it be sustained from above, is absolutely nothing: which the Psalmist confirms by crying out: *Unless the Lord builds the house, they have labored in vain who build it. Unless the Lord guards the city, he watches in vain who guards it.* <margin>Psalm 126 <note>original: "Pfal. 126." In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 127:1.</note></margin> 

Therefore, it is necessary that we continually and with great courage strive to acquire salvation, and ask in prayer for the help of God by which we may be protected. By His help, we shall easily overcome the powers of the devil—unless we obey him when provoked to pleasures and other modes of sinning, or unless we, even without being tempted, grant him the reins of our will. For if we come to his snare by our own choice and negligence, whom else shall we blame rather than ourselves? Is this not what Solomon writes: *The foolishness of a man destroys his ways, and he blames God in his heart.* <margin>Proverbs 19 <note>Proverbs 19:3</note></margin> 

If the traitor had not had the help of the Savior equally with the other disciples, these things would be said by us in vain. But if he was ruled by divine grace no less than the others, but fell into the depth of perdition by his own choice, how can it be said that Christ did not also keep him? Christ offered him His protection; and as far as providing help was concerned, He would have saved the man, had he not leaped into perdition of his own accord. Therefore, grace shone forth in the others, and saved all those who surrendered a cooperating will to it. For in this way the manner of our salvation is arranged.

Solomon makes this meaning of sanctification according to the law clear, saying: [Marginal note: Prov. 20] *It is a snare for a man to quickly sanctify anything holy.* <note>Proverbs 20:25. In this context, "sanctifying" refers to dedicating something to God, which should not be done impulsively.</note> For repentance usually follows a vow. Thus, to sanctify is to offer anything to God according to the custom of the law. Therefore, for us, Christ **sanctified himself**: indeed, he offered himself to God the Father as a holy sacrifice, reconciling the world to Him and restoring the fallen human race to His friendship. For [Marginal note: Ephes. 5] **He himself is our peace**, as it is written. Furthermore, the return of our race to God was brought about through Christ the Savior in no other way than through the participation and sanctification of the Spirit. For it is the Spirit who joins us to God; having become partakers of Him, we are made partakers of the supreme nature, receiving also the Father himself in the Son and through the Son. [Marginal note: 1 John 4] *In this,* says John, *we know that we remain in Christ and He in us, because He has given us of His Spirit.* And Paul: [Marginal note: Gal. 4] *Because you are sons,* he says, *God sent the Spirit of His Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.* For if we were devoid of the Holy Spirit, God would never be in us; if we did not have the Spirit through whom we are adopted as sons of God, we would in no way be sons of God. But now we are partakers of the supreme nature and temples of God. For on account of our sins, the only-begotten Son of God became man, so that he might offer himself as a sacred sacrifice in an odor of sweetness to God the Father; so that when that which separates us from God—that is, sin—has been removed from our midst, nothing may hinder us, if we so wish, from clinging to God and enjoying participation in Him through the Holy Spirit, reforming ourselves to righteousness, to sanctification, and to the original image. For if sin separates us from God, then righteousness certainly joins us, and in no intermediate way makes us stand before God. [Marginal note: Rom. 3. 4.] We have been **justified through faith in Christ**, who was handed over for our sins, as it is written: and rose again to justify us. For in Him, as in the first-fruits, the nature of man, having been repaired for a new life, ascends to its original condition and sanctification. *Sanctify them, therefore, in your truth,* he says, *that is, in me, Father*: for your word—that is, I—is truth. Moreover, he sanctified himself for us, that is, he offered himself, since he died for all so that he might reform all to a new life, so that he might sancti-

<column-break/>

-fy <note>Continuing the word "sanctificare" from the previous column.</note> and join: so that he might restore [human nature] in himself first, and through himself, to its original beauty; and so that he himself, the heavenly man and the **second Adam**, being established first of all in a new life—namely, in incorruption, in righteousness, and in spiritual sanctification—might transmit all good things to our race through himself. Thus, although he is life itself according to his nature, he nevertheless died so that, our death being destroyed in us, he might reform us to his own life. And since he himself is the righteousness of God the Father, he was made sin for our sake. For he himself (as [Marginal note: Isa. 53. Coloss. 3.] the Prophet says) bore our sins, and being counted among the wicked, and having torn the **handwritten bond** <note>original: "chirographo." Refers to the "handwriting of requirements" or debt of sin mentioned in Colossians 2:14, which Christ "cancelled" by nailing it to the cross.</note> that we made against ourselves through his cross, he justified us. Since, therefore, he is holy by nature as God, and since he himself sends the sanctification of the Spirit into creatures, and causes the creature to both exist and endure in the Holy Spirit, he is sanctified for our sake—not acquiring that from another, but he himself sending sanctification into his own flesh. Thus he provides the Spirit to himself as God, and receives it as man, which he did not do for his own sake but for ours, so that the grace of sanctification, having been received in him first, might pass to the whole race. For just as by the transgression of the first man, we were sentenced to death in the first-fruits of our race, hearing in that first man, *Earth you are, and to earth you shall return*: in the same way, I believe, through the obedience and righteousness of Christ (insofar as he subjected himself to the law, although he was the author of the law), the blessing and life-giving which is through the Spirit has penetrated to our whole nature. For that which was corrupted by sin, the Spirit reforms to incorruption; and he restores to a new life that which suffered destruction through negligence. How then, someone will perhaps say, was he sanctified by participation, when he is holy according to his nature? How is he, who bestows his Spirit on celestial and terrestrial beings, said to bestow it upon himself also? These things are difficult and entirely insoluble if you consider the Word of God as naked, having sanctified the flesh through himself; but if you keep in mind his ineffable union with our nature, all confusion will immediately depart from your soul. For when you believe the Son to be both God and man, those things which befit a man, even if they converge in the one and same person of the Only-begotten, will not seem absurd. Is it not entirely foreign, I ask, to think of death in relation to the life-giving Word? Yet he is believed to have suffered it in the flesh, which is susceptible to death; and we say that he himself was dead, since as a man he died.

# 562 ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

His human nature, while not holy by its own nature, was sanctified in Christ by the Word of God dwelling within it. The Word sanctified His own temple through His Spirit and transferred this to the sanctification of His own nature. For this reason, the Holy Spirit descended upon Him from heaven in the form of a dove, [Marginal note: John 1.] as John testified. We learn from this that the Spirit descended upon Christ first—as upon a man capable of receiving sanctification—for the renewal of our own nature. We do not say that Christ was only sanctified according to the flesh at the moment the Baptist saw the Spirit descending in the form of a dove. [Marginal note: Luke 1.] For He was holy even in His mother's womb. Thus it was said to the Virgin: *The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.* Rather, this descent was given as a sign for the Baptist. We believe, however, that the Lord’s flesh was sanctified through the Spirit, similar to other creatures, as the Son of God anointed His own temple. [Marginal note: Psalm 44.] Likewise, the Psalmist, considering the person of the Only-begotten in union with His humanity, cries out: *Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.* <note>original: "Propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus oleo læticiæ præ consortibus tuis." This is Psalm 45:7 in modern bibles, a key text used by early theologians to explain Christ's status as the "Anointed One" (Messiah).</note> For when the Son anoints His own temple, the Father—who does all things through the Son—is also said to perform it. All things the Son does are referred back to the Father, for the Father is the root and source of the Son. It is not surprising, therefore, that although He is holy by nature, He professes to be sanctified. Even though He is God by nature, Scripture speaks of God as His Father. We shall not err if we attribute all these things to His human nature. For just as He died as a man, though He is God by nature; and just as He was under the yoke of the law, though He is Lord of all; and just as He calls God His Father, though He is Himself God; so for our sake He sanctifies Himself. He does this so that, as sanctification overflows from Him to us, we ourselves might be sanctified in the truth—that is, in the Holy Spirit, for as John says, the Spirit is truth. [Marginal note: John 16.] The Spirit is not distinct from the Son in terms of substance, for the Spirit is in Him and proceeds through Him. Christ says He was "sent" into the world, though He was never absent from it. [Marginal note: NOTE.] For he says, *He was in the world, and the world did not know Him.* By "mission," He means nothing other than that He became man and was anointed with the Spirit, taking the likeness of the prophetic ministry as the **Messenger of Great Counsel**. <note>original: "magni fuit cōsilij angelus." This title for Christ comes from the Septuagint version of Isaiah 9:6.</note> He says that His disciples, who were appointed and sent by Him in imitation of Himself to preach heavenly and Gospel doctrine to the world, necessarily need to be sanctified in truth so they can complete the course of their ministry.

### CHAPTER XXVI.
**I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you: that they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.**

The beginning of the restoration into new life was the first heavenly man, Christ. For the second Adam is the Lord from heaven, [Marginal note: 2 Cor. 15.] <note>2 Corinthians 15:47. Paul contrasts Adam, the first man of earth, with Christ, the second man from heaven.</note> as Paul says. Therefore He said: *No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.* Those who were first chosen and honored with the dignity of following Christ were much closer to this beginning and origin.

[Marginal marker: A] They saw His glory with their own eyes; they clung to Him always and gathered the saving precepts into their souls. Rightly, then, after the Head of all, they became the most precious members of His body. Christ sought the blessing of the Spirit from the Father for them, to be given through Himself, as was said above. But lest anyone, out of fickleness or malice, should think that the Spirit of Christ was requested by the Lord only for the disciples, and that nothing was said for us who come after them by the high priest and mediator of our souls, He necessarily added that He prayed not for them alone, but for those who would believe in Him through their preaching. [Marginal marker: B] It would certainly be absurd and inconsistent if, while the entire race was condemned through the sin of one first man, the whole of nature was not similarly justified through the righteousness of Christ. For just as the image of the earthly Adam is known by sin, filth, weakness, the pleasure of the flesh, and finally destruction and death, so the image of the heavenly Adam is perceived by life, incorruptibility, sanctification, and other such qualities. 

It was not possible for us to be restored to our original beauty once we were reformed, unless we were joined to God; for thus we were adorned from the beginning. No one can be joined to God except through participation in the Holy Spirit, who imparts His own sanctification to us and reforms human nature—which is subject to destruction—toward His own life. For the Son is the pure image of the Father; [Marginal marker: C] and the Spirit is believed to be, and is, the natural likeness of the Son. Therefore, when the Spirit reforms a human soul in Himself, He imprints the divine image upon it. 

Our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, prays not only for the twelve disciples but for all who were to believe in Him through the Gospel teaching at various times. He wanted this request of His to be clear to us so that we might learn the path of righteousness we must walk to keep His commands. What, then, is the manner of this request? *That they may be one,* He says, *as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us.* He asks for the bond of love, peace, and concord, which leads believers to such a great spiritual union [Marginal marker: D] that it imitates the likeness of the natural and substantial union that exists in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Yet the power and connection of this love can never cause us to be so unchangeably joined in identity of substance that we could be seen to have attained the nature of the divine unity. For that divine unity, being natural and true, is seen in the character of substance; ours, however, imitates that state of unity. How can we, through imitation, equal the primary Truth? For truth and the imitation of truth are not the same thing. Although they may seem to have equality in proportion and likeness, they are separated by vast differences. Therefore, when a heretic brings forward this passage to overturn the natural identity of the Trinity—saying that we are not joined by an absolute identity of bodies, nor... [Marginal note: Ephes. 2.]

That we are thus united to the Holy Spirit is also perceived in a certain way through this reasoning: For if we have looked down upon the animal life <note>original: "animalem uitam," referring to life led by the natural soul or physical senses rather than the spirit.</note>, and have subjected ourselves to the spiritual law, making the Spirit our master in all things, it is clear that we are transformed, as it were, into another nature; for by fleeing the animalistic way of living, we have received the wondrous conformation of the Spirit dwelling within us. **CHAPTER XXVII.**
**"The glory which you gave me, I have given them, that they may be one, even as we are one. I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one. And let the world know that you sent me, and loved them, even as you loved me."** <note>John 17:22-23</note> The Only-begotten has a natural and <term>consubstantial</term> <note>meaning "of the same substance" or "essence."</note> union with the Father, from whom he was truly born and in whom he exists. For he is one with the Father by identity of substance, although he exists in his own person <note>original: "subsistentia," often used to distinguish the persons of the Trinity.</note>. But because for the sake of our salvation he stepped out, as it were, from his own dignity and glory (for this is what it means when it says, "he emptied himself") <note>A reference to Philippians 2:7, describing Christ's "kenosis" or self-emptying to become human.</note>, he therefore received back, along with his flesh, the radiance and glory which he always possesses as God. Since the temple <note>A common patristic term for Christ's human body.</note> which he received from the Virgin is not consubstantial with God the Father, it is nevertheless so united with the Word that its person is with him (for there is one Christ and one Son, even when made man). Therefore, he is said to have received unity with God: since his temple, which is not God by itself, was made one with God the Word. To speak more briefly and clearly: the Only-begotten says that what was given to his temple was given to himself—given, that is, by the Father through him in the Spirit. For there is no other way for the manner of unity with God to exist. For it is understood that in Christ, by an ineffable unity, the sanctified flesh ascends without any confusion to the unity of the Word, and through the Word to the unity of the Father—in a certain state of being, that is, and not by nature. Therefore, he says: "This glory and radiance, Father, which you gave to me, which is that I might be one with you, I have given to them, so that they may be one, just as we are one." For the faithful are united among themselves in those ways we have already explained. They are also united to God, and the Savior himself opened the way, saying: "I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one." For the Son is united to us physically as a man through the mystic blessing <note>original: "benedictionem mysticam," a reference to the Sacrament of the Eucharist.</note>, but spiritually as God, by the grace of his Spirit, renewing our spirit to a new life and a participation in the divine nature. Therefore, the bond of our union to God the Father is Christ: united to us as a man, but naturally united to God the Father as God. For it was not possible for the nature of man, which was subject to corruption,

to ascend to immortality, unless the immortal and unchangeable nature had descended to it, and by communion and participation in itself, raised those reformed from the limits of our mortality to its own good. We are therefore perfected and led back to the union of God the Father through the mediation of the Savior, that is, Christ. For by receiving the Son of God, who is naturally united to the Father, both physically and substantially (as has been said), we are clarified and glorified, having been made partakers of the supreme nature. Christ wishes us to be received into the union of God the Father so that he may both provide this glory to our nature through himself, and by the power of this grace, refute those who deny that he is from God. Therefore, he says: "When they are joined to you through me, Father, then the world will know that you sent me: and that you loved them—whom you have joined to yourself through me—just as you loved me." For how could he, who gave Christ as a man the radiance and glory of the deity, and gave us the power to acquire this by grace, not love us with an equal measure of charity? But let no one of sound mind be disturbed by this. For it is clear that a servant nature can in no way contend with its Lord, nor will God love a creature and his own Son with an equal measure. Nevertheless, the Son of God, who is loved by the Father before all ages, began to be loved as a man, which he acquired not for himself, but for us. Therefore, just as we will be conformed to his resurrection and glory, and were first renewed in Christ, so also we have received a conformity of love (so to speak) in Christ. We ought therefore to marvel at the kindness of the divine nature, which deigns to communicate to the creature those things which are its own.

**CHAPTER XXVIII.**
**"Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me: that they may see my glory, which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world."** <note>John 17:24</note> Since he has prayed for his disciples—indeed, for all people—and has asked for the charity of the Father, and for union and sanctification, he added these things. He did this to show that no others would be with him or see his glory except those who, having been joined to the Father through him, are loved with that love with which he himself is commanded to be loved. For we are loved as children, after the likeness of the natural Son. For even if not in equal measure, yet an exquisite imitation of a thing seems to be made equal to the truth in some way. "I will therefore," he says, "that those who have been given to me by you through the illumination of faith, may be with me, and see my glory." What speech can explain how sweet it is to be with Christ? Truly these things are ineffable; neither has eye seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man, what things God has prepared for those who love him. For what is greater than to be with Christ? "It is better to be dissolved and to be with him," as Paul says. <note>Philippians 1:23</note> With those words, Paul even preferred the status of being friends of God to this life, which is (as he testifies elsewhere) to be with Christ. ### CHAPTER 35

**Simon Peter, therefore, having a sword, drew it and struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his right ear; and the servant's name was Malchus.** Someone might ask: what compelled the Evangelist <note>The "Evangelist" refers to John, the author of this Gospel account.</note> to make mention of these things? Why did he diligently record that Peter rose up against the enemy with a sword more fervently—if not more cruelly—and that he was rebuked by Christ? Perhaps you think these details are unnecessary, but it is not so. For this matter brings us great utility, as we learn from it exactly how far a zealous devotion <note>original: "pietatis aemulatio"</note> is permitted to go. We are taught, therefore, if we do not wish to offend God in a similar struggle, that we must not take up iron <note>Here, "iron" refers to a sword or any lethal weapon.</note>, nor throw stones, nor raise clubs against the adversaries of Christ—

Since Christ offered himself voluntarily to those seeking him—not unwillingly, nor overcome by Jewish force—why then were the snares of the Jews to be repelled? He says that this cup was given to him by the Father, even though it was devised by the impiety of the Jews: because they could have done nothing unless the Father had permitted it for our sake. ### CHAPTER XXXVII.
**The cohort therefore, and the Tribune <note>A Roman military officer commanding a large group of soldiers.</note> and the servants of the Jews took Jesus, and bound him, and led him to Annas first; for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was the High Priest of that year.** <margin>John 19</margin> Now, with every hindrance removed, Peter being quiet, and no one defending him—and with Christ himself offering himself voluntarily though he could have escaped—the excessively puffed-up soldiers cast bonds upon the Lord of all things: he who descended to our nature so that he might snatch us from the bonds of sin and the devil. But they lead him first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas. From this, it is given to be understood that he was the architect of the snares himself, and had promised the agreed-upon reward to the traitor. Therefore, Christ is first handed over bound to him. Then it was demonstrated in actual fact that what the Jews said through the prophet was true: <margin>Wisdom 2</margin> "Let us circumvent the righteous man, for he is useless to us." Not because he himself was such <note>i.e., actually useless</note>, but because to sinners and those given to pleasures, by teaching a justice above the legal requirements and clearly opening up the things that pleased God, he was useless and troublesome to them. Certainly, the Law did not hold that way of teaching. For the legal discipline teaches us not openly, but through shadows and enigmas, which, being little understood, brought little utility then. Therefore, just as the solar splendor brings no utility to the blind, and sweet foods seem bitter to those with a fever: so the Lord, although he was the author of salvation, nevertheless seemed troublesome to the Jews; because, hindered by their sickness, they could not bear the Savior.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.
**But they sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest. Now it was Caiaphas who gave counsel to the Jews, that it is expedient that one man should die for the people. And Peter followed Jesus, and another disciple.** Caiaphas presided over the impiety against Christ by his authority and counsel, and a little later he will receive the bound Jesus as if the fruit of his own counsel. But with the rest of the disciples now struck by great fear and scattered, Peter, who was more fervent, follows, and another disciple with him. This was John, who wrote this divinely inspired gospel for us; he, driving out all ostentation far from his mind, hid his own name. And certainly, things that are done with a brave and great spirit ought to be proclaimed not by our own tongue, but by the tongues of others. For it is most shameful to be praised not by the voice of others, but by our own mouth. Whence <margin>Proverbs 27</margin> it is said in Proverbs: Let your neighbor praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.
<margin>A</margin> **Now that disciple was known to the high priest, and entered with Jesus into the court of the high priest.** Not without cause did he write even these minute details for us. For since he is about to narrate the deeds done in the court of the high priest, he necessarily placed those things first by which it is proved that he writes what he himself saw, and was not taught by another: for he entered with Jesus into the court, because he was known to the high priest.

### CHAPTER XL.
**But Peter stood at the door outside. Therefore the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the portress, and brought in Peter.** Peter would not have remained outside unless the observation of the portress <note>A female doorkeeper.</note> made entry unsafe for unknown persons. <margin>B</margin> Nor did he push the poor woman aside, though he easily could have, because he did not want to be subjected to a charge of opportunism. Therefore he stood outside mourning, until John, not being ignorant that he was grieving even because of this, obtained the favor of his admission from the portress.

### CHAPTER XLI.
**The maidservant who was the portress then said to Peter: Art thou not also one of this man's disciples? He said: I am not.** The Lord had already predicted to Peter that he would deny him three times before the cock crowed, having become somewhat weaker in faith: but now the Evangelist narrates where and how that happened. Certainly the poor woman who was the doorkeeper asked him, since she was curious about the disciples of that man who was injuriously captured. Peter repelled this as if it were no small crime, not so much out of fear of being captured, <margin>C</margin> nor because he had no care for the truth, but perhaps because he wanted to endure all things as long as he might see Christ. Therefore he fell out of love, and for the sake of devotion <note>original: "pietatis causa"</note> he seems to have denied—not indeed by a right reason, nor one approved by exquisite logic—but which nevertheless caused him to be present with Christ and to see him: which Peter desired above all things.

### CHAPTER XLII.
**Now the servants and ministers stood at a fire of coals, because it was cold, and warmed themselves. And Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.** When Peter had entered, lest he seem to commiserate with the captive with a mournful face and thus be expelled and unable to see what he wished, he mixed himself with the servants; and while pressing down his grief deep in his heart, he pretends to do what they were doing. <margin>D</margin> For it is not likely that Peter, in such great sorrow, sought a remedy for the cold—he who would reject much greater pleasures while Christ was thus bound. As if indeed nothing impelled him to sorrow itself, he repels the harm of the cold with the fire alongside the servants. So that since he appeared to be one of the household of the high priest, he might be asked by no one who he was, and thus avoid the crime of denying again: but the Savior could not lie. For what he foresaw as God, that he announced to the disciple would come to pass.

...he was able, he interrogated him about his disciples and about his doctrine. He questioned him, however, to see whether it agreed with the Mosaic law, or if his doctrine was foreign to the law; and what the mind of his disciples was—whether they followed the customs of the ancestors, or were entering a new way of worship and ceremonies. But he did this with the greatest malice. For he thought that Christ would say something against the law of Moses, which among them was nothing other than to rebel against God himself. They attended to Christ as if he were a mere man <note>original: "homini nudo," literally "a naked man," meaning a man stripped of divine status</note>, and they were eager to condemn the Lord of the law for a transgression of the law—forgetting what was said to them: <margin>Proverbs 16</margin> **He is wicked who says to a king, you act against the law.** <note>original: "Impius est, qui regi dicit, præter legem facis."</note>

### CHAPTER XLIV.
**Jesus answered him: I have spoken openly to the world, I always taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, where all the Jews gather: and in secret I have spoken nothing.** He says that he who examines a matter known to everyone as if it were hidden labors in vain. For how shall that which is open to all be concealed? I think these things were said by Christ so that he might reject the maliciously composed false charges. But I believe something more hidden is also suggested by these words: **I,** he says, **have spoken openly to the world.** That is, the things written for you through Moses do not openly explain whatever pleases God, but signify them through shadows and figures and through riddles <note>term: "enigmata" — obscure allegories or symbolic prophecies</note>; and the letters, covered in unrefinedness, do not openly set forth the things necessary to be known. **But I have spoken openly to the world.** For I have preached the way of piety to the world not enigmatically, but clearly. He says **to the world**, because even if the sound of the Gospel had not yet gone out into the whole world at that time, it would do so at the opportune time. **I,** he says, **always taught in the synagogue.** It is worthwhile to see what he is driving at: he strives to bring back to their memory, even if they are unwilling, what Isaiah predicted in the person of Christ: <margin>Isaiah 45</margin> **I have not spoken in secret, nor in a dark place of the earth.** And again: <margin>Isaiah 65</margin> **All day long,** he says, **I have stretched out my hands to an unbelieving and contradicting people.** For it is no different to say that he did not speak in an obscure place or in secret than to say he spoke openly, in the synagogue, and where many were present. Moreover, he conveniently brings this prophecy to mind so that they might learn that they were acting impiously by binding as a criminal the one they hoped would come, after he had arrived. For he was promised to the Jews, according to Paul. <margin>Romans 15</margin>

### CHAPTER XLV.
**Why do you ask me? Ask those who heard what I spoke to them, behold they know what I said.** He rebukes the legal experts as if they were ignorant of the law in which they boasted so much. For they were seeking crimes in vain after they had already bound him. Why then, he says, do you ask? Why do you provoke one who has been captured to a defense before he has been accused? And in another way: You who have already disgraced me as much as you can, he says, if I speak truly, you will cry out that I am lying. Therefore, ask others about me; it is not difficult to find witnesses, for these men heard me. Nor, as someone might perhaps think, did he point out some people present who heard him because he knew the hearts of men as God. Rather, he openly pointed to some of the ministers <note>term: "ministris" — the temple guards or officials serving the High Priest</note> who both heard and had been amazed; how or when, I will say briefly, so that this

While the Lord was preaching, as this Evangelist <note>The author refers to the Apostle John</note> narrated elsewhere, <margin>John 7</margin> the leaders of the Jews were bursting with rage, and they sent ministers to seize him. These men, having wondered at the doctrine of Christ, listened attentively; and after the preaching of Christ, they returned to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to them: "Why did you not bring him?" ### CHAPTER XLVI.
**But when he had said these things, one of the ministers standing by gave Jesus a blow, saying: Is this how you answer the High Priest?** This was also predicted concerning Christ by a prophetic voice: <margin>Isaiah 50</margin> **I gave my body to the strikers, and my cheeks to those plucking them.** This has now reached its conclusion for the condemnation of Jewish pride and the overturning of our disgrace. For we were disgraced by sin, which the unjust mark of disgrace upon Christ wiped away. For he himself takes away our sins and labors for us. For just as his death destroyed our death, similarly I believe the disgrace of our transgression was deleted by the blow <note>term: "alapa" — a strike with the open hand; a slap</note> inflicted on Christ. For one labored for all, and one was dishonored for all. But I think all creation itself shuddered <margin>Psalm 73</margin> if it had a sense of this thing. For the Lord of glory was struck by the impious hand of a man. It is not out of place to ask, however, for what reason that impious minister struck Jesus so impudently, <margin>Psalm 102</margin> since he had neither answered anything harsh nor had the High Priest ordered such a thing. Someone might perhaps say it was the custom of the ministers to force those they brought to the leaders to speak more modestly, and if they said anything somewhat unrefined, to suppress them with both words and blows. But in no way can these things apply to the most mild response of Jesus. We think, therefore, the cause of the impudence was consistent with what was said above. Some of the ministers had offended the leaders of the Jews (as we have already said), <margin>Psalms 10 and 28; Matthew 18</margin> who, having been ordered to seize Christ, so wondered at him that they said in praise: "Never has a man spoken thus." At which response, as if stirred by madness, the Pharisees said: "Have you also been deceived? Has anyone of the leaders believed in him, or of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the law, are cursed." Since, therefore, the response of the Savior brought back the memory <margin>John 7</margin> of this matter to the leaders (for he cited the ministers as witnesses, saying: **Behold, these know what I said**), for that reason, lest the leaders should suspect his heart and goodwill—since he had been rebuked another time because he wondered at Christ—he strikes Christ with a blow. For ministers are accustomed to not being able to bear anything being reported to the leaders against themselves.

### CHAPTER XLVII.
**Jesus answered him: If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?** He accuses the minister of a great crime of injustice. For even if some ignoble person were undergoing judgment, it would still not be proper to strike him.

But the common sense of this passage is this: however, I think these words look toward something else. For perhaps the official is argued to be especially injurious, not only because he inflicted a blow <note>original: "alapam," a slap or strike with the open hand</note>, but also because he now strikes for no reason the one whose teaching he once admired. "For if you had not otherwise approved of my doctrine," he says, "if I had not seemed to you a wonderful interpreter of scripture: if you had not exclaimed, 'never has a man spoken thus': perhaps some pardon could be given to your ignorance. But observe, I pray, the supreme clemency of the Savior, just as if it were now painted on a tablet by the Evangelist. He is struck like a servant, though he could have destroyed all the Jews with only a nod, yet he performs no vengeance. For he is not conquered by anger, nor by sadness, nor by pain. Rather, he strives to calm and improve the official, when he says it is not right to strike one who has spoken nothing evil. Thus he does not forget his own gentleness, even in matters that bring terror to others: but with the best reasoning, he induces the servant of Jewish pride to beware of <margin>Psalm 73</margin> such rashness: and he who held evil for us, as it is written, returned good for evil. But that Lord of all and true God bore it mercifully. We, however, miserable creatures of earth and mud, who are compared by scripture to the greenness of the grass— <margin>Psalm 102</margin> (**For man is like grass, his days are like the flower of the field, so shall he flourish**) —if any of our neighbors says even the smallest thing against us by a slip of the tongue, we rise up against him in the manner of dragons, and disparaging him with a thousand words for one, we cannot be satisfied: not because he slipped as a human, nor do we suppress our anger because of the common infirmity of men, but rushing to vengeance, we do not look back to Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith: nor do we remember what was written just now: that their ways lead to death, who are <margin>Ecclesiasticus 10 and 28</margin> mindful of injuries. And again: **leave to your neighbor the harm done to you, and then when you pray, your sins shall be forgiven.** <margin>Matthew 18</margin> Therefore let us hold Christ as an example of clemency and gentleness, who for this reason says to us: **The disciple is not above the teacher, nor the servant above his master.**

### CHAPTER I.

[Decorative initial M] **Annas therefore sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest. Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. They said therefore to him: Are you not also one of his disciples? He denied it and said: I am not. One of the servants of the high priest, a kinsman of him whose ear Peter cut off, said: Did I not see you in the garden with** <column-break/> **him? Again therefore Peter denied: and immediately the cock crowed.** As if recalling the progress of a running horse in narration, the Evangelist usefully returns and leads the discourse back to earlier events. Why so? Because he wished to explain the denial of Peter made for the third time. He repeats briefly, therefore, and says again that Jesus was sent by Annas to Caiaphas: and he explains that Peter was questioned both by the servants who were warming themselves and by a certain kinsman of that servant whose ear he himself had cut off. Thus he remembers that Peter denied for the third time, and the cock crowed: showing that no word of the Savior had fallen away, who knew and predicted the infirmity of the disciple <term>ad unguem</term> <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," meaning perfectly or with high precision</note>. He explained all these things diligently, lest any of the adversaries of Christ should insult us, inquiring how and where Peter had denied. But since these things were so carefully narrated by the Evangelist, perhaps no one will say these things: but will rise up against Peter, accusing him of the crime of fear. "For he had not yet," such a one will say, "seen danger, and yet out of levity he denied him thrice." To these people, having cast away their frivolous claims, I think it must be said: these things were also recorded in detail for this reason, so that readers might understand what sort of people the apostles were before the resurrection of Christ and the coming of the Spirit, and what they became after they received **power from on high**. For it is certain that they were men of invincible mind and truly divine; but before the empire of death was destroyed by the Savior, the dread of dying was terrible to them. For when they did not yet have the Spirit, nor were strengthened by heavenly grace, held back by human faint-heartedness, they were broken by the fear of suffering, as men are. And just as iron, although it is hard by itself, is nevertheless easily blunted by stones unless it is tempered by a certain liquid: so the mind of man, even if it boasts that it will despise all dangers for the love of virtue, is nevertheless conquered by the harshness of contests, unless it is corroborated by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore the apostles were weaker before, as men; but afterward they overcame human infirmity by the grace of the Spirit, having been conformed to an invincible mind by the strength of the Spirit. The infirmity of the disciples was therefore recorded for the glory of God, which raises the smallness of our nature into a strength like an impregnable tower. Moreover, what happened to one of the saints will be of the greatest consolation to us. For from this we learn that no despair ought to affect us when considering human fragility: but rather it is necessary to trust, believing that we shall have strength from him who generously grants to those who love him the sinews and strength for virtue.

### CHAPTER II.
**They lead Jesus therefore from Caiaphas into the governor's headquarters <note>original: "praetorium," the residence of the Roman governor</note>: and it was morning. And they themselves did not enter into the headquarters, so that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.** <margin>Exodus 23</margin> Although the law commands to judge a just judgment, and not to kill the innocent and the just: these miserable men, being unwilling because they find no fault, blush with shame. Therefore, finding no cause, because they were now about to celebrate the Passover, lest they themselves should be stained by the killing of a man, they lead him to another: not thinking, in the madness of their heart, that the crime would redound to them if they killed him through another. This is also most ridiculous: that they lead the innocent man as if he were a criminal...

### The Encounter with Pilate

**"Then Pilate went out to them and said, 'What accusation do you bring against this man?' They answered and said to him, 'If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have delivered him to you.'"** <note>John 18:29-30</note>

Do you see how they pretend to be holy and spotless themselves, while portraying Christ as a criminal? They offer no evidence or specific argument for his supposed "wickedness," but instead they want him condemned based solely on their own authority. They seem to suggest that their own judgment should be sufficient for the Roman governor, as if to say: "Our testimony alone is proof enough of his guilt; your role is simply to provide the punishment."

They avoid the "defilement" of a Roman house, yet they carry the stain of a murderous intent within their hearts. They are careful not to step across a physical threshold, but they leap over every boundary of justice and truth. By refusing to name a specific crime, they reveal their own lack of a legitimate case. They rely on their status and the gravity of their accusation to bypass the usual requirements of the law. 

Thus, the very ones who claim to be the guardians of the Law are the ones who most flagrantly violate its spirit, seeking the death of the Innocent through pride and prestige rather than through the truth.

<summary>Cyril of Alexandria critiques the Jewish leaders for demanding Jesus's execution based on their personal authority rather than evidence, highlighting the contrast between their ritual purity and their moral corruption.</summary>

...shows that he was falsely accused of this crime. For a Roman prefect would never release someone accused of seeking a tyranny <note>the Latin *tyrannidis* here refers to a rebellion or an illegal seizure of power against the state</note> against the Romans, if any evidence were provided. A

But let these points suffice for the explanation of this passage. However, as I reflect on where this custom originated—that the assembly <note>original: *synagoga*</note> should rescue a thief or a murderer from death—at first it seemed that this, too, was their own invention (much like many other divine mandates they have altered). <margin>Numbers 35</margin> If someone, by accident and without hatred or enmity, should strike a person by throwing a stone or some other object—not out of an ambush, nor intending to kill—and that person dies, and if these things are proven in the hearing of the people: then the assembly <note>original: *synagoga*</note> shall judge between the one who struck the blow and the next of kin <term>original: *propinquum sanguinis*, literally "neighbor of blood," referring to the "avenger of blood" who had the legal right to retaliate</term>... ### [Page 588]

...and the assembly <note>original: *synagoga*</note> shall deliver the slayer from the hand of the avenger of blood <term>original: *vindicis sanguinis*; in ancient Hebrew law, this was a relative of a deceased person who had the right to take vengeance</term>, and the assembly shall restore him to the city of refuge, to which he had fled; and he shall remain there until the death of the high priest <note>The death of the High Priest functioned as a legal amnesty, allowing those living in exile in 'Cities of Refuge' to return to their homes without fear of retaliation.</note>, who was anointed with the holy oil. **C**

<margin>Numbers 35</margin> This is the law of God. You see here also the authority of the assembly <note>original: *synagogae authoritatem*</note> in these judgments. But observe how greatly this current custom of the Jews <note>Referring to the 'Paschal privilege' of releasing a prisoner at Passover.</note> differs from this divine Law. In the Law, a man is set free who killed not by malice, but by accident; here, Barabbas is requested, a man who had been cast into prison for rebellion and murder. **D**

In the former case, the assembly acts to preserve the life of the innocent from the avenger; in the latter, the synagogue <note>original: *synagoga*</note> acts to protect a criminal from justice. Furthermore, there is a hidden mystery in the death of the High Priest mentioned in the Law. For just as the slayer could not return home until the High Priest had died, so too the human race—guilty of death—could never be restored to its true heavenly homeland except through the death of the eternal High Priest, Jesus Christ. 

But these men, blinded by their hatred, ignore the spiritual meaning of their own Law. They prefer a murderer over the Author of Life, and they use a shadow of the Law <note>The 'shadow' refers to an Old Testament practice that prefigures a New Testament truth.</note> to justify their rejection of the Truth. They use their authority to release a man who brought death to others, while condemning the very High Priest whose death alone brings life to the world.

If someone speaks evil against a god, even if a false one, they seem to have taken a step from which they might more easily ascend to blasphemy against the true God. Therefore, it is also said elsewhere: <margin>Exodus 22</margin> *You shall not revile the gods.* <note>original: *Deos non maledices*; in this context, the author interprets the "gods" in Exodus 22:28 as a protection for the sanctity of the divine name itself, even when misapplied by others.</note> For even if the name of God is placed upon some false things, he [the Lawgiver] thought it should nevertheless be honored. He did not command the worship of creatures for that reason, but rather that the name of divinity be venerated. 

Since, therefore, the law is that a blasphemer must die, they say the Lord is guilty of this crime, <margin>John 5</margin> because he made himself the Son of God. But where was this said by the Lord? At the pool which was called the "Sheep Pool," <note>original: *piscina quae ouilis dicebatur*; also known as Bethesda, located near the Sheep Gate in Jerusalem.</note> on the Sabbath day, he miraculously delivered a man from a divine disease. <note>original: *diuino morbo*; likely referring to the man's thirty-eight-year paralysis, viewed as a significant or "sacred" affliction.</note> And while the Jews were more disturbed because it was on the Sabbath than they were marvelling at Christ’s power, he said: *My Father is working until now, and I am working.* 

Therefore, the Evangelist says, <margin>John 10</margin> <note>The text here cites John 10, though the narrative describes the events and discourse found in John 5:17-18.</note> the Jews persecuted Christ, who not only broke the Sabbath but also said that God was his own Father, making himself equal to God.

...from anyone? This error he <note>Jesus</note> pulls out by the roots, saying: *unless it were given to you from above.* <note>original: "nisi tibi esset datum desuper" from John 19:11.</note> Now, he says "from above" because the Only-begotten offered himself with the Father's consent, so that the mystery of the incarnation might be fulfilled. Therefore, "it was given from above," he says—that is, the Father granted and consented together with the Son. For not only by reason—since God cannot be forced—but also by the many instances of danger, it was clear that the Jews had often wanted to attack Christ but had been unable. 
<margin>John 8</margin> Elsewhere, as the Evangelist notes here, they wanted to seize him, but he, passing through their midst, <margin>Luke 4</margin> went his way. He spoke thus, not as one who is fearful, nor as those fleeing in secret usually do, but walking with a free step as he was accustomed. In this way, he escaped their eyes by his own power then, because the time for his suffering <term>passion<gloss>the period of Jesus's suffering leading to the crucifixion</gloss></term> had not yet arrived. Therefore, by his own nod and the Father's will, he says power was given to Pilate so that he could do anything against him. 

However, a greater sin rested on the one who handed him over than on Pilate. The former was the origin and the path of this wickedness, while Pilate, out of fear, merely acted as a servant to the Jews. Who, then, handed him over, or whom does the greater crime weigh upon? I believe it was the traitorous disciple <note>Judas Iscariot</note>; then the high priests and the priests; and finally the Jewish people themselves. Although he testifies that their sin is greater, he shows that Pilate was by no means free from the sin of wickedness.

### CHAPTER XXIII.
AND from then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, saying: "If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar." <note>John 19:12</note> Pilate was terrified when he heard that Christ made himself the Son of God, and for that reason, he was eager to free him from every false charge. When the cunning of the Jews realized this, they turned back to their first false charge: that he desired a kingdom for himself and was attempting to cast the Roman yoke far from the Jews. 

But look, I ask you, how craftily their malice turns this way and that. For when they first presented this as a crime, because they had been rejected, they immediately said he ought to die according to the Law because he made himself the Son of God—intending to force Pilate to act against the Savior out of a sense of piety toward God. But because this did them no good, they fled back to the first charge and shouted that he desired the kingdom of Judea in opposition to Caesar. For this reason, unless Pilate wished to punish him, they contended he was no friend of Caesar, since he allowed a man to live who contradicts Caesar—that is, who usurps the title of king against Caesar. 

And certainly, Caesar held an earthly dominion (which also depends on Christ), but Christ the Lord is primarily the ruler of the heavenly kingdom. For by him kings reign <margin>Proverbs 8</margin> and tyrants rule, as it is written. Therefore, they talk nonsense and in vain disparage the glory of the Savior; Isaiah rightly rebukes them, saying: <margin>Isaiah 57</margin> *But you, draw near here, you sons of the wicked, the seed of the adulterer and the prostitute, over whom have you opened your mouth and stuck out your tongue? Are you not children of perdition, a wicked seed?* For they were shamelessly using a false accusation not simply against some man, but against him who holds the sovereignty of all things with the Father; for this reason, they became children of perdition and a wicked seed.

593
### CHAPTER XXIV.
THEREFORE, when Pilate heard this speech, he led Jesus outside and sat before the judgment seat, in the place called *Lithostrotos*, <note>original: "Licostratos," a transcription of the Greek word for "stone pavement."</note> but in Hebrew, *Gabbatha*. Now it was the Day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour, and he said to the Jews: "Behold your king." 

We see now that all this wickedness is attributed mostly to the Jews; for Pilate, conquered even by the sight of their shouting, yielded. He did this to the extent that he neither feared justice nor cared much that he was acting with extreme inconsistency. For he who had repeatedly said in public that he found no fault in him now deferred to their will, becoming a witness to his own impiety. 

Therefore, he ascended the customary judgment seat to pronounce the savage sentence against Jesus. Now, the day and the hour are necessarily recorded, both because of the resurrection and the three-day period under the earth, so that the word of the Lord spoken to the Jews might be understood to have reached its fulfillment. <margin>Matthew 12</margin> "For as Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days <margin>Jonah 2</margin> and three nights," he says, "so also the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights." From the judgment seat itself, he points to Jesus, saying: "Behold your king." What then is this? Either he is mocking the people, whose thirst for innocent blood he is gratifying, or perhaps he seeks to insult them because they strive to afflict him with so many and such great evils—the very one whom they call the King of the Jews.

For he who places obstacles in the way <note>original: "scandala ponit"</note> and seduces men from the right path in whatever way he can is no different from Satan. Which even Christ seems to show with those words: <margin>Matthew 5</margin> **If, he says, your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away.** <note>original: "Si oculus, inquit, dexter tuus scãdalizat te, erue eũ, & proijce abs te."</note> For whatever removes us from our happiness—even if it is joined to us by the law of friendship, even if it is linked by nature itself and the closeness of blood—must be considered not as our own, but as something alien and hostile. 

Now, he was crucified between two thieves by the malice of the Jews: who, in order to show his death as most shameful, condemned the righteous man with the wicked. Indeed, these two thieves seem to me to signify the two peoples who were afterwards joined to Christ—I mean the Jewish and the Gentile peoples. They were rightly condemned as thieves, because the Jews, by transgressing the law, were guilty of the crime of <term>unfaithfulness<gloss>Original: "praevaricationis." In a legal sense, this refers to a breach of duty or a "falling away" from the requirements of the law.</gloss></term>, and the Gentiles worshipped the creature rather than the Creator. 

Nevertheless, in another sense, those who cling to Christ are crucified together with him. For, having been reformed to a new and evangelical life, they undergo the death of their former way of life. Whence Paul says concerning Christ: <margin>Galatians 5</margin> **But those who are Christ’s have crucified their flesh with its vices and lusts.** <note>original: "Qui autē sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum uitijs & concupiscentijs."</note> And regarding everyone in his own person: <margin>Galatians 2</margin> **For I, through the law, am dead to the law, that I might live for God: I have been fixed to the cross with Christ; yet I no longer live, but Christ lives in me.** <note>original: "Ego enim per legem legi mortuus sum, ut Deo uiuā: Christo confixus sum cruci, uiuo autem iam nō ego, uiuit uerò in me Christus."</note> And again: <margin>Colossians 2</margin> **If therefore you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why do you still decree as if living for the world?** <note>original: "Si ergo mortui estis cũ Christo, ab elemētis huius mundi, quid adhuc tanquã uiuentes mundo decernitis?"</note> For the death of the worldly way of life is the origin and foundation of the evangelical life. Therefore, the cross of the two thieves, as we have learned from the event, signified the joining of the two peoples with Christ, who were in a certain way dead together with Christ, having despised carnal pleasure and buried the worldly life, so that they might live spiritually with their Lord.

### CHAPTER XXIX.

**And Pilate also wrote a title and placed it upon the cross. And it was written: Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.** <note>original: "Iesus Nazarenus rex Iudæorum"</note> This is surely that <term>record of debt<gloss>Original: "chirographum." A Greek-derived legal term for a handwritten document or bond of debt that a person signed to acknowledge what they owed.</gloss></term> against us, which Paul says was fixed to the cross by the Lord, in which he triumphed over principalities and powers as over the conquered. <margin>Colossians 2</margin> For even if not the Savior, but the servant of the Jews' fury, affixed this title, yet he himself <note>Christ</note> is written to have affixed it—he who triumphed—because the sign placed there signified to those reading it that he was that Christ who gave his life for the redemption of all. For all men were weighed down by the yoke of sin. **For all,** he says, **have turned aside, and have together become useless,** <margin>Psalm 13</margin> and serving the devil, we lived most shamefully. 

The devil held a record of debt against our nature: the curse of the divine law owed by transgressors, and that ancient sentence of God which was most justly brought against the first man, in whom our race was universally condemned (because no one is without sin). For just as Adam sinned, so also others after him neglected the command of God. Therefore, the sentence was brought regarding one against all. 

TWELFTH BOOK. 597

This record of debt against our race, therefore, the Savior blotted out by the title fixed to the cross. For this title clearly signified his death on the wood, which he suffered for the life of the condemned, and he paid a sufficient penalty for their sins. For even if only one suffered, yet as God he is worthy above every creature, and his life is far more excellent than the life of all. Therefore **all iniquity has stopped its mouth,** <margin>Psalm 106</margin> as the Psalmist sings, and the tongue of sin has fallen silent, since it cannot accuse those who fall short. For we have been justified since Christ paid our debts for us. **For by his bruises we are all healed,** <margin>Isaiah 53</margin> as it is written. But just as our fall was devised through wood <note>Referring to the tree in the Garden of Eden</note>, so through wood, having been renewed from our fall, we have received heavenly goods, since Christ for our sake purified in himself the very beginning of the sickness.

### CHAPTER XXX.

**Many of the Jews therefore read this title, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. And it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.** It was done by divine providence, as I think, that the title was written in the letters of the three languages that are primary. For it signified that the kingdom of all nations was attributed to Christ. For to him, says Daniel, **honor and kingdom were given, and all tribes and tongues shall serve him.** <margin>Daniel 7</margin> And as Paul says: <margin>Philippians 2</margin> **Every knee shall bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth: and every tongue shall confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.** This title, therefore, through the primary languages, preached that Jesus would be the leader of all languages, and it proved the Jews guilty of the crime of impiety. It shouted with the great voice of those who read it that they had crucified their Lord and King.

### CHAPTER XXXI.

**Therefore the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate: Do not write, "The King of the Jews," but that he said, "I am the King of the Jews." Pilate answered: What I have written, I have written.** The leaders of the Jews cannot bear a title of this kind, but, disturbed by sharp envy, they utterly deny the kingdom of Christ. For they say, "This man was never king, whom we never received as king; but he himself used words of this kind." Thus, out of ignorance, they did not see that the nature of truth cannot lie—and Christ is the Truth. Therefore, he is the King of the Jews if he said so himself, and even if you, O Jews, affirm it <note>Perhaps meaning that their very opposition confirms his status</note>. Pilate, however, does not wish to change the title, because it was not divinely permitted to him to rage against the glory of the Savior in all things. For the kingdom of Christ is stable and above all false accusations, even if the Jews are unwilling, and even if they do not allow his glory to be confessed.

[let us cast lots] <note>The page begins mid-sentence, likely completing the Latin "sortiamur" (let us cast lots).</note> about it, to decide whose it shall be, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says: **They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.** (And indeed, the soldiers did these things.)

The soldiers divided the Savior’s garments among themselves. For those who act as the executors of public law <note>original: "publicarum rerum uindices." He did not die against his will, but as the Master of life and death, choosing the exact moment when all things were perfected.

### CHAPTER XL.
**After these things, Joseph of Arimathea—who was a disciple of Jesus, though a secret one for fear of the Jews—asked Pilate if he might take away the body of Jesus; and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took the body of Jesus.** <margin>John 19</margin> This brief account again accuses the impiety of the Jews, showing that it was not without great danger to embrace the teachings of Christ. For this upright man, although he loved Christ and preferred his teaching over the Law, nevertheless remained hidden, fearing the threats of the Jews who threatened death to those who believed in Christ. But see here also how much cruelty was in the hearts of the Jews. Indeed, they did not even wish to perform the funeral rites for Christ after he was dead, though they were not ignorant that he was the Christ; they had seen many of his signs and miracles, yet, driven by the sting of envy, they gained no benefit from them. Therefore, to their condemnation, and especially that of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Joseph of Arimathea honors the body of Jesus with burial.

### CHAPTER XLI.
**Nicodemus, who had first come to Jesus by night, also came, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, weighing about a hundred pounds.** <margin>John 3</margin> The author shows that not just one man of great courage came to bury the most holy body of Christ, but a second as well, establishing the matter by the authority of the Law. <margin>Deuteronomy 19</margin> For the Law commands that **every word shall be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses.** There were, therefore, two "undertakers" <note>original: "pollinctores." In ancient Rome, these were the officials who prepared a body for burial by washing and anointing it.</note>, Joseph and Nicodemus: believing in their hearts, but weighed down by fear, they still preferred earthly glory to heavenly glory; and for that reason, they honored Christ not freely or openly, but more secretly and timidly.

### CHAPTER XLII.
**They took the body of Jesus and wrapped it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews. Now in the place where he was crucified, there was a garden; and in the garden, a new tomb in which no one had ever been laid.** He was indeed numbered among the dead according to the flesh for our sake—he who is so by nature and truly by himself—so that he might fulfill all the righteousness that belongs to our race, and he voluntarily surrendered his body to death and burial. He says the tomb was in a garden, and that it was new; this signifies that through the death of Christ, our return to Paradise has been prepared for us. <margin>A</margin> For the Forerunner himself has entered there on our behalf. <margin>Hebrews 6</margin> The novelty of the tomb, moreover, signifies the new and unheard-of return from death to life. <margin>Isaiah 26</margin> For death itself was made new in the death of Christ, changed into the condition of sleep. <margin>1 Thessalonians 4</margin> For we live for God, and our very bodies shall live again according to the Scriptures. Therefore the dead are now called "those who sleep" by everyone, and especially by Paul. <margin>Romans 5</margin> For formerly, death reigned most openly even over those who did not sin in the likeness of the transgression of Adam (clothed in whose image, all were subjected to the curse). But after the Second Adam shone forth, and by the death of his flesh redeemed the life of the human race, and rose again having destroyed the empire of destruction, we were

<column-break/>

->605<-
reformed, subjected to a certain "new death"—not an eternal one, but one most similar to sleep, namely after the likeness of Christ, who prepared this way for us. If anyone believes the tomb is called "new" because no one had been placed there before Christ, we not only do not reject this, but we strongly approve of it. For it was a new tomb, and no one was placed there before Christ, so that it would not be believed that someone else had risen from the dead.

### CHAPTER XLIII.
**And so, because of the Jewish day of Preparation, as the tomb was nearby, they laid Jesus there.** He not only indicated that the tomb was new and in a garden, but also described the body of Christ being placed in the tomb, omitting not even the smallest detail. For it is necessary for the knowledge of the mystery <margin>B</margin> to confess that Christ truly died. For this reason Paul, delivering the rule of faith, says: **Because if you confess with your mouth, "Jesus is Lord," and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.** <margin>Romans 10</margin> For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. And elsewhere: **I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.** <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> Necessarily, therefore, the Evangelist explains even these minute details to us. Because it is necessary to believe he was dead and buried, so that later we can truly believe that, having broken the bonds of destruction, he returned to his own life. <margin>Acts 17</margin> For it was not naturally possible for life to be held by death; <margin>C</margin> nor could He in whom we live and move and have our being be perpetually subject to the laws of our nature, but as God, he gives life to our nature which stands in need of life.

Thus, seeing that the outcome of events agreed with the true predictions, they were greatly strengthened in their faith. It should be noted, however, that while this Evangelist signifies the time of the resurrection by saying, **"On the first day of the week, early in the morning, while it was still dark,"** <margin>Matthew 28</margin> Matthew left it written, **"In the evening of the Sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week."** Yet there is no discrepancy between them. For the same time is signified by "deep evening" and "deep morning," since both modes of speaking reach toward midnight. For one, starting from the end of the night, and the other from the beginning, proceeded toward the depths of the night. And so, starting from opposite ends of the night, they meet at the deep and middle of the night.

### CHAPTER XLV.
**The disciples therefore went away again to their own homes. But Mary stood outside at the tomb weeping.** Strengthened now by a firm faith in the resurrection, John and Peter returned home again to preach to the disciples and to deliberate on what they ought to do. I believe they returned quite quickly because they were not ignorant of the Jews' anger against Christ's disciples. Hence, they did not think it safe for themselves to linger around the tomb until daylight. We shall not say they were overwhelmed by fear, but they did not wish to undergo danger before the appointed time, as Christ had warned their souls when he said to the Father concerning them: <margin>John 17</margin> **"Holy Father, keep them in your name whom you have given me, that they may be one as we are one; while I was with them, I kept them in your name... and none of them is lost except the son of perdition."** Therefore, departing quickly from there and returning to their own, they kept the Savior's commands, who ordered them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the promise of the Father which they had heard from him. <margin>Acts 1</margin> **"For John truly baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now."** <margin>Acts 2</margin> This matter reached its fulfillment on the day of Pentecost, when divided tongues, as if of fire, appeared to them and sat upon each of them. For then, reformed from human weakness to a certain greater strength, they thought little of the snares of the Jews. But while the disciples (as we said) withdrew to more secret places, <margin>Acts</margin> Mary, free from all fear because she suspected nothing of the Jews' anger, remained around the tomb and (as is the custom of women) added weeping upon weeping. Nor did she weep only because he was dead, but also because he seemed to have been moved elsewhere from the tomb.

### CHAPTER XLVI.
**As she wept, she stooped down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels in white sitting: one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been laid. They said to her: Woman, why are you weeping?** See again that she did not weep in vain, nor did she lack a reward for her love toward Christ. For as she persevered in weeping around the tomb, she was aided by the voice of the angels to recognize Christ. She saw them in white robes, so that by the brightness of the garments, the beauty of their purity might be signified. Turning her away from weeping, they said: **"Woman, why are you weeping?"** For they did not ask the cause of her tears because they were ignorant of it, but as is clear from the matter itself, they were admonishing her not to weep. For since death and destruction were now destroyed, they were saying it was no longer a time for tears. <margin>Genesis 3</margin> Since the Lord by his resurrection had recalled the human race to life, why must you weep, O woman? For the outcome of things invites the opposite instead. Why therefore do you weep, you who ought now to rejoice and be glad? Furthermore, they appeared sitting, one at the head and the other at the feet where the body of Jesus had been laid, <margin>Psalm 118</margin> to signify to the woman (who thought the Lord's body had been moved) that no one could have inflicted violence upon that most holy body, which was defended by angels. One might not unjustly wonder why the angels did not appear to the disciples (I mean Peter and John), but to the woman they both appear and speak. We say, therefore, that the mystery of the Lord—by his own arrangement and will—was more certainly planted in the minds of men in many diverse ways, as a suitable mode of manifestation was adapted to each person. For the outcome of events, agreeing with the scriptures and Christ's own preaching, led the disciples to a most firm faith. It was therefore superfluous for those who firmly believed to be taught by the voice of angels. But it was entirely necessary for the woman, who neither knew letters <note>Meaning she was likely uneducated or unable to read the prophecies for herself.</note> nor could perceive the sublime mystery of the resurrection in any other way.

### CHAPTER XLVII.
