For she did not yet understand what that vision signified, but merely explained the cause of her weeping. But because she always called Christ "Lord" and showed her fervent love for him in this way, she was judged worthy to see him. She sees Jesus, therefore, but does not recognize him: either because by divine power he did not permit himself to be recognized, or because since it was still dark, she could not discern him clearly.

### THE BREATH OF THE WORD
**When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them: Receive the Holy Spirit.** 

We must observe how the Savior, by his physical act of breathing, demonstrates that the Holy Spirit is not someone foreign or external to him. Rather, the Spirit proceeds from his own substance, just as the breath of a human being proceeds from their innermost self. <margin>Genesis 2</margin> He also brings to mind the original creation of man. In the beginning, God **breathed** the breath of life into man’s face; now, at the dawn of the new creation, Christ breathes again to restore the grace that had been lost through the ancient fall.

<gloss>The act of breathing represents the "new creation" of humanity.</gloss>

**Receive the Holy Spirit.** Although the full outpouring of the Spirit would later occur at Pentecost in the form of fiery tongues, here he grants them a specific **sanctification** <term>sanctification<gloss>The process of being made holy or set apart for a sacred purpose.</gloss></term> and the spiritual authority required for their upcoming mission.

<column-break/>

### THE POWER TO FORGIVE SINS
**Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them: and whose sins you retain, they are retained.** 

This is truly a magnificent and divine dignity! To forgive sins is a power that belongs to the nature of God alone. Yet, the Lord shares this glory with his servants. By saying this, he makes the Apostles the distributors of his divine mercy.

<margin>Matthew 16</margin> 

What was previously promised to Peter—the "Power of the Keys"—is now bestowed upon all the Apostles together. However, we should understand that it is not the men themselves who forgive sins by their own human will. Rather, it is the **Holy Spirit** dwelling within them who performs the cleansing. The Apostles act as the instruments and ministers of that Spirit.

<note>The author emphasizes that the priest's role is ministerial; the power itself is purely divine.</note>

Therefore, when they loose a man from the bonds of sin through the preaching of the Gospel or the administration of the sacraments, it is God himself who looses him. Conversely, when someone remains in a state of unrepentant unbelief, the Apostles "retain" those sins, signifying that the person remains bound by their own choices. Through this sacred ministry, the Church is governed and the faithful are led toward the hope of eternal life.

This was permitted to Thomas because he, together with the others, had obtained the Spirit; for that voice passed through to the entire company of the disciples by the generosity of the giver: **"Receive the Holy Spirit."** <note>original: *Accipite spiritum sanctum*. A reference to John 20:22, where Jesus breathes on the disciples.</note> 

<column-break/>

But it seems to me that this must also be asked: Thomas touched the Savior’s side, and quite curiously handled the wound from the soldier’s spear, and more diligently examined the marks of the nails. How then (someone might ask) did the signs of destruction appear in an **incorruptible body** <term>incorruptible body<gloss>In Christian theology, this refers to the "glorified" state of the body after resurrection, which is believed to be physical yet no longer subject to pain, decay, or death.</gloss></term>? For the wounds of the hands and side, and the iron piercings, are signs of bodily corruption. However, the body of Christ, having been reformed for **incorruptibility** <term>incorruptibility<gloss>The state of being free from physical decay or the possibility of dying again.</gloss></term>, ought to have cast aside everything belonging to corruption—that is, destruction—along with the corruption itself. Or perhaps those who were lame will walk with a limp in that other life as well, or the one-eyed will rise with only one eye? And how will the human race be completely freed from corruption, if the things that precede or follow destruction <note>The text cuts off here, but the author is posing a rhetorical question about whether the imperfections of our mortal lives will persist in the afterlife.</note>

->622 ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN<-

We have said that Thomas doubted more from [excessive joy] than from a weakness of mind, since we are not ignorant that Luke said the same of the others: <margin>Luke 24</margin> **And while they yet believed not for joy, and wondered.** <note>original: *Adhuc autem illis non credentibus, & mirantibus præ gaudio*. See Luke 24:41.</note> Truly, since the sight of him removed every cause for doubt, Thomas rightly cried out at once: **"My Lord and my God."** For he who is by nature the Lord and God of all things must also be the true God, a fact that also works in reverse: for he who is God by nature necessarily rules over all things. Both titles are used with the definite article <note>The author refers to the Greek grammar (*ho Kyrios* and *ho Theos*), where the "the" indicates a unique, supreme status.</note> so that no one might think he is being called "lord" or "god" in the way we or the angels are, but rather that he is being called **the** Lord and **the** God in a singular sense. For as Paul says, <margin>1 Corinthians 8</margin> there are many "gods" and "lords" in heaven and on earth. But Thomas, in a singular way, calls him **the** Lord and **the** God, as the Son of the true God.

[B] What is more, when the Savior heard the disciple say these things, he did not rebuke him or push him away; instead, he praised and embraced him, and urged the others to preach the same: <margin>Matthew 28</margin> **"Go,"** he said, **"and teach all nations."** When Thomas heard this along with the others, what else could he say but what he himself believed? It is clear, therefore, that the Lord wishes us to confess him in the same way that Thomas did. For he is Lord and God by nature, even after he took on humanity. Notice also that the disciple who touched his feet and his side confessed him in such a way that he did not divide him into "two sons." <note>This is a theological point against "Nestorianism," an early Christian debate. The author insists that Jesus is one single person—both God and man—not two separate beings (a divine "Son of God" and a human "son of Mary") joined together.</note> For he recognized one and the same Lord Jesus Christ in the flesh.

### CHAPTER 60
[C] <margin>John 20:29</margin> **Jesus said to him: "Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen, and yet have believed."** The Savior’s words are full of great foresight and bring us the highest benefit. For after he showed his pierced side and the marks of the nails to confirm the world's faith—and after he even ate food (though he did not need it), so that no cause for unbelief remained—he also confirmed by his words what must be believed. For he was not unaware that some would arise who would not confess the resurrection of the dead, and who would say they wanted to see and touch for themselves just as Thomas did, contending that they were right to do so because they were imitating the Savior's disciple. 

Therefore, Christ prevents this fall with these words, calling those **blessed** who have not seen and yet have believed. [D] And not without reason: for no cause for doubt is left to the one who sees. But the one who believes what he has not seen, but has heard through the words of teachers, certainly honors him in whom he believes in an extraordinary way. Blessed, therefore, are all who have believed through the preaching of the apostles. For they (as Luke says) <margin>Luke 10</margin> saw with their eyes the wonders performed by Jesus and were ministers of his word. We must place our faith in them if we desire to possess eternal life and reign in heaven.

### CHAPTER 61
**Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.** By repeating what he has written, he reveals the purpose of the Gospel: for these things were published by me, he says, so that you might believe, and by believing have eternal life. He says there were more signs of the Savior than were recorded by him, which were left out because he thought these were sufficient to persuade readers that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. These are the words of the Evangelist.

->ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 623<-

[A] But I will say this, and not without reason: if the power of the Gospel and the greatness of the miracles are sufficient to persuade us—because the son of the Virgin, who was named Jesus by the voice of the angel, is the same one who is called "Christ" by the scriptures and is the Son of God (not like others, but uniquely and properly so, even after he was joined to human nature)—then those who dare to deny their Lord are completely in error. For when we consider the nature of the Word, we find that the temple <note>In early Christian writing, the "temple" is a common metaphor for the human body of Jesus in which the divine Word (God) dwelt.</note> which he took from the Virgin is different from him by nature. [B] But when we look at the power of the union, and (as far as we are able) investigate this supernatural mystery, then we understand the Word and his temple to be one. He was not changed into flesh (for we do not say this, as the nature of the Word is by no means susceptible to change), but rather, according to the scriptures, Jesus Christ is one: one Son, I say, who is understood to consist of the temple of his flesh (which receives the definition of a complete human nature) and of the living Word of God. This can be easily understood by looking at noble men. For each of us is one man, even though we consist of soul and body, both of which differ from the other by the reason of their nature.

### CHAPTER 62
[C] <margin>Chapter 21</margin> **Afterward, Jesus manifested himself again at the Sea of Tiberias; and he manifested himself in this way. There were together Simon Peter, and Thomas called Didymus, and Nathanael who was from Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples. Simon Peter said to them: "I am going fishing." They said: "We will come with you." And they went out and entered the boat, and that night they caught nothing. But when morning came, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know it was Jesus. Jesus therefore said to them: "Children, do you have any food?" They answered him: "No." He said to them: "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." But they said: "We have labored all night and caught nothing, but in your name we will cast it." [D] They cast the net, therefore, and now they were not able to draw it in for the multitude of fish.**

Now the Lord appears freely to the disciples for the third time, so that he might strengthen their faith with invincible firmness. For since they have seen him so often, how could they not be removed from all doubt and become true teachers of piety to others? Peter went out to fish, and the others joined him—perhaps by Christ's divine plan. For when he called them to the apostolate, <margin>Matthew 4</margin> he said: **"Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men."** He signified by this event, as if by a sign, that this was soon to happen. For certain disciples labor all night and catch nothing; but as the sun was now rising, Jesus stood on the shore and asked if they had caught anything. When they replied they had caught nothing at all, he ordered them to the right side of the ship...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Gospel of John, specifically addressing the appearance of Jesus to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias (John 21). It picks up with the disciples being told to cast their nets after a night of unsuccessful fishing.</meta>

->624 BOOK TWELVE 625<-

...to cast the nets on that side. But they, although they had labored in vain all night, and although they did not know it was the Lord himself, replied: "In your name we will do it." When they did this, a miraculous multitude of fish was caught. Thus says the Evangelist. But since we were just saying that this event signified what the Lord had previously told them—that they would be "fishers of men"—let us now investigate the details and offer some reasons for spiritual contemplation to the readers. **"Give an occasion to a wise man,"** it says, <margin>Proverbs 9</margin> **"and he will be wiser."** <note>original: *Da enim sapienti causam, & sapientior erit.* See Proverbs 9:9.</note> Therefore, from the fact that they labored in vain all night, we think it is signified that through the preaching of the ancients <note>The "ancients" refers to the Old Testament prophets and patriarchs.</note>, almost no one adhered to God, or so few that we can say without injustice that no one did. For when compared to the whole world, the few seem like none. <margin>B</margin> What then prevented it, or what caused their preaching to bear no fruit? It was night, and mental darkness (if I may say so) clouded the eyes of the mind, and demonic error led them away from the knowledge of truth. For there was **"none who did good, not even one,"** but all turned aside and became useless together. <margin>Psalm 13</margin> <note>Modern Bibles usually list this as Psalm 14 or 53.</note> For even Israel itself, whom Moses "fished for," being instructed in shadows and figures <note>Refers to the ceremonies and laws of the Old Testament which were seen as "shadows" of the reality to come in Christ.</note>, could not reach perfection.

For the worship of God through figures was not acceptable to God, which is easily understood because he rejected sacrifices and blood and every kind of earthly and bodily offering, saying: <margin>Jeremiah 6</margin> **"To what purpose do you offer me cinnamon and incense from a far country? Your burnt offerings are not pleasing to me, and your sacrifices do not delight me."** <margin>C</margin> We say these things not to accuse the Law, but to show that while God the Creator of all looked toward the beauty of Gospel teaching alone, even those who worshipped God through the shadows and figures of the Law were far from the truth. For Christ is the truth. <margin>John 5</margin> Furthermore, those called to the legal worship through the Law of Moses, having despised the Law and turned to the mandates of men, became so hardened that the doctrine of the prophets could do nothing among them. Hence one cried out: <margin>Isaiah 53</margin> **"Lord, who has believed our report?"** Another said: <margin>Jeremiah 15</margin> **"Woe is me, my mother, why did you bear me a man of strife and discord in all the earth? I have been of no use to anyone, nor anyone to me."** Why then should we not consider the Jews similar to those who had no Law, since they despised the Law they were given? <margin>D</margin> For regarding the Gentiles, no one will ever doubt that, wrapped in errors, they were far from God's teaching.

Therefore, night and deep darkness prevented people from seeing the light of true piety. For these reasons, those who tried to "fish" for men before the coming of Christ labored through the whole night and caught nothing. But when morning came, and the darkness of the devil was driven away by the rising of the true light, Jesus Christ—who asks the laborers if they have anything that could be food for the Savior God who hungers for the salvation of men—because they answer they have caught nothing, they are ordered to cast the nets on the **right side** of the boat. For blessed Moses cast the nets through the mandates of the Law, but that fishing was done, in a sense, on the **left side**. For the **right side** is attributed to the Savior's teaching, which is beyond all comparison greater and more glorious than that of Moses.

<column-break/>

[A] For truth is much more sublime than figures, the Lord is superior to the servant, and the grace of the justifying Spirit is superior to the condemning letter. Therefore, the **right side** signifies excellence and superiority. But when the nets were cast on the right side, a great multitude of fish was caught. This was done by the Lord's command, because they did not seize grace for themselves, but obeyed the command of Christ saying: <margin>Matthew 28</margin> **"Go and teach all nations."** Hence they even said: **"In your name we will cast the net."** For the apostles do not fish in any other way than in the name of the Savior, and by his words and teaching. A truly great multitude of fish was caught, so many that the disciples could not pull them in. For the faithful are innumerable, and such a great matter entirely exceeds the strength of the apostles. <margin>B</margin> This is therefore the work of Christ, who by his power gathers the multitude of men into this earthly church as if into nets.

### CHAPTER 63.
That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter: **"It is the Lord."** When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his tunic around him (for he was naked) and threw himself into the sea; but the other disciples came in the boat. For they were not far from the land, but about two hundred cubits away, dragging the net of fish. When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire laid there, with fish placed on it and bread. Jesus said to them: **"Bring some of the fish you have just caught."** Simon Peter went up and dragged the net to land, full of very large fish, one hundred and fifty-three of them; <margin>C</margin> and although there were so many, the net was not torn. Jesus said to them: **"Come and eat."** But none of those sitting down to eat dared to ask him: "Who are you?" knowing that it was the Lord. And Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and the fish likewise. (This was now the third time Jesus was revealed to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.)

He calls himself "the beloved disciple" again, he who wrote this Gospel for us. He was loved most because, due to the purity of his mind and the sharpness of the "eyes of his heart," he was most fit for understanding. Hence he alone immediately understood the sign and knew Christ was present, and without hesitation signaled it to the others. For with a firm spirit he cried out: **"It is the Lord."** And Peter, burning with love for Christ (as was his habit), leaped out, realizing the boat would reach the shore too slowly. <margin>D</margin> But the others came in the boat, dragging the net. They see the charcoal fire laid, and the fish placed upon it, which Christ had fished for miraculously. For the spiritual fishing did not begin with the apostles, but our Savior first laid his hand to it and fished for one as the "first-fruits." <note>The "first-fruits" refers to the first part of a harvest dedicated to God; here, it signifies Christ starting the mission himself.</note> We do not understand "one" literally, but we believe a small number is signified in this way; afterward, the disciples, strengthened by his command, fished for a huge multitude.

It highlights the roles of John, who recognizes Jesus first through spiritual insight, and Peter, who acts with characteristic fervor.</summary>

        CHAPTER LXVI.
Then Peter, turning around, saw following them the disciple whom Jesus loved, who also had leaned back against his chest at the supper and said: Lord, who is it who will betray you? When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus: "Lord, what about this man?" Jesus said to him: "If I want him to remain until I come, what is it to you? You follow me." Therefore this saying went out among the brothers, that this disciple would not die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he would not die, but: "If I want him to remain, what is it to you?") The Evangelist <note>The author of the Gospel, John.</note> again signifies himself. For he was both the beloved disciple of the Lord, and the one who leaned against his chest at the supper and asked who was going to betray him. Therefore, when Peter looked back at this man so beloved by the Lord, he immediately asked what end of life was threatening him. But since an inquiry into the affairs of others is more curious than it is useful, he responds indeed, but in such a way that he leads the mind of the asker away to other things. 
<margin>John 21</margin> He does not say that John would be free from death, but: "If I want him to remain until I come, what is it to you?" That is: "You have heard, Peter, the things that pertain to you; why do you seek other things? Why do you search into the secrets of divine justice? For even if I were to wish that this man should not die at all, what profit or what consolation would you ever obtain?" Therefore, a curious person will not be prudent if he asks what he himself is to suffer, and whether others will also undergo the same things or not; for his own dangers are not mitigated by the calamity of others. Although it seems to be commonly implanted in humans that, if they are to undergo some danger, they hope they are not alone, but that they might see others suffering similar things, or at least hear that they have endured them, or will suffer the same things entirely.

                      C

        CHAPTER LXVII.
This is the disciple who gives testimony concerning these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true.) I think no one can doubt that John was loved by Christ because of his exceptional virtue and a mind ready for doing good. For the Lord was not moved by vain affections, as naked <note>The term "naked" (*nudi*) here implies "mere" or "fallen" humans without divine grace.</note> men are; rather, he imparted his love based on the weight of the facts and the virtue of the disciples. Therefore, this preacher of truth wrote these things about the Lord and gave testimony concerning them: "and we know that his testimony is true." For he would not have been loved by the Truth <note>Referring to Christ, who is Truth itself.</note> unless he had been removed far from all falsehood.

        CHAPTER LXVIII.
But there are also many other things that Jesus did; which if they were written one by one, I do not think the world itself could contain the books that would be written.) Great, he says, is the multitude of the Lord's signs, and the number is immense; but these things which we have reported are sufficient to produce the fullest faith in those who read attentively. Nor should I be accused, he says, if I have not written everything down. For if each thing were considered individually, with absolutely nothing omitted, the world would not contain the multitude of books. We say this, however, using <term>hyperbole</term> <note>original: *Hyperbolicè*—a literary device involving deliberate exaggeration for emphasis.</note> to bring forth the power of this speech. Therefore, not everything the Lord did was written down, but only those things which the writers thought would suffice for <term>morality</term> <note>original: *mores*—refers to ethical conduct and character.</note> as much as for <term>dogma</term> <note>original: *dogmata*—the core doctrines or teachings of the faith.</note>; so that, shining with right faith and works and virtue, we may reach the kingdom of heaven, in our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom and through whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit. 
Amen.

The end of the twelfth and final book of the commentaries of Cyril on John.

If, however, it should be the sin of the entire **synagogue** <note>original: "synagogæ"; here referring to the collective assembly or congregation of Israel</note>, the law commands the synagogue to nonetheless offer a calf as a burnt offering. But regarding the sin of the synagogue, it is said: "if it acted in ignorance, and the matter was hidden from the eyes of the synagogue, and it did what is against the commandment of the Lord." From this it appears that even the entire synagogue falls into transgression through ignorance; a point which the Lord also confirms in the <margin>Luke 23</margin> Gospel <note>original: "euã" (evangelio); the author refers to Luke 23:34, where Jesus says, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do."</note>

If anyone touches these things—that is, if someone follows another into sin—he shall be unclean. And if anyone touches the carcass <note>original: "morticinum"; in the Mosaic Law, this refers to the body of an animal that died of natural causes rather than being ritually slaughtered. Cyril interprets this as a person who has died spiritually.</note> of such a person—that is, of one who at first lived according to reason and exercised himself in the word of God, but afterwards fell into sin—if anyone follows or imitates him, he touches a human carcass and shall be unclean. 

But also, if you touch one caught by a wild beast, you shall be unclean. What is this beast? Is it the lion, or the wolf that snatches away men or cattle? I believe it is that beast of which the apostle Peter speaks: <margin>1 Peter 5</margin> *Because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour; resist him, firm in your faith.* And again, of those of whom the apostle Paul speaks: <margin>Acts 20</margin> *For after my departure, ravenous wolves will enter, not sparing the flock.* Therefore, if you see someone captured by these beasts, do not follow him, do not touch him, lest you also become unclean. 

There are, moreover, other unclean animals whose carcasses he forbids to be touched. Unclean animals are people who are outside of Christ, in whom there is neither reason nor any religion. Therefore, if you see the carcasses—that is, the sins—of all these, the Lawgiver <note>Refers to God or Moses as the author of the Law.</note> says to you: do not touch, do not approach, do not handle them. 

And these are the uncleannesses which ought deservedly to be shunned. However, to shrink from the touch of a human being, or from a dead body <note>original: "motui corporis"; likely a typesetter's error for "mortui corporis," meaning a corpse.</note> to which burial ought rather to be religiously granted—these are Jewish and useless fables, having indeed an appearance of piety, but denying its power. <note>Cyril is arguing that the Christian "purity" is moral/spiritual, whereas the literal Jewish avoidance of physical corpses is, in his view, a "useless fable" that ignores the duty of burial.</note>

The first law, therefore, given concerning uncleanness: If anyone was a witness of some oath or of a crime and did not make it known, through this [he shall be] unclean...

652 BOOK FOUR.

<margin>1 Thess. 5</margin> ...all things, holding fast to what is good. For our Lord Jesus Christ is the only one who can teach you this kind of art, through which you may know how to discern which "money" <note>original: "pecunia"; used here as a metaphor for faith or doctrine.</note> holds the image of the true King, and which is counterfeit—or as it is commonly said, "formed outside the mint"—which might have the name of the king but does not possess the truth of the royal figure. For there are many who have the name of Christ, <margin>1 Cor. 11</margin> but do not have the truth of Christ; and because of these, Paul says: *For there must also be heresies, that those who are approved may be made manifest among you.* Therefore, even in the present reading, the Lawgiver, looking entirely toward a mystical and spiritual sense, added that this ram—which is provided so that it might absolve sin—should be purchased not with just any shekel, <term>shekel</term><note>A "siclo" or shekel was a standard unit of weight and currency in ancient Israel.</note> that is, not with just any money, but with a **holy shekel**. If he were not looking toward a mystery, what reason would there seem to be that a ram offered as a sacrifice must be bought for a certain price? The name of the money called a "shekel" was not enough; he added, "and a holy shekel." What if someone had the finest rams in his flocks, worthy of divine sacrifices? Or what if someone is so poor that he cannot have a holy shekel? This would be a strange restriction by the Lawgiver, that unless someone has a specific amount of money, his sin cannot be absolved. This is clearly absurd according to the letter, but according to spiritual understanding it is certain: that no one will receive the remission of sins unless they bring an entire, approved, and holy faith, through which they may "purchase" the ram; whose nature is such that it wipes away the sins of the believer. And this is the **holy shekel**: a faith that is approved and sincere, as we said. That is, where no deceit of faithlessness and no perversity of heretical cunning is mixed in. Thus, by offering a sincere faith, we are washed by the precious blood of Christ as if by an unblemished sacrifice; with whom is glory and power to God the Father Almighty and with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

**The end of the Third Book.**

### SAINT CYRIL ON LEVITICUS
### BOOK FOUR.

Regarding that which is written: *If a soul shall sin, and in bypassing shall bypass the commandments of the Lord, and shall lie to his neighbor,* and so forth.

**S**I <note>The large decorative initial 'S' begins the new book.</note> IF, according to the faith of the divine law, the Lord spoke these things which are read to us to Moses, I think that such great words of God ought not to be understood according to the incapacity of the listeners, but according to the majesty of the Speaker. The Lord, <margin>1 Cor. 3</margin> he says, has spoken. What is "the Lord"? Let the Apostle answer you, and learn from him, that *the Lord is the Spirit.* But if the word of the Apostle is not enough for you, hear the Lord himself in the Gospels, saying: <margin>John 4</margin> *Because God is Spirit.* If therefore the Lord and God is Spirit, we ought to hear what the Spirit speaks in a spiritual way. I say even further:

BOOK FOUR. 653

because the things which the Lord speaks are to be believed not only as spiritual, but as Spirit itself. I shall not prove this from my own <margin>John 6</margin> opinion, but from the Gospels. Hear our Lord and Savior saying to his disciples: *The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life.* If therefore we learn by the voice of the Savior himself that the words he spoke to the apostles are spirit and life, we must in no way doubt that even the things he spoke through Moses are to be believed as spirit and life. But let us see what those things are about which we ought now, as far as we are able, to say something. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: *Whatever soul <margin>Levit. 6</margin> shall sin, and shall bypass the commandments of the Lord, and lies to his neighbor regarding a deposit, or a partnership, or a robbery, or has harmed his neighbor in some way, or has found something lost and lies about it, and has sworn falsely about any one of all the things a man might do so as to sin in them: and it shall be when he has sinned and is guilty, he shall restore the robbery which he seized, or the injury which he inflicted, or the deposit which was entrusted to him, or the lost thing which he found; from everything about which he swore unjustly, he shall restore the principal itself, and shall add a fifth part besides, and shall give it to him to whom it belongs on the day he is convicted.*

Thus far the types of sin are set forth; afterward, however, the purging of it through sacrifices is commanded. If any are weak and incapable of a deeper mystery, let them be built up by the letter; let them know that if anyone "in bypassing bypasses" <note>This repetitive phrasing mimics the Hebrew idiom for emphasis, often translated as "surely violates."</note> the commandments of the Lord and lies to his neighbor regarding a deposit, a partnership, or a robbery, he is determined to be guilty of a great sin. But far be it from the Church that I should believe there is anyone in it—or that any of the saints should act so unhappily—as to deny a neighbor's deposit, or contaminate a partnership with fraud, or himself snatch away the property of another, or receive things stolen by others, and regarding these things, if he is questioned, should swear against his conscience. Far be it, I say, that I should think these things of any of the faithful. For I say of you with confidence, that *you have not so learned Christ,* nor have you been so taught. Indeed, <margin>Ephes. 4</margin> the law itself did not command these things to the holy and the faithful. Do you wish to know that these things are not said to the holy and the just? Hear the Apostle distinguishing them: *The law,* he says, <margin>1 Tim. 1</margin> *is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust and the disobedient, for the impious and the contaminated, for parricides, matricides, and those like them.* Since therefore the Apostle says the law was imposed on such men, let the Church of God—which far be it from being stained by such crimes—leave the "letter" to others and be built up more holily by the Spirit. Let us see, then, what "deposit" <note>original: "depositum"; something entrusted to another's care.</note> it is that each of the faithful has received. I think that we receive our very soul and body as a deposit from God. And do you wish to see another even greater deposit which you have received from God? God has entrusted His own image and likeness to your very soul. Therefore, this deposit must be restored by you as holily as it is known to have been received. For if you are merciful, just as your Father in heaven <margin>Luke 6</margin> is merciful, the image of God is in you, and you keep the <margin>Matt. 5</margin> deposit whole. If you are perfect, just as your Father...

it is written: "He shall restore," he says, "what he found," both the one who found a lost thing, and the one who committed robbery. We have said in the preceding sections what it means to offer a ram, and that this ram is bought at the price of a **holy shekel** <term>sicli sancti</term><note>The "holy shekel" was the standard weight used in the Sanctuary, representing a higher or purer value than common currency.</note>: now it remains for us to discuss that difference—why in that case he set the price as a holy shekel, but here he only mentioned "a price": he designated neither the quantity of the price nor the name of the currency. For in the previous sections, where the law gave instructions for a sin committed against holy things, we said the holy shekel was named, and that "shekel" is the name of a currency: just as elsewhere it is called an **obol**, elsewhere a **drachma**, elsewhere a **mina**, or a **talent**, or a **mite**, **brass**, or a **denarius**. Do you wish to see this very distinction elsewhere? Listen to how <margin>1 Samuel 2</margin> **Eli the priest** says to his sons: "If a man sins against a man, the priest shall pray for him; but if he sins against God, who shall pray for him?" Because, therefore, there is a diversity of sins, we must learn from the spiritual law in which sins a ram must only be "bought," and in which it must be "purchased with a holy shekel": let us also seek out who these people are who "sell" the rams. I think they are those very ones who distribute rams for sacrifice, who are also those who sell oil for the lamps of the virgins, of whom the wise virgins said to the <margin>Matthew 25</margin> foolish ones: "Go to those who sell, and buy for yourselves." Who else, then, sells either oil for the lights or rams for the sacrifices, if not the holy **Prophets and Apostles**? When I have sinned, they show me and give me counsel on how I ought to correct my errors and amend my sins. <margin>Isaiah 1</margin> **Isaiah** sells me a ram for sacrificing for sin when he says to me, as if in the person of God: "I do not want your burnt offerings of rams, nor the fat of lambs, nor the blood of bulls and goats." is interpreted as **weight** <note>original: "pondus"</note>. But here, where the law is given regarding a sin committed against a neighbor, it says: "he shall offer a ram at a price," but it does not add the phrase "of a holy shekel." Why is this? Because when an offense is committed in holy matters, a specific weight of merit is required; but where one sins against a fellow human being, only a "price" is named. Now, if you ask what this "weight" is, it is the weight of faith, the weight of love, and the weight of your deeds. For as the Scripture says, "The Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed" <note>1 Samuel 2:3</note>. Therefore, let each of us take care that we do not lack weight in our actions, weight in our words, or weight in our feelings.

### The Perpetual Fire
"And the **fire**," it says, "on the altar shall burn, and shall not be extinguished" <note>Leviticus 6:12</note>. This is the fire that the Lord Jesus came to cast upon the earth, and he says: "How I wish it were already kindled!" <note>Luke 12:49</note>. This fire must always burn on the altar of our heart. For the altar is the heart of the person, from which the incense of prayer and the sacrifices of mercy are offered to God. The priest—who represents the Word of God or the spiritual understanding—must nourish this fire daily with the "wood" of the divine scriptures, so that the light of knowledge and the warmth of charity may never fail in us. If you neglect the study of the Word, the fire on your altar will grow cold.

## HOMILY FIVE
**Regarding the Law of the Burnt Offering and the Priest’s Garments**

"And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the **law of the burnt offering** <term>holocausti</term><note>The 'holocaust' or burnt offering refers to a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire, symbolizing total dedication to God.</note>: it is the burnt offering in its burning on the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn in it" <note>Leviticus 6:8-9</note>.

Having completed the previous discussion on the variety of sins and the diverse remedies of repentance, the Word of God now leads us to the "law of the burnt offering." But perhaps a listener will say: "What is this to me? I am a Christian, living under the grace of the Gospel, not under the burden of the Law. Why should I hear about the 'burning on the altar all night'?" Listen to what the Apostle Paul says: "The law is spiritual" <note>Romans 7:14</note>. If it is spiritual, then it speaks to your spirit. If you are a "spiritual person," you must understand it spiritually. Let us see, therefore, what it means for the burnt offering to burn "all night." This night is the present life, in which we walk as if in darkness, until the "day of the Lord" dawns. In this night, your sacrifice—your faith and your devotion—must burn continuously, so that when the morning of the resurrection comes, you may be found as a "child of light."

that is, the sense or spirit of the law, according to which the law A is spiritual, let it be offered sprinkled with oil and tender. Oil is referred to mercy, which ought to abound in priests; "tender" pertains to a subtle and pure understanding. Regarding what is said about the **frying pan** <note>original: "fartaginem"</note>, I think it means he wants the priest to be strict and parched by much continence <note>In this context, "continence" refers to self-restraint and ascetic discipline.</note>, in whom nothing can be held as loose toward luxury, and nothing wavering toward lust. And when all were satisfied, he said, twelve baskets of fragments remained. This, therefore, is the sacrifice of fragments, when we discuss the holy things of the law bit by bit, so that we may take from them a spiritual and pure food. And this, he says, is an **eternal law**. Indeed, John the apostle in the **Revelation** <margin>Rev. 14</margin> said it was the **eternal gospel**. We find it written here also that it is the eternal law. But those who wish to follow the law according to the letter—I would like them to tell me now how the law of this sacrifice can be eternal; especially since, with the temple destroyed, the altar overturned, and all things that were called holy profaned, this rite of sacrifices has not been able to remain. How then will they call "eternal" that which is well known to have ceased long ago and is already finished? It remains that this law is called eternal according to that C part by which we say the law is spiritual, and through it spiritual sacrifices can be offered, which can neither be broken nor ever cease. For they are not in a place that is overturned, nor in a time that changes; but in the faith of the believer and in the heart of the one sacrificing. Certainly, what he says—"It shall not be eaten from the sacrifice of the priest, but it shall be a whole burnt offering" <term>holocaustum</term> <note>A "holocaust" in the biblical sense refers to a sacrifice that is entirely consumed by fire, symbolizing total devotion to God.</note>—is certain to refer to the person of our Lord and Savior. For from His sacrifice, it shall not be eaten, but it shall be a whole burnt offering. In this place "sacrifice" must be understood as the Word itself and the doctrine, of which no one "eats"—that is, no one disputes it, no one retracts it—but it is a whole burnt offering; for whatever He said, whatever He established, endures by an eternal consecration. Nor is anyone found so insane or profane who D can retract anything from His words, which we ought to hold in all worship and veneration as a whole burnt offering offered to God. Because heaven and earth will pass away, but His words <margin>Luke 21</margin> will not pass away; rather, they remain forever, just as He Himself remains forever with God the Father and the Holy Spirit: to whom be glory and power forever and ever, Amen.

**eternal law** for the sons of Aaron. And for the priest who shall be anointed in his place from among his sons, it shall be offered in its entirety. It shall not be eaten; for every sacrifice of a priest shall be consumed by fire, and it shall not be eaten. <note>original: "omne enim sacrificium sacerdotis igne cremabitur, et non comedetur." Refers to Leviticus 6:22-23.</note> We must observe the distinction here: when a layman offers a sacrifice for himself, the priest eats a portion of it, signifying that the priest "carries" or "consumes" the sins of the people. But when the priest himself offers a sacrifice for his own soul, it must be entirely consumed by fire. This teaches us that the priest has no one higher than himself to act as a mediator or to consume his failings; therefore, his offering is surrendered entirely to God.

### HOMILY V

**On the Law of the Sin Offering**

**And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the sin offering.** <margin>Levit. 6:24</margin> In the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, they shall slaughter the sin offering before the Lord; it is **Holy of Holies**. The priest who offers it shall eat it; in a holy place it shall be eaten, in the court of the tabernacle of witness.

We have often noted that the Holy Spirit, through the mouth of the lawgiver, distinguishes between a **sin** <term>original: *peccatum*; a generic term for missing the mark</term> and a **guilt** <term>original: *delictum*; often implying a specific legal or moral trespass</term>. Though the rituals for their cleansing are similar, the roots of the offenses differ. The "soul that has sinned" <note>original: "Anima quae peccaverit"</note> must bring its offering to the door of the tabernacle.

Notice, however, that the text calls this sacrifice the **Holy of Holies**. <margin>Levit. 6:25</margin> Why is a sacrifice for sin called "most holy"? It is because the confession of a sin is itself a holy act. When a person turns away from their transgression and offers their heart to God, the very process of atonement transforms the "sin" into a "holy of holies" through the fire of the altar and the mediation of the priest. 

Furthermore, the law states that the sacrifice must be slaughtered **in the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered.** This signifies that there is no forgiveness of sin without the "whole burnt offering" of a devoted life. Just as the burnt offering is entirely dedicated to God, the sinner must offer their entire will to God in order for the sin offering to be effective. 

<column-break/>

Whatever touches the flesh of this sacrifice shall be sanctified. And if any of its blood is sprinkled on a garment, that which was sprinkled shall be washed in a holy place. <margin>Levit. 6:27</margin> This suggests a profound mystery: the "garment" represents our outer conduct or our physical life. If the "blood" of the sacrifice—which represents the life-force and the passion of the Savior—touches our life, we are made holy, but we must also "wash" ourselves in the "holy place" of the Church, through the grace of baptism and the tears of repentance.

The vessel of earthenware in which it is boiled shall be broken; but if it is boiled in a vessel of bronze, it shall be scoured and rinsed with water. <margin>Levit. 6:28</margin> This refers to the "earthenware" of our own fragile mortality. If the word of God is "boiled" or cooked within us—that is, if it is deeply meditated upon—our old, fragile self must be "broken" so that a new spirit may be formed. But if we are "bronze," strong and enduring in faith, we are merely "scoured" of our surface impurities and rinsed clean.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the "law of the sin offering" (Leviticus 6) from page 664. <margin>Genesis 4.</margin> sacrifices for sin. See how great the mercy and kindness of God is: so that where the burnt offering is slaughtered—that which is offered to God alone—there also the sacrifice which is for sin is commanded to be immolated. This is so that the one who has sinned may understand and, having turned back to the Lord in repentance, may slaughter the sacrifice of a "contrite spirit," <note>original: "contribulati spiritus hostiam." A reference to Psalm 51:17, where a broken spirit is the sacrifice God desires.</note> knowing that they now stand in a holy place and are joined to those who belong to God. Therefore, the sacrifice for sin is immolated in the same place as the burnt offering. It is, the text says, **in the sight of the Lord**. Perhaps there is a way to offer a sacrifice in the sight of the Lord, and a way to offer it *not* in the sight of the Lord. Who then is he who offers in the sight of the Lord? It is he, I believe, who has not "gone out from the sight of the Lord," like Cain, <note>Genesis 4:16. In the biblical narrative, Cain is described as leaving the presence of God after his crime.</note> who became trembling and fearful. If there is someone who has the confidence to stand in the sight of the Lord, and does not flee from His face, nor avoids His gaze due to a guilty conscience, that person offers the sacrifice in the sight of the Lord. 

Now, regarding this sacrifice which is offered for sins, the text calls it the **Holy of Holies**. This word wishes to venture something greater, if only your hearing can follow it. What is the sacrifice that is offered for sins and is the **Holy of Holies**, if not my Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God? He alone is the sacrifice for sins, and He Himself is the sacrifice that is the Holy of Holies. But what was added—**the priest, he says, who offers it, shall eat it**—seems difficult to understand. For that which is said to be "eaten" <margin>Hosea 4.</margin> seems to refer to the sin itself, just as the prophet says elsewhere of the priests: **They shall eat the sins of my people.** <note>original: "Peccata populi mei manducabunt." Quoting Hosea 4:8, where the corrupt priests are accused of feeding on the people's transgressions.</note> Hence, here too he shows that the priest ought to "eat" the sin of the one offering it. 

We have often shown from the divine scriptures that Christ is both the sacrifice which is offered for the sin of the world, and the priest who offers the sacrifice. The Apostle explains this in a single word <margin>Eph. 3.</margin> when he says: **Who offered himself to God.** <note>referencing Ephesians 5:2 or Hebrews 9:14.</note> This, therefore, is the priest who eats and consumes the sins of the people, of whom it was said: **You are a priest according to the order of Melchizedek.** <margin>Psal. 109.</margin> Therefore, my Savior and Lord shall "eat" the sins of the people. How will he eat the sins of the people? Hear what is written: **Our God,** it says, **is a consuming fire.** <margin>Deut. 4.</margin> What does God as fire consume? Shall we be so foolish as to think that God the fire consumes wood, or straw, or hay? No; God consumes human sins; He consumes them, He devours them, He purges them, according to what He says elsewhere: <margin>Esa. 1.</margin> **And I will purge you with fire to purity.** <note>original: "Et purgabo te igni ad purum." Isaiah 1:25.</note> This is what it means to "eat the sin" of the one who offers the sacrifice for sin. For He took our sins upon Himself; He ate and consumed them like a fire. Conversely, death is said to have "swallowed up" those who remain in their sins, as it is written: <margin>Esa. 5.</margin> **Death has swallowed them up in its power.** <note>Isaiah 25:8 or 5:14.</note> This, I believe, is what the Savior was saying in the Gospel: <margin>Luke 12.</margin> **I came to send fire upon the earth, and what do I wish but that it be kindled?** And would that my own "earth" be kindled by this divine fire, <margin>Hiere. 15.</margin> so that it no longer brings forth thorns and thistles! You should understand in the same way that which is written: **A fire is kindled by my wrath, it shall eat the earth and its generations.** 

The law says, therefore: **The priest who offered it shall eat it in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle of witness.** For it follows that, according to the im-

-age of Him who gave the priesthood to the church, the ministers and priests of the church should also receive the sins of the people; and they, imitating the Master, grant the remission of sins to the people. Therefore, the priests themselves ought to be so perfect and so learned in their priestly duties that they may consume the sins of the people in a holy place—in the courts of the tabernacle of witness—by not sinning themselves. 

But what does it mean to "eat sin in a holy place"? The place where Moses had arrived was holy, according to what was said to him: <margin>Exod. 3.</margin> **For the place where you stand is holy ground.** Similarly, in the church of God, the "holy place" is a whole faith, charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience. Whoever stands in these within the church should know that he stands in a holy place. For a "holy place" is not to be sought on the physical earth, upon which a sentence was once given by the Lord saying: <margin>Gen. 3.</margin> **Cursed is the earth in your works.** Therefore, an intact faith and a holy way of life is the "holy place." Thus, the priest of the church, positioned in this "place," consumes the sins of the people when, by slaughtering the sacrifice of the Word of God and offering the victims of holy doctrine, he purges the consciences of his listeners from sins. 

The priest, then, was given the flesh of the sacrifice in the court of the tabernacle of witness when he was able to understand what the reason or what the mysteries are that are described concerning the courts of the tabernacle of witness. For no one approaches these secret and hidden courts. They are open to none but the priests—if indeed they are "open," that is, if by their knowledge and mystical understanding they are able to penetrate their secrets. I know, however, that there are also certain other more secret dogmas in the church which even the priests themselves may not approach. I speak of the place where the ark is hidden, where the urn with manna and the tablets of the testament are kept. To that place, it is not granted even to the priests themselves

...which is commanded to be offered for sin upon the altar of the Lord. **And this,** he says, **is the law of the ram which is for a guilt offering; it is the Holy of Holies. In the place where they slaughter the burnt offerings, they shall also slaughter the ram which is for the guilt offering before the Lord,** and so forth. It is true that in the Divine Scriptures, "sin" and "guilt" <note>original: "peccatum" and "delictum." While often used interchangeably, the author here seeks a technical distinction between a general sin and a specific "guilt" or "trespass" offering.</note> are frequently used interchangeably and without any clear distinction. However, in this passage, a distinction is found. For while the text had previously delivered the rite and order of the sacrifice for a *sin offering*, it now separately commands a sacrifice for a *guilt offering*. And although they are commanded with the same order and observance—and he adds at the very end: **just as it is for the sin offering, so it is for the guilt offering; there shall be one law for them**—nevertheless, he wished to show that there is some difference between these things for which he commanded divided sacrifices.

Certainly, I think that a "guilt offering" <term>delictum: an offense or trespass</term> refers to something committed that is somewhat lighter than a "sin" <term>peccatum: a more serious moral failure or state of sin</term>. For we find it said of sin that there is <margin>1 John 5</margin> a **sin unto death**; but of a "guilt," we do not read that it is said to be "unto death." I am also aware of another distinction that has seemed correct to some of the wise: that in a "guilt" or "omission," we fail to do the things we ought to do; but it is a "sin" when we actually commit the things we ought not to do. But because we do not always find this distinction maintained in the Divine Scriptures, we cannot affirm it as a general rule. 

Therefore, the sacrifice offered for a guilt offering must be understood in the same way and by the same tradition that we previously explained regarding the sin offering. For in the same way, the fat of the ram—the fat around the kidneys and that which covers the internal organs—is commanded to <margin>Psalm 102</margin> be placed upon the altar. This is so that you who hear these things may know that everything within you that is "coarse" <note>original: "crassius," referring to the thick fat, but metaphorically to dull or worldly thoughts.</note> and covers your inner self must be offered to the fire of the altar. In this way, all your inner parts may be purged, so that you too may say, as David said: **Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless His holy name.** For unless that "thickness" which covers your inner parts is removed, they cannot grasp a subtle and spiritual sense, nor can they grasp the understanding of wisdom; and for that reason, they cannot praise the Lord. But if everything that is fat from the kidneys and from all the internal organs is offered, then, truly purged of every vice of lust, you have slaughtered the victim for your guilt and offered a sacrifice to God as a **sweet-smelling savor.** 

**The priest,** it says, **who offers it and makes atonement for the guilt, it shall belong to him.** Let the priests of the Lord who preside over the churches learn that a portion is given to them along with those for whose guilt they have made atonement. But what does it mean to "atone for guilt"? If you take up a sinner and—by warning, exhorting, teaching, and instructing—lead them to repentance, correct them from error, mend them from their vices, and make them such a person that God becomes favorable to them once they have turned back, you are said to "atone for the guilt." If, therefore, you are such a priest, and such is your teaching and your word, a portion is given to you from those you have corrected, so that their merit becomes your <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> reward, and their salvation becomes your glory. Does the Apostle not also show this when he says that **whatever someone builds upon, he shall receive a reward**? Let the priests of the Lord understand, therefore, where their portion is given, 

<column-break/>

and let them devote themselves and their labor to this. Let them not entangle themselves in empty and superfluous acts, but let them know that they will have a portion with the Lord in nothing else except in that which they offer for sins—that is, in the sinners they have turned away from the vices of sin. 

It should also be noted that the things offered as a burnt offering are the internal parts; however, that which is external is not offered to the Lord. The skin is not offered to the Lord, nor does it go into the burnt offerings. Such was that son of Judah, who was called <margin>Genesis 38</margin> Er <note>The author connects the name "Er" with the Hebrew word 'Or' (עוֹר), meaning skin or hide. In the biblical text, Er was the firstborn of Judah who was "wicked in the sight of the Lord."</note>, which is interpreted as "skin"; for that reason he was most wicked, and God killed him, because such as these are not offered to the Lord. 

**And every sacrifice that is made in an oven, and everything made on a griddle or in a frying pan, shall belong to the priest who offers it.** What shall we say? Do we think that the Almighty God, who gave the responses to Moses from heaven, was giving instructions about ovens, griddles, and frying pans? And was it so the people might learn through Moses that God would be favorable to them if they fried some things in a pan, baked others in an oven, and roasted others on a griddle? The children of the Church have not learned Christ in this way, nor were they so instructed in Him by the Apostles as to suspect anything so lowly and so cheap concerning the Lord of Majesty. 

Rather, according to the spiritual sense which the Spirit grants to the Church, let us see what this sacrifice is that is cooked in an oven, or what this "oven" ought to be understood to mean. But where will I suddenly find a Divine Scripture to teach me what an oven is? I must call upon my Lord Jesus, that He may make me—as one who seeks—to find, and open to me as I knock, so that I may find an "oven" in the Scriptures where I can cook my sacrifice so that God may accept it. And indeed, I think I have found it in the <margin>Hosea 7</margin> prophet Hosea, where he says: **All of them are adulterers, like an oven heated for burning.** And again, he says: **Their hearts have grown hot like an oven.** <margin>Ibid.</margin> 

Therefore, the "oven" is the heart of man. Now, if vices take over this heart, or if the devil inflames it, it will not "cook" the sacrifice, but burn it up. But if He kindles it—He who said, <margin>Luke 12</margin> **I have come to send fire upon the earth**—then the "loaves" of the Scriptures and the words of God which I receive into my heart, I do not burn up to destruction, but I cook into a sacrifice. And perhaps those things are said to be cooked in an "oven" which are internal and hidden, and cannot easily be brought out to the common people. For there are many things of this kind in the Divine Scriptures, such as in <margin>Ezekiel 10</margin> Ezekiel, when he describes either the Cherubim or God and that magnificent vision. If these things are not "cooked" in the oven, they cannot be eaten as they are, for they are "raw." For we must not believe that there is some animal <margin>Ezekiel 1</margin> set in the form of a lion upon which God is carried, or another in the form of a calf or an eagle. Therefore, these things—and any like them—must not be brought forth "raw," but must be "cooked" in the oven of the heart.

There are these three things in which he says sacrifices ought to be prepared: in the oven, in the frying pan, and on the griddle. ...bread is received. Let us see, then, what this might mean. In the Gospels, the Lord calls the human teaching of the Pharisees—who passed down the traditions and commandments of men—"leaven," when He says to the disciples: "Watch out for the leaven of the Pharisees." Therefore, "leaven" is human doctrine: for example, the art of Grammar, or Rhetoric, or even Dialectic <note>The "Liberal Arts" of the classical world. The author argues they are tools for communication but should not be the source of divine truth.</note>. From such doctrine, nothing is to be taken for the sacrifice—that is, in those matters which are to be believed concerning God. However, clear speech, the splendor of eloquence, and the method of disputation are rightly commanded to be admitted for the ministry of the Word of God. Did not he who said, [Marginal note: 1 Corinthians 15] "**Bad conversations corrupt good morals**" <note>original: "Corrumpūt mores bonos colloquia mala"</note>—and also, [Marginal note: Titus 1] "**Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies**" <note>original: "Cretenses semper mendaces, malę bestię, uentres pigri"</note>, and other similar things taken from the "leaven" of the Greeks—have the sacrifice of God's Word placed upon this leaven? 

Regarding what the law says—that it shall be eaten on that day, and nothing shall be left of it until morning—let us compare this with the other sacrifices. Let us see the reason why, in this sacrifice of well-being <term>sacrificio salutari: traditionally known as the Peace Offering or Fellowship Offering</term>, He commanded it to be eaten on the same day it is offered. Yet in another sacrifice, He allows it to be kept even into the second day, and even until the third; but on the third day, whatever remains is to be committed to the fire, so that it does not pollute the one offering it. 

Let us see, then, what this difference signifies. Truly, we need the help of God—who deigns to cut away all the "fat" covering our inner parts and remove every veil of duller perception—so that we may be able to notice these things according to what is commanded by God. Let us, therefore, compare the Divine Scripture to itself, and let us follow the path of explanation wherever it opens to us. We find [Marginal note: Exodus 12] in the sacrifice of the Passover, which is commanded to be sacrificed in the evening, a similar command given: that nothing of the meat should remain until morning. It is not without reason that the Divine Word does not want us to eat "yesterday's meat," but rather meat that is always recent and new. To those especially who offer a sacrifice of Passover or a sacrifice of praise to God, He commands them to eat new meat, fresh to that very day, and forbids what is from yesterday. 

[Marginal note: Ezekiel 4] I remember the prophet Ezekiel saying something similar when the Lord had commanded him to cook his bread over human dung. For he answered the Lord and said: "O Lord, my soul has never been contaminated by a carcass, nor has anything unclean entered my mouth; nor has 'yesterday's meat' entered my mouth." I have often asked myself what this boast of the prophet was, as if he were bringing something great before God by saying he had never eaten "yesterday's meat." But as I see it, having been taught from these mysteries, the prophet was saying to God: "I am not such a lowly or degenerate priest as to feed on 'yesterday's'—that is, ancient—meat." 

Listen to this, all you priests of the Lord, and understand more intently what is being said. The "meat" from the sacrifices assigned to the priests is the Word of God, which they teach in the church. Through these mystical figures, they are warned that when they begin to bring forth a sermon to the people, they should not bring forth "yesterday's" things; they should not speak ancient things according to the literal sense...

<column-break/>

[Right Page, 673]

[Paragraph marker: A]
...but through the grace of God, they should always bring forth new things and always discover spiritual meanings. For if you bring forth today in the church those things which you learned from the Jews "yesterday," <note>The author uses "yesterday" and "Jews" to represent a literalist, old-covenant understanding of the Bible that he believes Christians should transcend.</note> this is to eat the "yesterday's meat" of the sacrifice. Furthermore, if you remember, the Lawgiver used the same language regarding the offering of the firstfruits, saying they must be "new and fresh." You see everywhere that those things which pertain to the praises of God (for this is the sacrifice of praise) ought to be new and fresh. Otherwise, when you bring forth "old things" in the church, your lips might speak while your mind remains without fruit. But hear what the Apostle says: [Marginal note: 1 Corinthians 14] "If I speak in tongues, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit." What then? He says, "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind; I will sing a psalm with the spirit, and I will sing a psalm with the mind."

[Paragraph marker: B]
So it is with you: if you do not bring forth a present and fresh word in the praises of God from spiritual learning and the doctrine of God’s grace, your mouth indeed offers a sacrifice of praise, but your mind is accused of "yesterday's meat" because of its sterility. For the Lord also said to his disciples regarding the bread He gave them: [Marginal note: Matthew 26] "Take and eat." He did not delay, nor did He command it to be saved for the next day. Perhaps this mystery is also contained in the fact [Marginal note: Mark 6] that He commands them not to carry bread on the road, so that you may always bring forth the fresh "loaves" of God’s word which you carry within you. Finally, those Gibeonites [Marginal note: Joshua 9] were condemned and became woodcutters and water carriers because they brought "old bread" to the Israelites, whom the spiritual law commanded to always use what is fresh and new. 

There is surely another symbolic pattern [Paragraph marker: C] of the sacred mysteries which commands that what remains be eaten even on the second day, but nothing be reserved for the third. We shall see about this in its proper place. But let this not escape us: there is a certain time in which it is a blessing to eat "old things." For concerning the seventh year—which is called the year of release or the Sabbatical year—it is said: [Marginal note: Leviticus 26] "You shall eat the old, and the old of the old." At that time, under the mystery of the seventh year (as we said), it is a blessing to eat old things, though now it is forbidden. But it would be too much to go into each of these points in excess and wander too far based on the opportunity of these testimonies, since the explanation of the sacrifices is what we currently have in hand. 

It is said, therefore, in the following verses: [Marginal note: Leviticus 7] "But if the sacrifice of his offering is a vow or a voluntary gift, it shall be eaten on whatever day he offers his sacrifice; and on the second day, [Paragraph marker: D] whatever remains of the meat of the sacrifice shall be eaten. But whatever remains of the meat of the sacrifice until the third day shall be burned with fire. If anyone eats of the meat on the third day, it shall not be accepted from him who offers it; it shall not be credited to him; it is an abomination. And any soul who eats of it shall bear their sin." 

This is undoubtedly what David says in the Psalms: [Marginal note: Psalm 108] "Let his prayer be turned into sin"—when not only is no merit gained from the sacrifices, but even much guilt is sought. For you hear the Lawgiver decreeing that if anyone eats of what remains on the third day, they shall bear their sin. From this, it must be recognized how great a stain of sin hangs over the human condition, since sin can arise even from the very place where the victim of atonement is offered. I believe the blessed David, considering these things, said in the Psalms: [Marginal note: Psalm 18] "Who [can understand his] sins?"

# 638 SAINT CYRILL ON LEVITICUS <note>original: "DIVI CYRILLI IN LEVITICVM". While attributed here to Cyril, these are historically the homilies of Origen as translated into Latin by Rufinus.</note>

unless some edification were provided to the listeners from these things. If, therefore, a priest of the Church, through words and doctrine, and through his great solicitude and the labor of his vigils, is able to convert a sinner and teach him to follow a better way—returning him to the fear of God, leading him to reflect on the hope of future things, causing him to cease from evil acts and turn to good ones—if, I say, he performs such a work, it follows that the one who is saved by his labor gives thanks to God and offers a sacrifice of salvation for the fact that he has obtained health. In this sacrifice, a portion is made for the priest: the breast and the right arm. This serves as a sign that his breast and heart, which previously thought upon evil things, have received good thoughts through the priest’s labor of conversion; thus, it is cleansed so that he may even be able to see the Lord.

Similarly, in the arm, there is a sign that his evil and "left-handed" works—which are certainly perverse and not good—he has turned into "right-handed" works, so that they may be according to God. And this is the "right arm," in which the text says the priest’s portion lies. But we also beseech you who hear these things: give your breasts, offer your hearts to the priests of God, so that they may take away from them everything that is thick and coarse, making them a priestly portion. Give us also your arms; we ask for right arms from you, we do not want the left at all—we require right-handed works from you. 

But also this, which he adds—that it is called the "breast of addition" and the "arm of removal" <note>original: "pectusculum appositionis & brachium demptionis". These terms refer to what modern Bibles call the "wave breast" and "heave shoulder" from Leviticus 7:34.</note>—does not seem to be said without cause. Therefore, I would like to inquire: what is it that must be "added" to the breast, so that it becomes a "breast of addition"? After every coarse thing has been taken away from your heart, and it has been cleansed of every covering that must be surrendered to the fire, it remains for the grace of the Holy Spirit to be "added" to it; then it will become a "breast of addition." 

But how will it be an "arm of separation" or "removal"? An arm of separation: know and understand how to discern which are the works of light and which are the works of darkness, and separate the acts of light from the darkness, so that your works may be in the light. Your arm is then made an arm of separation—either when you separate yourself from every brother who walks in a disorderly way, or certainly when, according to the prophet, you separate yourself <margin>Numbers 16</margin> and go out from the midst of sinners, you who carry the vessels of the Lord. 

Finally, by a certain local custom of the Scripture, that which is "unclean" is said to be "common," just as the voice from heaven said to Peter: <margin>Acts 10</margin> "What God has cleansed, you shall not call common." <note>original: "Quod deus mundauit, tu commune ne dixeris." In biblical Latin, *commune* (common) refers to things that are ritually profane or shared with the pagan world, rather than set apart for God.</note> Consequently, therefore, if that which is unclean is called "common," then that which is holy shall be named "separated." But we add this as well: if anyone is a servant of God alone, he cannot be called "common." But if anyone is "common," there is no doubt that he belongs to many, and for that reason is called "common." 

There is a great mystery in this discourse, which Israel according to the flesh uses in practice but does not understand in its "common" sense. They also call a man unclean, but why he is called "common," they do not know. Let them learn, therefore, from the Church of God, that he who is holy belongs to God alone, and has no communion with anything else; but he who is a sinner and unclean belongs to many. For many demons possess him, and for that reason he is called "common."

<column-break/>

# 639

Finally, that man in the Gospels who was cured by the Lord, when he was asked, "What is your name?" said: <margin>Mark 5</margin> "Legion, for we are many." These things, though said as a sort of digression, nevertheless seem necessarily added so that we might discuss the mystery of why the "breast of addition" and the "arm of separation" were written, which is the eternal portion given to the priests. <margin>Leviticus 8</margin> May God deign to make us worthy of this, so that through purity of heart and uprightness of works, we may deserve to have a share in the divine sacrifice: through the eternal High Priest, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, with whom is glory and empire to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever, Amen.

## THE SIXTH BOOK OF SAINT CYRILL ON LEVITICUS
### Concerning the garments of the High Priest and the priests.

[Ornate initial C] THE REASON why these things being read to us can be understood, or not understood, the Apostle briefly shows, <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> saying: that the veil of the Old Testament can be taken away from the eyes of the one who has been converted to the Lord. From this he wished it to be known that the less these things are plain to us, the greater our conversion to the Lord ought to be. And therefore we must strive with all our strength to be free from the occupations of the age and from worldly acts—even leaving behind (if it can be done) the superfluous stories of companions <margin>1 Peter 2</margin>—and give our labor to the word of God. We should meditate on His law day and night, so that having turned with our whole heart, we may be able to behold the revealed and open face of Moses. 

This is especially true in these things that have now been read concerning the priestly garments or the consecration of the High Priest. In these matters, such things are said <margin>Isaiah 52</margin> that they utterly exclude even that "carnal Israel" from a literal historical understanding. And therefore, to explain these things, we must not rely on the strength of human genius, but our minds must be turned toward God with orisons and prayers. <margin>Romans 13</margin> In this I also need your help, so that God, the Father of the Word, may give us a word in the opening of our mouth, that we may be able to consider the wonders of His law. 

The beginning of what was read today is in these words: <margin>Leviticus 7</margin> "This is the anointing of Aaron and the anointing of his sons from the sacrifices of the Lord, on the day he brought them forward to sacrifice to the Lord, just as the Lord commanded to give to them on the day he anointed them from among the sons of Israel, by a perpetual law throughout their generations. <margin>Luke 16</margin> This is the law of burnt offerings, and for sin, and for guilt, and of consecration and the sacrifice of salvation, just as the Lord commanded Moses on Mount Sinai, on the day he commanded the sons of Israel to offer their gifts before the Lord in the desert of Sinai." 

When the Lawgiver proposed to say, "This is the anointing of Aaron and his sons," he did not immediately add what the anointing was, nor did he explain how he had anointed them—though he does this in what follows. But now, after saying "this is the anointing," he adds nothing about anointing. <margin>Isaiah 66</margin> He does this surely to show that those things he spoke of above—that is, the "breast of addition" and the "arm of separation"—were themselves the anointing of Aaron and his sons. We should not think those things were said for carnal reasons, but rather to teach that those very things...
