Listen to the consecration of the high priest or priest with attentive ears and a vigilant heart: because you also, according to the promises of God, are the priests of the Lord: for you are a *holy nation and a priesthood.* <margin>1 Peter 2</margin> For Moses took Aaron and his sons according to the command of the Lord: and first indeed he washes them, and afterward he clothes them. Consider the order of the words more diligently: first he washes, afterward he clothes. For one cannot be clothed unless he has first been washed. Be washed, therefore, and be clean; take away the wickedness from your souls. For unless you have been washed in this way, you will not be able to "put on" the Lord Jesus Christ, according to what the Apostle says: *Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh* <margin>Romans 13</margin> *in its lusts.* Therefore, let Moses wash you—let him wash you himself, and let him clothe you himself. You have heard frequently how Moses can wash you. For we have often said that Moses, in the Holy Scriptures, stands for the Law, just as it is said in the Gospel: *They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.* <margin>Luke 16</margin> It is the Law of God, therefore, which washes you. It washes away your filth; if you listen to it, it wipes away the stains of your sins. It is Moses himself, that is the Law, who consecrates priests; nor can anyone be a priest whom the Law has not established as a priest. For there are many priests, but those whom the Law has not washed, nor has the word of God rendered pure, nor has the divine discourse washed away the filth of their sins.

But you also, who desire to receive sacred baptism and to earn the grace of the Spirit, must first be purged by the Law; having heard the word of God, you must first cut away brutish vices and settle your barbaric and wild habits, so that having taken up gentleness and humility, you may be able to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. For so the Lord says through the prophet: *Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at* <margin>Isaiah 66</margin> *my words?* If you are not humble and quiet, the grace of the Holy Spirit cannot dwell in you; nor

**BOOK SIX. 681**

will the Spirit of the Lord rest in you if you do not receive the divine words with trembling. For the Holy Spirit flees from a proud and defiant soul, and one that is deceitful. <margin>Wisdom 1</margin> You must, therefore, first meditate upon the Law of God, so that if by chance your acts are intemperate and your habits disordered, the Law may amend and correct you. Do you wish to see that Moses is always with Jesus—that is, the Law with the Gospels? Let the Gospel teach you. Because when Jesus was transformed into glory, Moses and Elijah also <margin>Matthew 17</margin> appeared together with him in glory. So that you may know that the Law and the Prophets and the Gospel always come together as one, and remain in one glory. Finally, even Peter, when he wanted to make three tents for them, is noted for his lack of skill, as one who did not know what he was saying. For the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel, there are not three tents, but one: which is the Church of the Lord.

Therefore, Moses first washes the priest of God, and when he has washed him and rendered him purged from the filth of vices, after this he clothes him. But let us consider what these garments are, with which Moses clothes his brother Aaron, the first high priest: to see if perhaps it is possible for you also to be clothed in these same vestments and to be a high priest. There is indeed one great High Priest, our Lord Jesus Christ: but He is not the High Priest of priests, but the High Priest of high priests; nor is He the prince of priests, but the Prince of the princes of priests. Just as He is not called the King of the common people, but the *King of kings*; and not the Lord of servants, but the *Lord of lords.* It can happen, therefore, if someone has been washed by Moses and has become as clean as one whom Moses has washed, that such a person might also reach these garments which Moses brings forth—these robes with which he clothes his brother Aaron and his sons.

But not only garments are needed for the priestly <term>insignia [insulas]</term>, but also sashes. Before we begin to speak about the appearance of the garments themselves, I would like to compare those unhappy garments with which the first man was clothed when he had sinned, with these holy and faithful garments. Indeed, it says that God made those: *For God made,* it says, *tunics of skins, and clothed Adam and* <margin>Genesis 3</margin> *his wife.* Those tunics, therefore, were of skins taken from animals. For it was fitting for a sinner to be clothed in such things—in tunics of skins, I say—which were a sign of the mortality he had received for his sin, and of his fragility, <margin>2 Corinthians 5</margin> which came from the corruption of the flesh. But if you have already been washed from these and purified through the Law of God, Moses will clothe you with the garment of incorruption, so that your shame may nowhere appear, and *that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.*

Let us see, then, in what order the high priest is appointed. *Moses called together the congregation,* it says, *and said to them: This is the word which the Lord commanded.* Although the Lord had commanded concerning the appointment of the high priest and the Lord had chosen him, nevertheless the congregation is also called together. For in the ordaining of a priest, the presence of the people is required, so that all may know and be certain that the one chosen is the most outstanding from among all the people. The one who is more learned, more holy, and more eminent in every virtue—he is chosen for the priesthood. And this happens with the people standing by, so that no one may later have cause to reconsider, or lest

<meta>This page continues the discussion on spiritual states, moving from the metaphor of intoxication to the biblical prohibition of wine for priests in the Tabernacle. It interprets Christ as the High Priest who "abstains from wine" (joy) as long as His body, the Church, remains in sin.</meta>

**690 SAINT CYRILL ON LEVITICUS** <note>Although the title attributes this to Saint Cyril of Alexandria, this text is actually a Latin translation by Rufinus of Origen’s *Homilies on Leviticus*. Such misattributions were common in early printed editions.</note>

He waits, therefore, for us to be converted, that we may imitate His example and follow His footsteps, so that He may rejoice with us and drink wine with us in the kingdom of His Father. For now, because the Lord is merciful and compassionate, He—with an even greater affection than His apostle—weeps <margin>Romans 12</margin> with those who weep and desires to rejoice with those who rejoice. And He mourns much more for those who have previously sinned <margin>2 Corinthians 12</margin> and have not performed penance. For it must not be thought that while Paul indeed mourns for sinners and weeps for those who go astray, my Lord Jesus abstains from weeping when He approaches the Father and stands at the altar to offer atonement <note>original: "repropitiationem"</note> for us. And this is what it means for the one approaching the altar not to drink the wine of joy: because He still suffers the bitterness of our sins. Therefore, He does not wish to drink wine alone in the kingdom of God; He waits for us. 

[Paragraph marker B] For if He said, "until I drink it with you," then it is we who, by neglecting our lives, delay His joy. He waits for us so that He may drink from the fruit of this vine. Which vine? The one of which He was the truth: *I am the vine, you are the branches.* <margin>John 15</margin> Whence He also says: *For my blood is truly drink, and my flesh is truly food.* <margin>John 6</margin> For truly, in the blood of the grape, He washed His robe. <margin>Genesis 49</margin> What, then, does He wait for? Joy. When does He expect it? "When I have finished your work," He says. When does He finish this work? When He has made me—who am the last and most wicked of all sinners—complete and perfect; then His work is finished. For now, His work is still incomplete as long as I remain imperfect. Indeed, as long as I am not subject to the Father, He Himself is not said to be subject to the Father. It is not that He lacks subjection in His own person before the Father, but for my sake—in whom He has not yet finished His work—He Himself is said not to be subject. For so we read, that we are the body of Christ and members in part. <margin>Ephesians 5</margin> 

But let us see what He means by "in part." For example, I am now subject to God according to the spirit—that is, in purpose and will. But as long as the flesh in me lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, and I have not yet been able to subject the flesh to the spirit, I am indeed subject to God, but not entirely—only in part. However, if I can draw even my flesh and all my members into harmony with the spirit, then I shall appear perfectly subject. If you have understood what it means to be subject "in part" and "entirely," return [Paragraph marker D] now to what we proposed regarding the subjection of the Lord. See how, since we are all said to be His body and members, as long as there are some among us who are not yet subject with perfect subjection, He Himself is said not to be subject. But when He has finished His work and brought the entire creation to the height of perfection, then He Himself is said to be subject in those whom He has subjected to the Father, and in whom He has finished the work the Father gave Him, so that *God may be all in all.* <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> 

But where does this lead? To our understanding of what we discussed above: how He drank wine before He entered the tabernacle, before He approached the altar; and yet He does not drink now, because He stands at the altar and mourns my sins. And He will drink again after this, when all things have been subjected to Him, and when all things are set free and the death of sin is destroyed. 

***

**SAINT CYRILL ON LEVITICUS 691**

Then it will no longer be necessary to offer sacrifices for sin. For then there will be gladness and joy, and then <margin>Psalm 50</margin> the "humbled bones" shall rejoice; and that which is written shall be fulfilled: *Sorrow and sadness and groaning have fled away.* <margin>Revelation 7</margin> <note>This is a composite reference to Isaiah 35:10 and Revelation 21:4.</note> But let us not omit this: that it is said not only of Aaron that he should not drink wine, but also of his sons when they enter the holy places. <margin>Leviticus 10; 1 Corinthians 13</margin> For they have not yet received their joy—not even the apostles. They too wait, so that I also may become a participant in their joy. For the saints departing from this life do not immediately receive the full rewards of their merits; they wait for us as well, even though we are lingering and lazy. <margin>Galatians 2</margin> For their joy is not perfect as long as they grieve for our errors and mourn our sins. Perhaps you do not believe me when I say this. [Paragraph marker B] For who am I to dare to confirm the opinion of such a great doctrine? But I bring a witness for these things about whom there can be no doubt. For the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth is the apostle Paul. <margin>1 Timothy 2; Psalm 34</margin> He himself, writing to the Hebrews, when he had enumerated <margin>Hebrews 11</margin> all the holy fathers who were justified through faith...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of Leviticus 10, where the priests are forbidden from drinking wine when entering the Tabernacle. 692                                                                                                                                                                                                                               

For truly, in this vine He even drinks of our works and our progress. <margin>John 15</margin> For just as He is the vine and we are the branches, so also are our good deeds the fruit of that vine. Because He Himself is the one who planted this vine and gave it growth, He is also the one who, in a certain sense, is "intoxicated" <note>This refers to a spiritual ecstasy or deep satisfaction derived from the holiness of the faithful.</note> by our progress. This is why the Scripture says in the Song of Songs: *Eat, my neighbors, and drink; be intoxicated, my brothers.* <margin>Song of Songs 5</margin> <note>original: "Et inebriamini fratres"</note> For He is the one who is delighted by the faith and the virtues of His people.

[Paragraph marker] But do not think that He drinks this wine of joy alone. He waits for us, as He said, "until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father." <margin>Matthew 26</margin> Therefore, as long as we remain in our sins and fail to reach that kingdom, He—our High Priest—stands before the altar and "abstains from wine." This is the sorrow He feels for our delay. For how can He be in perfect joy while I, who am a member of His body, remain in grief? How can He be in gladness while I am in sin? 

[Paragraph marker] Therefore, He waits for us to be perfected. He waits for the "fullness of the nations" <margin>Romans 11</margin> to come in, and for the "remnant of Israel" to be saved. Only then, when the whole body of the Church is gathered and every member is joined to the Head, will the Great High Priest celebrate that feast of joy. Until that time, the prohibition remains: *He shall drink no wine nor strong drink when he enters the Tabernacle,* <margin>Leviticus 10</margin> because the time of His ministry for our atonement <note>original: "propitiationis"</note> is not yet finished.

He has already entered the Holy of Holies, it is true; but He has not yet completed the work of reconciling the whole world to God. He is even now interceding for us, and as long as the work of intercession continues, the "wine of joy" is deferred. Thus, we should realize that our own holiness and our own conversion contribute to the joy of our Lord, while our negligence prolongs His "fasting" and His wait.

In investigating these matters, we require the testimonies of Divine Scripture. <margin>*Psalm 63*</margin> I say this lest anyone think—for men love to "sharpen their tongues like a sword"—lest anyone think, I say, that I am doing violence to the Divine Scriptures. ->698 SAINT CYRILLUS ON LEVITICUS 699<-

...but do not divide the hooves. He makes another category of those who, conversely, divide the hoof but do not chew the cud <note>original: "ruminant." In Latin, *ruminatio* refers both to a cow chewing its cud and to a person deeply meditating or "mulling over" a thought.</note>. First, therefore, let us see who those are who chew the cud and divide the hoof, whom he calls "clean." I believe he is said to chew the cud who devotes himself to knowledge and meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. But hear how it is said: "he divides," it says, "the hoof and brings back the cud." He "brings back the cud" who recalls those things which he reads according to the letter to a spiritual sense, and climbs from the lowest and visible things to the invisible and higher things. 

But if you meditate on the divine law and recall what you read to a subtle and spiritual understanding—yet your life and your actions are not such that they have a discernment between the present life and the future, between this world and the world to come—if you do not discern and divide these things with competent reason, you will be a "crooked camel." For although you have received understanding from meditation on the divine law, you do not divide nor separate the present from the future, nor the narrow way from the spacious way. 

But let us explain what is being said even more clearly. There are those who take up the covenant of God with their mouth, and while they have the law of God in their mouths, their life and actions differ far from their words and speeches. For they speak, and <margin>Matthew 23</margin> they do not act; of whom the prophet also says: <margin>Psalm 49</margin> "But to the sinner God said: why do you declare my justices and take up my covenant through your mouth?" <note>original: "quare tu enarras iusticias meas, & assumis testamentum meum per os tuū?" This is Psalm 50:16 in modern numbering.</note> 

You see, therefore, how this man "chews the cud," since he has the covenant of God in his mouth. But what is said to him in the following verses? "But you have hated discipline and have cast my words behind you." In this, he evidently shows that this man is indeed chewing the cud, but not dividing the hoof; and therefore, whoever is like this is "unclean." 

And again, there is another type, either from those who are outside our religion <note>Meaning non-Christians or pagans.</note> or from those who are with us, who indeed divide the hoof and walk in their ways in such a way that they prepare their actions for the future world. For many of the philosophers think this way and believe there is a future judgment. For they perceive the soul to be immortal and they confess that a reward is set aside for all good people. Some heretics also do this, and as far as this is concerned, they carry a fear of the future judgment and temper their actions more cautiously as if they were to be required by a divine examination. 

But neither of these groups "chews the cud" or "brings back the cud." For they do not meditate upon hearing those things described in the Law, nor do they recall them to a subtle and spiritual understanding; rather, as soon as they have heard something, they either despise it or look down on it, nor do they seek what precious meaning might lie hidden within the more common words. And these are unclean, indeed dividing the hoof, but not bringing back the cud. 

But you, if you wish to be clean, have a life that is suitable and in harmony with your knowledge, and actions in harmony with your understanding, so that you may be clean in both; so that you both bring back the cud and divide the hoof—but also that you might "grow out" or "cast away" your hooves. Let us seek the testimony for this matter as well: how we grow out our hooves, or as it is read elsewhere, how we cast them away. <margin>Deuteronomy 21</margin> It is written in Deuteronomy: "If," it says, "you go out to war against your enemies, and you see there a woman of beautiful face, and you desire her: you shall take her and shave all the hair of her head and her nails <note>original: "ungues." In the context of the law of the captive woman, this refers to paring the nails.</note>, and clothe her in mourning garments, and she shall sit in the house mourning her father and her mother and her paternal home for thirty days, and after that she shall be your wife." 

But the purpose now is not to explain these things which have been called as testimony. We mentioned it because mention was made of "hooves" <note>In Latin, *ungula* (hoof) and *unguis* (nail) are closely related terms.</note> here. Nevertheless, I too have frequently gone out to war against my enemies, and I have seen there in the spoils a woman of beautiful face. For whatever things we find well and rationally said among our enemies <note>Cyril refers here to pagan Greek philosophy and literature.</note>—if we read anything said wisely and knowingly among them—it is necessary for us to cleanse it. That is, to take away from the knowledge which is among them and cut back everything that is dead and empty (for this is what the hair of the head and the nails of the woman taken from the spoils of enemies are) and only then make her a wife to ourselves, when she no longer has anything of those things which are called "dead" through infidelity, having nothing dead on her head and nothing on her hands: so that she carries nothing unclean or dead in either her thoughts or her actions. For the women of our enemies have nothing clean, because there is no wisdom among them with which some uncleanness is not mixed. 

I would like, however, for the Jews to tell me how these things are kept among them: what is the cause, what is the reason for a woman to be made bald and her nails to be cut off? For example, if we suppose that the one who is said to have found her found her in such a state that she had neither <margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin> hair nor nails: what would he have to remove according to the law? 

But for us, whose <term>warfare is spiritual</term> <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 10:4: "the weapons of our warfare are not carnal."</note>, and whose weapons are not fleshly but powerful from God for destroying plans—if a beautiful woman is found among the enemies, and some rational discipline is found, we will purify her in this way which we said above. It is necessary, therefore, for him who is clean not only to divide the hooves—and not only to discern the acts and works of the present and future world—but to grow out the hooves or (as we read elsewhere) to cast them away, so that purifying ourselves from dead works, we may remain in life. 

Let these things be said in a general way about the land animals. Concerning those which are in the waters, these things are said: if they have fins and scales, they are clean; if they do not have them, they are unclean and must not be eaten. In these things, it is shown that if anyone is in these waters—and in the sea of this life and placed in the waves of the world—he ought nevertheless to strive enough so that he does not lie in the depths of the waters, like those fish which are said to have neither fins nor scales. For this is reported to be their nature: that they always stay at the bottom and around the mud itself, just like eels and similar things, which cannot ascend to the surface of the water nor reach its higher parts. 

But those fish which are aided by fins and protected by scales ascend more to the higher parts and become closer to this air, as if they were seeking the freedom of the spirit. Therefore, every holy person, shut within the nets of faith, is called a "good fish" by the Savior and is put into a vessel, as if <margin>Matthew 13</margin> having fins...

<column-break/>

Conversely, there are others who "divide the hoof" but do not "chew the cud." These represent people who may perform outward works of the law or maintain a certain discipline in their lives, but they do not possess the internal "rumination" of the Word; they do not meditate on the spiritual depth of the scriptures to nourish their souls. 

The Law labels such creatures "unclean" to teach us that neither knowledge without works nor works without spiritual understanding is sufficient for a pure life. One must both "chew the cud"—meditating on the mysteries of God—and "divide the hoof"—living with the moral discernment that distinguishes the holy from the profane.

...in the world from the eighth day, and she remains in the "blood of purification" <note>original: *in sanguine mundo*; a reference to the period after childbirth where the mother is technically "clean" but restricted from the sanctuary</note> for thirty-three days—that is, three decades and three monads <note>original: *tribus decadibus, & tribus monadibus*; the author is using Pythagorean/mathematical terms for tens and ones to break down the number 33</note>. When she who has given birth begins to be in this state of clean blood, she then circumcises the infant. For on the eighth day, the Law says, you shall circumcise the flesh of his foreskin. But you must seek out which circumcision the Apostle <margin>Colossians 2; Psalm 57 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 58:3: "The wicked are estranged from the womb."</note></margin> preaches, which he commands us both to receive and to hold. "For we," he says, "are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit." And as it says in the Psalm: "Sinners are alienated from the womb." Consider if he is not saying this about those who receive that [literal] circumcision which the Apostle forbids us from undergoing; it is then that sinners are alienated from the womb, when they are circumcised not in spirit, but in the flesh. For those who are circumcised according to the Law have fallen away from grace. 

[Marginal letter: B] Therefore, a woman is said to become "unclean" when she has conceived seed and given birth to a male. But she who gives birth to a female shall not only be unclean, but doubly unclean: for she is recorded to remain unclean for twice seven days <note>Leviticus 12:5 states a woman is unclean for two weeks after bearing a daughter, compared to one week for a son.</note>. However, for the one who bore a male, on the eighth day the one who was born is circumcised, and she becomes clean. You know that it is a laborious task to touch upon these things in such a short space of time; nevertheless, to say something in passing, this "week" can be seen as the time of this present life. For the world was completed in a week of days. As long as we are placed in the flesh within this world, we cannot be purely clean until the "eighth day" arrives—that is, until the time of the future age is present. On that day, however, he who is "male" and has acted manfully is immediately purged at the very arrival of the future age, and the mother who bore him is immediately made clean. 

[Marginal letter: C] For she will receive her flesh back from the resurrection, purged of its vices. But if he had nothing manly in himself against sin, but was remiss and effeminate in his actions—whose sin is such that it is not forgiven in the present age nor in the future—he passes into a second week in his uncleanness. Only when a third week begins to dawn is he purged from the uncleanness which the "female" contracted in giving birth. 

As for the sacrificial victims which are commanded to be offered for this kind of uncleanness, they are distinguished in two ways. First, a yearling lamb without blemish is commanded to be offered as a burnt offering, along with young pigeons or turtledoves for a sin offering. Second, however, the offering is changed: "If," the Law says, "her hand cannot <margin>Leviticus 12 <note>The text mistakenly references Leviticus 2, but the law of the poor is in chapter 12.</note></margin> [Marginal letter: D] find enough for a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering." 

From this, it seems marvelous that the offering of Mary did not have the first victim—that is, the yearling lamb—but the second, as if her hand did not suffice for the first. For it is written of her: "His parents came to offer a sacrifice for him, according to what is written in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons." In this, the truth of that which is written is displayed: <margin>2 Corinthians 8; Micah 5</margin> "That Jesus Christ, though he was rich, became poor." For this reason, he chose a poor mother from whom to be born, and a poor homeland, of which it is said: "And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means the least among the leaders of Judah," and so forth. 

[Marginal letter: A] Truly, we are forced to run through these things briefly and not discuss every single thing written, since we are hurrying to treat something of the laws of leprosy which have been recited. 

We find, therefore, six species of leprosy in humans proposed, which are described in this manner: <margin>Leviticus 13</margin> 1. Either a scar and a bright white spot forms on the skin of the body, and the contagion of leprosy is in the skin. 2. Or the leprosy will break out and cover the entire skin with contagion from head to foot. 3. The third species is when an ulcer forms in the skin of the flesh and is healed, but a white scar remains in the place of the ulcer. 4. Or there is a burn from fire in the skin of the flesh, and after this the healed burn is shiny and white, or white with a reddish tint. 5. The fifth species is when a contagion of leprosy occurs on the head or the beard of a man or woman. 6. The final species is written as occurring in a bald head or a receding hairline, a reddish contagion of leprosy which breaks out there. 

To use a summary of the exposition (since our purpose now is to briefly remind the listeners of these things that were recited, and there is no time to discuss every single detail clearly), it seems to me these should be referred to various types of sins, and in them, the stains of the soul that happen because of sins must be examined. Therefore, it must first be said that these designate the sins we commit while placed in this life: some of which can be cured now, while others cannot. Secondly, it must be understood that even concerning those sins that pass with us after this life, some are so fixed in souls that they cannot be abolished. Others, however, can receive a cleansing, according to the inspection and judgment of that High Priest <note>referring to Christ</note> from whom secrets cannot be hidden. He will distribute the souls of individuals according to whether he sees the stains of leprosy in them as either expiable or inexpiable. This present discourse does not permit us to gather the differences of this matter from the current reading, nor to search out every detail according to the evidence of this Scripture, as I have already said above. Indeed, these things could scarcely be composed in many volumes by those from whom the Lord has removed the "veil" <margin>Hebrews 10</margin> from the reading of the Old Testament. We, therefore, according to our strength, shall follow as much as is appropriate to bring forth, with the Apostle Paul opening the way of understanding for us, where he says that the Law has a "shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things," and according to that which is written <margin>1 Corinthians 9</margin> regarding oxen in the Law—that it was not written for oxen, for whom God has no care...

706 SAINT CYRILL ON LEVITICUS

[Margin: A] If we now move from that shadow of the law <note>original: *legis umbra*; a common Patristic term meaning the Old Testament laws are a "shadow" of the spiritual truth revealed in Christ</note> to its truth, observe how a soul that has received the wound of sin—even if it is cured—nevertheless retains a scar residing in the place of the wound. This scar is seen not only by God, but also by those who have received grace from Him, through which they are able to see the sicknesses of the soul. They can discern which soul has been so cured that it has cast off every trace of the inflicted wound, and which has indeed been cured, but still carries the evidence of the old disease in the very trace of the scar. 

[Margin: Isaiah 1] That there are indeed certain wounds of the soul, Isaiah teaches, saying: "From the feet even to the head there is no health in him: but wounds, and bruises, and swelling sores." <note>Isaiah 1:6</note> Speaking these things to the people with burning heat concerning their delights, he suggests that there are some for whom a softening poultice <term>malagma: a medical paste or plaster used to soften skin or reduce inflammation</term> might still be applied. But others, [Margin: B] who are sinners to such an extent that no care can be applied to them, the same prophet describes in this way: "There is no," he says, "poultice to apply, nor oil, nor bandages." 

That the crushing and the blow of pain is applied to the soul through correction for the sake of a cure, [Margin: Jeremiah 30] Jeremiah teaches, saying: "Thus says the Lord: I have stirred up crushing; your blow is full of pain. There is no one to judge your judgment; you have been cured with pain, there is no use in you. All your friends have forgotten you, and will no longer ask about you, because I have struck you with the blow of an enemy, a mighty correction, for all your iniquity. How your sins have multiplied! Why do you cry out over your crushing? Your pain is violent; because of the multitude of your iniquities your sins have prevailed, and they have done these things to you. Therefore all who [Margin: C] devour you shall be devoured, and all your enemies shall devour your flesh. And those who afflicted you shall be in affliction: and all who devastated you, I will give over to be plundered: for I will restore your health, and I will call back the pain of your wound from you, says the Lord." <note>Jeremiah 30:12–17</note> 

Remember carefully what you have heard from the prophet regarding wounds, scars, and swellings. For these things are necessary for us for the exposition of the scars or wounds, or other things of this sort, which are mentioned in the inspections of leprosy. 

We will add [Margin: Jeremiah 30] yet further what the same Jeremiah mentions in another place regarding the soul's wounds and cures—in which, however, traces of the wounds remain after the scar has formed—using these words: "Behold, I will bring [Margin: D] its scar, and at the same time I will heal them, and I will manifest to them peace and faith, and I will turn back the captivity of Judah and the captivity of Jerusalem." <note>Jeremiah 33:6–7; in the Vulgate/Septuagint numbering this is often grouped with chapter 30 in commentary traditions</note> 

If, therefore, we have sufficiently learned from the prophet about the wounds and scars of souls, and the cures and healings which are brought about by God the Physician: look now at that soul of which God says, "Because I have brought its scar." After the wounds, He undoubtedly brings the scar for the sake of health. "And I have healed them," He says, "and I will manifest to them peace and faith." If, therefore, after the knowledge and medicine of God, if after the manifestation of peace and faith which we receive through Christ, there should again depart from that scar some evidence of the prior sin, or if some sign of the old error is renewed:

Now, the second species of leprosy is this: "If it blooms," he says, "in the skin, so that it covers all the skin of the body from the head to the feet, through all things whatsoever the priest shall inspect." When, therefore, it has covered all the skin of the body, then the priest pronounces him clean from the contagion. But on whatever day a living color <note>original: *color uiuus*; referring to "raw flesh" in Leviticus 13:14</note> appears in him, he is again judged unclean, because of this fact—that a living color appeared in him which he did not have before.

For although it is placed in the soul, as long as it does not have use, if any sin is committed, it is not reckoned against him, because he who transgresses is seen to not yet be [Margin: B] capable of reason. However, when reason has found its place and time in him, if he then acts against reason, he is rightly seen to be blameworthy.

### The Numbering of the Hairs

Truly <note>original: "uerè"</note>, for <note>original: "nanq[ue]"</note> it is written in the Gospel that **all the hairs of the head are said to be numbered** <note>original: "capilli capitis dicuntur esse numerati"; a reference to Matthew 10:30, used here to suggest that even the smallest, most "dead" parts of our lives are known to God</note> by the Lord <note>original: "dñi"</note>. ### The Shaving of the Eyebrows

And afterwards <note>original: "posteaq[ue]"</note>, when the process of cleansing begins, the ritual becomes even more rigorous. If you contract <note>original: "cōtrahas"</note> the disease of arrogance, you must remove even the appearance of loftiness to be restored to the community.

## BOOK NINE.

->On what is written concerning the sacrifices of atonement: and about the two goats, one of which is the lot of the Lord, and one is the scapegoat <note>original: "apopompæi"</note>, which is sent into the wilderness, and regarding the entry of the High Priest into the Holy of Holies.<-

<margin>ἀποπομπαῖος <note>apopompaios</note>, that is, the emissary.</margin>

**D**ay of atonement <note>original: "propitiationis"</note> is needed by all who have sinned; and therefore among the solemnities of the law, which contain the figures of heavenly mysteries, one particular solemnity is held, which is called the Day of Atonement. These things which have just been recited are the legislation of that very solemnity: which day (as we have said) is called the Day of Atonement. But let us first see what the contents of the letter itself mean: so that as you pray (if indeed we are so suppliant to the Lord that we deserve to be heard) you may be able to receive the grace of the Spirit, through which we may be strong enough to explain the mysteries contained in the law. 

<margin>Leviticus 10.</margin>
The two sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, have died, who offered "strange fire" <note>original: "ignem alienū"; referring to unauthorized incense or fire not taken from the sacred altar</note> at the altar of the Lord. It was necessary, therefore, that Aaron be instructed by heavenly doctrine on how he ought to approach the altar, and by what rite of supplication he might make the Lord merciful: so that he himself might not encounter those same things which his sons encountered, who approached the altar of God carelessly and improperly, offering a strange fire, and not that which had been divinely given. Therefore, the law spoke about these things in this way: And the Lord spoke to Moses: 

<margin>Leviticus 16.</margin>
Speak to Aaron your brother, that he should not enter at every hour <note>original: "omni hora"</note> into the sanctuary, which is within the veil before the sight of the mercy seat <note>original: "propitiatorij"</note>, which is above the ark of the testimony, so that he does not die. From this it is shown that if he enters into the holy place at every hour—unprepared, not clothed in the high-priestly garments, nor with the sacrifices that have been established, nor having first made peace with God—he will die; and justly so, as one who has not done those things which are fitting to be done before approaching the altar of God. 

This discourse touches us all; what the law speaks here pertains to everyone. For it commanded that we should know how we ought to approach the altar of God. For the altar is that upon which we offer our prayers to God, so that we may know how we ought to offer them: namely, that we lay aside "dirty garments," which are the uncleanness of the flesh, the vices of character, and the stains of lusts. Or are you unaware that a priesthood has been given to you also—that is, to the whole Church of God and the people of believers? 

<margin>1 Peter 2.</margin>
Listen to how Peter speaks of the faithful: "A chosen race," he says, "a royal priesthood <note>original: "regale sacerdotīū"</note>, a holy nation, a people for His possession." You have a priesthood, therefore, because you are a priestly race, and for that reason, you ought to offer to God a sacrifice of praise, a sacrifice of prayers, a sacrifice of mercy, a sacrifice of purity, a sacrifice of justice, a sacrifice of holiness. But so that you may offer these worthily, you have need of clean garments, set apart from the common garments of other men, and you have need of the necessary divine fire. Not some fire "strange" to God, but that which is given by God to men, of which the Son of God says: "I have come to send fire upon the earth, and what do I desire

...is said to be bound with linen breeches and a belt, it is also fitting to speak of him according to the literal sense <note>original: "secundum literam"</note>, because our uncomely parts have more abundant honor. Thus, everyone who lives in chastity and imitates Christ—who alone knew nothing of human failings—is himself clothed in sanctified linen breeches, and has surrounded his uncomely parts with more abundant honor. Therefore, he is clothed in a sanctified linen tunic, and the linen breeches are upon his body. But lest these breeches, which cover the private parts, should fall loose and reveal his shame (for He said: *you shall not go up by steps to my altar, lest your shame be revealed upon them*), and lest your shame be revealed by falling breeches, He says: let the breeches be bound by a belt. 

At one time, while explaining John the Baptist and elsewhere Jeremiah—noting that Jeremiah was said to have a belt, while John had a leather belt around his waist—we sufficiently showed how these things declare that the part of the body in such men is so deadened to the world that no movement toward the allurements of the flesh, nor any other impulse, was believed to reside in their loins, but only chastity and pure modesty. Therefore, the High Priest is girded with a linen belt and places a linen miter <note>original: "cydarim"; a priestly turban or headdress</note> upon his head; everything is linen. What he calls a miter is a certain ornament placed upon the head, used by the High Priest and other priests when offering sacrifices. But each of us ought to adorn our head with priestly ornaments. For since Christ is the head of every man, whoever acts in such a way that his deeds bring glory to Christ has adorned his head, which is Christ. 

The ornament of the head can also be understood in us in another way: since the mind is the first and highest part of us, and the "head" of all our faculties. Thus, a person cultivates his head for the dignity of the high priesthood if he adorns his mind with wisdom and learning. There are, therefore, these four garments with which the High Priest is commanded to be clothed, and only then to enter the Holy of Holies, lest he die for lacking them. Now, regarding the sacrifices, some are commanded to be provided by the High Priest himself, and some are to be taken from the people. A calf is said to be his own, as it is the most precious and robust of animals. And the second animal is a ram, which is undoubtedly the most precious among the sheep. From the people, however, gifts are ordered to be offered: a ram from the leaders, and two goats from the people. One is to be sent away into the wilderness, which is called the scapegoat <note>original: "apopompæus"; literally 'the one sent away'</note>, and one is to be offered to the Lord. 

If all the people of God were holy and all were blessed, two lots would not be cast over the goats—one to be sent into the wilderness and the other offered to the Lord—but there would be a single lot and a single sacrifice for the Lord alone. Now, however, since among the multitude of those who come to the Lord there are some who belong to the Lord Himself, but others who must be sent to the wilderness—that is, those who deserve to be rejected and separated from the Lord's sacrifice—therefore a part of the sacrifice offered by the people consists of only one goat sacrificed to the Lord, while the other is rejected and sent into the wilderness as the scapegoat. The lot, how- <column-break/> -ever, falls upon both. And indeed, that one which is sent into the wilderness is said to take upon himself the sins of the sons of Israel, their injustices, and their iniquities. For it is not the goat which becomes the Lord's lot, but the one whose lot it is to be sent into the wilderness, that is said to carry them away. This is according to what I believe is written: *I have given Egypt as your ransom, and Ethiopia and Syene in your place, since you have become honorable in my sight.* <margin>Isaiah 43.</margin> 

Therefore, the sins of those who have performed penance and those who have abandoned malice are taken upon the heads of those who have become the lot of the one sent into the wilderness—those who have made themselves worthy of such a role or such a fate. It will be fitting, as if by contrast, to apply to these that which was said: <margin>Luke 19.</margin> [Marker B] *To him who has, it shall be given.* For just as to him who has righteousness, more is added, so too to him who has sins to such an extent that he is found in the lot of the scapegoat sent into the wilderness, more sins shall be added to him; and these sins are wiped away from the saints, so that in them what is written may be fulfilled: *From him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away,* so that it may be added to him who has much filth of sin. 

But because he who is in the lot of the Lord places his hope not in the present world but in the future, and he whose lot is the Lord's "dies daily," therefore the one upon whom the Lord's lot falls is slaughtered and dies, so that by his blood he may purify the people of God. That other one, however, who falls into the contrary lot, is not even worthy to die. Because he who is in the Lord's lot is not of this world; [Marker C] but the other is of this world, and the world loves its own. Therefore he is not killed, nor is he worthy to be slaughtered at the altar of God, nor does his blood deserve to be poured out at the base of the altar. 

But let us see who this is who receives the one whose lot has become that of the scapegoat, to cast him out into the wilderness. *A man*, it says, *who is prepared shall receive the goat* which fell to the lot of the scapegoat, and shall lead him into the wilderness. The end of this lot is the wilderness—that is, a place deserted of virtues, deserted of God, deserted of justice, deserted of Christ, and deserted of every good thing. 

And thus one of two lots awaits each of us individually. For either by acting well we are the Lord's lot, or by [Marker D] acting poorly our own lot leads us to the wilderness. Do you wish for me to show you clearly how these two lots are always at work, and how each of us becomes either the Lord's lot or the lot of the scapegoat and the wilderness? <margin>Luke 16.</margin> Consider in the Gospels that rich man living splendidly and luxuriously, and Lazarus lying at his gate full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table. What end is designated for each? *Lazarus died*, it says, *and was carried by angels to the bosom of Abraham.* Similarly, the rich man also died, and was led to a place of torment. You clearly perceive the distinct locations of each lot. See also who they are who lead them away: the *angels*, it says, who are always "prepared" to lead away. For they are the ministers of God designated for this very purpose, to fulfill the lot which you have prepared for yourself. For if you have lived well, if you have shared your bread with the hungry from your soul, if you have clothed the naked and judged with righteous judgment, then when you face the unjust...

### 718 SAINT CYRILL ON LEVITICUS

If you have resisted your iniquity, and have not placed your counsel with those who prepare snares for the innocent: you will make your lot <note>original: "fortem," likely a common printing error for "sortem," meaning "lot" or "fate"</note> the Lord's. But if you serve lust, and are a lover of pleasure more than a lover of God, loving the world, and do not hate malice, you have made your lot that of the *apopompaeus* <note>original: "apopompæi"; the Greek term for the "scapegoat" or the "goat of removal" sent into the wilderness</note>, so that you may be led away into the wilderness by the hands of a minister of God, who was ordained by God for this very purpose, and is therefore called "prepared": because he blushes for no person, neither the rich, nor the powerful, nor kings, nor priests. 

But do you wish to know why these animals, which receive these lots, belong to the Lord? They are not unclean, nor foreign to the altars of God: but they are clean, and are those which are accustomed to be offered in sacrifices: so that you may know these represent a figure <note>original: "figuram tenere"; to serve as a symbolic type</note>, not of those who are outside the faith, but of those who are within the faith. For a goat is a clean animal, and consecrated to the divine altars. And you therefore, through the grace of baptism, have been consecrated to the altars of God, and have become a clean animal. 

But if you do not keep that command of the Lord which said: *Behold, you are now made healthy; sin no more, <margin>John 5</margin> lest something worse happen to you,* but although you were clean, you stained yourself again with the filth of sin, and by your own fault you turned away from virtue to lust, and from purity to uncleanness: when you were a clean animal, by your own lot you surrendered yourself to the *apopompaeus*, to the wilderness. 

But perhaps the "prepared and clean" person (who leads him away, for whom the lot fell to the wilderness, and by the very fact that he leads him, as if he had touched something unclean, is said to be required to wash his clothes until evening and be clean) can also be understood as the Lord and Savior himself in that respect where he took up the garments of our nature—that is, of flesh and blood—which he washed toward evening. For this reason the prophet long ago said of him: *And I saw Jesus <note>original: "Iesum"; referring to Joshua the High Priest in the book of Zechariah, whose name is identical to Jesus in Greek and Latin</note> the high priest clothed in <margin>Zechariah 3</margin> filthy garments, and the devil standing at his right hand to oppose him.* He washed...

[Column 1]

We must take care lest perhaps it becomes even more grave for us at some time, we who are by no means punished by this common death for a common sin, compared to those whom the sentence of the law condemned corporally. For vengeance is reserved for us in the future, while for those others, their crimes were absolved through the punishments they paid. But if there is anyone who perhaps falls more frequently into sins of this kind, having now been admonished by the word of God, let him flee to the help of **repentance**; so that if he has committed a sin once, he may not do it a second time; or if he has already been overtaken a second time or third, let him add no more. For with the Just Judge, there is a moderation of punishment not only according to the quality of the act, but also according to the quantity. Among other sins, therefore, which are punished by death, the divine law records that **"whoever curses his father or mother shall die the death."** <note>original: "quí maledixerit patri aut matri, morte moriatur." From Leviticus 20:9.</note>

The name of a father is a great mystery, and the name of a mother is a secret reverence. God is called your Father according to the spirit; your mother is the **Heavenly Jerusalem**. <note>A common allegorical trope in early Christian writing, identifying the Church or the celestial city as the mother of believers.</note> Learn these things from the testimonies of the prophets and apostles. <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> Moses himself wrote this in his Song: **"Is he not your father, who acquired you and possessed you?"** <margin>Galatians 4</margin> Truly, the Apostle says of the Heavenly Jerusalem that **"she is free, who is our mother."** First, therefore, God is your Father, who begot your spirit, and who says: <margin>Isaiah 1</margin> **"I have begotten sons and exalted them."** But also the apostle Paul <margin>Hebrews 12</margin> says: **"Let us obey the Father of spirits, and we shall live."**

Secondly, your father is the father of your flesh, by whose ministry you were born in the flesh, from whom you came into this world, and who carried you in his loins, just as it is said of Levi: <margin>Hebrews 7</margin> **"Because he was still in the loins of Abraham when Melchizedek met him as he returned from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him, and received tithes from him."** Therefore, because the name of a father is so sacred and so venerable, for that reason **"whoever curses father or mother shall die the death."** Similar things must be considered regarding the mother, by whose labor, care, and ministry you were both born and nourished. And therefore it is necessary for you, according to the Apostle, to return a portion of grace to your parents. For if you dishonor a carnal father, a contempt of this kind is referred back to the spiritual Father. And if you do an injury to a carnal mother, the injury overflows to that mother, the Heavenly Jerusalem.

In the same way, if a servant is irreverent to a master, through this corporal master, contempt is cast upon the Lord of Majesty; for He has placed His own name upon this carnal master. And therefore, in no way should a contest be held or a contradiction moved against a father, not even in word. He is a father, she is a mother; let them act, do, say, and command as it seems best to them. However much obedience we offer, we do not yet return the favor of the grace by which we were born, by which we were carried, by which we drew light, and by which we were nourished—and perhaps even educated and instructed in honorable arts. And perhaps through these very authors we recognized the Lord, came to the church of God, and heard the word of the divine law. For all these reasons, therefore, **"whoever curses father or mother shall die the death."**

If these things are decreed concerning corporal parents, what will those do who provoke God the Father with cursing voices, who deny that He is the Creator of the world? Or those who, understanding the Heavenly Jerusalem (which is the mother of us all) with unworthy senses, drag the prophetic sayings down to the condition of some earthly city? It is good, therefore, to observe that we never worship either our carnal father or our heavenly Father with less than worthy honor; similarly to observe the mother, and even every commandment which commends modesty and chastity to us; so that we may neither be liable to death in the present life according to the spiritual law, nor may the future punishment of eternal fire await us. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant that we all flee and escape from this, to whom is glory and power for ages of ages. Amen.

**SAINT CYRIL'S TWELFTH BOOK ON LEVITICUS.**
**Concerning the high priest.**

Every priest who is among men is small and slight compared to that Priest of whom the Lord said: <margin>Psalm 109</margin> **"You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek."** For He is the **Great High Priest** who was able to penetrate the heavens, and to go beyond the entire creation, and to ascend to Him who dwells in inaccessible light, the Lord and Father of the universe. For this reason, even he who was called the "Great Priest" among the Jews entered indeed into the holy places, but into those made by hands, built of stones; he did not ascend into heaven, nor could he stand before the Father of lights. But because he filled the shadow and image of these things, for that reason he also bore the name of the Great High Priest through a shadow and image.

From this, the Jews—who ought to have been closest to the faith because a certain foreshadowing and image of the truth had shone before them—while they thought the <term>types</term> <note>Historical patterns or symbols in the Old Testament that prefigure New Testament realities.</note> were the truth, rejected the Truth itself as if it were a lie. We, however, who have received the Great High Priest, ought to understand how He truly is the Great High Priest. He is truly the Great High Priest who forgives sins: not through the blood of bulls and goats, but through His own blood. Because we have recognized who the Great High Priest is, and that the things written in the Law concerning the high priest are fulfilled in the Savior—whom the previous discourse showed to be the truly Great High Priest—let us now see what things the Law wrote about Him in a prophetic spirit.

**"And the priest,"** it says, <margin>Leviticus 21</margin> **"who is great among his brothers, upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured, and whose hands have been perfected so that he may put on the holy garments: he shall not take the turban from his head, nor shall he rend his clothes, and he shall not go in to any dead soul. He shall not be contaminated for his father or his mother, and he shall not go out of the sanctuary, nor shall he defile the name of his God which has been sanctified upon him, because the holy oil of the anointing of his God is upon him. I am the Lord. This man shall take a virgin as his wife from his own kin; but a widow, or one cast out, or a defiled woman, or a harlot, these he shall not take; but he shall take a virgin from his own kin as a wife, so that he does not stain his seed among his people. ...clothed in the light of [justice] and wisdom, which are truly holy garments. **He shall not,** he says, **take the turban from his head.** <note>original: "Non, inquit, auferet de capite suo cydarim." The "cydarim" is the distinctive turban or mitre worn by the High Priest.</note> We have said before that the turban is a type of covering which, when placed upon the head, provides an ornament for the priest. This great high priest of mine, therefore, never puts aside the ornament of his sacred head. Learn from the Apostle what the "head" of Christ is, for he [Marginal note: 1 Corinthians 11; John 14] says: **The head of Christ, however, is God.** <note>original: "Caput autem Christi, Deus."</note> Rightly, then, he never sets aside the ornament of his head, who is God: because the Father is always in the Son, just as the Son is always in the Father. **And he shall not tear his clothes.** Truly, this is the one who does not tear his garments, but has always kept them clean, always whole, and always chaste. **And he shall not enter where there is any dead soul.** What is a "defunct" soul; what is a "dead" soul? [Marginal note: Ezekiel 18] The Prophet says: **The soul that sins, it shall die.** <note>original: "Anima quæ peccauerit, ipsa morietur."</note> Christ, therefore, does not come upon this dead soul: because he is wisdom, and [Marginal note: Wisdom 1] **wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul.** For that soul is dead, because where malice is present, sin is present. [Marginal note: James 1] **Sin, however, when it is finished,** he says, **brings forth death.** For this reason, Jesus does not enter a dead soul. But if the soul lives—that is, if it does not have mortal sin within itself—then Christ, who is life, enters the living soul: because just as light cannot be with darkness, nor justice with iniquity, so life cannot be with death. And therefore, if anyone is conscious within himself that he has mortal sin, and has not cast it from him through the penance of the fullest satisfaction, let him not hope that Christ will enter his soul, because he does not enter any dead soul. Then the text adds: **Because he is the great priest, he shall not be defiled by his father or his mother.** This passage of Scripture is very difficult to explain; but if you pray to God, the Father of the Word, that he might deign to illuminate us, it can be explained by his gift. Everyone who enters this world is said to be made in a certain state of defilement, which is why the Scripture says: [Marginal note: Job 25] **No one is clean from filth, not even if his life has been but a single day.** <note>original: "Nemo mundus à sorde..." Cyril is referring to the concept of original sin or the inherent frailty of human birth.</note> Therefore, the very fact that he is placed in the mother's womb, and that he takes the material of the body from the origin of the father’s seed, can be called being "defiled" in father and mother. Or do you [Marginal note: Leviticus 12] not know that when a male child has reached forty days, he is offered at the altar to be purified there, as one who was polluted by the very conception, either of the father’s seed or the mother’s womb? Every human being, therefore, is polluted in father and mother. But only the Lord Jesus Christ, my Lord, having entered into this generation of the world, was not polluted in his mother. For he entered an undefiled body; for it was he who long ago had said through Solomon: [Marginal note: Wisdom 8] **But rather, since I was good, I came into an undefiled body.** <note>original: "Magis autem quum essem bonus, ueni ad corpus incoinquinatum."</note> He was not, therefore, defiled in his mother; but neither was he in his father. For Joseph provided nothing in his generation except for his service and affection; for which reason the Scripture granted him the title of "father" because of his faithful service. [Marginal note: Luke 2] For thus his mother Mary says in the Gospel: **Behold, your father and I were searching for you sorrowing.** <note>original: "Ecce ego & pater tuus dolentes quærebamus te."</note> So

741

A therefore, he alone is this great priest who was polluted neither in his father nor in his mother. But let us see if we can find something even more sublime, and worthy of the dignity of such a great high priest. The true Father of all is called God; and the [Marginal note: Galatians 4] Apostle says that the "mother" is the **heavenly Jerusalem.** All those, therefore, who sin are defiled in the Father by whom they were created. For whether we have done something impious, or spoken it, or thought it against the Lord, when we have not believed in God, we are defiled in the Father. But would that it had happened then only through unbelief, and ceased after we believed! We are also defiled in the mother in this way: if, while believing in God, we either harm the Church or stain the liberty of the heavenly mother by the unworthy slavery of sin. But only the Lord B Jesus Christ, who knows no sin, was defiled neither in his father nor in his mother, and **he did not go out from the sanctuary.** There were indeed several points to be proposed to the Jews regarding the above things, to which they could not respond. But leaving those aside, what do they—or those who wish the law to be understood according to their [literal] sense—say to us about this discourse? If these things are not referred to our Priest and Savior, how can it be proven according to the letter that the great priest **did not go out from the sanctuary**, when he certainly took a wife (as is said below), a virgin of his own kin? If he did not go out from the sanctuary—if he never goes forth—how and for what purpose is he seen to take a wife? For it must not be thought that he could remain within the holy places with a wife. But let those who take pleasure in C **Jewish fables** <note>original: "Iudaicæ fabulæ." A common patristic term for literalist interpretations of the Old Testament that ignore the allegorical or Christological meaning.</note> think such things. We, however, [Marginal note: Hebrews 7] have a great priest according to the **order of Melchizedek**, Jesus Christ, who never goes out from the sanctuary. For he is always in holy things, and he always remains holy in his words, holy in his acts, holy in all his wills, and he is the only one who is never found outside the sanctuary. For he who sins goes out from the holy; and as often as anyone sins, so often is he made to be outside the holy. Christ, however, who never sinned, never went out from the sanctuary. But you also, who follow Christ and are an imitator of him—if you remain in the word of God, if you meditate on his law day and night, if you are exercised in his commandments—you are always in the sanctuary, nor will you ever depart from there. For holy things are not to be sought in D places, but in actions, life, and character. If these are according to the Lord, and are held according to the command of God, even if you are not in the house of God, even if you are in the marketplace—and what am I saying, "in the marketplace"?—even if you are found in the theater, serving the word of God, do not doubt that you are in the sanctuary. Does it not seem to you that Paul, when he entered the theater [Marginal note: Acts 19 and 17] and entered the Areopagus and preached Christ to the Athenians, was in the sanctuary? Even when he walked among the altars and idols of the Athenians, where he found the inscription, **To the Unknown God**, and from this word took the beginning of his preaching of Christ—even there, surveying the altars of the Gentiles, he was placed in the sanctuary because he was thinking holy thoughts. But whoever also guards himself after receiving the grace of God, so that he does not fall into murder, adultery, theft, or false testimony and other things like these, but remains clean from all defilement...

Concerning the feast days and the lamp, and the candlestick, and concerning the oil for the light, and concerning the table and the loaves of proposition.

<margin>A</margin> He who is perfect is taught by God himself concerning the rationale of the solemnities, and does not use a man as a teacher to learn these things; but he learns from God, if he is able to grasp the voice of God. One is that where the mind, illuminated through the prophetic spirit, is taught: in which (if I may say so) it is learned more by the intuition of the mind than by the sound of the voice, through which the truth itself is recognized, rather than the shadow and image of truth. 
<margin>B</margin> Therefore, those who cannot grasp the truth of God itself, nor behold the full brightness of the truth with the intent gaze of the mind, hear about the solemnities in the second place from those who learned them in the first. ...from two-tenths <note>The Latin "decimis" refers to the measure of flour used for each loaf, specifically two-tenths of an ephah as prescribed in Leviticus 24:5.</note>, twelve loaves of bread are set before the Lord, and all twelve consist of an equal and similar measure. They are commanded to be set forth upon a clean table. Who among us possesses such a clean table that loaves may be offered upon it to the Lord? "If you sit," it says, <margin>Proverbs 23</margin> "to dine at the table of a powerful man, understand intelligently those things which are set before you." What then is the "table of the powerful man," if not the table of Him who said: "I can <margin>Philippians 4</margin> do all things in Him who strengthens me, Christ Jesus," and "when I am weak, then I am powerful"? <margin>2 Corinthians 12</margin> On the clean table of this powerful man—that is, in his heart and in his mind—bread is offered to the Lord. If you sit down to dine at the table of such a powerful Apostle, understand intelligently what is set before you; that is, observe spiritually what is said by him, so that you too may be able to do what he adds. For he says: "Knowing that it is necessary for you to prepare such things."

But let us see how the twelve loaves are placed. "Two," it says, "arrangements." In one arrangement, there are six loaves. Do you think that this division is idle—that is, that the number twelve is again divided into six? For the number six <term>senarius numerus; the number six was considered "perfect" in antiquity because it is the sum of its parts (1+2+3) and represents the six days of creation</term> has a certain closeness with this world. For in six days this visible world was made. Therefore, there are two orders held in this world, that is, two peoples <note>Likely referring to the Jews and the Gentiles, or perhaps the clergy and the laity within the Church.</note>, who guard the faith of the Father and the Son in the Church, as if upon one clean table.

"And there shall be placed," it says, "upon the arrangement, pure frankincense." <note>original: "thus mundum"</note> The substance of frankincense holds the form of prayers. It is necessary, therefore, to join the vigilance and purity of prayers to the "loaves of faith." Moreover, a pure prayer is, as the Apostle says: "Lifting up pure hands without anger and dispute." <margin>1 Timothy 2</margin> At the same time, let him cause that which is written to be filled with fragrance: "Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight." <margin>Psalm 140/141</margin> If anyone indeed offers prayers to God, but does not have a clean conscience from evil works, he may seem to place frankincense upon the loaves, but he does not place *pure* frankincense. For if all were pure frankincense, the Scripture certainly would not have added that "pure" frankincense was to be placed upon the loaves of the presence before the Lord. Do not think that Almighty God commanded this, or enacted this by law, so that frankincense would be brought to Him from Arabia. Rather, this is the "incense" which God seeks to be offered to Him by men, from which He receives a "sweet-smelling odor": prayers from a pure heart and a good conscience, in which God truly receives a fragrance of sweetness.

"And the loaves shall be," it says, "for a commemoration of what is set forth before the Lord. On the Sabbath day you shall set them forth." If it is not yet manifest to you that these loaves are the Word of God, I shall confirm it now from these words. For what is it that makes a commemoration of God for us? What is it that recalls us to the memory of justice and of every good thing, if not the Word of God? Therefore, he says, "they shall be for a commemoration of what is set forth before the Lord." He adds, "and on the Sabbath day," that is, in the rest of souls. And what greater rest is there for a faithful soul than the memory of God, than to dwell in the sight of the Lord, than to remain in the faith of the Father and the Son, than to offer prayers to the Lord as a sweet-smelling odor? "It shall be," it says, "an eternal covenant..."

<column-break/>

# 751

"...for Aaron and his sons; and Aaron and his sons shall eat them in a holy place." This is the "chosen race, the priestly race," <margin>1 Peter 2</margin> to whom this portion of holy things is granted by God; which is all of us who believe in Christ. However, I do not look for the "holy place" to be situated upon the earth, but in the heart. For the rational soul is called a "holy place," because of which the Apostle also says: "Do not give a place to the devil." <margin>Ephesians 4</margin> Therefore, my soul is a place: if I act wickedly, it is the devil's; if well, it is God's. Finally, the malignant spirit, "when," it says, "he has gone out from a man, and has wandered through dry places, and has not found rest, he says then: I will return to my place from which I came out." <margin>Luke 11</margin>

Therefore, the holy place is a pure soul, in which place we are commanded to eat the food of the Word of God. For it is not fitting that a holy soul should receive unholy words; but when it has purified itself from every defilement of the flesh and of character, then having been made a holy place, let it receive the food of that "bread which descended from heaven." <margin>John 6</margin> Is not the "holy place" better understood this way than if we were to think that a structure of unfeeling stones is named a holy place? From this, by a certain similarity, this Law is also set before you: that when you receive the mystical bread <note>A reference to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, you eat it in a clean place. That is, do not perceive the sacraments of the Lord's body in a soul contaminated and polluted by sins. "For whoever," it says, "eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily, will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let each one examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup." <margin>1 Corinthians 11</margin> For they are the "Holy of Holies." <margin>Leviticus</margin>

You see how it did not say "holy" only, but "Holy of Holies"—as if it were saying: This holy food is not common to everyone, nor to any unworthy person, but it belongs to the holy. How much more rightly and deservedly do we say this also concerning the Word of God: this speech is not for everyone, nor can just anyone hear the mystery of this Word. It belongs only to the holy, who are purified in mind, who are clean in heart, who are simple in spirit, who are irreproachable in life, who are free in conscience. It is for them to hear concerning this Word; to them these mysteries can be explained. "For to you it is given," it says, "to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God." <margin>Luke 8</margin> But to those who do not deserve the same, who are not the kind who deserve it, they cannot be capable of understanding the secrets; to them this "priestly bread"—which is the mystical and secret Word—cannot be given, except in parables, which is common to the crowd.

"This shall be a legitimate and eternal [statute]." For everything that is mystical is legitimate and eternal. For these present and everywhere-visible things are temporal and quickly reach an end. "For the fashion of this world passes away." <margin>1 Corinthians 7</margin> But if the figure of this world passes away, without doubt the fashion of the literal [text] also passes away, and those things remain which are eternal, which the spiritual sense contains. If, therefore, we have understood first how God speaks to Moses and Moses to the children of Israel; second, the reasoning of the clean lampstand and its lamps and its oil; and third, the loaves of the presence, each one made from two-tenths according to the will of the Spirit; let us give our effort, so that we also... <margin>Leviticus 24</margin>

<summary>Cyril provides a spiritual interpretation of the twelve loaves of Showbread and the frankincense from Leviticus 24, arguing that the "holy place" where these are consumed represents a pure soul rather than a physical building. He links the bread both to the Word of God and the Eucharist, emphasizing that only those with a clear conscience should partake of these mysteries.</summary>

Therefore, let those who turn their mouths to this vice by almost daily habit see what danger hangs over them. For thinking this to be a light and easy sin, they do not easily take heed; but let them consider the Apostle, how he excludes the abusive person from the kingdom of God, and how God through Moses shows how the abusive person ought to be punished.

756 BOOK FOURTEEN.

[Column 1]

...this man is named: the "inner man," I say, who was made in the image of God and is able to see the Lord. After these things, the matters reported in the later parts are not without a certain difficulty; many have asked about this, but not many have been able to explain it. But if you help me with your prayers, we will also attempt to bring forward what the Lord provides. "A man," he says, "if he curses God, shall receive his sin; but he who names the name of the Lord, let him die the death." <note>original: "Homo, inquit, si maledixerit deum, peccatum accipiet: qui autem nominat nomen domini, morte moriatur." Cyril is quoting Leviticus 24:15–16.</note> What is this? He who curses God does not have the penalty of death, but he who names the name of the Lord does? Is it not much more serious to curse God than to name Him, even if it is said to have been named in vain? And how is it that he who curses only "receives sin," while he who names Him "dies the death"? These are the things in this place that usually raise a question, which to those ignorant of the meaning of the scriptures seem to be stated inconsistently and inappropriately. For they think that he who curses the name of the Lord ought to be punished immediately; but for him who names the name of the Lord—that is, names it superfluously and in vain—it should be enough to have "received the sin." 

But we hold that the logic of the discourse can be opened with a certain understanding of this kind. We cannot doubt that the sin in which God is cursed is greater than that in which He is merely named. It remains for us to show that it is much more serious to "receive sin" and have it with oneself, than to be punished by death. Death, which is inflicted as a punishment for sin, is a cleansing <note>term: "purgatio" - here meaning a temporal payment or satisfaction that settles the debt of the sin.</note> of the very sin for which it is ordered to be inflicted. Therefore, the sin is absolved by the penalty of death, and nothing remains of it that the day of judgment would find worthy of the penalty of eternal fire for this crime. 

However, where someone "receives sin" and keeps it with himself, and it remains with him without being washed away by any suffering or punishment, it passes with him even after death. And because he did not pay temporal penalties here, he pays eternal punishments there. Do you see, therefore, how much more serious it is to "receive sin" than to be punished by death? For here, death is given for vengeance, and before God, the just judge, "He does not judge twice for the same thing," <margin>Zephaniah 1 <note>The Latin text cites "Sopho. 1" (Sophonias/Zephaniah), though this specific phrasing "not judged twice" is famously associated with Nahum 1:9 in the Vulgate tradition.</note></margin> as the prophet said. But where the vengeance has not been paid, the sin remains to be punished by those eternal fires. 

That these things are so, I can bring you witnesses from the divine volumes: the patriarchs Reuben and Judah, speaking to their father Jacob when they wanted to take Benjamin with them and lead him to Egypt because of the promises they had pledged with their brother Joseph. There, Reuben says to his father: "Kill both my sons unless I bring Benjamin back to you." <margin>Genesis 42</margin> But Judah says: "I shall be a sinner against you unless I bring him back to you." <margin>Genesis 43</margin> Jacob their father, knowing that what Judah had promised—who said "I shall be a sinner against you"—was much more serious than what he had said who promised "kill my sons," did not trust his son to Reuben, as to one who had chosen a lighter penalty; but he handed him over to Judah, knowing that what he had chosen was more significant. In this way, therefore, the divine scripture appropriately assigned that he who curses God "receives sin," but he who commits a lighter offense "dies the death." Do you wish also from the Gos-
