And men who are ignorant of the judgments of God, which are "a great abyss," <margin>Psalm 35 <note>In modern numbering, Psalm 36:6.</note></margin> are accustomed to complain against the Lord and say: "Why do unjust and iniquitous men—robbers, the impious, the wicked—suffer no adversity in this life, but all things fall to them with prosperous success? Honors, riches, power, and even health and physical fitness serve them. And on the contrary, for the innocent and pious who worship God, innumerable hardships come upon them; they live rejected, humble, despised, and under the blows of the powerful, and sometimes—quite often—diseases of the body itself dominate them." 

But they complain of these things, as I said, being ignorant of the order of divine judgments. For as much as they want those whose power and iniquities they groan under to be punished more severely, so much more is it necessary for the punishments to be deferred. If they were not deferred, they would certainly be temporal and lighter, because they would receive an end with death; but now, because they are deferred, it is certain that they will be eternal and will extend through the ages. 

On the contrary, therefore, if they wished for good things to be returned to the just and innocent in the present age, those good things would also be temporal and concluded by a swift end. But the more they are deferred into the future, the more they will be perpetual and know no end. This is what this passage of scripture, though contained in few words, has taught us: so that we may know it is much more serious to "receive sin" and keep it, and carry it with oneself to the underworld, than to pay the penalties for the crime in the present. 

And therefore, knowing these things to be profitable for the faithful, the apostle Paul says of the one who had sinned: "Whom I have delivered," he says, "to Satan for the destruction of the flesh," <margin>1 Corinthians 5</margin>—that is, to death. That many fruits follow this death, he shows in what follows, saying: "So that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ." You see, therefore, how clearly the Apostle explained the utility of this death when he said, "I have delivered him to the destruction of the flesh"—that is, into the affliction of the body, which is usually paid by those who are penitent; and he called it the destruction of the flesh, which nonetheless confers life upon the spirit. 

Wherefore, even now, if any of us remembers in himself the consciousness of any sin, if anyone knows himself to be liable for a fault, let him flee to repentance and undertake a voluntary "destruction of the flesh." Thus, with our spirit purged in the present life, let it proceed clean and pure to Christ our Lord: 
to whom is glory and power 
forever and ever, 
Amen.

# SAINT CYRIL ON LEVITICUS
## Book Fifteen.
### On the sale of houses and redemptions.

**[T]**hree different laws regarding the sale and redemption of houses are given through Moses in Leviticus. We shall first examine their content according to the historical narrative <note>Cyril uses "history" here to mean the literal, factual events or laws as they were originally recorded.</note>, so that after this we may also ascend to the spiritual sense. Some houses are in walled cities, while others are in villages or fields that do not have walls. <margin>Leviticus 25</margin> He says, therefore, that if someone sells a house in a walled city, he shall have the opportunity to redeem it for a full year. After a year, however, no power of recovery is granted. For, he says, the house shall become the certain possession of the buyer if the one who sold it could not liberate it within the year. The second law is that if the house which was sold is in a village that has no wall, but to which a field is adjacent, the seller is allowed—even after a year, and whenever he is able—to return the price and recover the house he had sold. The third law is that if the house happens to belong to a Levite or a priest: wherever such a house may be, whether in a walled city or in a village without a wall, it is always permitted, and at any time, for the Levite or priest to redeem his house whenever he is able. Divine laws never permit a priestly or Levitical possession to be confirmed to another who is not of the same order. These, then, are the laws used by that former people <note>Referring to the ancient Israelites under the Old Covenant.</note>, observing them religiously and piously in consideration of the priestly or Levitical orders, even according to the literal meaning. 

But let us more quickly refer these things to ourselves, for whom the law of Christ—if we follow it—permits us to have neither possessions on earth nor houses in cities. And why do I say houses? It does not even grant us many tunics, nor the possession of much money. <margin>1 Timothy 6</margin> For "having food and clothing," it says, "let us be content with these." How, then, shall we observe the laws given concerning houses, whether placed within a walled city or in villages without walls? We find in other places of Scripture that the divine word names a "house" with a certain greater mystery: as when it speaks of Jacob and offers it as praise for him: "For Jacob was," it says, "a simple man, dwelling in a house." <margin>Genesis 25</margin> And again I find it written concerning the midwives of the Hebrews: "And because," it says, "the midwives feared God, they made houses for themselves." <margin>Exodus 1</margin> Let us see, therefore, that the cause for making houses for the midwives was the fear of God; but for Jacob, simplicity and innocence gave him cause to dwell in a house. Finally, concerning Esau, who was wicked, it is not written that he dwelt in a house; nor is it written of any other who did not fear God that he built a house for himself. What then is this house, and what kind of building is it? The Apostle Paul explains more clearly when he says: "We have a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." <margin>2 Corinthians 5</margin> This, therefore, is the house which no one can build except in simplicity of mind and purity of heart. But since it often happens that even one who has built well, and has constructed 

<column-break/>

SAINT CYRIL ON LEVITICUS 759

A a heavenly house for himself by acting well, living well, and believing rightly, may incur the debt of some sin and be forced to sell this house to a most cruel usurer <note>Typically interpreted as the devil or the weight of sin.</note>, transferring his labors to another, the piety and mercy of the Lawgiver intervenes so that it can be redeemed within a certain time—if, however, it says, "your hand finds the price to restore it." What kind of price? Doubtless one gathered from the tears of repentance, <margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin> and found by the "hands," that is, by the labor of good work. Moreover, the "year" itself can be understood as that which the Lord came to call the "acceptable year," <margin>Isaiah 61</margin> in which He releases the broken in forgiveness and offers salvation to those confessing their sins. As for his saying "a house in a walled city," I believe the house which is said to be in heaven is rightly understood as being in a walled city. B For the wall for houses of this kind is the very firmament of heaven. But only a rare few are able to have such a house: those perhaps who, though walking upon the earth, have their "conversation in the heavens," <margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin> and of whom the Apostle says: "You are God's building." <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> But others have houses in villages which have no wall, yet there is a fertile field adjacent to it; and these are perhaps those who prepare a dwelling for themselves in the "land of the living," and in that land which the Lord promises to the meek, saying: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth." <margin>Matthew 5</margin> Regarding these houses, therefore, if someone happens to fall (as we explained above), there is always the faculty of recovery; so that, to give an example, if some mortal fault finds us—not a mortal crime, <margin>Ephesians 2</margin> not a blasphemy of the faith (which is surrounded by the ecclesiastical wall and the apostolic dogma) <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> C but a fault in speech or a vice of character—this is to have "sold a house which is in a field," or in a village which has no wall. This sale, and a fault of this kind, can always be repaired; never are you forbidden from performing penance for such committed acts. For in more serious crimes, a place for penance is granted only once. <margin>This refers to public penance, which [unclear] is to be understood according to the judgment of the church.</margin> But these common things, which we frequently fall into, always receive penance and are redeemed without intermission. 

"But if it was a priestly house," he says, "or a Levitical one, wherever it may be, whether in a city or in a field, it always has redemption." In this place, I seek a priestly sense and a Levitical understanding. For the author of these things <note>The interpreter/preacher.</note> ought not to be inferior (if possible) to the one who wrote and ordained them. What is it then, that the priest and the Levite always have redemption of their house, and wherever they are, they have redemption? D According to the spiritual understanding, the "priest" is said to be the mind consecrated to God; and the "Levite" is called he who stands unceasingly before God and ministers to His will. Therefore, the "priest and Levite" are to be understood as perfection in intellect and work, in faith and actions. Thus, if it happens at some time to this perfect mind to sell the house it has—not made with hands, but eternal in the heavens—and to give it into the hands of another (as happened once to the great patriarch David, when from his roof he beheld the wife of Uriah the Hittite), he redeems it immediately, <margin>2 Corinthians 5. 2 Kings 11.</margin> he repairs it immediately, for he says immediately: "I have sinned." Nay, even...

<summary>Cyril provides a spiritual interpretation of the Levitical laws regarding property redemption, equating the "house" with the soul's heavenly dwelling and the "price of redemption" with the labor of repentance.</summary>

...a similar rain of the word. Was this the blessing of so great a patriarch? Do you want me to show you even further how elsewhere the wicked have a multitude of grain? Look at that man in the Gospel,

...the Lord might give rain in its season: and the harvest was made. <note>original: "daret dominus pluuiam in tempore: & facta est messis."</note> After this, I do not remain idle, but I sow again; I take up the prophetic scripture, and from it I sow the lands and the *fallow fields* of my listeners; after these, I sow other things from the Gospel discourses. <term>fallow fields</term><note>The Latin *noualia* refers to land newly broken by the plow; here, Cyril uses it to describe the minds of those hearing the Word for the first time.</note> Different are the things which are sown. There is always something to be sown in all our life: there is no time for idleness. <margin>Galatians 6</margin> As long as we breathe, let us sow: only let us sow in the spirit, so that from the spirit we may reap eternal life. <note>Cyril is referencing Galatians 6:8: "For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life."</note> "And you shall eat," he says, "your bread in fullness." <note>original: "in satietate," meaning to the point of being completely satisfied or full.</note> Nor do I take this to be a physical blessing—as if someone who keeps the law of God should obtain this common bread in abundance. For why? Do not the impious and the wicked eat bread not only in abundance, but even in delicacies? <margin>1 Cor. 15</margin> ...to say: Before the man from heaven came, and the heavenly man was born, we were all earthly and bore the image of the earthly; but when the new man came, who was created according to God, we cast out old things from his sight:

**"And I will place my tabernacle among you."** <note>Leviticus 26:11. Cyril interprets the "tabernacle" not as a physical tent, but as the presence of God within the human heart.</note> If we have these things in us which were mentioned above—if, by casting aside the old man, our heart is renewed—then God comes to us and dwells in us, he who said: **"And I will place my tabernacle among you, and my soul shall not abhor you."** The soul of God will not abhor us if we observe those things which are written. Nevertheless, I wish to ask: what is the **"soul of God"**? <note>original: "anima dei"</note> Do we truly think that God has a soul just as a human does? It is absurd to feel this way about God. I, however, dare to say that the **"soul of God"** is Christ. For just as Christ is the **Word of God** and the **Wisdom of God**, so also is he the **Soul of God**. And in this way he says: **"Because my soul shall not abhor you,"** 

<column-break/>

[Right Column]

that is, my Son; **"but I will walk among you."** It does not seem to me that God is promising this—that he is going to walk in the land of the Jews—but rather that if anyone deserves to be so pure of heart that they are capable of containing God, God says that he "walks" in that person. **"And you shall be my people, and I will be your Lord God, who led you out of the land of Egypt, when you were slaves, and I broke the yoke of your chains."** <note>Leviticus 26:12-13. Cyril moves from the physical liberation of Israel to a spiritual liberation of the soul.</note> Truly he led us out of the **house of bondage**; for we were **slaves of sin**. 
<margin>John 8</margin> **"Because everyone who sins is a slave to sin,"** <note>John 8:34. Therefore, our Lord Jesus Christ broke the chains of sin and shook off the yoke of our captivity; and he placed upon us his own **sweet yoke** of faith, and charity, and hope, and of all holiness. To him be glory for eternal ages of ages, Amen.

# THE SECOND VOLUME CONTAINS,
## [THE WORKS] OF THE BLESSED CYRIL,
### ARCHBISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

The distinguished work entitled the **THESAURUS**, concerning the consubstantiality <term>consubstantiality: the theological doctrine that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share the same essential nature or "substance"</term> of the Son and the Holy Spirit with God the Father, written against the heretics.

Seven books of **Dialogues with Hermias on the Trinity**, including an appendix of arguments [proving] that the Holy Spirit is God.

That the Son is consubstantial and co-eternal with God the Father, **Book I.**
That the Son is co-eternal with God the Father, and was begotten from Him according to nature, **Book II.**
That the Son is true God, just as the Father is, **Book III.**
That the Son is neither a creature nor a created thing <note>original: "factura"</note>, **Book IV.**
That the properties and glory of divinity are naturally within the Son, just as they are in the Father, **Book V.**
That the properties of humanity, and those things said of the Son that do not sound divine, pertain more to the "dispensation" <term>dispensation: also known as the "economy" of salvation, this refers to the Way God manages human history, specifically through the Incarnation—God taking on human flesh</term> of the flesh, and not to the nature of the Word insofar as He is understood to be God, **Book VI.**
Concerning the Holy Spirit: that He is both God and is from God, according to nature, **Book VII.**

**On adoration and worship in spirit and truth, in one book.**

# THE SECOND VOLUME CONTAINS
## THE WORKS OF BLESSED CYRIL,
### ARCHBISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA.

i. **Twelve objections**, by which he teaches that his anathematisms <term>anathematisms: formal ecclesiastical denunciations or curses against specific heretical doctrines</term> are correct, against those in Syria who wrote on behalf of Nestorius <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century Bishop of Constantinople who was accused of dividing Christ into two separate persons, divine and human</note>.
ii. **A Dialogue on the incarnation of the Only-Begotten**, in which it is shown that Christ is one, and not two, against those who divide him into two, and that he is one [being] from two natures.
iii. **That the blessed Virgin Mary is the Mother of God** <note>original Latin: "Dei genitrix," a translation of the Greek "Theotokos"</note>, and not only the mother of a man.
iiii. **That Christ is God**, and not only a man.
v. **That Christ is one**, and not two.
vi. **That the divinity is impassible** <term>impassible: the theological concept that God's divine nature is incapable of suffering, pain, or change</term>, and that the flesh is life-giving, and that it belongs specifically to the Word of God, and not to another.
vii. **That the humanity belongs specifically to the Word of God**, and not to another, and that it is united according to hypostasis <term>hypostasis: the fundamental reality of Christ's personhood in which his divine and human natures are perfectly joined</term>.
viii. **A distinguished and very useful discourse** against those who do not wish to confess that the blessed Virgin is the Mother of God, and that Christ is God, and not only a man.
ix. **On the explanation of the Creed** <note>original: "symboli," referring to the formal statement of Christian belief, likely the Nicene Creed</note>, that there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and that he is the Only-Begotten Son of God.
x. **On adoration and worship in spirit and truth**, in seventeen books.

## OF THIS BOOK WHICH IS
### called the Treasury.

->**CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST BOOK.**<-
How one ought to respond to the Arians <note>Arians were followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being and not of the same substance as God the Father</note> when they ask whether there is only one "begotten" or two. Chapter 1.
Why it is better and worthier for God to be called "Father" than "Unbegotten." Chapter 2.
That "unbegotten" is not a substance <term>substance: in this context, the essential nature or "whatness" of God</term>, but a term signifying the mode of his substance. Chapter 3.
That "unbegotten" is not a substance, but only signifies that God was not begotten. Chapter 4.
Against those who say there was a duration of time when the Son did not exist: and the testimonies of Scripture from which it is gathered that the Word of God is eternal. Chapter 5.
That the Father did not exist before the Son, even though He is unbegotten; rather, the begotten Son has always been co-eternal with Him. Chapter 6.
That the Father generates the Son from Himself indivisibly and without corruption. Chapter 7.
Regarding those who ask whether the Father begat the Son by choice or by necessity <note>original Latin: "uolens an nolens," literally "willing or unwilling"</note>. Chapter 8.
Against those who say the Son is similar to the Father's will, but not to the Father Himself. Chapter 9.

->**THE SECOND BOOK.**<-
That the Son is consubstantial <term>consubstantial: of the very same essence or being</term> with the Father. Chapter 1.
That the Son is consubstantial with the Father, based on the proposed text: *I go to my Father and your Father: to my God and your God.* Chapter 2.
Regarding the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son, based on the proposed text: *Because my Father is greater than I.* Chapter 3.
That the Son is equal to the Father, based on the proposed Gospel text: *Among those born of women, there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist.* Chapter 4.

->**THE THIRD BOOK.**<-
Refutation of the heretical interpretation, and an exposition of the true sense of the Gospel text: *I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.* Chapter 1.
Regarding the likeness of the Son to the Father, and that the Son is not of a changeable nature, nor does He exist from the outside, but was begotten from the very substance of the Father, as a true Son. Chapter 2.
That the Son is from the substance of the Father, and was not produced from the outside as the heretics say. And since He was not produced from the outside, He is therefore like the Father. Chapter 3.
Regarding the likeness of the Father and the Son, similarly based on the proposed text: *No one is good, except God alone.* Chapter 4.

->**THE FOURTH BOOK.**<-
That we are formed into the image of God through participation. Chapter 1.
Likewise, regarding the essential likeness of the Father and the Son, based on the proposed Gospel text: *For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave also to the Son to have life in himself.* Chapter 2.

Against the Arians, who, by proposing the text from Proverbs: *The Lord created me, the beginning of his ways for his works,* were seducing the simpler folk by saying the Son was a creature <note>The Arians used Proverbs 8:22 to argue that Christ was a "creation" of the Father rather than being eternally God</note>. Chapter 1.
Against the reason for which heretics think the Son of God is a creature. Chapter 2.
Against the objections of heretics, by which they attempt to teach that because the Son is a creator (which is not characteristic of creatures), he is still a creature. Chapter 3.
How one must understand: *The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways.* Chapter 4.
That the Word of God is not a creature. Chapter 5.
That Scripture sometimes misuses words <note>This refers to "catachresis," where a word is applied in a non-literal or broad sense to describe divine mysteries</note>. Chapter 6.
Regarding the same text from Proverbs: *The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, and before all the hills he begat me.* Chapter 7.
How that phrase in the text of Proverbs is understood: *He founded me before the ages.* Chapter 8.

->**THE SIXTH BOOK.**<-
Regarding the eternity of the Son, and that He emanates inseparably from the substance of the Father. Chapter 1.
Regarding the same, namely that the Son is not a creature. Chapter 2.
That "to generate" and "to create" are not the same thing in God. Chapter 3.

->**THE SEVENTH BOOK.**<-
Against those who say that the Son is not the Father's true Word, but is of a different nature than the Father. Chapter 1.
Regarding the same, in another manner. Chapter 2.
Against another objection of Eunomius <note>Eunomius of Cyzicus was a prominent leader of the radical Arians who argued the Son was "unlike" the Father</note>. Chapter 3.
That the name "Word" is sufficient to signify the eternal generation of the Son from the Father. Chapter 4.

The objection of Eunomius from the text of the Apostle: *Therefore God also exalted him, and gave him a name which is above every name.* Chapter 1.
That the Son is immutable according to His nature, based on the proposed text of the Apostle: *He sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having been made so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they.* Chapter 2.

## THE THIRTEENTH BOOK.

<meta>This page continues the theological discourse from the previous page, shifting from the scriptural names of God to a logical and linguistic analysis of the term "unbegotten." The author is refuting the Arian claim that "unbegotten" is the essential definition of the Father’s nature.</meta>

4 BOOK ONE.

A definition seeks [to state] not what a thing is not, but what that which is proposed actually is. However, the word <term>unbegotten: "ingenitum." A technical term used to describe God the Father’s unique property of having no origin or beginning from another.</term> signifies not what God is, but rather what He is not. For because He is not begotten, He is therefore called "unbegotten." Therefore, the name "unbegotten" is not a definition. 

Furthermore, the professors who teach the art of definition <note>The author is likely referring to classical logicians or followers of Aristotle, who established the rules for how to define things by their genus and specific difference.</note> demonstrate that definitions of substances, or even of accidents, are not to be made from opposites, but from the components of which they consist. For a person does not define white who says it is "that which is not black." For that phrase signifies not what the defined object is, but rather what it is not. 

But the word "unbegotten" signifies "not being begotten," which is the opposite of "begotten." You will never define something correctly through opposites; therefore, the name "unbegotten" is not a definition. 

Add to this that the word "unbegotten" signifies many things and is rightly numbered among <term>equivocal terms: "aequivoca." Words that have the same sound or spelling but multiple, distinct meanings.</term> Definitions of substances, however, do not consist of equivocal terms, nor of terms that signify many different things. For that which one seeks to define will not be made clear if it is defined through words of this kind. Wherefore, "unbegotten" cannot be a definition. Finally, if the word "unbegotten" [is a] definition... <note>The sentence continues on the following page.</note>

<summary>The author argues that "unbegotten" is a negative description rather than a formal definition of God's essence, using classical logic to show that a definition must state what a thing is, not what it is not.</summary>

He generates by sight. Do you not see that even from fire light is born, yet it suffers no division <note>original: "diuisionem." FIRST. 9

A For we call the Father "God," and the Word "Son" and "God": not so that we understand it in the manner of men, as if one existed before and the other was born later, but so that we may adore one as "generating" (which is the notion of a Father) and the other as ineffably "begotten" from the substance of the Father. The Father, therefore, is Father because He begets; the Son is Son because He is begotten. And it is only the use of these names, based on a similarity to us, that signifies this. 

If, therefore, in God the name of "Father" signifies only "to generate," no reason will compel God—who generates without time—to have existed before His own Son. Because if no duration can be understood between the begetter and the begotten, the Son is surely co-eternal with the Father.

# 12

...that **there was a time when the Son was not**, <note>original: "erat quando non erat Filius." This was the primary slogan of Arianism, a 4th-century belief that Jesus was a created being rather than eternally God.</note> he imagines the Father to be a **dry fountain**. <note>original: "siccum fontem." Cyril uses this "absurd" image to show that a Father without a Son is as logically impossible as a fountain that does not flow.</note> Yet He is explicitly called the Fountain of Wisdom. How is it not completely absurd to suggest that a fountain could exist without ever having had water? For if the Father is a fountain—and a fountain is by definition that which produces a flow—how can the Son not be present? 

Or how can He truly be called "Father," if He does not have a Son? A fountain is named for its flow, and a father is named for his child. If, therefore, there was a time when the Son did not exist, then there was also a time when the Father was neither a fountain nor a father. But if He is the **eternal Fountain** and the **eternal Father**, then it follows that His "flow"—which is the Son—must also be eternal.

->On the Eternal Radiance<-

<margin>Hebrews 1</margin>
Consider also what is written of the Son being the *radiance of His glory and the exact representation of His being.* <note>Hebrews 1:3. This is another of Cyril's favorite analogies: just as you cannot have the sun without its light, you cannot have the Father without the Son.</note> If the glory of the Father is eternal, then the radiance that shines from it must be eternal as well. To say the radiance had a beginning is to say the glory itself was once dark. Therefore, we confess that the Son exists co-eternally with the Father, flowing from Him like water from an ever-springing well, never having a beginning and never ceasing to be.

<margin>Solution to the objection <note>original: "Solutio Cavilli." A 'cavil' is a trivial or petty objection used in formal logic to avoid the truth.</note></margin> 
But if, they say, the Father is perfect in His own greatness, and nothing is lacking for the perfection of His nature, then the Son is joined to Him redundantly, as if to provide a fullness of the Godhead that was otherwise missing. 

Certainly, the Father is found to be perfect in His greatness; no one of sound mind would deny this. Yet He is perfect not only because He is God, but also because He is a **Father**. Therefore, he who denies that God is a Father takes away **fecundity** <term>fecundity: from the Latin *fecunditas*, meaning fruitfulness or the inherent power to produce life.</term> from the divine nature, so that it would no longer be perfect, since it would lack the power of generating. 

The very concept of perfection, therefore, is fecundity; and the seal which demonstrates the Father's perfection is the Son, who comes forth from God. Furthermore, if fecundity were not inherent to the Father’s substance by nature, and if He were "perfect" even without the power of generating, then the act of generation would be something superfluous and brought in from the outside. But anything brought in from the outside is something that was previously lacking; how then can He be "perfect" if He were in need? Or how could something brought in from the outside...

Likewise, when Philip wished to investigate the divine nature with such curiosity <margin>John 14</margin>, he said: "Show us the **Father**," and not, "Show us [God]..."

<meta>This page continues the defense of the eternal generation of the Son against the Arian heretic Eunomius. The previous discussion established that the name "Father" is more fundamental to God's nature than the title "God." Now, Cyril refutes the argument that divine generation implies a physical change or a loss of substance in the Father.</meta>

**28 THE TREASURY OF SAINT CYRIL**

If you think that God is diminished by outflows during generation in the same way that humans are—as if something flows out from Him into His Word and becomes separated—what prevents you from applying such similar impiety to other matters? For if He generates with **passion** <term>passion: from the Latin *passio*, meaning "undergoing change" or physical sensation, rather than just emotion</term> like a man, why would He not also create with labor like a man? But if it is absurd to suggest that God does anything with labor like a man, it is also absurd to say He generates through physical change like a man. If He generates like a man and acts like a man, then because we humans must stretch out our hands over pre-existing matter to make something from it, you would have to say the same about God. 

But without hands or matter, God brought all things into being from nothing by His Word, surpassing every nature of created things. Therefore, in generating, He shall also surpass that nature. If you apply words to God in no other way than if they were spoken of physical bodies—even though God is written to contain the universe—and since those things are said to "contain" which surround a larger physical space and are more extended, you would be forced to understand the incorporeal God as being stretched out through all places. But this I know you will avoid as an impious thought. Therefore, just as God does not contain all things by the law of physical bodies, so He does not generate in the manner of bodies. 

Furthermore, that which is in all things and penetrates the universe must be connected to all things. Now, God is in all things and penetrates all things, yet we do not believe that He Himself is "connected" to bodies in a physical sense. For God remains in His own purity and is not mixed with other things, even though He is everywhere and penetrates all. It is impious, therefore, to apply the power of words to Him as if He were a physical body. Add to this that God is not a composite being, but **simple** <note>In theology, "simplicity" means God is not made of parts; His essence and His existence are the same.</note>; and yet He works diverse and various things, and His simplicity is in no way harmed even though He works differently in individual things. Therefore, just as He exceeds physical nature in these and all other things, so He does as well in 

<margin>The sophistry of the heretics.</margin> 

generating. But it is necessary (says Eunomius) that if the Son proceeds from the Father's substance, He must have been implanted in Him by power beforehand: for in this way He seems to proceed from Him. Then, if the Father generated no Son after the Word (for He is the **Only-begotten**), you might say He is deprived of the power of generating; but you cannot deny that He is also found to be diminished in part: since the Son once proceeded from Him, and is no longer implanted in Him as He was before. 

Are you not ashamed, O man, to attribute the properties of bodies to God? And to keep saying that the Son was "inside" the Father like one body inside another? For the Son is not contained beforehand in the loins of the parent as happens among men; the same does not apply to God. What would stop someone—if they reduce the divine essence to the misery of physical bodies—from thinking that the Father could in no way generate because He has neither a female sex, nor even a male one? For these things are found only in bodies, but He Himself is simple and incorporeal, and the most pure intellect. Therefore, if anyone wishes to investigate that generation as far as is permitted to man, they ought to consider the things that proceed from the mind and intellect, and from a likeness of this sort, to understand the generation of the Word as much as we are able in this life,

...composed of parts, because it is spread throughout all things. <margin>A</margin> But if God is simple and not composed of parts, why do you not also believe that His generation is simple and without parts? For we, because we are composed of many parts, are subject to division and outflows; but since God is simple, if He generates, He generates simply. And if He generates simply, He certainly generates without **passion** <term>passion: from the Latin *passio*, meaning "undergoing change" or physical sensation, rather than just emotion</term>. For how can He who is always the same and never changes suffer any change in His nature? For it is not possible: <margin>B</margin> <note>original: *potest*</note> that the divine and unchangeable nature should undergo the laws of human birth.

If you say that the generation of the Son is a "passion," you are essentially saying that God is changeable, which is a great impiety. We must consider that God does not generate in the same way as humans do. In humans, the father is older than the son, but in God, the Father is not prior in time to the Son. As light is never without its radiance, so the Father is never without His Word. We must speak of these things quite often <margin>C</margin> <note>original: *saepius*</note> because the craftiness of the heretics <note>Cyril is referring to the Arians and Eunomians who used human logic to limit God</note> attempts to lead the simple-minded astray by using human analogies for the divine nature.

If God is truly incorporeal—and I do not think even you would dare to say He has a body—then it follows that His generation must be incorporeal. If there is no body, there is no flow; if there is no flow, there is no division of substance; and if there is no division, there is no diminution. Therefore, the Father generates the Son while remaining whole and perfect, losing nothing <margin>D</margin> <note>original: *non*</note> of His own essence.

For the Father is the source, and the Son is the power, <margin>A</margin> <note>original: *uirtus*</note> and the radiance of His glory. If the Son is the power of the Father, and the Father's power is eternal and inseparable from Him, then the Son is eternal and inseparable. The heretics argue that "there was a time when the Son was not," but they do not understand that the things of God are not like the things of men, which have a beginning and have passed away. Why <margin>B</margin> <note>original: *transierunt. Qua-*</note> then do they seek to measure the divine by the human?

For if they admit that God is the eternal Father, they must admit He has an eternal Son <margin>C</margin> <note>original: *fili-*</note> because a father is only defined by his relation to a child. Therefore, if He is the Father from eternity, the Son exists from eternity. You cannot name the one without implying the other. Just as you cannot speak of a "creator" without something being created, you cannot speak of a Father <margin>D</margin> <note>original: *pater*</note> without a Son.

<summary>Cyril argues that God’s simple and incorporeal nature ensures that the Son is generated without change or division of the Father's substance. He concludes that the Father and Son are co-eternal, as the title "Father" necessitates the eternal existence of the Son.</summary>

But the Son, as the will of the Father, was eternally in the Father. Why is it that when they ask whether the Father begat the Son willingly, they do not also ask whether He begat Him in **prudence**? For counsel and prudence seem to be the same thing: for he who is prudent rightly wills what he wills. <margin>Proverbs 8</margin> For this reason, these qualities are joined together in the Savior as if they were equivalent. 

**B** "Counsel and protection are mine," He says, "mine is prudence and power." <note>original: "Meum conſiliū & tutela, mea eſt prudēn-tia & potentia." A reference to Proverbs 8:14, where Wisdom (the Son) speaks.</note> For just as protection and power are reduced to the same thing, so are counsel and prudence. Furthermore, Paul, showing the unchanging likeness of the Son to the Father, calls Him the **radiance of His glory** and the **exact representation** <term>exact representation: the Latin 'character' refers to an engraved mark or a seal’s impression that perfectly matches the original</term> of His substance. If, therefore, according to you, He was born by a preceding act of will, then since it is necessary that the Father not be unlike the image and His own radiance in essence, the Father Himself would also be preceded by a will—which is utterly absurd. For the Father’s **hypostasis** <term>hypostasis: the distinct person or underlying reality of the Father</term> cannot in any way exist from a preceding will; therefore, neither can the Son’s. 

But how, they say, will it not be impious to admit the Son was born from an unwilling Father? I pray they should revere the Savior Himself when He says: "Because the Father loves the Son." For just as He is good and omnipotent—qualities which, although He does not possess them by a preceding will or choice of counsel, He nevertheless does not possess unwillingly, for He wills to be what He is—so, although He did not beget the Son from a choice of will, He nevertheless does not have Him unwillingly, but loves Him, as it is written. Just as the Father’s hypostasis exists, not because He willed it to exist, but because it simply **is**, nor does He wish it not to exist; so also the Son is born from the Father not unwillingly, and yet a choice of will does not precede His generation. 

Furthermore, if the Son, as the radiance and representation, was made by will and counsel according to you, then certainly the Father was at one time without His radiance and representation. It follows then that the Father’s hypostasis was not always generative, but was changed by counsel and finally reached that state. But if it is impious even to think such a thing, let them believe that the Father is generative according to **nature**, just as He is naturally good. 

Besides, if will does not exist without an interior word—for will is an occult word implanted in the heart—and since the Son of the Father is His Word, He Himself will also be His Will. How then is will begotten from will? Or how is a word from a word? For the Son is all these things to the Father: counsel, will, word, wisdom; therefore, nothing exists in the Father before Him. 

In addition, it is naturally implanted in humans that they are able to procreate children; they are not "fathers" in the same way they are "honest" or "wicked" by an act of will. Rather, they have the latter by will, but the former by nature; we are masters of one, while nature masters the other. Therefore, just as we do not become fathers of our children by an act of choice, but by nature, so also God the Fa-

**A** -ther is not a Father by an act of will, but naturally. And just as our children are like us according to substance, so also the Son of God—since He did not come to the Father from the outside, but proceeded from His own essence—is like the Parent in all things. And just as the Father is not Father by will, so also the Son is not a Son of "will," but is from the Father according to nature, since He is the radiance and representation of His Parent. 

But <margin>The captious questioning of the heretics</margin> these people (says Eunomius) who think they believe correctly should be asked: Did the Father beget the Son willingly or unwillingly? For if the Son was within the Father’s substance, even if He were distinct from Him, He was not born by will: for it was necessary for Him who was naturally implanted to be brought forth and emitted. But if He was not in the Father, but was born because the Father willed it, then necessarily the Father’s will preceded Him. Therefore, the Son is not co-eternal with the Father. 

I cannot marvel enough at how carelessly these people run into every blasphemy, like the unlearned. For they are not ashamed to subject God Himself to **necessity**, and to say that something is contained in the essence of the Father as if in human bodies, or that the Son is in the Father like a little vessel within a vessel. But we, who strive to believe correctly, confess that the essence of God is above all necessity. We believe the Son is in the Father, not as a body within a body, or as if contained by a body, but as inseparable from the Father and emanating from Him according to the law of nature. 

If they think they are offering something clever when they say He was necessarily born either by will or not by will, let them answer us: **C** If someone imagined there was a "will" in fire, would its heat flow from it by its will, or the opposite? They will be able to answer nothing. For things that come forth by nature undergo neither of these; but things produced from the outside undergo both, for they are within our power if we are able to do them. Therefore, just as we also work by willing, but we give birth from ourselves—and "willing" or "not willing" has no place in that process—likewise God produces external things because He wills to; but He generates the Son eternally from Himself, and "willing" or "not willing" has no place in this generation, although the Son is not begotten of an unwilling Father. For the Father (says the Savior) loves the Son. 

But if the Father (says Eunomius) did not beget the Son by will and <margin>John 14</margin> judgment, but has Him from nature, it is clear that even the knowledge by which He knows the Son was not held by His own consideration, but by nature. **D** Therefore, He "learned" that He would have a Son through whom He would create all things; and thus the Father’s knowledge of the Son came to the Father from the outside, for He learned it from His own nature—which is absurd. Therefore, He produced Him by will, and foreknew that He would exist, and thus the will precedes the generation. 

As if we would ever concede that the Father was "taught" that a Son would be born to Him before He brought Him forth! Thus does this most untruthful man argue. Let him not ignore that there is no space between the Father and the Son, and therefore no place for such pre-knowledge. For if He used counsel beforehand, and learned beforehand that He would have a Son, then certainly some spaces of time would precede the Son. But He Himself is the creator of both time and all space.

Since, therefore, the Father is capable of all things and always wills what is better, the Son is born from God consubstantial with Himself...

the substance of the parent, and not be consubstan-
<margin>B</margin> tial <term>consubstantialis; sharing the same fundamental "stuff" or essence</term> 
with him, if he is truly begotten from him, as if his 
natural fruit? But if they say "begotten from the 
Father" only with their voice <note>Meaning they say the words but don't believe the reality behind them.</note>, let them say openly that he is a creature, 
and stop pretending many things and hiding many things, 
trying to deceive the simpler Christians.

<margin>Aetius</margin> But if God (says Aetius <note>Aetius was a radical Arian theologian who argued that the Son was "unlike" the Father because God is indivisible and cannot beget anything from his own essence.</note>) is indivisible 
according to his substance, the Son is not begotten from him: 
since generation happens through the dividing of substance; 
rather, he was produced by him according to his 
will. How then will a nature produced by will be of the same 
substance with the one who produced it? God is of an 
indivisible nature, 
O Aetius, and he shall not therefore be deprived of the power of begetting. 
For he can be both indivisible and a parent at the same time. 
You, however, wishing to honor God, attribute indivisibi-
<margin>C</margin> lity to him. But when you deprive him of the power 
of begetting, and think his Son is a creature, you certainly 
do not honor him: for a most beautiful and 
excellent thing is natural action, or operation. 
If you wish to speak this way, honor God also with that which we 
call the power of begetting. Truly, however, you will honor 
God if you are willing to confess and preach that he, 
without being divided, begets from himself a 
consubstantial Son in an ineffable <note>Beyond the power of words to describe.</note> and incompre-
hensible way. But when you say the Son was produced 
by the will of the Father, I do not see why you call him "Son." For 
how will he truly be a Son who does not flow out from the 
substance of the Father? But he is truly a Son; therefore 
he is also consubstantial: for the same nature is found in the one begotten 
and the one who begets. Furthermore, if—as 
<margin>D</margin> you say, you deceived and deceiving ones—the Son does not 
flow from the substance of the Father, but was produced 
because the Father willed it, since he himself is both the Wisdom and 
the Power of the Father: then the Father will not be wise by nature, 
nor powerful in his own strength. For if his 
Wisdom and Power were produced outside his substance, they will not be 
innate to him, which is most absurd. His 
Father is such by nature: therefore the Son flows from his substance, 
and is of the same substance with him. But tell 
me, I ask, what compelled the Father to produce the Son 
outside his substance, as you say? Was it some necessity, 
or because he wanted to show his grace and goodness in him 
(as he does in other creatures)? If you say he was compelled by necessity, 
the Father will be subject to necessity; but if it was because he wanted to show his grace in the Son, 

->BOOK TWO. 37<-

<margin>A</margin> he is found to have gratified himself more than the Son. 
For through the Son he is found to be both Creator and wise, and 
mighty in power. For the Scripture cries out that **"All things 
<margin>John 1, 1 Cor 1</margin> were made through him"** and again: **"Christ, 
the power of God and the wisdom of God."** But it is foolishness 
to say the Father gratified himself in these things, and not to believe 
that he is naturally wise, and the rest of 
this sort. Therefore, he did not produce the Son because he willed it, 
as you contend: but he brings him forth naturally from himself, 
and therefore consubstantiality is necessarily pre-
served in them. In addition, we believe the Son is consubstan-
tial with men insofar as he is a man, because he took on our 
form. But he is also in the form of God the Fa-
ther: he is therefore also consubstantial with God the Father. 
Furthermore, if the radiance of this light <note>Meaning physical light, like the sun.</note> is of the same 
<margin>B</margin> nature and essence as its source, the Son, since 
he is the radiance of eternal light, will be consubstantial with it. 
In all such examples, however, we bring 
a certain weak similarity to that supreme 
nature: since every creature 
is infinitely distant from its Creator. Added to this is that 
equality—which in bodies is spoken of according to 
size—is in intellectual and 
incorporeal things (where size has no place) spoken of 
according to the identity of substance: but the Son is preached 
as equal to the Father according to the Scriptures; 
he is therefore necessarily consubstantial with him. For things which 
are truly from someone by nature are of the same substance with the 
begetter. And he who possesses all the natural 
goods of the parent is truly born from him: but the Son 
<margin>C</margin> has all things that belong to the Father. Furthermore, he who 
produces created things out of nothing cannot be of the na-
ture of the things produced, but is necessarily of the nature of the producer. 
But the Son produces and makes crea-
tures out of nothing, even according to you; therefore he is found to be 
of the same substance, not with the creatures, but with the 
producing and creating Father. For those things which have the same 
action and operation are proven to be of the same 
essence. By nature, truly, God is Father; therefore by nature 
the Son is also God; otherwise he will be God by 
participation, just like the creatures: and there will be 
no difference between him and the creatures. But he 
is the Lord and Creator of creatures: therefore he does not 
agree in substance with any creature, but with the Father. 
To this, every rational nature operates not by 
<margin>D</margin> will alone, but by acting and suffering; 
God alone operates by will alone, but the Son 
operates by will alone: he is therefore consubstantial with God the Father, 
not with any creature. Add to this, that 
God begets his only-begotten Son not as we do, but in a 
nobler way. Our 
sons are consubstantial with us; therefore his 
Son will also be so with God the Father. And we indeed are born before 
our [sons]: but the Son of God is co-eternal with the Father, and from him 
he is not (as our sons are) separable. Furthermore, of all 
things that exist, one is God, the other is creature: therefore the Son 
will be consubstantial with either the creature or with God. 
But he is not consubstantial with the creature: for a creature 
cannot receive creative power. Therefore to God the Fa-
ther, the Creator of all, he who is also the Creator of all 
will likewise be consubstantial.

Specifically, he addresses the Arian claim that because Jesus said "The Father is greater than I," the two cannot share the same divine nature.</meta>

38 SAINT CYRIL’S TREASURY

<margin>Objection of the / heretics.</margin>
On the shared essence of the Father and the Son, regarding the proposed 
text: **"Because my Father is greater than I."**
CHAPTER III.
"Things that are of the same nature and the same substance," Eunomius <note>Eunomius (died c. 393) was a leading radical Arian who argued that the Son was a created being, fundamentally "unlike" the Father.</note> says, "do not admit 
'greater' or 'lesser.' For one man is not more a man than another 
according to the definition of his substance, nor is one donkey greater 
than another [in its 'donkey-ness']. If, therefore, in things of shared essence 
no place is given for 'greater' or 'lesser,' and the Son 
plainly taught that the Father was greater than himself, he is not 
of the same essence." All heretics would do 
well if they would strive to hunt for the true 
meaning of the Scriptures from every angle, and not twist 
everything to their own will, and from there weave together false syllogisms. 
For if it offends them that the Father 
<margin>Philippians 2</margin> is written as being greater than the Son, let that which is said 
of the Son help them: **"Who, though he was in the form of God, did not 
think it robbery to be equal to God."** And John says 
most clearly: **"He called God his own Father,"** he says, **"making 
himself equal to God."** <note>original: "Patrem... deum dicebat, æqualem seipsum faciens deo" from John 5:18.</note> How then is he of a different 
substance, if he is equal? For things that are naturally 
equal are entirely of the same substance, 
such as men or horses. Furthermore, in incorporeal <term>incorporeal; things without physical bodies, like spirits or the soul</term> 
matters, "greater" and "lesser" are not perceived according to size, 
as in physical bodies, but according to service. 
<margin>1 Corinthians 12</margin> This is what Paul shows: **"To one,"** he says, **"is 
given the word of wisdom by the Spirit, to another the grace of 
healing,"** and having counted many such things, he concludes: 
**"But one and the same Spirit works all these things."** 
Then again he encourages us that we ought to ask for greater 
graces from God. Will they say, then, that the Spirit differs within 
himself, or is of some dissimilar substance, 
because he is "small" in small things and "greater" in 
greater things, according to the capacity 
of those receiving him? No one is so insane as to dare 
think this. Since, therefore, an incorporeal nature does 
not admit "greater" or "lesser," when the Father is said 
to be greater than the Son, the statement must be attributed 
to his humanity, not his divinity. For when Christ says: **"The Father who 
sent me is greater than I,"** and the Apostle says of him: **"He did not 
think it robbery to be equal to God,"** we must 
diligently seek how the Son can be both equal to the Father and 
lesser; so that we neither despise the equality because 
the Father is called greater, nor deny that the Father is 
greater because the Son is written as equal to him, 
but rather understand both piously. Since, therefore, the nature 
of the deity is not composite but simple, it would never 
be distinguished into several persons unless some 
difference were found: not according to essence, but 
according to relationship, understood as it were from the outside, 
through which the person of each is established in their own 
hypostasis <term>hypostasis; the distinct individual existence or "person" of the Father, Son, or Spirit</term>, and cannot be excluded from the unity of the deity 
because of their natural identity. Thus, 
no confusion and no "mixing" of the Father and Son 
can be imagined. For since there is such great likeness and 
perfect identity that some have even suspected the Father 
and Son to be the same person <note>A reference to Sabellianism, a heresy that taught God was one person appearing in different "modes."</note>, and did not distinguish 
a duality of persons, divine Scripture used the names 
of Father and Son to distinguish the "notions" of the hypostasis 
that begets and the one that is begotten. It did this so that 
"Light from Light" might be correctly understood, each in its own 
hypostasis, while the identity of substance is preserved.

SAINT CYRIL’S TREASURY 39

<margin>A</margin> Following our human custom, Scripture calls the 
Father "greater" so that the person *from whom* he is 
signified, and the person who is *from* that one, might be 
clearly seen from every side. It also testifies to their equality, 
lest any lack of likeness or difference be found in the essence 
of the Father and the Son. Although, therefore, according to the 
definition of substance he is equal and entirely similar to the Father, 
the Father who begets him is nevertheless greater 
than him in this alone: because the Son is *from* him. Thus, 
the Father is the "principle" or beginning of the Son according 
to origin. And certainly, things that are of the same 
nature admit such a comparison; 
but things of different natures are not compared in this way. 
For no one rightly says an ox is greater 
than a man, nor a man than an ox. 
If, therefore, according to the heretics, the Father is greater than the Son, 
<margin>B</margin> and this cannot be said according to essence (for one 
man is not said to be greater than another according to essence, 
nor insofar as he is a man), and since things of different substances 
do not admit "greater" and "lesser" in this way, as we have said, 
it remains that the Father is called greater than the Son 
in Scripture either because the Son is *from* the Father, or (which 
we believe more firmly) because of the "dispensation of the 
incarnation" <term>dispensation of the incarnation; the theological term for God's plan to take on human flesh and live as a man</term>. 
Furthermore, things that are compared to one 
another are entirely of the same nature; 
they do not receive comparison from their essence (for 
man is not greater than man *as* man) but from 
accidents <term>accidents; in philosophy, qualities like height or strength that can change without changing what a thing fundamentally is</term>, 
by which they differ. These usually arise 
from some "passion" or from an entirely external 
cause which is clearly not inherent in the definition of the thing. 
For example: a man is greater than another man 
<margin>C</margin> in the size of his body, the strength of his soul, or the 
sharpness of his mind. But in all men, the definition 
of substance is one and the same, and is said equally of each. 
Accidents, however, flow from "passion" <note>original: "passione"; in this context, it refers to the state of being acted upon or having physical/emotional experiences.</note> as if from a root. 
For slowness of mind and fear of the soul flow from passion. 
If, therefore, any comparison is founded on accidents, 
and accidents arise from passion or an external cause: 
if no passion can exist in God, and no external cause can 
happen to him, it follows necessarily that the Father is 
greater than the Son either by way of origin (because he is 
called his principle) or because of the incarnation, as we said. 
"But the Son," says Eunomius, "proclaims himself 
<margin>Eunomius’s / desire.</margin> 
lesser than the Father not ambiguously, but openly. 
What need is there for more words? For you will grant 
that the Truth speaks truly; and Christ is the Truth. Therefore, the 
<margin>D</margin> Father is greater than the Son, and therefore dissimilar 
and not consubstantial." First, therefore, we will ask him 
*when* the Father was greater than the Son. For he cannot 
have been greater within a determined time. 
For the Son is the creator of all times and ages. 
It follows, then, that the Father is greater than the Son 
always and eternally. And since "greater" is said in relation to 
"lesser," and "greater" and "lesser" exist at the same time: 
if the Father is greater than the Son, the Father and Son 
are co-eternal. How then will the eternal be dissimilar to the eternal, 
or how will it be "greater"? Next, we marvel that even though 
they set out from the wisdom of this world and 
follow Aristotelian disciplines, and try to strike us with them, 
they are found to be unlearned even according to those rules. 
For they do not follow through logically when they make 
this argument about "greater" and "lesser"...

He uses logical and scriptural proofs to show that if the Father and Son are co-eternal, they must share the same essence.</summary>

[Column 1]

...they might do, they fell into a discussion of similarity and dissimilarity. For even according to Aristotle (whom these men boast of most frequently), "similar" and "dissimilar" are not placed in the same category as "greater" and "lesser." For Aristotle calls these latter terms <term>relative terms (ad aliquid): things defined by their relationship to something else, like "larger" or "smaller"</term>, a category in which we do not see "similar" and "dissimilar" placed. Why then, weaving your argument from "greater" and "lesser," did you introduce a conclusion from a different category, saying: "The Son is less than the Father; therefore he is dissimilar"? It would have been better had you said, "therefore he is unequal," or "not as great"—although even that would not be correct. For even if "greater" and "lesser" are properly spoken of in regard to quantity, they are not placed in that category <note>Cyril is arguing that God has no "quantity" or "size," so terms like "greater" cannot be applied to His essence in a physical way.</note>. Therefore, Eunomius has ignorantly deviated from "greater" and "lesser" to "similar" and "dissimilar," saying: "The Son is less than the Father, therefore he is dissimilar." <margin>B</margin> Nor will he speak any less ignorantly if he says: "He is less, therefore he is unequal, or not as great." [Left Column]

there is no place for "more" or "less" according to nature. For how could the Son be granted equality again if he were inherently lesser than the Father? Paul says: *Who, though he did not think it robbery to be equal to God,* <margin>Philippians 2</margin> *emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself.* Therefore, if the incarnation involves "humility" and "emptying," as it is said here, it is necessary that—when the incarnation is separated out by the intellect—he is found to be always equal to the Father, just as he was before the incarnation. From this, we can clearly perceive that humility and emptying. For if he were already lesser than the Father even before the humility of the incarnation, how would he be seen to have "descended," or what would the nature of his humiliation be? Certainly, this same Paul very openly called the Son equal to God, yet also declared him to be "lesser" because of the suffering of death. Since he cannot be both equal and lesser at the same time, let us ask in what way he is equal, and in what way he is lesser. Insofar as his nature is God, the Son is equal to the Father who begat him; but insofar as he was made man, and as a man was crucified and died, he is lesser.

[Heading]
### That the Son is equal to the Father, based on the proposed Gospel text: "Among those born of women there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist."
### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Matthew 11</margin> But how, asks Eunomius <note>Eunomius was a leading radical Arian who argued that the Son was "unlike" the Father in substance.</note>, will the Son be similar or equal to the Father, when he openly says in the Gospel that no one greater than John the Baptist has risen among those born of women, and then immediately adds: "but he who is less in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he"? For [Jesus] himself is "less" because of the time at which he was born of the holy Virgin. And he confesses that he will only reach greater things because of his excellent virtues when the kingdom of heaven arrives, as if he were to receive this as a reward for his administration of human salvation. How then can one who is of such a nature, and lesser than John, be equal or similar to God the Father? 

Those who explain it this way have perverted the meaning of Christ’s words. For why would he claim it as a great thing for himself to exceed John—he who dares to possess by nature all the dignities of God the Father? <margin>John 1</margin> *All things,* he says, *that the Father has are mine.* But the Father is perfect; therefore the Son is also perfect and stands in need of nothing. He who is such by nature, how shall he not be equal and similar to his Parent? Furthermore, if Christ is called "lesser" than John because of the span of time in which he lived among men, and it is added that no one "greater" than John has risen, this would also be understood as referring to the length of one's life—which is not true. <margin>Genesis 4</margin> For Adam (as Scripture testifies) lived nine hundred and fifty years, and almost all others born of women at that time lived nearly as long. Yet the Forerunner John, while still quite a young man, exchanged life for death. Therefore, he is not called "greater" among those born of women because of time, but because of the sublimity of his virtue, by which he reached the furthest limits that human nature can attain. Therefore, Christ is likewise not called "lesser" because of time. For it would be ridiculous to attribute the heights of virtue to the length of time.

<column-break/>

[Right Column]

It necessarily follows, therefore, that the comparison is being made in terms of virtue and holiness; and thus Christ would appear "lesser" than John in holiness—which is most absurd. Since this interpretation leads to an absurdity, it must be rejected entirely. 

But our opponents say: "We bring forward a true and simple explanation of the Savior’s words, not one scrutinized with great care. Christ is 'lesser' than John according to the length of time starting from his incarnation, but he will be 'greater' even than John in the kingdom of heaven, having reached the perfection of human virtue." Thus, "lesser" here would signify the person of the Lord. And when it is said that no one greater than John the Baptist has risen among those born of women, it signifies that John reached the perfection of human virtue. Nevertheless, Christ will exceed even that great man in that [future] time. 

What is absurd about this explanation? <note>Cyril is speaking sarcastically here, mimicking the opponent's tone before tearing their argument apart.</note> Scriptures are not to be explained so simply as you think, but with great diligence and care. First, it is entirely trivial to believe the Lord is called "lesser" than John merely because of the span of time since the Word was incarnate. For clearly, he who is called "greater in the kingdom of heaven" is meant to be more sublime in holiness. For how else could anyone understand "greater" here? If, therefore, the Savior will only appear "greater" than the Baptist in the time of the kingdom of heaven, he is currently either "lesser" or "equal." To say "lesser" is quite impious; but even to think him "equal" is impious. For we hear the Baptist saying: <margin>Matthew 3</margin> *I need to be baptized by you.* Now, the inferior is baptized and sanctified by the superior. <margin>John 1</margin> And he said to the Jews: *I baptize you with water; but one comes after me, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire; his winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather the wheat into his barns, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.* <margin>John 3</margin> How then was the Lord equal to or lesser than John according to these men? Or for what reason did John preach that he himself only baptized with water, while affirming that Christ was the giver of the Spirit? Do you not see that, as a servant, John does not even dare to touch the straps of his sandals? Do you not perceive that Christ is the Master of the threshing floor? This is what is signified when it is said, *And he will clear his threshing floor.* He also shows that Christ is the Judge, who will lead the just and good like wheat into the heavenly barns, but will hand over the unjust like chaff to the fire. 

If John were then "greater" or "equal" to Christ, why does he not also baptize in the Holy Spirit? <margin>John 20. Acts 16.</margin> But these men do not even listen to Isaiah, by whom it is written of Christ: <margin>Isaiah 43</margin> *I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember your sins.* And when he was born of the Virgin and lived among men, John pointed him out, saying: <margin>John 1</margin> *Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.* How then, according to these men, did Christ only have a "hope" of becoming greater than John in the kingdom of heaven? <margin>John 16</margin> Or how was John equal or greater than Christ—John, who desired to be baptized by Christ—while Christ himself was the one who could take away the sin of the world, and do so as the true Lord? For just as God, he forgives their sins.

...sends: which John could in no way do. Furthermore, **A** if Christ was then lesser than or equal to John, why did he himself not hear from the Father: *You are my Son, today I have begotten you*? Moreover, what great thing do they think they are attributing to Christ by contending that he will be "greater than John" in the future? For even the angels are greater than John by nature and by their love for God—yet Christ stands as far above the angels as the Creator exceeds his creatures. *For to which of the angels* (says Paul) <margin>Hebrews 1, Psalm 109</margin> *did he ever say: Sit at my right hand? Are they not all ministering spirits?* Therefore, how can he who exceeds even the angels, who is placed on the throne of God the Father, claim it as a "great thing" for himself that he will be "greater than John" in the kingdom of heaven? For he is always and simply greater than every creature, being equal to God the Father. 

Furthermore, the Baptist will be a lamp, but Christ is the Light. <margin>Note: original *lucerna* (lamp) vs. *lux* (light)</margin> How then shall the Light, whose nature it is to illuminate, **C** be equal to or lesser than the lamp which stands in need of light? And certainly the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears the bridegroom who has the bride, cannot be found equal to or greater than the bridegroom in dignity and honor. <margin>John 3</margin> In addition to this, John himself says of the Savior: *He who comes from above is above all*. Then, showing his own measure, he says, *He who is of the earth speaks earthly things*. But if, according to you <note>referring to the Arians</note>, John is greater than Christ outside the kingdom of heaven, you must understand that the Baptist "comes from above" and the Lord "speaks earthly things" and "is from the earth." This is utterly absurd; for the one is God by nature and above all, while the other is a creature and therefore from the earth. Therefore, Christ is not equal; rather, he exceeds John incomparably. How then can he expect an "excess of dignity" in the kingdom of heaven by hope alone? 

Furthermore, after the resurrection, **D** when the Savior was renewing the ancient grace of the Spirit within us, <margin>John 20, Acts 16</margin> he breathed on the disciples, saying: *Receive the Holy Spirit*. And the Holy Spirit himself is called the Spirit of Christ. And when they had passed through Asia and the region of Galatia (as it is written in the Acts), they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them. Let John, therefore, also renew the grace of the Spirit in us, if he is equal to Christ; and let the Spirit of God the Father also be called *his* Spirit. And if you wish, let him also say of the Spirit, *He shall receive of mine*. <margin>John 16</margin> But to even think all these things is impious. Therefore, he is not equal to Christ, nor will he ever be lesser; rather, Christ as a man is always lesser than God. In addition to this, the Evangelist John, showing the natural

dignity of Christ, and revealing the measure of John as a servant, says: *There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. <margin>John 1</margin> He came as a witness, to bear witness to the light, that all might believe through him. Or when did the servant and precursor ascend to equality with his natural Lord? 

From all these things it is clear that John was never greater than Christ, nor can it be said of Christ himself that he is "now" lesser than John but will be "greater" in the kingdom of heaven. However, since we have refuted the sense of our adversaries, let us now examine the true sense of the Gospel's words, so that by the application of the true exposition, the false one may be refuted again. To do this correctly, let us recall the whole matter from its source. 

When John, in prison, heard of the miracles of Christ, he sent two of his disciples to say to Christ: *Are you he who is to come, or do we look for another?* To this, Christ said: *Go and tell John what you have heard and seen,* and then he enumerated many miracles. I say to you, and more than a prophet. The blessed Baptist led a wondrous and unheard-of life, at which men marveled so much that he was rightly judged to be a great man. He bore witness to Christ; indeed, he pointed him out with his finger as he stood there, saying:
<margin>John 1</margin> Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. But the Lord, to whom he bore witness, seemed to oppose the observance of the Mosaic Law by introducing the evangelical <note>The "evangelical life" refers to the life of the Gospel (Evangelium), moving beyond the Old Testament rules.</note> life in its place—or rather, leading the figures and shadows toward the truth. The Jews complained about the Baptist, claiming that by his authority he favored one who would overturn the teachings of the Law, as they believed. What, then, did John do in response? He fought for the Law, lest he should seem to despise the Mosaic doctrine. He did this either to repel or to mitigate the Jews' suspicion of him: **A** not because he himself held this of great importance, but so that his testimony concerning Christ might become more credible **B** among them. Therefore, although many were then transgressing in many and various ways, he rebuked only Herod—who was the prince—so that by his own danger he might recall the Jews to his favor and become more credible to them. For because he suffered, as it were, for the Law, they became more ready to believe him; thus, by his death, he sought to benefit the rest. But when, through the prophetic spirit (with which he was filled from his mother’s womb), <margin>Luke 1</margin> he saw the naked sword already threatening him, he wished to confirm his disciples in the faith of Christ and to teach them openly, so they would know that Jesus was the one expected for the salvation of all. Therefore, in the divine **C** plan <note>original: "dispensatione." This refers to a strategic management of a situation for a higher purpose.</note>, he feigned ignorance, so that the disciples, being led by their own experiences, might believe more firmly. For as men, they attributed much to themselves, and did not believe their master as much as their own reasonings. Therefore, he showed himself to be ignorant of who was to come. But Jesus, when they arrived—since as true God he knew the whole matter—shone forth even more then than before with miracles. He did those things as part of the plan which the prophets wrote would happen when <margin>Isaiah 35</margin> Christ came. Therefore, when asked if he was the one to come, he did not immediately answer, nor did he say, "I am the one"; but by the magnitude and multitude of his miracles, he showed that he was. "Go, therefore," he said, <margin>Matthew 11</margin> "and tell John what you have heard and seen. You heard these things from the prophets, and now you have seen them **D** fulfilled through me." Thus, when they had departed, turning to the crowd, he said: "What did you go out to see?" and the rest that follows. Necessarily, Christ spoke afterward about John. For since the crowd saw John's disciples and heard them questioning—not what they themselves wanted, but what John seemed to want to say—Christ spoke so they would not be troubled concerning John or think him a fickle man because he had first said, "Behold the lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world," <margin>John 1</margin> and then seemed to doubt if he was the one to come. Therefore, lest they should judge him for this or otherwise as a fickle man, and profit less because of this disturbance, he said to them: "What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind?" You were amazed by the Baptist,
