he said, and for that reason, you made long journeys into the desert to see him. Why then do you now think him a man of a fickle mind, like a reed, and driven here and there by inconstancy for some slight reason? "But did you see a man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who are so adorned are in the houses of kings." Those who are clothed in soft things are likewise of a softer mind. But as for John, who always inhabited the wilderness, who by the strength of his soul subjected the flesh to reason—why should he be like a light reed? If therefore you admired John because of his very harsh life, which he led most constantly, you ought also to grant him a firmness of mind consistent with such a life. But if the desert, the most humble clothing, and the most lowly food seem to bring you nothing more toward constancy than soft clothing does, why did you leave these behind to seek the Baptist in the desert? Was it because you think him a prophet? "Truly I say to you, John is more than a prophet." For the prophets foretold that Christ would come, but could not see him; John, however, both preached that he would come and saw him. Thus, he first exalted John, and then brought forward the testimony of the Father as well. "For this is he," he said, <margin>Malachi 3</margin> "of whom it is written: Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you." And he added: "Amen I say to you, among those born of women there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist; yet he who is minor in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he." When he had said so many and such great things about John, and had affirmed him to be the greatest among those born of women because he had reached the summit of human virtue, he then places a greater good: he says that he who has already touched the kingdom of heaven and has been made a son of God, reborn through the Holy Spirit, is better and greater. He did this to show that John was wonderful because of his excellent virtues, but those who participate in the kingdom of heaven are even more wonderful than him. By this reasoning, he encouraged them to strive to seize it with great courage, which makes them even greater than John. For we say that the kingdom of heaven is the gift of the Spirit, according to that saying of Christ: <margin>John 14, Acts 17</margin> "The kingdom of heaven is within you." Therefore, he who is reborn through the Spirit is found to be greater than all those born of women. For the latter are still called children of the flesh, while the former are children of God, whom they call upon in prayer: <margin>Galatians 4</margin> "Abba, Father." Therefore, although John may be wonderful among those born of women according to human virtue, those who seem "lesser" than him in the kingdom of heaven—that is, those reborn through the Holy Spirit—are greater. Because they are not born of women, but are partakers of God, they are therefore called children of God, even if they seem like infants, the smallest in the perfection of virtue, because they are newly reborn. That this regeneration which happens through the Holy Spirit exceeds John and all those born of women by a great interval, we do not have to seek far for a witness, since John himself said to Jesus that <margin>Matthew 3</margin> he had need to be baptized by him. For although he was perfect in virtue, he nevertheless sought the grace of being born again through the Spirit, so that he might ascend to a greater degree, and no longer be merely one born of a woman, but be reshaped into divine nobility—which the Savior greatly affirms... From this, men who indulge their own whims and do not follow the guidance of right reason, but rather a brute and unrestrained appetite, are judged by the names of those animals whose innate and natural passions they follow. And this is indeed a frequent occurrence found in the scriptures. For instance, what is written by the Psalmist: <margin>Psalm 31 and 48</margin> *Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.* And again: *Man, when he was in honor, did not understand, but was compared to the beasts and brutes, and was made like unto them.* And elsewhere: <margin>Jeremiah 5</margin> *They became like raging horses after mares.* <note>original: "Equi furentes in equas facti sunt." This refers to a biblical metaphor for people following carnal lusts rather than spiritual reason.</note> The Savior made these things clearer to his disciples, saying: <margin>Matthew 10</margin> *Be wise as serpents and simple as doves.* And again: <margin>Luke 6</margin> *Be merciful, just as your Father in heaven is merciful.* 

If, therefore, those who have followed a lack of reason are made like beasts and brutes according to their behavior—and again, if the disciples, by imitating the wisdom of the serpent, the simplicity of the dove, and the mercy of the heavenly Father, are called "serpents," "doves," and even "gods" by their imitation—nothing prevents us from thinking that when we are said to be "one with the Lord," or with God the Father himself, we have not been made one with God <term>essentially: Sharing the same fundamental substance or being (Latin: *essentialiter*).</term> Rather, if a similarity in some action causes us to be called "serpents" or "doves" and so on, we will not be the same as God according to our substance simply because we are said to be "one with him." But just as he is one by nature with his own Word, so we too are brought back to a unity among ourselves through a joining of our will and through concord, when we do not disagree in any way, but are joined in unity by a single bond of charity.

Furthermore, our Savior and Lord is accustomed to set forth the good things that exist in him naturally and to exhort us to imitate them, so that he may reform us to the divine image in which we were made. <margin>Matthew 11</margin> Therefore, when he exhorts us to be mild, he says: *Learn from me, for I am humble and mild of heart.* Yet, if by imitating him we become mild, we will not therefore be similar to him in our nature, but we will be made like him only in gentleness, as far as is possible. 

Thus, when he says of us, *that they may be one, just as we are one,* he is exhorting us to follow a pattern. He does not say this because we could ever become one with God by nature, but so that, just as he is naturally one with the Father, we might be one through concord and consensus. By following the <term>natural identity: The state of being exactly the same in essence or substance (Latin: *naturalem identitatem*).</term> of the Father and the Son as a model, we might imitate it through a joining of our will, which makes us, as it were, one body and one soul. For so it is written of those <margin>Acts 4</margin> who believed: *That the heart and soul of the multitude of them was one.* For those qualities that belong to some beings by nature become, as it were, firm images for those who wish to conform their own will to them, such as: <margin>Matthew 10</margin> *Be like serpents; be like doves.* 

Therefore, he proposes to us the natural identity that he has with the Father—as an image, a likeness, and a model—so that by looking upon it, we might be united in our will. When, therefore, he says of us, *That they also may be one, just as we are one,* he is not saying that we should cast off our own nature and be changed into the nature of the Son, but rather that (as 

<column-break/>

->BOOK THREE 57<-

has been said) we might become that through our will which he is by nature with the Father. Wherefore, if anyone thinks that there will be a natural union between us and the Son of God, he errs greatly, imagining impossible things. For if he had wanted to say that we would be one with the Son by nature, he surely would have said, *That they may be one with me, just as I am with you.* But now he does not say it that way, but uses the plural: *that just as I and you are one, so they also may be one in us.* Thus he clearly teaches that we are not joined to God by nature—which is impossible—but that it is possible through faith and charity, when we strive to become one by a unity of wills, following the model of the natural unity of the Son and the Father, which exists in them by a unity of nature. 

Furthermore, when something is said to happen "in God," it does not signify a change of nature, but that it happens from him or through him. <margin>Psalm 43 and 17</margin> *In you,* says the Psalmist, *we shall toss our enemies with our horn.* And again: *In my God I shall leap over a wall.* For it is evident that he does not say he will leap over a wall or toss with a horn because he has naturally become "in God," but he shows that he will do these things in the name of God and by his power. When, therefore, he says *that they also may be one in us,* he does not say it because human nature is converted into the nature of God, but because in the name and power of the Father and the Son, they will have one will and one consensus. 

He added, *just as we are one,* so that he might propose his own natural unity with the Father to the believers as a model for the uniting of their wills. For adverbs of similarity, such as "just as," "as if," "as," and others of this kind, do not signify that the whole thing is the same as the other in its entirety, but they show a certain likeness. Therefore he added, *that they may be perfected into one,* so that this might be the sense of the whole text. For because the Son of God wished to confer a great, indeed an immense, grace upon the human race, he therefore sought to draw all people into a union with himself. For he was made in us because he, who has the Father in himself as his Word and his radiance, put on the human person. Just as therefore...

<margin>1 John 4</margin> because Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God. If, therefore, because of a confession of this kind we are in God and he in us—while the Son is not in the Father for that same reason (for he did not receive being in God as a gift in return for the merit of confession)—it is not ambiguous that men are one with God by grace and by a gift, and they receive this gift from God because of such faith and confession. However, the Word of God is naturally in the Father, not by gift or grace, and he likewise has the Father in himself. 

To understand this more clearly, let us suppose that someone now confesses through faith and charity that Jesus is the Son of God. He, therefore, according to the words of John, has received the Holy Spirit because of this confession; and since he has received God into himself, God is in him, and he is in God. Let us also suppose that afterward, at the suggestion of the devil, the man changes this opinion and denies that Jesus is the Son of God. He has therefore lost grace, and being deserted by the Holy Spirit, neither will he be in God, nor will God be in him. 

In this case, surely, just as he was a man before his confession, so too will he be a man during his confession and during his denial. We are not, therefore, naturally joined to God, nor are we the faithful "one" with him by nature; rather, just as grace and charity join us to him, so vice removes us from him. If, therefore, by trusting in charity because Jesus is the Son of God, we are in God—and by denying him we are alienated from him—while the Son is with God not by gift, nor because of such a confession, then surely he is not in the Father in the same way we are. 

Instead, he is in him naturally and unchangeably, as one born from him; but we are in him by grace and <term>participation: The theological idea that humans do not "become" God by nature, but "share in" his life and qualities through his generosity (Latin: *participatione*).</term>. Therefore, just as he is naturally both Son and God, so we are made sons of God and "gods" by grace and participation.

->### On the likeness of the Son to the Father: and that the Son is not of a changeable nature, nor subsisting from without, but begotten from the very substance of the Father, as a true son.<-

->### CHAPTER II.<-

<margin>A deceitful objection from the adversaries.</margin> "If the Son," they say, "is the unchanging image of the Father..."

<summary>Cyril argues that while humans become one with God through the "gift" of faith and can lose that connection through sin, the Son's unity with the Father is "natural" and unchangeable. This distinguishes the biological-essential Sonship of Christ from the adoptive sonship of believers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cyril’s refutation of Arianism. He is arguing that the Son’s divinity is not a "reward" for good behavior, but a natural, unchangeable quality. He transitions from discussing the Son's unity with the Father to his absolute immutability (unchangeability).</meta>

60 BOOK THREE.

[The Son] is with the Father, not by some effort or because he was changed into the likeness of the Father. For he is perfect from the perfect, and immutable from the immutable. For how could he not be perfect, who <note>Philippians 2:6</note> **did not consider it robbery to be equal to God**? <note>This famous phrase means Christ did not have to "steal" or "seize" equality with God; it belonged to him by nature.</note> Or how is he not immutable, for whom being one and the same with the Father is his very nature? Furthermore, <note>Matthew 7:17</note> **a tree is known by its fruit**; but the "fruit" of the Father is his Word—that is, his Son. Therefore, let them either show that the "tree" is also changeable, or if the tree is immutable (as they themselves believe), let them believe the Son is also immutable. This is especially true since there are many testimonies of Scripture by which the Son is demonstrated to be unchangeable. For when Philip said, <note>John 14:8-9</note> **"Show us the Father,"** and so on, Jesus responded: **"Have I been with you for so long, and yet you do not know me, Philip? He who sees me sees my Father also."** If, therefore, the knowledge of the Son is the knowledge of the Father, the Son must be exactly as the Father is. But the Father is immutable; therefore, the Son is immutable. And Paul says: <note>Hebrews 13:8</note> **Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.** And the Psalmist: <note>Psalm 101:26-28 in the Latin Vulgate numbering; Psalm 102 in modern Bibles.</note> **In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and all of them shall grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you shall change them, and they shall be changed: but you are the same yourself, and your years shall not fail.** And the Savior says of himself: <note>Malachi 3:6</note> **"See me, see me, for I am, and I do not change."** <note>Cyril attributes this quote from Malachi to "the Savior" directly, identifying the God of the Old Testament with Christ.</note> And Jeremiah: <note>Baruch 3:3 in some versions.</note> **"For you sit forever, and we perish forever."** For here the prophet indicated the stability and perfection of the divine nature, while he indicated the continuous change of created things when he said, "And we perish forever." If, therefore, Scripture recognizes change and destruction only in created things, and excludes the Son from these when it says, "But you are the same yourself," then the Son is certainly not of a changeable nature. For he who can be changed is not "the same." 

Furthermore, if he were not immutable by nature, but attained this <term>accidentally</term> <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that is not part of a thing's essential nature. For example, being "happy" is an accident of a human, but being "rational" is essential.</note> and was made like the Father later because of his virtues, he would have at one time been *dissimilar* to the Father. And how can he be a "Son" who was at one time of a dissimilar nature? Or how will blessedness, goodness, and such things be stable in him if these things happened to him by "accident"? For things that are accidental can also cease to exist. It is therefore impious to think the Son is changeable, of whom Scripture says: **But you are the same yourself,** and in whom all the dignities of the deity are shown to exist. Furthermore, that which can change cannot truly say of itself: **"I am the truth."** For that which is one way now, and another way later, is changed within itself. But the Son truly says of himself: <note>John 14:6</note> **"I am the truth."** Therefore he is not changeable, but like the Father and immutable. 

The heretics <note>The Arians, who argued that Jesus was a created being who "became" God as a reward for his obedience.</note> strive to show the Son is changeable so that, from this, he might appear to be a creature and dissimilar to the Father. They bring forward many things from the Scriptures to prove their madness, so that they may seduce simpler folk with the authority of the texts. Among other things, they cite that word of the Apostle: <note>Philippians 2:9-10</note> **"Therefore God has also exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow."** And that of the Psalmist: <note>Psalm 44:8 (Vulgate); Psalm 45:7 (English).</note> 

<column-break/>

"Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows." <note>original: "oleo exultationis præ participibus tuis"</note> Next, they cavil, saying that "therefore," "for this reason," and other words of this kind signify a *cause* for which he was exalted, and for which that name above every name was given to him, and for which he was anointed with the oil of gladness. "If therefore," they say, "he had these things for some cause, he was necessarily changed, and became such as he was not before these things were given to him. Furthermore, any dignity that is given can be taken away: but if someone is of such a condition that a dignity can be given to him or taken away, how will he be entirely like the immutable Father? And how will he be the true image of him who is always the same?" 

[Cyril responds:] If, according to you, the Son of God was exalted and anointed with the oil of gladness for some "cause," then if that cause had not existed, he would not be what he is. And thus he would not be God by nature, but by grace; nor a Son by nature, but by grace. His title would have been a reward given to him, so that he might be called both God and the Son of God. There would, therefore, be no difference between him and us; for it would also be permitted to us through faith and charity to attain similar things, since we too are called "gods" and "sons of God" by grace, and are anointed with the oil of gladness. 

But it is most absurd to think that the true Son of God—through whom the Father is truly "Father" because he is "God from God" <note>original: "deus ex deo"</note> just as a human is from a human—it is most absurd, I say, to think the Son of God is equal to us, we who are not truly sons and gods, but are so by grace because of the mercy of the Giver. Furthermore, the Apostle Paul says of him: <note>Philippians 2:6-7</note> **Who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.** And a little later: **"Therefore God exalted him, and gave him the name which is above every name."** It is written that the name was given to him, and he is said to have been exalted, at the time *when he was made man*. Was he, therefore, not of this kind before the incarnation? For if he was already like this, it is superfluous to say he received it afterward; but if he was not such, and did not have these things, he was surely changed when he received them. 

What, therefore, was he according to you before he received these things? If he received these things as a man when he was made man, then certainly he was always the Wisdom, Power, Truth, and Light from Light, Life, and Image of the Father, and always will be. For if he did not have these things before his humiliation <note>The "humiliation" refers to the Incarnation, where the Word became flesh.</note>, see, I pray, how the order of all things is overturned by the highest impiety. For the divine Scriptures preach that the incarnation of the Son of Man was done for the restoration of the whole human race. But if (as they say) the Son of God was exalted and made sublime *after* the incarnation—receiving something he did not have before—he would have been incarnated more for his own sake than for men. For according to you, he profited himself more than he profited men. Thus he would have been made man not so much for our salvation, but so that he himself might be exalted and attain the greatest name. How then do the prophets and apostles call him our Savior, if he profited himself more than us? Or how did he die for us, if God himself [repaid him] for that death...

<summary>Cyril argues that the Son is immutable and divine by nature, not by reward. He refutes the Arian claim that Christ was "exalted" as a prize for his human life, noting that this would imply Christ was not God before the incarnation and that he became man for his own benefit rather than for human salvation.</summary>

64 BOOK FOUR.

A | He brings forth all things from nothing: thus he cannot generate a son from himself: therefore the son will not be naturally similar to the father, since he was produced by him not from himself, but from outside himself. How then, O most ingenious men, is he written to be the "only-begotten" <note>The term "only-begotten" (unigenitus) is central to Cyril’s argument; he argues it implies a unique birth from the Father’s own essence, not a creation like the rest of the universe.</note> son, if even he was created from the outside just like a creature? Or how is he truly a son, who did not shine forth from the substance of the parent? For if it were possible for those things which are produced from nothing—that is, from the outside—to be naturally called "sons," the Word of God would not be the only-begotten son, since in this he would agree with all creatures. But if it is not possible, and only the son of God is the only-begotten, then he was not called from non-existence to existence like a creature: but just as a true son he proceeded from the father, and therefore he is like him. Furthermore, if all things were produced from nothing, and the son himself similarly, for what reason is he by nature B | Lord, while all other creatures are by nature servants? For either it is right that all things be naturally honored by the name of "Lord," or the son himself must also be called a servant along with all others, if he was produced from the outside from nothing similarly to the creatures. But that is never read in divine scripture: rather, the son is written to be Lord by nature, but creatures are by nature <margin>Psalm 118</margin> servants. **"Behold,"** it says, **"all things serve you."** And we read indeed that the son is to be adored and glorified together with the father, but that creatures are to adore and glorify. He was not, therefore, produced from the outside (like the rest), but is generated from the father as a son by nature: therefore he is naturally similar to the parent in all things. But those men seem to be ignorant, who boast with empty syllogisms and a great sound C | of words rather than with the truth: because that which truly "is," and which can truly generate from its own substance, is God. For he himself is "He who is": for all other things "are not" before they are produced. Therefore, he who truly is, whose proper name is "To Be," <margin>Exodus 3</margin> <note>original: "esse." This refers to the divine name revealed to Moses in the burning bush, interpreted here as God being the only source of true, independent existence.</note> he alone generates from his own substance. For other things (as for example, men) do not seem to generate from their own substance in this way, because they do not have this power from themselves, but are called to this by the divine will. For the divine law, which is the creator's will, makes it so that a man generates. This is clear, because not all things generate, but only those which he himself willed. Therefore, that which properly generates from itself is God: other things do it in imitation of him. How then is it not absurd to say that creatures, who imitate God in this, D | give birth to sons from themselves, but that the very Exemplar <term>Exemplar</term> <note>An "exemplar" is the original pattern or model. Cyril argues that if humans (the copies) can have children of the same nature, God (the original model) must be able to as well.</note> according to which they were created does not generate from himself, but produced his son from the outside? Since therefore that is absurd, the father truly generates the son from himself, and therefore the son is similar to him in all things, and the eternity and immutability of the father will also be naturally in the son.

CHAPTER IV.
IF no one, he says, is good but God, as the son himself testifies, how will he be like the father: he who <margin>Mark 10</margin> is not good by nature? especially since he most clearly excludes himself from natural and substantial goodness. For why, he said to the scribe, do you call me good? No one is good except God. Either they do not see how 

BOOK FOUR. 65

much danger follows from these words: or if they see it, they wish to play games in a matter where one should least of all play. For they wish the father alone to be naturally good, but the son not at all: how then will he be the son, if he is not naturally like the father? But in this, they say, we call him "similar," because the father willed to make him such as the father himself is. Just as when a builder builds a house, the house is a likeness and image of the pattern that is in the builder's mind: and yet on account of the material, the built house is one thing, and that which is in the builder's mind is another, and he is far different from the builder himself. So, they say, as the house is the image and likeness of the mind, so also the son is of the father: but he is not an image and likeness according to nature and substance, as you preach. All these things are ridiculous, or rather worthy of tears. For who would not groan, considering such great impiety of men? For if he is unlike the father according to essence, but similar according to a phantom and an image of the mind, it will be necessary first that he be composed of the most diverse and contrary things: I say from the "similar" and the "dissimilar," and thus he will not be entirely Light, nor entirely Truth, nor entirely the image of the father. Then, in addition to this, it is necessary that this impiety pass over to the father himself. For he himself will necessarily be composed of substance and mind, or that image which he has in his mind: since according to those men, the son is indeed substantially dissimilar to the father, but similar according to that mental pattern. How then will the father be the principle of all things, if he is not simple, but composite? For the "First" simply can by no means be composite, because nothing can be understood prior to him from which he might be composed, nor is there any diversity in the "First" simply. But composite things have a gathering of diverse simple parts, which are necessarily understood to exist before them. Since therefore all these things are impious and impossible, the son will necessarily be similar to the father according to essence. For if he is not substantially similar, he will not be perfectly similar: how then did he not consider it robbery to be equal to God? <note>A reference to Philippians 2:6. Cyril argues that Christ could only claim equality with God if he shared the same divine nature.</note> For he who is equal to God is also substantially similar.

THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE SAME.
That we are formed in the image of God through participation.
CHAPTER I.
MAN could not be in the image of the <margin>Phil. 2.</margin> creator unless he participated in the Holy Spirit. For if anyone (Paul says) does not have the spirit of Christ, he is not of Christ. But if we could be in the image of God without the participation of the spirit, we would certainly all be Christ’s, even if we did not participate in the Holy Spirit. John also says: He who keeps <margin>John 14.</margin> <margin>Rom. 8.</margin> his commandments remains in him, and he in him. And we know that he remains in us, from the spirit which he gave us. If therefore those keeping the commandments participate in the Holy Spirit, by which participation they are formed in the image of the creator: it is clear that man cannot be made like God, except in a certain way by participating in him...

68 BOOK FOUR

Concerning the essential similarity of the Father and the Son, based on the proposed Gospel text: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself."

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>John 5</margin> "But how," they <note>The "they" refers to the Arian heretics, who used the language of "giving" and "receiving" in the Bible to argue that the Son was a created being and therefore lesser than the Father.</note> ask, "will the Son be essentially similar to the Father? Or how will He not be posterior <note>In this context, "posterior" means coming after in time or being lower in rank.</note> to the one who, as the Giver, bestows many things upon Him? For as it says, 'the Father has life in Himself, so also He has given to the Son to have life in Himself.'"

There is nothing, oh you <note>Cyril is addressing his opponents directly here.</note>, that prevents the Father from being said to give something to the Son, and the Son to receive from the Father, without the Father being "prior" to the Son. For it is not as if the Son did not previously exist, possessing nothing from the Father, and only then received something from Him. Rather, because He is naturally born of the Father, He naturally possesses all things that belong to the Father's nature by the very fact of His birth. 

It is just as if someone were to say that the light which comes forth from the sun "receives" something from the sun for this reason: because everything that is in the light, and the light itself, originates from the sun. Yet, even so, the sun is not seen to exist before the light <note>Cyril uses this classic analogy to show that while the sun "causes" the light, they both exist at the exact same moment; you cannot have a sun that does not shine.</note>.

<summary>Cyril refutes the Arian claim that the Son is inferior to the Father because He "receives" life from Him, using the analogy of the sun and its light to prove co-eternity.</summary>

will be in you? He who understands it in this way is guilty of great impiety. How will the giver of incorruption be corruptible? Or how will He be seen as God by nature? Or how will He not be wise, about whom it is written,
<margin>1 Cor. 1</margin> "Because He is the power and wisdom of God"? It is certainly a wonder how you dare to say that the wisdom of God is unwise. Therefore, even if you say that the Father alone possesses something by nature, the Son is not thereby deprived of that same thing by nature. For the Father alone is said to possess these things insofar as He receives them from no one; but the Son, proceeding from Him, naturally attains all things that are naturally in the Father. For Truth does not lie about Himself, saying:

Furthermore, if the Son is the unchangeable character <note>original: "character" — here used in the theological sense of an "exact imprint" or "perfect image," referencing Hebrews 1:3.</note> of the Father’s substance, how will He not be life by nature, since the Father possesses it? For He would be a distorted and false image rather than a true one. In addition to this, if anyone sees the Son, he sees the Father also; since the Father is life essentially, the Son will also be life essentially. For if He were life not essentially, but by participation in life, then because he who sees the Son sees the Father, the Father too would be life by participation; which is an impious thing to say. It follows that things which are necessarily different cannot have the same operation <note>original: "operationem" — referring to "energy" or "activity." Cyril argues that if two beings perform the exact same divine act, they must share the same nature.</note>. For a natural operation is necessarily different in different natures. No one would attribute the same operation to water and fire. If, therefore, the Father is life by nature, but the Son is not—as the heretics claim—how is the operation of the Father and the Son the same? Truth Himself certainly says: 
<margin>John 5</margin> "As the Father gives life to whom He will, so also the Son gives life to whom He will." For He does not say the Father gives life in one way and the Son in another, but "just as the Father, so also the Son," always attributing the same operation to Himself and the Father. Therefore, the Son is not unlike the Begetter, but just as the Father is life by nature, so also is the Son. Furthermore, if they believe John spoke truly, they must all confess that the Father works through the Son. Now, it is also a single operation of the Father to give life to whom He wills; therefore, He will give them life through the Son. The Son, therefore, will also be life according to nature, otherwise nothing could be given life through Him. In addition, if the Son is the mediator between God and men because He joined the extremes in Himself alone, it is necessary that just as He truly took on humanity and is truly man, so also He is true God according to nature. And since the true God is essentially life, He Himself will also be, just as the Father is, essentially life. Add to this that the divine Scriptures call the Son "Truth"; how then will He be the Truth if He speaks falsely, saying: 
<margin>John 14</margin> "I am the way, the truth, and the life"? For he who is not essentially life is not life at all. But since Truth cannot lie—for it is impious to say so—the Son will be life substantially, not by participation. For how is He not essentially life, whose knowledge gives life to those who know Him, just as the knowledge of the Father does? 
<margin>John 17</margin> "This," He says, "is eternal life: that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent." But many, because they are led by human ways of thinking (for they cannot be described otherwise, and the things themselves are ineffable <note>original: "ineffabiles" — things that cannot be expressed in words.</note> in their own right), are unwilling to understand correctly while following the words, and so they fall into great impiety. 72 [centered] BOOK FIVE

... [conside]red, how will He not be like one of the creatures? <note>The text begins mid-word, likely "consideratur." Cyril is finishing a point about why the Son cannot be classified as a created being without losing His divine status.</note> But perhaps you think you are bestowing a certain special honor upon the Son by calling Him a creature, "but not like one of the creatures." <note>original: "non sicut una creaturarum" — This was a specific phrase used by Arians to argue that Jesus was a special, first-born creation of God, distinct from the rest of the world but still not God by nature.</note> Yet this is not truly honoring the Son. For if He were created like other creatures, it would matter little if He were of a different nature. For indeed, the same could be said of all creatures, of which one naturally surpasses another. 

For of individual species you might rightly say, "it is a creature, but not like one of the creatures." As for example: the Sun is a creature, but not like one of the creatures; for no other creature except the sun is of this kind. Man also is a creature, but not like one of the creatures; for no other species besides man is "man." 

B [marginal marker] Therefore, any species of creatures is a creature, but not like one of the creatures. For only this one thing is common to all creatures: that they were produced from nothing. But in form and nature, individual species differ among themselves.

<summary>Cyril refutes the Arian claim that the Son is a "unique creature," arguing that every creature (like the sun or humanity) is unique in its own way, and therefore "uniqueness" does not prove divinity.</summary>

On the previous page, Cyril argued that every species is "unique" in its own way, so being a "unique creature" does not make the Son divine. Here, he addresses the Arian idea that the Son was created as a necessary "buffer" or "instrument" because the world could not handle the direct power of the Father.</meta>

# ->74 THE TREASURY OF THE HOLY CYRIL<-

...[The Fi]lious <note>The text begins mid-word: "Filius."</note> was able to do this; even if he were a creature, every creature would then be able to do it. Or, if other things cannot do it because they are created, then he himself would not be able to do it either, since according to you, he is also created. But if you think it is unbecoming for God’s providence to descend even to the smallest things, I ask you to blush <margin>Matthew 10</margin> a little when you hear the words of Christ: *Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And yet not one of them falls to the ground without your Father who is in heaven.* <margin>Matthew 6</margin> And again: *Look at the birds of the air, that they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them.* And again: *If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you?* 

Now, what can be thought of as more lowly than grass and sparrows, for which He provides out of His own goodness? Or how can He not be the Creator of all things for which He deigns to provide? You surely attempt to brand God with the vice of pride when you say it is not becoming for Him to be the creator of the smallest things. Yet He Himself is the creator of all things, even the smallest, and He provides for all, and through His mercy, He offers Himself to be shared. 

Furthermore, if the Son were created (as you say) because creatures could not bear the power of the Father, then since he himself would be a creature, he also would not be capable of containing the full power of the Father. It would then be necessary for you to invent another "medium" <note>original: "medium" — a go-between or buffer</note> that could receive the entire operation of the Father. Then another, and another, which leads at once to infinity and to the impossible, and it overturns the entire creation of things.

<margin>Against the objections of the heretics by which they try to teach that although the Son is a creature, he is nevertheless the Creator, which is not a property belonging to creatures.</margin>

### CHAPTER III.

**C**reature, they say, is the Son, and yet he creates, because he learned it from God as if from a master and craftsman, so that he might be a servant for His works. 

If something is not implanted by nature, but is acquired in some way by happenstance, that thing can also be lost at some point. Therefore, according to your view, the Son would be able to lose the power of creating, and thus he would be stripped of the very dignity by which he is a creator, if he "unlearned" what he had learned. For he who has attained through teaching what he did not know before, surely he will also be able to unlearn it through forgetfulness. 

Furthermore, it is not the job of "art" <note>original: "artis" — here meaning a technical skill or craft</note> to produce creatures out of nothing; rather, that is the work of an ineffable and creative power. For the role of art is merely to change those things that already exist through an underlying material. But the power of creating produces the very substance of things from nothing into being. If, therefore, the Son were made a creator by art and teaching, what would they say if someone applied the same logic to the Father? 

Certainly, nothing else remains for them but to say that the Father is creator by nature, while the Son is creator by teaching. It follows, then, that it is possible to learn the power of God by which He creates through natural means, and to become through teaching what He is by nature. There would then be no difference between the Son and the creatures except for a certain "superfluous" teaching; and so, the Son would surpass us not by the excellence of his nature, but by teaching alone. If we possessed that teaching, we would all be creators. Since these ideas are utterly foolish, it remains that the power of creating in the Son is not a taught skill, but a natural power. 

In addition to this, wisdom is one thing, and a "wise person" is another. For Wisdom is that by which one is wise; but a wise person is one who possesses

# ->THE TREASURY OF THE HOLY CYRIL 75<-

A wisdom. How, then, could the Son become wise through teaching, when he is Wisdom itself? For if he were in need of teaching, he was not Wisdom itself; and if he learned wisdom, he could also unlearn it through forgetfulness. But he who is always Wisdom, as the Scriptures proclaim, did not learn it. 

Furthermore, they brand the Father with the vice of envy by speaking this way: for He could have taught the art of creating to many, yet He did not. For what was stopping Him—if creation is given through teaching—from making many creators, just as there are many angels and archangels? But now the Son alone, to the exclusion of all creatures, creates together with the Father in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, he creates not through teaching, but through a natural power. Nor did the Father teach him, but from Himself He begot the Son, who is **consubstantial** <note>original: "consubstantialem" — of the same essence or substance</note> with Him, through whom He creates all things. 

B Add to this: if the Father produced the Son for the purpose of creating, as you preach, then the Father's own work of creation would have ceased with the Son. How then does the Savior say: *My Father works even until now, and I work?* <margin>John 5</margin> If the Father is working even now, then according to your view, the Son was created in vain. <margin>Ibid.</margin> These are most absurd claims. Therefore, the Son was not "made" to produce creatures, but was born of the Father, and like a Son he works all things with the Father, being God by nature and Creator by nature. 

Furthermore, God works with total finality and by His will alone; what need is there for a medium? Does the Son not seem superfluous in your view? But if it is found to be impious even to think this, then the Son himself is the subsisting and living Will of the Father, through whom He produced all things from nothing. 

But the things that follow are much more inconvenient and absurd. For if it <margin>Genesis 1</margin> C happened that God produced us and the rest of creatures through the Son, but produced the Son himself (as the heretics say) from nothing, then he himself was made for our sake, not we for his. <margin>Genesis 15, Exodus 3, Zechariah 1, Habakkuk 2</margin> And thus, we would be a more excellent creature than he is; while he would merely be an instrument for creating the rest of the creatures. Why then should he not also give thanks to us, he who exists for our sake? He would also be our glory in the same way a woman is to a man. For Paul says: *The woman is the glory of the man.* <margin>1 Corinthians 11</margin> For the man was not created for the woman, but the woman for the man. For if the Son was made for us, and not we for the Son, we would be much more excellent than he; which is most absurd. Therefore, he is not a creature, nor was he born for our sake, but since he is God by nature, so that He is also the Father <note>The Latin "ut etiam pater sit" likely refers to the Son possessing the same nature as the Father, or perhaps a typo for "as the Father is."</note>, he produced us from nothing into being together with the Father and the Spirit. 

D Furthermore, if the Son were made for our sake, as they dare to say, we would be the first in God’s priority. For God would seem to have intended us first, and then the Son for our sake. Additionally, God would be seen as driven by necessity: since He could not create us otherwise, He produced the Son—whom, according to them, He would not have produced unless He wanted to create us. Therefore, once we were created, the Son would seem to be superfluous, <margin>John 10</margin> since the Father no longer needs him once the creatures have been produced. 

Finally, it would mean that like a frail and weak man, God created us through the Son, about whom He first deliberated; and He produced the Son first, whom He considered last, <margin>Proverbs 8, Proverbs 5</margin> merely as an instrument. Why then should He call him "Son" and "Heir," while we are called...

...creature, he himself could not have borne <note>original: *ferre potuisset*</note> the hand of the Creator. For if the divine nature is so immense and unbearable <margin>A logical contradiction</margin> that it cannot be sustained by a created nature, and the Son—as you claim—is a creature, how did he withstand the force of God working within him? He would have needed another mediator for himself, and that one yet another, and so on to infinity. 

But if you say that he was able to bear God even though he is a creature, then there was no need for him to be created as a "middle-man" for the sake of the others; for if one creature could withstand God, then the rest could have done so as well. Thus, your argument that the Son was created because of our weakness is proven to be a foolish invention.

<margin>Assertio 16</margin>
### THAT THE SON IS NOT CALLED "ONLY-BEGOTTEN" BECAUSE HE ALONE WAS CREATED BY THE FATHER ALONE.

Since they <note>The Arians, who argued that the Son was a subordinate being.</note> are trapped by these truths, they turn to another sophistry to support their error. They say: "The Son is called 'Only-begotten' <term>Only-begotten (Unigenitus)<gloss>In Greek, *monogenēs*; the Arians argued this meant 'the only one created directly by God'.</gloss></term> because he alone was created and produced by the Father alone; but all other things were created by the Father through the Son as an instrument." 

Let us see how much poison this idea contains. If you say he is "Only-begotten" because he alone was made by the Father, you are saying that "Only-begotten" and "Only-created" mean the same thing. But the Holy Scripture knows how to distinguish between "begotten" <note>original: *genitum*</note> and "made" <note>original: *factum*</note>. Furthermore, if he is the "Only-begotten" simply because of the *manner* of his creation—being made by one person rather than through another—then the name refers to a method of manufacturing rather than a relationship of nature. 

<margin>John 1</margin>
But the Evangelist John says: *We saw his glory, the glory as of the Only-begotten of the Father.* He does not say "the glory of the only-one-made-by-the-Father," but points to the unique excellence of his nature. If he were a creature, even one made "alone," his glory would still be that of a slave, not of a Son. For what does it matter if a servant is made by the master's own hand or through a steward? He is no less a slave because of the way he was manufactured.

<summary>Cyril concludes that the Son cannot be a "buffer" between God and creation, as this leads to an infinite regress of mediators. He begins a new argument (Assertio 16) refuting the Arian claim that "Only-begotten" merely means "the only being created directly by the Father."</summary>

<margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> Wherefore Paul also writes: "No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ." If, therefore, Christ has been laid as the foundation, it is necessary that the things built upon it be of the same nature as the foundation (for in this way a coherent structure will be built into a holy temple). It is clear that he was not "founded" <note>original: *fundata est*. Cyril is arguing that the term 'founded' in Proverbs 8:23 refers to Christ’s role as the basis of human salvation.</note> as the Word—that is, that <term>Wisdom<note>A common title for Christ in the early Church, derived from the Book of Proverbs.</note></term> became the foundation—because no creature can naturally be built together with a foundation of that kind <note>i.e., a purely divine foundation</note>. Therefore, Wisdom was made a foundation as a man in all things, sin alone excepted, and in this man the faithful are built up because of the identity of nature. And just as <margin>John 15</margin> elsewhere he calls himself the vine and us the branches of that vine, so in this place he says he is the foundation to reveal his natural connection with those who are to be built upon him. For we are built into a new creature, so that we may be made a temple for the Spirit dwelling in us. 

->B<-

But it will not be inconvenient to refute the false opinions of the heretics even with examples. For perhaps, out of shame, they will either be converted or at least attack the lesser ones with less force. That which is "founded"—that is, which serves the use of a foundation—certainly did not first begin to exist at the moment it was laid as a foundation. For stones (for example) buried in the earth are made into a foundation; yet they did not begin to be stones when they were founded. Rather, since they were stones even before, they were afterwards made a foundation, and did not lose their prior nature. 

<margin>John 1. Daniel 2.</margin> Thus, therefore, you will piously understand that the Wisdom of God was made a foundation: for he was in the beginning with God, and the Word was God, as it is written. 

->C<-

When, however, like a "stone cut without hands from a mountain" <note>original: *lapis aliquis absq; manibus de monte demissus*. This is a reference to Daniel 2:34, traditionally interpreted by Christians as the Virgin Birth of Christ.</note>—that is, proceeding from the substance of the Father—he was buried in our flesh as if in the earth, then he says he was "founded," as if saying: "I am the true Son of God, but I have been made man, so that I may become the beginning and the foundation for those built up through faith, and that I may join them to myself because of the shared nature of the flesh."

<margin>The quibbling of the heretics.</margin> "But how," they say, "can the incarnation of the Word be understood through this text? For <margin>Proverbs 8</margin> Wisdom itself cries out that she was 'founded before the ages, before the earth was founded, before the mountains were established,' whereas the incarnation took place in the last times." The response seems easy to any of us, yet we are forced to speak at greater length and repeat many things often to shut the mouths of the heretics. 

->D<-

No one will deny, therefore, that the incarnation of the Word took place in the last times. But God, who knows all future things, also eternally founded His Son—insofar as His own knowledge is concerned. That is, He established him to be that future foundation, so that we, built up in him, might rise again from corruption into <term>incorruption<note>The state of being no longer subject to decay or death.</note></term>. For He knew that we would be mortal because of sin, and therefore in His mercy He established before the ages that His Word should become man, the "beginning of ways," and the foundation, and that he should renew man in himself, having been made the firstborn among many brothers <margin>Romans 8. 2 Timothy 1.</margin> and the source of the resurrection. This is what Paul shows to Timothy: "Take your part in suffering for the gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with

->A<-

his holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages of time; but has now been manifested through the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ, who indeed destroyed death, but brought life and incorruption to light." If, therefore, before the age and before we were made—namely, by the grace of God who foreknows all things—we were called in Christ Jesus, it is clear that in this way, even before the ages (insofar as it pertains to the foreknowledge and, so to speak, the deliberation of God), our Lord Jesus Christ was "founded." 

<margin>Ephesians 1</margin> Paul also, writing to the Ephesians, says: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ; just as He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in His sight in love, He predestined us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ." If, therefore, before we were created, we were chosen for adoption through Jesus Christ and are blessed with a spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, why should we doubt that, in a similar way, it is said by Wisdom regarding the foreknowledge of God: "Before the ages he founded me"? The Lord also showed this same thing, saying: <margin>Matthew 25</margin> "Come, you blessed of my Father, and possess the kingdom which was prepared for you before the beginning of the world." 

If, however, before the beginning of the world the kingdom was prepared for those not yet made, and prepared in Christ, he does not speak irrationally <margin>Proverbs 8</margin> concerning himself: "Before the ages he founded me, before the mountains were established, before the springs of water broke forth"—all of which signify the production of creatures from nothing into being. 

<margin>John 14</margin> Truly the cause, so to speak, why we were foreknown in Christ and called to adoption out of the love of God the Father, is this: God foresaw that man would sin and fall into death; He also foresaw what would be beneficial for his race, and how he might be renewed and return to immortality. Therefore, He placed the roots of this hope for us in His Son, through whom He called us to adoption and fortified us—though not yet made—with every spiritual blessing. <margin>John 10</margin> This was done so that when we fell into death through transgression, we might rise again to life from that ancient root, and as those already blessed, we could not lie prostrate forever. 

Christ, therefore, is "pre-founded" before us, and in him we are all built up; and this happened before the beginning of the world in the foreknowledge of God. Thus, when in the divine order the blessing preceded the curse, the promise of life preceded the condemnation to death, and the freedom of adoption preceded the slavery to the devil, human nature—having overcome the evils that happened in the meantime—could return through the grace of Christ (who founded it with good things in the midst of good things) to its original dignity, and become such as God, out of love, determined it should be through His Son. 

We will understand how the Wisdom of God was "founded" before the ages by the Father's counsel through this comparison: A wise architect, for example, about to build a royal palace, likely considers whether the structure of the palace might suffer anything as time goes on. <margin>The quibbling of the heretics.</margin> For this reason, he lays a most firm foundation and constructs the strongest roots for the works, so that if the upper parts should suffer anything...

Therefore, in regards to the foreknowledge, the counsel, and the purpose of the Father and the entire <term>Godhead<note>original: "deitatis". Refers to the divine nature or essence of the Trinity.</note></term>, Christ was founded before the ages and born of the Virgin in the fullness of time. In him we have been restored, we who possessed that foundation of our salvation even before the beginning of the world.

->End of the fifth book of Cyril’s *Thesaurus*.<-

*Concerning the eternity of the Son, and how he emanates inseparably from the substance of the Father.*

### CHAPTER I.

**B**UT how (ask the <term>Arians<note>Followers of Arius, who argued that Jesus was a created being and not of the same eternal substance as God the Father. This was the primary theological conflict of the 4th century.</note></term>) can the Son be eternal, or how could he have emanated inseparably from the Father? For whatever comes forth from something is a part of the <term>substance<note>original: "substantia". In this context, it refers to the essential nature or "stuff" of God.</note></term> of that from which it proceeds; but what has been once separated and divided cannot be the whole. What then do you say of the sun, which emits its light through this brilliance <note>original: "splendore". Cyril is beginning a common patristic analogy: just as light cannot be separated from the sun, the Son cannot be separated from the Father.</note>?

<meta>This page continues Cyril’s refutation of Arianism, specifically addressing the claim that the Son was created for the sake of humanity, similar to how the sun was made to provide light. Cyril argues that the Son is co-eternal and shares the same divine essence as the Father.</meta>

If we were the cause [of his existence], according to your view, so that he might be brought forth—just as the heavens were made for the sake of generating things that can be born, the sun to illuminate dark places, and the earth to sustain animals—then there would be nothing great in the Son that is not also in <term>creatures<note>original: "creaturis". In this theological context, a "creature" refers to anything that has been created by God, rather than being part of the eternal Godhead itself.</note></term>. For he would also be a servant just like a creature; indeed, other creatures would seem to be of greater dignity, since he was brought forth for their sake. You see what impious conclusions follow from the false opinion of the heretics. Yet they confess that the innate wisdom and power of God is not created. Therefore, when they hear that the Son is uncreated and <term>co-eternal<note>Existing together eternally, without beginning or end.</note></term> with the Father, they should not think of two uncreated beings. For we believe that the Son himself is that very wisdom and power of God, co-eternal with the Father, who <margin>John 1</margin> made all things and who became flesh for our sake, as John says. Furthermore, why does the Father perform all things through the Son? Why is he numbered with the Father in baptism if he is a creature and not the Creator? What need was there for a creature for our sanctification? Or why do we invoke him as our protector, since we flee to no creature as we do to him? For we flee to him alone as to the co-eternal Son of the Father. Why also is he believed in, if he is not truly God just as the Father is? Or why is he called the "Creator of all" by the heretics themselves, unless he is Creator in the same way as the Father? <margin>John 16</margin> "All things that the Father has," he says, "are mine." Now, the power of creating is in the Father; therefore, the same power is also in the Son. Similarly, to save, to sanctify, and all things which befit God are in the Son just as they are in the Father. Therefore, he is true God, no differently than the Father is; he is not "made" (as the heretics imagine) but is <term>properly flowing forth from the substance of the Father<note>original: "ex patris substantia proprie profluens". This emphasizes that the Son’s existence is an eternal emanation of the Father’s own being, not a separate act of creation.</note></term>.

*Concerning the same subject: namely, that the Son is not a creature.*
### CHAPTER 11.

IF every creature is ignorant of the Father, but only the Son knows him (<margin>Matthew 11</margin> for he says, "no one knows the Father except the Son"), then the Son is certainly not a creature. Furthermore, none of the creatures is God; but the Son is God by nature, therefore he is not a creature. For if the Son were not God by nature, the human race would now be in a more miserable state than before: because while humanity believes itself to be liberated from the slavery of false gods, it would fall into the same impiety by serving a God who is not God by nature. In addition to this, every created thing is of an entirely different nature than the uncreated, nor can that which is created <margin>Isaiah 42</margin> enjoy the glory of the uncreated equally. For he says, "I will not give my glory to another." But the Son comes in the glory of the Father and possesses it equally; therefore, he is not a creature. It follows that the Scriptures affirm the Son to be the true God, and we all now <margin>Psalm 80</margin> believe this. But that which is created is "recent," and it is not lawful to believe in a "recent" God <note>A "recent" or "new" God would be a secondary deity created in time, which contradicts the Jewish and Christian doctrine of one eternal God.</note>. Therefore, the Son is uncreated and the true God. For the created is far different from the uncreated. And just as we are commanded to adore the uncreated, so we are forbidden by Scripture from the adoration of the created. But we are commanded to adore the Son: therefore the Son is not something other than God, nor a creature, but the true God and uncreated. It follows that no creature can bestow freedom, since it is itself a servant. But the Son has set us free: therefore he is not a servant,

<column-break/>

**THE TREASURES OF SAINT CYRIL 91**

but Lord and God according to nature. For all creatures follow the nature given to them by God, and thus they serve God. But God himself exceeds every necessity of this kind of nature, and therefore he does not serve, but rules. For he himself imposed nature upon each species as a law. But the Son is free, and Lord by nature: therefore he is not a creature. Add to this that no creature is naturally similar to God the Father; but the Son is so naturally similar that he who sees him sees the Father. Therefore, he is uncreated, just as the Father is. For the Son is called the Lord and King of Glory. But creatures serve the divine glory. Add to this that all things which were produced from nothing can also, if the Creator wills it, be reduced to nothing: which is a wicked thing to say about the Son. Therefore, he was not produced from nothing like a creature, <margin>Hebrews</margin> but was begotten of the Father as a true Son. Furthermore, every rational creature can err; but the Son can in no way err. In addition, no creature will ever be able to produce <term>substance<note>original: "substantiam". Here meaning the fundamental matter or existence of a thing.</note></term> from nothing; for that cannot belong to a finite power. But the Son is the Creator of all: how then can he be a creature? It follows that all created things, insofar as they are created, agree among themselves and have no difference in this regard; therefore, if the Son were also a creature, he would necessarily agree in this with other creatures. But he agrees with the others in nothing: how then is he not the true God? Furthermore, every creature was made in time, but no time preceded the generation of the Son, nor any space, nor any duration: therefore he was not made, but begotten. For if time, or some created duration, had preceded the generation of the Son, he himself would not be the Creator of all; and if the space or duration which preceded the generation of the Son were uncreated, there would be something uncreated besides God, which is a wicked thing to say. If therefore neither time, nor space, nor any duration existed before the Son, how can the Father be said to have existed before the Son, when they cannot find by what [measure] he preceded him? It follows that the Scriptures call rational creatures "gods" not by nature, but by participation and grace; but they name the Son "God" not by participation and grace, but by nature. For adoration is owed only to God by nature, yet we are commanded to adore the Son: therefore he is something other than a creature. Finally, they [the Arians] concede that the Son is the Creator, yet they also concede that he is created; wherefore, if the Creator is created, and the Father is also the Creator, why do they not say that he [the Father] also was produced from nothing? Because, clearly, it is impossible for the Creator of all nature to be created by another. How then do they think the Son is both the Creator of all and created? Can anyone of sound mind devise such a thing—to create that which is created, and to produce from nothing that which is produced from nothing? I pray they would more diligently weigh what they say. For the chief property of the true God is that he can produce substances from nothing. They do not deny that the Son can do this; how then is he not the true God, but a creature?

just as he is <term>consubstantial<note>original: "consubstantialis". Meaning "of the same essence" or "of the same nature." This is the core term used to describe the relationship between the Father and the Son in the Trinity.</note></term>, so he is the Father’s true Word. Furthermore, the names of substances signify the substances themselves, especially those names which are primary and proper to them; yet we see a great difference within them. For some have a universal meaning: these signify more general things that apply to individuals. For example: the word "man," simply and absolutely, signifies the human race itself, which is the very essence of being human. But "Paul," "Peter," and "James," and other such names, divide that universal meaning of "man" into individuals. Yet this difference of individuals, noted by their specific names, does not mean that the nature of these individuals is one thing in one person and something else in another. Therefore, the Father is Father, and the Son is the Word; yet a diversity of nature is not introduced because of this. They are distinguished by nothing other than the diversity of their relationship, which is signified by different names. Moreover, the different relations of consubstantial beings, and the different names of those relations, cannot (as we have shown by example) destroy their natural union. Wherefore it is necessary that the Son be of the same substance as the Father, even though the former is always only the Father, and the latter is always only the Son and the Word. For since the essence of the Father is most simple, and his Word proceeds from him, nothing else can be understood to exist between the generation of the Word and the Father that could prevent his Word from being of the same nature as the one whose Word he is. 

<margin>The sophistry of the adversaries.</margin>
But in the Gospel, they say, we know the Son says to the Father: *Father, glorify your Son*; and the Father responded to him, *I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again*. How, then, will the Son be the true Word of the Father when the Father speaks to him? For speech cannot happen without a word. Either the Father speaks to the Son through the Son himself (if he is the true Word), or, if this is absurd, there must be another internal and natural word which the Father used to speak to the Son. 

It is no small impiety if anyone believes the divine Word is emitted in a human fashion through lips, throat, and tongue, striking the ears of listeners. Certainly, such a fiction does not suit an incorporeal nature. Nor was that voice properly and naturally the Father’s; rather, it was a certain sound produced to signify how great the Son’s dignity is in the eyes of the Father. For not only did the Lord hear it, but all the disciples did as well. That the voice was made by a physical <term>vibration<note>original: "collisione". ...unless perhaps they say that the Father himself is ignorant and finds things out by thinking? Here used in the sense of a "stamp" or "exact imprint," referring to the Son as the perfect representation of the Father's essence.</note></term> should not be the same. "Are you so unlearned," they say, "as to contend that the names given to things are nothing other than the things themselves? Look at heaven, God's chief work: its name is far different, for it is not the thing itself. Moreover, heaven is a visible thing, but its name is perceived by hearing, not sight. Therefore, the Son of God is called 'the Word,' yet he is not a 'word' in the way many understand it, but something naturally different from a word." We ought to remain silent and not respond to such arguments; and yet, lest the simpler folk be led astray by them, we cannot remain silent. We say, therefore, that names given to things signify the very essences of the things, even if they are distinct from them. For example, the word "man"—this sound I speak—is different from the man himself, yet it signifies the subject of the man. For if it did not signify the man himself, upon hearing this name, one would not understand "man" but something else, which is the height of foolishness to say. We should not, therefore, understand anything other than what is signified by the name, and thus the madness of the heretics is suppressed. Or let Eunomius demonstrate to us that "the Word" is not the proper name of the Son of God, so that he may be found an enemy of the Divine Scriptures, and especially of John the Evangelist, who set down this title as the most proper to the Son of God.

CHAPTER III.

"But how," he asks, "will the Son of God be both Word and Wisdom? Since wisdom is a kind of knowledge, and a word is a pronunciation of the voice; yet voices are neither <term>subsistences<note>original: "subsistentiæ". Referring to things that have their own independent existence or substance.</note></term> nor living beings. But the Son is a living being; therefore he is neither the wisdom nor the word of the Father." He descends again to human things, forgetting that these words are spoken of God; but perhaps he does not know that we use human words regarding God, where everything is to be understood far differently than in human affairs. For a man’s word does not subsist, but the voice brought forth from the mouth vanishes; however, the word of God is not like that, but is living from the living, and subsisting from the subsisting. The same must be said about wisdom and knowledge: for our wisdom does not subsist, but God’s wisdom subsists. For he ought to understand that things said of God exceed the human manner just as much as the divine substance exceeds human substance. But I do not know how, perhaps through ignorance, he fell into such great impiety. For he calls the Son of God a <term>living being<note>original: "animal". In a philosophical context, this means a being endowed with life (anima), not necessarily a "beast."</note></term>, and did not consider that a living being is one thing, and life is another, just as a knower is different from knowledge. For life is that thing which, being shared, gives life; but a living being is that which shares in life. But the Lord does not call himself a "living being," but "the Life." If, because he is life, he were also a "living being" according to him, why does he not also call the Father a "living being"? Of whom it is written: "As I live, says the Lord." Therefore, rightly saying that apostolic word to Eunomius: "May your clever inventions be with you unto destruction": not a "living being" like himself, but...

That the title "the Word" is sufficient to signify the generation of the Son from the Father.
CHAPTER IV.

"But the title 'the Word' is not sufficient," Eunomius says, "to signify a true Son. For the very being of the Son cannot be manifested through it. For many other things are called by the name 'word' which do not have their own existence." By this same logic, even the title "God" would not be sufficient to signify God himself. For many others are so called, though they are not gods by nature, according to that saying: "I have said, you are gods." Someone could also say that because "good," "holy," and other such things are said of men through <term>participation<note>original: "participationem". The theological concept that creatures possess qualities like "goodness" only by sharing in God's perfect version of them.</note></term> in the True Good and the True Holy, these are not properly said of God. But if many names are common to both God and creatures, and yet are said of him alone according to nature, what shall prevent "the Word" also from being properly called the Son of God? And through this title, the very being of the Son is signified as much as humans can perceive, even though many other words are called such <term>abusively<note>original: "abusiue". A technical term in rhetoric meaning a word used in an extended or figurative sense rather than its strict, proper sense.</note></term> and in imitation of the True Word. For this reason, he says of himself: "I am the Truth." Therefore, whatever you say of God, as it truly applies to him: do not doubt that it is said properly of him, but of others only by extension. "But he is called 'the Word' by the Scriptures," Eunomius says, "not because he is from the Father according to nature, or because the Son himself is an internal word implanted in the Father, but because hearing the Father’s word, he announces it to us; just as the Son is also called 'sanctification' because he sanctifies, and 'justice' because he justifies." If he is called the Word of God, according to Eunomius, not because he is from the Father by nature and demonstrates the essence of the Begetter in himself, but because he hears a word from the Father and reports it to us, he would keep...

He is life as God; he died as man. Therefore, just as death does not diminish the Word of God, so too for him who receives many things from God as a man, this act of receiving will take nothing away from his divine status. And therefore Jesus Christ exists in the glory of God the Father. <margin>Philippians 3</margin> <note>original: "Phil. 3." Though the margin cites chapter 3, Cyril is quoting the sense of Philippians 2:11: "and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father."</note> For having been made man, he found us when we were lost, restored us when we were worn down, and called us back from error to himself: all of which things tend toward the glory of God the Father.

Let no one, therefore, be troubled if those things which are suitable to the "condition of servants" <note>A reference to the *kenosis* or "emptying" described in Philippians 2:7, where Christ takes the form of a servant/slave.</note> are applied to him. he was not ignorant: but lest he should cause grief to his still-tender disciples, who were longing to know that day, he truly said that as a **man** he did not know. For he took upon himself all our infirmities: for this reason, he said he was ignorant, as is evident from what follows. For after the resurrection, when he was already about to ascend into the heavens and was asked about future things, he responded more sharply, saying: *It is not for you to know the times and moments, which the Father <margin>Acts 1</margin> has put in his own power.* If indeed (as the heretics claim) he had been utterly ignorant, he certainly would not have responded in such a way, but would have said: "I have already told you that I do not know." But now he does not do so; rather, he rebukes those questioning him as if they were asking irrationally, and he discourages them from inquiring into matters greater than what concerns them. From this, therefore, it is clear that he then said he did not know that day and hour as a **man**, because the knowledge of that matter was greater than the disciples were then able to grasp.

<margin>B</margin> But let them answer, I pray: when God called our father Adam in paradise, <margin>Genesis 3, 4</margin> saying: *Adam, Adam, where are you?* and when he asked Cain: *Where is your brother Abel?* what will they say? For if they assert that God asked because he was ignorant, they will be held in manifest impiety. But if they say that God asked in this way as a form of **divine plan** <term>dispensation: God’s intentional way of dealing with humanity, often masking his full power or knowledge for a specific purpose</term>, why do they wonder if the Son of God—through whom that very question was asked back then—also usefully claims to be ignorant of that hour as a man, even though he knows all things as the **Wisdom of the Father**?

Moreover, that the Savior was accustomed to attribute ignorance to himself for the sake of the **divine plan** is clearly stated by the Evangelist himself in another place. For when he wished to feed his followers after the loaves were miraculously multiplied, he asked as if he were ignorant: <margin>John 6</margin> *How many loaves do you have?* But the Evangelist added: *He said this, however, to test Philip: for he himself knew what he was going to do.* If, therefore, although he knew what he was going to do, he nevertheless questioned as if ignorant, what prevents us now from thinking that he said he was ignorant of that day and hour for the sake of a useful **divine plan**?
