**THE TENTH BOOK BY THE SAME AUTHOR.**

On the same subject, that is, on the **consubstantiality** <term>consubstantiality: being of the same "substance" or "essence"; the doctrine that the Father and Son are the same God</term> of the Son and the Father, with the following text proposed: *Because the Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.* And, *That all things have been delivered to me by the Father.* And, *That I can do nothing of myself: but as I hear, so I judge,* and other such passages.

CHAPTER I.

<margin>C</margin> **B**ut how, they ask, will the Son be like the Father, he who openly says that he has received all things from the Father? For if he had them from himself, he would not have received them; but since he truly says he has received them, he certainly did not have them from himself. What will you do, O you [heretics], when you hear him say, *All things that the Father has are mine, and all mine are likewise the Father's*? For if the Son has nothing from himself, then the Father will also have nothing from himself: for all things that are the Son's are the Father's. But if the Father has all things naturally, then the Son also has those very same things naturally. Wherefore it will be necessary as a consequence to impose this very defect, which they strive to impose on the Son, upon the Father as well, lest any of those things which are the Son's should seem not to be in the Father. If that is impious, as it certainly is, it will be necessary to confess that all the Father's things are naturally in the Son, and all the Son's things are likewise in the Father.

For while the Son is born of the Father, he has all things naturally—even his very being—from the Father, and therefore he is said to "receive" from the Father. It is not, therefore, because he does not have them that he is written to receive something from the Father. For he has all things naturally, since he is the **Word** and the **Splendor of the Father’s light**, with only one exception: that he is not the Father. He said he received things from the Father, however, so that he might radically overturn the future opinions of heretics. For lest anyone, seeing all the Father's attributes in the Son, should think the Father and the Son are the same person because of the unchangeable likeness and identity—which happened to **Sabellius** <note>Sabellius was a 3rd-century teacher who claimed the Father, Son, and Spirit were just three roles played by one single person, rather than three distinct persons</note>—he necessarily says he receives from the Father what he has naturally from him: so that while one gives and the other receives, the **duality of persons** may be demonstrated, distinct not only in name, but truly and personally. Yet the statement is not false. For since the Son proceeds from the substance of the Father, he has all things of the Father eternally: and for this reason, he eternally receives from him all things which belong to the Father himself. Wherefore nothing is taken away from the deity of the Son when it is said by him, *All things are delivered to me by my Father*: <margin>Matthew 11</margin> but rather this speech demonstrates that he is naturally the Son of God. For if all things were delivered to him, and there is nothing outside the number of "all things," he himself will not be

He is not merely one of all those things which were handed over to him, but he is properly born from the Father; and as a son by nature, he possesses everything that is characteristic of the Father. Now, it is the Father's own nature to possess all things; therefore, let the Son also possess all things. In this way, he alone is the natural **heir** <note>original: "hæres". Cyril uses the legal concept of inheritance to show that the Son receives the Father's full nature not by grace, but by birthright.</note> of the Father, into whom all things belonging to the Father naturally—if I may speak this way—flow down. Furthermore, he says of himself elsewhere <margin>John 5</margin>: *Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted to the Son also to have life in himself.* This, too, shall be understood in a similar way. For because it is written that he "gave," it signifies that the Son possesses this life naturally from the Father; it also demonstrates that he exists as a distinct **person** <term>personally: from "personaliter," referring to the distinct existence of the Son (Hypostasis) compared to the Father, even though they share one divine nature.</term> from the one who gave. Since indeed he says, "as the Father has, so also the Son has," he teaches most clearly,

<summary>Cyril argues that Christ is the natural heir to the Father's essence, possessing "life in himself" not as a gift to a creature, but as a natural attribute of his divine Sonship.</summary>

The previous text ended while discussing John 5:26 ("As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son to have life in himself"). Cyril is now clarifying that this "granting" does not imply the Son is a created being who once lacked life, but rather describes his eternal origin from the Father.</meta>

### Page 128

->128 BOOK TEN<-

[Right column]
<column-break/>
that through the phrase "as the Father has," a single and identical **substance** <term>substance: from "substantia," referring to the underlying divine essence or "what it is to be God."</term> and a property of nature are signified. However, when it is said that he "gave" <note>original: "dedit"</note>, this designates his origin from the Father. For we do not say that the Son is **unbegotten** <note>original: "ingenitum." To be unbegotten is the unique property of the Father (the source); the Son is "begotten" or generated from that source.</note>, lest we should imply there are two Fathers; instead, we confess that the Son is from the Father, while still possessing everything that belongs to the Father by nature. 

Therefore, he has life in himself, not as something added from the outside, but as a natural property of his being. <margin>Psalm 36:9</margin> *For with you is the fountain of life,* the Psalmist says; and since the Son is the Wisdom and Power of the Father, he is truly the fountain of life from the fountain of life. <insert>Just as light is generated from light, so life is generated from life.</insert> 

We must also observe that the scripture does not say "the Father gave him life," but "granted him to **have life in himself**." This distinction is crucial: a creature might "receive life" as a gift that can be lost, but only God "has life in himself" as an inherent and eternal power. If the Son were of a different nature than the Father, this equality of "having life" would be impossible. Thus, the distinction between the "Giver" and the "Receiver" here does not imply a difference in rank or essence, but simply the order of their **eternal relationship**. <note>Cyril is refuting the Arian claim that if the Son "received" anything from the Father, he must be a subordinate creature rather than equal God.</note>

Furthermore, if the Father is truly life by nature, and the Son is his natural offspring, the Son must also be life by nature. <margin>1 John 5:20</margin> For if the one begotten were not like the one who begat him, the very definition of "Sonship" would be destroyed. The Son, therefore, is not a participant in life, but is Life itself.

they will say all these things were written in the usual way. Therefore, they do not understand that after he became man, all these things are to be applied not to the nature of the Word <note>The "Word" (Logos) refers to the divine nature of Christ before the Incarnation.</note>, but to the human nature (which he truly took up with all its sufferings, yet without sin).

**CHAPTER 4.**
On the same subject, namely that the Son is not a creature, based on the proposed text: "The Firstborn of all creation."

<margin>Colossians 1</margin> **I**f he were not a creature, they say, he would not be called the firstborn of all creatures. For because he has a great connection with creatures, even though he is the first of them and exists before them all, he was called by this name. And while it is not difficult to respond to the matter itself immediately, this must be said first: If, because he is called the firstborn of all creatures, he seems to be numbered among creatures, he will likewise be seen to exceed every creature, because he alone is called "only-begotten." For just as he is called "firstborn" when he has many brothers, so he is not "only-begotten" unless he alone was born in such a way that he has no brothers. How then will he be both "firstborn" and "only-begotten" at the same time, since these things clearly contradict each other? For since he is named both ways by Scripture, it is necessary to ask diligently how he is the only-begotten and how he is the firstborn. He is therefore the **only-begotten** because he alone is born from the Father, and he alone is the Son of God by nature.

<margin>Romans 8</margin> But he is written as the **firstborn** not simply, but "among many brothers." When, therefore, he who is God by nature became our brother by assuming humanity, then he also became the firstborn among many brothers, because he made many into "sons of God" through grace. He is called "firstborn," therefore, in regards to the time he preceded us, not because he himself, insofar as he is the Word of God, shares the same essence with creatures; but because in him we were first deified <term>deified: "theosis" or "deification," the ancient Christian teaching that humans are transformed by God's grace to share in the divine nature.</term>. For this reason, he is called "only-begotten" simply, without any added cause, because he alone is in the bosom of the Father as the true Son.

But he is called "firstborn" in such a way that both the cause and those of whom he is the first are immediately added. For he says, "the firstborn among many brothers" and "the firstborn from the dead." For since he is uncreated by nature, and the Lord and creator of all things, having also become a creature, he is found to be the first among all men, whom he reformed by his assumed human nature. Therefore, he himself, as the Word, is not a creature. For if all things were created in him (as Paul says), nothing was created that was not created through him.

<margin>Colossians 1</margin> Or if all things that were created were made through him, then he created himself—if he is a creature according to the heretics—which is found to be utterly impossible. Therefore, "firstborn among many brothers" is understood piously, as we have said: because having become man and our brother, he first sanctified us in himself.

<margin>Colossians 1</margin> Moreover, he is the "firstborn from the dead" because he himself, having trampled death, was the first to rise, and the first to lead our flesh back into the heavens. Therefore he says:
<margin>John 14</margin> "I am the way, and I am the door," for through him our nature was taught to make a new journey, and enters the heavens as if through a certain gate.
<margin>John 10</margin> Because of his mercy, therefore, having become man, he numbered himself among creatures, and having become their firstborn, he reformed all things. The Son is therefore "only-begotten" of the Father

<column-break/>

123

<margin>John 1</margin> according to nature. And "we saw," he says, "his glory, as the glory of the only-begotten from the Father." For he is **true God** from **true God**, **light** from **light**. But he is the "firstborn" for our sake, so that just as all things were made through him, so also they might be saved by being reformed in him. For this reason, just as he was created as "the beginning of ways" <note>original: "initium viarum." A reference to Proverbs 8:22, a central text in the Arian controversy regarding the creation of Wisdom.</note>, because through him all can return to salvation; so he is called "firstborn among many brothers" because he called us all to the adoption of God through grace. And again, he is "firstborn from the dead" because he was the first to rise from death and called our nature back into incorruption.

<margin>Colossians</margin> But "only-begotten," they [the heretics] say, "is used because he alone was created by the Father alone, while all other things were created through him." If the Son of the Father is called "only-begotten" for this reason, the Father will not be the universal creator of all things; yet Scripture cries out that all things are from Him. Therefore, he is called "only-begotten" not because he alone was created by the Father, but because he alone is born by nature from the Father.

<margin>John</margin> For if he were called "only-begotten" because he alone was made by the Father alone, would not a **day** also be called "only-begotten," since it is made alone? Would not many **arts**, or **statues**, or **works** which someone alone and by himself made, be called "only-begotten"?
<margin>4 Esdras</margin> Would not the **sun** and **moon**, the **heaven** also, and many other things be called "only-begotten," because they were made unique in their kind? But surely no one calls that which is *made* "only-begotten," even if it were made by one alone. Therefore, neither is the Son called "only-begotten" because he was made alone by one alone, but because he was begotten <note>original: "genitus." Cyril emphasizes the distinction between "begotten" (from the same nature) and "made" (from a different nature).</note> alone by one alone.

For a work that is made is not called an "offspring"; but the Son is truly begotten from the Father, because proceeding naturally from him, he is found through generation to be the true heir of the paternal essence. But if he were called "only-begotten" (as some say) because he alone exceeds all things, the Father would also be called "only-begotten" by this reasoning; and whatever seemed to exceed others in its kind would be called "only-begotten." Therefore, he is only-begotten not because of excellence, but because he alone is born from the Father.

<margin>Matthew</margin> But they say he is "only-begotten" because he alone is the "Angel of Paternal Counsel."
<margin>The cavils of the heretics</margin> If, therefore, the word we produce also alone announces the thoughts of the mind, it could rightly be called the "only-begotten of the mind"—which no one is ever found to have said.

<margin>Colossians</margin> But they say he is called "only-begotten" because he is the creator of only those things that were created after him, lest he be thought to be the creator of himself as well. But Scripture, O you [heretics], proclaims that all things were made simply in him and through him.

Furthermore, we sometimes call him "firstborn" who was born first: in this way, Christ is called the "firstborn of the Virgin" according to the flesh—not because she gave birth to others (for she remained a virgin even after the birth), but because "first" is often used both absolutely and in itself, and not in comparison to others.
<margin>Luke</margin> So, therefore, he is also the firstborn from God, not as the first of many [created things], but as the only one begotten from God. In addition, those things which are "first" in a simple sense are the cause of those things that are in the second place. The Son of God, therefore, can be called the "firstborn" of others because he himself is the primary cause, so that the name of "son" may be applied to all others. Thus also God the Father is the "First Father," because he first of all begot him who is eternally begotten.

<summary>Cyril explains that "Only-begotten" refers to Christ’s unique divine nature as the Father's natural Son, while "Firstborn" refers to his role as the head of the human race and the first to conquer death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cyril’s rebuttal of Arian arguments. Having previously discussed the tension between Christ being the "Only-begotten" (unique in nature) and "Firstborn" (head of a family), he now addresses specific scriptural objections used by his opponents to claim the Son is a created being or subordinate in power.</meta>

124 BOOK TEN 125

Furthermore, the heretics <note>Cyril is referring to the Arians, who argued that Jesus was a created being, not eternally God.</note> contradict themselves. For they say he is the "Firstborn" son because he alone was made by the Father, while they concede that all other things were produced through the Son. These ideas certainly clash. For if he is the "Firstborn" for that reason, then the other things—in comparison to which he is called the first produced—would certainly have been produced by the Father alone, and not by the Son. 

But how, they ask, if the Word <note>original: "verbum," referring to the divine Logos</note> is the true Son of God, does Scripture number him among the rest, saying: 
<margin>Colossians 1</margin> **The firstborn of all creation?** 
For they claim it is absolutely necessary that the Word be of the same nature as those things of which he is the first. There is great impiety in such a statement. For the Son is not called the firstborn of all creation because he himself is a creature, but because all of us are made adopted sons of God through grace in him and through him. He himself is the author of this grace, making those who believe in him like himself through his mercy. 

Because he is truly the firstborn, he is shown to be the true image of the Father. For just as he is truly the first Son, so also the Father is the first Father. For the first Father is in him, and he, the first Son, is in the first Father. 
<margin>John 1</margin> And through him all things were made, and through him every rational creature is adopted. Finally, if you believe he is a creature simply because he is called the "first" son of all creation, what do you say when the Father says of himself: 
<margin>Isaiah 44</margin> **I am the first and I am after these things** <note>original: "Ego primus et ego post haec." Modern versions usually read "I am the first and I am the last."</note>? 
Will you dare to preach that he, too, is the first of creatures and a creature himself? I think not. Therefore, just as the Father is not a creature although he is called "first," so it is with the Son. And just as the Father, showing himself to be the beginning of all things, says, "I am the first," so the Son is called the first of all creation because all things were made through him, and he himself is the beginning and creator of all.

### On the Gospel text: "But to sit at my right hand, or at my left, is not mine to give."
## CHAPTER 5.

<margin>Matthew 20</margin> **B**ut how, they ask, if the Son is equal to the Father, did he say to the sons of Zebedee: **It is not mine to give?** For that clearly shows, they argue, that he does not have the power to give what was being asked; therefore, he is not equal to the Father, since the Father has power over all things. 

Certainly, one ought not to explain the Savior’s words so inconsiderately. For if you are willing to examine each point diligently, you will find nothing that can help your impiety. The sons of Zebedee <note>The apostles James and John.</note> approached Christ and asked for the highest honors, which were owed to others. To this petition, the Savior appropriately replied: "It is not mine to give"—not because he lacks the power to give, but because rewards are given proportionally to those who strive for them. 

For it is just as if someone established a contest and announced the prizes; if people asked for the greatest rewards, he might say, "It is not mine to give." This does not mean he lacks the prizes, but that "The rewards of the contest are not set before me in such a way that I should give them to anyone who asks, but only to those who will win by competing." 

So also the Savior says: "It is not mine to give" this supreme honor to you who ask for it, which is reserved in the foreknowledge of the Father for those whose excellence in the struggle will recommend them. Therefore, this response of the Lord does not deny his power, but shows the divine arrangement <note>original: "dispensationem," referring to the 'economy' or plan of God.</note>. 

For how could he not be able to give to whom he wills, when he is found to have bestowed this very thing upon all the disciples? 
<margin>Matthew 19</margin> **Amen, amen, I say to you,** he said, **when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve seats.** 
He does not predict this merely as a prophet, but graciously bestows it as the Author. How then could he, who was able to give to all, not be able to give to two? Unless, perhaps, you dare to say that the apostles will not actually have what was promised. If you do that, no one should speak to you as Christians any longer, but as despisers of the truth. Therefore, just as he would not be equal to the Father if he could not give this to the sons of Zebedee, since he was able to give it to all the disciples, he is equal to the Father in all things.

Furthermore, if he truly says that all things have been handed over to him by the Father, and this favor is included among all things, he does not deny the power of giving when he says, "It is not mine to give"; rather, it is a statement of the divine arrangement. For Isaiah cries out openly, saying of the Savior: 
<margin>Isaiah 53</margin> **Therefore he shall have dominion over many, and shall divide the spoils of the strong, because his soul was delivered unto death.** 
If, therefore, he himself distributes honors to holy men, how can you say he is unable to give to those who ask, if he wills? Certainly, the Father works all things through him, one of which is the distribution of rewards to each of the saints; he, therefore, is the distributor of rewards. 

But let us explain the sense of the Gospel words more deeply. When our Lord Jesus Christ was encouraging and warning his disciples to desire nothing in this life, but to attend to divine worship, promising great honors to those who keep his commandments, the disciples approached, saying: 
<margin>Matthew 19</margin> **Behold, we have now left all things and followed you alone; what then shall there be for us?** 
Christ replied: "When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, then in that regeneration you also shall sit on twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." 

When the sons of Zebedee heard this, they coveted a reward that was not appropriate for them. For they sought to snatch for themselves alone what had been proposed to all the disciples as a reward for their goodwill toward Christ. But lest they should seem overcome by a desire for empty glory, they themselves remained silent out of shame and used the service of their mother. She, therefore, approached the Lord, saying: 
<margin>Matthew 20</margin> **Command that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left.** 
Clearly, then, through these words, the woman is seen wanting to transfer to her sons alone that which was owed to everyone. For if this were not the case, for what reason would she ask again for what had already been given to all the disciples—among whose number her sons were included? Obviously for no other reason than to transfer a reward common to all to her own sons. 

The Savior, knowing these things as God, called the sons of Zebedee to himself. In his mercy, he did not rebuke them harshly, lest he should overwhelm them with the greatness of grief and sadness; instead, he said it was "not his to give." By these words, he did not show an impotence of his nature (as the heretics claim)—for such a statement is entirely foolish, especially since he is found to have already provided this to everyone. But he said: "Because you ask for an unjust favor which it is not fitting for me to bestow upon you, **it is not mine to give.**"

<summary>Cyril argues that Christ's title as "Firstborn" refers to his role as the head of adopted humanity rather than being a created being, and explains that Christ's refusal to grant specific seats in heaven to the sons of Zebedee was a rejection of favoritism, not a lack of divine power.</summary>

### CHAPTER VII.
How, they ask, shall the Son be substantially equal to the Father, if he is not perfect? For he is found to increase in wisdom. But that which is not perfect increases; the Father, however, is perfect, lacking nothing, and therefore undergoes no progress toward something better. These heretics must be asked: about whom do they think it was written that he increased in wisdom and grace? They will certainly say of Christ; furthermore, who do they judge Christ to have been? For if he were a common and naked man, in whom there was nothing beyond our nature, let him increase as a man; but if he is God and was made man for our sake, as it is written, how shall he receive increase? Or how shall he be imperfect, who *thought it not robbery to be equal with God*? But if he is equal to God, as Paul asserts, and yet he increased, it will now be necessary according to you to say he is greater than the Father: which is most absurd. Since therefore he is perfect, and the Son of a perfect Father, you should accept that this was said on account of the incarnation. For if he increased as the Word made man, he himself did not benefit us, but rather the flesh which he assumed brought progress to itself, and led the imperfect toward perfection. How then do we give thanks to him, as to one made man for our sake? Since it would surely be proper that he should return thanks to us! Because it is impious even to think this, he did not increase as the Word, but it was said on account of the incarnation, as we shall now say more extensively. Furthermore, the Word of God is called God not by empty but by true names, and the Wisdom of God, and Power, and Form, and Image of the Father. How then, since he truly is all these things, was he susceptible to increase? For there would be something greater than God, and Wisdom, and Power, and the Form and Image of God: which is impossible. Moreover, principalities, dominions, angels, archangels, and every rational creature are perfected by participation in the Word. How then is he himself imperfect, by whom all other things are perfected? And how can the Wisdom of God increase in wisdom? Or how does he increase in grace, who is the giver of all graces? Unless perhaps they do not believe Paul, who calls the Son the Wisdom of God and the giver of grace.
It is added, that what is imperfect always strives to ascend to perfection: and neglects the first place in which it is, desiring a greater and better one: as men (for example) gradually increasing in wisdom and every virtue,

<margin>Philip. 2.
A quibble of the heretics.</margin>
[Right Column]
ascend to a life of perfection. But the Word of God, that is, the Son of God, since he is entirely in the Father, and has the Father entirely in himself, where shall he ascend? For he who fills the Father (to speak now of bodies) and is filled by the Father, if he receives an increase, he will seem greater than the Father, which is altogether a wicked thing to say. Therefore he who is perfect does not increase, nor is he who is immutable changed. Just as when Paul says, *he humbled himself, taking the form of a servant*: we are not troubled, nor do we think less of the Word of God, but we marvel at his mercy and grace: so it is not right to be troubled when we read that he increased. For just as the deity suffered nothing from that humiliation of the Word; so from this increase it suffered nothing at all: but just as he humbled himself for our sake, so also for our sake he willed to increase: so that we might increase in wisdom in him, we who on account of sin had become like beasts, so that we might likewise increase in grace in him, we who were [estranged] from the former grace of God because of the first man's transgression. For Christ undertook all our things for our sake without sin, so that with all our things reformed for the better, he might become the principle of all our goods. But let us now investigate the sense of the text itself more deeply.
A certain natural law brings it about that a man does not increase in wisdom and every virtue suddenly or in a short time, but gradually according to the progress of the body. Therefore the Word of God, who is described as being made flesh, although he is the perfect wisdom and power of the Father: nevertheless, because it was necessary for him to show himself truly made man, not contrary to the nature of men, but according to nature as the body gradually grew, he also gradually appeared wiser. Therefore he revealed his hidden wisdom gradually, following the law of our nature. When therefore you hear that he increased in wisdom and grace, do not think that anything was added to him, who can never lack anything. But because to those seeing and hearing him, he showed himself daily wiser and more gracious, for that reason he is written to have increased. Thus by uncovering himself daily, not he himself, but those who wondered at him and loved him, increased. And certainly that which increases in some thing is different from the thing itself in which it increases. If therefore Christ, who is Wisdom, is written to have increased in wisdom, it was surely not he himself (for Wisdom cannot increase in itself) therefore not he, but the human nature increased. For while the deity was manifested in him daily, he appeared more wonderful and wiser. Moreover, human nature increased in him in this way: the Wisdom of God, that is the Son of God, assumed our nature, and gradually revealing the deification of the assumed man both by words and deeds, he made him increase by revealing it. And so the nature itself increased in wisdom, in which it was deified, through which we also have been made sons of God by grace. And so in Christ our nature increased so much, that it arrived from corruption to incorruption, and to the dignity of the deity in Christ.
But they say, we have heard through the scripture that the Son himself...

the Son of God made man is called Jesus Christ. Therefore, it is the Son of God himself who progressed; nor do we accept those distinctions of yours, since <margin>1 Corinthians 8</margin> Paul preaches one Jesus Christ. If, therefore, he is one, and this one progressed, he was certainly imperfect: how then shall he be equal to the most perfect Father? Truly, the Lord Jesus Christ is one, and not two, and one <term>hypostatically</term> <note>meaning existing as a single, distinct person or individual reality</note> and personally in two natures. For God assumed and put on man, <margin>John 1</margin> and therefore the Word is said to have been made flesh. Why then do you not also attribute to the Word all things which belong to man without sin? Especially since the deity of the Word is in no way diminished by this. Since, therefore, it is characteristic of the flesh to progress, you may say that he progressed as a man: for he attributes to himself the things which belong to the flesh. For in this way we also preach that he suffered death, and we believe he suffered it not as God, but as man. Since, therefore, you heretics also do not dare to deny that the Word of God truly became man: just as when you hear that Christ himself is the brightness, and the wisdom, and the character of the Father, you understand not the man whom he assumed, but the Son of God who assumed him: so when something is said in the Scriptures which is appropriate not to God, but to man, you ought to refer it not to the Word of God, but to the man who is hypostatically united to the Word. It is therefore evident on all sides that not Wisdom itself, insofar as it is Wisdom, but the human nature progressed in wisdom. For by degrees our nature was manifested as being the instrument of the deity which dwelt in it: therefore he does not say the Word of God progressed, but Jesus: lest, of course, the Word should seem to progress, but rather the human nature, which is capable of progress. Thus, therefore, the things written about Christ are to be understood, so that neither are those things which belong to the deity attributed to his humanity, nor are those things proper to his humanity twisted toward his deity.

CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> AND how, they say, will the Son be equal to the Father according to nature, if Paul truly says that the Son himself also shall be subjected to the Father? For no one can deny that what is subjected is less than that which subjects: just as the conquered is less than the victor. The heretics do not understand that they are saying conflicting and altogether absurd things. For they contend that the Father is less than the Son, and they try to affirm this because Paul says "then" (for he proposes a determinate time) the Son shall be subjected to the Father. From which it follows, according to them, that the Son is not currently subjected to the Father; but when a rational nature is not subjected, it is then in its own proper will. What then will they <margin>John 6</margin> say upon hearing Christ: *I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father*? Let those men, who boast that they understand the Scriptures acutely, answer us: is he who does the will of another not subjected to him? Since they will be afraid to say this, how is it that if the Son is now 

131

also subjected to the Father, he shall finally be subjected in a future time? Let them believe, therefore, that we can truly say of them: *You were in error, not knowing the Scriptures.* <margin>Matthew 22, Psalm 118</margin> Furthermore, they contend that the Son is a creature. If therefore, as the Scriptures cry out, every creature serves God, how is he not now subjected to the Father? It must be, however, that either the Father cannot now subject him, and the Son will now be greater than the Father, which is against their own position; or if it is honorable that the Son be subjected to the Father, it must be granted by them that he acts basely, he who is to be subjected later and is not subjected now. How then was it said of him that <margin>Isaiah 53</margin> he committed no sin? Rather, they say, how is the Son not less than the Father, who according to you is always subjected to him? It is clear to everyone that equality is not destroyed by subjection. For an equal is often subjected to an equal in a certain manner of <term>dispensation</term> <note>the divine plan or arrangement of events in salvation history</note>. Do you not grant that one and the same Spirit is in the prophets? Why then did Paul write that <margin>1 Corinthians 14</margin> the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets? How, moreover, can subjection drive the Son away from equality with the Father? Are not sons among men also subjected to fathers, yet they are in no way less as far as substance and the reason of nature are concerned? If, therefore, no one will deny that it ought to be so among us, nor will anyone say on that account that those who subject or those who are subjected are greater or lesser in nature: why shall we not think that it happens similarly in God without impiety? For subjection is not the essence of the Son, nor is the essence of the Son in subjection: but while he is in his own hypostasis, he is said to be subjected to the Father. Whence subjection cannot show the nature of the Son to be less than the Father. But if you think subjection is, as it were, the definition of the Son himself, see how far this speech will drive you into impiety. For then it will be necessary for you to say: that the Son is to be (when previously he was not) when the time of subjection shall come: which Paul shows has not yet come, but is to come. But what will you say if the Father also is found to be subjected to the Son? Certainly, he who ministers to another is subjected to him. But the Father ministers to the Son, as the Psalmist sings: <margin>Psalm 109</margin> *Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.* If therefore the Father, although he ministers to the Son, is nevertheless not less than him on that account: neither is the Son to be thought less than the Father because he is subjected to the Father. But let us now consider the sense of the Apostle's words. The Father works all things through the Son: and that is the condition of subjection, that the Son should have the will of the Father in all things. For there is one will of both, whence when the Father says: *Let us make man*: <margin>Genesis 1</margin> man is divinely formed by the Son. <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> Paul teaches, therefore, that in the future age also the Father dwells in us no other way than through the Son; therefore he writes: *When all things shall be subjected to the Son, then he himself also shall be subjected to the Father, who subjected all things to himself.* And he adds: *That God may be all in all.* He seems therefore to say, let no one think we shall be partakers of the Father in the coming age otherwise than through the Son. By subjection, therefore, he wished to signify nothing else than that the Son would even then bestow the Father upon us. And thus subjection does not show the Son to be lesser, but shows identity.

The unity of the Trinity demonstrates an unchangeable nature, which will never be otherwise than it is. Even in that future age, the Father through the Son will be all in all: life, incorruptibility, joy, power, and whatever grace is given to the saints shall be given from the Father through the Son in the Spirit. But I ask you to see how prudently—indeed, how divinely—these words of Paul are written. ### On the Properties of the Elements

It is necessary to consider the **primary qualities** <note>The fundamental characteristics of matter in Aristotelian physics: hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note> that govern the composition of all earthly bodies. As the ancient masters have written, "Nature does nothing in vain" <note>original: "Natura nihil facit frustra"</note>, and thus we see a perfect balance in the arrangement of the spheres.

<margin>The movement of the heavens influences the lower realms.</margin>

The element of **Air** is by its nature hot and moist, serving as a bridge between the fiery heavens and the watery depths of the earth. Without this mediation, the sharp heat of the sun would consume the delicate spirits of living creatures. <insert>Note that some later physicians argue air is primarily cold, but they confuse the substance with the wind.</insert>

#### Table of Elemental Harmonies

| Element | Primary Quality | Secondary Quality |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Fire | Hot | Dry |
| Air | Moist | Hot |
| Water | Cold | Moist |
| Earth | Dry | Cold |

<column-break/>

Furthermore, we must observe the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth element" or ether, thought to be the pure substance of the stars, distinct from the four earthly elements.</note> which permeates the celestial bodies. Unlike the four elements of our sublunary world, which are subject to decay and change, the heavens remain constant. 

->**The Unity of the Macrocosm**<-

As it is said in the Greek tongue, "The universe is a single living being" <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν ζῷον ἕν"</note>. This interconnectedness ensures that the physician must look to the stars just as the farmer looks to the soil. <gloss>The stars incline, but do not compel.</gloss> If the humors of the body are out of alignment, one must seek the remedy in the corresponding plant or mineral that shares the same elemental signature.

<summary>This page details the Aristotelian system of the four elements and their qualities, emphasizing the role of Air as a mediator and the existence of the celestial Quintessence. It argues for a "macrocosm-microcosm" relationship where the universe functions as a single, interconnected organism.</summary>

If it belongs to a Lord to set free—and Christ has set us free, and by his mercy claimed us from the yoke of servitude into sonship—he himself will certainly not be a servant, but the Lord, and a Son according to nature, who also led the others through grace to adoption by God the Father.

For it is necessary that a perfect image have the likeness of that of which it is an image. Therefore, just as the Father is uncreated, so also the Son shall be uncreated;

and just as the Father is true God, so also the Son is true God. Then a little later: "Wherefore remember [margin] Ephesians 2. How then shall he be a creature: he who, being known as God, saves those who believe in him, and brings a weak hope, saying: [margin] Matthew 25. [/margin] "Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things, [margin] Ephesians 2. [/margin] I will set you over many things, enter into the joy of your lord." It is certainly written concerning the law of God, that no one should dare either to add anything to it or subtract from it: for it is not lawful for a creature to do that. But Christ alone, as the Lord of the law, [margin] Deuteronomy 4. [/margin] did this: for he subtracted, when he abolished the law of commandments; and he added the dogmas of faith and evangelical piety. How then shall the Lord of the divine law be a creature? To these things he adds: "Therefore now you are [margin] Ephesians 2. [/margin] no longer guests and strangers, but you are fellow citizens of the saints, and members of the household of God." How then shall the Son not be God, since all of us who are joined to him through faith are made members of the household of God because of this? But he himself also, showing the manner of spiritual union, says: [margin] Matthew 12. [/margin] "Whoever does the will of my Father, he is my brother and sister and mother." Furthermore, Paul adds: "For this cause I bow my knees to the Father, from whom all fatherhood in heaven [margin] Ephesians 3. [/margin] and on earth is named." Those things which exist by position—that is, not by nature, but by grace or adoption—are as similar as possible to natural things. Likewise, all things which are made in imitation of something, although they do not entirely attain the natural and proper qualities of those things they imitate, nevertheless have no small likeness to them. [margin] Matthew 5. [/margin] If, therefore, the name of fatherhood passes from God to us, as Paul asserts: how will it not be impious to think that we are indeed fathers of our children by nature—we who are called fathers through imitation, by which the creature [margin] John 1. [/margin] imitates its Creator by nature—but to think that God the Father is not truly a Father first, nor to confess that the Son proceeds from him essentially, but to judge him foreign to the paternal substance? Or how shall he be a Father, if he did not beget from himself? Since that name properly signifies this very thing. Since, therefore, the Father truly says to the Son: "From the womb before the [margin] Psalm 109. [/margin] morning star I have begotten you"—and he begot him from himself (for this is what "from the womb" signifies)—the Son will not be a creature, who proceeds naturally from God as from a Father. Again in the same place: "One Lord, one faith, [margin] Ephesians 4. [/margin] one..."

### On the Division of Things

The definition of a **thing** <note>Latin: *res*</note> is generally understood as anything that can be of use to man, or that which is the object of a right. In this sense, it encompasses both physical objects and legal rights themselves.

#### I. Things of Divine Right
These are things which are held to belong to no one among men, but are consecrated to God.
*   **Sacred things:** Such as churches and offerings properly dedicated to God by the authority of the Church.
*   **Religious things:** Such as burial places or tombs, which become religious by the very act of burying a body.
*   **Holy things:** <note>Latin: *sanctae*</note> Such as the walls and gates of a city, which are protected against the injury of men by a certain religious sanction.

#### II. Things of Human Right
These are divided into several categories based on their ownership and use:

1.  **Common things:** <note>Latin: *res communes*</note> Those which by natural law belong to all, such as the air, flowing water, the sea, and consequently the shores of the sea.
2.  **Public things:** Those which belong to the whole people or the state, such as rivers and ports.
3.  **University things:** <note>Latin: *res universitatis*</note> Those belonging to a corporation or a city, intended for the use of the citizens, such as theaters and racecourses.
4.  **Private things:** Those which belong to individuals and are acquired in various ways.

<column-break/>

#### III. Corporeal and Incorporeal Things
*   **Corporeal things:** Those which can be touched by their nature, such as land, a slave, a garment, gold, or silver.
*   **Incorporeal things:** Those which cannot be touched; they consist of rights, such as an inheritance, a <term>usufruct</term> <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it</note>, or obligations however contracted.

<margin>Note on the distinction between ownership and possession.</margin>

#### IV. Movable and Immovable Things
*   **Movable:** Things that can move themselves (like animals) or be moved by external force (like furniture).
*   **Immovable:** Things that cannot be moved from their place, such as fields, houses, and trees attached to the soil.

<insert>It should be noted that certain rights attached to land are also treated as immovable.</insert>

<summary>This page outlines the fundamental legal classification of "things" (res), distinguishing between divine and human law, corporeal and incorporeal property, and the various categories of public and private ownership.</summary>

<keywords>property law, res sacrae, res communes, corporeal things, incorporeal things, usufruct, Roman law categories</keywords>

CHAPTER IX.
<margin>Hebrews 1</margin> **God, who in many parts and in many ways spoke long ago to the fathers through the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the worlds.** <note>original: "secula" - often translated as 'ages' or 'worlds' in a cosmological sense.</note> When Paul wished to show that the Gospel doctrine was more excellent than the Mosaic law and all prophetic scripture, he did so by the diversity of the persons involved: he says that God spoke to the fathers through the prophets, and in this manner issued the law and the Old Testament. But in these last days, he says He has spoken to us through the Son, who exceeds all the prophets as much as a lord by nature is more excellent than servants by nature. For all the prophets, like true ministers, cry out: "Thus says the Lord"; but the Son is truly the Lord: <margin>Matthew 5</margin> **It was said to those of old,** he says, **you shall not commit adultery: But I say to you.** How then shall the Son of God be a creature according to nature, or how shall he be a servant, who is the Lord of all and the heir of all? For it is necessary that he himself be something other than all the things of which he is the heir. But through him even the worlds were made: therefore he existed before the worlds. Truly, no creature existed before the worlds: for all things are within time, except God alone. Therefore the Son is true God and not a creature. Then the Apostle adds: <margin>Hebrews 2</margin> **For if the word spoken through angels was made firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just retribution of reward: how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? Which, having begun to be narrated by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard him.** Here he demonstrates most clearly, through the difference of the persons, how much the Gospel preaching exceeds the shadows of the Law. For if, he says, the authority of the Law—which was given through the ministry of angels—was so great that its transgressors and despisers were severely punished: how much more shall those be punished who despise the Gospel doctrine, which the Son of God himself delivered to us? Moreover, how much the Son stands above the angels is evident: because they are ministers and are sent to minister; but the Son is glorified with the Father, and the angels minister to him, as it is written in the Gospel: <margin>Matthew 4</margin> **And behold, angels came and ministered to him.** How then shall he who is Lord by nature be a minister by nature? Or how shall he who is King by nature be placed among those who are servants by nature? Furthermore, the blessed Paul, referring to Christ what is written in the eighth Psalm, <margin>Hebrews 2</margin> says: **What is man, that you are mindful of him? or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels, you crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands: you have subjected all things under his feet.** Then he immediately infers: **For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing not subject to him.** Shall he not therefore be rightly proclaimed by all as King by nature and Lord by nature, to whom all things are subject? Certainly, all things are subjected to God alone. How then shall he be numbered among creatures, who is over all things, and to whom all things are subject and serve, and who rules over all things with them subjected under his feet? As

A he says through a certain prophet: **Heaven is my throne, but the earth is my footstool.** <margin>Isaiah 66</margin> Furthermore, Paul adds in that place: <margin>Hebrews 3</margin> **Wherefore, holy brothers, sharers of the heavenly calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus Christ, who is faithful to him who made him, just as Moses was in all his house.** For this one was deemed worthy of greater glory than Moses, inasmuch as he who built the house has greater honor than the house itself. For every house is built by someone; but he who created all things is God. Since he teaches that the creature and the creator are not to be honored equally, it is clear that he shows the Son is not to be numbered among creatures. For he says he who built the house has greater honor. Moreover, that the Son B produced all things, Paul teaches both here and in many other places: **For through him,** he says, **all things were created, whether visible or invisible, whether principalities or powers, all things were created in him and through him: and he is before all things.** <margin>Colossians 1</margin> How then shall the creator of all things, even of the worlds and times themselves (for these also are among all things), be a creature, he who is before every creature? For he would be within time if he were a creature. For all things are within time, except God, who is eternal. But he himself is before times, as the creator of times; how then shall he be a creature? Furthermore, the Apostle immediately connects: <margin>Hebrews 3</margin> **And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant: but Christ as a Son in his own house, which house we are.** C Thus, by both names and realities, he shows how great a difference in dignity there is between Moses and Christ—that is, between all creatures; for the discourse is led to this conclusion. For Moses is a faithful servant: but Christ is the Son, and as a Son, faithful in his own house as the heir. If, therefore, both are faithful in the same house: the former as a servant, the latter as the Son and the builder of the house itself, how shall he be a created thing? Since he who constructs and builds is one thing by nature, and that which is constructed is another. Thus from the realities—that is, from the dignity which each holds in the house of God—the Son is also demonstrated to be God and the Lord of the house. For the person of Moses and the house itself are taken to represent every creature. Furthermore, it is God who speaks through a certain prophet: <margin>Leviticus 26</margin> **I will dwell in them, and I will be their God, D and they shall be my people.** How then are we the house of the Son, if the Son is not God? But we are the house of the Son because we pray (as Paul says) for Christ to dwell in the inner man. <margin>Ephesians 3; Hebrews 3; John 6</margin> Therefore Christ is God, and not a creature. Then Paul adds: **See, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God.** Faith is in Christ, and through it eternal life is given to us. **He who believes in me,** the Savior says, **has eternal life.** But he who neglects this faith departs from the living God in his heart and wicked thoughts. How then shall the Son not be the living God? But the Father is also the living God: therefore the Father and the Son are the same God by nature. Again in the same place: <margin>Hebrews 4</margin> **For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of the soul...**

And after a few words: "Trembling," it says, "the jailer fell at the knees of Paul and Silas: and leading them outside he said, 'Lord, what must I do to be saved?' But they said: 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you shall be saved, you and your household.' And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all his house. And taking them in that hour of the night, he washed their wounds, and he himself was baptized, and all his family immediately. And leading them into his house, he set a table, and rejoiced: because with his whole household he believed in God." <note>This passage cites Acts 16:25-34 to demonstrate that believing in Jesus is equated with believing in God.</note> See how he who believed in the Lord Jesus, according to the commands of the apostles, rejoiced with his whole house as one believing in God. But if the Son of God were a creature, according to the heretics <note>The "heretics" here refers to the Arians, who denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>: why is the truth not revealed to the jailer by the apostles? Why are they exhorted to believe in the Lord Jesus? Why, when he had believed in him, is he said to have believed in God, and not in a creature? It is manifest therefore even from this, that the Son is God according to nature, and not a creature.

Concerning the same, from the Gospel according to Matthew.
CHAPTER XIV.

Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife: for that which she has in her womb is of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, she shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus: for he himself shall save his people from their sins. <note>Matthew 1:20-21</note> The Son saves his people, and forgives the sins of the people as God and Lord of the Law. Who, therefore, among creatures will dare to place him there, except the rash and the impious? Since no one can forgive sins except God alone: and since a people can be called the "own" of no one except God alone, who is the God and Creator of all peoples. Again in the same place: Now all this was done that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet Isaiah, saying: *Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel, which is interpreted, God with us.* Unless the Son were God by nature, his name would not be called Emmanuel, which is *God with us*. For through the holy virgin, and by the Holy Spirit, he was made man: whom no angel, nor any creature, but God himself called Emmanuel: just as the prophet himself shows, saying of Christ: *And they shall call his name a new name, which the Lord shall name.* For the new name Emmanuel was imposed upon the Son. For before the incarnation he is called God only: but after the incarnation not only God, but also *God with us*, that is, God made man. Since, therefore, the Lord and Father himself calls the Son his God, let those who rashly dare to count him among creatures finally blush with shame. Furthermore, Matthew adds: *You have heard that it was said to the ancients, you shall not kill: but whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.* From this, the true deity of the Son is rightly gathered (as it seems to me). For the making of laws is most fitting for a King, and therefore God the King permits no one to add or take away anything from the Mosaic law. <note>referring to Deuteronomy 4:2</note> But the Son took away what was lesser, and added what is greater and more perfect. As God, therefore, and Lord of the law, he did this. Or if he is not true God, as the heretics say, he will seem unjust, because he added not small nor few things to the Mosaic law. But he is not unjust. For *he committed no sin*, as it is written. As God, therefore, and Lord of the law, he added with great liberty, saying: *But I say to you.* How then shall he be a creature, who as true God changes the Mosaic law for the better and more perfect with great power? Afterward Matthew adds: *A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor a bad tree bear good fruit.* This sentence, spoken thus universally by our Savior, is most true. Wherefore it is now pleasing to reduce this very sentence to the divine essence. A good tree, he says, produces good fruit. For that which is produced is entirely similar to that which produces it. But the Father himself is uncreated; he cannot, therefore, naturally beget a created Son from himself. For if he, being uncreated, could naturally beget a created Son from himself, a good tree could produce bad fruit. For the uncreated Father, naturally good, is goodness itself: whereas any creature cannot be goodness itself. Wherefore if the Father is uncreated, and the Son created, the fruit of the tree would not be good, though the tree is good: which is against the stated sentence of the Savior. Therefore the Son is not a creature, but consubstantial <term>consubstantial: of the same substance or essence (Greek: homoousios)</term> with the Father. Consequently Matthew says: *And behold, a leper worshipped him, saying: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. For *all things*, he says, *that the Lord willed, he did.* He, therefore, who shines with this power and omnipotence as the Father: how shall he not be consubstantial with the Father? Especially since all things are always of the same substance whose operation is one. But the Son is the living and consubstantial action, and power, and wisdom of the Father: he cannot, therefore, be a creature. Again in the same place: *Then rising he rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm. But the men wondered, saying: What sort of man is this? for even the sea and the winds obey him.* Furthermore, to show his omnipotence, God says through one of the prophets against the wicked words of this kind: *Will you not fear me, says the Lord? will you not tremble at my presence, who have placed the sand as a bound for the sea, an eternal decree, which it shall not pass?* Something similar is also in Job: *He placed* (he says) *bounds for the sea, and imposed bars and doors, and said to it: thus far you shall come, and you shall not pass, but in yourself your waves shall be broken.* The blessed Psalmist also, striking a spiritual lyre, thus sings to God, saying: *You rule the power of the sea, and you mitigate the movement of its waves.* Since, therefore, it is the property of the divine nature to rule the sea also, and to impose laws on the waters, and to tame all elements under his yoke, and the Son of God does this with supreme power: how shall he not be God by nature? Or how shall he be a creature?

And "in the beginning he was": how, therefore, do these men <note>Referring to the Arians, who argued that Jesus was a created being rather than eternally God.</note> suppose him to be a creature? Especially since they cannot say he was deified through grace. For whatever is given to someone through grace must necessarily be added afterward. For the nature, essence, and hypostasis <term>hypostasis: the distinct personhood or individual existence of a being</term> to which grace is granted must necessarily be understood to exist beforehand. Just as we, being humans by nature, are called "gods" through the grace of God; and it is understood that we are humans prior to being deified through grace. But those who falsely claim the Son is a creature cannot say what the Son is understood to be by nature prior to being called God. For "the Word was God," according to John. "This one was in the beginning with God." He shows that the Son was not produced as something external, but emanates from the very substance of the Father, as one shining forth within him and from him according to nature; nor did this happen in time. For he says this: "he was in the beginning with God." How, then, shall the true fruit of the parent be anything other by nature than his own parent? For just as grapes do not grow from brambles, so brambles do not grow from the vine. Since, therefore, the Father is God by nature, the Son will also be God by nature. Otherwise, he would be of less dignity than his own creatures. For creatures produce fruit from themselves that is of the same substance <term>consubstantial: sharing the same fundamental nature or essence</term> as themselves; but according to these men, God will not generate God from himself by nature—which is utterly absurd. "All things were made through him." Nothing was made that was not made by him, as he himself asserts. Therefore, he who is not included in the number of things made is something other than the things made themselves. He is the Son of God, who called the universe into existence. The creator of all things is therefore not a creature, but true God, and consubstantial with the Father. For it is written, he says: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve." <margin>Luke 6 <note>The text cites Luke 6, though the quote is more famously from Luke 4:8 or Matthew 4:10.</note></margin> <margin>Deuteronomy 6</margin> How then, if the Son is a creature according to these men, is he worshipped both by us and by the angels? Paul is a witness to this matter: "But when he brings the first-born into the world, he says: let all the angels of God worship him." <margin>Hebrews 1</margin> Certainly, if only humans worshipped him, these men might perhaps say it is no wonder if we are in error; but now the powers of the heavens worship him, and they will not dare to say that they are in error (since they are angels of God). Furthermore, rewards are laid up in heaven for those who worship Christ. He is therefore not a "new god," <margin>Psalm 80 <note>Refers to the prohibition against "strange" or "new" gods.</note></margin> whom we are forbidden to worship; but the true God, and God by nature, because we are commanded to worship him. <margin>John 1</margin> ...of the world. <note>original: "ecce agnus dei qui tollit peccata mundi" — Behold the lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.</note> But since the Savior says that he does not receive testimony from man, but that there is another who bears witness of himself: who is this other, greater than John, or rather, simply greater than any man? It is clear he speaks of the Father. For the Father said to John: Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining on him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. Moreover, as the Spirit descended upon Jesus, the voice of the Father was heard saying: This is my beloved Son. Since, therefore, God the Father himself calls Christ his Son, and that testimony is true—because it is spoken by Truth itself about the Truth—do not those people manifestly condemn themselves with the crime of impiety who dare to preach that the Son of God is a creature? I (Christ says thereafter) have a testimony greater than the testimony of John. For the works which the Father gave me to do, these very works that I do, bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me. Christ says that John’s testimony has little power: not because John did not bear true witness (for he came as a witness sent by God, to bear witness of the light) but because already among the Jews his testimony, although he was a great man and most upright in every kind of virtue, was little valued; the Savior rightly says that he is demonstrated by the magnitude of his works and miracles, because he went out and came from the Father himself. For he would not have done so many and such great things beyond nature by his own power as God, unless he were truly the Son of God. Since, therefore, what the Father is able to do, the Son also is able to do: must not all those be shunned as impious who dare to call him not God, but a creature? Afterward in the same place he adds: I have come in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me: if another comes in his own name, him you will receive. How does the Son come in the name of the Father? Clearly as God, as Lord, as life, as almighty, as light, as he who is able to make the dead live. For the Father is able to do all these things. Wherefore, if the Son is not also all these things, he has not come in the name of the Father. But he came in the name of the Father: because everything that the Father is, he also is, with only one exception, that he is not the Father. <note>A reference to the distinction of persons in the Trinity: they share one essence, but the Son is not the Father.</note> How then shall he be a creature? Again: As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father. And, He who eats me, shall live because of me. The Son says he is sent by the Father, either according to the manner of the incarnation—because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and was made obedient even unto death—or because just as light is sent out from the sun, or heat from fire, so he emanates inseparably from the Father. Moreover, he is said to live because of the Father, not because he is a participant in life (as we are): but because all things proper to the Father’s substance pass naturally into him, as into a Son. Now, it is proper to the Father to live: or to say it more clearly, he is essentially life itself: therefore the Son is also this because of the Father, since he is born of him. For a non-living son cannot be born of a living father, nor a created one from the uncreated. Afterward we read in the same Evangelist that Jesus answered: You know neither me, nor my Father. From this also observe that the Son is the true image of the Father. For if

<column-break/>

[Right Column - Page 173]

A from the knowledge of the Son himself the knowledge of the Father is obtained: how will it not be necessary that the nature, that is, the essence of the Father and the Son, be the same? If therefore there is no difference between the Father and the Son, except for the personal one—because this one is the Father, that one the Son—how shall the Son be created, when the Father is uncreated? Especially since relative names are spoken one in relation to the other, and by one word, the other is immediately understood: for he who has said "Father," has therein understood "Son": and he who has called him "Son," has immediately referred back to the "Father." If B therefore the Son is a creature, he cannot be truly referred to the Father, but to the Creator: and thus no one would be able to have knowledge of the Father from knowledge of the Son. But he who knows the Son, knows also the Father. Truly therefore he is the Son, and consubstantial <term>consubstantial: of the same substance or essence (Greek: homoousios)</term> with the Father. Rightly therefore can these people hear, together with the Jews: If you knew me, you would know my Father also. Furthermore, the Evangelist says: The Jews answered: We were not born of fornication, we have one father, God. Jesus said to them: If God were your father, you would surely love me: for I proceeded and came from God. For I did not come of myself, but he sent me. Those who did not love the Son of God, how can they be said to have loved God the Father, from whom the Son is? And those who did not honor the fruit, how shall they be seen to have honored the tree? But if the Son himself is the fruit of God the Father (for this is what it means, that he proceeded and came from the Father), how shall he be a creature? Or how can a non-god be naturally born from God the Father himself, when not even any creature C suffers this? For a human is born from a human, and an ox from an ox. It is necessary, therefore, for true God to be born of true God. Otherwise, generation would be found to be more true in creatures than in God: which is absurd. Moreover, the Son says he is sent by the Father, not by a change of places (for God is not in a place) but just as heat from fire, or illumination from light. Again John says: My Father who gave them to me is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father. I and the Father are one. The Father is greater than all, not as a body to bodies, but as the creator to creatures: for thus he exceeds all things, and is over all things. But the Father himself, who is over all things, is one with the Son. Wherefore the Son himself likewise, like the Father, is greater than all, and is over all things. He is not therefore a creature, but one and the D same essentially with the Father. Furthermore he says: Many good works I have shown you from my Father, for which of them therefore do you stone me? The Jews answered: We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy: because you, though you are a man, make yourself God. When our Savior said, I and the Father are one: the Jews, not understanding by whom that was said, and looking only at the flesh, accused him of the crime of impiety, and tried to stone him. For they understood this much correctly: that they thought he was making himself God, he who said, I and the Father are one. Therefore the Jews seem better than the Arians <note>Arians: followers of Arius who believed Jesus was a created being, not equal to God the Father.</note>: since they, because Christ said, I and the Father are one, saw that if this were admitted, it was necessary for Christ to be God.

176          BOOK THIRTEEN. <note>original: "LIBER DECIMVSTERTIVS" - Note that the header says Book 13, but the text below concludes Book 12 of the "Treasury." This likely refers to the volume division of this specific edition.</note>

A is in reality truly the Son of God. For he could not, if he himself were also a god merely by grace, bestow a similar dignity. Therefore, the Son of God is not a creature, but true God. *Peace be unto you*, the Savior said to the disciples: *As the Father has sent me, even so send I you.* And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them: *Receive the Holy Spirit.* That the Holy Spirit is creative by nature is also proclaimed by the Psalmist: <margin>Psalm 103 <note>Modern Psalm 104:30</note></margin> *For you shall send forth* (he says to God the Father) *your spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth.* Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit both creates and renews all things, as one who is substantially true God: how can the Son be a creature, who is the giver of the Creator's Spirit? Furthermore, when the disciples told their fellow disciple Thomas that the Savior had risen from the dead, and that they had seen him, Thomas, doubting, replied: <margin>John 20</margin> *Unless I put my hands into the places of the nails, I will not believe.* When the Lord afterwards appeared again, and showed his hands and side to Thomas, B having been recalled to a firm faith, he cried out with a loud voice: *My Lord, and my God.* Having said this, he was praised then, and is held in admiration by us now: because he truly called the Savior both Lord and God. No less blessed are those called by Christ himself, who although they have not seen him, nevertheless confess him as Lord and God (as Thomas did). How then can he be a creature, if he is God and Lord? Since these titles truly and according to nature belong only to the uncreated nature. But if the Son were a creature, as those men falsely claim, surely one would not err if he called other creatures as well (such as angels, for example) lords and gods. But he does err, and is considered impious, whoever makes for himself a "recent"—that is, a created—God and Lord. C Therefore, the Son of God is not a creature, but co-eternal with the Father. Finally, the Evangelist says: *Many other signs also Jesus did in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book: but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.* Truly the heretics do not consider what the difference is between a creature and a son. For a creature is not from the substance of the creator itself, but is produced from the outside. But that which is born from someone, and from his very nature, this we ought to properly trace back from the likeness of creatures to God: and thus we rightly understand divine things from our own. For what reason, then, if the Son of God were a creature, does the Evangelist say many signs were done by Christ, so that we might believe he is the Son of God? D Is it because it would be difficult to believe he was a creature? Certainly not; for he says the signs were written, which Jesus did, so that you might believe Christ is the Son of God, true God from true God. For those signs and miracles, with the highest power, impel us toward this understanding.

The end of the twelfth book of the Treasury by Cyril.

That the Holy Spirit is true God, that he emanates from the substance of the Father and the Son, and that he is given to creatures through the Son.

CHAPTER I.

The objection of the heretics.

**I**f, because the Spirit is said by the scriptures to be "from God," he is therefore consubstantial <note>of the same substance or essence</note> with the Father, then all things will be consubstantial with the Father. For all things are written to be "from God," and thus an innumerable multitude of gods would be introduced, which is not only impious, but even foolish. **The Solution.** It is necessary that those who wish to understand the scriptures rightly be prepared for faith. *For unless you believe, you shall not understand,* as a certain prophet said. <margin>Isaiah 7</margin> B But because many impudently hurl these objections at us, it is necessary that we strive to the best of our ability to lead them back to the truth, or at least to repel their arrows from those who believe rightly. We say, therefore, that the Holy Spirit and all other things are not said to be "from God" in the same way. For the Holy Spirit is essentially in God himself, and proceeds inseparably from him: but creatures were produced from God the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit toward the outside. But if all things are said to be from God the Father, and the Holy Spirit likewise, and they contend that there is no difference between creatures and the Holy Spirit: let them tell us, I pray, why none of the creatures knows the things that are of God? And why does none search the deep things of God? Why also does God the Father reveal his secrets through no creature, but only through the Holy Spirit? C Since, therefore, revelation is made to creatures through the Spirit, and the Spirit himself knows the deep things of God: it is clear that he is not produced from the outside like creatures, but is in God himself, and is inseparably from him: and thus he is true God, one with the Father and the Son, and not a creature. Paul testifies that these things are so, saying: <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> *But we have received the Spirit of God, that we might know the things that are given to us by God.* And again: *What man knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? Even so the things of God no one knows, except the Spirit of God who is in him.* And elsewhere: <margin>ibid.</margin> *For God has revealed them to us through the Holy Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God.* Notice that the spirit of a man does not know what is in a man through revelation, but properly and naturally knows the secrets of the heart. But the Holy Spirit likewise knows the things that are in God the Father, according to Paul. D Therefore, just as the human spirit is not foreign to the nature of man: so also the Spirit of God the Father is of the same substance with God the Father himself. *But you* (for the same Paul says) <margin>Romans 8</margin> *are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.* Learn again from Paul the right opinions concerning the Holy Spirit: for from this you have it that the Holy Spirit is from the substance of the Savior, and not foreign to the essence of the one deity. For when he called him the Spirit of God, he immediately also called him the Spirit of Christ: to show that all things which...

And so, if anyone receives the Holy Spirit, he has similarly received both the Son and the Father.
How then shall the Holy Spirit, since he is the unchangeable
image of the Son of God, be numbered among the creatures?
I do not think anyone is so insane as to dare to say that any creature
can be the unchangeable image of the Creator, and a true and perfect one,
namely so that all things are in itself which are in him whose image
it is. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is true God, since he is the most perfect

### That the Holy Spirit is perfect, and nothing in him is imperfect. CHAPTER III.
#### The objection of the heretics.

**S**ince this is so, they ask: how is it not foolish to preach that the Spirit is from the substance of God the Father, and to consider him to be God himself? For God is perfect and has no imperfection; yet the Spirit is imperfect, since he has nothing from himself, but whatever he possesses, he possesses by participation. ### On the Divine Will and Human Action

It is necessary to consider how the **Divine Will** <note>original: "Voluntas Divina"</note> relates to the actions of created beings. For as we have established in the preceding chapters, nothing occurs in the created order without the concurrence of the First Cause. 

<margin>The distinction between the hidden and revealed will.</margin>
