# **THE PROLOGUE OF SAINT CYRIL, ARCHBISHOP**
# **OF ALEXANDRIA, TO THE BOOKS OF DIALOGUES**
on the Trinity, addressed to Nemesinus, translated by Johannes Oecolampadius. <insert>by a condemned author</insert> <note>original: "auctore damnato." This handwritten note likely refers to Oecolampadius, whose works were often censored or banned by Catholic authorities during the Reformation.</note>

**D**ivine matters are difficult to comprehend, even for those who are highly practiced in contemplating secrets and things that transcend the grasp of the mind. For as human reason is exceedingly dull, and unequal to these things due to frequent [distracting] thoughts, even they see—according to the most wise Paul—as if in a mirror and a riddle. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12.</note> Hence it is no wonder if speaking of God is dangerous; so much so, that the wise judge silence to be more preferable, which would nonetheless be detrimental to those to whom the duty of teaching has been entrusted. Knowing this, the blessed Paul said: "Woe to me, if I do not preach the gospel." Approaching therefore the labors of the present book, I have prepared for you, Nemesinus, most learned brother, this work concerning the holy and consubstantial <term>consubstantial: of the same essence or substance</term> Trinity. I have divided the entire body of the volume into seven books, having brought together those things which are usually questioned regarding each point, whether in general or in specific. I have spoken with Hermias, a man both most learned and most fair, which is why the style of speaking is quite humble, being in the form of a dialogue between two persons conversing with one another, one of whom is marked by **α** [Alpha], the other by **β** [Beta]. The introduction of characters seemed necessary because of the great subtlety required in frequent questioning, while that which is being investigated is always being confirmed or refuted. Therefore, let the aforementioned letters be diligently observed, so that a distinct and orderly discovery of the meanings, and thus the order and virtue of the whole book, may be maintained. I pray that you fare well in the Lord, beloved.

**Contents in this volume of dialogues on the Trinity.**

That the Son is consubstantial and co-eternal with God the Father. **Book I.**

That the Son is both co-eternal with God the Father, and begotten from Him according to nature. **Book II.**

That the Son is true God, just as the Father is. **Book III.**

That the Son is neither a creature nor a thing made. **Book IV.**

That the properties and glory of the Deity are naturally in the Son, just as in the Father. **Book V.**

That the properties of humanity, and those things said of the Son that do not sound divine, belong rather to the dispensation <term>dispensation: the "economy" or plan of God regarding Christ's human life</term> in the flesh, and not to the nature of the Word, according to which He is understood to be and is God. **Book VI.**

Concerning the Holy Spirit: that He is both God and from God according to nature. **Book VII.**

<margin>God is indicated in two ways.</margin>
For he is known by us either through those things which he *is*, or through those things which he *is not*. deed, the power of the names repels confusion in a way, and requires a firm and, as it were, immobile seat in the thing itself, attributed to each in such a way. For the Father is Father, and not Son, because he begat; and the Son, again, is Son, because he was begotten. Therefore, that which is his and his alone is proper to the one, although other things are said of them indiscriminately. For those other things are left in the order of natural dignities, but these [names] are not so; rather, they demonstrate partly the Begetter and partly the Begotten.

I have spoken blamelessly in saying that he is indeed called unbegotten <note>original: *ingenitus*</note>, yet not because he is Father in every respect *because* he is unbegotten, but because he is not begotten by anyone. It is true that in being unbegotten, he has from himself and in himself his own begotten Son, and for this reason he is named Father. HERMAS: And let these things be so, they will say; nevertheless, that which exists in an unbegotten way will be different from that which exists in a begotten way, and they will not be understood as the same. For if they are not different things—imagine indeed that they were the same—it would follow again that a change would occur inseparably in both, and the property of the names would be the same for the Father and the Son, just as he is called incorruptible and invisible, etc.
CYRIL: No one can dodge the fact that being in an unbegotten way is one thing, and being in a begotten way is another. For we do not forget the order of what is honest and true; nevertheless, in such matters, the difference of names does not imply a diversity of nature, as of God compared to God, but signifies only that he is not in such a manner—that is, not begotten. Therefore, what will they say to this, they who confuse all things indiscriminately among themselves, even though they are very severe in these matters and are puffed up with a haughty brow? HERMAS: Does "unbegotten," then, happen to be an accident <term>accident: a philosophical term for a quality that is not essential to a thing's nature, like hair color on a person</term> in God the Father? CYRIL: Not at
<margin>In God, "unbegotten" is not an accident.</margin>
all. For God is understood simultaneously with all things that are his, and no accident is understood to be in him. Do not wonder at this, since even in ourselves, those who wish to see the matter thus perceive it without difficulty. For we, who began to exist in time, define ourselves together with those things which are substantially and inseparably within us. Nothing, therefore, is rightly understood in God that "happens" to him as an accident. And even if there were accidents which naturally exist in the substances of certain things, they are not entirely the things themselves in their own distinct difference, as we understand in a human being, or at least in anything else that exists. It seems rather that we ought to conjecture what place "unbegotten" holds in God regarding the essences of things. For if "unbegotten" stood by itself and had its own existence, and if this were, as they say, the property of God the Father, it would be something different from him to whom it belongs. For that which is and exists as a properly subsisting thing is certainly entirely different from that to which it belongs, and consequently the simple nature of the Father would be made double, composed of "Father" and "unbegotten." We must attend, however, not to their shadowy wisdom, but to the words of the Savior, who distinguishes well between his own nature and the nature of him who begot him. He never named him "the Unbegotten" to us, but rather

And again: "I confess to thee, O Lord, Father of heaven and earth." Moreover, he says this: "I came out from the Father and have come." Why, then, did he not also establish this term ["unbegotten"] in holy baptism, and lay it in the beginning as the foundation of the immaculate faith for those in the whole world? Did he not, passing over the fact that they are incorruptible and unbegotten, command to baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit? By which I am led by clear reasons, as I think, to see that the holy Trinity is not declared to us by those [other] terms; rather, he collected and proposed before others the names that most distinctly establish for us the proper existence of each signified person. For those things which are innate to the supreme substance would be called "common," so to speak, to the whole Trinity. And indeed, if anyone were to name the "divine nature," he would show us the holy Trinity immediately as a whole in one meaning, which is understood in one deity. Nevertheless, one would not yet manifest the person properly. But by saying Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit, he does not make a manifestation of all the nature of the deity indiscriminately, but of those in whom the identity of the holy Trinity is discerned, into the substance of those who are understood in their own subsistences <term>subsistence: the individual reality or "personhood" of the Father, Son, or Spirit</term>, the discourse distributing to each the convenient name and placing them in their own subsistences, which are substantially united. For you shall understand the Father as the supreme root beyond which you understand nothing, and you shall receive the Son as born and begotten from the supreme root—not having obtained his condition in time on an equal rank with the creatures, nor declaring the beauty of his nature in lesser things than those in which the Father is, but being simultaneous and co-eternal, and having an equal measure through all things, except for this: that he [the Father] begot, which belongs to God the Father alone. Likewise, we name the Holy Spirit as flowing naturally from God the Father through the Son, and as if in the figure of the breath <note>original: *spirationis*</note> which is from his mouth, to designate the subsistence to us. For thus, preserving the manifest and unconfused property of the three subsistences in their own existences, you shall adore one and consubstantial nature, the queen of all. HERMAS: You have spoken excellently; for these things were said by me not because they are so [in reality]. They say, nonetheless, that the nature is properly defined by the word "unbegotten" of God the Father, so that afterwards they may declare without labor that the Son is of another nature, since "begotten" is not the same as "unbegotten."
CYRIL: Therefore we shall say to them most rightly, and deservedly: if "begotten" defines the nature of the Son, and for this reason he is of another nature and foreign to the substance of the Father, what follows from that? Truly stupendous crimes and blasphemous opinions which would rashly dare to strike down the supreme substance of the Only-begotten to inferior things, although he says clearly to us as to created beings: "You are from below," but of his own subsistence,
<margin>John 8.</margin>
"I am from above." How, then, is he supreme and from above...

<summary>Cyril argues that "Father" and "Son" are the proper names for the divine persons because they describe their relationship and shared substance, whereas "unbegotten" is merely a description of how the Father exists, not a definition of his essence that would exclude the Son.</summary>

Therefore, I would not say that anyone should grant that the Only-begotten shares every common definition with the Unbegotten <note>original: "ingenito"; referring to God the Father who was not created or born</note>, at least in regard to the manner of being unbegotten. For in that case, according to the logic that follows such reasoning, the Begotten <note>the Son</note> would also have a similar and equal definition with everything else that is created. Furthermore, how is this ambiguous? For the same reasoning exists in both cases without change. And so, O Hermias, you will speak of an impiety that is by no means to be despised; or rather, you can forget the deceitful speech of our adversaries, which indeed has a painted-on appearance and is adorned with divine little words, so that it is able to carry away the minds of the simpler folk and give birth to the most foul blasphemy. # DIALOGUES OF THE DIVINE CYRIL
## ON THE TRINITY

receive the force of a definition, whether they wish that A word to be a **genus**, or a signifier of a **difference**. <note>In Aristotelian logic, a definition consists of a "genus" (a broad category) and a "specific difference" (the trait that distinguishes a species within that category).</note> Therefore, if they say it is a genus, let it signify nothing else and be exempt from others, so that we are not caught adding the force of a specific difference to a genus, and removing it from its own proper force. But if they pass over this and say it is a difference, let them show us at the same time what it is a difference *of*, since no word for a genus has yet been put forward. How then will a substantial definition be sufficient, and be composed of a difference alone according to its own proper reasoning? Will they not necessarily provoke laughter if they continue to behave this way? HERMES: They will clearly provoke it; there is no doubt. CYRIL: Therefore, if someone wished to say to these things—which completely defiles their dogma and is full of the extreme of false accusation—how would he not speak the truest things? HERMES: Tell me with an example, what? CYRIL: As I said before, a definition of substance is never rightly made from one thing alone. B For a genus is always understood in a certain way before the proper differences; from which, as if starting from a barrier, the discourse goes forth succinctly and sends itself distinctly into the things that follow, and makes a right and indubitable manifestation. If, therefore, "unbegotten" fulfills the force of a term, they contend unskillfully, for it will not be a difference. For it signifies to us nothing further than that it is not begotten, but neither will we permit the word to have such power. Let it rather be assumed among them as a genus, simply and indistinctly, even though it does not have a congruent reason; nevertheless, let it be supposed that "unbegotten" is the genus in Him, according to what pleases those inconsiderate men. C But a genus signifies nothing at all to us if it does not take the place and force of a difference; while the voice of the "unbegotten" brings no further exposition than that of not being begotten, what kind of difference will it exhibit to us of the Father with the Son? Or how will He have less according to something, even if He is understood to exist as begotten? Indeed, I certainly do not understand; but what do you say, Hermes? HERMES: What could possibly be said to this, I pray? CYRIL: Now I think we have refuted sufficiently and clearly that "unbegotten" receives the force of a definition neither healthily nor learnedly. Nor is it our custom to use such discourses, but we grant this to necessity, because against our will and beyond what is D owed, we are occupied in their discipline. It is not difficult, however, to add other opinions to those already found. I will attempt it as far as I can. For those who are very eloquent and studious, and exercised in such matters, say that **conversion** <note>In logic, "conversion" means the subject and predicate can be swapped while remaining true (e.g., "Every human is a rational animal" and "Every rational animal is a human").</note> applies to every definition. HERMES: And what is this? How eagerly I would hear it from you. CYRIL: Therefore, I am in the same discourses, and I shall ask in a scholarly way. For we define a man with such a speech: "He is a rational, mortal animal"; and a horse with such: "It is a neighing animal." We shall also make another manifestation of the aforementioned things, not at all from the first, but from the last words going backward to the definition of the principle. For if something is a mortal

-> 231 <-

and rational animal, you will understand it to be a man: or again, if something is a neighing animal, this will show the nature of a horse. If, therefore, "unbegotten" is a definition, why does it not accept conversion? For they confess that if anything is unbegotten, this is the term and substance of God the Father; but it is not a true speech. For there are innumerable things <note>Cyril likely refers to things like "space" or "time" which some philosophers argued were unbegotten, or simply that the term is too vague.</note>, and it would be difficult to enumerate them. Do you perceive into how great an absurdity the discourse reaches? HERMES: Yes, into a very grave one. CYRIL: We shall consider, moreover, if by another reason than that one, "unbegotten" cannot be a definition. For we define each one of these things from those things out of which it is believed to be, and truly is. For it does not happen that one is deprived of those things from which he is not, as if from some things. HERMES: How do you say? CYRIL: For wishing to preach by nature what or of what sort fire or water each may be: concerning fire indeed we say that it is a hot and dry body; but concerning the other, that it is moist and cold; and this, I think, is to define them from those things out of which they are. But if we were to say, explaining the nature of fire, that it is neither cold nor moist, and we omitted to say that it is hot and dry; and concerning water, that it is neither hot nor dry, when it ought to be said that it is cold and moist—from what would we seem to you to have made a manifestation? HERMES: From those things of which they are deprived, and which by confession they are not. CYRIL: Therefore, if it seems to anyone that he should think and speak thus about any matter, would he have demonstrated the truth distinctly and simply in each one? HERMES: Not at all. CYRIL: Accordingly, if concerning God and the Father, "unbegotten" only manifests to us that He is not begotten, in what way does it have the force of a definition? Because it signifies in this way not *what* He is, but *what He is not*. HERMES: You say that He is not begotten at all? CYRIL: So I said, for the force of the word has this in a certain way. But what does he think again, if we add and say that the substantiality of a term has no opposite difference necessarily, nor will they be received into the order of relatives, so that if someone names one, he also remembers the other in some way. For always through both, the manifestation of the other is judged at the same time. HERMES: The speech is not very clear to me. CYRIL: Nevertheless, nothing prevents it from being clearly understood by you. For if someone names a "Father," he certainly leads the mind of the listeners to think of a "Son," or simply and rudely of "offspring": that which would also be true conversely of a "Son." For the "begetter" comes at the same time with the significance of the "offspring." Similarly, "right" and "left" behave in an equal way, for the one is named with these and is born at the same time. But he who utters the definition of the substance of a man, or of any other animal, joins no opposite to it—that is, something that must arise from the opposite, just as "left" is in "right," or "Son" in "Father," or "that which is begotten" in "the begetter." For a man is a man, and a stone is a stone, and nothing to them...

<summary>Cyril argues that "unbegotten" is a negative attribute rather than a formal definition of God's essence, using Aristotelian logic to show that a definition must state what a thing is, not what it is not.</summary>

234 SAINT CYRIL

...to call God "Father," is it because he himself perfected the race of all creatures, or because we have been crowned with the glory of the adoption of sons, and are reckoned among his children? HERMIAS: By nature, certainly, we are as creatures; but by grace, we are sons. CYRIL: But in this case, if he were not named "Father," and the "Son" likewise, would it not imply that the Son is a mere creation, and that the relationship of a created thing would then seem incidental to him? For the Father has a relationship to the Son, and the Son to the Father, without any obstacle, just as the creator relates to the creature, and the creature to the creator. Now, if I take away from each what is proper to them, and the power of those terms which are spoken in relation to something else, we shall be found to inflict an insult: treating the Father as a creature, and assigning to the Son some relational force derived from terms used for a maker. How shall we not then, and quite deservedly, provoke laughter at such extreme madness? HERMIAS: We shall call God "Father" as sons do, but I think it would be the mark of the foolish to contend over superfluities. CYRIL: But he would not be a Father according to the truth, nor would there be a Son, unless one understands him who begat and him who is begotten. HERMIAS: You have spoken rightly. CYRIL: Let God be so called, then, if it pleases you, by an abusive figure of speech <note>original: "tropo abusiuo" — a rhetorical term meaning a word used outside its strict literal sense, a catachresis</note>; from where then did he kindly find this title, if indeed he is not a Father according to nature? Perhaps from us, who will say we are fathers by nature and in truth? HERMIAS: From those he has benefited, for they say this too. CYRIL: What exactly? Shall we not posit that the blessed Paul attributes the beginning of fatherhood not to us, nor to any of the creatures, but sets it apart and consecrates it, in a way, to God alone, the first Father? For one may hear him writing to us: *From whom all <margin>Ephesians 3</margin> fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.* Answer then, O Hermias, to exercise our discourse. If we wish to learn: Was God made "unbegotten" in time, having not been so from the beginning, or is he understood to be unbegotten and to have existed in an unbegotten way simultaneously? HERMIAS: He existed in an unbegotten way. For to say anything other than this—how could it not be utterly absurd? CYRIL: Does the word "unbegotten" signify "not having been begotten," or what? HERMIAS: Certainly, not having been begotten. CYRIL: Why was it necessary for God, who lacks a beginning, to appear entirely as such? Or what distinction did the speech or nature form against certain people, if indeed his nature is unbegotten, when as yet nothing was begotten or co-existing? For they say the Father is not the begetter of the Son. To what end is he "unbegotten," if the substance of the begotten is still entirely hidden? For they would not say this, lest those things created in the manner of the begotten should seem to lack a beginning and be co-eternal with the unbegotten God. And if indeed the Father were always unbegotten, since he is God, it must be absolutely assumed that he is so called because of him for whose sake he is "unbegotten"—that is, because of the Son who is in the manner of the born. Enriched by his image, and having attained a configuration through virtue and piety, we call God "Father," and we too, according to the likeness of the

highest and first Father, are named fathers. The originals are older than the images. HERMIAS: And what prevents our adversaries from calling God "Father" in an abusive sense, since we are fathers entirely according to nature, while he is called Father because he was the author of existence for those who were made? Having existence as an unbegotten power in his substance. CYRIL: Yet the divine Paul truly testified to us how the name of fatherhood is received from him, against every rational creation, according to the likeness and imitation of the First, clearly showing that this is so even in ourselves. But he did not say that from him is every "unbegottenness" in heaven and on earth. Is it necessary that nothing be born at all, so that the image of the Unbegotten might be signified in the saints? For nothing so adorns a creature as to be shaped and fashioned after that which is above all things. CYRIL: Not this, I say, but I think the absurdity of the senses should be gathered from there; the wise word will persuade us to depart as far as possible from them: *Keep yourself pure, and do not <margin>1 Timothy 5</margin> share in the sins of others,* adding this well. For since we ought to love and hold fast to the blameless opinion of the holy fathers: why do we delight in foreign things, and become participants in such a fierce mind? For it is a fierce mind that barks against the glory of the Son, and speaks against the justice of God, as it is written. For it seemed quite right to those famous men, who were the calm and most approved stewards of the mysteries of our Savior, that the substance of God is in no way "unbegotten," but the word only signifies to listeners "not begotten," which we certainly say exists in the discourse concerning the subsistence of the God and Father, <margin>Some things are substances, others are accidents.</margin> not as the very thing of God's substance. For to those who wish to consider it, because all things that belong to us, or even that they exist, are in our conjecture, as if in a fashioned state of substance: some things are in their own seats, and have obtained in their subsistences to be what they are; but others are not so, but are rather "seats": not founded in their own natures, but they surround the essences of things, because of which they can happen <note>term: "accidere" — to occur as an 'accident,' a philosophical property that is not essential to a thing's nature</note> to someone, or certainly it must be said to appear to someone, that they subsist with those who have them, and put on a foreign nature as if it were their own. HERMIAS: How do you mean? CYRIL: Do you not remember the discourse we made, which was well demonstrated to the best of our ability? That those things which are numbered in the order of accidents, or simply of inherent things, are by no means seen to exist in themselves, but rather in others: and they seem indeed to exist and be spoken of according to themselves, but they have the nature of that which they have obtained as if it were their own. For a thing does not exist as the same thing by itself and in substance which is "begotten" and "unbegotten," but these only manifest to us either being begotten or not being begotten. HERMIAS: You speak well. CYRIL:

CYRIL: Therefore, one must consider that "unbegottenness" itself exists as a description of the subsistence <note>Greek: *hypostasis*, the distinct personhood</note> of God the Father; it should be placed as belonging to His essence, but not as the essence itself. For consider the absurdity here, if you please. For if they say that "unbegotten" truly constitutes the substance, what is to stop us from thinking and saying that the countless things which exist as "begotten" <note>created things</note> do not actually possess any substance, even though they have obtained existence in a begotten way? For whatever was not unbegotten would depart and fall away from essence, so as not to exist at all. HERMES: It would indeed fall away. CYRIL: And how should that not also be appropriately said to them? For if they say the substance of God the Father is "unbegotten," and they set this apart as His own unique nature to the exclusion of others, then God—who is above all substance and beyond all things—must consequently be thought of as existing in a begotten way, lying within a certain private nature that has nothing naturally in common with the other. For what would be the relationship of the begotten to the unbegotten, regarding the substantial quality in which it exists? Then what evil would those men say—bold as they are in anything—who see those things which are proper to God the Father also in the offspring, that is, the Son? For the Father is Life and Light and true God, but the Son is these things also, not by participation or by comparison, but substantially and in an equal manner. Do you not perceive that hereafter, they would rather call the unique and excellent qualities of the deity the "reason and mode of unbegottenness," so that we might not say those things belong to others which are seen to exist and subsist without birth? But it is more fitting for God the Father. For in this way they later pass, as it were, to the Son, who is also from Him by nature. I think this alone: that He is the same in substance. Therefore, "unbegotten" is by no means the substance of God, but signifies, as I said, only that the Father is not begotten, and it is not a self-subsisting thing. HERMES: That is correct. But perhaps the adversaries might say: "If you say the Son exists in identity as begotten, and is consubstantial <note>of the same substance; *homoousios*</note> with God the Father, you will not be troubled now to understand that He also always co-exists, and was born not without passion <note>suffering or change</note> and 'outflow' from Him by whom He is said to be born—even though it entirely persuades us that the cause of anything pre-exists the effect, and that everything which is produced follows in some way the nature of that which is born, for it precedes it as a parent. Let birth, therefore, precede in nature and truth, in every way and entirely bringing about the necessity of a 'flow' or change in that nature which is above all passion and free from harm." CYRIL: Now, is this not plainly what I was saying? For by their own words they achieve what they want to be understood. Just as dyes, when a new color is introduced, change into other forms and turn readily to whatever they are moved toward. Nor do I think those who are affected by such a small argument differ from a reed. Although it was not to be allowed that they should love such things and become like children; rather, they ought to cast away those adulterated things as useless. For they destroy the best mind, so that they are moved incautiously toward anything, seizing whatever comes into the mind and valuing every rotten and weak argument. Furthermore, I would call this a slavish thing and

of a weak mind. But to us Paul said: *Brothers, do not be children in your senses, but be children in malice, and be perfect in your senses.* <margin>1 Corinthians 14</margin> For to understand less than one ought, and to pass toward the knowledge of truth less than is sufficient—even in more perfect men, and those no longer youths or poorly taught, but coming into the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ—is indecorous and least worthy of the saints. There is no doubt what damage this brings to those in whom it settles, so that it is difficult to erase. HERMES: It is not otherwise; you speak rightly. CYRIL: Do you wish, then, that we leave these things—let them be however they wish—and proceed so that we may oppose the truth to their trifles? HERMES: Certainly. For this will be more useful. CYRIL: Therefore, I do not know from where they have taken and named "cause" and "effect," for they do not say this from the divine Scripture; why then do they believe themselves to be wise? HERMES: For you recently heard them saying how the cause is always in some way in an older knowledge and subsistence than the effect, and that a generator never generates without passion and "outflow," and circulating that, they affirm the Son is less than the Father. They make Him out to be such, and in a way "late-born," and perhaps even impiously spreading this untrue birth, they slander the sincerity which comes from the substance. CYRIL: Therefore, let them tell those saying that: do they perhaps believe the Father is something to the Son as if to one existing in the order of creation and the arranged manner of craftsmanship in creatures, or not so? At the same time they will say that, according to the true mode of birth, that which is begotten proceeds from our own substance. HERMES: Just as they call Him Father or Founder. For being simple and above substance, just as God is understood to found, so also to generate. For they say that He who is simple does not compose an operation of only one species. CYRIL: This also would be to turn everything upside down, and to greatly confound the well-distinguished nature of things without composition, and to throw into a promiscuous sewer those things which a long and diligent discourse separates like the flowing of equal rivers. For so a certain Gentile philosopher used to say: "It is one thing to found and another to beget," and every reason will support us in this. <margin>To beget and to found are different.</margin> I certainly think that he who rightly holds foreign opinions <note>secular philosophy</note> and is founded in good faith, does not absurdly attribute simplicity to the Father, nor confound the discourse concerning Him. For if He founds just as He begets, and no distinction is understood between them, nor do they relate in different ways, I would not fear to say that of whomever one is the craftsman, of those he is also the father; and everything that is made would be understood to be His offspring. How many such things there are, and in how many species and differences, is indeed difficult to say; yet among those who wish to weigh it, there is nothing that does not admit the statement that it was made. There are, in all ways, among beings even those which are extreme outcasts, nor does anyone deny this. Therefore, will God be the Father of all things, if such things be true? HERMES: And how would that not be most absurd?

**SAINT CYRILL’S DIALOGUE ON THE** <note>The title is truncated; likely "On the Holy Trinity." Cyril of Alexandria was a 5th-century Church Father known for defending the divinity of Christ.</note>

->Is this discourse?<- CYRIL. Certainly, you would rather call it beyond the height of impiety, if you wish to speak correctly. For if they say that with God the Father, "to create" and "to beget" are the same thing, and truly indistinct, and that they do not exist in a different manner because of the simplicity of His substance, then first of all they are asserting that the Holy Scripture is a fable when it names Him the "only-begotten" Son. For in that case, He would truly be (as the adversaries claim) merely one among many brothers—indeed, among all things together which have been granted existence. He would be perhaps "begotten" only in the sense of being produced into existence by the industry of a craftsman. For to those people, both of these things seem to be the same and not to differ in manner. Furthermore, even our great teacher John himself would have committed a slip of the tongue while pronouncing the mysteries concerning the Son, stating that He is the "only-begotten" in the bosom of God the Father <note>original: "unigenitus sit in sinu dei ac pat[ris]" - a reference to the Gospel of John 1:18.</note>

We shall therefore receive the operation of fulfillment in two ways and dissimilarly; and unless the fullness of the Father were to be sufficient for those in whom he works for salvation (being a certain divine thing and the other better), what would the Son have perfectly worked in us, since he would have applied something inferior, if indeed he did not work in the same way as the Father? But if we understand the fulfillment we receive through the Son as a useful and necessary provision for salvation, it must certainly be said that the more excellent thing had need of the inferior, and that he applied a lesser thing to that which was lacking in the more excellent, since the fulfillment of God the Father would not have been sufficient in all things to save us. Truly, to think and say that this is irreproachable, I would say is a crime and fault of the highest stupidity. Therefore, let us cast away that madness as most absurd; let us judge and believe that there is one efficacy and fulfillment in us through both. For there is one nature. Now, natures which are forced into a difference between themselves, understood according to diversity and declared as most foreign, would not have uniformity according to act and equality in all ways in any matters; but where the reason for being in some things were different, it would entirely follow there that even what is according to act does not behave similarly. HERMIAS: It is true, yet I would gladly hear from you how the fulfillment of both the Father and the Son is understood and happens in us, since it is one certain thing and not diverse. HERMIAS: It would not be otherwise. CYRILLVS: Therefore we must now proceed to the nature of the Holy Spirit itself, which we shall consider with diligent examination. # On the Internal Senses

## Chapter 10
### On the Common Sense

The **Common Sense** <note>Latin: *sensus communis*</note> is an internal power of the sensitive soul, by which the perceptions of the five external senses are received, distinguished, and judged. It is called "common" because it is the common center or goal where all the lines of the external senses meet, just as lines from the circumference of a circle meet at the center.

Its functions are twofold:
1. **To perceive the actions of the external senses.** For example, when we see, we *know* that we see. The eye itself sees, but it does not perceive that it sees; that is the task of the common sense.
2. **To distinguish between the objects of different senses.** For example, to discern the difference between white and sweet. The eye knows white but not sweet; the tongue knows sweet but not white. Therefore, there must be a higher, internal faculty that perceives both and can judge the difference between them.

## Chapter 11
### On the Phantasy or Imagination

The **Phantasy** <note>also known as the Imaginative faculty</note> is an internal power of the sensitive soul that retains the forms <note>mental images or "species"</note> received from the common sense and can combine or divide them.

Its functions are:
1. **Retention:** It acts as a storehouse for the images brought in by the senses, keeping them even when the physical object is no longer present.
2. **Apprehension:** It gazes upon these stored images.
3. **Composition and Division:** It can join different images together—such as imagining a "Golden Mountain" by combining the image of gold with the image of a mountain—or separate them.

->**The Difference between Common Sense and Phantasy**<-

| Common Sense | Phantasy |
| :--- | :--- |
| Perceives objects only when they are **present**. | Perceives objects even when they are **absent**. |
| Only receives forms from the external senses. | Can create new forms by combining existing ones. |
| Located in the anterior <note>front</note> part of the brain. | Located in the middle part of the brain. |

<margin>The Phantasy is more noble than the common sense because it is less tied to the immediate presence of matter.</margin>

<column-break/>

### On the Estimative and Memorative Faculties

The **Estimative Faculty** <note>often called "Instinct" in animals</note> is that by which the soul perceives "intentions" that are not captured by the external senses, such as usefulness or danger. 
<gloss>Example: A sheep flees from a wolf not because of its color or sound, but because it perceives "enmity" through this faculty.</gloss>

The **Memorative Faculty** <note>Memory</note> is the storehouse of these "intentions." While the Phantasy stores the *forms* of things (how they look/smell), the Memory stores the *judgments* made about them (whether they were good or bad).

<insert>In humans, this is called the **Cogitative Faculty**, because it is guided by reason.</insert>

<summary>This section defines the internal senses—Common Sense, Phantasy, Estimation, and Memory—explaining how the mind processes, stores, and judges sensory information beyond simple physical contact.</summary>

<keywords>internal senses, common sense, phantasy, imagination, estimative faculty, memory, cognition, psychology</keywords>

### On the Nature of the Elements

It is necessary to consider the primary qualities that govern the physical world. As the ancients taught, the balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness forms the foundation of all material existence. <note>The author refers to the four Aristotelian qualities.</note>

->**The First Principle**<-

When we observe the transformation of water into vapor, we see the action of heat overcoming the natural density of the liquid. <margin>See the commentary on Aristotle's *Physics*, Book II</margin> This process is not a destruction of the substance, but a change in its outward form. <gloss>The essence remains unchanged</gloss>

| Element | Primary Quality | Secondary Quality |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Fire | Hot | Dry |

We must also note that "nothing comes from nothing" <note>original: "ex nihilo nihil fit"</note>, a principle that guides our understanding of chemical reactions. Even when a substance seems to vanish, it has merely dispersed into the surrounding air. <insert>This is especially true of volatile spirits.</insert>

The prophet Isaiah will also cry out with his words, <margin>Isaiah 26</margin> saying: *Lord our God, give us your peace, for you have given us all things: Lord, besides you we know no other, we name your name.* <note>original: "Domine deus noster, tuam pacem da nobis..." Cyril is quoting the Septuagint version of Isaiah 26:12-13.</note> And so I think they meant that peace is every good thing. HERMIAS: It is so. CYRIL: Therefore, peace is the fruit and the gift of heavenly power, and as I have already said, it belongs to no creature, but to God alone by nature. HERMIAS: And what is this? CYRIL: Namely, that he is God by nature and truly the Son. For the wise Paul says of God the Father: *The God and Father of our <margin>2 Corinthians 11</margin> <note>The margin says 2 Cor 12, but the quote is from 11:31.</note> Lord Jesus Christ knows, who is blessed forever, that I do not lie.* Now, immediately placing an equal crown of honor and glory upon the Son, fearing nothing—since he knew him to be God by nature and in truth—he writes in his epistle where he declares the rejection of the Jews: <margin>Romans 9</margin> *For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites... whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever, Amen.* Shall we then place him, who is God over all, under God along with all other things, as if he were not truly God, and count him among those who are adopted by grace? Although he has been allotted to be "over all"—I speak of that great and divine dignity—and to be "blessed over all," and that perpetually and without end, with the seal of the word "Amen": will opponents of a sound mind think this? HERMIAS: Not at all; he has a more sound mind who confesses the Son to be true God and born of true God, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father with the Holy Spirit forever and ever, Amen.

ST. CYRIL'S DIALOGUES ON THE [TRINITY] 287

<margin>A</margin> THE FOURTH BOOK of the dialogues of ST. CYRIL, ARCHBISHOP of Alexandria, with Hermias: that the Son is not a creature nor a thing made.

CYRIL.

**N**ONE is there who, failing to place him who was brought forth from God according to an ineffable birth in the glory of a natural son, but instead asserting that he was made and formed, deserves the punishment which we say is intended for those who blaspheme the glory of God? Sacred Scripture supports this: *He who curses his God shall bear his sin, and he who names the name of the Lord, let him <margin>Leviticus 24</margin> die the death; let all the congregation stone him, whether he be a stranger or a native, because he named the name of the Lord, let him die.* <margin>B</margin> HERMIAS: I do not think he will escape without receiving the punishment he deserves. CYRIL: It would be best then, Hermias, not to care for the insolence of others who take away our proven mind, but rather to applaud the right and not perverse rule of faith—that is, the discourses made by the apostles—and no others than those themselves, and to say: *It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.* HERMIAS: Most rightly then. Therefore, they know how to adore the only-begotten Word of God, not as something made, nor as having obtained a transition to being created; but they say he is the co-eternal and concurrent fruit of the substance of the Begetter, and they name him Son and true God, and eternal life. <margin>C</margin> Whence John, the teacher of divine mysteries, says: *And we know that the Son of God has come, and has given us understanding, that we may know the true God, and we are in his true [Son] Jesus Christ. This is the true <margin>1 John 5</margin> God and eternal life.* CYRIL: But, my good man, even if the Son is true God, is he nonetheless a creature and a thing made, even though he has obtained such noble glory? Does not this assertion also prejudice the substance of God the Father, with nothing to stop it? HERMIAS: How so? CYRIL: Was not God himself also named "true," and does he not give life to all things, being life according to nature? For *in him we live, and <margin>Acts 17</margin> move, and have our being,* as the wise word also said? HERMIAS: True. CYRIL: Let that crude and blasphemous speech then reach him too, and <margin>D</margin> let him be called "made." For there is nothing to prohibit or hinder it, once true deity allows the Son to be among creatures, and somehow to be moved away from eternal life, so that he is life for other creatures indiscriminately, as if by necessity, and received an existence measured in time. For that which is made is not without a beginning, nor older than all time. HERMIAS: My friend, what a grave matter this is, and an accusation of impiety truly hard to avoid! CYRIL: And so it can be well avoided. For it allows those who wish to depart easily, and by repelling the destructive and harmful speech of the adversaries, they piously attribute victory to the voices of the saints. For nowhere did they celebrate the Father as the "maker" of the only-begotten, but rather as the "begetter," whom they also placed as the light of the world, not being ignorant of his own [nature].

A learns what the "left" is. Furthermore, each one will testify to this truth by its opposite. Therefore, the name "Father" is a relative term, and just as that is, so equally is "Son." Toward what, then, will these look to create this relation and mutual habit, the fitting logic of which they never abandon? And to whom is this obscure? Therefore, if the word is true, either God the Father must be brought down into the ranks of creatures, lest He seem to give more glory to the Son than is due, or certainly the Son must be raised up into the dignity of the Godhead and the nature of Sonship, which is understood substantially. For He would be in no way and by no means less than God the Father, if it is seen to be so. And the wise John will support us, saying: "He who comes from above is above all." Furthermore, that the word "from above" commends to us a high and supreme nature, the disciple of the Savior will teach, saying: "Every good <margin>James 1</margin> gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights." Therefore the Son descends to us from the Father as from a fountain, and born from the highest root.

How then do they not speak proudly and ignorantly against the Father, when they deny that he is the founder of those things of which they say he is God, although they hear Christ speaking, who admires the providence of God the Father: *Are not two sparrows sold for a penny, and not one of them falls to the ground without your Father, who is in heaven?* <note>Matthew 10:29</note> But he who extends his providence even to sparrows, how would he reject founding the angels and strengthening the heaven, and joining the earth, and bringing forth the sun and moon and C stars, in which he is also admirable in praises, with the holy angels following him as magnificent? For he said when the stars were made: *All my angels praised me with a loud voice.* <note>Job 38:7</note> Do I not seem to you to have considered probable things, and to speak rightly? HER. Very much so. CYR. Tell me, I pray, would you not say that there is nothing, neither small nor great among creatures, that is not from divine power? HER. Not at all. CYR. Now how is it not foolish for them to be named divine works, and said to be made through the Son, yet not to believe that he himself is God, but to count him among the things made as if he were of the same nature with them? For that which is made is no longer God. Furthermore, creatures would no longer be D demonstrative of the eminence of their substantial maker, having obtained a nature no less and no different than how the founder is perhaps understood. And understanding this well, the divine Paul writes to us: *For his invisible things are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and divinity.* <note>Romans 1:20</note> Is his divinity known, and his eternal and similarly-situated power, while the Word, the founder of all, is understood as being made? For these things are eternal. But I think nothing at all will now prevent the creature from being called by the name of deity, so that it too might boast. And how then will visible things show us his deity, and no longer God's? HER. What then, if they should say the deity of the Father and his eternal power are declared through the magnificence of the things made—

<summary>Cyril argues against the idea that God the Father is too exalted to create "lowly" things like sparrows or insects, asserting that both the Father and the Son are involved in all levels of creation. He uses Platonic philosophy and Biblical citations to prove that God's goodness and providence extend to the smallest creatures, affirming the Son's divinity as the Creator.</summary>

306 DIVINE CYRIL.

And it is similarly the case with anything nature has ever seen, which at some point did not exist and was made. HERMIAS: So it is.
CYRIL: But I also think the opposite is true. For in that which never was, we would not have seen something always and similarly existing. HERMIAS: True.
CYRIL: What, then, is now worthy of admiration in us from that configuration to Christ? Or where is the divine beauty in the souls of believers, as something unusual? Since for everything that is made, in relation to that which is made—insofar as it is understood to be made—the law of nature dictates that nothing of the same species is foreign to it. Every creature would therefore always be conformed to the Son if he were made; what kind of beauty, then, is instilled in our souls through the Spirit, who would be acting superfluously and adding in vain that which one would attain even if they did not wish it? For that which we possess according to nature, and which one has intrinsically, one has not received from another. But every right reason, free from error, will laugh at this. We who have believed are all partners in the divine nature, because of our relationship with the Son through the Spirit—not so much in mere opinion, but in truth—and we are configured to God, returning to the highest beauty. For Christ is formed ineffably <note>original: "ineffabiliter" — in a way that cannot be expressed in words</note> in us, not as one made among made things, but as one not made; and God, in a created and made nature, forms us to his own image, which he carves through the Spirit, and transfers the creature—that is, us—to a dignity that is above the creature. HERMIAS: Therefore, there is nothing that turns away or transfers the Only-begotten from true sonship. But we shall grant that he is both made and not made. CYRIL: Yes, if indeed we have received him as God in this way, and have judged him worthy of worship by us and the holy angels, and deign to crown him with the eminent glory of the deity; so that, having not passed over the Creator and the Queen of the universe <note>referring to the Divine Nature</note>, we do not serve a creature, and—giving the glory of the unmade to the made—justly hear: "Behold the fool, and the one without a heart."
HERMIAS: For would they not also say that he is both Son and God? CYRIL: And how is it not stupid and ridiculous to color him with mere names and differences of words, as if with an image or a painting, while stripping him of divine glory by placing him among creatures? Is it not very shameful to say that he was made, if indeed God is to be adored?
HERMIAS: You speak well. CYRIL: Therefore, if it is necessary to think thus, and to mock by setting aside useful discourse so that the Son may be cast out from the order of the divine deity, let them say it with a loud voice and blaspheme openly. For they are soon to hear from us and the holy angels: "Go to the light of your fire, and <margin>Isaiah 50.</margin> to the flame which you have kindled." For we are turned toward the path lacking error, believing the Word proceeding from God according to an ineffable nature to be God, and true. But if they return to a mind that is not entirely unteachable and foolish, they will not deny it with blasphemy, I think, being less troublesome. However, they are accustomed to confessing him as God, yet they remove him from the substance of the God and Father. They say he is in some way better than a creature, as if placed in the middle of unbegotten and begotten nature; let them hear how the nature of the Deity could be understood as varied? For God, as

DIALOGUE ON THE TRINITY 307

though toward God, does not exist in different ways, specifically in that he is God, just as one might see even in ourselves. For we would say that the nature of humanity is one, and the definition of substance is one, and it is not varied in the universal or the particular. Therefore, either believing him to be God, let them free him entirely from being among creatures; or if they are not persuaded of this, let them not confess him to be God at all. For laughing broadly we shall say: "Either make the tree rotten and its fruit rotten, or make the tree good and its fruit good." For the tree is known by its fruit. Is it not, O friend, that we clearly and without error know what each thing is according to nature from those things by which it is truly believed to be? HERMIAS: Certainly. CYRIL:
[B] Come then, let us consider what the nature of the Son of God is, and let us keep in mind that if he is not God according to nature, he was made, and was brought forth to be with us, according to the talk of those drunkards and madmen. How then did the world recede from him, and the creation become separated? Was it perhaps according to intervals measured by space? But how is this not nonsense? For where, or how, does that which is incorporeal distinguish, or what kind of place will circumscribe it? Whence also the blessed John bore witness: "He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world knew him not." Shall we then, O Hermias, as those who think rightly, grant that the manner of apostasy and the intervening falling away was something else from him—I mean, that the world did not know him who always [C] existed together as the Creator? HERMIAS: How could we not?
CYRIL: Therefore the world was a fugitive, fleeing from communion with him, because it did not know the Creator who is above the creature, and it cast away its relationship through the Spirit, having fallen into wickedness. For as soon as the nature of man was brought forth by the ineffable nods of the Craftsman, it was also honored with a certain relationship with the Spirit. For he breathed into his face the spirit of life, not otherwise, I think, than into a living being, which would expire clearly in holiness and familiarity with God, unless it were honored by the presence of the Holy Spirit. For when the Only-begotten became man, finding the nature of man destitute of its ancient and primary goods, he urged it to return to them again, as if [D] sending it from the fountain of his fullness, and saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit," and thus shadowing forth the nature of the Spirit with a fleshly and more manifest breath. It will therefore be equal to the first beginning, to be renewed to the beginning; and in this receding way the made nature suffered—not by distance according to place, far from it—but by being expelled and falling away from God and the union with God through the Spirit. Therefore, if indeed the Son is among the made things according to them, in what way did the creature go out and become separated from him? For that which is kindred is always friendly, and a made thing is not separated from a fellow-made thing, insofar as they are made. For that which is of a different genus or a different species always seems in some way foreign, but not in those things which have obtained one and the same boundary of nature. How then does the Son dwell through the Spirit in the creature,

For indeed, certain wretched Jews—whom it behooved to admire Christ as famous and to congratulate him with praises and glorify him as God on account of the narrations which were above the law and the rigor of the Mosaic speech, and on account of miracles exceeding reason—did not do this, but being exasperated into anger, and moving almost everyone with envy, they provoked him, falling into impious calumny. For they said at times: *This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub the prince of demons*; and at other times: *From whence has this man wisdom and power?* But it was still, in a way, harsh to those who shrunk from that most prudent dispensation, that he who was indeed God from God had appeared for our sake and been made man, and should say clearly: "I am indeed, O you people, wisdom and power, and the worker of wonders, having neither a power that is added from without, nor do I boast in foreign dignities, but in my very own." For if he had said these things, those who were accustomed to clamor against even moderate speeches would not have endured it; they would have dared to bark, attacking like dogs, if he had spoken anything beyond the conditions of humanity. Therefore, leading them away from their wickedness and bringing them to a better consideration, and instructing them in a civil manner, he did not think it right to suppose that the Lord and God of all worked in Beelzebub; rather, he attributed the clearer works to the ineffable power of the Father, and assigned to the divine nature those things which were most suitable to it. And thus, he himself existing in the Father, and having the Father as his own within himself because of their identity without variation, he said that the **substantial** Father, remaining in him, fulfilled the works. For no one endowed with a mind would truly suppose a work fitting for God to be properly called a work of the flesh—that is, of humanity alone and by itself. Do you suppose that this argument wanders from a true and evident opinion? HERMAS: Not at all, for it is well-stated. <margin>John 20 / Psalm 49 / John 4</margin>

...that he might remain stable in the good things in which he was, although he was made flesh and dwelt among us. HER. That is necessary. CYR. Therefore, we now attribute to the same one those things which belong to the flesh, [A] or because of the flesh. He who was impalpable <note>original: *impalpabilis*; meaning incapable of being touched or felt</note> was made palpable. For which reason Thomas, touching the marks of the nails with his hand and fingers, said: *My Lord and my God.* He who was invisible appeared visibly; and bringing a sweet song concerning this, the divine David said: *The God of gods, the Lord has spoken, and called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting; our God shall come manifestly, and shall not keep silence.* For when, or where, or how did God come to us manifestly—he who also called the whole earth—except for when the Only-begotten was made man? And because he was seen by none of the creatures, [B] he was shown visibly because of the flesh. He labored from his journey when he passed through the city of the Samaritans, and he stood in need of bodily food, although he gave strength to the hungry according to the voice of the prophet. He in whom we live and move and have our being is said to have been with us even in the death of the flesh. Therefore, O friend, if you grant these things to the Only-begotten even before the flesh, do you not bring forth a sound and pious discourse concerning him? HER. So it is gathered. CYR. Let us therefore refute the most impious reproach and the crimes of impiety. For whatever things are more divine and above our nature, let us attribute to the Son as not yet made like us. But whatever things are humbler and hold the character of our own properties, let us interpret according to the dispensation <note>term: *dispensation* (Greek: *oikonomia*); the divine plan by which God took on human form for salvation</note>, and let us lead every thought captive into obedience to him, according to the Scriptures. 

<margin>2 Corinthians 10 / John 3</margin>

Lest we suffer from madness when Christ says: *And no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man*, let us also consider that flesh itself came from heaven, although the prophet clearly shows us the Holy Virgin and cries out openly: <margin>Isaiah 7</margin> *Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.* For we do not think that the Word from God, while in a bodily womb, possessed that excellence of existence which he had in the beginning, when Paul—calling him the brightness of glory and the express image of the Father's substance—designated his incorporeal and ineffable nativity in terms exceeding our reason. HER. In every way. CYR. Therefore, one must understand his works and what is fitting to each nature; for thus, arriving rightly at the truth, we shall neither twist the sublimity of the Word into ignobility because of the flesh and the things of the flesh, nor shall we refer those things which are of the flesh entirely to his divine nature because of the dispensation. Rather, we preserve the truth that the Only-begotten is immutable. For we know him to be the very same both before his union with the flesh and when he was made flesh, regardless of whatever humble and lowly things are said of him because of his humanity. HER. But if you wish to turn everything, as it pleases you, toward the dispensation with the flesh, by what means shall we then find what the nature of the Word truly is? CYR. Therefore, I would hardly say to you, my excellent friend, if you wish everything to be twisted into what the nature of the Word is at any given time, so that you might interpret how he was made man—how would you know, or from where? For one does not know human nature [321] [A] from the properties of the deity. --- Page 581 ---


The soul is the form of the body, and the body is the matter of the soul. Therefore, the soul and the body are not two things, but one thing. For just as the wax and the shape of the wax are one thing, so the soul and the body are one thing. <note>This is a classic Aristotelian analogy (Hylomorphism) explaining that the soul is the "organization" or "actuality" of the body, not a separate object inside it.</note>

### On the Powers of the Soul

The soul has three powers:
1. **The vegetative power**, which is the power of nourishment, growth, and reproduction.
2. **The sensitive power**, which is the power of the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.
3. **The rational power**, which is the power of understanding and will.

The vegetative power is common to all living things, including plants. The sensitive power is common to all animals. The rational power is proper to humans alone.

<column-break/>

The soul is not in the body as a place, but as a form. For the soul is not in the body as a sailor is in a ship, but as the form is in the matter. <note>original: "sicut nauta in navi"</note> <note>This refutes the Platonic view that the soul is a separate entity merely "driving" the body.</note>

#### The Five Internal Senses

Besides the five external senses, there are five internal senses:
*   **Common Sense** <note>The faculty that integrates data from the five external senses into a single perception.</note>
*   **Phantasy** <note>The ability to form mental images.</note>
*   **Imagination**
*   **Estimation** <note>The instinctual ability to perceive intentions or qualities not given by the senses, such as a sheep "estimating" that a wolf is dangerous.</note>
*   **Memory**

<margin>The soul is the first act of a natural organic body having the potential for life.</margin> <note>This is the standard scholastic definition of the soul derived from Aristotle's *De Anima*.</note>

The intellect is twofold: the **agent intellect** and the **possible intellect**. The agent intellect makes the species <term>species: mental representations or concepts</term> intelligible, while the possible intellect receives them.

<keywords>Aristotle, Hylomorphism, vegetative power, sensitive power, rational power, internal senses, agent intellect, possible intellect, scholasticism</keywords>

### DIALOGUES OF SAINT CYRIL ON THE TRINITY

<note>original: "DIVI CYRIL. DIALOG. DE [TRINITATE]"</note>

...not as an angel from an angel, nor as one of us from another: he is distinct as a whole from a whole. Nor does the principle of difference establish a one on both sides separately in every way for each. Would there not even be two gods, since the deity is understood as one and alone? See the living and subsisting Son in the Father, and conversely the Father in the Son, for he is the <term>character</term><note>The Greek term 'charaktēr' refers to the exact imprint or representation of a person's substance.</note> of his subsistence. HERMES: I agree. CYRIL: Therefore, of one nature there is also one Spirit; and he proceeds indeed as if from the Father as a source, but he is not foreign to the Son, having the property of all things in himself. And since he is the fruit of the supreme divinity, how could he be understood as stripped of the goods of divinity? Now, the proper attribute of deity is sanctification, of which the Spirit is capable: for he is Holy by nature, and the sanctifier of every creature.

<margin>The Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son.</margin>

HERMES: And what will be the faith concerning these things, or how might I clearly discern that the Holy Spirit is the Son's own, just as he is the Father's? CYRIL: I will bring forward no foreign words, but Christ himself saying: *I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; but when that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come.* Does that speech not teach those who understand, with sufficient arguments, that he calls the Paraclete <note>The Comforter or Advocate; a title for the Holy Spirit.</note> his own? For he named him the Spirit of truth, and the Truth is not something other than himself. Adding, "because he will receive from what is mine," he clearly shows a substantial and natural property, according to which his Spirit is one with him. For he does not say the Spirit will be wise by participating in him, nor that he will bring the Son's words in the manner of servants; but as if a most fragrant flower were to spread its own scent, and pouring itself into the senses of those standing around should say: "It will receive from what is mine," it would signify a natural property, and not something as if participating separately. Understand the Son and the Spirit in this way. For being the Spirit of wisdom and power, he is entirely wisdom and power, emitting the whole efficacy from the whole, preserving it in himself, and as if in his own nature well-demonstrating that of which he is. But after he said, "He will receive from what is mine," he necessarily added: *All things whatsoever the Father has are mine: for this reason I said to you, that he receives from what is mine.* For just as the Spirit is always according to nature, since he is the Spirit of the holy Father, so also he is wise, since he is the Spirit of wisdom—or rather, substantially and as if by nature, a certain quality of the holy and wise divinity, which is understood in the Father and the Son, and in the Spirit himself. But that the Spirit of the Father is the Spirit of the Son, let him teach by himself, saying: *When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he,* he says, *will bear witness concerning me.* Do you understand, therefore, how he promises to send us his own from the Father, and calls him the Spirit of truth, and defines that he emanates from the Father himself, and foretells that he will also bear witness concerning him?

CYRIL. So I say; for it comes to me and occupies a favorable ear, like a melody played upon a reed. And so, because he performed a certain work even on the Sabbath—which was truly admirable—the Jews, being bitter and troublesome, began to carp at him. Opening their impudent and unrestrained mouths, even provoking him with the harshest speeches, they thought they spoke excellently and objected that he was breaking the Law: "If this man were from God," they said, "he would by no means break the Sabbath." But Christ refuted their arguments and demonstrated that the Father himself works on the Sabbath, and is not negligent in giving life to men. For he said: "My Father
<margin>John 5</margin> works until now, and I work." Moreover, that

there is one will and one power of the Father and the Son in all things that exist, he demonstrates with certainty by adding: "Amen I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing." CYRIL: But I do not think the Father and God himself would keep his glory safe if he were ignorant of what is, according to truth, the counsel and wisdom of God. He was accustomed to do such a thing especially among the holy apostles: if they asked anything that carried a weight of doctrine greater than their opinion, he would provide a narration without further scrutiny, and diligently urge that it be examined as subtly as possible. But if they wished to know something that was beyond their grasp, he restrained them with quietness, and persuaded them
<margin>C</margin> most diligently that they should wish to inquire into more fitting matters, and do those things through which they might become illustrious, and possess a most decent clarity before God through good works. Then, thinking they were still following Jewish [customs], they made a weak argument of doctrine, saying: "Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?" <note>John 9:2</note> Because they were touching upon divine judgments—which are so uninvestigable and incomprehensible to men—and wished these to be declared to them, going further than was fitting, he restrained them again in this, lest they wish to know curious things. If someone says of a certain thing that it is a "rational animal, mortal, capable of intellect and knowledge," what would you say he is defining, my good man? HERMAS: Clearly, a human being. CYRIL: And if he says "animal," but adds that it is "capable of neighing"? HERMAS: I would say, a horse. CYRIL: Now, if he keeps silent the names of both things defined, how will you yourself say "human" and "horse"? HERMAS: Because he has defined the nature of the human and the horse. CYRIL: But if someone should rebuke you for saying this, and say that neither is the human a rational animal, nor is the horse "neighing," because the names were not added to the definitions—would we not refute him as a stupid, useless, and hardly wise man, calling him quite unrefined? HERMAS: Certainly. CYRIL: And if someone asked you why he did this, and wanted to learn, what would you answer? HERMAS: I would say that to rebuke things well and diligently defined is the mark of a rustic and unlearned person; for there is a speech proper to each thing, demonstrating truly what it is. <note>Hermas argues that the definition of a thing's essence is more important than its label.</note> Often, however, names are uttered under the same name. CYRIL: Therefore, the manifestation of things is truer and more certain if they are examined from those qualities which belong to each according to nature, and not entirely from names. Shall we not rightly attribute to the supreme nature, the Queen of all things, that which is incorruptible, subject to no decay, eternal, and unchangeable? HERMAS: And why not? CYRIL: What then, tell me I pray, is God? HERMAS: You say it yourself, it is fitting. CYRIL: Indeed, it is proper to Him to be incorruptible and not subject to decay; but the name "God" is common to angels, and even common to ourselves, though it is adventitious <note>meaning "added from the outside" or "granted," rather than inherent to our nature</note> and given. Similarly, it is so in the case of "rational," for the name "human" is even given to those made of stone, or certainly formed well from other material into our likeness <note>referring to statues or idols</note>. Go then into yourself, as you are fervent: whether the Spirit is God and in God naturally—as being substantially visible in the properties of the Godhead—or whether, according to those others, he has received a true title and sufficient cause such that he ought to fall away from consubstantiality <term>consubstantiality: the doctrine that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the exact same substance or essence</term> with God, as if he were not otherwise named God. Although, even in this, we shall without labor refute those wishing to speak falsely, and using arguments pertaining to the contest and taken from Holy Scripture, we shall free our minds from the harm of cold, vain talk. HERMAS: I would certainly grant that something vastly and incomparably better should be extolled (if the Holy Spirit is conspicuous in the properties of the Godhead, and nothing less is in him than in the Father and in the Son) than to speak imprudently and anxiously, and to sweat in vain over the mere investigation of words. CYRIL: Discreetly and quite rightly, O Hermas. For I think this is better and more evident. Yet the adversaries, if they search more diligently, can see that the Spirit is named God. For the divine and most holy Peter brought destruction upon Ananias, who had stolen from the holy offerings, and rebuked him saying: <margin>Acts 5</margin> "Why has Satan filled your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit, and keep back part of the price of the field? While it remained, did it not remain your own? and after it was sold, was it not in your own power? Why have you conceived this thing in your heart? You have not lied to men, but to God." HERMAS: Yes, for he lies to God, he says, even if

one wishes to do this against the Holy Spirit. CYRIL: But how could this be, unless the Holy Spirit were God? HERMAS: But they say that even if one wished to act piously toward the saints, he acts piously toward God. Furthermore, Christ clearly said to the holy apostles: "He who receives you, receives me." <margin>Matthew 10</margin> And yet we do not say, following right and necessary reasoning, that the disciples are gods by nature, even though one receives the Son by receiving the saints into his house. there the deity would also exist according to nature: thus everything, whether it had begotten or been begotten, would be entirely and truly God. Yet that line of reasoning is clearly reckless. For the Father is not God because he begat, nor is the Son God because he was begotten; rather, the Father, already existing as God, begat, and the Son, already existing as God, is the Son. Therefore, nothing yet rejects or prohibits us from believing that the Holy Spirit—who is from that nature and in that nature naturally—belongs to the divine nature, even if he is neither Father nor Son. For God somewhere, he says, spoke to certain ancients: *I am the Lord, strengthening the thunder and creating the spirit, and announcing his Christ to men, making the dawn and the mist, and ascending above the high places of the earth.* <note>A reference to Amos 4:13. **CYRIL:** Why, my friend, those words by no means designated the glory of the Holy Spirit, unless one has a weak and corrupt mind. For "Spirit," when named simply and without addition, does not always and everywhere designate the Divine and Holy Spirit; otherwise, I would not say that they blaspheme. But the same names are very often pronounced for things that are of a most dissimilar nature. For an angel is a "spirit," and the soul of man, and the movement of the air or the wind. Now why do they pass over what is due to its own context and would be manifest, and instead think, in their madness, that this should be attributed to God the Creator as being above the creature? But the prophet—or rather God through him—did not say his own Spirit was being brought forth. Far be it from us to think so! 

But this is the meaning: Since there were certain people who, out of excessive stupidity, thought they could do good for themselves and others without any heavenly grace, God—who is over all—attributes to himself the royal thrones, illustrious princedoms, and the dominion of the scepter. He shows that every creature is dispensed by his laws and commands, and says: *I am the Lord strengthening the thunder,* sending it to those in the world who are powerless against spirits <note>original: "spirituum," here meaning winds or storms</note>. For in this way I "create the spirit" <note>meaning the wind</note>. And he makes the narrative manifest. For he says, *He shall be the Christ* <note>The "Anointed One"</note> *of whomsoever I wish*: that is, of him who has obtained the kingdom and empire by being anointed, not against my will, but by my commands. And the "dawn and mist" are summoned, that is, night and day, light and darkness. Otherwise, let them say what thunder and the Holy Spirit have in common, or what the dawn and mist have to do with Him who is from God and in God? Is the speech not manifest?

**HERMES:** It seems so. For that which is named is not of the same nature, and it is not consistent with their opinion; it proves they speak unbecomingly.

**CYRIL:** How, by another reason, could he be understood to be a creature or a thing made, who is a creator together with the only Creator? He has in this a virtue and power that is not brought in from the outside, nor ignoble, nor that which he received from another, but from himself and his own... <margin>Job 24</margin>

<margin>Psalm 32</margin> CYRIL: Do you hear the blessed David singing and plucking a certain spiritual lyre, who says clearly: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath <note>original: "spiritu" - can mean both breath and Spirit</note> of his mouth all their power*? Therefore, tell me: that which makes the heavens firm, and is the power of all things—is it God, or a creature? HERMIAS: I say it is God, and rightly so. For I would not allow that creatures have no need of God, but could benefit themselves and be saved by some other means than through those things by which they can be saved and well-established, since they naturally fall away toward corruption. CYRIL: Therefore the Spirit makes the heavens firm, not by providing them with a participation in some created or manufactured substance, but by granting them the very efficacy of God. For to cherish and maintain well those things which exist, and to strengthen them so that corruptible things—which are weak in their own nature and threaten to return to nothingness—may endure, must belong to the Nature that governs the universe. Whence also the divine Paul urges us to understand and soberly recognize from the things that are made, <margin>Romans 1</margin> what the nature of God is.
