Furthermore, power strengthens everything, and the Spirit makes the heavens firm, not as if he were one creature taken up by Him as an assistant—for it would be stupidity to think or say this—but as being the proper Spirit of the God who creates and strengthens all things. # On the Divine Substance

The majesty of the Creator is revealed in this: that he is **consubstantial** <note>original: "consubstantialis"; meaning of the same essence or substance, a key term from the Council of Nicaea</note> with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For the divine nature does not consist of parts, nor is it subject to the failings of the created world.

<column-break/>

We must understand that the excellence of the supreme substance <note>original: "substantię"</note> far surpasses all things that have been made. While the creature is subject to change, the Creator remains eternal. The blind <note>original: "cæci"</note> of heart do not perceive this light, which is why they fail to recognize the grace that is blessed <note>original: "benedicītur"</note> by the faithful.

Every creature <note>original: "creaturæ"</note> owes its beginning to the one who is without beginning. This is the eminence <note>original: "eminētię"</note> of the heavenly <note>original: "supernæ"</note> power, which governs all things. It is necessary that we understand <note>original: "intelligant"</note> these truths as they are written <note>original: "scriptum"</note> in the holy books, lest we fall into the errors of those who think the Creator is like the things he has fashioned.

The condition of the world is temporary, but the essence of the Maker is everlasting. Therefore, let us acknowledge the distinction between the one who was never made and the things that were brought into being from nothing.

# Chapter 10
## On the Nature of the Soul

The soul is the primary principle of life in those things which, among us, are living; for we call living things "animated" <note>original: "animata"</note>, and those which are not living "inanimate." Now, the word "soul" is used in many ways, but we must first define it in its most general sense.

### I. The Definition of the Soul

The soul is defined by the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and early modern texts.</note> as the **first act** of a natural body that has life potentially.

1. It is called an **act** <note>term: *Actus* (Act) — In Aristotelian philosophy, the state of being actual or realized, as opposed to just being a possibility.</note> because it is that by which the body actually exists and operates.
2. It is the **first** act, to distinguish it from the **second** acts, which are the operations of life themselves (such as thinking, sensing, or moving).
3. It belongs to a **natural body**, because the soul is not found in artificial things like a clock or a statue.
4. It is a body **having life potentially**, meaning it possesses the necessary organs and structure to carry out the functions of life.

### II. The Threefold Division of the Soul

There are commonly held to be three types of souls, or rather, three levels of the soul's power:

| Type of Soul | Primary Functions | Found In |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Vegetative** | Growth, Nutrition, Procreation | Plants |
| **Sensitive** | Sensation, Movement, Appetite | Animals |
| **Rational** | Reason, Intellect, Free Will | Humans |

<column-break/>

<margin>The soul is not a body, but the form of a body.</margin>

It must be understood that in humans, these are not three distinct souls, but one single soul that contains all these powers. Just as a triangle is contained within a quadrangle <note>A geometric analogy: a four-sided shape "contains" the properties of a three-sided one, just as the human soul contains the powers of the plant and animal souls.</note>, so the rational soul contains the powers of the lower souls.

<insert>Note: Some moderns dispute this Aristotelian definition, yet it remains the most useful for our study.</insert>

The soul is also said to be *immaterial* and *immortal*, at least in its rational part. While the vegetative and sensitive powers depend on the organs of the body and perish with it, the **Intellect** <note>original: "Nous" or "Intellectus"</note> is of a higher nature. As the Greeks say, it is "something divine" <note>original: "τι θεῖον" (ti theion)</note> that enters from without.

<gloss>The soul is the form of the body.</gloss>

<summary>This page defines the soul using Aristotelian principles, categorizing it as the "first act" of a living body and outlining the hierarchy of vegetative, sensitive, and rational powers.</summary>
<keywords>soul, Aristotle, vegetative soul, sensitive soul, rational soul, act and potency, immortality, philosophy of mind</keywords>

Those who show their craftsmanship in panels and pictures do not, immediately when they begin to paint, express a finished and in every part perfect likeness; but they first sketch it out and fashion it with darker colors, and then, as they please, they illuminate the still-dim lines with becoming and fitting colors, and so they transform the figure into a clear likeness, which appears incomparably better than it did at the beginning. Is it not so? PAL. I would certainly say so. CYR. Furthermore, even the coppersmiths, when about to cast a solid statue, first make a dim likeness in wax; then they pour bronze into that wax melted by fire, and so they produce their work so that it has a new appearance and beauty, with various kinds of colors added to the shadows.

[Column 2]

[Section marker: A] And it appears indeed, while the bronze melts the wax, that the first outlines are abolished, but the reality is not so. For that which appeared so obscurely and shapelessly in shadows and figures alone, is now conspicuous, having been brought forth into a better and clearer form. PAL. You have spoken well. CYR. And <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> indeed, if anyone wishes to rightly scrutinize the sacred and divinely inspired scripture, he will clearly know that what I say is true. For Moses put a veil over his face, because the children of Israel could not look upon his face on account of the brightness of that face, just as it is written. PAL. And what did this [Section marker: B] signify? CYR. The duller minds of the Jews, which were able to bear in a way the external things of the law—that is, those things said through the letter of the law—but the things that lay hidden within, and so to speak, the true face of the meanings, were intolerable and inaccessible. For that reason also the divine Paul writes to us: *Until this day the same veil remains unlifted in the reading of the Old Testament, because it is abolished through Christ; but until this day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed over their heart.* Thus far have the affairs of the Jews progressed. *But we all,* he says, *beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face as in a mirror, are transformed into that same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. Now the Lord is the Spirit.* [Section marker: C] For just as those who look into a mirror behold the image and figure of the truth, and not the truth itself: so also those who desire to see the beauty of the Christian life, and use the law as a mirror, will certainly obtain their wishes; for transforming that image of things into the truth, they will purely know what most pleases God and is acceptable. PAL. But in what way was it fitting that of old and from the beginning, the new and Evangelical law was not given to the ancients, but only figures and shadows were prescribed for them? CYR. The more evident manner of how the <term>dispensation</term> <note>God's plan or arrangement of history</note> holds itself must be left to God, who knows all things. Nevertheless, the thoughts of good reasons, which are more certain, lead us at least into a modest knowledge, [Section marker: D] or at least so that we may seem to know the occasion of the dispensation. Therefore we say, that those liberated from Egypt had need of instruction and education as if for children. For they were still dull, and easily led astray to every absurdity. For those who were weak in the indelible and immoderate love of the flesh, and subject to almost inevitable affections, it was nearly impossible, and not at all sound, that they should immediately seize upon a certain arduous citizenship and way of life, which is so noble and admirable that one walks indeed upon the earth, but is considered to have his name in heaven, according to what is written. Is it not so that <margin>Hebrews 5</margin> solid food is for the perfect, but for infants milk is more profitable? PAL. Certainly. CYRILLUS. Therefore children had need of the education which is through—

PAL. You judge most rightly.

But when this animal <note>original: "animal" - here meaning a living being or creature</note> was set free by the creator God within the reasons of its own nature, it immediately received a likeness to Him. PAL. Was the divine Spirit made into a soul for man?

CYR. And how is it not absurd even to think such a thing? Did the soul remain immutable and the same, and is it now mutable? But that which is mutable is by no means the Spirit; or if indeed it suffers from mutability, C a stain immediately passes into the divine nature itself: since the Spirit, who substantially proceeds from both—that is, from the Father through the Son—is of God and the Father and the Son. Therefore, they think ignorantly who suppose the Spirit was transmuted into a soul and passed into the nature of man. Rather, that which was created was animated by an ineffable <margin>How the divine image is in us.</margin> power, and was immediately adorned by the gift of the Spirit: for we are not otherwise capable of the divine image.

PAL. You speak well.

PALLADIUS: What then is this? CYRIL: How is it not manifest that when God calls us to follow spiritual things, and wishes those whom He deems worthy of this honor to go out from the worldly life, and from pleasures and the lusts of the flesh, it is foolish if anyone thinks anything is better than this? # 428 BOOK ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

Be teachable, for virtue is not seized immediately nor at the first attempt by those who have recently escaped from malice and believe they must walk the path of salvation; nor can they reach it just as they might wish. No one is led back to an extraordinary way of life all at once, nor will anyone be suddenly alienated from the passions deeply implanted within them. Instead, one distances oneself from these things little by little. As far as readiness and the beginnings of greater and more sublime efforts are concerned, one must yield to a more upright life as if moving toward another land—yet not yet to that high ground which is conspicuous on all sides with glory. Such, of course, is the instruction of the Law <note>original: "instructio legalis"; referring to the Old Testament Law as a preliminary stage of spiritual growth</note>, leading to the beginnings of the best way. For it is written: *The beginning of a good way is to do what is just.* <note>Proverbs 16:7</note> Just as for those desiring to learn and longing for mystical contemplations, the word of initiation is indeed useful and most suitable at the start. However, when they have grown into a perfect man, and into the stature of the fullness of Christ <note>Ephesians 4:13</note>, a more sublime contemplation will then, in a sense, be appropriate. So also I say here regarding morals and good works...

For as soon as useful desire and right reason lead us back, so that we wish for those things approved by God and are mindful of the law that teaches piety, the enemy of all urges us to have it worse. Nevertheless, God comes forward and tames his ferocity. For when Satan turns us away and destitute of every good desire and inclination toward that by which we can be driven: the law of God exhorts us to good will, showing indeed an immortal helper, and stimulating us with thick hope toward boldness and faith, attributing salvation to God as savior and redeemer. PALLADIUS. How good and salutary a thing it is to believe and desire to follow God? CYRIL. You have said rightly. Faith comes to a good end, if indeed we direct our discourse to its proper goal. But he rather commanded his own men to do the same, as if crying out through this: We are not ignorant of these works, for there are many among the Egyptians like you, and it is the study of the wicked to work wonders, of whose number you also are. But he says this: If we sacrifice to the God of the Hebrews, we shall provoke the Egyptians to anger on all sides and entirely, doing an intolerable thing. Meanwhile, the probable discourse, as far as spiritual contemplation is concerned, has no small utility. For that which the multitude of demons is most accustomed to worship, and which they most do while harrassing us, from that we pay the most grateful worship to God. PALLADIUS. How did you say? CYRIL. CYRIL: Indeed, friend, the discourse is manifest. For he who struggles against those who wish to act, and fights them, does so unless it is permitted for some to be subject to him, even if he desires to have them only in part. But the divine law teaches us to make a most swift departure, and to permit nothing at all to be left behind or remain under him—not a particle of the soul, nor an occasion for bodily sense. For when God commanded them to despoil the Egyptians, He said they should borrow vessels of gold and silver from their neighbors and housemates, which was also accomplished through the women. For a woman is always a shrill and most talkative thing, and fit for deception <note>Cyril uses a common ancient trope here to explain why women were the ones to "borrow" the goods—implying a clever ruse</note>. Now the silver and gold vessels of the Egyptians, as I have already said, are those things with which men think themselves adorned, even if they have not acknowledged the true God. For what I say is something like this: the movements of the mind and B soul are common to all men, and in everyone there is a pursuit of good and evil; but some, using the goods of nature well, lead an excellent and distinguished life; while others, perverting the goods of nature toward what is not fitting, turn them so that they go toward shameful things. Both strength and prudence are good for those who use them well, but harmful to those who do not conduct themselves rightly. For it is possible to act and think manfully with applause and praise, but it is also possible to possess the same and end in great lamentation. These things are common, both in those who err and those who know God. Therefore, when we convert our former strength and prudence in evil toward those things that please God, they will be as if received from the Egyptians and from worldly life, sacred and acceptable to God; for they are C adapted to the use of virtue and the ministry of sanctification, just as the gold and silver vessels from Egypt were declared useful for the construction and perfection of the holy tabernacle. Furthermore, after the Egyptians were despoiled and the firstborn died, the children of Israel were finally redeemed, a lamb having been sacrificed as a figure of Christ. For redemption could not be obtained otherwise, since all of it is through Christ, and through Him every good gift. They were sent out around midnight from the land of the Egyptians, those who were being liberated from darkness and slavery. For the slavery of sin is always accustomed to be, in a way, in spiritual darkness and not in divine light. For whoever acts wickedly hates the light, according to the voice of the Lord. <margin>John 3</margin> D Moreover, the flour is carried out without leaven, and they flee without cooked food. For the Egyptians, it says, urged the people to cast them out of the land in haste. For they said: "We are all dying." For I do not think those who are to adhere closely to God ought to carry out any remnants of malice, nor should they scrape together foreign and profane nourishment for their journey—namely spiritual nourishment—but they should love the unleavened and desire hereafter the bread of Him who gives life to the world. For those who are such celebrate the feast purely, and performing a worship acceptable to God, they remain under Him forever.
